N] = printed page of Part II; one printed paragraph per line; line-end hyphenation joined. [p. 1] Now, we shall explain the true nature of Brahman. [p. 2] In this regard, some maintain that Brahman is characterized by the cessation of all mental modifications (*sarvavṛttinirodha*). [p. 3] Others hold that it is characterized by the cessation of the mind alone (*manonirodha*). [p. 4] Still others maintain that it is characterized by the cessation of the activity of the mind and the senses (*manendriyavyāpāranivṛtti*). [p. 5] Furthermore, some say it is characterized by the cessation of the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavyāpāranivṛtti*). [p. 6] And yet others maintain that it is characterized by the cessation of the activity of the intellect (*buddhivyāpāranivṛtti*). [p. 7] Among these, the first view—that it is characterized by the cessation of all mental modifications—is untenable. For, if all mental modifications were to cease, there would be no means of knowing Brahman, and thus it could not be established as an object of knowledge. [p. 8] Nor can it be characterized by the cessation of the mind alone, because the mind is an instrument for the perception of objects, and its cessation would result in the non-perception of anything at all. [p. 9] The view that it is characterized by the cessation of the activity of the mind and the senses is also incorrect, for the senses are merely instruments for the mind, and their cessation does not constitute the cessation of the mind itself. [p. 10] Likewise, the view that it is characterized by the cessation of the activity of the internal organ is untenable, as the internal organ is synonymous with the mind, and the arguments against the previous view apply here as well. [p. 11] Finally, the view that it is characterized by the cessation of the activity of the intellect is also flawed, since the intellect is a specific modification of the internal organ, and its cessation does not imply the cessation of the internal organ as a whole. [p. 12] Therefore, none of these definitions are appropriate. Rather, Brahman is characterized by the cessation of the superimposition of the unreal upon the real (*adhyāsanivṛtti*). [p. 13] For, when the false notion that "the body is the self" is removed through the realization of the truth, the Self is revealed in its true nature as pure consciousness. Thus, the cessation of such superimposition constitutes the true nature of Brahman. [p. 14] This is the correct view, as it avoids the defects of the other positions and accounts for the possibility of Brahman being known through the scriptures. [p. 15] Thus, it is established that Brahman is the reality free from all superimpositions, which is to be realized through the cessation of the erroneous identification of the Self with the non-Self. [p. 16] In this way, the nature of Brahman has been explained according to the tradition of the Vedānta. [p. 17] Now, we shall consider the means of attaining this realization. [p. 18] It is generally accepted that the means consist of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*).

[p. 19] Among these, hearing refers to the study of the Upaniṣads under a qualified teacher. [p. 20] Reflection consists of the logical deliberation upon the meaning of those teachings to remove doubts. [p. 21] Meditative concentration is the continuous application of the mind toward the object of meditation until it becomes firmly established. [p. 22] Through these three means, the veil of ignorance is removed, and the Self is realized as identical with Brahman. [p. 23] This realization leads to the destruction of all karma, both past and future, and results in liberation (*mokṣa*). [p. 24] Therefore, one who desires liberation should diligently apply oneself to these means of knowledge. [p. 25] Thus ends the exposition of the nature of Brahman and the path to its realization. [p. 26] May this work contribute to the welfare of all beings. [p. 27] [End of Part II] [p. 28] [Appendix: Index of Subjects] [p. 29] [End of Document]
"P. x-y. = the editor’s marginal references to the page and line of the *mūla* in Part I; ^n^ = footnote markers; [fn] = footnote text.

[Page 1] Om. *Brahmasiddhivyākhyā* composed by Śaṅkhapāṇi. The Section on Brahman (*Brahmakāṇḍa*). May that Reality known as Gaṇādhipati, upon whom even the commencement and completion of the lords of the gods depend, always grant me my desired goal. At the beginning of this treatise, for the removal of obstacles, he pays homage with praise to the deity who is intended as the subject to be expounded here: "Ānanda" (Bliss). In the performance of an act of salutation at the start of an undertaking, the practice of those whose conduct is unimpeachable serves as authoritative evidence.

Nor should one suspect a contradiction on the grounds that Jaimini did not offer a salutation; for non-performance is not a contradiction, but rather a statement of censure. Thus it is established that even rites such as the *holākā*, which have restricted performers such as those from the East, possess authority. Yet, such a salutation is not found here [in his work]. Alternatively, we infer that Jaimini certainly performed a salutation—whether by speech or by mind—though it was not recorded, because of his distinguished character. Furthermore, that salutation is practiced by the learned at the commencement of a task precisely with the intention of attaining its completion as its fruit.

Therefore, since it is only a recollection (*smṛti*) that possesses a specific fruit, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) must be inferred as having that very same fruit; thus, there is no possibility of heaven being the fruit according to the logic of the Viśvajit sacrifice. Furthermore, from the act of salutation (*namaskāra*), a particular merit (*dharma*) arises; from that, the destruction of demerit (*adharma*) which is the cause of obstacles; and from the absence of that cause, the non-arising of obstacles, resulting in the completion of the work intended to be undertaken—such is the purpose of the salutation as the completion of the task. Moreover, a salutation preceded by praise is more powerful; therefore, it was performed in that very manner.

In this regard, this treatise must be commenced for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman; and that [knowledge] is established through the Vedāntas alone. Anticipating the objection, "What is the use of this [treatise]?", the author states the purpose for the sake of engaging the audience with the passage beginning with "In the Vedāntas" and ending with "is commenced. The Vedāntas, their power being obscured by doubts regarding validity and other factors arising from the conflicting views of various disputants, are not capable of producing the knowledge of Brahman.

But when all doubts have been dispelled by this treatise (*prakaraṇa*), those very [Upaniṣadic passages], their power having become manifest, make known Brahman; therefore, just as the injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*) have the *Dharma-mīmāṃsā* as their auxiliary (*aṅga*) by way of removing contradictions while producing knowledge of Dharma, so too this treatise is an auxiliary to the Vedāntas while they produce knowledge of Brahman. And whatever is the fruit of the principal [action], that alone is the fruit of its auxiliary; as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices].

It is like the fruit resulting from the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; therefore, the knowledge of Brahman is its purpose (*prayojana*). This being the case, it follows by implication that Brahman is the subject matter (*viṣaya*), and that there exists a relationship (*saṃbandha*) characterized by the means and the end. Thus, the intention is that this treatise (*prakaraṇa*), being complete with its subject matter, purpose, and relationship, ought to be commenced. Now, one might object: "But here too, the *Mīmāṃsā-śāstra* on Brahman already exists as an auxiliary (*aṅga*); therefore, what is the use of this treatise which is almost redundant? True, it does exist.

However, since that which was stated there in various places—in brief, as established by implication and as established by direct proof—is now being stated here in one place at length, directly, and with supporting arguments, this is a new undertaking. Among those [topics], he first states the initial disagreement: "Some... Why? He says: "And of the self (ātman). Is it the *vijñānātman* (the individual self) that is to be established by the Vedāntas, or the *paramātman* (the supreme self)?

In that regard, as for the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānātman*), since it is established by the notion of "I," those Vedānta texts would lack authority because they would merely be restating what is already known; even if the self were self-luminous, its being established by itself would mean that the Vedānta texts are equally restatements; and the claim that it is established by other means of knowledge was stated only in the context of introducing the presentation of the opponent's view.

Since the Supreme Self (paramātman) is not established by any other means of knowledge, and because the apprehension of a relation is impossible when the related term is not grasped, the relationship characterized as the signified-signifier (vācyavācaka) between that [Self] and the word denoting it cannot be apprehended. Consequently, since it is not the meaning of a word (apadārthatva), it cannot be the subject matter of a sentence; for it is held that the meaning of a sentence consists precisely of the meanings of the words. Therefore, the meaning is that the Vedāntas lack authority precisely because they do not produce cognition.

Now, even if one were to argue that sentences such as "neither gross nor subtle" (*asthūlam anaṇu*) do not merely restate what is already established by other means of knowledge—since they convey the Self as devoid of all attributes—and that the connection of the meanings of words like "gross" and the negative particle *nañ* with words like "Brahman" in their respective senses is possible through their association with meanings such as "vastness," and thus, being word-meanings, they can be the objects of a sentence; nevertheless, because they do not provide instruction for engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), they would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*) due to not serving the purposes of man (*puruṣārtha*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is characterized by "determinative cognition" (*pariccheda-lakṣaṇa*), and not by "usefulness for human goals" (*puruṣārtha-upayogitva-lakṣaṇa*); for even jars and the like, though useful for human goals, lack validity, whereas even things that do not serve human goals—such as cognitions of objects that are not required—possess validity? Since the Vedāntas possess this quality of determinative cognition, how can they be invalid? [Reply: It is said: The validity of the Upaniṣads does not consist in mere determinative cognition, which would be equivalent to the cognition of an unrequired object; rather, it consists in their usefulness for human goals.

And they are not equal, because [the Vedas] are traditional and are the object of the injunction to study; for an injunction does not impel a person toward that which is of no utility to the person. Furthermore, the utility of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) lies in its being useful to the person, and it is the means to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) that constitutes such utility. And worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is the means to the human goal, and that consists of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and desistance (*nivṛtti*). If the Vedantas do not teach these two, they possess no validity as they are found [in common experience]; thus, the statement "they lack validity" is made.

For what purpose, then, does the injunction for study cause one to teach them? We reply: for the purpose of recitation (*japa*). But does it not then follow that [the Veda] has attained [a worldly purpose]?

They possess utility for human goals (*puruṣārtha*); certainly so, by way of being objects of knowledge (*prameya*), but not by way of being means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And here it is to be established that they lack utility for human goals by way of being means of valid cognition, due to their application toward invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), and not in every respect. Now, one might object: "The injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) is for the purpose of comprehending the meaning, not for the purpose of recitation (*japa*). True; however, because that [purpose] is impossible according to the reasoning stated previously, it will serve the purpose of recitation in the case of the Vedāntas. But is it not improper for a single injunction to have two purposes?

Even that which is improper will be resorted to as a last resort, just like conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, just as there is no fault in the case of the Vedāntas being for the purpose of recitation (*japa*), despite the lack of distinction in their being objects of the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*)—since, although the injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras are all equally subjects of that injunction, they serve specific purposes according to their respective capacities through their connection with "that which one is able to do" (*yat śaknuyāt*), resulting in [the former] serving as injunctions, praises, or reminders—so too is it here. Thus, there is no defect.

Others, however, considering the Veda to have authority only regarding matters to be accomplished (*kāryārtha*), maintain that the Upaniṣads possess authority because they enter into the sphere of what is to be accomplished; for when it is said, "The Self is to be realized," and the question arises, "Of what nature is it?", the Upaniṣads provide the required information on the nature of the Self to be realized by stating, "It is of such a nature. Thus, they believe its authority lies in its involvement with an action to be performed.

They argue: "This being the case, since a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) would otherwise be untenable, the very nature of the Self, which serves as the qualifier, will also be established by the Upaniṣads—just as the substance and the deity are established in an injunction for a sacrifice qualified by a specific substance and deity. Furthermore, there will be no lack of human purpose (*apuruṣārthatva*) nor any futility regarding the injunction to study the Vedas. However, this is merely their pretense; in reality, the authority of the Upaniṣads with respect to the nature of the Self is not established at that time, because the Upaniṣads do not have that as their primary purport.

In that case, the statement is expressed as "the Self is to be understood as being thus," and not simply as "the Self is thus. [Objection: But how can that which is not thus be understood as being thus? [Reply: No, for it is possible even through superimposition (*adhyāropa*), just as in the case of "one should meditate on speech as a cow. For this very reason, even from an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there is no establishment of the essential nature of the Self; whereas, since a sacrifice cannot be accomplished without a substance and a deity, it is logical that it implies them—this is the point of difference.

Furthermore, [the Veda] lacks authority because it is impossible to follow its injunctions; this is what they say. To express this, he says: "But others... He states another point of disagreement: "But others... [One... P. 1-6.

The meaning is as follows: others hold that because statements such as "this is non-dual" (advitīya) would contradict the injunctions for ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) if their primary literal sense were accepted—since those injunctions concern distinctions such as the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—and because they would contradict perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge if they concerned distinctions such as blue and so forth, the terms "one" and "non-dual" are used figuratively (*upacāreṇa*) to mean non-distinction in terms of place, time, genus, and so on. These conflicting views (*vipratipattayaḥ*) have been stated by way of illustration; others should also be understood from the refutations that will be presented later.

Thus, having stated that this [work] was commenced in order to refute those misconceptions, he asks: "For the sake of refuting that"? To which he replies: "The Bliss" (*ānanda*). By the word "Bliss," he indicates this treatise by way of its title; the meaning is "the treatise. He states the purport of the first verse therein: "The Supreme," etc. Although for the Advaitins Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), [the verse says] "Bliss"—[page 4].

Moreover, compassion (*dayā*) is His very nature, not a mere attribute (*guṇa*); nevertheless, based upon the distinction between quality and the possessor of quality—which is established by ignorance (*avidyā*) just like the distinction between the object of praise and the praiser—a hymn consisting of the glorification of attributes has been composed. Therefore, by means of that hymn and by prostration (*praṇati*), which consists of the humility of body, speech, and mind, one worships the Deity who is supreme over the body, senses, mind, and intellect, whose nature is untouched by them, who is radiant, and who shines forth by Himself.

Because of the grammatical rule (*smaraṇa*) stating that the suffix *kyac* is used in the sense of "reverence" (*namas*) and "worship" (*pūjā*), it is implied that [the salutation] is preceded by praise. Furthermore, the phrase "characterized by the prostration of body, speech, and mind" provides the definition of mere prostration in general; however, it should be understood that in this context, a specific form of verbal prostration is intended. We ascertain from the very words of the author of the treatise that this verbal homage is indeed preceded by body and mind. In this regard, the praise is expressed by the words beginning with "Bliss" (*ānanda*), and the prostration is performed by the words "we shall bow down" (*namasyāmaḥ*).

The first verse is for the purpose of salutation (*namaskāra*). Since the commencement of a treatise (*prakaraṇa*) must be preceded by a salutation, one might ask: "Why is the word *ānanda* (bliss) mentioned here as if it were a representative title (*pratīka*) of the treatise? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For the sake of the meaning of the treatise" (*prakaraṇārtham*). This means that the very qualities which were stated for the purpose of praising the subject matter are precisely what are to be established by the treatise; thus, by implication, he also briefly indicates the meaning of the treatise itself.

Therefore, the sense is that because this [treatise] is contained within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), it is appropriate for it to have the status of a *prakaraṇa-pratīka* (a representative symbol of the context). Now, one might object: "It has been stated that 'this treatise is for the purpose of removing misconceptions' (*vipratipatti-nirāsa*); therefore, since the logical establishment of that removal is its subject matter (*pratipādya*), the subject (*viṣaya*) is that [removal] itself, and not bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Misconception," etc. The statement regarding the logical establishment of the removal of misconceptions is not for its own sake, but rather for the purpose of establishing the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman, whose nature is bliss and so forth.

This is intended to establish that even that [Brahman] has the nature of bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth, being the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattva*). Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman, though possessing the nature of bliss and so forth, is also the "object" (*viṣaya*) because it is that which is to be established. The sense of the word "also" (*api*) is that not only the removal of conflicting views (*vipratipatti-nirāsa*) is the object, but the nature of bliss and so forth as well. Now, wishing to explain the nature of bliss and so forth first, he sets forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding it, beginning with the words "here" (*atra*). The word "they say" (*āhuḥ*) is to be supplied.

Or rather, the word "they think" (*manyante*) should be supplied from a distance by way of syntactic connection. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Because of passion," etc. The word "iti" has the sense of a reason. That activity rooted in passion is the cause of *saṃsāra* is understood from such scriptural and traditional texts as: "Selfishness is not praised," "One should cut off this enemy here," and "When all desires that dwell in his heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal"; and it is also established by inference.

To explain: for one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), activity rooted in passion (*rāga*) is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is the seed of *saṃsāra*" is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*); because it is activity rooted in passion, like activity directed toward the enjoyment of women and so forth. Furthermore, he states that if the activity of one desiring liberation were due to passion, even a qualified person (*adhikārī*) as prescribed would not be found: "of the peaceful one" (*śāntasya*), whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is restrained; "of the self-controlled one" (*dāntasya*), whose external organs (*bahiṣkaraṇa*) are restrained; regarding the Self as the object, there is "vision" (*darśana*). "Therefore... [p. 5]

It is stated in the Śruti: "Having become tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and composed, one should see the Self in the very Self. Nor does it mean that one becomes tranquil by proceeding from attachment to bliss. [Objection: But if tranquility is impossible, then the prior mention of self-control is also useless. [Reply: It is not useless; for its purpose is to make known that tranquility is based on the Śruti. Indeed, when many words are employed, the Śruti itself is brought to mind.

Therefore, there arises the knowledge that tranquility (*śāntatva*) is based on scripture. Alternatively, if one does not possess a restrained internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then, because the activity of the external organs is rooted in that [internal organ], one would certainly not be self-controlled (*dānta*) either; thus, the mention of "tranquil" should be understood as being illustrative (*upalakṣaṇārtha*). Now, it may be argued: "It is not proper to discard the bliss (*ānanda*) heard in the scripture, 'Brahman is consciousness and bliss,' on account of some practical purpose; for a restriction regarding what is prescribed by scripture is not appropriate to be made on the basis of a purpose. Certainly so.

We do not abandon the scriptural mention of bliss (*ānanda*) on account of some practical purpose; rather, we interpret it otherwise solely by the force of other scriptural passages concerning liberation (*mukti*). Nor do we abandon it entirely, so there is no fault. Now, one might object: if Brahman were not of the nature of bliss, there would be no inclination toward it because it would not be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); yet there can be no inclination unless there is a desire for it, since inclination is impossible for one who lacks desire; and that very desire is passion (*rāga*).

Therefore, anticipating the objection, "How then can even you possess tranquility?", the opponent demonstrates that the seeker who engages in his own school must indeed be tranquil—starting with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). The meaning is: since such a fault exists when activity proceeds from attachment to bliss, therefore [one must be tranquil]. (P. 1-16)

The meaning is that one who has transcended the multitude of sufferings—divided into all categories such as internal and so forth—and who, being distressed by those very sufferings and having lost all longing for even the pleasures of Hiraṇyagarbha through reflection on defects such as their perishability, proceeds [toward liberation], is liberated. For the desire for the cessation of suffering is not attachment (*rāga*); rather, it is the desire for pleasure; yet in the world, activity even for the sake of the cessation of suffering is observed.

Therefore, the sense is that both the engagement [in practice] and the qualified aspirant are possible according to our position. Now, one might object: "If Brahman is not of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), then what is the status of such scriptural passages as 'Brahman is consciousness and bliss'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Bliss," etc. They declare—that is, they lead to—the transcendence, meaning the absence, of the threefold [distinctions] divided into the internal and so forth; this is by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For happiness is invariably concomitant with the absence of suffering.

Even if pleasure and pain were to exist simultaneously, even there, pain—which is invariably concomitant with pleasure—would be absent through the door of pleasure; and this is untenable in Brahman according to the reasoning stated previously. Therefore, in the scriptural passages concerning bliss (*ānanda*), figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone is logical. Some, however, maintain that because the word "pleasure" is used both for actual pleasure and for the absence of pain, it possesses multiple meanings, like the word "akṣa" (which means dice, axle, etc.). That is incorrect, because the usage in the other case is justified by figurative indication based on a single primary meaning; thus, it is improper to postulate a separate denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*).

With the intention that this secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) is well-established and not merely imagined by us, he says: "For it is seen" (*dṛṣṭo hi*). With the intention that once the use of the word "pleasure" (*sukha*) for the cessation of suffering is established, the use of its synonym "bliss" (*ānanda*) for that same thing is also established, [he says on page 6]:

The application of the word "sukha" (pleasure) has been shown. Alternatively, "sukhaśabdaḥ" refers to the word that denotes pleasure; it should be understood as being synonymous with the word "ānanda" (bliss). He states another view: "saiva" (that very same); the meaning is "the cessation of suffering. The verb "they think" (*manyante*) is to be supplied. For indeed, when there is the cessation of pain and so forth, the word "sukha" is observed in the expression "I am happy" (*sukhy aham*). And since its primary denotation of pleasure is possible, it is not appropriate to regard it as merely figurative.

Furthermore, the certainty of suffering is established for both parties, since even one who maintains that pleasure consists in existence accepts that [certainty] in those cases; therefore, let that very [certainty] be pleasure—what is the point of postulating a separate property (*dharma*)? This is the sense. Now, raising the objection that if this were so, then because the certainty of suffering is no different in the case of a stone and the like, it would follow that they too are happy, he says: "And not... (the word *sukhitvasya* is to be supplied). Why? He says: "Because of the inner self" (*pratyag-iti*).

That which has turned back (*prati*) and is withdrawn from the "this" (*idam*) portions—meaning it goes toward (*eti*) and comes from (*cet*) them—is the *pratyak*, the inner self (*cidātman*). Regarding this, the scripture (*śruti*) states: "That cessation of suffering which belongs to the inner self is the *pratyak-śruti*. This is a compound formed despite the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), because the meaning is clearly conveyed. The implication is that the individual soul (*jīvātman*) does not exist in stones and such things. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "being perceived" (*upalabhyamāna*) is intended to prevent the unwarranted conclusion that pleasure exists even in states such as fainting, where the cessation of suffering—which is the *pratyak-śruti*—is not actually perceived.

The notion “this” is an outward-turning function of consciousness (*citti*), whereas the notion “I” is an inward-turning function of consciousness; therefore, the state of happiness belongs to that consciousness which perceives [the self] as free from suffering. Nor is there the notion “I” in stones and the like—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: “Happiness is well known to be a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*); how can it be determined to be the absence of suffering? Anticipating this doubt, he states another position: “That,” etc.

Since there is the perception of a self characterized by the cessation of suffering, or because pleasure is indeed of a positive nature, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to stones and the like; therefore, let pleasure be either the cessation of suffering or the perception of a self characterized by it. The point is that in any case, pleasure is not some distinct entity (*dharmāntara*). Having thus raised an objection against Brahman’s nature as bliss (*ānandātmakatva*), he provides the resolution with the words “to them” (*tān*). In that regard, according to the view that pleasure is the absence of suffering, which was previously mentioned, the word “bliss” (*ānanda*) would apply to Brahman only in a figurative sense.

Consequently, the position that [the term "bliss"] is secondary would not recur. Although, in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the position of the absence of suffering as bliss was presented after introducing the secondary position, nevertheless, because there is much to be said, because the secondary position is easily refuted once the primary position is established, and because the consideration of the secondary follows the primary, he first refutes the position of the cessation of suffering as bliss with the words "Not, first of all" (*na tāvat*). For if bliss were the absence of suffering, existence and non-existence of a single thing could not occur simultaneously in one and the same place.

But if it (pleasure) were of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), then even two contradictory things, such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), could coexist in one place simultaneously. And just as merit and demerit exist together in a single self, their simultaneous presence in a single birth is indeed possible; for by a single action, there may be both the restraint of one and the favoring of another. Furthermore, in the case of one suffering from heat who plunges into a cool lake, pleasure and pain are seen to occur simultaneously through the two parts of his body—one submerged and the other half-submerged. Therefore, the meaning is that pleasure is not merely the absence of pain. [p. 7]

Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of perceiving smell, taste, and so forth while eating a *kulī* fruit, there is an appearance of simultaneity due to rapid succession even though there is no actual simultaneity; for in that case, because the sense organs that grasp taste and the rest are distinct, it is logical that there is no simultaneity, since the internal organ (*manas*) is incapable of presiding over them all at once.

In this case, however, a single cognition grasping both cold and heat is produced by a single part of the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*), which pervades the entire body and is in contact with water that occupies half [of it], and by a mind (*citta*) presided over by successive conjunctions with the internal organ (*manas*). By means of that [cognition], pleasure and pain are produced simultaneously; and because there is no distinction in the conjunction with the mind, these two appear together as one in the cognition. Therefore, it is well said: "Because pleasure and pain are observed to occur simultaneously. Here, he raises an objection with the word "atha" (now/if).

The meaning is this: even though there is suffering for one whose body is half-submerged in a cold lake, the other person, whose body is fully submerged, is said to be happy because of the absence of that suffering. Having raised this objection, he refutes it with the word "kumbhī" (cauldron). For a person being cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell, there would follow the absurd consequence of being happy, since there is no *pradhvaṃsābhāva* (non-existence through destruction) of the sufferings already experienced in other hells such as Raurava, and no *prāgabhāva* (prior non-existence) of those not yet experienced. And that is not desired.

For in hell, there is absolute suffering unmixed with happiness. This [point] is easily understood through scripture alone as being beyond the world (*alaukika*); thus, he states the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding worldly objects with the word "eka" (one). A person for whom suffering exists through the gateway of a single sense-organ is described as such. Because that person lacks suffering through the gateways of other sense-organs, the consequence follows that they would be happy. He states another reason with the words "and from this": the meaning is that for this reason also, happiness is not the mere absence of suffering. Why? He says: "of one who is without suffering."

The meaning is this: a person for whom there is no suffering is "one without suffering" (*aduḥkha*); because of his contact with specific objects such as camphor and the like, there arises a pleasure that is experienced as a joyous sensation (*hrāda*). The inclusion of the term "experienced" (*saṃvedya*) is intended to show that, since it is established by direct experience, it cannot be said that "this does not exist. Furthermore, pleasure is not the destruction of suffering for one who is already without suffering, because for us [Buddhists] destruction is impossible; nor is it the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of suffering, because that is not produced by objects, whereas this [pleasure] is produced by objects.

The sense is that a quite different kind of happiness is experienced there by those two. Now, one might raise the objection: "In a case where there is the suffering of hunger and so forth, why should the destruction of that [suffering] through food, drink, and the like not be considered happiness? Anticipating this, he says: "Even where... Why? To this he replies: "By means of food... The meaning is: "by taking up food and drink that are flavorful, cool, and refreshing. One might further object: "Surely, by taking up specific kinds of food and drink, there will simply be the cessation of that suffering. Anticipating this, he says: "By whatever [means]..."

The meaning is: "by whatever [means], even by those that are tasteless. Now, one might object: "The acquisition of specific foods and drinks must be for the sake of a specific cessation of suffering; for a specific effect is indeed observed to arise from a specific cause. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not... The sense is that there is no gradation (atiśaya) in the absence of suffering. However, in the case of pleasure (*sukha*), which is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), since it possesses gradation, the requirement for specific means of pleasure for its sake is logical. As it has been said: "But in the case of pleasure... [p. 8]

Regarding what was stated [in the verse], "of that which is not suffering" (*aduḥkhasya*), he raises an objection with the words "even that which... (*yad api*). The meaning is: since desire itself is suffering in the absence of the attainment of its object, therefore the cessation of that [desire] will indeed be happiness. He refutes that position with the words "in that case" (*tatra*); that is, even under that alternative view, a person who is without desire—that is, one for whom desire does not exist—would not experience happiness when enjoying specific objects such as the scent of a campaka flower brought by the wind without having thought of it. If it is argued, "Let it not be so," he replies to that with the words "if it were so" (*bhavati cet*).

"Neutral" (*madhyastha*) means existing in the middle between attachment and detachment. The phrase "even for one who is without desire" (*akāmasyāpi*) is stated to show that the state of being happy is not invariably concomitant with the cessation of desire; regarding this, he raises an objection: "It might be so. An object is "pleasurable" (*sukha*) because it produces pleasure (*sukhayati*); the suffix *ac* is added after the root ending in the causative marker (*ṇi*). He states the validity of his own position: "But by the cessation of desire... The term "inclination" (*abhiruci*) is an explanation of "desire" (*kāma*).

Anticipating the objection—"In that case, what is the status of that pleasure which arises from the union with a particular object for one who has desire?"—the author says: "Therein... For innate passion exists in all men, but it manifests through a particular object; with this in mind, he says: "Upon the manifestation of desire. The proponent replies: "Even that... "Nivarhaṇas" means destroyers. The word "become" (*bhavanti*) is to be supplied. He strengthens this very point with the words of an authoritative scholar: "For it has been said..."

Likewise, Patañjali also confirms this with his words: "Enjoyment," etc. The meaning is that just as the habituation to enjoyment increases—that is, it increases specifically—so too does passion increase. He states another defect: "The defects of the objects," etc.; the sense is that there would be no distinction because the cessation of desire would be non-substantial (avastu). He states yet another defect: "And if [the cause] were the same," etc.; the meaning is that when one person obtains the desired object, there would be a great joy, while for another it might be merely pleasant; thus, there would be no difference in the resulting joy.

He asks "Why? and says: "Because of the cessation of desire. Now the opponent states a distinction: "It might be so. For one whose desire is excessive and great, upon its cessation, he considers even non-excessive pleasure to be excessive; yet it is not actually excessive, because there is no difference in the cessation of desire itself. But in the other case, where desire is not excessive, it is otherwise—that is, it is not superlative. He points out the flaw in that position with the words: "And that..."

The meaning is this: even when there is an abundance of desire, because there is no excess of happiness in an object that is a dwelling place of afflictions (*kleśa*), and because an excess of happiness is observed even in the absence of an abundance of desire when [the object] is obtained without affliction, the conceit of an excess of happiness is not based on an abundance of desire. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: an object obtained does not please a person who undergoes exertion and affliction for the sake of an abundance of desire in the same way that an object which has arrived unasked and without exertion pleases.

He confirms this point by means of an experience established in the world, beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*). "Unhoped for" (*anāśaṃsitam*) means not sought after (*aprārthitam*). Furthermore, is happiness merely the absence of desire, or is it its destruction? Regarding the first position, he states the fault:

"And [the state] consisting merely in the absence of desire. This means: when one is enjoying an object that was previously undesired, there is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of desire before the enjoyment; during the state of enjoyment and thereafter, there is the non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of the desire awakened by the attainment of the object. Therefore, since the absence of desire is indistinguishable [in these two cases], the states preceding and following the state of enjoyment would not differ from it; consequently, one should be happy in those two states just as one is in the state of enjoyment itself. But this is not the case—this is the intended meaning. He states the flaw in the second alternative: "the destruction of desire" (*kāmadhvaṃsa*).

Furthermore, if happiness were merely the destruction of desire, the state beyond [the worldly] would not differ from the state of enjoyment; for since the destruction of desire is identical in both cases, one would be happy after that state as well, just as one is during the state of enjoyment. Alternatively, if the person possesses desire during the state of enjoyment but is free from desire in the preceding and succeeding states, then the preceding and succeeding states would differ from the state of enjoyment only insofar as there is an absence of desire; and the state beyond would differ from the state where happiness consists in the total destruction of desire.

Therefore, it is said that the faults mentioned for both positions do not apply. This is incorrect; for in the first position, one would be happy in the states prior to and subsequent to the state of enjoyment because of the existence of happiness consisting merely in the absence of desire; and in the second position, one would be happy in the future because of the existence of happiness consisting in the destruction of desire; however, during the state of enjoyment itself, one would be miserable due to the existence of misery consisting in desire—and this contradicts experience.

He states all of this with due reservation: "In the state of enjoyment" (*bhogāvasthāyām*). The analysis of the compound is: "one whose desire (*kāma*) has been awakened and destroyed. The phrase "of the former and the latter" is an elliptical expression; it should be understood as including the phrase "and in the subsequent [state]" (*paratra*). It was stated that even for one who is without desire, when desire is manifested through the enjoyment of an object, its cessation is pleasure; however, that is not tenable. For an object that has not yet been attained, when remembered as a cause of pleasure, excites desire, whereas once attained, it brings that desire to an end.

Even when an object is obtained, since it does not cause the cessation of desire but rather inflames it, there would be no cessation of desire from that object; therefore, such [cessation] does not exist. To the question, "What then will be the happiness? he says: "And when unobtained. This means that when it is unobtained and not being enjoyed, as opposed to when it is obtained and being enjoyed. Furthermore, if the cessation of desire were happiness, then wherever there is desire, happiness must necessarily follow, because the cessation of desire, being something produced, is necessarily bound to occur.

And this is not the case, as he says: "Nor is it... Why? He says: "Because of the hundredfold desires... The meaning is that even for some object sought after with hundreds of desires, such as a wicked wife, one observes suffering at the time of its enjoyment. Furthermore, having raised the objection that there would be no desire or, due to desire, no inclination toward suckling the breast and so forth on the part of calves and others who possess specific species such as cows, he says: "That which... "Previous existence" (*prāgbhava*) means a former birth; "arising from that" (*prāgbhavīya*) means an experience belonging to that [former birth]; the meaning is "by means of the memory of that."

This is what is meant: in this beginningless *saṃsāra*, for those whose selves have assumed the bodies of cows and other such beings hundreds of times, there arises from the experience of pleasures such as suckling at the breast a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). From that impression, there arises a memory of pleasure, triggered by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which is the cause for assuming the body of a cow or similar being. From that follows the impulse of desire (*kāma*); therefore, even in that case, desire is preceded by the experience of pleasure, and from desire comes activity. As it has been said: "Knowledge and action [follow] him."

"Where there is desire, there is happiness; otherwise, that which is pleasant for one would have to be pleasant for everyone, which would result in a lack of order. To this, he replies: "And just as... Desire also does not arise for everyone everywhere; what then? It arises in a particular place for someone of a certain class, a certain age, and a certain condition—for example, for a cow in eating grass, for a youth in the company of women, or for a sick person in unwholesome food. Happiness is likewise determined by distinctions such as class and so forth; thus, the sense is that there is no lack of order.

Furthermore, the cessation of desire is not happiness; rather, it is suffering, as he says: "Moreover, some whose senses are afflicted by bile and other humors suffer with pain and are tormented by distress; if the cessation of desire were happiness, they too would be happy; but this is not the case. Therefore, the point is that it is not happiness. To the question "Why do they suffer?", he says: "In the absence of that"; the meaning is, "in the absence of that," namely, the absence of desire. Another says: "Then it is not so"; if they suffer, then they have not ceased their desires.

The sense is that no one is distressed by the cessation of desire for what is undesirable. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) says: “Cessation...”. Regarding objects such as sugar-candy which appear bitter due to a defect of bile (*pitta*), those whose desire has ceased and whose relish has vanished do not desire them; they desire only what is relished, grasping the object with the thought, “How might we have a relish for this? He states the reason: “Of that... This means that because of some defect such as bile, that object is unfit for enjoyment and thus lacks the quality of being a cause of pleasure.

If they are free from desire regarding sense objects, for what reason then are they distressed by those objects being unenjoyable? With the intention that suffering is not observed when undesirable objects are not enjoyed, the opponent asks for the reason—"Why? The proponent states the reason: "Because of the recollection of what was previously experienced. The meaning is that because they do not now obtain through senses impaired by bile (*pitta*) and other defects the pleasure previously experienced from objects such as sugar-candy, they are distressed by the memory thereof. He provides an illustration here: "Just as..."

He concludes: "Therefore... By the fact that it is established through experience as being perceivable by each individual person (*pratipuruṣavedyatva*), he confirms its very non-rejectability. If pleasure is an existing reality (*vastubhūta*), then for what purpose is it said: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self"?

“Birth is suffering, a dark abyss, resembling a rain-bubble; it consists mostly of destruction, is dependent on pleasure, and is followed by destruction, leading to non-existence. With such words, teachers such as Vyāsa and Patañjali have declared that there is an absence of happiness in saṃsāra. Having raised the doubt: “Why then have some scholars stated that the cessation of suffering is happiness? he says: *sukhasaṃgīti*. (P. 3-14)

The meaning is that we infer that the venerable teachers, being established in reality, have described how no entity exists with its own intrinsic nature (*sasva-nāma-vastu*) in order to win over people who are excessively attached to sensual pleasures and averse to the supreme good. Having formulated the conclusion of the present inquiry, he states: "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*). The word "established" (*siddham*) is to be supplied. Now, he refutes the claim previously made—that the scriptural texts concerning bliss (*ānanda-śruti*) speak of the absence of suffering through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*)—with the words: "And that" (*sa ca*).

Therefore, the ellipsis of the sentence is that "that alone is to be accepted. Now, one might object: "Why is the non-primary meaning not accepted, as in the case of sentences such as 'The sound [of cows] at the Ganges'? Anticipating this doubt, he states the distinction with the words "śabda... (by the word). In those cases, it might be so because the object falls within the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); but here, that is not the case, because the nature of the Self (*ātman*) is accessible through the word alone. Therefore, in this instance, the comprehension of the meaning is logically based solely on the power of the word, and not on another means of knowledge, just as from the word "Ganges" the meaning "bank" is understood.

One might object: "Metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) occurs due to the impossibility [of the literal sense], and that [impossibility] exists here as well," as was stated in the passage beginning with "from passion for bliss" (*ānandarāgāt*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "And not so. Why? To this he replies: "For not... The meaning is that in common worldly usage, an ascetic who desires the fruits of his austerities is not called "passionate" (*rāgin*). What, then, is that [which is called passion]? He says: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). Ignorance is the cognition of the unreal as real and of the non-self as the self. The wise declare that the attachment (*abhiniveśa*) produced by that [ignorance] toward the qualities of form, taste, and so forth—which are inherently unpeaceful—is what is termed "passion" (*rāga*).

For one who, through ignorance (*avidyā*), conceives of the qualities of the field (*kṣetra*) such as pleasure and the like as belonging to the self, there arises an attachment (*abhiniveśa*) toward their causes—form, taste, and so forth—which, though unreal, are falsely regarded as real by that ignorance; this is what is projected by ignorance. He states the distinction [from passion] with the words "But that" (*tac ca*). But that, however, which is the tranquility of the mind—the absence of desire—arising from the vision of Brahman, whose nature is bliss, and which is free from the stains of doubt and error, is not classified by the wise as falling within the category of passion (*rāga*).

This is what is meant: not every desire is passion (*rāga*); rather, it is that which has a non-existent object as its domain. "Serene clarity," "delight," and "intense longing" are synonymous designations; the purpose is to show that in common worldly usage, such a state is well-known by these terms and not by the word "passion. To show that for you, mere distress is not hatred (*dveṣa*), he says "just as. "From that" means from *saṃsāra*. He says "otherwise" to show that if mere distress were hatred, then even for you there would be no liberation. "From that" means from suffering; "hatred" is the aversion toward it, and "wealth" means its cessation. Thus far... [p. 12]

It has been stated that the desire for the reality that is eternal and unsurpassed bliss does not constitute passion (*rāga*). Now, let us grant that it is passion; nevertheless, it is not prohibited by such scriptural passages as those concerning "peace" (*śānta*), but rather the desire that arises toward its opposite—that is, toward the side of that [passion]—as its adversary. This is just as in the case of those who are passionate regarding the supreme excellence of sovereignty and so forth in a universal monarch seen through other means of knowledge; or for those who are passionate because they have perceived a supreme excellence or intensity [in worldly objects].

Alternatively, "superiority over others" (*parotkarṣa*) refers to the sight and hearing of the excellence of others; regarding those who are attached to such things, mastery over the senses—which consists in the renunciation of desire and greed—is taught as the means for attaining that [excellence]. He says "Moreover" (*api ca*) to indicate that the same will apply here as well.

Since the prohibition of all passion and the like entails the prohibition of even the passion for universal sovereignty, there would be the fault that the instruction [for such sovereignty] would be rendered useless because one would not engage in it either. Just as in that case, attachment—that is, clinging or an excess of passion—toward anything other than the desired universal sovereignty, specifically toward its opposite, is prohibited; so too here, by means of the rule of tranquility (*śama*), the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) is instructed to desist from attachment to any inferior sensual pleasure, whether it be present or imminent, other than the passion for the supreme bliss of Brahman.

Thus he says: "In that manner. This is what is meant: with the exception of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), attachment to other things is prohibited by the injunction for tranquility (*śama*); therefore, even when there is attachment to the bliss of Brahman, there is no contradiction with the injunction for tranquility regarding the engagement of one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). And so, he says "And thus it has been said by others as well," referring to the fact that an excessive state of being driven by desire (*kāmatman*) is not praised; yet even for one seeking liberation, there is not an absolute absence of desire, for even such a person possesses a desire for liberation.

Thus, having resolved the contradiction regarding the method of tranquility (*śama*), the opponent again challenges the existence of bliss in Brahman, saying: "It might be so. If bliss were an object of cognition (*saṃvedya*), then, because the object of cognition would be something other than the agent who cognizes, duality (*dvaita*) would necessarily follow; the sense is that there is a contradiction in action being directed toward oneself. He states that duality follows for this reason as well: "The agent... The sense is that since the relationship between an object and an agent is inherently rooted in action, and since action cannot exist without an instrument (*karaṇa*).

He states that if there were a distinction between bliss (*ānanda*) and Brahman by way of the relationship of agent and object, as in the case of a pot and a cloth, even grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not be possible; thus he says: "Bliss" (*ānandam*). Now, if it is argued that "Brahman-bliss" (*ānandam brahma*) is expressed as "the cloth is white" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*), meaning Brahman possesses bliss, then because of that second [attribute], it would not be tenable to say "that Brahman is non-dual" (*advitīyam brahma*); consequently, there would be a contradiction with the scriptures on non-duality (*advaita-śruti*). With this intention, he says: "by possessing that" (*tadvattayā*). Furthermore, if it is argued that bliss is imperceptible, he says in response: "in the absence of perception" (*asaṃvedane*).

The meaning is: "Consciousness is bliss," as stated in the Śruti. Anticipating the objection, "How is it useless?", he says: "Because it is the human goal" (*puruṣārtha*). Here he provides the solution: "It is said. "Fruit" (*phala*) means the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is experience (*anubhava*); and because of proximity, the Self is the experiencer of that very experience; such is the meaning. [p. 13]

He elaborates on this very point by first demonstrating the actual existence of the fruit, beginning with the words "tathā hi" (for instance). Whether the fruit be something distinct from the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of an axe [being distinct] from the act of cutting, or whether it be non-distinct according to the Buddhist view—as expressed in the verse: "That which appears is the object of cognition (*prameya*); that same [appearance], through the consciousness of the form of the cognizer, is the fruit; therefore, it is not made separate from that"—in either case, all this is accepted by every investigator. However, an inquiry into its specific nature is of no use here.

The point is that, therefore, the example is not unestablished (*asiddha*). Others say that the statement "it is not a different thing" was made with the intention of distinguishing between the two etymological derivations (*vyutpatti*) of the word *pramāṇa*: as an abstract state (*bhāva*) or as an instrument (*karaṇa*). He first negates its non-manifestation, saying "and not" (*na ca*). Why? He says: "Because of that" (*tat*). If that [light] does not manifest, then, like a hare's horn, it simply does not exist; therefore, the state of being cognizable (*saṃvedyatva*) of entities could not be caused by it. This is the point; for when there is no light from a lamp, there is no light from the sense-organ.

Therefore, the point is that even if that [consciousness] exists, if it does not manifest, the cognizability of objects produced by it would not occur. Why, then, does the result (phala), while itself unknown, not cause the object to be cognized, as the sense organ does? Because of the difference between them: for the sense organ produces a result, and a producer may remain unknown, just as a seed is to a sprout; but a result does not produce another result, because that would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā). Therefore, that [result] itself is the experience (anubhava) of the jar.

If it is argued that when the jar appears as permeated by that [consciousness], it indeed shines forth; that the cognition "this is a jar" is one thing, and the cognition "the jar is being experienced" is another; and therefore, in the cognition "this is a jar," only the jar appears, not the experience of the jar—this is not so. For if the jar were thus shining forth, there would arise a separate inquiry: "Do I have the experience of the jar, or not? But such is not the case. Therefore, the experience itself appears as the jar.

Furthermore, if this were the case, experience would have to exist through another experience; and if that were so, there would be an infinite regress. Moreover, what is that other experience by which the experience itself shines forth? If you say it is a perception produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind, that cannot be simultaneous with the experience, because the non-simultaneity of cognitions is accepted [by you]. Nor can it occur at a time prior to or subsequent to the experience, because perception cannot have a past or future experience as its object. Its being inferable must also be rejected, due to the absence of any logical mark (*liṅga*).

An object is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) by its mere existence, because that which is unknown cannot be a mark. If it is argued that it is so when known, we say no; for the relationship has not been ascertained. Indeed, when the experience—the related term—is itself unknown, it is impossible to know its relationship with the mark. If it is known and then known [to be related], by what is it known? Not by this very mark, because that would involve mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Nor by another mark, because that would lead to the same fault and render further marks useless.
Therefore, if the knowledge of the relationship between the mark and the experience is desired when the experience is already known, [page 14]...

From that, it follows by necessity that [cognition] is known through itself; therefore, our position is established. Furthermore, at that time, inference would also be fruitless. As for what was said—"Cognition [is known] by virtue of its cognizedness" (jñātatā)—that too is incorrect. For cognizedness is the relation between cognition and the object of cognition; as it has been stated: "The expression of a relation [is formed] from kṛt, taddhita, and compound [words], by means of the suffixes -ta and -tva. And since cognizedness cannot be known when the related cognition is unknown, it is not a valid logical mark (liṅga).

Now, if "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*), which resides in the object, is what is called "known-ness" (*jñātatā*), that too, if unknown, cannot serve as a probans (*liṅga*). If it is known, then—just like the object itself—another manifestness would have to arise for that manifestness, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*), then let experience (*anubhava*) itself be so; what is the use of that [separate manifestness]? Furthermore, manifestness residing in the object would persist even after the cognition has passed away, just as the color and other qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja-rūpādi*) persist after the act of cooking has ceased. And, being located in the object, it would be indistinguishable with respect to all persons, just like those qualities.

By this, it is established that even by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), experience is not itself experienced. Furthermore, when cognition alone—which is intrinsically connected with the object—is manifest, it is said that "the object is manifest"; however, there is no separate manifestation of the object, because, as we shall explain, it is impossible for an insentient thing to be manifest. Moreover, cognition cannot be manifested by another cognition, because they belong to the same genus; whatever belongs to the same genus as something else cannot be manifested by that thing.

Therefore, experience manifests the object only while it is itself manifesting, and not like a sense organ, which does so even while remaining unmanifest; rather, it is like a lamp, being known by itself. Thus it is well said that "if it were not manifest, the object would not be manifest"—that is, "it would be unperceived. Now, if it is held that the result (phala) is what is perceived, he says: "And not... The result is not something perceived, for it is the object of consciousness (*saṃvitti-karman*); for in that case, there would have to be the apprehension of another consciousness within it, and it has already been stated that such [an infinite regress] does not exist.

The meaning is that there would likewise be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding the fruit, another fruit, and so on, even in that case. He concludes with "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Having thus elaborated upon what was stated as "like the fruit," he now elaborates upon what was stated as "like the agent"—namely, "and just as... He asks, "Why would it not be so? and answers, "Because it does not... The meaning is that the object would not appear as being related to that [self]. He asks, "Why? and says, "Because it does not..."

The meaning is that the Self, not appearing [as an object] in the case of "this" (the object) or "it is known" (the result), cannot be connected as the knower by means of the notion "by me. He states what the fault would be in that case: "in the absence of connection" (*ananusaṃdhāne*). What is the distinction between one's own and another's objects of cognition? The meaning is: none at all. Let it then be that [the Self] is cognizable; he says "no" to that as well: "nor... Why? He says: "because of being an object" (*karmatve*).

If the self were the object of its own cognition, there would be a contradiction of action upon itself; therefore, the cognizer would have to be distinct from it. Consequently, the self would be a non-self because it is an object of cognition, like a jar; furthermore, there would be an infinite regress—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: the self does not appear as "this" like an external object, but rather knows itself as the cognizer through the thought "I am"; so how can there be a distinction between the cognizer and the cognized? [P. 4-6, p. 15]

What is the consequence? Even a contradictory relationship between object and agent would apply to that which is established by cognition as being one. This might indeed be so if the notion of "I" were such [an entity]; however, that very notion is difficult to find when it pertains to the self as an object of awareness. For instance, like a jar or other objects, there would be the notion "this," not "I. Therefore, this objection extends only as far as the notion of "I"; consequently, on the strength of that notion, there is neither non-difference between the knower and the known, nor is there an absence of contradiction.

Indeed, there exists this haughty notion “I”; it cannot be removed otherwise. If it cannot be removed, then hear its course: the notion “I” is not actually [the self], but rather it is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) itself, which, illuminated by the self-established, impermanent consciousness, appears as if inherently manifest within the Self conditioned by it. It is due to this very [ego-sense] that the delusion of a notion arises among the ignorant that “the Self is perceived. Consequently, there is no contradiction regarding action upon one's own Self.

Furthermore, when a non-contradictory explanation is possible, it is not appropriate to assume a contradiction. Moreover, the *ahaṃkāra* possesses only the power of agency and does not manifest even in the slightest degree as an object of action (*karman*). Therefore, how could that which is delimited by such an *ahaṃkāra* be self-cognizable? Consequently, the self-cognizability of the Self would not be like that of a jar; rather, it would belong to something other than it, namely, the cognizer of that [Self]. Thus, if the Self were an object of cognition, it would follow by necessity that it is cognized by the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*).

And in that regard, it is well said that there is a distinction between the knower and the known—“because of the consequence of such a distinction. Thus, relying on the impossibility of consciousness being an object [of cognition], he states the self's intended self-luminosity with the words “therefore” (*tasmāt*). The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is that the self’s state of being cognized consists precisely in its self-luminosity, and not in its being an object of consciousness. The term “state of being cognized” (*saṃvedyatā*) is an indication of being cognized without intending the sense of being an object. Furthermore, the self does not appear in the cognition of an object, because it is not the object of that [cognition].

Whatever is not an object of consciousness in a particular instance does not appear therein, just as blue does not appear in the consciousness of yellow. Having thus established self-luminosity through these two examples—that of the fruit and that of the agent—he applies it to the subject at hand with the word "tathā" (so too). Bliss does not fail to appear; even when it does appear, it does not appear as an object of consciousness, because its status as self-luminous is established in the same manner as the fruit and the agent. Therefore, it is not the case that bliss is not a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*).

Nor does it follow that there is duality in the sense that the object of action is other than the agent; nor does it imply dependence on instruments of action and the like—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of Brahman is established by such scriptural passages as “The Self is light, O King” (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.6) and “For there is no loss of the seer’s sight” (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.23). The term “intrinsic nature” (*svabhāvaḥ*) is the reason for bliss being self-luminous; the point is that since bliss has the self-luminous Brahman as its intrinsic nature, it is logical that bliss itself is also self-luminous, because it is non-different from that [Brahman].

But surely bliss (*ānanda*) is an attribute (*guṇa*) of Brahman, not its essential nature (*svabhāva*). This is not so, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "Brahman is bliss. But is this not observed even between an attribute and its possessor, as in the case of a white cloth and the like? No, because of the difference in the cases. For words such as "white" are denotative of attributes; they express the attribute and— [p. 16]

Let [terms] such as "white" and the like apply to the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*); however, bliss and the others reside in the abstracted quality (*guṇa*) itself and do not deserve to apply to the possessor of qualities. For it is not the case that one says, "Sandalwood is fragrance. As it has been said: "The application of the expression 'sandalwood is fragrance' never occurs. Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the possessor of qualities is not possible for a word denoting a quality that does not apply to that possessor. We shall explain later how this is possible according to our own position; for now, we shall desist.

Now, if the Self is self-luminous, why does it not manifest during deep sleep? To whom would it manifest? If it manifests to itself, that is exactly what we maintain; for the Self is eternally manifest to itself, according to the Śruti: "For the vision of the seer is never lost. If you say it manifests to other individual souls (jīvas), that is not so.

For those [individual selves], whose distinctions are imagined through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect and so forth—which are effects of ignorance—how could they perceive [anything] during deep sleep? In that state, all effects are withdrawn, and ignorance remains merely as a seed, having concealed the true nature [of the self] and leaving behind only residual impressions (saṃskāra). Therefore, this is not a fault. Now, one might object: "If Brahman is eternally perceived due to its self-luminosity, then the prohibition of seeing it is untenable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By what? The word "what" (kam) is an elliptical reference (ākṣepa) to the entire class of objects of sight, and not to the act of seeing itself. This is the meaning.

This very point is strengthened by the sequence of the scriptural passages—thus it is said. The meaning is that the negation is stated solely on account of the dissolution of the entire range of the visible, which is the object of seeing. When, for this wise one, the entire range of the visible has become the Self alone and nothing exists apart from the Self, then what could he see? The sense of the sentence is "nothing at all. Thus, the phrase "he would see" indicates that it is the perception of the visible that is negated here, not the perception of the Self.

In this regard, some others raise an objection once more, seeking to establish that the word *ānanda* denotes the absence of suffering in Brahman rather than signifying happiness itself—the text says "others. He distinguishes between types of properties with the words "of two kinds," namely "positive" (*bhāva*) and so forth. Among these, he states that those which are negative in form are not defective with the word "therein. He provides examples with the words "for example. He states the reason with the words "it does not," meaning that because cessation (*nivṛtti*) is a non-entity, it does not bring about duality; therefore, it does not destroy non-duality (*advaita*).

One should distinguish as follows: “one” (*ekam*) signifies the cessation of the difference or manifoldness between the self and non-self objects; “unborn” (*ajam*) signifies the cessation of arising or birth; and “immortal” (*amṛtam*) signifies the cessation of decay or destruction. However, if bliss (*ānanda*) were admitted to be a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*), then non-duality (*advaita*) would be destroyed; thus he says: “And bliss... Now, one might object: since there is a distinction between a property (*dharma*) and its substratum (*dharmin*), non-duality would be destroyed; [we reply] that such a distinction does not exist there, because if they were distinct like a cow and a horse, the relationship of property and substratum would be impossible.

Therefore, he raises the objection that there would be no destruction of non-duality by saying, "It might be so. He refutes that with the words, "That [is not so]. The meaning is that even if there were absolute non-difference between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substrate (*dharmin*), the status of being attribute and substrate would be untenable for the attribute in relation to itself, just as it is for the substrate. Since the relationship of attribute and substrate is excluded from both absolute difference and absolute non-difference, therefore, there is a partial (or qualified) distinction.

He states that dharma must be accepted by saying "therefore" (tasmāt). He asks "what follows from that? and says "and so" (tathā ca). Furthermore, the fact that the Śruti intends the absence of absolute difference should be understood from its repeated use of the words "one," "without a second," and "alone. Now, one might object: there is no relationship of property and property-bearer between bliss and consciousness; rather, Brahman is a single entity whose nature consists of both consciousness and bliss. Therefore, the Śruti on non-duality is not contradicted. Anticipating this doubt, he says "in this way" (evam).

The connection with the preceding argument is as follows: even for one who asserts that Brahman possesses a dual nature consisting of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and bliss (*ānanda*), the scriptural teaching of the absolute absence of difference is untenable, because he must admit a distinction between these two forms and their substrate (the possessor of the forms). Having thus utilized the objection raised against the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) as a synonym for happiness, the opponent establishes his own position, beginning with the words "Therefore... and "by means of the self of consciousness (*vijñānātman*)."

It has been stated that because consciousness (*vijñāna*) is of a single nature, there is no fault of falling into duality caused by a distinction between two forms called "consciousness" and "bliss. Furthermore, it should be understood that regarding the view that bliss is the absence of suffering (*duḥkhābhāva*), since non-existence is not a real entity, that same fault—caused by a distinction between attribute and substratum (*dharma-dharmin*)—does not exist, as is the case with the position that bliss is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*). Now, one might object: consciousness and bliss do not stand in the relation of attribute and substratum, nor is there a single reality consisting of multiple parts; rather, this single reality alone is expressed by the two words "consciousness" and "bliss."

Anticipating the objection that "therefore, there is no consequence of duality" according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), he says: "And not [so]. Why? He says: "Because of the words," etc. For if they had the same meaning, they would be synonyms; and the simultaneous use of synonyms is neither observed nor logical—this is the sense. Furthermore, in common usage, the non-synonymy of the words *vijñāna* and *ānanda* is well known; nor is it logical for their referents to be identical, as in the case of a pot and a cloth. Thus he says: "And how," etc. Therefore, in this way, the identity of *vijñāna* and *ānanda* is not tenable.

Since the distinction between those two remains, thereby establishing the position of the Advaitavādin, the opponent concludes his own view with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Let it be granted that elsewhere the word *ānanda* denotes pleasure; however, in the case of Brahman, due to the aforementioned logical inconsistency, its indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) must be the mere absence of suffering. For this very reason, the phrase "in Brahman" (*brahmaṇi*) was stated. Here, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the word "here" (*atra*).

The meaning is that there is no fault of contradicting the scriptures on non-duality (*advaita-śruti*), because the two terms "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*) designate a specific luminosity—distinct from the three worlds, consisting of radiance, and having the nature of happiness—but do not designate its substratum (*dharmin*), which is comparable to moonlight. This is what is being said: bliss is consciousness itself, not a quality of it; nor is it a single entity possessing two forms. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the doctrine of non-duality.

As for the claim that it is never observed that non-synonymous words have a single referent, he provides an example to refute that: "Just as... He states that there is no contradiction because they are non-synonymous due to a difference in their primary denotations (*abhidheya*), yet they possess a single referent through the identity of what is indicated (*lakṣyamāṇa*). He asks, "What is that? and replies, "Illumination" (*prakāśa*). Now, if these two are non-synonyms, then they must have different meanings; therefore, like the letters *na* and *li*, they cannot stand in the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*).

It might be so; therefore, a light qualified by excellence would have to be established. And from that, since there is equality between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and bliss (*ānanda*), one might suspect the consequence of duality due to the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified. Anticipating this, he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). This connects with the end of the passage: "...is understood through the means of two words."

Consequently, this is the meaning: from the two words [“prakāśa” and “savitṛ”], no excellence (*prakarṣa*) distinct from or different from the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), which is of the nature of light, is perceived as belonging to the sun; nor is the reverse the case. What, then, is perceived? To this he says: "But rather... The intention is as follows: when someone asks, "What is the sun?", then, because the answer must correspond to the question, that which is to be established is precisely an excellence of light characterized as the essence of the sun.

It is neither light distinguished by excellence nor its opposite, because that would not correspond to the question; therefore, at that time, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) pertains solely to the nature of the sun. And since the primary referent of a word is its actual meaning (*śabdārtha*), it is established that through two words whose literal senses are not intended, that single [nature] alone is indicated (*lakṣyate*) by means of their respective literal senses. Thus, their non-synonymy and their identity of meaning are proven. He applies this point to the subject under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*) as well with the word "likewise" (*tathā*).

The meaning is as follows: "distinction of bliss" (*ānandabheda*) refers to a specific kind of bliss, which is happiness, or rather, Brahman whose nature is bliss is understood through these two words as self-luminous consciousness itself; it does not, however, imply a relationship of quality and qualified (*guṇaguṇibhāva*) between consciousness and bliss. Now, one might object: if there is no difference between consciousness and bliss, then because the two words would be synonyms, they could not be used together; whereas in cases such as "excellent light" (*prakṛṣṭaprakāśa*), co-usage is justified because there is a difference in the objects denoted, and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs by means of two distinct literal senses.
