Furthermore, there is no connection here between two primary meanings (svārtha); and when there is no connection between primary meanings, there can be no secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Nor is that which is indicated (lakṣya) itself the indicator (lakṣaṇa). In that context, it was stated that two non-synonymous terms attain a single referent through secondary indication; however, if consciousness (vijñāna) and bliss (ānanda) were non-different, they could not be non-synonymous. Therefore, in every respect, the illustrative example is dissimilar.

Now, if it is maintained that there is a difference between the referents of the words *vijñāna* (consciousness) and *ānanda* (bliss) in order to avoid [the charge of] all these defects, then it follows by necessity that Brahman possesses the qualities of consciousness and bliss as its possessor (*guṇin*), and duality would consequently result. To this it is replied: even here, a difference between the referents is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*). For it is only on the plane of ignorance that the linguistic convention regarding the difference between word and meaning is accepted for the world of the ignorant, not on the non-dual plane of reality (*tattva-bhūmi*); therein, consciousness and bliss are not established as separate entities.

And this well-established distinction between the two, which consists of ignorance, is sublated by the scriptural text, "One only, without a second. Furthermore, by this very scripture which teaches reality (*tattva*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is made known through the mode of usage—as in "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) regarding the individual self and the supreme Self. For in that case, neither the meaning of "thou" qualified by the meaning of "that," nor the meaning of "that" qualified by the meaning of "thou," is what is to be established.

However, by the power of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words *tat* and *tvam*, the reality (*tattvam*) is non-different from the perspective of sublation by the Veda, despite the difference between objects established through ignorance (*avidyā*). And therefore, just as in that case, those things established through ignorance— [p.

Because of the difference in their referents (*artha*), those two [words] are not synonyms; nevertheless, through those two, which have as their referents objects established by ignorance (*avidyā*), a single transcendent reality (*tattva*) is indicated—not denoted—precisely because the Self is transcendent and because it is devoid of the fourfold set [of categories] such as genus (*jāti*), which are the grounds for the application of words. It is the same here as well. Consequently, there is no disparity between the example and the case at hand, nor is there the fault of redundant co-usage, nor does the consequence of duality follow, since the distinction between the denotable objects consists in their being of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*).

For a difference consisting of ignorance does not produce the appearance of duality in cases such as the double moon. If it is asked how that which is imagined can serve as a means (*upāya*), we have already stated this and shall explain it further. But if this is so, and the well-known meaning is sublated, how can there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when the primary sense is not applicable? We reply: it does occur, just as in the passage, "The cows indeed performed this sacrificial session," where, since the sitting of cows is impossible, praise is indicated; and thus it has been said: "Just as the sitting of cows for a sacrificial session, though non-existent, has become a subordinate element of praise..."

“Likewise, knowledge and bliss are the limbs of the self-abiding consciousness of happiness. Now, one might object: that [previous case] was appropriate because the sentence was intended to express the non-difference between those two objects; however, this sentence is intended to describe the very nature of Brahman, not to express the non-difference between bliss and consciousness, for if it were intended to convey both, there would be the contingency of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, how can there be a cognition of their non-difference here? No, for it is established by the sense of the matter (*arthasiddhatvāt*).

Just as in a sentence primarily concerned with an injunction regarding an action, there is a necessary restriction of substance and quality toward a single effect, so too here, because both are bound to a single [subject], there is a mutual restriction between them.

Furthermore, since it has been stated that the word *ānanda* (bliss), which denotes an extracted quality (*guṇa*), cannot enter into grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [with consciousness], it is understood through the relation of quality and qualified (*guṇaguṇibhāva*), like words such as *aruṇa* (red) which reside in the possessor of the quality; thus, by implication, it is established as identical [to consciousness]. Therefore, the non-difference between these two is proven: "Consciousness itself is bliss" and "Bliss itself is consciousness"—thus all is faultless. Alternatively, excellence (*prakarṣa*) is not a quality, because even a quality can possess it, as in the expression "sandalwood with excellent fragrance."

For it has been stated: "A quality (guṇa) is that which resides in a substance (dravya) and possesses qualities. Therefore, it is not a separate substance. Nor is it action (karman), because it exists even when there is no action—as in the expression "the horse has swift movement" (*prakṛṣṭagatiraśvaḥ*). As for its being a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, such possibilities are far removed from the case. Consequently, what is called "excellence" (*prakarṣa*) is in reality a particular individual (*vyaktiviśeṣa*) itself; it is differentiated only by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). And this particularity of the individual is intrinsic (*svata eva*), not due to its connection with excellence.

Because there is no excellence where there is no prior excellence, and because otherwise there would be an infinite regress. But surely, even when the excellence has long since vanished, there remains another excellence in the form of the persistence of the sandalwood fragrance on the nail? Not so; even that fragrance there is not something that arrived from the previous state. Rather, understand that due to contact with water and other elements, a transformation of the fragrance of the sandalwood—which had perished for some reason—has arisen after a long time. Thus, by this conceptualization, there is a difference in meaning, and therefore they are not synonyms.

There is no lack of established usage; furthermore, in reality, excellence in the sun is nothing other than a specific manifestation of light, and this is understood through two words, since it is not understood from either one alone—thus, the statement beginning with "nor [is there a lack of usage] for the words *prakṛṣṭa* and *prakāśa*" is well-said.

Having thus refuted the view that the word *ānanda* has the absence of suffering as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and that it signifies the absence of suffering, [the author] now addresses the "supremacy" (*paramatā*) of bliss heard in the scripture, "This is his supreme bliss. They say that this supremacy is merely figurative (*aupacārikī*), because there is an absence of the state of being miserable—which consists in dependence on external means for sensual pleasure such as garlands and sandalwood (according to the principle that "everything dependent on another is suffering")—as well as the absence of misery in the form of the cessation [of such dependence]. They maintain that this is what is meant by the supremacy of the term "supreme bliss."

The meaning is this: that which falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is described in accordance with them, whereas that which falls solely within the scope of verbal testimony is properly grasped in accordance with the power of the words themselves. He asks "Why? and says: "For... (*ja hi*). "Because of the non-creation of food that is opposed [to bliss]" means because of the absence of suffering, which is the opposite of bliss. He concludes the subject matter of the section with: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).

It should be discerned that the term "self-luminous" (ātmaprakāśa) indicates its nature as consciousness by virtue of being self-manifesting; "supreme" (prakṛṣṭa) indicates its primary status as the highest reality; and "of the nature of bliss" (ānandasvabhāva) indicates that since the mere absence of suffering cannot logically constitute a positive state, bliss must be a positive entity and is non-different from it.

And since Brahman has the nature of unconditioned bliss which is of the form of existence, even that which is stated in the passage, "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction (*mātrā*) of this very bliss," namely that worldly happiness is but a fraction of supreme bliss, is also rendered consistent; thus he says: "If this is so. *Mātrā* means a single part, that is to say, a small portion. Why? He says: "Because of limitation (*avacchedāt*)."

For existence (*bhāva*), being unlimited, can be delimited and made small by objects, just as space is by jars and the like; but non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot, like the non-existence of a sky-flower and such. This has been stated: "in the cessation of suffering. He states another reason for bliss being of the nature of existence: "for this reason also" (*itaśca*). He establishes the reason—that it is the object of supreme love—by means of scripture: "it is heard [in the Upanishads]. He says that it is not only heard, but is also established by experience: "and it is perceived."

He states the experience: "For thus" (*tathā hi*). "Self-directed desire" (*ātmāśīḥ*) means one who desires for the self. He states that [desire]: "May I... (*mā...*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that too" (*sāpi*). The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that it is not only the Vedic scripture, but that desire for the self as well. Nevertheless, to the question "Even so, what?", he says: "And love" (*prema ca*). The distinction is this: there is aversion toward suffering, and indifference toward that which is devoid of both pleasure and pain. Regarding the experience of the self as being of the nature of happiness, he states another view: "But others... (*anye tu*).

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that immediately after deep sleep (*suṣupta*), there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) for one who has awakened. But how, from this reflective awareness, is the existence of experience established? To this he says: "For not... Since reflective awareness is preceded by experience, that experience is inferred from it; such is the meaning. Furthermore, if there were no experience whatsoever, even the admission that "I slept" would not occur; thus he says: "In deep sleep... The word "would not exist" (*na syāt*) is understood to carry over. Now, [page 21]...

Experience is indeed [of the nature of] *va* (pleasure); why is there the distinction that it is "the experience of pleasure" (*sukhānubhava*)? Why could it not be "the experience of pain" (*duḥkhānubhava*) instead? To this he says: "Not so" (*na ca*). The word "it would be" (*syāt*) connects with what precedes. The sense is that the establishment of experience as qualified by the subsequent recollection of pleasure is thus proven. Now, let us grant that there is an experience of pleasure; nevertheless, how can the Self have pleasure as its very nature (*sukhasvabhāvatva*)? Why could it not be that pleasure is experienced as something entirely separate? To this he says: "Not so."

In that state of deep sleep, because all the instruments [of perception] have ceased their activity, nothing other than the Self is experienced; therefore, it is established that the Self, being of the nature of bliss, shines forth by itself, and thus its identity with bliss is proven. He confirms this point with scripture, saying "And so" (*tathā ca*). The scripture states: "In this very way, all these creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it. Others, however, do not accept this, because experience must be postulated on the grounds that the subsequent reflection (*parāmarśa*) would otherwise be inexplicable.

"And that [experience of pleasure] can also arise from the absence of pain"; thus he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). In this context, those who maintain that the experience of pleasure has inference by means of recollection (*parāmarśa*) as its mark say: since the Self is essentially pleasure, if its being otherwise—that is, its being non-pleasure—were understood through another means of knowledge, then the word "pleasure" would be assumed to be used figuratively (*gauṇa*) on account of the absence of pain; otherwise, if its being non-pleasure were not understood, it is proper that it be used in its primary sense (*mukhya*). Thus he says: "To them" (*tān*). He refutes this with: "In that regard" (*tatra*).

For experience must be postulated as belonging only to the individual soul (*jīva*) who has awakened, upon reflection, and not to anyone else. Furthermore, for that soul at that time—whose all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have been withdrawn, who remains as mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and whose self is veiled by ignorance—the perception of deep-sleep bliss is impossible. Therefore, this is merely a recollection in the form of "I was happy. And such [recollection] is observed both in the case of actual happiness and in the cessation of pain; moreover, it is logical that the cessation of pain occurs invariably concomitant with happiness.

Consequently, there is no establishment of an object consisting of the experience of pleasure from that [sleep]. Thus he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). Alternatively, because of the two-fold designation—"I slept happily" and "nothing was cognized by me"—there is total ignorance during sleep; and since the reflection on pleasure is caused by the cessation of pain, both designations are thus justified. Therefore, the meaning is that the experience of pleasure is not established merely by virtue of such designations. [Objection: But even the cessation of pain is not known during sleep. [Reply: True.

Upon waking, however, one connects with pleasure and realizes the cessation of suffering. [Objection: But surely even the non-experience of suffering was not known at that time; how then can it be connected? If one had experienced suffering, then one would have remembered the suffering; but this is not the case. Therefore, it follows that one connects with the absence of the experience of suffering, thinking, "I did not experience suffering. Now, in order to explain the single word [of the verse], he first sets forth the mutual difference between the self and the objects of the self's vision, as well as among the objects themselves—which is the view held by others—introducing it with the words "In this regard" (*atra*). Someone is happy, someone...

The distinction that "one is suffering" as a result of the distribution of experiences, and the differentiation that "one is liberated while another is transmigrating," is only possible if there is a difference between selves; otherwise, if there were only one self, when one person is happy or liberated, all would have to be happy or liberated. This is the logical argument for the plurality of selves. Furthermore, without an object of perception, the power of vision belonging to the self would be fruitless. If it is argued that the self will perceive itself by means of that power, the author replies: "In regard to its own self. The meaning is that it is contradictory for the self to be its own object of action by virtue of being pervaded by its own operation.

Furthermore, that which is visible must be pervaded by vision; and since vision is an effect, it leads to the inference of its inherent cause, the seer—thus, the seer is inferred from the visible. Therefore, there exists a visible distinct from the seer: this is the reasoning for the difference between the self and the visible. It should be understood that the phrase "of the visible," etc., refers to the reasoning for the mutual difference among various objects of perception. Moreover, because sound and other objects are born of the three *guṇas*, they are like the differences in pleasure and so forth; thus, it should be seen that the distinction between types of the visible, characterized as pleasure and the rest, is also implied.

The meaning is that just as there is the perception of difference among mutually opposed states such as pleasure and so forth, so too there is the perception of difference among mutually opposed things such as sound and so forth. Thus, since there is indeed difference, those who think that the scriptural statement regarding the oneness of the Self—“This is one alone, without a second”—is based on the non-difference of the genus *ātmatva* (selfhood) and the non-difference of space and time; and that the scriptural statement regarding the oneness of the world—“All this is indeed the Self”—is figurative due to oneness in the form of existence (*sattā*); and that the word "that" in such passages is used in that sense—to them it is replied: "One. Here, he cites the scripture: "Indra... [and so forth].

"Māyā" is that by which one is measured; thus, it means the intellect (*buddhi*), through which the self is perceived in the form of bipeds and so forth. If it is asked, "In that case, how can multiplicity be false?", [the answer is: no, because [the word] is etymological (*yaugika*). For the word *māyā* is etymologically derived when applied to the intellect, whereas it is conventional (*rūḍha*) when applied to the state of falsity. And the rule is that conventional meaning is stronger than etymological meaning. Therefore, the intellect alone should be understood [here]. Even though there is an inclusion of this term among the names for the intellect in some lists, nevertheless, it is not to be accepted here.

For whatever is perceived is perceived by the intellect (*buddhi*) alone; therefore, the qualification "illusion" (*māyā*) would be redundant. Furthermore, the word *māyā* does not everywhere in the Veda denote the intellect, because it is seen to deviate from that meaning in such passages as, "Know *prakṛti* to be illusion" (*māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ viddhi*). To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). If there were multiplicity, then oneness would be merely figurative (*upacarita*); however, since that [multiplicity] is not real, the oneness declared by the scripture must be understood as truly real, not figurative. He states the contradiction with another scriptural passage should oneness be taken figuratively: "Likewise" (*tathā*).

The phrase "it is not possible [to apply it] in the sense of identity" (nopacarita ekatve 'vakalpate) is to be connected with everything that follows. Previously, the plurality of objects was negated by referring to them as "illusion" (māyā); here, however, because it is stated directly, it is called "manifestation" (vyakti). On this point, some say: since the generic form (ākṛti) is the referent of words, the word expresses plurality; therefore, in the context of the cause of the world, the passage "this was indeed non-existent" (asadevedam) negates plurality within that causal substrate, but does not negate that the world consists of diverse entities. To this we reply: even though the word for plurality expresses plurality, the word "plurality" (nānā) [is used] as in the expression "the cloth is different from the jars" (vaṭebhyo nānā paṭaḥ). [Page 23]

But [the word "one"] exists in reference to that world (*jagat*). If it is argued that it exists there because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "cloth," as in the expression "white cloth," then here too, the coreferentiality with the world—whose specific nature is not determined by the term "something" (*kiñcana*)—is no different. Therefore, it is established that it is the world itself in its state of multiplicity that is negated, not multiplicity per se. Nor should this meaning be imagined—that "in one abode there is only one non-dual enjoyer, not many"—because that would entail the fallacy of imagining what is not stated in the scripture.

In that very context, he states the contradiction with another scriptural passage: "nānātva" (diversity). The sense is that if unity were merely figurative, then diversity would be the ultimate reality; and it is not proper to censure that [ultimate reality]. Again, in that same context, he states the contradiction with another scriptural passage: "bheda" (difference). The meaning is that the word "as if" (iva) is appropriate when there is something other than the perception of difference—as in a mere semblance of it—but not when it refers to that [perception] itself.

Nor should it be said that the word *iva* in the phrase "as if there were a perception of difference" (*bhedadṛṣṭiriva*) has the sense of restriction—as in the expression "these grains are as if minute"—and not the sense of indicating unreality; for [if that were so], the statement "due to delusion" (*bhramāt*) would be untenable. Precisely because the perception of difference is established as an error, and difference is therefore false, it is proven that this *iva* in the word "manifold" (*nānā*) serves to indicate falsity and not to signify restriction; otherwise, it would have a meaning contrary to that.

Furthermore, because multiplicity is prohibited by the statement "not here is diversity," and because it is improper to abandon a well-established meaning without a compelling reason, there is a distinction in that case [of the Śruti passage] due to the mention of the feminine gender, which serves as another reason for its transcendence. It was stated previously that the scriptural teaching regarding the cessation of multiplicity does not imply a figurative application of unity; now, however, he says "Granted... (kāmam), while provisionally accepting that unity is figurative, to show that even then the scriptural teaching on the cessation of multiplicity would not be tenable. The term "bhāvikasya" means "of that which is real" (tāttvikasya).

One might object: "Even the cessation of multiplicity will occur through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), since there is no multiplicity when there is non-difference in terms of existence (*sattā*) and so forth. Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "That too" (*sāpi*). One might further object: "Let there be no purpose; let the non-difference of the universal (*jāti*) such as existence be the cause for that metaphorical usage. What is the need for a purpose? Anticipating this, he says: "When there is a metaphorical usage based on a cause, a purpose must be required. For the word "sun" is not metaphorically applied to a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) merely because of the presence of the cause of brilliance, without regard for a purpose such as praise.

The intention is that the Scripture does not demonstrate the non-existence of the multiplicity of existing things for no purpose at all. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And not... It is not only that [the teaching] is purposeless, but rather it is contrary to the purpose; to this extent he says: "And because of the opposite. That which is the purpose and how the figurative usage occurs—it is contrary to that; thus he says: "Abhyudaya... (regarding spiritual prosperity).

That cessation of diversity is the heaven to be attained; sacrifice is the means; and the *prayāja* offerings and so forth constitute the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). By negating this distinction, [the notion of non-duality] stands in opposition to spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*), because without that [distinction], there can be no performance [of ritual]. Regarding all objects, [one should realize] "this is indeed the Self. [p. 24]

The compound is formed with a word ending in the dual number. Having set aside the fact that [attachment] is opposed to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) because it is well known, he states the reason for its opposition to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*). "A human being does not find liberation anywhere except through the renunciation of everything"—thus liberation is heard in scripture as resulting from the renunciation of all things. And since it is impossible to renounce sons, wife, and so forth while there is the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) toward them, liberation would not occur; this is the meaning.

The metaphorical designation of oneness was stated merely as a concession, but it is not what the Śruti intends; with this intention, he says "tathā" (so). An *avadhāraṇa* is that by which something is determined—the particle *eva*. Because the meaning of that very non-dual form is expressed again and again by those two [terms] (*advitīya* and *eka*), the purport of the Śruti is seen to be the cessation of difference in every way—not only in the form of genus and so forth, but also in the form of the individual. He states the reason for this: "For in repetition... (*abhyāse hi*).

"Abundance" (*bhūyastva*) means being preeminent or superior; that is to say, there is not even a scent of difference in any way. Thus, it should be understood that even those who maintain the doctrine of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda-vādin*) are refuted by scripture itself. Having thus established the non-dual nature of the Self (*ātma-advaita*) based on the scriptures whose purport is non-difference, [the author] now restates and refutes the reason for the difference between selves (*ātman*) as stated by the opponent—namely, "on account of the regulation of experience"—with the words "As for what... (*yattu*).

The meaning is as follows: even though the Self is one, the regulation of experience will be established—just like the distinction between smallness and largeness based on the difference between a water-jar and a room, which is imagined due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*). Nor is this an assumption of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*); for it is observed that the regulation of experience occurs from a difference that is merely imagined. He says "For instance" (*tathā hi*): "in one"; the meaning is "in the individual soul residing in a single body. And he says "for not" (*na hi*) to show that the sensation there does not belong exclusively to the feet or the head.

Now, one might object: let it be granted that for the all-pervading, partless self, the regulation of experience (*bhoga-vyavasthā*) is based on mere conceptual construction; however, for the self whose size is coextensive with the body, since it possesses parts due to its capacity for contraction and expansion, [the regulation of experience] will be established as real through the perception of those parts. To this, he says: "The body... It is not only the parts of the self that are the locus of sensation, but rather the whole composed of those parts (*ātmāvayavin*) as well; otherwise, there would be no sensation belonging to the self as a whole.

And for this reason, because there would be a difference between the two parts of the self, the mutual connection of cognitions would be impossible; consequently, there would be no single unifier of the sensations in the foot and the head, yet such a one does exist. Furthermore, he does not connect the sensation of another, because of the lack of identification expressed in the thought, "this is my sensation. Therefore, even the self as a composite whole must be the locus of sensation; yet, while it pervades the entire body, it is not the case that it experiences sensation everywhere, but rather only in the foot and the head.

And therefore, because it is partless (*anavayava*), there would be no fixed determination of sensation based on the distinctions among its own parts as characterized by the feet and so forth; this is the meaning. Now, if even for the naked ones (*nagna*) the self is partless, then this passage must be interpreted with reference to the limbs such as the feet. Thus, [p.

And the intention behind the separate mention [of the two bodies] must be stated. Here, the opponent objects: "It might be so. (P. 7-6) The meaning is this: just as in a single body a single self connects the sensations of the foot and the head, why does a single self not likewise connect them across two bodies? The proponent, however, states that pointing out a flaw in another's position is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), saying: "Because they are different. If there were identity of self, there would be connection between the two bodies just as within one body; yet that is not the case.

Therefore, since the objection that "there is no identity of the self" does not constitute a refutation of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) presented here, the author states another solution out of dissatisfaction with the previous one, beginning with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). The meaning is as follows: just as within a single body, the portions of the individual soul (*jīva*) demarcated by the head and the feet do not experience each other's sensations, so too the individual souls (*jīvas*), though belonging to the one Supreme Self (*paramātman*), are differentiated by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*). As for the Supreme Self, however, such a lack of coordination is ruled out by impossibility; furthermore, that [lack of coordination] is a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

And the sense is that it does not belong to him [the Self]. He provides another illustration regarding the systematic arrangement based on imagined difference with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). The meaning is that even though there is no difference in the face and so forth, a distinction in the arrangement of color—such as dark—and of configuration—the specific arrangement of parts—is observed in the case of a jewel, a sword, and so on; it is the same here as well. Having thus established the systematic arrangement of experience (*bhoga*), he extends this very principle to the systematic arrangement of the liberated and the transmigrating souls, saying "thus" (*evam*).

He confirms this very point by means of an illustration with the words "tathā hi" (for instance). Just as a single individual soul (*jīva*), though appearing divided by way of locations defined by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the head and feet, becomes associated with pleasure and so forth; and where it is associated with those, it is understood to be bound there, while elsewhere it is understood to be associated with them [in a different state]—so too will it be for us. This is the intended meaning. To provide another illustration on this very point, he says "tathā" (likewise).

Just as a single face appears both dirty and clean in mirrors that are respectively dirty and clean, so too the single Self appears both miserable and happy in internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that are respectively impure and pure; this is the explanation for the two-fold nature of transmigratory existence. Or, just as that very same face becomes free from the defects [of the mirror], so too the Self, when not associated with the internal organ, becomes free from those defects such as misery; thus the systematic consistency (*vyavasthā*) is established—this is the intended meaning. Here, an objection is raised: "It might be... The term *kalpanā* (conceptual construction) is used here with the abstract sense as the primary referent.

The meaning is this: the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) and the state of having an unreal object are attributes of the cognizer’s cognition (*pratyaya*), not attributes of the external object; therefore, they are not capable of establishing the reality of the thing itself. Alternatively, "cognition" (*pratyaya*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), as that by which something is perceived; its attribute is false knowledge, which is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). However, in the phrase "not indeed," it is the conceptual construction itself that is the cognition. Why is this so? He says: "Not indeed. For it is not the case that whatever is known in a certain way must exist exactly in that way.

For indeed, a mother-of-pearl shell known as silver does not thereby become silver itself; consequently, the Self, though known as divided by the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), would not be divided in reality. Therefore, there would be no established order regarding experience and so forth—this is the sense. Furthermore, from an imagined individual soul (*jīva*), neither seen nor unseen effects could arise, just as they do not from an imagined person such as a boy named Bhāṇavaka; thus he says: "And not... (*na ca*).

[Page 26] But was it not stated that the systematic arrangement [of things] is established even through distinctions imagined by way of the head, feet, and so forth? True, it was stated; however, that is an illusion and not according to reality. Thus he says: "That which has been cited... The word "true" is used in the sense of acceptance. The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), however, says: "In this case too... The meaning is: for us as well, everything is indeed nothing but an illusion. The systematic arrangement that was cited is precisely our final position.

In this regard, when the opponent objects that [the example] is "real," the text should be applied as a further rebuttal stating that even here there is delusion (*vibhrama*). As for the statement that "an effect is not seen from the imagined (*kalpita*"), he refutes that by saying, "even though imagined. "Imagined" means determined through error (*bhrānti*) in the absence of an actual bite. Nor should it be said that it is the cognition (*jñāna*) there that is the cause of death, rather than the unreal thing; for cognition in its mere form is indistinguishable everywhere.

Now, if it is argued that this [snake] is distinguished by being a snake-bite, then it follows that just as it is a cause of death, so too is it imagined; thus there is no fault. The bite is entirely imagined, whereas in the case of the living being, it is merely a difference; therefore, they are not identical in every respect. To clarify this point, he cites the example of a reflected sun (*pratisūryaka*); the meaning is that the reflection of the sun in a mirror or similar surface, though consisting of a mere imagined difference, is capable of performing the function of illumination.

Having thus established the regularity of experiences and so forth—even while the self is non-dual—as the reason for the apparent difference between selves, [the author] now restates the opponent's argument in order to refute the reasons for the mutual difference between the seer and the seen, and among the objects seen themselves, beginning with the words "yadapi" (as for that which...). First, he refutes the initial reason by showing its lack of proof, beginning with "tadapi" (that too). The meaning is as follows: the cognition of the object is preceded by the cognition of the subject, and not vice versa; how this is possible has been explained in the passage beginning with "yathā ca kartaryasaṃvedye" (and just as when the agent is not perceived).

He refutes the second reason as well by showing its lack of proof (*asiddhatva*) with the words "the visible" (*dṛśya*); the meaning is that the distinction between the visible and the means of knowledge, such as perception, cannot be apprehended. He says "will be stated" (*vakṣyate*), meaning in the passage: "They say that perception is an affirmer" (*āhurvidhātṛ pratyakṣam*). As for the one who holds that the existence of distinct visible objects is due to the power of the seer's capacity, he too must admit their connection even in the absence of the visible; thus he says "the seer" (*dṛk*); the meaning is that the seer will perceive only the Self through that [power].

Anticipating the objection that "it has been stated that the status of being an agent is contradictory to the status of being an object," he says: "And not so" (*na ca*). The point is that just as a lamp shines by itself independently of another lamp, so too does the Self; therefore, there is no contradiction. Even if a lamp indeed shines independently of another lamp, it is nevertheless known by the intellect (*buddhi*); thus, he provides the example of the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), which is self-established and not known by the intellect, saying: "the means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is that this has already been stated in the passage "nor is it an object of cognition. Now, however, he states the advantage in his own position with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*); the meaning is "in the case of the identity of the seer and the seen. To the question "Why? he says: "Of the seer" (*draṣṭuḥ*). "Because of transformation into various forms of the seen"—this is the view of the opponent (*paramata*). "Because of illusory manifestation" (*vivartanāt*); "because of the superimposition of that form upon what does not have that form through delusion"—this is your own view (*tvamata*). What is there in this? [p. 27]

The sense is that, even according to both systems, the status of objects as "seen" (dṛśyatva) is possible because they are related to the seer (draṣṭṛ) by way of having the same form as the vision (dṛksarūpeṇa). However, if there were difference (bheda), then for the Self and the non-Self—which lack a relationship characterized by identity (tādātmya)—there could be no relationship of seer and seen. This is because, being partless like two separate iron balls, they would not be in contact with one another, and thus, being unconnected, the relationship of seer and seen would not exist. To this he says: "But if there is plurality (nānātve tu). Why would it not exist? He says: "For not... (na hi). [P. 7-24] From its own nature... (svato).

The sense is that objects are insentient (*jaḍa*). Now, one might raise the objection: "If the mind is like a crystal, then objects transmitted through the channel of the senses will become its objects of perception once they are connected with the self-consciousness (*ātma-caitanya*) that has likewise been transmitted into it. Anticipating this, he says: "Not so" (*na*). Even though consciousness (*cit*) has been transmitted into the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is no turbidity caused by contact with objects, because it is pure (*viśuddhatvāt*).

Nor does consciousness, even when pure, undergo transformation into the form of an object upon being reflected therein, because it is immutable (*kauṭasthya*) and thus incapable of change. This statement was made with reference to the theory of reflection; however, in reality, such reflection does not exist for consciousness because it is inactive, nor for the object. Therefore, the point is: how could the object possess the quality of being cognized through that connection? Now, it might be argued: "The external object is not what is perceived; rather, it is the intellect (*buddhi*) itself that, having transformed into the form of the object, is perceived in the form of the object."

And that [intellect], due to its proximity to the conscious self, bears the reflection of consciousness; therefore, it is said that "the object is seen. However, this does not imply that consciousness possesses impurity, undergoes transformation, or that there is a transference [of qualities]. Thus he says: "as the seen" (*dṛśya*). He refutes that [objection] with: "Now" (*atha*). If the intellect, which is non-conscious by nature, were to possess the nature of consciousness, that would be its being a reflection; in that case, it would be false. And an object is not truly seen through a connection with consciousness that is itself false.

Furthermore, it cannot be asserted that what is not perceived from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha) exists as something distinct from the object seen or the seer; therefore, the intended meaning is that the duality of the seer is established. As for the Mīmāṃsaka who maintains: "The status of the object seen is determined solely by its being an object of perception, not by a [separate] relation; the relationship between these two is precisely the state of being the seer and the seen, like that between the signified and the signifier, and nothing else. This is the sense.

Furthermore, perception [in the form] "this is blue" presents the blue as distinct [from itself], not [as] non-distinct [in the form] "I am blue"; therefore, the object of sight is distinct from the seer. To this he must be answered: "It is true that perception has for its object a thing distinct [from itself], but because of a delusory determination (*bhrānty-adhyavasāya*), even though there is no actual distinction, one perceives that distinction due to the single Self appearing in various distinct forms such as blue and so forth. He states all of this with the words "He who also... and provides an illustration here with the words "like a mirror..."

"Of the self" (ātmanaḥ) means "of one's own body. He elaborates on that very point with the words "for thus" (tathā hi). The meaning is that just as a reflection, though non-different from the original object, is perceived as different, so it is here. Now, one might object: "Granted that this may be so there because of sublation, but what is not possible here that would justify such a hypothesis? To this he says: "But for consciousness... (citeḥ tu). It is difficult to understand how consciousness could perceive itself as something distinct, non-identical, or unconnected; therefore, its being an object of cognition is simply untenable. [p. 28]

The sense is that it is "conceived" (*kalpyate*). There is a relationship between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) that contains the act of denotation (*abhidhāna-kriyā*); however, since consciousness (*cit*) possesses no such action, there is a disparity. Furthermore, regarding the non-difference of the object of perception from the Self, he states in P. 8-11, "And thus," that there is even scriptural authority (*śruti*). Since everything other than the Self is non-existent, the Self alone is the reality (*tattva*) of all; therefore, the meaning of the scripture—"when the Self is known, all is known"—is established.

Nor can it be asserted that everything is both identical to and different from the Self, such that by knowing the Self through its aspect of non-difference, everything becomes known; for this would entail the assumption of what is not heard [in scripture], and because knowledge would be incomplete due to the aspect of difference, making absolute knowledge impossible, and because identity and difference will be refuted later. Therefore, he concludes that the term "one" is well-stated: "Therefore... and so forth.

Now, in order to explain [the Brahman] as "immortal" and "unborn," the author first presents the Mādhyamika view while setting aside two Buddhist positions, beginning with the verse starting with *kṣaṇika*. As it has been said: "The liberation of that Protector (Tāyin) is like the extinguishing of a lamp. This means that there is a complete eradication of the afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding sense objects. Due to the destruction of the latent impressions of sense objects, there is an absence of the apprehended (*grāhya*); and due to the absence of that, there is an absence of the apprehender (*grāhaka*).

The non-existence of an ungraspable object of cognition (*agrāhya*) implies the impossibility of a grasper (*grāhaka*); this is the cause for the cessation of consciousness. For the Mādhyamika, Brahman has the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnya*); therefore, the attainment of that [emptiness] alone is the attainment of Brahman. He confirms this point with scripture: "And thus," meaning that after departing from saṃsāra, there is no [empirical] knowledge. He states the view of the Yogācāra: "But others" etc.; one whose entire latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding objects and so forth have been completely severed is described as such, because of that reality—that is the meaning.

The connection with the forms of objects has been shaken off and removed; therefore, there arises a purified consciousness—this is how the ancient teachers describe the attainment of Brahman, characterized by that [purification]. This is the connection with what precedes. Now, he states the defect for those who maintain the existence of an eternal self: "beginningless," etc. The meaning is: in the state of immutability, which is free from birth and destruction. To the question, "What is the defect in that? he says: "Thus" (*iti*); here *iti* signifies the reason. "For the sake of that" means: for the purpose of removal and acquisition.

He elaborates on the very absence of anything to be removed or added, beginning with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). He asks "Why? and replies: "Because of ignorance" (*avidyāyāḥ*). First of all, ignorance is not something to be removed, because it does not exist within the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*); nor is it something to be added by means of knowledge, because it is established as its own inherent nature. Furthermore, Brahman does not have ignorance as its nature; otherwise, one would have to say that ignorance is removed from it. For if the eternal Brahman were to lose its own nature, the consequence would be its impermanence.

The meaning is as follows: because the prior nature of ignorance cannot be abandoned; because the nature of knowledge, being without any adventitious excellence, does not undergo any change; and because if it possessed the dual nature of both knowledge and ignorance, then since knowledge would already be attained, it could not be further acquired, and since ignorance would be of that very same nature, it could not be removed. Thus, "there is nothing to be set aside" (p. 29).

The phrase "or [the word] *bhava* is not [to be taken as] *asavyam*" follows from the two preceding alternatives. To those who say this, he replies: "Immortal and unerring" (*amṛtam ajām iti*). Therein, he first dispels the two faults mentioned by the opponent with the words "not so" (*na ca*). Now, one might object: "If ignorance (*avidyā*) is beginningless like Brahman, it cannot be destroyed. To this he says: "all" (*sarva-*). The point is that since this is established for all disputants, we alone are not to be blamed; furthermore, it is observed that even a beginningless antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) can be destroyed. The opponent now says: "No. (*na iti*)

The connection with what precedes is as follows: we say that there is no cessation of that which has the nature of eternal Brahman and consists of ignorance. He raises this very doubt and refutes it with the words "Now, if... (atha). The implication is that, in that case, the consequence of duality would follow. Now, if it is argued that she [ignorance] is not accepted even as something other than this [Brahman], then she is neither its nature nor a separate entity; thus, she does not exist at all. Therefore, he asks: "What is there to be removed? with the words "And if not... (na cet). The opponent, however, raises another objection with the words "Now, if... (atha).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of Brahman; nevertheless, there is no consequence of duality (*dvaitaprasaṅga*), because, being of the nature of a non-apprehension, it is a non-entity and thus not a separate thing. Nor is it for that very reason indestructible, since all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have as their purpose the cessation of the non-apprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). This is the meaning. The sense is that even if the means of valid cognition do not remove it, the ignorance regarding the object of knowledge would still persist. Having raised this objection, he refutes it with the words "that too" (*tadapi*). He asks "Why? and replies with "And that" (*tacca*).

The point is this: since that ignorance consists of non-apprehension and is opposed to knowledge—which consists of apprehension of that [Brahman]—it can be removed only by knowledge and not by anything else; and because it is of the very nature of Brahman, it is eternal. Therefore, ignorance is eternally sublated, and thus the scriptures and so forth do not have their purpose in bringing about its removal. Now, suppose one argues: ignorance does not belong to Brahman, but rather to the individual souls (jīvas) with respect to Brahman as its object; and that ignorance is removed from them by adventitious knowledge concerning Brahman, which is acquired through efforts such as hearing the scriptures.

Therefore, it is said that there is no consequence of the perpetual cessation of ignorance; yet even that is not so, because if one accepts a living being (jīva) distinct from Brahman, the consequence of duality follows. With this intention, he says: "And not... [na ca]. If it is then argued that ignorance resides in Brahman itself, he says: "In Brahman... [brahmaṇi]. It should be understood that this is restated with the desire to state another refutation. Now, if out of fear of these defects their non-contradiction were admitted, he says: "There would be no contradiction" [avipratiṣedhaḥ].

For knowledge, being opposed [to ignorance], would remove it, but not that which is not opposed to it, just as taste does not remove color; this is the sense. Having thus refuted ignorance as consisting in non-apprehension, he now refutes it as consisting in erroneous apprehension—with the words "But for whom... The sense is that if it were not of the nature of Brahman, it would be a different entity, and thus non-duality would be destroyed. He states another defect with the words "And of whom..."; the sense is that an erroneous apprehension is impossible without a substratum.

First of all, that grasping of the opposite cannot belong to anything other than Brahman, because such a thing does not exist; nor can it belong to Brahman itself, because it is impossible for that which is of the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*) to be the locus of the contradictory ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus he says: "of Brahman. Then, regarding the lack of contradiction therein, he says: "non-contradiction" (*avipratiṣedha*). [p. 30]

By what could it be removed? The meaning is: by nothing at all. The sense is that, because knowledge is not contradictory [to it], it cannot remove it, and no other remover of it is observed. (P. 9-11) Here he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "To this it is said. By the statement, "It is neither the nature [of Brahman] nor a different entity," he refutes the faults mentioned regarding the positions of it being either the nature or a non-nature, simply by not accepting them. To the objection—"If ignorance is neither the nature of Brahman nor a different entity, then it does not exist at all"—he says: "No."

If it is neither different from Brahman nor non-different, neither existent nor non-existent, what indeed is it? To this he says: "In this way"; the meaning is that it is precisely such, having no fixed single form. Nor is this something extraordinary; thus he says: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*); the word "in the world" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. He employs these specific synonyms to show that it is conventionally established by words such as these, and not by words such as "existent" or "non-existent. Regarding its lack of existence, he first states the proof: "For its nature is... and so forth.

The sense is that, regarding its non-existence as a real entity, the very impossibility of its being ignorance otherwise is the proof. Likewise, since it would be real if it were of the nature of Brahman, the impossibility of its sublation—just like Brahman—is also to be inferred as a proof in that regard. Its non-distinctness from other objects is not mentioned separately because it shares the same defect, or because it is equivalent to the position that its nature is different; for in the case of its absolute non-existence, the impossibility of its serving as a factor in empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*) is the proof.

With the intention that "for what is non-existent, the status of being a constituent of worldly transaction (*vyavahārāṅgatva*) is never observed," he says: "absolutely" (*atyanta*). This is also an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication); for even perception (*upalambha*) of a non-existent thing would not be possible, as in the case of a sky-flower; thus, that [perception] too is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Objection: If it is a constituent of worldly transaction, then because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), how could it not be existent? [Reply: Not so; for even the identification of the body with the self (*dehātmabhāva*), though it is a constituent of all worldly transactions, is non-existent. [Objection: If it is argued that the knowledge of that [body] is indeed existent and is the constituent of the transaction therein, [Reply: That too is not the case.

Since mere cognition is not a constituent of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*): [Objection] If ignorance (*avidyā*) is apprehended by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then it must be real like Brahman; if it is not, then it must be unreal like a sky-flower. How, then, can it be "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*)? [Reply] Not so; for it indeed appears, yet not by means of a valid knowledge, as in the case of the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. For this very reason, it is distinguished from a sky-flower. Nor is it both real and unreal, because that would involve a contradiction. Therefore, by force of logic, it follows that the indefinable is a third category, distinct from both the real and the unreal. [Objection] But nothing other than those two has ever been observed.

Granted that it may not be seen [in this way], nevertheless, the indefinability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), established by the force of the aforementioned proofs, cannot be denied; for the fact that earth possesses odor is not denied simply because it is not observed elsewhere, even though it is observed there. [Objection: But if it is called "indefinable," how can it be indefinable? [Reply: Not so, because it is specified as being neither existent nor non-existent (*sadasadbhyām*). [Objection: If ignorance is admitted, it must necessarily be either different from or non-different from Brahman, since no other category is possible.
[Reply: Not so, as in the case of the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell (*śuktirūpya*).

Because it has already been answered by the statement "vāda" (in the case of debate); for silver in a mother-of-pearl shell cannot logically be distinct from the shell, non-distinct, or both distinct and non-distinct. Therefore, there exists the possibility of another mode [of relation]. He concludes by accepting all these positions—*tasmāt* (therefore). This [mode] must indeed be admitted by all disputants; thus, he makes everyone accept it through the force of reasoning so that we alone are not to be blamed—*sarvaiḥ* (by all). He elaborates on this very point—*tathā hi* (for instance).

For the Mādhyamikas, who maintain that everything is empty, if the world as it is perceived were real in that very way, then, being the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it would not be ignorance (*avidyā*). On the other hand, if it were absolutely non-existent, then like a sky-flower, it could not be a constituent of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) nor would it appear. Likewise, for the Yogācāra, who maintains that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), since he does not deny the appearance of external objects, if they were real in that way, there would be no denial of objects; yet if they were absolutely non-existent, they could not be constituents of worldly transaction, just like a sky-flower.

Even for Patañjali, who maintains the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), this notion of permanence and so forth—defined as "ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cognition of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in that which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self"—is accepted as false. If the object appearing as permanent and so forth were real, that cognition would not be false; if it were unreal, there could be no worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) based upon it. Therefore, the meaning is that ignorance must be admitted by all to be truly indefinable (*anirvacanīya*). Now, one might object: in an illusion such as [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the silver is unreal, but the cognition of it is not.

"And that [appearance] is ignorance; therefore, while it exists, how can there be indeterminability?"—thus he objects with the words "This might be so. But the proponent replies: "This is not so. When an object is appearing yet is unreal, its appearance cannot be established as real either; rather, only the act of appearing would be real. Even the phrase "its appearance" is merely an error, because that [object] itself does not exist. The meaning is that not only is the object non-existent, but even the appearance of the object is likewise unreal.

This is what is meant: mere experience (*anubhava-mātra*), devoid of connection with an object, is indeed eternally existent for us; its status as ignorance (*avidyātva*) is due to the illusory connection with an object, not by itself. Because it does not exist in the form of a connection with a non-existent object, it is said to be "not existent" even though it is existent by itself. Having thus resolved the objection regarding indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*), he concludes with the words "therefore. He demonstrates that very point with the words "hence."

He asks "Why? and replies: "Because its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not abandoned. If ignorance were of the nature of existence, it would not abandon its own nature, just as fire does not abandon its heat. Furthermore, there can be no transformation into something else for that which already exists in such a state; and if that which has already been transformed were to transform again, there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, it could not be altered by a subverting cognition (bādhaka-jñāna). Alternatively, if it were non-existent, then because it would be ascertained as such by its very nature, it could not be removed by that [cognition]. This is the meaning.

Having thus established the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), he addresses the two objections raised by opponents—that "if it were real, there would be the consequence of duality; and if it were unreal, there would be no object to be removed"—with the word "thus" (*evam*). Now, having restated what was asked regarding "whose is this ignorance?", he provides the answer with the words "as for that which... (*yattu*). Here, the opponent raises an objection with the word "but" (*nanu*): the sense is that ignorance cannot belong to Brahman, because its very nature is knowledge (*vidyā*). [p. 32]

P 10-4. To the question "Why?", he says: "For thus... The scriptural text [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20] records grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Self" (*ātman*), which denotes Brahman, in the phrase "by the living self" (*jīvenātmanā*). The sense is that such coreferentiality would not be possible between two distinct entities, like a jar and a cloth. Likewise, one should infer that there would be contradiction with such passages as "Know me also as the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajñaṃ cāpi māṃ viddhi*), and the consequence of duality (*dvaitāpatti*) would follow if there were a difference between the two. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*), however, says: "True"; the phrase "is not different" (*na bhidyate*) is understood to carry over. To the question "In what way, then, are they different?", he says: "By conceptual construction" (*kalpanayā*).

The meaning is: "of a cognition that does not correspond to reality. Although the individual souls (*jīvas*) are in fact non-different from Brahman, they appear as distinct from it through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), due to false cognition (*mithyābuddhi*), like a reflection and its original, or like the moon and its reflections. Thus, it is stated that here only the difference is conceptual, and not the reality of the soul itself. For this very reason, in the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), it is the difference alone that is sublated, and not the soul itself as expressed by "Thou art That. He raises an objection again with the word "whose": the meaning is, "Whose conceptual construction serves to differentiate the individual soul and the Supreme?"

In this regard, wishing to state two solutions according to different views, he first states one: "In this case" (*atrety*). If that which is called *avidyā* were a real entity (*vastu*), then it would not be unestablished and would be sufficient for the establishment of the reality of the individual soul (*jīva*); yet, without the soul, its own establishment would not be possible—thus there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). But it is merely *māyā*; therefore, there is no fault. Why? He says: "For not... Why? He says: "For it has only an impossible object. That *māyā* has only an unreal subject matter.

If that [scripture] were to have a real referent, it would be consistent with reality (*yathārthatva*), and thus its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) would be lost; therefore, the fact that its referent is unreal is its ornament, not its defect—this is the meaning. He states another solution: "But others... From the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, the individual soul (*jīva*) is delimited by them and consists of their qualities (*tadguṇasāra*), like the space within a jar; from that [soul], the conceptualization [of the ego] arises. Thus, like a seed and a sprout, they should be understood as beginningless (*anāditva*). However, the causal ignorance (*kāraṇavidyā*) is indeed beginningless.

He confirms the very beginninglessness [of the world] by means of the statement of those belonging to his own school—with the words “And thus” (*tathā ca*). This means: by those who maintain that the phenomenal world of difference has ignorance as its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). Regarding that, he states the result of beginninglessness with the word “But there” (*tatra*). He states the result of the lack of purpose mentioned in the context of the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) with the words “Not so, because of the lack of purpose” (*aprayojanatvāt na*); the meaning is that there is no room for the objection: “What is the purpose of the creation of the phenomenal world that is being differentiated?”

In this regard, he first states the objection: "If [it were] one," etc. Although even prior to creation there exist individual souls (*jīvas*) in a state possessing seeds who are to be favored—since otherwise the impossibility of renewed creation would follow—nevertheless, because they are as if dissolved in Brahman upon the dissolution of their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is stated that there is an absence of distinct individuals to be favored, as observed in experience. Furthermore, he says: "And because [the world] is followed by suffering," to show that favoring others is not the motive [for creation]. For through favor, He would create only those who are happy, not those who suffer. [p. 33]

The meaning is that creation is full of suffering; as it has been said: "And [if He were motivated by compassion], He would create only what is auspicious. Nor is there any purpose useful to Himself, as he says: "No," because "His desires are fulfilled" (āptakāmatvāt). According to the Śruti, "He whose desire is for the Self is one whose desires are fulfilled"; thus, the meaning is that He has achieved His goal because all objects of desire have been attained. As it has been said: "If His activity were for the sake of sport, His state of having achieved His goal would be impaired. By the word "sport and so forth" (krīḍādi), curiosity (kutūhala) is implied.

Having thus stated the objection, he declares its lack of foundation with the words "of that" (*tasya*). He asks "Why? and replies "For not... (*na hi*). He demonstrates this very point through worldly examples with the words "not" (*na*). He states "likewise" (*tathā*) to show that even the defect mentioned regarding the position of cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra*) does not affect our own position; the sense is that even in the case of the pure sky, an illusion such as "the surface is dark" is observed. It has been stated that creation produced by ignorance is without purpose.

Now, having for the sake of argument accepted that activity is for the purpose of sport (*krīḍā*), he states the absence of the previously mentioned defects, beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*). "Activity for the purpose of sport": the word "sport" (*krīḍā*) is to be supplied [as the predicate]. "From encouragement" (*ucchvāsāt*): this means from stimulation (*protsāhāt*). "Prayer" (*prārthanā*): the sense is that activity performed by one possessing the prayer of desire is itself called "sport," and not activity for the sake of some task to be accomplished. [Objection: But surely, since the sight of the happy and the suffering is a cause of attachment and aversion, the Lord, as a seer, would possess those [qualities] and thus there would be partiality (*vaiṣamya*).

Likewise, there would be cruelty on the part of one who creates beings in suffering; therefore, he says "not so" (*na ca*). Why? He says "for not" (*na hi*). A "magician" (*māyākara*) is a conjurer; just as that magician, when displaying the manifold world (*prapañca*) of Rudra and others—whether complete or incomplete in its limbs—has neither passion nor hatred, such is the case here. This is an illustration from his own position (*svapakṣa*). He states the same for the position of those who maintain that the manifold world is real: "various" (*citram*). "Model" (*pustam*) means a painting; "of the created" (*kṛtām*) is the genitive plural from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *kvip*.

"Defective or non-defective" means having incomplete or complete limbs. "Variegated" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), by which paintings and other such things are also to be understood. "Image" means a likeness. He states another solution: "By action. For God, like the rain-cloud, is the common cause; however, the distinction between those who experience pleasure and those who experience pain arises from the distinction of their own actions, just as the distinction between sprouts arises from the distinction between seeds. Therefore, the meaning is that He is not subject to defects such as partiality.

[Objection: But in this way, because the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) is dependent [on something else], sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), which is characterized by independence, would not exist. To this he says: "And not... This is what is meant: mere dependence on another does not constitute a lack of sovereignty; for in the world, a lord who bestows a result while depending on a particular service is not thereby rendered a non-lord. Just as one who, though depending on a support, is capable of giving a result, is a lord—and not the other.

Likewise, even when dependent upon karma, it is that [Self] alone—and no other—that is capable of bestowing the fruit; thus, sovereignty belongs to that alone. And as for the statement, "For the pure Person, there is no impure modification," this is the primary [point].

Previously, this was refuted by relying on the illusory nature of creation (*māyikī sṛṣṭi*) and by not accepting the position of transformation (*vikārapakṣa*). Now, with the intention that even if that [transformation] were accepted, this fault would not arise—and how much less so for us proponents of *māyā* (Māyāvādins)—he says: "In the same way" (*tathā*). The meaning is as follows: if there were an absolute lack of distinction between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*), then, like the material cause alone, there would be no differentiation consisting in the state of being cause and effect. Therefore, there is a distinction between the two; and thus, even from the pure, an impure modification may come to be.

A difference between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) is observed elsewhere as well; with the intention that the same might be the case here, he says: "of liquids" (*dravāṇām*). The non-conscious and the conscious should be understood as being respectively uncontrolled and controlled by consciousness. Now, he raises an objection again from the perspective of the Advaita school: "But surely" (*nanu*). "Of pure nature" means having the nature of stainless knowledge (*vidyā*). The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), however, shows that even though [the impure] is non-different from the pure, it nevertheless appears as impure; thus he says: "it is a mere pittance" (*vārtam*), meaning it is worthless.

The news arrived from hearsay; the meaning is that it is without proof. Why is this so? He says: "Not, first of all," and so forth. But how is it that the reflection is not distinct from the original object (*bimba*)? Because it is impossible for something possessing parts to exist without a conjunction of those parts. It is not the case that its parts are not perceived; nor can they be merely postulated, since the cognition of it is established even otherwise. Furthermore, it is impossible for something with parts to abide in a mirror that is without intervals; because there is recognition of the form of the original object; and because it is not perceived by touch.

Because that which possesses parts cannot perish without the destruction of its parts and their conjunctions, whereas this [reflection] appears through the mere proximity of the original object (*bimba*); therefore, it is established that the original object itself appears as if divided due to error. Now, one might object: "Impurity in that which is non-different from the pure is not possible in reality; rather, that impurity belongs to the reflection, which is an illusion. Anticipating this, he states that here too there is an illusion, saying: "The delusion" (*vibhrama*). He further confirms its status as an illusion with the words: "Otherwise... (*anyathā*).

The meaning is that, from the ultimate standpoint (*tattvataḥ*), if the individual souls (*jīvas*) were impure by nature, there could be no purification; this was stated in the passage "because their nature would not be abandoned. Here, the opponent raises an objection with the word "it might be" (*syāt*); his intention is that for one who maintains the doctrine of non-duality (*aikātmyavādin*), there can be no adventitious cause external to that [non-dual reality]. The proponent, however, says: "What is the need here for another adventitious cause? For such a cause would be required in the case of adventitious errors like reflections; but this error regarding the soul is beginningless (*anādi*)."

Therefore, since this [non-apprehension] is beginningless and is established by that very non-apprehension, it is improper to search for an adventitious external cause; with this intention, he says: "In the beginningless... He further states: "And thus," meaning that the objection regarding the absence of a cause for the activity of ignorance is also refuted because of its beginninglessness. Here, an opponent objects: "But surely... For the cessation of that which possesses a cause is seen to result from the destruction of the cause; however, ignorance, being beginningless, is innate and thus lacks a cause. Therefore, how could it be destroyed? This is the sense of the objection. The proponent replies: Ignorance is indeed destroyed even though it is innate; otherwise, [p. 35]...

With the intention that treatises whose objects are established upon that [nature] would otherwise become useless, he says: "All... He further states: "Moreover... because even the natural [state] is seen to be subject to cessation. But the opponent, raising an objection by pointing out the disparity with cases such as blackness and so forth, asks: "Now... "Pratyaya" means "cause. That which has no adventitious second object is described as such. "Because of its state" means: because of the absence of the occurrence of a heterogeneous cause.

From what does cessation arise? The word "from ignorance" (*avidyāyāḥ*) is to be supplied. Now, one might object: let there be no adventitious cause; since the Self consists of knowledge (*vidyā*), knowledge, being its very nature, will simply remove ignorance. To this he says: "Certainly not. If you maintain that knowledge and ignorance coexist in the same single Self, then, because they would abide as its inherent natures, there would be no opposition between them, and thus no relationship of the remover and the removed.

Alternatively, in case of a contradiction, the meaning is that since ignorance (*avidyā*) is eternally dispelled from the Self by knowledge (*vidyā*), the world would be eternally liberated due to the absence of any basis for it [in the Self]. The term "of ignorance" (*avidyāyāḥ*) connects with both [sides] like the eye of a crow (i.e., it functions in both contexts). "By that" means by knowledge. If it is argued that another adventitious knowledge produced by hearing and so forth will remove ignorance, he says "and not" (*na ca*). If it is argued that even though this other adventitious knowledge is adventitious, there is no loss of non-duality because it is the very nature of Brahman, he says "adventitious" (*āgantuka*).

The meaning is that it is not possible for that which is impermanent to possess the nature of permanence. Regarding this very point, he cites what has been stated by another: "As it has been said. Here he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "In this regard. The meaning is that this was explained by means of the analogy of a reflection. He asks why it does not belong to Brahman and answers: "Because of that fear" (*tadbhīti*). The meaning is that there is no adventitious object for it that could remove ignorance (*avidyā*). Alternatively, the meaning is that it possesses no adventitious object, i.e., it is incapable of having any excellence added to it (*anādheyātiśaya*). In that context, it has been stated that because of its eternal luminosity, there is no innate ignorance.

The distinction here is that it has been stated that even adventitious [impurity] does not exist, because its meaning is non-adventitious. It has been stated that there is no defilement by ignorance in Brahman, whose nature is knowledge; for if such were the case, a great fault would ensue—thus he says, "otherwise. Regarding the phrase "one who has attained the state of Brahman" (*brahmabhūyaṃ gatasya*), the meaning is "one who has reached the condition of Brahman. To the question "What follows from that?", he says, "therein. Their view is that Brahman alone transmigrates and is liberated, and not the individual souls (*jīvas*).

Having restated that, he refutes it: "By implication. The meaning is: "Brahman alone [is liberated], not the individual souls (jīvas). He asks, "Why? and says: "Because," etc. The meaning is that since liberation occurs in Brahman through the vision of non-difference, and because there would be no other bound soul who perceives difference once all distinctions have vanished, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that everyone is liberated simultaneously. He concludes his own position with: "Therefore," etc. Now, let it be granted that ignorance belongs to the individual souls; [but...]

Nevertheless, having raised the previously mentioned objection—asking how there can be the cessation of ignorance if there is oneness (*aikātmya*) due to the absence of a distinct cause—the author offers a rebuttal with the words "of them" (*teṣām*). The meaning is this: even though there is an absence of a distinct real cause, the cessation of ignorance is possible for individual souls (*jīva*) who are defiled by ignorance, because knowledge arises through causes characterized by hearing and so forth, which are themselves imagined by ignorance. That whose cause is a "distinct cognition" is described as such; it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the arising of knowledge which is a distinct cognition," or alternatively, "the arising of knowledge that is a distinct cognition. (P. 12-8)

[Objection: But surely the knowledge that leads to liberation exists even for the individual souls (*jīvas*); therefore, it is that very [knowledge] which removes ignorance, not some adventitious and distinct [knowledge]. To this he says: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). The meaning is that the individual soul is said to consist of ignorance itself. [Objection: Since the individual souls are non-different from Brahman, whose nature is knowledge, how can they consist of ignorance? To this he says: "Even though there is no distinction" (*avyatireke 'pi*).

The meaning is that just as a reflection of a face and so forth is pure, while its reflection in a sword or similar surface is impure, so too, even though Brahman is of the nature of knowledge (*vidyā-ātman*), there is the established distinction that for individual souls (*jīvas*) there is ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, [one might object]: first of all, it cannot be the remover of the ignorance regarding Brahman, because that would entail the consequence of its being eternally removed; nor can it be another ignorance, because since there is no difference in their both being ignorance, they could not stand in the relation of counter-positive and antagonist; furthermore, this would entail the consequence that the remover itself would not be removed, and if one were to postulate yet another remover, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

With the intention that there is no other subverter [of ignorance] than either Brahman or ignorance itself, he asks: "By what? The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin), however, says: "By hearing (śravaṇa)," with the intention that although there is no difference in their being dust, just as the dust of the clearing-nut (kataka) is the counter-agent to other dust and its subverter, so too, although there is no difference in their being ignorance, the ignorance consisting of hearing and so forth will be the counter-agent and the subverter of the ignorance of the phenomenal world (prapañca).

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) are means for the cessation of ignorance through the sequence of the arising of scriptural knowledge; celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the like, through the sequence of the non-destruction of [merit] over a kalpa; and meditation (*dhyāna*) and the like, through the sequence of the manifestation of the light of the non-dual Self.
