Hearing is the study of the Vedānta; reflection is the investigation of its meaning by means of reasoning; and the practice of meditation is the repeated contemplation of that meaning.

The opponent, intending to show that it is impossible for something of a similar kind, such as hearing and so forth, to serve as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), asks again: "How? The proponent replies: "What is there to say here? Even though there is no difference in their being forms of ignorance (*avidyā*), this practice of meditation—which is preceded by hearing and reflection, and not preceded by instruction at the ear's root—concerning the entire differentiated phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as negated by the repetition 'not this, not this' (*neti neti*), is for that very reason the counter-correlate to the perception of the phenomenal world."

Therefore, he says "this which... to show that it turns that [ignorance] away. That in which the entire manifold of difference (*bhedaprapañca*) has been negated is described as such. If it is argued that this is a negation of the body and so forth being the Self, and not a negation of the entire manifold, we say no; for the body and so forth are not mentioned [in the text], and there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for assuming what is not heard. Therefore, since no specific [object of negation] is perceived when there is a requirement for something to be negated, it is well said—"in which the entire manifold of difference has been negated"—that this is indeed the negation of the entire manifold.
But even so, [one might ask], is there not a need for a negator of hearing and so forth, which themselves negate the perception of difference? [Page 37]

Anticipating the opponent’s objection—that if [the means] do not cease, liberation would not occur because there is no intermediate state—he offers a rebuttal with the words "And that" (1.12–14). The term "generally" (sāmānyena) means "without distinction. By the word "that" (saḥ), the practice of meditation preceded by hearing and so forth is referred to. He elaborates on this very point through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the words "For not... If hearing and the rest were to dissolve other distinctions while leaving aside the distinction between the hearer and the act of hearing, then this fault would indeed arise.

The sense is that they, by specifically dissolving all distinctions, dissolve even the Self because [the Self] is included within them; consequently, there is no non-cessation of those [distinctions], nor is there a dependence on another means of cessation. Therefore, he says "And thus" (tathā ca) to show that the fault of non-liberation does not apply. By "clear" (svaccha), he expresses the natural purity of its own nature. By "perfectly pure" (pariśuddha), the meaning is that adventitious impurity consisting of ignorance has been removed. He provides an illustration for this with "Just as" (yathā).

Just as the dust in the form of powder from a specific substance such as *kataka* acts as the agent that, having been cast into [the water], removes other impurities; and while being itself removed, it brings the water—which is the object of the action and turbid due to contact with impurities—back to its own natural state. Having stated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he applies it to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) as well, saying "in this way" (*evam*).

The meaning is that, because there is no distinction in the nature of perceiving difference, when the difference residing in hearing and so forth likewise dissolves, the individual soul (jīva) abides in its own pure essential nature. Now, one might object: even if the individual soul, which was distinct from Brahman, remains in its own nature upon the dissolution of ignorance, it would still remain in that same [separate] state; thus, its becoming one with Brahman (brahmībhāva) would not occur. Anticipating this objection—and noting that the scripture declares, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—the author says: "by ignorance" (avidyayā).

If the individual soul (*jīva*) were different from Brahman in reality, then this [distinction] would indeed exist; however, it is so only through ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, the meaning is that upon the cessation of ignorance through knowledge (*vidyā*), one becomes exactly of the nature of Brahman. Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "as" (*yathā*). "In division" (*bhede*) means in the sense of splitting apart. "That space" (*tadākāśa*) means the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*). Now, the opponent objects again, out of the conceit that the power of counteracting heat, cold, and so forth is observed to be caused by heterogeneity (*vijātīyatva*): "It might be so," he says.

How can the manifold world (*prapañca*) be sublated through the distinctions of hearing and so forth? The sense is that [the opponent argues] it cannot, because there is no difference in their being ignorance (*avidyā*). The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), however, maintains that it is observed that even a similar *rajas* (passion/impurity) acts as the sublater of another *rajas* when it serves as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*); whereas it is not observed that things of a different class, such as color (*rūpa*) or taste (*rasa*), act as sublaters when they are not counter-correlatives. Therefore, even in cases like cold and heat, the power of sublation is conditioned solely by the status of being a counter-correlative. And since this [status of being a counter-correlative] is clearly present in the case of the distinctions of hearing and so forth, even though they are produced by ignorance, he says: "by the distinction" (*bhedeti*).

He states its nature as an antidote with the word "manifestly" (*vyaktam*). He provides two further examples to illustrate how hearing and so forth cease by themselves and also cause the cessation of their own kind: "And just as... (*yathā ca...*) Although milk is digested by the digestive fire within the stomach, it is nevertheless described as "ceasing by itself" on the basis of this much similarity—that it is digested without depending on another instance of milk.

The point is that a complete identity with the illustrative example does not occur in every respect. He confirms with scripture the idea that hearing and so forth—which are themselves a form of ignorance—bring about the cessation of ignorance, stating "as it has been said. He clarifies the meaning of the mantra with the words "this," etc.: knowledge is pure consciousness which is eternal; ignorance consists of hearing and so forth; for these two are joined and connected by way of the relationship between means and end, and thus they are related respectively. [Objection: But if knowledge is the goal (upeya), then it must be something to be accomplished (sādhya).

For it is not possible for that which is unattainable (asādhya) to be an object of attainment (upeya); therefore, having raised the objection that [knowledge] must be impermanent, he provides the answer through the latter part of the mantra, beginning with "sādhyā" (to be attained). He explains this with "eṣa" (this): ignorance does not produce knowledge, but rather it is one who is established in ignorance [who produces it]; however, [the mantra] reveals knowledge. Thus, knowledge is an object of attainment by way of being revealed, not by way of being produced; therefore, it is not impermanent. This is stated with reference to the eternal knowledge that constitutes the very nature of the Self.

An objection is raised: "Is it not the case that by the words 'having crossed over death' (*mṛtyuṃ tīrtvā*), the cessation of death is heard in the scripture, and not the cessation of ignorance? How then can it be said that ignorance is what is removed? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Death... He connects the fourth quarter of the mantra with the words: "In that... The instrumental case in the word *vidyayā* is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇe*). The phrase "abiding in one's own nature" (*svarūpāvasthānam*) is an explanation of the term "immortality" (*amṛta*). An objection is raised: "If ignorance removes ignorance, then no effort need be made for the sake of attaining one's true nature. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Like a crystal..."

The meaning is as follows: just as in the case of a crystal gem, through effort alone one removes the limiting adjuncts such as the *japā* flower, and by the abandonment of the redness caused by them, the gem abides in its own true nature without requiring further effort—so it is here as well. Regarding this, some say: "Based on the mantra 'performing indeed actions here,' action is mentioned by the word 'ignorance' (*avidyā*) through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of knowledge; therefore, this mantra is devoted to the combination of knowledge and action. That is incorrect.

The word ‘avidyā’—through the negative particle (nan) and its own inherent power—denotes a lack of knowledge (*ajñāna*) that is the opposite of true knowledge (*vidyā*), namely false cognition (*asamyag-jñāna*), and not merely something other than it. In this context, the direct statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative than the contextual setting (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, this mantra does not intend to teach the combination of knowledge and ritual action. He states another meaning of the mantra with the words "anya" (other): the meaning is that the manifestation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-darśana*), which is ignorance, does not exist apart from true knowledge, which is the illumination of the immutable Self (*kūṭasthātma-prakāśa*). He demonstrates this very point with the words "tathā hi" (for thus).

The manifestation of an insentient thing cannot occur through itself; nor can it occur through another, because that would entail the loss of its own nature. Nor can it occur through another manifestation residing within the Self that is self-luminous, because the Self is changeless. Furthermore, the implication is that there can be no manifestation of something that is not connected with manifestation. He concludes: "Therefore... "In such and such a way" means by way of this or that form of phenomenal expansion. He confirms this very point by means of scripture: "Just as... Here, someone says: [p. 39]

This word "all" refers to the subject under discussion; and what is under discussion here is the sun and so forth, beginning from the passage: "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars. Therefore, the meaning is this: by the light—that is, the power—of that Brahman, all this, beginning with the sun, shines or is illumined; it does not mean that the entire world is illumined by its [the sun's] own light. That is incorrect; for the word *bhās* denotes "light. If it were taken to signify "power," "influence," or "capacity," an unconventional meaning would be imagined.

Therefore, the meaning is simply this: by its light—that is, its illumination—everything is illumined. Now, an objection might be raised: since Brahman is of the nature of light itself, the use of the distinct term “its” (tasya) would not be appropriate. This is not so, for it is justifiable as a figurative expression, like the phrase “the head of Rāhu. Furthermore, one might argue that even so, because of the immediate context, it would be only the sun and other luminaries that are said to be illumined by the light of Brahman, rather than the entire universe. This is not the case; for, by virtue of their commonality with those luminaries, the same status applies to all others, and because it is logically consistent to take the terms as figurative indicators (upalakṣaṇa), just as in the case of the terms “Brahmin” and “Kṣatriya” [which stand for all classes].

The word "all" (sarva), by its own inherent force, denotes the entirety [of things]; yet, when its primary meaning is found to be untenable, it is restricted by means of context and other such factors—as in the expression, "All food has been eaten. However, that is not the case here; therefore, a restriction of the literal sense of the scripture is not appropriate. It has been stated that the Supreme Light itself shines forth in various ways. Does this occur through a change in its own nature or through transformation? He says "no"—rather, as follows. Regarding this point, he cites the words of an authoritative teacher: "As... (P. 13-14).

All seeing is all knowing; it is without deficiency, complete, and—so to speak—of the nature of supreme illumination. "Free from conceptual construction" (avikalpa) means devoid of conceptual constructions such as lightning and so forth; however, the meaning is that this internal living being (jīva), situated within the body, imagines itself as if being conceptualized in the form of lightning and the like. Alternatively, "conceptual construction" (vikalpa) refers to the cognition of a non-existent object; "free from conceptual construction" means that it is not such [a cognition], yet it imagines itself as if it were an unreal conceptualization, as if it were a cognition of a non-existent object.

Previously, the coexistence of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) was stated in terms of the relationship between the means and the end; here, however, the distinction is that ignorance is connected to knowledge by way of the manifestation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Now, it was previously stated that ignorance belongs to the individual souls (*jīvas*) and not to Brahman; how is it now said that ignorance is connected to that very [Brahman]? Previously, it was stated that ignorance belongs to the souls because they do not know the true nature of Brahman.

But now, since an error without a substrate is untenable, it is stated that Brahman, by virtue of its being unknown, is bound by the ignorance of the effect, just like mother-of-pearl; thus there is no contradiction. Having thus explained the coexistence of the ignorance of the phenomenal world with eternal knowledge, he states the coexistence of the knowledge consisting of hearing and so forth with ignorance—beginning with "In the same way. This means that knowledge and ignorance are mutually coexistent. For this very reason it was said: "Both together. He asks, "Why? and answers: "Because of the hearer," and so on.

Having thus explained the first half of the mantra, he explains its second half with the word "tathā" (so). The meaning is: having crossed over the perception of the phenomenal world—that ignorance residing within eternal knowledge—which is caused by the ignorance consisting of the distinctions such as hearing and so forth. Now, [if it is argued that] regarding its being ignorance...

Anticipating the objection—"If [the self] is equal [to the Self], what is the distinction by which one might say that the perception of difference in the world is ignorance?"—the distinction is stated [in verses 13–17]: "proximate to knowledge" (*vidyāpratyāsannā*). The distinction is this: because it is proximate to ignorance regarding the differences in the hearer, the hearing, and so forth—acting as the manifestor of knowledge (which consists of the hearing of the identity of the Self and the like) and of that which has the nature of eternal luminosity—it is said to be "proximate to knowledge. The phrase "characterized by knowledge" (*vidyālakṣaṇa*) means "characterized by eternal luminosity. The phrase "upon its cessation" (*tannivṛttau*) means "upon the cessation of turbidity."

Now, an opponent raises an objection: "If there is only one Self (*aikātmya*), then because difference is unreal, the acts of hearing and so forth—which depend on the differences of the auditory organ and the rest—must also be unreal. Consequently, how could they produce the effect that is the cessation of ignorance? This is expressed by the word *syāt*. The underlying thought is that no such effects as bathing are observed in the case of water in a mirage. Furthermore, he says *asatyācca* (and from the unreal), meaning that the realization of Brahman would also be unreal because the means of realization, such as hearing, are unreal. The word *vahneḥ* (of fire) is to be supplied and connected with the word *pratipatti* (realization).

The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), however, states "It is said" (*ucyate*), asserting that even from what is unreal, a real effect and the comprehension of a real object are observed. The distinction is this: an illusion of a woman and so forth displayed by a magician is the cause of pleasure, while an illusion of a tiger and so forth is the cause of fear. In the phrase "of the comprehension of the real," the word "cause" (*nimitta*) is to be supplied; this is the example cited. Although a line is unreal in the form of a *gavaya* or other such animal, it is nonetheless real in its own nature as a line.

The opponent, however, objects again, pointing out the distinction that the means such as hearing are unreal even in their own nature, saying: "It might be so. The proponent, however, states that there is no such distinction: although things like a line-drawn gavaya are real in the form of the lines themselves, the form by which they convey a real gavaya and the like is indeed unreal; furthermore, the reality of the line-form is utterly useless and incapable of serving the purpose of producing the cognition of a real gavaya and so forth. Thus he says: "It is replied."

But if you are not satisfied unless there is truth in some form, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*) to show that even that exists. The meaning is that Brahman itself, when apprehended through ignorance in the form of hearing and so forth, is the means for attaining pure Brahman. He demonstrates the complete similarity by saying "Just as," showing that even lines and the like, though real in their own nature, indicate letters and so forth only through a form such as ignorance—that is, as the representation of letters—and not in their own essential nature. Here, having set forth the view of another school, he refutes it with the words "Even he who... (*yo 'pi*).

He demonstrates the contradiction with worldly experience by saying "tathā hi" (for instance). To provide another example for the comprehension of a real object from that which is unreal, he says "tathā" (so too). The meaning is that the inference of the original object (*bimba*) in the house, based on perceiving a mirror marked by a reflection outside, is not false. In this very context, he gives another example, saying "śabdācca" (and from sound). "Eternality" (*nityatva*) means existence at all times; it should be understood that this is stated in order to indicate the unreality of [properties] such as length, which are characterized by existing in two points of time.

Having thus provided examples by way of distinction for the comprehension of unreal objects and unreal effects, he now states that there is a single example for both cases, beginning with "tathā" (likewise). Even when there is a snake-bite...

Fearing that the reason (*hetu*) might be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the non-perception of death or fainting [in certain cases], he qualifies it with the words "at a particular time, etc. (*kālādi*). Therefore, one should infer as follows: "This person will die or fall into a faint, because he has been bitten by a *rāhu* [serpent] at a specific time or in a specific place such as an anthill, just like those previously observed [to have died or fainted]. Thus, the status of being a reason should be understood through the qualification of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Having thus refuted the objection raised by the opponent against his own position, and attributing it instead to the opponent, he says: "Of whomsoever... (*yasyaiva*).

One might object: "Surely knowledge itself will be removed by these [means]; therefore, how can there be an absence of anything to be removed? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "of that which is momentary" (*kṣaṇikasya*). For the removal of knowledge is its destruction, and that is already established by its very nature for that which is momentary; such is the meaning. One might further object: "Surely the excellence consisting in the purification of previously impure knowledge will be brought about by them; therefore, how can there be an absence of anything to be brought about? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "not to be added" (*anadheya*). The point is that if purity were produced in knowledge at a second moment, it would not exist [in the first], and thus [the means] would be purposeful; however, since that is not the case, [the means are useless].

Alternatively, in the second moment, something would have to be removed or added; yet that is not possible for a momentary thing, because it perishes by its own inherent nature (*svarasa*). Furthermore, such a state [of modification] is impossible; for some [might argue] that by producing an excellence (*atiśaya*) or a transformation (*vikāra*), something could be added or removed. But for a momentary thing, there can be no production of excellence precisely because of its momentariness—this is the meaning. Moreover, excellence and non-excellence cannot coexist in a single moment due to their contradiction; thus he says: "In one... (*ekasmin...*).

Nor can there be a lack of contradiction between those two within a single moment by means of a distinction between its prior and posterior halves, because a distinction between prior and posterior halves is impossible within a single moment; thus he says: "of the moment. As for one who asserts that from a pure moment there arises another pure moment, for him it results in the untenable conclusion that one person is bound while another is liberated. Having thus stated the impossibility of applying [the concepts of bondage and liberation] to the possessor of the continuum (*saṃtānin*), he raises an objection regarding the continuum itself: "If... The sense is that the continuum is indeed stable.

He refutes that [position] with the words, "That is incorrect. Only a transmigrating being (saṃsārin) has the qualification for liberation; and that [qualification] consists of the characteristics of being an agent and an enjoyer. But the continuum (saṃtati) is not such [a thing], because it is not a real entity (avastu). Therefore, since the continuum lacks qualification for liberation, neither what is to be added nor what is to be removed can affect it—this is the sense. Furthermore, the unreality of the continuum should be understood as resulting from the non-acceptance of its distinction from the members of the continuum (saṃtānin). He states another refutation with the words, "And how?"—the sense being that [such a thing] is never observed in cases like a sky-flower.

Right here, he anticipates the opposing view with the words "Now, however" (*atha*). He refutes this with the words "In that case, they would be imagined" (*kalpitastarhi*). He states what he himself has said with the words "It has been stated" (*uktam iti*). The meaning is as follows: the individual soul (*jīva*) is imagined as distinct from the Supreme Self; bondage and liberation pertain to that [imagined soul], and do not truly exist in the Supreme Self. This is what was stated in such passages as "Therefore, by means of ignorance, the souls... Furthermore, since transmigratory existence and liberation have imagined things as their objects, it follows that they too are imagined. Moreover, [page 42]...

Since neither liberation nor saṃsāra are possible for a self that has no beginning or end, the position of momentariness (kṣaṇika-pakṣa) has been accepted. Yet, even having accepted that, if those two [liberation and saṃsāra] are desired for the continuum (saṃtati) alone—which is itself without beginning or end—then what wrong has the self done that these two are not desired for it? With this intention, he says: "Moreover" (api ca). He establishes the very fact that the continuum is without beginning or end with the words: "For instance" (tathā hi). There is no origination of the continuum, because saṃsāra is beginningless; for if there were origination, it could not be beginningless.

Furthermore, because the continuum (*saṃtati*) is not a real entity (*avastu*), there is no arising; nor is there annihilation, precisely because it is not a real entity. The meaning is that neither birth nor destruction exists for that which is not a real entity. For this reason as well, he says "it passes away" (*antyeti*) to show that there is no annihilation. He states the logical inconsistency [of the opponent's view] with "for that... (*sa hi*). Another says: "from the beginning" (*ārambhataḥ*). Because the final moment of the yogin has all things as its object, it performs the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) of the knowledge of the Omniscient One; therefore, it is not non-existent. Consequently, the preceding moments are not non-existent on account of that [final moment] being non-existent. Thus, there is no absence of the continuum.

Nor is there its non-interruption, because when there is another continuum (*saṃtāna*), there is the interruption of one's own continuum—this is the sense. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), however, [argues]: previously, when the relation of cause and effect persisted, there was a single continuum; if even now the relation of cause and effect exists between the final moment of the yogi and the omniscient knowledge, then there is no distinctness of continuum. For there is no other cause for a single continuum apart from a succession of cause and effect; therefore, there is no interruption of the continuum.

And for this reason, with the intention that liberation does not possess that characteristic, he says: "It exists" (*satī*). But the opponent states a distinction: "No. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And not... The meaning is: "the final [moment] in the continuum of the yogi's cognition. If it is not the material cause (*upādāna*), then what is it? He says: "The objective support" (*ālambana*). "Condition" (*pratyaya*) means a cause; the meaning is: a cause in the form of an object. However, he says: "Immediately preceding," because the material cause is defined as the cause that exists immediately prior.

In that regard, within the omniscient cognition, every preceding moment existing in its own continuum is indeed [the cause], whereas the final moment, because it is apprehended by the omniscient cognition, is the cause in the form of an object; thus he says "sva" (its own). The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), however, maintains that the material cause (*upādāna*) is neither that which constitutes the nature of the effect, nor that which serves as its substratum (*āśraya*); for moments are mutually distinct in nature and lack a common substratum. If, on the other hand, the material cause must be of a similar class, then the cognition of a yogi would necessarily be the material cause of the omniscient cognition, since they are identical in being merely cognition.

Therefore, with the intention that there is no difference in the mental continuum (*saṃtānāntaratva*), he says: "If... If, however, because the cognitions of the yogin and the omniscient one do not have all things as their objects, they differ in their objects and thus lack a common genus (*anuvṛttajātīyatva*), then the yogin’s cognition would not be the material cause (*upādāna*). Consequently, it might be argued that when a distinct omniscient cognition arises, the continuum of the yogin’s cognition is severed. To this, he says: "Even if... For even when a cognition of taste occurs while a stream of cognitions of color is present, there would follow the consequence of liberation (*apavarga*) due to the severance of the prior continuum. Now, how could that be so in that case? [p. 43]

The similarity is stated by way of having the nature of aversion; that [similarity] is no different even for the knowledge of a yogin and an omniscient being. Consequently, due to the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*), there would be a single continuum (*ekasaṃtānatva*); and because the previous continuum is not severed, there would again be no final nirvāṇa. Thus he says: "In some way" (*kathaṃcit*). Now, in order to explain the term *vijñāna*, which comes next in the sequence, he introduces the view of another school as a necessary preliminary: "Some say" (*kecit*). The analysis of the compound is: "that whose quality (*guṇa*) is cognition (*vijñāna*) produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind."

"Having non-consciousness as its intrinsic nature (*avijñānasvabhāva*)," means being insentient by itself. The analysis of the compound is: that in which all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*)—known as cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)—have been completely uprooted because they have been rightly extinguished. "Of that" means of the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*). Even if [the self] has cognition as its intrinsic nature, if it cognizes only in dependence upon conjunction with the mind (*manas*), then knowledge arises from that [conjunction] alone; therefore, the postulation of that [self] having cognition as its intrinsic nature is useless. This is the opinion of Kaṇabhuj (Kaṇāda).

Anticipating the objection as to how the state of its own essential nature (*svarūpāvasthā*) is expressed by the word "Brahman," he states the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*): "For that [is... (*sā hi*). The reason for its vastness (*bṛhattva*) is its being unconditioned by the body and so forth; and because of this vastness, it is celebrated as "Brahman. The sense is that the word "Brahman" is derived from the roots *bṛh* or *bṛhi*, meaning "to grow" or "to increase. This should be understood as stated for the purpose of indicating even a slight trace of its scriptural authority (*śrautatva*). However, he points out the defect in the view that the Self has the nature of knowledge (*jñānasvabhāvatva*): "In the case of having the nature of knowledge... (*jñānasvabhāvatve*).

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of the word *tu* (but). First of all, it is not the case that [the Self] does not perceive everything due to non-proximity, because that which is omnipresent is proximate everywhere. Nor is it the case that, even though omnipresent, [the Self] does not perceive everything because it depends on a body, senses, and so forth that are not omnipresent; for it is for the sake of the production of knowledge that the body and other such things are required. Since the nature of knowledge belongs to the Self by virtue of its eternity, that knowledge is eternal. Consequently, because of the proximity of various specific objects of knowledge, the Self would perceive everything.

And thus, the meaning is that for one who is bound and for one who is liberated, there would be a greater cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) than the cycle of existence whose scope consists of determined objects as they are perceived, because of [the latter's] omniscience. Now, if it is said that [the liberated one] knows nothing at all out of fear of this defect, then insentience (*jaḍatva*) follows; for, just as there is no going without something to be gone to, the meaning of "knowing" does not arise without an object of knowledge. Nor can the Self itself be the object of knowledge, because of the contradiction between being the agent and the object. He states this very point, along with its doubt, beginning with "Now, if... (*atha*).

Having presented that very opposing view, he employs the term *vijñāna* (consciousness) in order to refute it, beginning with the words "those" (*tān*). The opponent, perceiving the aforementioned defect, asks: "Why? The proponent, however, thinking, "We do not assert the nature of consciousness on the strength of some practical purpose, but rather on the strength of scripture," says: "It is heard [in scripture]. Now, one might object: "On the strength of the previously mentioned defect, we shall assume a different meaning for the scripture. To this he replies: "And not so. The meaning is:
there would be an assumption of a different meaning for the scripture only if the stated defect were present; but that defect does not exist. [p. 44]

To the question "Why?", he says: "Just as... Just as fire, though it is a burner, does not burn everything; and just as a mirror or the like, having assumed the reflection of whatever is brought before it, shows that very thing, yet remains pure in the absence of anything being brought before it; so too the Self perceives only what is presented by the senses and other instruments, and not everything. Furthermore, the liberated one does not perceive external objects due to the absence of such presenters. "Incombustible" means unfit [to be perceived]. "Residing in the body, which is the locus of experience," etc.

The qualification [“by means of the body”] is for the purpose of excluding the enjoyment of objects even when they are present elsewhere; and it should be understood that the absence of a conductor (*upanāyaka*) is the cause for the absence of enjoyment in liberation. Now, one might object: “It is reasonable that fire and other non-omnipresent things require a conductor from an object to be burned that is not in contact with them; however, this is not the case for the Self, which is omnipresent and eternally in contact with all objects. Therefore, the liberated soul would possess omniscience and the perception of external objects. To this, the opponent says: “It would be so. But the proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*) replies: This same fault applies to you as well.

Therefore, with the intention that "whatever solution you offer shall also apply to us," he attributes that same fault to the opponent as well, saying: "It is said. Knowledge is produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind; and since that conjunction of self and mind is indistinguishable for all selves because of the omnipresence of all minds, the consequence is the perception of everything—this is the meaning.

One might object: "Even though there is no distinction in the conjunction of all selves with all minds, only that object which exists as an object for a particular self is perceived by that very self; thus, there would be no lack of determinacy. Anticipating this, he says: "The mind" (*manaḥ*). For objects do not possess objectivity toward the self inherently, but rather through the mediation of conjunction with the mind. Therefore, since there is no distinction in the conjunction with all minds that are conjoined with everything, the meaning is that all objects exist as objects for this [self].

Now, if it is argued that even though there is no distinction in the conjunction with all minds, the restriction is stated that one experiences only that which is to be enjoyed as brought forth by one’s own karma—because enjoyment is caused by one’s own karma—then for us as well, the self, although consisting of consciousness, is not independent but is subjugated by the bonds of karma; thus, it perceives only the object brought forth by those [bonds] and not everything. This is what he says with the word "atha" (now). [Objection: For one who maintains that knowledge is produced (*janya-jñāna-vādin*), a restriction is indeed logical: that through the power of karma, knowledge is produced in some cases and not in others.

However, for one who maintains that the self has the nature of eternal cognition, it must be explained how there can be a systematic order (*vyavasthā*) caused by karma. For its cognition—whose objects are restricted by karma—is not produced by actions, because it is eternal; and if it were produced, it would follow that the self, whose nature is that cognition, would itself be born. Nor could another object appear [to it], because that would entail the impermanence of the cognition and the consequent destruction of the self. In that case, the non-perception of everything would result, rather than a systematic order; for it is impossible for a single entity to both perish and not perish due to a difference in objects.

For this very reason, it is not hidden either. Nor is any portion of the all-pervading self removed by objects, nor is it covered by actions as a cloth is by a dye and so forth, whereby there might be a lack of uniformity. Furthermore, if this lack of uniformity were caused by karma, then...

For one who has attained liberation and whose karma is entirely exhausted, omniscience is unavoidable. It is argued: knowledge is the Self, but it is not the knower; and its state as a knower is a bondage resulting from the coloring of the power of agency and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Furthermore, the ego-sense, residing within the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*), manifests the state of being a knower precisely there. Consequently, even though the Self is all-pervading, its status as a knower is merely localized and not universal. Therefore, the Self is a knower only while situated in the locus of experience, and not elsewhere, even though it exists there.

Consequently, since that alone which has been brought into proximity with the enjoyer by means of actions that serve as the instruments of enjoyment is present to the knower, it is that alone which he knows, and not anything else; thus the established order is maintained. Now, one might object: "Since the Self, whose nature is consciousness, is all-pervading, there is a connection with all objects of knowledge. True. Why, then, does one not reflect, "I know all this"? Because one is not a knower [of everything]; reflection in the form "I know" occurs only for the sake of the knower’s own cognition.

It has been stated that the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) resides in the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*) and is not universal. For this very reason, even for one who is liberated, there is no knowledge of external objects; for it has been stated that such [knowledge] resides in the body. Therefore, it cannot belong to one who is bodiless. Consequently, in liberation, one remains as pure consciousness alone, not as a knower; thus, although the world is connected to him, it is not connected to him as an object of knowledge (*jñeyatayā*), for the connection with an action belongs to the agent. But surely, even knowledge does not exist without an object of knowledge?

If it is argued: "Since it has been stated that the meaning of 'to know' (*jñāna*) is transitive, how can liberated knowledge exist without an object of knowledge?"—we say: no; for this is logically possible, like the light of the sun. Just as the light of the sun is established independently of anything to be illuminated, so too is knowledge established independently of an object of knowledge. [Objection: But surely the meaning of the verb "to know" (*jānāti*) is transitive. [Reply: True; however, that [transitive action] is a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*). For that is an action involving an object, and it is logical that it requires an object. But knowledge is eternal; it is not an action.

For that [cognition] is indeed momentary. How then can there be a connection between that which has the status of a knower superimposed upon it and the object of knowledge? No; for that [connection] is centered on an action. And it has been stated that this [action] belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*). Furthermore, the relationship of object and agent cannot exist between two things when the action centered in one does not belong to the other. True, this is so when their difference is perceived; but when they are not distinguished, even though the action belongs to the one, the other may very well be its agent with respect to that object—just as, due to the movement residing in the body, the Self, which is distinct from it, thinks "I am going to the village."

In that case, are there now two kinds of knowledge? Consciousness (*cit*) itself, being self-luminous, is knowledge; however, due to a lack of discrimination from it, people employ the word "knowledge" with respect to the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*). [Objection: But surely the meaning of a word is to be understood through its usage in the world; therefore, because of its usage in that context, that alone should be the meaning of the word "knowledge," and not self-luminous consciousness. [Reply: No, for the usage with respect to the modification of the intellect occurs precisely through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of self-luminous knowledge upon it.

That very object upon which a word is applied through superimposition is its primary meaning, just as silver is the primary meaning of the word "silver" when applied to mother-of-pearl. But how is it understood that, in common worldly usage, the word "knowledge" (jñāna) is applied to the mental modification (buddhivṛtti), which is a superimposed self-luminous cognition?

This is because of the manifestation of the cognition, "I know the jar. And it has been stated that this manifestation cannot be accounted for by anything else. Nor does the modification of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) manifest itself by its own nature, because it is insentient (jaḍa). Furthermore, an insentient modification of the intellect cannot possess the capacity to illuminate an object like a jar or other things. The sense organ, however, is an illuminator, not illumination itself; this is the distinction. Moreover, the word "knowledge" (jñāna) is used for eternal knowledge in the Veda, as in: "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite."

For it is not possible for the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*), being momentary, to possess infinity; nor is there any connection between the seer and the seen other than that characterized by fitness (*yogyatā*), according to the Śruti: "For this Puruṣa is unattached. Furthermore, since the fitness of an object for perception belongs only to that which has ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*), there is no possibility of its being perceived elsewhere. Therefore, knowledge is primarily self-luminous alone; nothing else is. It is thus established that the mental modification is merely internal and secondary.

Since this very point is also applicable to our own position, it was stated in the context of introducing the Sāṃkhya doctrine (P. 16-9). Having thus established the position according to the view of others, he now states his own view with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). The perception of difference is ignorance (*avidyā*); when that [ignorance] has been terminated by knowledge (*vidyā*)—which consists in the perception of non-difference in the form "all this is indeed myself"—and the world remains as nothing but the Self alone, the object of sight (*dṛśya*) no longer exists at all. How, then, could there be omniscience for one who is liberated? This is the meaning.

However, for the bound soul (*baddhātman*), because of such scriptural passages as, "This atomic self (*aṇu*) is to be known as consciousness" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.1.1), its nature is atomic due to being delimited by the intellect (*buddhi*). Furthermore, because it perceives only those objects presented by ignorance (*avidyā*), the defect of omniscience mentioned in the case of the omnipresent [self] is far removed. This is the intended meaning. On this very point, he states two examples: "as of the seer" (*draṣṭuriva*). He confirms that same point with two scriptural citations: "so it has been said" (*taduktam*). In the phrase "of the visibility of the seeing self" (*draṣṭurātmano dṛśyatāyāḥ*), the two genitives are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

Having thus established his own position, he states the defect in the opposing view with the words "vijñāne" (in consciousness). He asks "Why? and replies "For not... The meaning is that for one devoid of qualities such as intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, who is eternally unperceiving, there is no existence; it does not differ from non-existence. Furthermore, the mere absence of the self cannot be the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*), because it is not sought after by persons; thus he says "Who indeed... Having raised an alternative view, he refutes it with "It might be... The connection with the preceding is that in the phrase "carrying [the burden]," those striving for their own destruction are seen.

But transmigrating beings are not of such a nature that they would strive for their own destruction; thus he says, "But not... The qualification beginning with "various" is intended to indicate that they are not of such a nature. He asks, "What follows from that? and answers, "In that case... Regarding his own position, however, he states that liberation possesses the status of a human goal because it is the absolute cessation of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable; thus he says, "But for whom... [p. 47]

Now he explains the syllable-word (*akṣarapada*) that follows in sequence, beginning with "the imperishable" (*akṣaram*). Regarding "the nature of sound" (*śabdātmatām*): the meaning is that he speaks of the nature of the syllable *oṃ*, which is to be understood solely through scripture (*āgama*), and which consists of the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), being the thread that runs through all specific sounds and meanings such as the letters 'a', 'u', and 'm'. [Objection: But does not the word "imperishable" (*akṣara*) refer to the specific form of the syllable *oṃ* as endowed with the letters 'a' and so forth?

How then can he say that the syllable *oṃ* is of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya-rūpa*), since it is devoid of any distinction of phonetic quality (*varṇa-vibhāga*) due to its being permeated by all words and their meanings? To this he says: "by way of distinction" (*viśeṣeṇa*). The meaning is that because there would be a contradiction with scripture regarding its being the self of all through the specific forms such as *a*, *ā*, and so forth—which are denoted by the word *akṣara* and perceived by the ear—the previously mentioned universal form of the supersensuous *oṃ* is what is indicated (*lakṣyate*). Alternatively, the word *akṣara* denotes a specific kind of sound consisting of phonemes (*varṇa-ātmaka*).

Anticipating the objection, "How then can it be said to have the nature of being merely sound devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*)," he says: "By means of a specific quality" (*viśeṣeṇa*). He states another interpretation: "Or, non-transformability" (*apariṇāmitvam*); the phrase "he calls it the Imperishable" (*akṣaram*) carries over from the previous context. To explain how it is designated by the word "Imperishable," he says: "Because of transformation" (*pariṇāme*). Since in the case of transformation there exists "perishing" (*kṣaraṇa*), which consists in the cessation of prior attributes, that which has no such perishing or falling away from its prior attributes is called "non-transformable" (*apariṇāmī*) through the exclusion of perishing; this is the meaning.

Regarding that, [the opponent], considering that Brahman consists of sound (*śabdātmaka*), that there is an absence of perception and other means of knowledge, and that the scriptural passages to be cited later are intended for the worship of symbols (*pratīkopāsana*), asks: "How? The proponent, however, considering that these scriptural passages are not intended for the worship of symbols, but rather refer to the true nature of Brahman itself, cites scripture as the authority: "The higher and the lower," etc. Now, Brahman is denoted by the syllable *oṃ*; as it has been said: "The *praṇava* is its designator."

Fearing that this might imply the supreme and inferior forms belong to the Brahman denoted by that [syllable] rather than to the syllable *oṃ* itself, he says: "And not... Now, one might object: since the rule "the suffix *kāra* follows a letter" intends a singular number, how can the suffix *kāra* be applied to the name ‘*oṃ*,’ which is a collection of letters? To this he replies: "from a non-*a*-letter" (*avarṇāt*); the meaning is "even from another [letter] besides a single letter. Therefore, the intention is that the singularity in the rule "from a letter" (*varṇāt*) is not intended to be significant. Here, he raises an objection: "Now, indeed... (nanv iti).

The "pratīka" (symbol) is the objective support (*ālambana*) or the object (*viṣaya*) for the intellect of meditation; the meaning is that the intellect should be directed toward Brahman with respect to the syllable *oṃ*. Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the words "just as" (*yathā*). Since direct worship of a deity is impossible due to its unmanifest nature, one performs the rite of worship with the thought that it is the deity itself upon whatever wood or stone bears its marks—the signs or emblems of that deity, such as the conch and the discus. The sense is: "just as," considering that the deity is thus worshipped and becomes propitious, so too [is the case here].

Alternatively, Brahman itself should be meditated upon by means of its name, "Om," through the differentiation of phonemes; thus he says, "And by this," indicating that it becomes propitious in that way. Having thus presented two views, he refutes them with the words, "It is said. Where [p.

It is heard that the syllable *om* is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); in those cases, let there be instruction regarding the meditation on symbols (*pratīka*) and so forth. However, where—as in the passage beginning with "That which one breathes out" (*yaj jīvaḥ*)—there is no such hearing [of it as a part], and because there is no authority for assuming what is not heard, the sentence culminates in the fact that Brahman and everything else have *om* as their self; in that case, there is no instruction regarding symbols and the like. He illustrates this with the example: "Just as all leaves are pierced by a single pin (*śaṅku*), even so all speech is pierced by *om*. (P. 17.11)

The sentence "Oṃkāra indeed is all this," which includes both the opening and the conclusion, has been recited; the meaning is that just as a leaf is pierced and pervaded by a single stalk (śaṅku) situated in its center through veins extending in every direction, so it is with everything.

Now, one might object: "Even if all speech is pervaded by the syllable *oṃ*, how can they have that as their essence? And even if they were identical with it, since the objects [denoted] by those words are not identical with it, how can *oṃ* possess the nature of everything? Anticipating this doubt, the author establishes both points with the words "For here... (*atra hi*). Because the syllable *oṃ* pervades all speech, it does not abandon the form of all speech; thus, it is non-deviating. That which is non-deviating is the Reality (*tattva*), whereas that which deviates—such as the appearance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—is not the Reality.

The specific forms of speech are mutually deviating, but the syllable *oṃ* is not; therefore, the syllable *oṃ* is the reality (*tattva*) of speech, its true form (*satyarūpa*), whereas its specific forms are not. This is because it has been shown by the passage ending with "all speeches are interwoven" that all objects, as perceived through conceptual cognitions permeated by speech, possess the nature of speech (*vāgrūpatva*) as before; thus, speech is the reality of objects, and the syllable *oṃ* is the reality of speech. With this intention, [the text] concludes: "All this is indeed the syllable *oṃ*. And all is Brahman.

Therefore, the sense is that "Oṃkāra is Brahman. Having thus stated that the fact of Oṃkāra being the self of all is understood from the statement regarding non-discrimination (*aviveka*), he now says—"even through discrimination"—to show that this is understood even when discrimination is present. By this, the meaning is: "by means of the Oṃkāra which consists of the aforementioned self-of-all-nature. Anticipating the objection that this is a metaphorical expression for the sake of praise because it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), he says—"and not so. Why? He says: "because [the word] has its primary meaning."

Even explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), because they are characterized by the expression of qualities—that is, praise—praise while expressing a certain meaning, since praise is understood precisely in this way. And for that praise, as in the case of the sun [in the passage] "it was seen at night," contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause [for resorting to a secondary meaning]. If such a contradiction does not exist, then it is not proper to abandon the primary, uncontradicted, required meaning that is being perceived, in favor of imagining an unmentioned secondary meaning; this is the sense.

Now, one might object: "If everything has the nature of the syllable *Om*, then it ought to be perceived through perception and other means of knowledge; yet this is not the case. Therefore, since this contradicts the non-perception of such things by perception and so forth, how can there be no contradiction? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For of everything... [p. 49]. Indeed, not...

The meaning is this: by virtue of its nature as phonemes (*varṇa*), everything has the nature of the syllable *oṃ* through that which is perceived by the auditory organ; however, it is not so by way of a nature that is inaccessible to perception and the like, but rather by a nature accessible through scripture (*āgama*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with the non-perception [of such a nature] by means of perception and the like. An objection is raised: "Even in the case of something accessible solely through scripture, there is indeed a contradiction with the non-perception of perception and the like; how then can there be no contradiction? Anticipating this, he says: "For not... (P.17-17).

"By another means of knowledge," such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, "non-apprehension" (*anavagama*), that is, non-perception, does not "take away"—meaning it does not subvert—the object of another means of knowledge, namely the scripture (*śāstra*), which is the fact that everything has the nature of the syllable *Om*, just as [the scripture does not subvert] dharma and so forth. For the meaning is this: dharma and other things accessible through scripture do not become non-existent simply because they are not perceived by perception and the like. Furthermore, he says "therefore" to show that the fact of the syllable *Om* being the self of all, even though stated as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), is indeed intended to be significant.

"Therefore, by means of this [Oṃ], the wise man [should perceive] the Supreme Person"—thus the qualification of the knower is heard in scripture. And the "knower" is one who, due to proximity, knows Oṃ to be the Self of all; and that [knowledge] does not come from any other source of valid cognition, because it is not perceived there. Therefore, what arises from the explanatory passage (arthavāda) based on proximity must be accepted. Consequently, the explanatory passage immediately following [the injunction] culminates in Oṃ being the Self of all; it does not culminate in a secondary sense by bypassing that. Furthermore, that [cognition] leads to the syntactical unity of the ritual duties with the injunction.

Therefore, it is established that this is an instruction for meditation for a person who has gained the knowledge of the syllable *om* as the self of all through the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); such is the sense that the syllable *om* is the self of all. He states another alternative: "Or else" (*athavā*). Regarding the word *viśvāḥ*, there is the elision of the case-ending *-s* according to the rule "the case-ending *-s* is frequently dropped after *viśva* when followed by a Vedic noun" (*seśchandasi bahulam*); the meaning is "all. In that context, by the statement "he gave birth to all worlds" (*viśvā bhuvanāni jajñe*), the fact that the class of objects of enjoyment has speech as its essence is stated, since speech is their material cause; however, the distinction is that in the subsequent part, the class of enjoyers [has speech as its essence] because of their non-difference from speech.

And there is non-difference of speech because speech, being the self of all, is Brahman; and the non-difference of individual souls from Brahman is to be understood. Likewise, he states with an illustration that by speech itself the selfhood of the Self as the self of all was declared: "In the same way," meaning "I move together with Vasus, Rudras, and others; I am inherent in them. Previously, the selfhood of all of *Oṃ* was stated.

But now, the distinction is that the all-pervading nature (*sarvātmatva*) of the reality of speech (*śabdatattva*), which is denoted by the word "speech" (*vākśabda*) and serves as the locus for all specific conceptualizations of names and forms, has been stated. As it has been said: "Brahman is without beginning or end, the imperishable reality of speech. Having thus established the all-pervading nature of speech through the authority of scripture (*āgama*), he now states it through the power of inference (*anumāna*), beginning with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). The statement "the modifications are endowed with the form of their material cause" expresses the pervasion (*vyāpti*); "endowed with speech" is the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopanaya*); and "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is the conclusion (*nigamana*).

Thus, the meaning of this formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) is that the world is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) or an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of speech; because it is endowed with the form of speech, which does not constitute a separate genus or quality (*ajāti-guṇa-bhūta*); for whatever is endowed with the form of something that does not constitute a separate genus or quality is either a transformation or an illusory manifestation of that thing; just as jars and other objects, being endowed with the form of clay, are transformations of clay; or just as a reflection, being endowed with the form of the original object (*bimba*), is an illusory manifestation of the original object.

Regarding the term *vivarta* (apparent transformation): individual instances (*vyakti*) are indeed associated with their respective universals (*jāti*), such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so on; therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) [of the reason] by means of them. The same should be understood regarding qualities (*guṇa*). Sound is merely a means for the comprehension of an object; thus, the opponent asks—"How?"—with the intention that the reason "being accompanied by the form of the word" (*śabdarūpānugatatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the object. "Its accompaniment" (*tadanugama*) means being accompanied by the form of the word. To this, he states the answer: "That," etc. Because objects are cognizable through that cognition which is colored by the form of air (*vāyu*).

The meaning is that because the cognition of an object is colored by the word, the objects themselves possess the form of the word, just as a jar or similar object possesses the form of clay because the cognition of it is colored by clay. He refutes the opponent’s position with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*): if the word were merely an instrument like the eye, then the perception of the object would occur upon the word just as it does upon the eye; however, there is no impression of the object, such as a jar, within the word itself. This is the meaning.

Now, one might raise the objection: "In that case, smoke, once it is known, will serve as the means [to the cognition of fire]. Anticipating this, he states the disparity between the two cases with the words "Nor even... (nāpi). If sound were a means in the same way as smoke, then just as there is a cognition of fire through smoke in the form of a subordinate relation (*nyūnakaraṇatayā*)—namely, "from smoke, fire"—and not in the form "smoke is fire," so too would it be in the case of sound. But such is not the case, because from the word "this is a jar" (*ghaṭo 'yam*), the object is cognized as non-different from the word; this is the meaning. He states another argument with the words "For this reason also" (*itaśca*).

For two words do not possess the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by virtue of themselves; rather, this [relationship] resides in the objects, and it is observed in the case of the two words "blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*). And that [relationship] is possible only when there is non-difference between the word and its object, not when [the word] is merely a means [to cognition]; otherwise, like "crow-possessing-ness" and "uprightness," they would not lead to the cognition of a single post (*sthāṇu*) which is distinct from them by its own nature.

However, the meaning is that, as in the case of "it is a post because it is tall and has a crow perched on it," there would be a cognition of an object distinct from the meanings of the two words *nīla* (blue) and *utpala* (lotus) through their respective denotative functions (*vācaka*). Furthermore, whereas in other cases—such as with smoke and so forth, which are merely means [of inference], and not only when they are means of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—certainty regarding fire does not occur until the form of smoke is ascertained; here, however, even when [the word] is a means of another means of knowledge, certainty occurs through the very form of the word itself.

Therefore, for this reason as well, the cognition of the form of the word is not a means [to the object] like smoke and so forth; rather, it is because the object possesses the form of the word. Thus he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*). Now, one might object: "In that case, the cognition of the object has the word as its very means, and not another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); since it follows immediately upon that [word], why should the cognition of the object not be an error? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the perception of that" (*taddarśanāt*).

The meaning is this: since an object that is apprehended by means of another instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is seen to possess the nature of a word, even in the case of verbal cognition (*śābda*), when there is the perception that the object itself is of the nature of the word, this is not a delusion regarding the object being identical with the word merely because it follows immediately upon the word which served as the means. Now, one might object: "Granted that in conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) the object has the nature of the word due to the cognition of the object as permeated by the word; but how is it so in the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) of infants and others? To this he says: "Of infants" (*bālānām*). Here, the activity of infants is the subject (*dharmin*), and "permeated by words" is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*), because their activity is preceded by a certain determination (*niścaya*), as is the case with ourselves and others.
[Page 51]

It is like the process of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*). The subject (*dharmin*) is the determinate cognition (*niścaya*) of infants and others, which is permeated by words (*śabdānuviddha*), just like our own determinate cognitions. Even though these [infants] lack the acquisition of linguistic conventions (*śabdavyutpatti*) in this present life, it is possible for them to have words residing in their hearts (*hṛdayastha-śabda-anuvedha*), since they possess the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of words acquired in previous births; the fact that they do not utter them, however, is due to a lack of proficiency in the vocal organs. Thus, the meaning is that even the non-perception of such speech by others is not a defect. He asks, "What follows from that? and says: "And so it is. By the two pronouns (*tad*), speech (*vāk*) is referred to.

Although transformation (*vipariṇāma*) was also mentioned previously, nevertheless, since *vivarta* alone is his own doctrine, that alone is summarized here. Furthermore, he states that the world is a *vivarta* of sound with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). Regarding the term "empirical" (*vyāvahārikāḥ*): it means they are capable of empirical usage, or established merely by way of empirical convention. To the objection that only those [entities] might then be *vivartas* of sound and not others, he replies with the word "that" (*tat*).

Other word-meanings as well are transformations (*vivarta*) of the word, because they are word-meanings, just like injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth; this is the formal argument (*prayoga*). He provides examples with the words "just as" (*yathā*): the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is a relation (*saṃsarga*), a collection such as a forest (*vana*), and non-existent things (*asantaḥ*) are indeed well-known. Among these, he states that injunctions and prohibitions consist of the transformation of the word with the words "therein" (*tatra*); by the phrase "activity and cessation" (*pravṛtti-nivṛttī*), he indicates the inciter and the dissuader.

The meaning is that these very two, when understood as effects through the form of human activity, constitute injunction and prohibition. Now, one might object with the intention that injunction and prohibition consist in engagement and withdrawal toward an effect, not toward something delimited by time; therefore, there is no lack of distinction in the threefold application [of the suffix]. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In an effect. He refutes this, saying: "No. The meaning is that no fourth alternative called "effect-ness" can be established apart from the three times.

The sense is that even "being an effect" (kāryatva) must be either past, future, or present. He concludes with the words "therefore" (tasmāt). "A non-entity" (avastu) means that which lacks the reality of external affirmation or negation. To the question "What follows from that?", he says "and not" (na ca). To the question "Even so, what? he says "and not" (na ca). He concludes the subject at hand with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).

Even when it is explained that injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*niṣedha*) are engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), even then injunction and prohibition consist in engagement and withdrawal as endowed with the property of being a task (*kāryatva*), not in their own essential form; therefore, considering that being a task alone is the motivator, there is no contradiction in stating "being a task" specifically as that which conforms to engagement and withdrawal. Likewise, the sentence-meaning of "a blue lotus" would also be either a relation (*saṃsarga*) or that which is qualified by it.

In this regard, it cannot first be *saṃsarga* (relation), because such a thing does not exist apart from the related entities. Why? Because if it were distinct from them, it would result in the necessity of yet another relation between the two, leading to an infinite regress; we shall explain later that neither distinction nor non-distinction is possible. If, however, it were non-distinct, they would simply be the individual word-meanings themselves, not a *saṃsarga*. For this very reason, there is no "related entity" distinct from the word-meanings—which are by nature unrelated—that could constitute the sentence-meaning. Therefore, this [sentence-meaning] is merely a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*).

Nor is that [cognition] possible without an objective support (*nirālambana*), nor does there exist a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-pratyaya*) devoid of the coloring of words (*śabdoparāga*). Therefore, he says "thus" (*evam*) to indicate that it is the very essence of speech (*vāktattva*) that shines forth in such and such ways. Likewise, he extends this principle with "thus" (*evam*) to show that even in the case of a forest and so forth, when a cognition of a real object arises despite the absence of a real object, it has recourse to the very essence of speech as its objective support.

Now, with regard to those who maintain that there is non-conceptual knowledge regarding the notes such as *ṣaḍja* and the syllables such as *ga*, which is devoid of the accompaniment of words—even though there is a conformity to general terms such as "this is a song" even in the absence of specific words like "ṣaḍja" for the notes; and even though there is the reply that subtle speech exists even in non-conceptual cognition—nevertheless, while relying on that very view, he establishes the accompaniment of words in all cognitions by means of another method, beginning with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).

He states this very lack of suchness [in the opponent's view] with the words "for they are undiscriminated" (*aviviktā hi*). And so it has been said: "Those who are not authorized therein know only the singing; but those whose minds are refined attain discrimination. He confirms that cognition permeated by words is possessed of discrimination through common worldly usage with the words "and thus" (*tathā ca*). To the question "What follows from this?", he says "And if this is so" (*evaṃ ca*).

Because, when there is contact with sound, we observe an excellence in the discernment of a person possessing discrimination—specifically, the discernment that is useful for practical activity—and because, upon its withdrawal in the absence of sound, even those things previously perceived become as if unperceived; why? Because for a man walking on a path, even the grasses and such being touched by his feet are disregarded. Therefore, the meaning is that through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it follows by necessity that the consciousness of the intellect (cit) is dependent solely upon speech (vāk).

For the nature of consciousness (*cit*) as the illuminator of objects consists in its being the act of cognizing, not merely in its being a substance; and that [nature] is enhanced when there is contact with speech, while it is diminished in its absence. Therefore, the form known as the consciousness of an object is dependent upon speech. He states another view: "the power of speech" (*vākśakti*); the power of speech is the capacity of speech to illuminate an object. If consciousness is the power of speech, then how is an object cognized when speech is withdrawn? To this he says: "the cognition thereof" (*tatpratīti*).

If it exists there in consciousness as well, then subtle speech exists, because consciousness has the power of speech (*vāk-śakti*) as its nature. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "In every way" (*sarvathā*); that is to say, whether it is dependent on speech as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) or whether it is the power of speech itself. The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason. "Of clay" (*mṛdaḥ*) is an example for a modification (*vikāra*), while "of the moon" (*candramasaḥ*) is an example for an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). Therefore, everything consists of speech; and speech, according to the Śruti text "As by a peg... (*yathā śaṅkunā*), consists of the syllable *oṃ*. Thus, *oṃ* is everything, and everything is Brahman; hence it is established that *oṃ* is Brahman. [p. 53]

Now, in order to state another meaning for the word *akṣara* and to introduce the view of others (*paramata*) to that extent, he begins with the words "another [says]... (P. 19-13). By the partial statement "because of the observation of examples such as clay," the entire syllogism of inference is indicated. This syllogism is as follows: Brahman undergoes transformation into the form of its effects, because it is the material cause (*prakṛti*), just as clay [transforms] into the form of a jar and so forth. And its status as the material cause is established by scriptural texts such as, "From which indeed these beings [are born]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1).

The meaning is that this is because the *Śruti* shows examples such as clay and so forth. Having thus presented the opponent's view, he applies the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) for the purpose of refuting it, saying "tat" (that); the meaning is that "that"—Brahman's state of undergoing transformation—is "apākīryate," i.e., rejected or set aside, by means of the term "akṣara. But the opponent, relying on the force of the previously stated inference, asks: "Why? The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*), considering an inference that contradicts the *Śruti* to be invalid, cites the *Śruti*: "bhruvaḥ" (of the eyebrows).

Here, he raises the opponent’s objection with the words "Now [if it be argued]... Even if the Self undergoes modification (*pariṇāmitva*), its eternity is not contradicted, just as in the case of clay in the form of a jar and so forth; for its essential nature (*tattva*) remains unimpaired, as it does not perish by losing its own form. Therefore, since eternity is established even while there is modification, the inference of modification sublates [the claim of eternity]; this is the sense. He confirms this very point with the words of an authoritative teacher: "As it has been said..."

That which, even when transformed into the nature of an effect, does not deviate from its essential reality (tattva) among those effects because it is recognized [as such], is also eternal; the meaning is that it is not only that which is immutable (kūṭastha). Having raised this objection, he refutes it with the words "True" (satyam): "It is true that eternity also exists in that which undergoes transformation; however, that is not possible in the case of the Self (ātman); for it would have to transform either in its entirety or in part."

In that regard, if transformation occurred in its entirety, the nature of the self would be destroyed, resulting in impermanence; and if transformation occurred only in part, the self would possess constituent parts, which would contradict its permanence. For whatever possesses parts is observed to be an effect, being produced by the conjunction of those parts; and whatever is an effect is observed to be impermanent. Thus, if the self possessed parts, there would be a distinction between the parts and the whole composed of them, whereby its oneness and non-duality would be contradicted—this is the meaning.

Having thus stated the impossibility of the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*), he states the logical consistency of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) with the words "This very [Brahman]": This very [Brahman], which is pure in its own form yet impure as the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), likewise possesses eternity by itself even when the phenomenal world is destroyed, and unity despite the diversity of the phenomenal world; this is possible in Brahman—which is like space due to its purity and partlessness, and comparable to space—when it is conceived as having limitations imagined through the phenomenal world constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*). The meaning is that it is not possible otherwise.

How is this possible? He says: "The imagined," etc. Just as space, although possessing imagined limitations, remains in reality unconditioned; although impermanent due to the destruction of its limitations, it is in truth eternal by virtue of its conceptual nature; and although it possesses imagined distinctions due to the difference in limitations, it is in reality one; so too, through that impurity... [p. 54]

Even that which is impure is pure from the perspective of reality (*tattvataḥ*); Brahman is likewise. The point is that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) does not alter the actual nature of a thing. Now, it might be argued: "If Brahman is limited by what is conceptually constructed, then let there be transformation (*pariṇāma*) only of those parts that are themselves conceptually constructed. This being so, its eternity and unity will not be contradicted, and yet transformation will be established. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the word "atha" (now/if).

The transformation of a fabricated portion—one that is falsely determined—would itself be merely a fabrication, for there is no reality in what is falsely determined. Therefore, since Brahman is indeed unchanging, our position is established; thus it is well said that it is "the Imperishable" (*akṣaram*). And this is another explanation of the word *akṣara*, not because of dissatisfaction with the previous one, for no objection was raised against the former.

Therefore, it should be understood that [the repetition] is for the purpose of pervading the object either by way of recurrence or by means of another function. Now, in order to explain the term "not all" (*asarva*), he first presents the view of those who maintain the reality of the phenomenal world (*sat-prapañca-vādin*) as the counter-position to be excluded—namely, "some" (*kecit*). The meaning is that some have accepted the nature of Brahman as being a real phenomenal world (*sat-prapañcātmatā*), based on such scriptural passages as, "He is the smell of all, the taste of all, the desire of all, the action of all," and so forth.

He says "thus" (evam) to show that this point is obtained not only from scripture, but also through logical implication (arthāpatti). The meaning is that the experience of objects is possible only when [Brahman] is the Self of all. He asks "how? and replies with "prakāśa... (illumination...). The meaning is that since objects are of the nature of illumination, it is logical that they shine forth within Brahman—the Self of all—which is itself of the nature of illumination. Thus, they are essentially one with the light of Brahman.

But if it were other than Brahman, the manifestation of an object—which is by nature insentient and conjoined with light—would not be possible. Thus, with the intention that the manifestation of objects, being untenable if Brahman were not the Self of all, leads to the understanding of Brahman’s being the Self of all, he says: "If it were other."

The scriptural passages concerning the non-differentiated Brahman, such as "not gross" and so forth, are intended to show that Brahman is to be meditated upon as being without phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*), and not to deny its nature as the self of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); this is the sense. Here, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "those [passages]. It means that Brahman is not the self of everything, but rather is exclusively non-dual (*advaya*). The opponent, however, asks "Why? by relying on that very same scriptural implication. He provides the answer: "Not gross," etc. "Appropriation" (*uparāga*) here means identity (*tādātmya*).

This scriptural passage is not intended for meditation (*upāsanā*), because meditation is not mentioned therein; because meditation is not the subject under discussion; and because there is no authority (*pramāṇa*) for supplying words by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Furthermore, the Upaniṣads possess authority only with respect to an already established reality (*siddha-artha*). Therefore, on account of the scriptural texts such as "not coarse" (*asthūla*), Brahman is not the self of all.
