But is there not also the scriptural text regarding "all odors" (*sarva-gandha*) and so forth? What then is the status of that? It is said: since Brahman is the locus for the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of all odors and the like, the statement "possessing all odors" (*sarva-gandhaḥ*) and so on is made; thus, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the enjoyment of objects is thereby rendered possible. [p. 55]

Since this has already been stated even under the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), it is not a mere repetition. Thus, having refuted the idea that Brahman possesses the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) through the absence of evidence and by means of contrary evidence, he now states the fault in accepting such a position: "All... (P. 20-2). The meaning is: because the Self is never dissociated from specific qualities such as all odors and so forth. He asks, "Why? and replies: "For not... (*na hi*). An objection is raised: "But even something possessing a nature may be separated from it; how so? Just as a pot is [separated] by baking. Anticipating this, he says: "Even though... (*athāpi*).

Even if separation were to occur, it would be through only a few manifestations (*prapañca*), and not through all those existing within the three worlds; for there is no total cessation of the entire continuous stream of manifestations. And thus, the meaning is that there would be eternal transmigratory existence (*nityasaṃsāritā*). Now, one might object: "Is it not observed that at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) there is a cessation of everything? Not so; this is because it refers to an absolute dissolution (*ātyantikalayābhiprāyatvāt*), for that [absolute dissolution] is conducive to liberation, whereas the other is not, since there is a subsequent re-creation. He makes manifest the non-cessation of the predominance of manifestations with the words "by all" (*sarvathā*).

Regarding the non-separation and separation from one's own nature (*sabhāva*): according to your position, the manifold of hunger and so forth constitutes the very nature of this self. Furthermore, no one accepts the eradication of the continuous stream of hunger and other such states that pervade all living beings, because if one were liberated, it would follow that everyone is liberated. The specific inclusion [of hunger] is because these internal states, such as hunger, are the most immediate and excessive cause of bondage for the person.

Regarding this, he says "therein" (*tatra*) to show that for you, who maintain that the one [Brahman] is the self of all, liberation would not exist. By this, the liberation of even the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a superimposed distinction, upon reaching Brahman is also refuted. To the question, "For whom indeed could there be no liberation?", he says "the Self" (*ātman*). For one who maintains the distinction of selves, there might be a division of a particular self from transmigratory existence through the cessation of the manifold world of hunger and so forth; however, the point is that the oneness of the Self with all things is not accepted by such a person. He concludes the subject at hand with "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

If the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not of the same nature as Brahman, then what is it? To this he says: "It is ignorance" (*avidyā*). The intention is this: if, in reality, Brahman were identical with the phenomenal world, then because the world is afflicted by many defects and is produced by those very defects, Brahman would inevitably experience eternal suffering through the foul odors and other qualities of impure things and the like; yet that [Brahman] is heard in scripture to be inconceivable and consisting solely of the essence of bliss, which would thus be contradicted.

If it is argued that those defects of transformation do not touch the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), then do you consider the clay in a jar defiled by excrement and such to be undefiled? For why would you think so? If it is argued that because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is both different and non-different [from Brahman], there is no staining by those defects due to this difference-and-non-difference, we say no; for by virtue of being both different and non-different, Brahman would be both defiled and undefiled. Yet it is heard in scripture that it is absolutely pure. However, this defect applies to the phenomenal world as it plays under the sway of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Indeed, reality is not defiled by the fault of being played with by ignorance, just as the sky is not defiled by impurity and the like. Therefore, Brahman, which is absolutely pure, should be worshipped precisely within the sphere of ignorance.

P. 20-8. Here now, the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādī) objects with the words "yadi" (if). If that Brahman is the ultimate reality, according to the Vedic scripture "That is Truth," and if, in the phenomenal world (prapañca) which is a play of ignorance (avidyā), its very emptiness is what is real, then let that [emptiness] itself be Brahman; this is the meaning. He confirms this point by means of scripture with the words "tathā ca" (and so too). To this, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta) with the word "tatra" (in that case). He explains how all-pervasiveness (sarvatva)—which is the opposite of the aforementioned non-universality—is revealed once delusion has been dispelled, with the words "etad" (this).

It has been stated that Brahman is not something distinct from all things; however, the meaning here is that everything has Brahman as its self, and by virtue of that self it exists, rather than being a void, and thus there is no contradiction. He states the reason for this: "eternal," etc. The meaning is that if everything were a void, liberation—which is characterized by the absence of phenomenal manifestation (niṣprapañca)—would be established without effort, and consequently, the instruction and activity directed toward liberation would be rendered purposeless. He raises an objection regarding the opposing view: "eternal," etc.

The meaning is: "Just as for you, whose self is eternally liberated, saṃsāra is based on ignorance (avidyā), so too will it be for me in relation to emptiness (śūnyatā). He states the reply with the words "If... He asks "Why? and replies with "Even in liberation... The point is that since the absence of apprehension is equal even in liberation, nothing would appear even in saṃsāra, because that [apprehension] is not a real entity. Then he says "Now, if... [to address the objection]: "If ignorance is the apprehension of error, then since its existence is admitted, there is no universal emptiness."

He states that there would also be a contradiction with scripture (śrutivirodha), saying "by that" (tena). The word "it would not be" (na syāt) is to be supplied. He says "how? (katham) to show that this position has been refuted by scripture itself. Furthermore, the contradiction with scripture was stated on the basis of [the author's] own conviction; however, for the Buddhist, the authority of scripture is not established. With the intention that, in the case of universal emptiness (sarvaśūnyatā), the delusion of the phenomenal world (prapañcavibhrama) would be causeless due to the absence of a substratum (niradhiṣṭhānatva), and that no effect can exist without a cause, he establishes the very meaning of scripture, saying "for existence... (bhāvo hi).

Just as a substratum such as a rope, though not appearing in its true form, manifests in the form of a superimposed, non-existent snake and so forth, [how could it be otherwise] in the case of the Void? Since there is no substratum in the Void, what could be superimposed upon what? And in the absence of that [superimposition], what could possibly manifest? Yet the phenomenal world (prapañca) does manifest; the meaning is that it would have to be without any cause. The point is that an error without a substratum is never observed. For this reason as well, he says "consciousness" (vijñāna), [to show] that the Void is not [the reality].

For it is not possible for that which is empty (śūnya) to possess the nature of consciousness and bliss; therefore, Brahman is not of the nature of emptiness. Rather, the meaning is that it is the Self—the innate essence—of everything imagined through ignorance (avidyā). Now, in order to explain the state of fearlessness (abhaya-pada), which follows in sequence, [the author] states the apprehension of fear regarding its opposite: "Some think... Because pleasure is invariably concomitant with pain, there is no state whatsoever free from contact with pain; therefore, some believe that even in liberation (mukti), there remains the fear of pain.

He asks, "How is there invariable concomitance? and answers with the word *kevala*; the meaning is "of that which is devoid of suffering. He establishes the lack of isolation (*akaivalya*) with the words "for not... [p. 57]. Now, one might object: the invariable concomitance of pleasure with suffering must be stated as "for no one is ever merely happy"; however, the phrase "merely miserable" is irrelevant to the present context, for the invariable concomitance of suffering with pleasure is not what is under discussion here. It is replied: the presentation of an established fact as something to be proven is for the sake of providing an illustration. This particle *vā* has the sense of *iva*; as it has been said: "The words *iva* and *vā* have the sense of comparison (*anupamāna*)."

Therefore, this is the meaning: just as no one is perceived as being in pain without pleasure, so too no one is [perceived] as being in pleasure without pain. For this reason as well, he says that there is no state devoid of suffering: "like pain" (*duḥkhavat*). Here he provides an illustration: "like heat" (*tāpavat*). By this, he means that in liberation, pleasure is accompanied by pain, because it is pleasure, like the pleasure of the wicked and others. To that, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "therein" (*tatra*). He explains "fearlessness" (*abhayam*): "all... He states the reason: "because of non-attachment" (*asaktāt*).

He cites scripture: "fearless" (*abhayam*). The sense is that this inference contradicts the sacred tradition (*āgama*). He confirms the meaning of the scripture through reasoning: "for thus" (*tathā hi*). "Fear" means the fear of suffering (*duḥkha*). He states that it is also incorrect to say that pleasure remains as pleasure only when accompanied by suffering: "nor" (*na ca*). If pleasure were merely the absence of suffering, then that might be so; however, since pleasure is a positive entity (*bhāvāntara*), it would indeed exist even in the absence of suffering. This is the meaning.

He states another meaning for the term "state of fearlessness" with the words "another [view]. In that context, he first indicates what is excluded by the term "fearlessness" with the word "here. To demonstrate that, he first describes the various divisions of the nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) by way of showing its manifold forms, beginning with "here. In this transmigratory world, the individual selves (*jīva*), who are of the nature of consciousness, may be either distinct from Brahman or non-distinct. And when they are distinct, there are two possible ways: they may be divided from the Self, or they may be divided by Brahman itself.

To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "for the sake of enjoyment," and so forth. Alternatively, it is not for the sake of enjoyment and the like, but rather due to its own nature (*svabhāva*); that this Brahman differentiates the individual souls (*jīvas*) is one way of explaining it. He states another way: "due to ignorance" (*avidyā*); that is, the differentiation is based on ignorance, like that between an original object and its reflection. He states yet another position: "the conscious selves" (*vijñānātman*). Regarding that as well, he states two ways of explaining it: "of them," and so forth. The superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the Self of the notion "I am doing" with respect to the body and other such things resulting from karma is "karmic ignorance" (*karmāvidyā*).

Regarding that, he first states the consequence of the fear of returning in the case of the immediate alternative: "In that regard" (*tatra*). If it is argued that the conscious self, the individual soul (*jīva*), is bound because it perceives objects through that fitness of the seer—the Self—and the seen—consisting of the three *guṇas* transformed into the form of objects—then, since such eternal fitness is permanent and thus cannot be removed, the fear of returning remains indeed present.

This is the meaning. Now, one might raise the following objection: "The primordial nature (prakṛti) transforms into the form of objects for the sake of the experience (bhoga) of the person (puruṣa); and since that has already been accomplished during the state of worldly existence (saṃsāra), it does not do so again for the liberated one. Therefore, there is no fear of returning [to bondage]. To this, he says: "Now" (*atha*). Here he states the flaw: "Once" (*sakṛt*). Having presented sound and the other objects once, primordial nature, having fulfilled its purpose, would not present them to itself again; consequently, even for one who is still in the state of worldly existence, there would be the perception of sound and the rest only once. This is the meaning.

Now, if primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which possesses infinite modifications, having been perceived by the Self in the form of all modifications, were not to transform again into the forms of objects such as sound and so forth; then, once sound and the rest have been perceived, there would be no perception of subsequent transformations of sound and the rest. Therefore, it is said that primordial nature must indeed transform again into the forms of sound and the rest, and thus the repeated perception of sound and the rest is logically established.

Consequently, because it possesses infinite modifications, the primordial nature (prakṛti) would undergo transformation once again into the form of objects for that liberated person, since its discernment from the Puruṣa had been experienced by him in his entirety; therefore, even he would certainly remain subject to the fear of saṃsāra, characterized by the enjoyment of objects once more.

This is what he says: "Now" (*atha*). Now, that aforementioned ignorance (*avidyā*), being prior to it, is said to be the cause of the bondage of action superimposed upon the Self. Consequently, because transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless and actions are infinite, even if the majority of actions have been exhausted, remnants of action are possible even for one who is liberated; thus, the fear of returning remains for him. If it is argued: "Actions that yield immediate results have ceased once they have bestowed their fruit immediately thereafter; therefore, how could they possibly exist in liberation?", [the answer is: no.

Because their time of ripening is indefinite; the analysis of the compound is: "those whose time for yielding fruit is indefinite. Consequently, even after the lapse of a very long period, they might sometimes bind one who is already liberated upon encountering their own auxiliary condition, namely Time. And thus, there would be a return from the state of liberation just as from the state of cosmic dissolution (pralaya). He states this with the word "ignorance" (avidyā). Even though bondage is based on ignorance, he speaks of the fear of returning [to saṃsāra] by means of the word "ignorance."

First of all, ignorance does not function for one who is liberated, either because of the absence of a cause or because of the absence of a purpose, since it is without cause and without purpose; it has no dependence upon causes or purposes. Consequently, the meaning is that it might at some point bind even the liberated person again. Nor is this impossible, for we observe the return from deep sleep of one who had attained Brahman; thus he says, "And so it is. If it is argued that ignorance exists here [in deep sleep], then it must also exist in liberation; therefore, there is parity.

It should be understood that the attainment of Brahman by one in deep sleep is stated in such scriptural passages as, "Having merged into the Existent, they do not know," and "Having merged into the Existent, we shall emerge. Likewise, even if Brahman is independent, if one were to accept that the bodies, senses, and objects of experience—which are either inherently distinct or non-distinct from Brahman—are produced for the sake of the individual souls (jīvas) through various causes such as the Lord's desire for the manifestation of the power of playful enjoyment, then there would still be the fear of future connection with a body and so forth; thus he says: "But if [Brahman] is independent... He asks, "Why? and replies: [p. 59]

Regarding the phrase "for [He] is independent," he provides an illustration here: "in the worldly case. Now, it may be argued that God is dependent upon karma, and thus He lacks independence regarding its bondage; or that He lacks independence over karmas themselves, such that He could summon them and bind [the soul] again. Therefore, it is not said that He binds [the soul] again in liberation in order to remove His own independence.

Nevertheless, because karma is infinite in this beginningless saṃsāra, and because the time for its transformation into fruit is not fixed, there remains indeed the fear of returning—even after hundreds of kalpas have passed, those [karmas] may, upon reaching the time for their own fruition, bind one who was previously liberated. Thus he says: "Now... (atha). [Objection: But surely, the accumulation of karma (karmāśaya)—that is, the collection of actions performed in each preceding birth—is completely exhausted by giving its fruits in the immediately following birth, due to its manifestation at the time of death.

Furthermore, since [karma] is exhausted with each birth, there would be no infinity of karmas. Therefore, one might suspect that because the accumulation of karma (*karmāśaya*) performed in the immediately preceding birth is destroyed in its entirety only in the final body, there is no possibility of rebirth. Anticipating this objection, he states the reason for its infinity, beginning with "because" (*yataḥ*). "A single existence" (*ekabhava*) means a single birth; that which exists therein is "pertaining to a single existence" (*aikabhavika*). Why is this so? He says: "For not" (*na hi*). For death alone is not the manifestor—that is, the illuminator that causes the fruit to be given—but rather [it is manifested] also by place and time.

Therefore, even though death occurs immediately thereafter, actions that depend upon their own place and time continue for a long duration; thus, they do not belong to a single lifetime—this is the meaning. But how can mere death be the manifestor of bondage? To this he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). If mere death were the manifestor, then all actions would have to yield their fruits simultaneously immediately after it.

But this is not so; for even within a single body, those [karmas] yield their fruits sequentially, depending upon their respective places and times. Therefore, the implication is that death alone is not their manifestor, but rather place and other factors as well. Furthermore, if death alone were the manifestor, then the karmas performed in previous births—which are causes for experiencing births as gods, humans, animals, or lower species that are mutually contradictory—would have to yield their own fruits simultaneously immediately after death.

In that regard, since it is impossible for multiple contradictory bodies to be assumed simultaneously, [one might suggest that] when one body is produced in a single instance, the others would undergo entry and exit—that is, they would enter therein and produce their own results. But even that is not possible; for it is impossible for births and enjoyments that are mutually contradictory to coexist in a single birth. Thus he says, "contradictory" (*viruddha*). Alternatively, there is a reading: "because of the impossibility of entry and exit" (*āvāpāpagamanāsaṃbhavāt*); in that case, the meaning is "because of the impossibility of introduction and removal" (*upanayāpanayāsaṃbhavāt*).

Regarding those who die in the womb or during birth due to the non-performance of actions, there is no karma that serves as the cause for the body and so forth to manifest death; thus, liberation would occur. To this he says: "garbha... (in the womb). Therefore, the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) does not belong to a single lifetime alone. Consequently, one might suspect that because karma is infinite within beginningless *saṃsāra*, there could be a result of returning even for one who is liberated. Anticipating this, he employs the term "state of fearlessness" (*abhayapada*) to dispel that doubt, saying: "To this it is replied... Why? He says: "For the higher... [p. 60]

"Supreme" (parā) means "excellent" (prakṛṣṭā). He asks, "Why does it not exist? and answers, "Not so," and so forth. Now, one might object: since actions are infinite and because they can only be destroyed by their own fruits, it is impossible for those whose fruits have not yet been experienced to be destroyed; therefore, why should transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), which is caused by action, not continue? To this he replies, "By knowledge" (vidyayā). The point is that there is no rule that actions are destroyed only by their fruits, for they are also destroyed by expiatory rites (prāyaścitta); nor is there non-destruction due to infinity, because knowledge possesses the power to burn away even infinite [actions].

Nor should it be said that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is merely occasional (*naimittika*) and that even this is exhausted only through experience (*bhoga*); for that would contradict the Smṛti text: "The killer of a cow is liberated from that sin after twelve years. Now, one might object: "Granted that expiation is a cause for the destruction of sin because it is established by scripture (*āgama*), but how can knowledge (*vidyā*) be a cause for the destruction of endless karma? Anticipating this doubt, he cites scripture on this point as well, saying: "For it has been said..."

Having thus stated, according to the view of others, that knowledge is the cause for the destruction of all karma through its unseen power (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*)—much like a penance—the author now states it according to his own view through its seen power (*dṛṣṭa-śakti*), beginning with "Or rather" (*atha vā*). The sense is: the distinction between agent, action, and so forth is caused by ignorance (*avidyā*); once that is removed by knowledge, how could there be any fear of returning for him? He says "Nor even... to show that even if bondage were based on ignorance, there is no fear of renewed transmigratory existence for one who is liberated; the phrase "renewed transmigratory existence" connects with what precedes.

He asks "Why? and answers with the word "that" (*tat*); by "that," he refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). Why is there no cause for its activity? He says: "beginningless" (*anādi*). Why, then, does it not require a beginningless cause? He says: "prior" (*prāk*). Even if ignorance is indeed causeless due to its beginninglessness, what follows from that? He says: "by knowledge" (*vidyayā*). First, the beginningless ignorance of one who is liberated has been destroyed by knowledge; and as for the other [ignorance], since it is causeless, it cannot possibly arise without a cause—this is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even though [ignorance] is severed as in deep sleep, it arises again? To this he says: "But in deep sleep... In deep sleep, only the expansion of ignorance in the form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has ceased; however, ignorance itself remains in the form of the non-apprehension of the true nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*) and in the form of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of mental distraction (*vikṣepa*). Therefore, upon awakening, it manifests the phenomenal world once more. But for the liberated one, it is severed in every respect—this is the distinction.

The meaning is that if [ignorance] were entirely severed even in deep sleep, then deep sleep would not be distinguished from liberation. If ignorance is not severed in deep sleep, then how is it that in passages such as "Every day these creatures go to the world of Brahman," the attainment of Brahman is mentioned? To this he says: "dispersion" (*vikṣepa*). Although causal ignorance (*kāraṇāvidyā*) exists there, nevertheless, because of the commonality of the cessation of the effects of ignorance (*kāryāvidyā*), the mention of attaining Brahman is figurative; this is the sense.

Regarding the two positions concerning the fitness for autonomy (*svātantrya-yogyatā*), however, the suspicion of a recurrence [of the same objection] has not been answered again, since it was already answered by the very fact that those two positions were not accepted. He concludes the subject at hand: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), moreover, is there an understanding of this reality of the non-dual self-nature mentioned in the first verse? (P.22-19) It cannot be by perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that has as its object distinctions such as blue and yellow, which are the opposite of non-duality. Nor can it be by inference (*anumāna*), because that is preceded by perception which grasps the distinction between the probandum (*liṅgin*) and the probans (*liṅga*), and because [inference] is absent when that [perception] is absent, being inherently opposed to non-duality. Nor can it be by comparison (*upamāna*), because that depends upon difference, having as its object a similarity based on difference.

Inference and comparison depend upon difference, yet they do not directly apprehend difference; perception, while apprehending an object as its subordinate element, does not directly apprehend that [difference] itself. Presumption (arthāpatti), however, is the direct means of knowledge regarding difference within the sphere of non-difference, and is thus even more opposed [to non-duality]; for without difference, the conventional usage of distinctions such as knower and known could never be established anywhere, and it is indeed required [for such usage], otherwise, even the realization of the undifferentiated Brahman would be impossible without it.

Even non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman, which is of the nature of existence. Nor is it a means of valid cognition regarding the non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because that [non-existence], being of the nature of the absence of the five means of valid cognition, cannot possibly occur within the scope of perception and the other [means of knowledge]. It should be understood that, since there is much to be said regarding scripture (*āgama*), the absence of comparison (*upamāna*) and the others was mentioned previously. The same applies to scripture: first, that which has a trustworthy person (*āpta*) as its author is not a means of valid cognition regarding Brahman, which is beyond the scope of that [scripture], because its subject matter consists of things already apprehended through other means of valid cognition.

Nor is the Veda [the means of knowledge], because it consists of injunctions and prohibitions; and injunctions and prohibitions are impossible once the reality of Brahman is established. Furthermore, it is not logical for a word to possess authority regarding an already established entity without depending on injunctions and prohibitions. To explain: if it were a mere restatement of what is already established—as in "this is a jar"—it would require dependence upon another means of knowledge; and since that is not possible in the case of the non-worldly Brahman, it would follow that the Veda lacks authority altogether. For this reason as well, the Veda has no authority regarding an established object.

Since the comprehension of a word's expressive capacity occurs in the world [only] through its relation to an action, and since words are employed there with reference solely to an action—because they must have a purpose, for otherwise they would be purposeless—and furthermore, because the relationship between a word and its denotation is not understood from a statement that merely restates an established fact, but rather from an injunctive sentence; [therefore, the Veda is authoritative only as an injunction].

For instance, when it is said, "Bring the cuckoo," the servant's activity—which would otherwise be inexplicable without a cognition of the object—leads one to infer that he possesses such a cognition. Since this cognition immediately follows the word and no other cause for it is perceived, one understands its capacity in that regard by thinking, "This [cognition] was produced by the word. Consequently, words whose powers have been established through their connection with such activity are not capable of making known an already established Brahman; therefore, they are not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding it.

Furthermore, if Brahman were established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the word [denoting it] would be non-authoritative because it would be merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*); if it were not so established, it would be even less so. For if Brahman is unknown, its relationship with a word cannot be known; and if it is not the referent of a word (*apadārtha*), it cannot logically be the referent of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). Why? Because it is precisely the referent of a word that becomes the referent of a sentence when qualified by the referents of other words. But the referent of the word "Brahman" is not [established] by any other means of valid cognition... [p. 62]

Because it has never been perceived by him, and because its relationship [to other words] is unknown, that which is not understood from a word cannot enter—either as a subordinate or as a primary element—into the meaning of a sentence, which consists of the connection between word-meanings. Therefore, Brahman is not established by the means of knowledge that is verbal testimony (*śabda*). Furthermore, the reality of Brahman, with all its attributes entirely set aside, does not even fall within the range of cognition.

How so? For every cognition proceeds by delimiting an object as "this is of such a nature, not of another nature"; otherwise, there would be no cognition at all. But how could there be a cognition of Brahman, in which all modes have been excluded? Thus, having raised the objection that non-dual Brahman lacks any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he states the authority for it: "It is declared in the sacred tradition" (*āmnāyata*). In the word "ascertainment" (*nirūpaṇam*), the verb "they declare" (*pracakṣate*) is understood to carry over.

As for what was stated—that if the Veda were merely a restatement of what is already established, it would depend upon other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—we shall demonstrate in the section on *niyoga* that this is not the case. Furthermore, as for the claim that all worldly sentences must terminate in something to be accomplished (*kārya*), that too is not an absolute rule; for there exist in the world sentences that do not terminate in something to be accomplished, such as pleasant reports—those by which a pleasant thing is communicated, like "A son is born to you"—which are devoid of the purpose of inciting action or cessation from action.

Nor are they [the words] devoid of purpose, since their purpose is the production of happiness for the father. Nor can it be assumed that there is an injunction to act with the words "Be happy" in that case, because the attainment of happiness is established by the very power of the known fact of the son's birth, without requiring an instruction. Now, if it is thought: "In that case, there is indeed the father’s activity toward his own happiness; therefore, the purport of the speech lies precisely there; thus, even that [speech] culminates in activity"—this is true.

Because the sentence is employed with the intention (*abhisaṃdhāna*) "the father’s happiness has arisen," its purport (*tātparya*) exists there in the form of [the father's] arising; however, from that sentence, there is no cognition in the form of a primary [purport] such as "let activity toward happiness be understood," because there is no word expressive of that [activity], and because what is not the meaning of a word cannot be the meaning of a sentence. For a cognition is restricted solely to an established fact (*siddhārtha*). This has been stated provisionally; however, he will later state that there is no activity toward happiness.

Furthermore, even if there were a purpose consisting in the production of pleasure for the father, it would not be possible to postulate that a word—which has already culminated in the communication of an accomplished fact—possesses an operation extending to incitement to action, as in the case of the statement "Pūṣan has the ground flour as his portion. Therefore, that sentence culminates solely in an accomplished fact and does not culminate in incitement to action. Moreover, even if it did culminate in incitement to action, a person who has not yet engaged in the birth of a son—which is a means to pleasure—is not one who needs to be incited, since that [birth] is already an established fact.

Nor can one who previously failed to act toward the happiness that is the goal due to ignorance of the means be incited by making known those means; for it is only after knowing the meaning of the sentence that a person is to be incited toward his own activity. And there is no other activity required for the accomplishment of happiness, since that arises from the very knowledge of the sentence-meaning, "A son has been born to you. By this, [the following is also explained:]...

The words of the wicked have also been explained. Likewise, in the case of one who is terrified by a delusion, when that delusion is dispelled, the statement "This is a rope, not a snake" is seen to be established solely in its own nature (*svarūpaniṣṭha*). Nor can an injunction such as "Do not fear" be postulated even there; for an injunction occurs only where, having understood it, a person acts or desists through its power and through a desire preceded by that [understanding].

In this case, since fear ceases for one who does not require either an injunction or a desire—merely through the knowledge of the reality of the rope, which is the cause of fearlessness, and because of the absence of the false conceit of the rope-snake's reality—there is no purpose served by an injunction. Furthermore, who is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)? Not with regard to the cessation of fear, because an injunction functions to impel toward what has not yet begun, and the cessation of fear occurs spontaneously, just as the world-process (*sarga*) and so forth do; nor can it be with regard to the means thereto, because that [knowledge] arises from the very word "this is a rope" through the knowledge of the rope's reality.

Furthermore, since an operation occurring subsequent to the cognition of word and meaning is observed elsewhere to be based on an injunction, it follows that even a sentence recounting events situated at an extremely remote distance—which, due to such extreme remoteness, cannot possibly involve the acts of abandoning or acquiring—is nonetheless restricted to its own form alone. Nor is it purposeless, for it serves to satisfy the curiosity of those who are interested.

Even in cases where the possibility of rejection or acceptance arises—such as "this path is beset by obstacles" or "this portion of ground contains a treasure"—one proceeds toward the object out of desire after recollecting the utility of the treasure as known through another means of valid cognition, and one desists out of aversion after recollecting the harmfulness of the obstacle; however, the word itself is exhausted merely in conveying the nature of the ground and does not express the rejection or acceptance.

Now, one might object: a speaker who acts with prior deliberation employs a sentence solely for the purpose of inciting activity (*pravṛtti*) or causing cessation (*nivṛtti*), and never for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); therefore, even that [sentence] must ultimately culminate in activity or cessation. It is simply that, due to laziness or other causes, this particular sentence—which is fit for use there—is not employed, namely: "Take this treasure" or "Do not go by this path. If it were intended to convey its own literal form (*svarūpa-paratva*), this sentence would be meaningless. This is not so.

If you argue that [the word] is purposeless in its own form, and therefore you must postulate that the function of the sentence extends as far as the commencement or cessation of activity—which has not been heard [directly from the word]—then do not postulate it so. For even while resting in its own form, this [word] can appropriately serve as a subordinate factor for activity or cessation by way of presenting its own form, just like perception and other means of knowledge. Indeed, perception and the others, having ceased their operation once they have determined an established object, do not at all take activity or cessation as their domain, yet they do not forfeit their status as subordinate factors [to them]. The same applies to the word; thus, there is no fault.

If it is argued that while in perception and other means of knowledge only the bare thing (*vastumātra*) is intended, and not engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), whereas this sentence is employed with a view toward engagement and withdrawal—therefore, those two alone are the word-meanings here—we say: not so. For it is not the case that whatever is intended is the word-meaning; rather, the word-meaning is that in which the word possesses expressive capacity (*vācaka-sāmarthya*). And this is not [the case here].

P. 25-3. The word "possessing a treasure" (*nidhimān*) has its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) in the sense of "take [it]"; for if the status of being a word-meaning were based on mere intention (*abhisandhāna*), then even the enjoyment and so forth to be accomplished by the treasure—which is also intended by that speaker—would have to be considered a word-meaning. Furthermore, when one intends, "I shall proceed toward the jar," or "I shall withdraw from the snake," and then investigates that object through perception and other means, those two intended objects are not the word-meaning.

If, on the other hand, activity were the meaning of a sentence concerning a treasure merely through the intention [of the speaker], then, because the power of the word is uniform, all people would have the cognition of activity; they would not have a cognition of indifference. Yet such a cognition does exist for some. Therefore, activity is not the meaning of the word. Consequently, that sentence is established as resting solely upon an accomplished fact (*siddhārtha*); thus, not every sentence in common usage is restricted to an action to be performed (*kāryaniṣṭha*).

As for what was also said—that since linguistic practice such as "bringing the cuckoo" arises from injunctive sentences, and from that the understanding of the relationship between signifier and signified occurs in the world, therefore all words must have activity (pravṛtti) as their ultimate purpose—that too is not correct, because we observe the understanding of the relationship even from statements describing the present (vartamānāpadeśa).

For instance, when it is said, "Devadatta cooks rice with wood," one who has mastered the meanings of the words and has mastered the meaning of the instrumental case, but has not yet mastered the meaning of the word "wood," perceives that which is the instrument in the act of cooking and thereby learns that the referent of the word "wood" is that very thing.

Likewise, from statements that communicate reality—such as "A son has been born to you," which serve purposes like joy—even though they concern established facts, there arises an understanding of the denotative power of words like "son" with respect to the sons and so forth who are the causes of joy, just as there is from injunctive sentences.

For just as a child, having observed a specific activity of a servant—such as bringing a cuckoo—which is the object of a linguistic usage like "bring the cuckoo," infers through the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability) that the servant possesses knowledge of that specific activity or knowledge of the injunction (*niyoga*) that is its cause; and since this occurs immediately after the word [is heard], and no other cause is perceived, and because it is illogical to abandon what is seen in favor of postulating what is unseen, one postulates that the word itself has the capacity for that knowledge—thus there is the acquisition of the understanding that the sentence-meaning is an action (*kārya*)—so too [the meaning is understood] from the father or others by means of their facial expressions, such as serenity, and so forth.

Having perceived joy and so forth through a mark (liṅga), and because an effect cannot arise without a cause, one infers a cognition of the cause of that joy and so forth; and since that [cognition] immediately follows the word, and no other cause is observed, it is concluded that it was produced by the word, whereby the capacity of the word to generate that cognition of the cause of joy and so forth is postulated.

Thus, when it has been understood in a general sense that "some cause for joy has been expressed by him through this word," and there arises a desire for the specific detail as to what that cause of joy is—since the birth of a son, which is known from one's own experience to be a cause of joy, is already established as the referent of the word "son" (though the child may not yet know it), and since this [cause] is understood as being connected to the father who is present in the sentence, and because no other cause of joy is perceived or exists—[the meaning is determined].

Furthermore, since it is illogical to postulate an unseen result when an observed one can be abandoned, this sentence was uttered by the father specifically upon the birth of a son; and it was precisely that [fact] which was understood by him from this sentence.

"He [did so]," thus the bystander observes. Therefore, in this manner, by means of the application of words uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*) as previously described, and by the two cognitions of the father regarding the birth of the son, the bystander perceives the capacity of the sentence to convey the meaning known as "the birth of a son. Consequently, there is linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) even from a sentence whose primary referent is an accomplished fact (*siddhārtha*); hence, linguistic acquisition does not arise solely from sentences concerning what is to be done (*kārya*).

Therefore, it is not by virtue of that [word] alone that all words have their finality fixed solely upon the action; thus, even when the meaning is established, the authority [of the word] is not contradicted. Although words depend upon linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) for their comprehension, while a sentence does not—since the understanding of meaning arises even from a sentence newly composed—nevertheless, linguistic usage arises from the employment of sentences, not from the employment of mere words. It is with reference to the word itself that it was stated that the capacity of the sentence is realized therein.

Now, it is stated [in response] even while granting [the opponent's point]: let it be that all words possess the capacity to incite action (*pravartakatva*), and from that alone there is the comprehension of the relationship between the signifier and the signified; nevertheless, in the very sentence that incites action, once the injunctive word (*vidhāyakapada*) has been extracted as the motivator, what is the purport (*tātparya*) of the remaining words? Is their expressive power (*śakti*) directed toward the mere individual meanings (*padārtha*)? Or toward the connection with an action (*kāryasaṃsarga*)? Or toward the connection with any other object (*padārthāntaramātra*) that is desired, capable, and proximate, whether it be an action or a non-action? This is what must be investigated.

Among those positions, if it were admitted that words have as their purport merely the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*), then all word-meanings would be like iron rods—mutually unconnected; consequently, there would be an absence of the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) in the form of a synthesis. Yet such a cognition does exist. Furthermore, since the mere apprehension of word-meanings is purposeless, the employment of words would be rendered futile.

Since these two defects arise in this view, therefore, in order to avoid these two defects, one must postulate a mutual connection—a reciprocal association—with a mere object (artha-mātra), whether it be an effect (kārya) or a non-effect (akārya), which is mutually required, fit, and proximate. And since the employment of words and the cognition of the sentence-meaning are established by such a connection with a mere object for another purpose, there is no evidence for a connection with a specific word-meaning in the form of an effect, as the speaker and the listener are already free from expectancy.

The point is this: since the employment and comprehension of words would otherwise be inexplicable if they were to terminate in their own individual meanings alone, these two factors lead us beyond that to the power of *tātparya* (intentional meaning), which culminates in the connection between the word-meanings themselves; and since those two are fully accounted for by that much alone, they are not capable of leading to a further connection with another meaning consisting of an action (*kārya*). Furthermore: whoever postulates a connection with another meaning consisting of an action must also postulate a connection with yet another meaning, because an action itself is also a distinct meaning.

Therefore, since it is established for both disputants, one must rely solely on the connection with another object (*arthāntaramātra*), and not on the connection with an effect (*kāryavyatiṣaṅga*); the sense is that this is because the subject under discussion is characterized by disagreement (*vimatyadhikṛtatvāt*). Furthermore, connection with an effect is inconstant, because an effect may be connected with what is not an effect; however, connection with another object in general is invariable.

...and thus it is a concomitant; therefore, that alone should be resorted to. If, in this way, the power of intention (*tātparya-śakti*) of words is determined to consist merely in their connection with another entity characterized by what is to be done or not to be done, then, insofar as a word is employed for worldly transaction in the world and in the Veda, there is a connection with that [intended entity] in each case.

However, in those cases where no action (*kārya*) is heard in the Vedānta, the cognition of established entities (*siddhārtha*) qualified by one another is established through the mutual relation of word-meanings even without such an action; thus, it is proven that the authority of words applies even to established entities. Consequently, although a connection with action is observed in the sentences used for linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) in common worldly usage, this connection to action must not be relied upon as the factor determining the power of a word’s intentionality (*tātparya-śakti*) when the word refers solely to an action.

And this must necessarily be admitted by you as well; otherwise, if everything observed in ordinary speech were accepted as the regulator of word-meaning, then—since in the world it is observed that the connection of word-meanings in a sentence depends on the speaker's intention—there would be no comprehension of meaning from injunctive passages in the Veda due to the absence of a speaker and, consequently, the absence of intention; yet such comprehension does exist.

Therefore, the connection with an action is not a necessary factor in the acquisition of word-meaning; since the relation between word-meanings is established even through non-actional entities, it is proven that the authority of words extends to established (siddha) objects as well. Moreover, if it were admitted that all words and their meanings are related only to an action, then there would be no mutual relationship characterized by the action-agent (kriyā-kāraka) relation between items such as "red" (aruṇā) and the verb "to buy" (krīṇāti).

In that case, the injunction (*niyoga*) would not be understood as having for its object a purchase qualified by causal factors (*kāraka*) such as "red" and so forth; rather, it would have as its object the act of purchase alone, accomplished by a single word-meaning. Now, if it is argued: "The injunction is indeed understood as having for its object the root-meaning qualified by the causal factors, and not the root-meaning alone; and the root-meaning does not become qualified without the connection with causal factors; therefore, with respect to the application (*viniyoga*), the injunction is not directed toward the individual meanings, but rather toward the [integrated] purpose."

And thus, even when there is a connection with the *niyoga* (the mandate), there is no contradiction in the mutual connection of the word-meanings. To this it is replied: "In that case, the application (*viniyoga*) must precede the *niyoga*. [The opponent continues: "Let the application be prior; nevertheless, the connection with the *niyoga* still exists," and he asks: "What follows from this if that is so? (Pa. 26-8). The proponent, however, reveals his own intention: "This being the case, even when there is a connection of the word-meaning distinct from the *niyoga*, the word possesses the capacity for *tātparya* (purport)."

Therefore, our position is established. [Objection: But surely there is a mutual connection between those things that are connected with the *niyoga* (the injunction), and not among those independent of it; therefore, this [connection] is based solely on the *niyoga*, and without it, words have no power of connection in the Upaniṣads. To this he replies: The capacity of words for mutual connection exists quite independently of the *niyoga*. Why? Because it is only after the words have first been mutually connected that they are subsequently connected with the *niyoga*.

This is the intention: for you maintain that the connection of the injunction (*niyoga*) is with a qualified object; yet that [object] does not become qualified unless it is connected with the factors of action (*kāraka*); nor is something unqualified connected with the injunction, because what is unqualified cannot be an object, and what is not an object [cannot be enjoined].

[The opponent argues: "There is necessarily no dependence [on other words], because this [syntactic relation] is based on dependence; therefore, the connection of words occurs prior to the connection with the *niyoga* (injunction). If it were independent of the connection with the *niyoga*, then even in the case of the Upaniṣads, where the object is already established, the connection [of words] would be established even without that [injunction]. [The author replies: "Granted, even if the connection of word-meanings does not occur prior to the connection with the *niyoga*, nevertheless, it is based on the requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the *niyoga*. For the *niyoga* requires the mutual connection of word-meanings in order to accomplish its own specific objective."

Otherwise, even the connection between word-meanings, being devoid of a connection with an action to be accomplished (*kārya*), would be useless, and there would be no unity of sentence (*ekavākyatā*). If this is so, he states that in the Upaniṣads the establishment of connection does not occur without an injunction (*niyoga*): "The mutual relation of word-meanings is not based on the requirement of an injunction"—this point he will explain in the section on injunction (*niyogakāṇḍa*).

As for what was said—that since Brahman is not established by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its relationship [with words] cannot be grasped, and thus, being a non-word-meaning (*apadārtha*), it cannot be expressed by a sentence—it is replied to this: even though Brahman is not apprehended by another means of knowledge, it can nevertheless be defined by such words as "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long" and so forth, precisely because its relationship with its own designating terms—such as "Brahman," "the Inner Controller" (*antaryāmin*), and the like—is capable of being established, even if that denotative relationship has not been previously apprehended.

How so? It is said: by means of negating specific attributes such as "gross," "subtle," and "short" which are superimposed through ignorance—as in the expressions "I am gross," "I am subtle," and "I am short. Nor should it be argued that the same fault of inconsistency applies to the word by which [the Self] is thus conveyed; for the words denoting specific attributes like "gross" and the negative particle *nañ* have their respective relationships with their meanings already established. Furthermore, there is no fault of inconsistency here, as there is in the case of words such as "Brahman" or "Inner Controller" (*antaryāmin*).

The sense is this: by means of the negation of specific attributes such as grossness and so forth, words like "not gross" (asthūla) possess the power to denote the reality that is free from all defects, namely the self-established *jīva*. Likewise, even according to the Śruti, in passages such as "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red... and so on, that Brahman is taught precisely in this way—by means of the negation of specific attributes like grossness—to be beyond all distinctions, transcending all particularities such as grossness; the sense is that we have not said this merely out of our own imagination.

He applies the meaning of the verse to the subject matter already stated: "This [verse] says this. And since this will be explained in the fourth book (*kāṇḍa*), it is not elaborated upon here. The word "iti" marks the conclusion. Another meaning of this very verse is now stated: As for what was said in the prima facie argument—that Brahman, in which all distinctions have subsided, is by its very nature not an object of comprehension—it is replied to this: it is precisely through the cessation of distinctions that that non-distinct reality is conveyed by words.

This may be stated as follows: two kinds of exposition are observed. One is by way of specifying particular attributes, such as “this one wears earrings, that one wears a *kaṭhaka* necklace”; and the other is by way of negating particular attributes, such as “he does not wear armlets, he does not wear a crown, he does not wear a *kaṭhaka* necklace. Therefore, even if the reality (*tattva*) is devoid of particulars and cannot be described by way of specifying particular attributes as being “of such a nature,” it will nevertheless be expounded and understood by way of negating the particulars superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*). On this point [p. 68]:

P. 26-16. He states an illustration: "Gold is like the reality (*tattva*). He elaborates upon this with the words "for not... Gold-reality, which is perceived through specific forms such as a lump or a necklace (*rucaka*), is free from that which constitutes an adjunct (*uparāga*), a state of being mixed (*saṃmiśratva*), or non-separateness (*apṛthagbhāva*). Being devoid of these, it possesses characteristics distinct from the necklace and so forth; yet, it is not seen as separate from them. Nor should it be said that the necklace and other forms are themselves the gold-reality, because [the gold] persists even when the necklace is discarded, in another form such as a *svastika*.

For if the gold-substance (*suvarṇatattva*) were non-different from the necklace (*rucaka*), then like the necklace, it too would not exist in the cross-shaped ornament (*svastika*); yet it does exist there. Therefore, it is distinct from that [necklace]. The same should be understood regarding the cross-shaped ornament as well. Thus, although the gold-substance is not seen as something separate from the necklace and so forth, nevertheless, even though it is of such a nature, it is not the cross-shaped ornament because it exists in the necklace; nor is it the necklace, because it exists in the cross-shaped ornament.

The meaning is as follows: by means of the discriminative cognition "it is other than this," and through the exclusion (*apoha*) of differences such as the *rucaka* (necklace) and so forth—expressed as "it is neither that *buddhaka* nor the *svastika*"—the specific forms like the *rucaka* are negated; thereby, the gold-essence (*suvarṇatattva*), which is internal to all those forms, is itself realized and communicated to another. It is the same with Brahman. The analysis of the compound is: "that for which no distinction is perceived because of the observation of differences in configuration" (*saṃsthānabheda*). This [principle] applies equally to the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) and so on; gold is merely an illustrative example.

He confirms this point by means of scripture: "This very one... He cites two statements from authoritative sources on this same subject: "Likewise... The ellipsis of the sentence is "it has been said. The meaning is that at the end, at the conclusion, when there is the withdrawal—that is, the dissolution—of the specific forms such as the gross and so forth, that which remains is the Truth. Likewise, it has been stated by others: "In the ultimate sense, Brahman is indeed devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*)."

The meaning is that by the superimposition of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) through ignorance (*avidyā*), and by its subsequent negation—that is, its denial—it is "proliferated" or explained. Having thus stated that Brahman is accessible through the Vedas (*āmnāya*) by means of the dissolution of the phenomenal world, the following is now investigated in order to determine the specific portion of the Veda: Does the entire Veda, which is established in [describing] both the nature and the effects [of Brahman], lead one to know non-dual Brahman by way of negating difference, or is there only a certain single part of this Veda known as the Vedānta?

Regarding that doubt, some say: "In every part of the sacred tradition (āmnāya), the dissolution of some [lower] Veda is perceived; therefore, by means of that [dissolution], the entire sacred tradition leads one to Brahman"—this is the sense. He demonstrates this: as from the scriptural injunction "One desiring offspring should sacrifice," the dissolution of the body's status as the Self is perceived; thus is the connection with what precedes.

How so? It is said: for in this sentence, since the body—which does not follow one to another world and is insentient—lacks the capacity for the enjoyment of heaven in a future birth, it is understood that there is an agent distinct from it, who persists through future births, is sentient, and is capable of enjoying heaven; and that very agent is understood to be the dissolution of the identification with the body in the phrase "these four.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is exactly as before. Likewise, in the case of the statement, "For one desiring cattle, [one should perform the sacrifice] with the *godohana* vessel," since the *godohana*—being non-actional in nature and lacking the inherent capacity to produce anything else directly—cannot be a direct means for obtaining cattle, it depends upon an action that serves as its substrate. By virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it takes recourse to the act of fetching water (*praṇayana*) belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Thus, by implication, its status as a means for obtaining cattle belongs to one who is already authorized for the Darśapūrṇamāsa; consequently, because the qualification is restricted to such a person, any distinct qualified agent is excluded. (P. 27-4)

One might object: "Granted that in such [passages] as these there may be the dissolution of difference; however, in the injunctions of prescriptions and prohibitions—which have as their sole fruit engagement and withdrawal—that is impossible. Therefore, the entire body of scripture does not aim at the dissolution of difference. Anticipating this doubt, he states that even there there is the dissolution of difference, with the words "In the same way" (*tathā*). The syntactical connection is as follows: "In the same way, even in the injunctions of prescriptions and prohibitions, a prohibition of external activities based on natural attachment and aversion is understood."

Regarding that, he says "In prohibitions" (*niṣedheṣu*), because in prohibitions such as "Do not do this," the prohibition of other activities is understood directly. Now, let this be so for prohibitions; but how is it in the case of injunctions, whose sole fruit is the instigation to act? To this he says "In injunctions" (*vidhiṣu*). In injunctions such as "One should perform the twilight worship" (*saṃdhyām upāsīta*), the prohibition of activity external to that time is understood through the prescription of another activity. What is meant is this: in both cases, the dissolution of external activity does not differ.

However, this is the distinction: that [the cessation of activity] occurs directly in the case of prohibitions, but by implication in the case of injunctions. He states that these two modes are observed in the world as well, saying "In the world. Even in the world, one observes a direct prevention from an undesired path, such as "Do not go by this way," or an implied prevention of the intended but undesired path through the instruction of an alternative route. Thus, it is established that even in the injunctions of injunctions and prohibitions, the dissolution of activity rooted in passion and other such factors is understood.

And this is the benefit: by means of dissolving the distinctions in the natural activity rooted in passion and so forth, the injunctions regarding ritual action (*karmavidhi*)—like the threshing of grain—act as direct auxiliaries (*sannipatyopakārin*) through their visible utility, thereby establishing for the seeker of liberation the qualification of tranquility (*śāntatā*) required for the mandate [to know the Self]. Thus, the injunctions such as "the Self is to be known" become applicable to the qualification for the knowledge of the Self; the sense is that there is no burden of postulating unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*).

He states that even by means of scripture (*śruti*), the cessation of all external activity rooted in passion (*rāga*) and so forth is shown to be a qualification of the qualified seeker (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*): "For thus... In this regard, the vision of the Self as the object is taught for one who is peaceful (*śānta*) and composed (*samāhita*): "Therefore, having become peaceful, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and composed, one should see the Self in the very Self," and so on, according to scripture. Therein, by the term "peaceful," the cessation of activity arising from passion and the like, preceded by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is stated to be a qualification of the qualified seeker.

"Self-controlled" (*dānta*) means the cessation of activity arising from passion and the like, preceded by the restraint of the external organs. Others, however, state the opposite: this must necessarily be understood as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), because one who is capable is the qualified person; and that knowledge of the Self is possible only for one who is peaceful, self-controlled, and concentrated, not for anyone else. Therefore, the sense is that such a person alone is qualified, and no other. Why, then, is knowledge of the Self impossible for another? To this he says: "For not... (*na hi*).

The sense is that one whose mind is attached—that is, one by whom the mind has been directed toward the means of an object while being drawn forward by the attractiveness of that object—is unable to achieve composure within the Self as his own subject, nor, when withdrawn from it, is he able to know the Self; therefore, due to this incapacity, such a person is not qualified.

Furthermore, one who has desisted from those natural activities rooted in passion—being tranquil and self-controlled, and consequently having a restrained mind with all internal and external distractions cast aside—is able to concentrate upon the Self; thus, by virtue of possessing the capacity for self-knowledge, such a person is qualified for the vision of the Self. Therefore, some maintain that since ritual injunctions, when aimed at prohibiting natural impulses, serve as a means to the qualification for knowledge through their visible effect, it is logical that they are intended solely for that purpose.

Others, however, consider the injunctions for ritual action to be useful for the qualification for the knowledge of the Self; how so? It is said: one whose desires are unattained—desires (*kāma*) being those things desired, such as heaven and the like—is one by whom desires have not been attained; one whose mind is afflicted by desire—desire (*kāma*) being longing, a craving for sensual pleasure—one whose mind is thus afflicted and rendered unstable is not fit for the vision of supreme non-duality and therefore is not qualified for it.

Indeed, one who is unfit does not attain the qualification [for this knowledge]. On the other hand, he who—beginning from the Āśrāvaṇa sacrifice up to the sacrificial session (*sattra*) known as the *sahasra-saṃvatsara*—has performed all rites that fulfill every desire, and by having attained all that is desired, has brought about the destruction of his desires; he for whom the destruction—that is, the eradication—of desire, which is the longing for the pleasure of sense-objects, has been accomplished, being thus one whose mind is unassailed because all desires have been attained, realizes the non-dual Self beyond the station of Prajāpati (the world of Prajāpati).

One proceeds [in this manner]. Thus, others maintain that the injunctions regarding ritual action (karmavidhi) serve as a means for the qualification for the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna) by way of the destruction of desire. And in this way, the meaning of the sentences throughout the entire Veda is understood: the collection of rituals, culminating in the thousand-year sacrifice, must be performed by one who desires to know the Self.

Moreover, in both of these immediately preceding positions—namely, the views that the injunctions regarding ritual action (*karmavidhi*) are subservient to the qualification for the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna-adhikāra*)—the entire Vedic corpus culminates in the single purpose of the knowledge of the Self; it finds its completion in that one purpose, which is the knowledge of the Self. In other words, it is "intent upon" that. The use of the singular term "one" [purpose] indicates that it does not culminate in any other kind of result.

Regarding this, the distinction is as follows: in the first position, the ritual injunctions, whose intermediate results are intended to be expressed, are connected to the supreme injunction of the knowledge of the Self; in the second, however, they are so connected by way of the intermediate results of the ritual injunctions themselves. [p. 71]

He states another opinion: "The view of others. [This means] they are indeed distinct effects; that is, distinct from the knowledge that has liberation as its fruit, they are distinct parts (*kalā*); or rather, they are "distinct instruments" (*pṛthakkaraṇa*), meaning those for whom the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the effect (*kārya*). In other words, they are independent. Being such distinct effects, they lead the person seeking liberation into the qualification for self-knowledge; that is, they render him fit for that qualification. This is a construction involving two objects, just as in the expression "he leads the goat to the village."

Why? Because one who has not discharged the three debts lacks the qualification for that knowledge of the Self—that is, for one by whom the three debts have not been discharged, there is no entitlement to it. Why is there no entitlement for him? From the statement of Manu: "Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation. And the three debts are declared by the Śruti itself: "Being born, one is born burdened with three debts: through studentship to the sages, through sacrifice to the gods, and through progeny to the ancestors."

But surely, even in the view that desires are to be eradicated, ritual injunctions still possess a distinct purpose; therefore, what is the distinction of this position? This is the distinction: for in that case, the fruit is not stated for the sake of the fruit itself, but rather, through the attainment of desire, when that desire ceases, it serves to secure for the desireless person the qualification for the knowledge of the Self; thus, in that context, an intermediate purpose is not intended.

In this context, however, there is no fault, because ritual injunctions whose function is to eliminate specific intermediate forms are indeed useful for the qualification for the knowledge of the Self, just as in the case of the statement: "Having sacrificed with the Bṛhaspatisava, one should sacrifice with the Vājapeya. And he states another opinion: "But others... and so forth.

For those [acts] connected with the fruits such as the creation [of the world] mentioned in scripture, and therefore independent of any other purpose, there is nonetheless heard a separate connection with knowledge (*jñāna*) through the injunction "They desire to know Him by means of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity" (*tam etam yajñena dānena tapasānāśakena vividiṣanti*), according to the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*). This is in accordance with the maxim "When one thing serves two purposes, there is separateness of connection," just as in the case of the [wooden post] "made of *khadira* wood": [the texts state] "The sacrificial post is made of *khadira* wood," "One binds the animal to the post," and "It is made of *khadira* for one desiring vigor"—thereby establishing the permanent (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) [applications] of the same object.

The connection is as follows: "But others say" refers to the fact that all ritual actions enter into the qualification for the knowledge of the Self precisely through their application (*viniyoga*). The word "but" (*tu*) is for the sake of distinction; the distinction here in this view is that there is an application of the connection of action to knowledge. Likewise, he cites another scriptural passage (*śrutyantara*) which shows how actions enter into the qualification for the knowledge of the Self by means of removing mental distraction: "By whatever [means]... He states another opinion: "But others say," meaning that a person who has been purified becomes fit for the qualification for the knowledge of the Self.

Regarding this point, he cites two traditional authorities (*smṛti*): "By the great sacrifices," and so forth. By the great sacrifices—the sacrifices to Brahman, the gods, the ancestors, humans, and spirits—and by other sacrifices, this body is made *brāhmī*, meaning it is made fit for Brahman; for the suffix *-aṇ* is prescribed in the rule "one who studies that or knows that" (*tad adhīte tad veda*) with respect to *brahma-vidyā*. The meaning is that it is "made. The word "body" (*tanu*) is used as a metaphorical designation for the Self (*ātman*) because the Self resides within it. For the Self alone is the one qualified for the knowledge of Brahman and is a knower of Brahman, whereas the body is not, because it is insentient (*jaḍa*).

For that man who has performed the following: the *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarman*, *nāmakaraṇa*, *annaprāśana*, *caula*, and *upanayana*; the four *vedavrata*s; the *snāna* together with the union with a wife; the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*); the seven *pākayajña* rites known as the *aṣṭakā*, *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, *śrāvaṇī*, *āgrahāyaṇī*, *caitrī*, and *āśvayujī*; the seven *haviryajña* rites known as the *ādhāna*, *agnihotra*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *cāturmāsya*, *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, *nirūḍhapaśubandha*, and *sautrāmaṇī*; and the [seven] *soma-saṃsthā*s known as the *agniṣṭoma*, *atyagniṣṭoma*, *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśin*, *vājapeya*, [atirātra, and āptoryāma]...

The seven forms of the Soma sacrifice known as Ātigrāhya, Aptoryāma, and so forth—these constitute the forty sacraments (saṃskāras). Furthermore, there are eight personal qualities (ātmaguṇas), namely: compassion, forbearance, freedom from malice, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of longing. Such a person attains union with Brahman—that is, oneness with Hiraṇyagarbha—and also the state of residing in the same world (sālokya). By stating that he is dissolved into the Supreme Brahman at the time of cosmic dissolution (pralaya), the text demonstrates the path of gradual liberation (kramamukti).

As it has been said: “When the time of universal dissolution arrives, at the end of the Supreme, all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state along with Brahmā. (P. 28-4) He states another view: “But others,” etc. They describe this very same process of purifying the person (*puruṣasaṃskārakatva*) in reverse—that which was stated regarding the eligibility for self-knowledge on the part of ritual actions—as being rather the eligibility for ritual action on the part of self-knowledge itself. He states that very point with the words beginning “Self-knowledge,” etc.

Only one who knows the Self as an eternal agent and enjoyer distinct from the body has the qualification for one's own ritual acts (*karma*), and no other. Thus it has been said: "For indeed, no one who is ignorant of the inner self (*adhyātma*) enjoys the fruit of action. Therefore, the sense is that this purification (*saṃskāra*) belongs to the agent who is about to employ himself in ritual acts. And there is another view: "But others... Ritual action has as its object the duality of the goal and the means, whereas the knowledge of the Self has as its object non-duality, according to the teaching: "One alone, without a second."

Therefore, others maintain that because these two are mutually contradictory, there is no connection between them at all. Having thus set forth seven positions, he refutes the first position with the words "In that case" (*tatra*). "Kalpa" means "conception" (*kalpanā*). He asks "Why? and replies "For not... By the word "karma-ādi" ("action, etc."), the injunctions regarding substances such as the *godohana* vessel are intended; alternatively, by the word "karma," dharma characterized by activity is meant, while by the word "ādi," austerity (*tapas*) characterized by cessation is meant—the injunctions for these. These have as their effects heaven and so forth, which are understood from their own respective sentences. [p. 73]

Those [injunctions] for which the fruit to be accomplished—such as heaven and so forth—is understood from their own sentences are described as such; therefore, they do not require another effect known as the knowledge of the Self, because there is no expectancy for anything other than the fruits heard in their own sentences—this is the sense. Now, one might object: "Let it be that the injunctions regarding ritual action (*karman*) are independent in this way; however, the injunction for the knowledge of the Self will depend upon them as its means, for a relationship can indeed exist through dependence on even a single factor. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Nor... (P. 28-9).

The meaning is this: such being the case, since there is no mutual relationship characterized by expectancy between the two when they are both devoid of expectancy, how can there be a single purpose or a single subject matter for the injunctions regarding ritual action and knowledge? Here, he anticipates the opponent's view with the words "Now (atha)": the idea is that ritual injunctions whose fruits are not understood within their own sentences will enter into the scope of the injunction for self-knowledge when they have a requirement for a fruit.

An objection is raised: "Is it not heard in scripture that 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice'? Therefore, how can it be said that the fruit is not understood? Anticipating this, he says: "Of heaven and so forth. It is true that heaven and so forth are heard in scripture; however, that [heaven] consists of substances such as sandalwood produced by pleasure. And whatever is a substance, in the context of the expression "the past and the future," it is taught that "the past is for the sake of the future"; thus, it is connected as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), meaning as a non-primary means (*sādhana*) to the ritual action (*karman*), and not as a primary factor in the sense of being the fruit. This is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, the meaning is that because heaven and so forth are connected as subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) by virtue of being qualifiers of the person—as in "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*)—they do not constitute the fruit. The proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*), however, says with derision: "Heaven," etc. For in that context, heaven is pleasure (*prīti*), not a material substance; and everything exists for the sake of pleasure, whereas pleasure does not exist for the sake of anything else. Therefore, it is connected as the primary element by way of being the fruit, and not as a subordinate qualifier of the person by way of being a means (*sādhana*).

Moreover, it is established that heaven and the like are the primary objects because they are what is desired; yet this has not been understood by this proponent who claims that heaven and the like are merely subordinate qualities (guṇa). Therefore, the meaning is that one should explain that section (adhikaraṇa) to him.

Furthermore, if it were accepted that the dissolution of the entire phenomenal world—which consists of both the names (śabda), i.e., the verbal forms, and the forms (rūpa), i.e., the meanings—is the sole purpose and final goal of all injunctions and prohibitions, then injunctions and prohibitions would lack any basis for authority, as they would be directed toward something else; consequently, there would be no such thing as the attainment of good or evil through what is enjoined or prohibited.
