In that case, those prosperities of living beings such as heaven and so forth, as well as those misfortunes even in hells and the like, would not have their cause in enjoined or prohibited actions; consequently, being without the cause of action, they would be accidental—that is, without a cause. And it is not logical for an effect to exist without a cause; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, if prosperity and misfortune were accidental, then liberation (*apavarga*) would likewise be accidental in the same manner; and thus, the scripture which teaches the means to attain it would be rendered useless. He states this with the word "tathā" (so too). The word "iti" has the sense of a reason.

[Page 74] Now, it might be argued: suppose someone says at some time or place, “Go to the city; first go to such-and-such a village there, and from there to another. In this case, just as the instructions to travel to the villages along the way—even though they result in reaching those respective villages—are included within the instruction to go to the city by virtue of being seen as subordinate to that [final] purpose, so too the injunctions regarding ritual actions (karma-vidhi), although they have results such as heaven understood from their own sentences, are included within the qualification for knowledge (jñāna-adhikāra) by virtue of being seen as subordinate to the result of heaven and the like.

Even though their functions are distinct, they may share a single ultimate objective; thus he says [in the commentary], "Now" (atha). When one engages in the injunctions for ritual action out of desire for heaven and the like, the cessation of external activity implies that heaven and such results must be regarded as mere means. He refutes that by way of a dissimilar example, stating, "That is incorrect. For in that case, the speaker's desired goal is the reaching of the city, not the reaching of the village along the way.

Therefore, the meaning is that instructions regarding the attainment of villages along the way—which are not themselves the desired goal—are rightly subsumed under the instructions for the attainment of the desired city. Why, then, is the attainment of the village on the path not the desired goal? To this he says: "For... (na hi). For upon reaching the city, there occurs the attainment of the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha) intended by the other person, whereas such is not the case upon reaching a village on the path; thus, it is the attainment of the city alone that is the speaker's desired goal, not the attainment of the village on the path.

Therefore, instructions regarding the path to a village, because they entail an expectation of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), enter into those instructions for reaching a city where the attainment of a human goal occurs; thus he says, "therefore" (*ataḥ*). He says, "but not so" (*na tv evam*) regarding the injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*); the sense is that heaven and the like are heard of within their own respective sentences. Nor can it be argued that even though they are heard of, they are not human goals, and therefore how could a human goal be attained through the injunctions for ritual action? To this he says, "of heaven and the like."

Indeed, there is no such thing as a "human goal" (puruṣārtha) by virtue of its genus; rather, that which is sought after by a person is a human goal. Since heaven and so forth are likewise [sought], they are human goals; thus, there is no attainment of a human goal within the injunctions regarding ritual actions (karma-vidhi). Nevertheless, he asks "What then? and replies: "In that case... This means that since those human goals such as heaven have been attained, the injunctions regarding ritual actions lack any further expectancy toward another human goal consisting of liberation; therefore, how could they enter into the other injunction regarding the knowledge of the Self?

Thus, having stated the disparity between the philosophical example and the case of human purposeful action, the opponent again seeks to establish their similarity, beginning with the word "atha" (now). Suppose a person is instructed: "Go to this village; there is this benefit for you, that you will obtain fine food and the like. Having reached that village and obtained the fine food, he is then led on by this very same sequence—through the presentation of further benefits in successive villages—until he is enticed toward the presentation of his desired city. In that case, the instructions regarding the previous villages have achieved their intended purpose.

Those by whom the desired object in the form of a human goal—such as delicious food and the like—has been attained or obtained are so described; that is to say, they are those who have no further desire for the human goals such as delicious food obtained through their own words. Just as they, being free from such desire, yet enter into other injunctions regarding going to the city, so too do the injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*), even though they are free from desire for objects such as heaven.

The sense is that they will enter into the procedure for knowledge. He refutes that with the word "yuktam" (it is proper). He explains this very point with the words "pramāṇāntara... (by means of another means of knowledge). This is what is meant: although the instructions regarding the previous village appear, according to the literal function of the words, to be directed toward the attainment of the previous village as their fruit, nevertheless, upon reaching the city, this [attainment] is understood to be the intended fruit of the speaker.

Having understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that "it was with this very intention that he taught the journey to various villages and cities," one realizes that the instructions regarding the previous villages are included within the instruction regarding the city. Therefore, because [the understanding] occurs when another means of knowledge exists, this is the result of that [other means], not of the operation of the word itself. He says "and for this reason" (*itaśca*) to show that this is so not only because it occurs when another means of knowledge exists, but also because it does not occur when it is absent.

In every village, when the speaker and the listener have attained their purpose—such as delicious food and the like—and the speaker’s intention to go to the city or the village is not perceived through any other means of knowledge, then bystanders and neutral recipients regard the previous instructions regarding the villages as having only those previous purposes—that is, they consider them to have only those previous purposes consisting of delicious food and so forth; they do not regard them as being for the purpose of reaching the city or the village, nor do they regard the instruction regarding the city as residing in themselves.

These [words] do not have a single referent (*ekārthatva*). However, if the earlier instructions were for the sake of the later ones merely by following the function of the words, then that would indeed apply there as well, because that function has a fixed form; but this is not the case. Therefore, the sense is that it is the grace of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) that constitutes that [referent]. Now, one might object: "Since the attainment of each subsequent city is impossible without first reaching each preceding village, why should these [earlier stages] not also be for the sake of that [final goal]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even though... The sense is that the unity of purpose (*maidamarthya*) of a word does not arise from mere assistance alone.

In this context, he states an example established by logic: "the acquisition of wealth and so forth. The meaning is as follows: just as, for instance, although the injunction regarding the rules for acquiring wealth for sacrifices serves to assist the injunction for the sacrifice itself—since a sacrifice cannot be accomplished without wealth—the [wealth] does not have its scriptural purpose (kratvaidamarthya) directed toward the sacrifice; so it is here. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the injunctions for the laying of the fires (adhāna) and other such rites are included.

Having thus established—in the case of the illustrative example—that even those [sentences] which are semantically complete still enter into other injunctions by depending on another means of knowledge, he states the impossibility of that in the case of injunctions regarding ritual action (*karmavidhi*), beginning with the words "by the operation of the word" (*śabdavṛtta*). In these injunctions regarding ritual action, it is proper that the intended meaning (*tātparya*) follows the function of the word itself; it is not determined by the force of another means of knowledge, because such [external means] are impossible in the case of a Vedic subject matter. Furthermore, the function of the word is sufficient for each respective injunctive meaning and does not extend as far as an injunction for knowledge (*jñānavidhi*); therefore, the sense is that there is no entry into that [injunction for knowledge].

Furthermore, even instructions regarding the villages along the way do not have the attainment of the destination as their ultimate purpose; therefore, the illustrative example is unestablished. For even when the intention to go to the destination is understood, it is only through the misconception that those instructions have the attainment of the villages along the way as their purpose—thinking "this and that are intended by him"—that one proceeds toward the villages along the way and attains the fruits such as delicious food. However, if the attainment of the city were the intended purpose, then since the attainment of the villages along the way would not be intended and only the attainment of the city would be intended, one might instead travel by another route. Moreover, the attainment of the fruit would not necessarily occur.

Because there is a declaration of fruit (*phalaśruti*) in passages whose primary intent is something else, according to the principle: "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals, the declaration of fruit must be an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), because they exist for the sake of another" (PMS 4.3.1). He states all of this with the words "Moreover... (*api ca*). Relying on this very logic, he says "That... (*tat*). The sense is that if injunctions and prohibitions were directed solely toward the production of knowledge, then they would not have creation and so forth as their effects; consequently, the prosperity and calamities of living beings would be without cause.

The analysis of the compound is: "those for whom creation and so forth are the objects to be accomplished. Although the subsequent discussion regarding ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) continues, nevertheless, because they share the same defect and were introduced at the outset, the prohibitions have been placed here. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "creation and so forth," hell and other such states are also to be understood.

One might object: "Just as the function of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—which is characterized by assisting the primary sacrifice—is not unintended even though it culminates in the creation (*sarga*) and other effects of the primary sacrifice, so too the effect of creation and so forth, although it culminates in the effect of self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), will likewise not be unintended. Consequently, why could injunctions and prohibitions, though intended for the effect of knowledge, not also have creation and other effects? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Their own... Since the function of the *prayāja* and so forth is not in itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), its inclusion within a function that is a human goal is appropriate.

But this does not apply to effects such as creation, because [the Self] is itself the human goal; this is the sense. Thus, it is established that ritual injunctions, which have become self-sufficient through the mention of heaven and so forth in the scriptures, do not enter into the domain of the inquiry into the knowledge of the Self. Now, he refutes what was previously stated—that ritual injunctions are useful for the inquiry into the knowledge of the Self by means of visible results alone—with the words "And how? Here, he anticipates the opponent's intention with the words "If..."

The meaning is this: if it is argued that ritual injunctions, by preventing activity directed toward visible ends prompted by passion, aversion, and so forth, thereby produce a state of composure (samāhitatva) and thus serve the purpose of the qualification for the knowledge of the Self through a visible means—that is refuted with the words "Let it be so" (bhavatu). Since prohibitions (pratiṣedha) serve the purpose of turning one away from activity already prompted by passion and the like, let them have a visible utility toward the qualification for knowledge; however, this does not apply to ritual injunctions (karmavidhi). He states the reason for this: "For not... (na hi).

For in the case of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), when there is a possibility of [the rule] applying both there and elsewhere due to passion, a statement such as "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten" or "the hare, the porcupine," etc., has the purpose of precluding the eating of five-nailed animals other than the hare and so forth, such as humans. Similarly, in the case of "one should sacrifice with rice," since any substance whatsoever required for the sacrifice is already applicable, and rice is included therein as well, the statement has the purpose of precluding other substances. However, injunctions regarding ritual acts (*karmavidhi*) are neither restrictive nor exclusive.

However, they are indeed prescriptive (*vidhāyaka*); therefore, the meaning is that they do not aim at the exclusion of other things. Why? To this he says: "Because [the object] is absolutely unattained" (*atyantam*). Those for whom the object (*viṣaya*) is not attained through passion (*rāga*) and so forth are described as such; the compound *karmaviṣaya* has its members in reverse order (*anyapadārtha*). The sense is that in the case of the *agnihotra* and other such rites, activity is not already attained through passion and the like. But why, even though the objects are absolutely unattained, would these injunctions regarding ritual acts not be restrictive (*niyāmaka*) or exclusive (*parisaṃkhyāyaka*)? To provide the reason for this, he says: "For an injunction whose object is already attained... (1.29–14). An injunction is one whose object is already attained through passion and the like.

The meaning is this: because [injunctions] that cause one to obtain what is already obtained would be purposeless, they are understood to have the exclusion of other things as their result. However, since injunctions concerning ritual actions (*karma*) are purposeful precisely by causing one to obtain what was absolutely unobtained, they are not understood to have the exclusion of other things as their purpose due to the fault of purposelessness. As it has been said: “An injunction (*vidhi*) applies when [the action] is absolutely unobtained; a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when it is optionally obtained; and when it is obtained both there and elsewhere, it is celebrated as an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).”

Even though the domain of ritual action (*karma*) does not have as its fruit the engagement in or desisting from activity born of passion and the like, nevertheless, through the opposition characterized by the fact that engagement prompted by passion and engagement prompted by injunction produce the same effect, the cessation of engagement born of passion will occur by means of engagement prompted by injunction. For instance, whatever pleasure results from engagement born of passion, that very same [pleasure] results from engagement in injunctions such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice.

If it were argued that this [cessation] is established precisely through engagement in what is ordained (*vaidhapravṛtti*), and therefore there is a cessation of activity born of passion and so forth because its purpose has been accomplished, he says "no" to that as well: "And not... Why? He says: "Because of the indefinite... The analysis of the compound is: "those whose fruits have an indefinite time. Activities arising from injunctions (*naiyogikyaḥ pravṛttayaḥ*) have fruits that yield results either in this world or the next; therefore, they have the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) as their purpose. However, activities prompted by passion and so forth—namely, natural activities born from the very nature of the person such as passion—are those that have visible purposes (*dṛṣṭārthāḥ*).

They indicate that [these practices] have results pertaining to this life (*aihika-phalatva*) because their purpose is perceptible; the meaning is that they yield results in this world. Consequently, since the two have effects occurring at different times, there is no contradiction between them; thus, activity born of passion and the like is not sublated by activity arising from a ritual injunction (*naiyogikī pravṛtti*). Alternatively, the sense is that because the perceptible purpose is more highly esteemed, it would sublate the imperceptible purpose. Now, one might object: "But the fruit of creation and so forth is indeed otherworldly (*āmuṣmika*)."

How then is it stated without qualification that "the fruits have an indefinite time"? This was said with reference to the power of the injunction (*vidhi-śakti*), not to the power of the thing itself (*vastu-śakti*). For the injunction does not specify whether the creation [of the fruit] occurs here or there, as no particular time is indicated; however, the power of the thing is such that if the creation cannot be experienced here, it must occur there. Alternatively, "indefinite time" is a mere illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); the fact that the fruit belongs to the next world (*āmuṣmika*) should also be understood. Even in that case, there is indeed a restriction due to the difference in time.

Or rather, the sublation would be the opposite. Furthermore, if there were a contradiction because activities for seen and unseen purposes had the same effect, then that contradiction would also apply to service and the grasping of sacrificial implements; but it is not so.

P. 29-17. He says "no" [to the objection]: there is no contradiction even though the *Sāṅgrahaṇī* sacrifice—which is performed for one desiring a village—and service to the Lord—which has a visible purpose—are both means to the same effect of obtaining a single village, because it is possible for one who desires the fruit to engage in both. Even if they were contradictory, the *Sāṅgrahaṇī* would supersede service only if the scriptural injunction for it were an authority for the cessation of other activities; however, that scripture is an authority only to the extent that "the *Sāṅgrahaṇī* is to be performed," not for the cessation of other activities.

Therefore, he says "to this extent" (*etāvatī*) to show that there is no contradiction between the two. Since there is thus no contradiction in that case, he asks: what contradiction could there be for one who desires the fruit of both *ūrmi* (the waves of worldly existence) and the fruit [of liberation], and who performs service and the grasping of the limbs [of yoga] either simultaneously or sequentially? He says "therein" (*tatra*). And so, just as there is no contradiction there despite the activities having equal effects, so too here, even though the activity impelled by ritual injunction (*naiyogika*) and the activity impelled by passion (*rāga*) have equal effects, there is no contradiction; thus, the sense is that they do not stand in a relationship of mutual sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*).

Furthermore, if it is admitted that activities prompted by passion (*rāga*) and so forth are obstructed by activities arising from an injunction (*niyoga*), then even those activities rooted in the injunction would be obstructed. Consequently, this position results in the subversion of what is desired (*iṣṭavighātakṛt*); with this intention, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*). He states the reason for this: "by one who has not acquired wealth."

For one by whom the means called wealth has not been acquired—that person who is thus "one whose wealth is unacquired"—and for that very reason, because such a person is deficient in the materials such as animals required for sacrifices and the like, they lack the qualification due to incapacity. Consequently, since those activities centered on injunctions (*niyoga*) which are to be accomplished through material substances are impossible for them, the acquisition of wealth must necessarily be performed. Furthermore, it is established in the *Karmakāṇḍa* that this [acquisition] is prompted by desire (*rāga*), and not prompted by the ritual sacrifice (*kratu*).

In that regard, if mandatory activities (*naiyogika-pravṛtti*) were to obstruct activities impelled by passion (*rāga-ākṣipta-pravṛtti*), then even the acquisition of wealth would be obstructed; therefore, since mandatory activity is impossible for that which lacks a means, those [passion-driven activities] too would be contradicted—this is the sense. He begins the presentation of another refutation with "Moreover" (*api ca*): there is no distinction whatsoever between an activity aimed at a visible result, such as sexual union, and an activity aimed at an invisible result, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, insofar as both are equally means to pleasure and are impelled by passion.

The meaning is that even those who are impelled by passion for pleasure [are included]. He demonstrates this very equality with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). The word *iti* is intended to indicate the essential nature [of the desire]. By the term "desire for heaven" (*sargakāma*), one refers to the activity already obtained through passion for heaven—according to the maxim "the desire for that [result] is indicated by its purpose"—and thereby prescribes a specific means for it, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; this is the meaning.

If it is granted that the engagement in activities for seen and unseen purposes is equally motivated by passion (*rāga*), then why is this so? To this he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). Even though the motivation by passion is equal, and likewise the attachment to the manifold of means for pleasure and so forth projected by passion is equal, what is the distinction such that the one [activity] pertaining to an injunction (*naiyogikī*) is conducive to the knowledge of the Self, while the other is not?

The meaning is that there is no practice whatsoever for the sake of visible ends (*dṛṣṭārtha*) that is not opposed to the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). He states the reason for this lack of distinction: "By desire" (*kāma*), etc. Desire (*kāma*) is attachment (*rāga*), which is the longing for pleasure; by means of it, the attraction of the mind is the same whether in an activity for a visible end or one for an invisible end (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Just as in an activity for a visible end, so too in an activity for an invisible end, the mind—drawn by the desire for pleasure such as heaven—is not concentrated and is incapable of the knowledge of the Self. Therefore, the sense is that even that [activity for an invisible end] is opposed to it.

Now, one might raise the following objection: "Since heaven is construed as a subordinate element (guṇa), the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices are not the means for attaining heaven as a desired object (kāmya); therefore, there is a distinction in that there is no mental projection of desire toward them. To this he says, "atha" (now). He states the refutation of that position: "varṇitam" (it has been described). The meaning is that it has already been explained that if the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites were not means for attaining desired objects, then the prosperity and misfortune of living beings would be accidental. He states another defect: "uktaśca" (and it has been said).

Furthermore, the principle stated by Jaimini in the sixth book—that heaven is connected as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—would be overturned; for the prefix *ud-* has the sense of "lifting up" or "extracting," while the prefix *prati-* signifies its opposite; thus, the meaning is that [the principle] would be cast down. He states that this position is also contradictory to what precedes and follows with the words "tulya... (equal...).

The meaning is as follows: since activities for seen and unseen ends have the same result, there is a contradiction; thus, the previous suspicion that there might be a cessation of activity for both seen and unseen ends would be cast far away and find no room, because if sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma were not means to [specific] desires, they would lack the quality of having the same result. (The analysis of the compound is: "that whose scope is cast far away. He raises a suspicion regarding the conformity of ritual injunctions to the knowledge of the Self by another method, starting with "Now" (*atha*).

When desire is not attained, a person who conforms to desires is unable to know the Self because of his lack of mental composure (*asamāhita*). When desirable objects are obtained through ritual injunctions, desires dissolve. Thus, by means of the attainment of desirable objects, the ritual injunctions cause desires and the longing for them to dissolve, thereby conforming to the qualification for the knowledge of the Self—this is the meaning. To support the point that liberation occurs for one whose desires have dissolved through the arising of knowledge, he cites scripture with the words "as it has been said. He refutes that [view] with the words "that too is incorrect."

He asks "Why? and answers with "Since... (yataḥ). You speak well: the meaning is that if those desires were to dissolve through the attainment of their objects, they would not, however, dissolve by that attainment. By what, then, do they dissolve? To this he says: "But rather... (api tu). The contemplation (*paribhāvanā*) of defects such as impermanence regarding sense-objects means reflecting upon them; dissolution occurs through *prasaṃkhyāna*, which is discernment (*viveka*) arising from that contemplation of defects. This is the meaning.

He states that contact with objects of desire causes the mind to go astray, using the word "even" (*kalayā*): even if the mind is touched by desirable things only to a slight degree (*mātrayā*), it is then indeed drawn away, completely captivated by those alluring things which have the power to steal the mind; the meaning is that the mind does not become free from desire for them. He confirms this very point with two citations from authoritative sources:

Regarding the phrase "it has been said": not only do the injunctions for ritual duties (*dharma*) not serve as causes for the dissolution of desires, but on the contrary, they produce the opposite effect. Thus he says: "Because they are not the means. In the absence of injunctions for action, this person would indeed turn away from desires because [action] is not the means, since sacrifices and other rites are merely means to desire. Furthermore, one should take recourse in the knowledge of the Self, which is "tranquility" (*upaśama*)—so called because by it one becomes tranquil—and which consists in the pacification of the entire residue of ignorance and the like.

But when ritual injunctions exist, a person for whom various means such as sacrifice and charity have been shown by them might become deeply attached to those very objects of desire—which, by their nature (prakṛti), are habitually captivating to the mind, or rather, which are habitually capable of captivating the mind’s nature (prakṛti) and instead tending to distort it; he would thus become even more firmly bound to them.

And there is the dissolution (*pravilaya*) of those desires; "dissolution" means that by which [desires] are dissolved. The meaning is that one should become weary of [the world] because self-knowledge and the like, being of that nature, act as destroyers of what is desired. Now, one might object: sensory pleasure is impermanent, meager, and accompanied by suffering; whereas the fruit of knowledge is supreme bliss, the opposite of that, according to the Vedic revelation, "For this is the supreme bliss. Therefore, it follows that desire should be directed toward that [bliss] alone, and that [knowledge] will eradicate the longing for sensory pleasure.

Thinking that, even though ritual injunctions exist, one might turn away from them out of a desire for their fruits and fail to become intent upon them, and might likewise be repelled by the knowledge of the Self, he says: "Even if heard" (*śruto’pi*). For the bliss of sense-objects has been experienced repeatedly; and it is precisely that which has been experienced which attracts the mind, not that which is accessible through mere hearing, because it has not been experienced—this is the sense. The phrase "even before" (*prāgevā*) means "how much more so. He concludes with: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Therefore, it is established that the injunctions regarding ritual action do not enter into the scope of the injunction for knowledge by means of the visible sublation of desire. Although the position that desire is sublated is the second [alternative], nevertheless, there is no fault in its being mentioned here in the context of refuting the view that ritual injunctions have utility only through a visible result. As for what was said—that in every part of the Veda, the sublation of some portion of the Veda is perceived—that too he restates and refutes with the words "As for what was said," the remainder of the sentence being "has been stated."

He asks how it is non-existent and says: "not this" (*anidam*); the remainder of the sentence is "of the statement 'one desiring creation should sacrifice'. He explains that very point with: "for not... The meaning of a word is that for which the word has purpose (*yatparaḥ śabdaḥ sa śabdārthaḥ*). However, this sentence regarding one desiring creation does not have as its primary purport the cognition of the reality of a self distinct from the body, because that would entail abandoning what is heard in the text and assuming what is not heard; rather, it has as its purport the injunction (*niyoga*) to perform the sacrifice. Therefore, its authority lies in this alone, and not in the former [the self]; this is the sense. Now, even if the reality of a self distinct from the body is not explicitly heard, nevertheless, since the body is impermanent... [p. 81]

Furthermore, because an insentient entity is incapable of experiencing heaven in another birth, it follows by implication that this reality of the Self is understood to be distinct from the body; and indeed, the meaning of the Veda may be understood even from passages intended for another purpose, as in the case of the injunction to wear [the sacred thread] above, which is derived from the explanatory passage stating, "For he holds it above for the gods. Therefore, with the intention that the sublation of the body as the Self is the purpose of the injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, he raises the objection with the words "Now, if... He refutes this with the words "That too... (P. 30-16).

The meaning is that this too is like the inference of an elephant by means of the word "elephant" when the elephant has already been seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); it is unnecessary because it is redundant. Now, one might object: "In that case, the elephant is established by perception, but here it is not so with the dissolution of the body and the self. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Directly" (*sākṣāt*). It is true that the injunction for the knowledge of the Self requires the dissolution of the body and the self, but since that [dissolution] is obtained through direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), it does not depend on that which is merely obtained through implication (*arthalabdha*).

Furthermore, there is the logical principle that "that which is a meaning derived from another meaning is not itself the primary meaning of the word. Consequently, the dissolution of the body and the self—which is to be understood through the [prior] meaning—is not the Vedic meaning within injunctions such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. On the other hand, since it is impossible to restate what has not already been established regarding the holding [of the breath], there is a difference in status: [the latter] is an injunction. Moreover, if even that which is established by the sense were to be considered the Vedic meaning, then for one who—believing that the impermanent body cannot be the enjoyer of fruits in future lives—possesses a mental knot consisting of desire for those fruits and the conceit of being the enjoyer, that knot might indeed become loosened.

Even though the Self is distinct from the body, just as that meaning of the Veda is to be understood through its own inherent sense, so too for a person who considers the enjoyment of fruits in another birth to belong to that eternal Self, the hardness—that is, the firmness—of the knot of desire and the like which results from that [Vedic teaching] must also be considered Vedic. Therefore, with the intention that injunctions such as the Jyotiṣṭoma would not achieve syntactic unity with the injunction for the knowledge of the detached Self because they are contrary to it, he says: "And by implication" (arthāt).

The meaning is that because various means are shown in the Vedas, the difficulty found in the section concerning desire and so forth would be Vedic in nature. The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the refutations. Having thus refuted the first position, he refutes the second position—that the injunctions for ritual action enter into the knowledge of the Self by way of suppressing desire—with the words "The second also... and so on.

The connection with the distant [conclusion] is as follows: because the capacity to sever desire for objects of desire has already been described in passages such as "Desire for desires never ceases," there is no evidence for the second position either—that ritual injunctions, which are self-sufficient regarding their own results such as heaven mentioned in their own sentences, enter into the injunction for the knowledge of the Self; thus, that second position is also inconsistent.

Furthermore, if ritual injunctions ending with those lasting a thousand years were subordinate to the injunction for knowledge, then—given that the subsidiary and the principal share a single qualification—a single seeker of liberation who is qualified for knowledge would have to perform the complete synthesis of all rituals. Consequently, there would be a combination (*samuccaya*) of all rituals with knowledge, and their performance by a single agent would be required; yet this is impossible, as he says: "In the case of a single qualification" (*ekādhikāratve*). The analysis of the compound is: "those in which there is the qualification of one. The particle *iti* marks the end of the section. 6 [p. 82]

Now, disregarding the subsequent positions which follow the order of the summary (uddesa), [the author] restates the position that self-knowledge is a subsidiary part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*) by way of purifying the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*), because much remains to be said regarding it; he does so with the words "Even those who... (*ye 'pi*). Previously it was stated that ritual action is a subsidiary part of knowledge; now, however, the meaning is the reverse—that knowledge is a subsidiary part of ritual action. He refutes that [position] with the words "By them... (*tair*).

The point is that even they must state some authority, such as direct scriptural testimony (*śruti*) or others, for the connection between knowledge and ritual actions; yet that is difficult to state. Now, one might object: "Just like the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) performed on rice-grains and so forth, self-knowledge is connected with rituals because it is a purificatory rite pertaining to the agent. Anticipating this, he states the dissimilarity between the two cases with the words "Not, first of all" (*na tāvat*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "There is no such authority for its connection with rituals as there is in those other cases."

Regarding that, he states the authority for the connection with the ritual action in sprinkling and so forth: "For in that case," etc. For in that case, since there would be no purpose for the sprinkling of the rice in its own form—which is not being employed in the ritual action and has not become a means—the word "rice" indicates elsewhere that which has become a means, because the sprinkling of the rice in its own form would otherwise be purposeless.

In that case as well, if the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) included by the context were connected with the means for the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of a non-contextual rite, there would be a sublation of the context; therefore, it is understood from the context that [the grain] is the means for the transcendental result of the contextual rite. Thus, the meaning is that the word *vrīhi* (rice/grain) makes known the connection of the sprinkling with the transcendental result of the contextual rite by way of defining it as being the means for the transcendental result of the contextual rite.

One might object: "Why should self-knowledge not be connected with ritual action even in the absence of a specific context, just as the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood [is connected]? To this he says: "Nor... The ellipsis of the sentence is: "Just as there is a connection with ritual action in the case of [the text], 'He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood,' so it is here. Why? He says: "Even there... Even there, the substance such as the *juhū* has an invariable connection with ritual action—that is, that whose connection with ritual action is not subject to deviation is so described.

For the substance such as the *juhū* ladle is indeed inherent in the ritual action (*karman*), and not elsewhere; therefore, even in the absence of a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), it brings the ritual action to mind—this is the meaning. Now, even if this is so, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is there a connection between the state of being made of *parṇa*-wood and the ritual action? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). In that case—that is, when [the ritual action] exists—or rather, in the sentence concerning the *parṇa*-wood, the connection with the ritual action occurs through the sentence itself; the words "of the state of being made of *parṇa*-wood" are to be supplied.

The sense is this: that sentence, by restating the *juhū* ladle—which has an inseparable connection with the sacrifice—prescribes the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood and thereby causes it to enter into the sacrifice. Having thus stated the reason for the connection with ritual action in the two examples, he declares its impossibility in the case of the subject at hand (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words: "But the knowledge of the Self... The knowledge of the Self is not heard of within the context (*prakaraṇa*), because the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*) lies outside the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*).

Nor does it have an invariable connection with a ritual (*kratu*), because the self’s status as an agent is accepted even in worldly action; this is the sense. Therefore, he says "by that" (*tena*), meaning that due to the absence of any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it cannot be asserted that the knowledge of the self is connected to ritual action by way of being a refinement of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*). Regarding the absence of such a connection between the knowledge of the self and ritual action [p.

He states what is intended as being established: "And thus" (tathā ca). Since there is no connection between the knowledge of the Self and ritual action, and since its purpose for another is unknown, the scriptural statement regarding the fruit—"and he does not return again"—is not a mere *arthavāda* (eulogistic supplement), according to the maxim: "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals, the mention of a fruit is an *arthavāda*. Therefore, because it possesses a distinct fruit, it possesses a distinct qualification; thus, the claim that "knowledge and action share a single qualification by way of mutual reversal" is refuted.

That which comes into being is called *bhāva*. Now, this would indeed be so if this were a scriptural statement of a result (*phala-śruti*); however, since this is a statement in the present tense—like the passage "streams of clarified butter flow"—and because there is no connection with a person desiring heaven (*svarga-kāma*) or the like, it is not by its own inherent force a statement of a result. Therefore, just as in the case of the *Rātri-satra*, where the phrase "they stand firm" (*pratitiṣṭhante*) was modified into "they should stand firm" (*pratitiṣṭheran*) and a result was thus postulated, so too must it be postulated here.

And that [result] would have to be postulated only if there were a desire for a result, as in the case of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice; however, when a visible result exists, there can be no desire for another result. Furthermore, the knowledge of the Self has a visible purpose: it is the motivation for engaging in ritual acts whose fruits are to be experienced in other bodies. Indeed, such engagement would not be possible without the knowledge of the eternal Self. Therefore, with the intention that one should not postulate a result by transforming the text, he raises the objection: "Now [atha]..."

Therefore, just as the injunction for Vedic study does not seek results such as explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) because its purpose is seen [in the study itself], so too is the injunction for the knowledge of the Self; thus he says, "Therefore. Furthermore, because there is no separate result, it is established that the qualification for the injunction of the knowledge of the Self is distinct from the qualification for ritual action; thus he says, "In the same way," where the particle *iti* signifies a reason. He refutes this by saying, "That too is incorrect. To the question "Why is it incorrect? he replies, "Because..."

Because the person who is to be inquired into in the Vedāntas is indeed other than the agent and enjoyer—the self required by the injunctions for ritual action—and is of the nature of a non-agent and non-enjoyer, known solely through the Upaniṣads and accessible only through them. Nor is knowledge of that [Upaniṣadic Self] a cause for engagement in ritual action; this is the meaning. Why is it not its cause? He says: "For not... An agent and an enjoyer engage in rituals; therefore, knowledge of that [agent/enjoyer] is the cause for engagement in ritual action, but knowledge of the Upaniṣadic Self is not.

The meaning is that agency and enjoyership do not belong to that which has the Self as its secret essence (upaniṣad). But why do agency and enjoyership not belong to it? To this he says: "Thus. "Does not eat" means he does not consume; "not eating" means not consuming—this is a negation of enjoyership. This is an illustration; one should also understand the negation of agency from such passages as "partless and actionless" and "he neither slays nor is slain."

Having thus stated that the Self, which is to be known through the Vedānta, does not engage in action, he says "But he who... (verse 6A) to show that one who engages in action as an agent and an enjoyer is not the Self known through the Vedānta.

The word *eva* (only/just) serves to emphasize. That which is the agent, the enjoyer, and the individual soul (*jīva*) is established by direct perception; it is self-evident through the immediate experience of "I" in worldly discourse. It is not the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because the latter has already been apprehended [by other means] and is therefore not accessible through the words of the Vedānta. This is the meaning. Here, an objection is raised: "But surely... The sense of the objection is: if there is non-difference between the individual soul and the Supreme Self, then when the Supreme Self is accessible through scripture, the individual soul must also be scriptural; how then can it be said that it is not accessible through scripture?

He confirms their identity through scripture with the word "thus" (evam). The scriptural passage, "Entering by means of this living self (jīva), let me manifest names and forms," expresses the non-difference between the living self and the Self (ātman) because of the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "by the living self" and because of the use of the first-person verb "let me manifest. The meaning is: how then can there be a difference between these two? The proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*), while accepting their real non-difference, states the distinction regarding what is accessible and inaccessible through words: "True," [he says].

However, that very *jīva*, which is non-different in its oneness yet possesses an imagined distinction like a reflection from its original (the *bimba*), has a single form called "the individual soul" (*jīva*) that is permeated by the power of agency, the *ahaṃkāra*, and ignorance—just as the original object appears darkened or otherwise when reflected in a mirror or similar medium. And because it is the cause for engaging in actions due to its agency, and because it is established through direct perception, it does not depend upon the Vedānta; therefore, it is not something to be known through the words [of the Upaniṣads].

However, that form of that very [Self] which is conjoined with ignorance (*avidyā*), which is self-luminous, and devoid of distinctions such as agency and so forth—that such a form is what is intended to be known through scripture, because it is not established in worldly transactions. Therefore, the meaning is this: even though there is non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), it is the Supreme, and not the individual soul, that is the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for scripture. Nor is it the case that the purpose seen for the activity in ritual acts is simply the knowledge of the Supreme born from the Vedāntas; thus he says: "And that... (*tac ca*).

Furthermore, that form which is to be known through the Vedānta is opposed to the engagement in ritual action; the meaning is: how could knowledge of that [form] have the observed engagement in ritual action as its purpose? He clarifies this opposition with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*). The meaning is that for a person who knows the Self whose nature is the bliss of Brahman and so forth, there exists neither a motive nor the capacity for engagement [in action]. The word *vā* is used in the sense of *ca* (and). Why, then, does one who knows the Self as Brahman lack both motive and capacity? To this he says: "because his desires are fulfilled" (*āptakāmatvāt*).

In this context, the state of having all desires fulfilled (*āptakāmatva*) is the reason for the absence of purpose (*niṣprayojanatva*). Furthermore, the absence of means such as instruments of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is the reason for incapacity regarding activity (*pravṛtti*). Regarding the state of having all desires fulfilled, the previously mentioned nature of supreme bliss (*paramānandarūpatva*) is the reason, because all forms of bliss are included therein. Moreover, non-duality (*advayatva*) is the reason for the absence of means such as the object of action (*karman*), the instrument (*sādhana*), and the agency (*itikartavyatā*); such is the distinction. Thus, it is the form bound by ignorance (*avidyā*) that is the cause for the engagement in action, and not the form taught in the Upaniṣads.

Therefore, it is established that such knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*). But surely, it is the knowledge of the Self taught in the Upaniṣads alone that is enjoined by the Śruti as an auxiliary to ritual action; so how can it be said that it is not?

The opponent raises an objection, stating "this might be so": even if the knowledge of the Self derived from the Upaniṣads is not an auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅga*) by way of a visible result, it might nevertheless serve as such through an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), just like the purpose (*prayojana*) and other factors. [The author replies: But it has already been stated that once activity has commenced, there may be an unseen purpose as in the case of the *prayojana* and so forth; however, for one who possesses the knowledge of the Self from the Upaniṣads, there is no engagement in ritual action at all, because such a person lacks both a purpose and a means [for performing action].

Therefore, it is asked: "In what way will the knowledge of the Self taught in the Upaniṣads become an auxiliary (aṅga) to the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa)? The opponent maintains that, based on these very scriptural passages to be cited hereafter, the scriptural statement regarding supreme non-dual bliss must be interpreted in a figurative sense; he cites those scriptural passages beginning with "That which... ("yadeva"). According to the opponent's intention, the word "by knowledge" ("vidyayā") refers to the knowledge of the Self.

Likewise, by means of showing that the fruits of rituals such as sacrifices are finite due to being devoid of the knowledge of Brahman—according to the Śruti: "O Gārgī, he who, not knowing this Imperishable, offers oblations, gives gifts, or performs austerities in this world for many thousands of years, his world is indeed finite"—there is a censure of mere ritual action. For it is said: "Censure is not intended to censure the object censured, but rather to praise something other than the censured. Thus, the praise of ritual action accompanied by knowledge is established.

And by the statement "and for the purpose of the injunction," it is shown that the knowledge of Brahman is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice. Likewise, in the passage "Knowledge and action both take hold of him," because the word *sam-* has the sense of "together," the coexistence of the knowledge of Brahman and action at the commencement [of the journey] is shown. And coexistence occurs in the commencement of an activity when there is a single performance; yet this is not like the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, because no fruit is heard of for the collection of those two as equal primaries, whereas a fruit is heard of from the sacrifice and so forth individually.

Sacrifices and the like are the primary acts because of their inherent capacity; knowledge is a subordinate part, according to the maxim: "That which is fruitless when in proximity to that which possesses fruit is a subordinate part of it. This is the sense. The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), however, says: "The former. That statement first presented—"Whatever one performs with knowledge"—refers specifically to the Udgītha-vidyā under discussion, which consists of the meditation on the syllables within the Udgītha, a division of the Sāman; it does not refer to the knowledge of Brahman.

Therefore, the meaning is that it does not indicate that this [meditation] is an auxiliary part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*). Although the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is a general term, the mention of the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) is used to show that it refers to a specific instance due to the particular context. The word *tāvat* signifies sequence. To the question, "In what way is the Udgītha-knowledge the subject under discussion?", he says: "Om."

Likewise, following the passage beginning with “Whatever one wins through knowledge,” the subsequent statement, “He who, not knowing this Imperishable,” performs a praise of the knowledge of the Imperishable by censuring ritual action as having perishable results; it does not, however, intend to establish that the knowledge of Brahman is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of ritual action. But [an objection may be raised]: is it not understood from the censure of mere ritual action that the injunction implies its association with knowledge? Not so; for if that were the case, the text would subsequently praise ritual action as being accompanied by knowledge.
But here, by such passages as, "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world having known this Imperishable, he is of Brahman," the knowledge of the mere Imperishable is praised; therefore— [p.

There is no fault [in our position], for the intent here is precisely to praise knowledge and the knower (*dakṣarajñāna*), and not to enjoin the conjunction of knowledge and action. Likewise, he states that even in the case of the simultaneous undertaking (*anvārambha*) of knowledge and action, there is no conjunction: "Knowledge... The word "separately" (*bhedena*) means "by way of distinction. He explains this very distinction: "One who possesses knowledge... Now, one might object: since the prefix *sam-* conveys the sense of "together," how can it be explained in this way? We reply: because the unity or conjunction of knowledge and action is impossible.

How is it that there is no possibility? It is said: first of all, there is no joint undertaking (*sāhitya*) of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) and ritual action (*karman*) in their commencement, because they are mutually independent. Their mutual independence follows from the scriptural mention of separate fruits, just as in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Agnihotra; for joint undertaking would only occur if there were a single fruit, as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. However, the higher knowledge is an obstacle to ritual action; how then could it be combined with action? Nor does it initiate another birth, since its fruit is liberation (*apavarga*).

Therefore, the status of being an auxiliary to action belongs only to the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) when it is distinguished [from higher knowledge]. As it has been said: “The distinction is like that of a hundred [coins]” (*vibhāgaḥ śatavat*). Furthermore, the word *sam* does not intend the sense of “together,” but is a restatement of the sense of “properly. Hence, it is well stated: “by way of distinction. He concludes the meaning of the section with the words “therefore” (*tasmāt*). The phrase “even so” (*evamapi*) means “even by way of reversal. Alternatively, it means that it is not only because self-knowledge has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), but even so, because it is enjoined by scripture as having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*).

Having thus refuted the opposing view that knowledge is an auxiliary to ritual action (*karma*), he restates another position in order to refute it, beginning with the words "those who also... The phrase "they consider [them] to be unrelated" is to be connected with what follows. To the question "How is there a contradiction between these two?", he says: "Because of duality... Ritual action has as its object the duality of means and so forth, whereas self-knowledge has as its object the Self devoid of duality; therefore, because of this contradiction, there is no connection (*ananvaya*). The word "iti" here signifies the reason. He states the refutation with the words "of them... To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth..."

If ritual action, having duality as its object, is incompatible with non-dual knowledge and thus does not connect with it, then the duality consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*) would likewise not connect with it. And without the connection to such means as the instruments of knowledge, knowledge cannot arise; consequently, the meaning is that non-dual knowledge itself would never be produced. Now, it might be argued: the distinction between the means of knowledge and so forth is the *upāya* (means), while non-dual knowledge is the *upeya* (the goal to be attained); and because of their temporal sequence, there is no simultaneity between the two.

Otherwise, there would be no relationship of means and end at all, like that between the left and right horns of an animal; therefore, since these two are not contradictory due to their difference in time, there is no fault of non-arising of the knowledge of non-duality when they are related to one another. To this he says: "Now" (*atha*). If there is no contradiction between the distinction of means and so forth and the realization of non-duality, then even when that realization has arisen, one must continue to proceed in exactly the same way by means of the distinction of means and so forth; consequently, there is no attainment of non-duality, and thus the undesirable consequence of the absence of liberation follows.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "It indeed dissolves. The meaning is that when the realization of non-duality (*advaita*) is attained, the entire distinction between the means of knowledge and so forth indeed dissolves; therefore, there is no consequence of the impossibility of liberation. If, upon the knowledge of non-duality, the duality of the means of knowledge and so forth dissolves, then it follows that there is a contradiction between the two—like that between light and shade—and that the distinction of the means of knowledge and so forth cannot serve as a means [to that knowledge]; for a thing that is itself being dissolved is never seen to function as a means to anything.

Therefore, there is neither contradiction nor the status of being a means for the differentiation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth; having raised this doubt, he says: "And not... In that regard, he first states the reason for the lack of contradiction: "Of the means... Contradiction does not arise merely from the relationship between that which is to be dissolved and that which dissolves, but rather from a difference in time; for even in the case of such things as shadow and sunlight, there is no contradiction when they exist at different times. And here, there is a difference in time between those two; therefore, the sense is that there is no contradiction. He states the reason for its being a means: "And when..."

The meaning is this: when this knowledge of Brahman arises, duality consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth dissolves; it does not exist prior [to that knowledge]. Furthermore, previously it serves as the means, and at that time, it remains undissolved. For this reason as well, it is not the case that [Brahman] lacks a means; thus he says: "Difference" (*bheda*). Since the knowledge of non-duality is an effect, there must necessarily be a cause for it. Nor can non-dual Brahman itself be its cause, because Brahman is not an agent (*akārakatvāt*), and because [if it were], there would follow the undesirable consequence of the effect being produced eternally.

Therefore, the sense is that by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), there must exist a duality consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth. Alternatively, the sense is that just as another kind of difference is seen to be a means for realizing the non-difference of universals (*sāmānya*) and so on, so too will there be a difference among the means of knowledge and the rest. Having thus raised the opponent's objection, he refutes the contradiction stated by the opponent—which serves as the reason for the lack of connection between action and knowledge—by relying on that very point, saying: "No."

If it is argued that the duality of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, being merely instrumental, exists at a different time [from the result] and therefore does not contradict the knowledge of non-duality (*advaita*), then in that case, there would likewise be no contradiction for that [knowledge] with ritual actions (*karman*), since they too are instrumental and thus exist at a different time; and consequently, the implication is that there is no connection between that [knowledge] and them. Now, the opponent, challenging the very instrumentality of ritual actions on the grounds of their lack of utility, challenges the connection by saying: "It might be so" (*syāt*). This [instrumentality] of ritual actions and the resulting connection might indeed exist, provided that they were actually useful.

However, that very [Brahman], because it is eternal and thus not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*), does not exist [as an object of action]. Nor can there be the status of a means for that which is not useful for the accomplishment of an effect; nor is there a requirement for what is not a means; nor is there a connection for that which is not required—this is the sense. He cites scripture regarding the uselessness of ritual actions: "It is heard," etc. The meaning of this is: liberation (*mokṣa*), which is uncreated and not an effect, being the very nature of Brahman, does not exist, does not come into being, and is not accomplished by means of performed action (*kṛta-karman*).

One might object: "Granted that there may be no utility for ritual actions regarding Brahman, which is unattainable through them; but who can prevent their utility in the arising of knowledge of It, just as the distinction between means of valid cognition and so forth is necessary? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not... He states the reason: "Of knowledge... Knowledge is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not dependent upon ritual action; otherwise, [p. 88]...

Action (*karman*) would also have to be a seventh means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, the meaning is that only the means of valid cognition is useful for the arising of knowledge, not actions. Now, one might object: "Even if actions have no utility in the arising of knowledge, they will nonetheless be useful as auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) in the arising of the effect of knowledge. Anticipating this, he says: "And not... Why? He says: "Of knowledge... For auxiliary status belongs to those things that act together to produce an effect, such as the earth and other elements in relation to a sprout.

The meaning is that for the knowledge of the Self, there is no other effect than the determination of its own object. Now, one might object: "But there is indeed another effect of knowledge, namely liberation (mokṣa); and thus liberation is heard to result from knowledge. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not of that" (*na tasya*). Liberation is the very nature of Brahman, and that is accepted as eternal; if it were an effect, it would consequently be non-eternal. Alternatively, the point is that if liberation were an effect, then because of its non-eternality, there would be a return to worldly existence for the liberated one.

[The opponent objects: "Granted that liberation (*mokṣa*) itself may not be the direct object to be accomplished, nevertheless, the destruction of the cause of bondage will be the object to be accomplished by knowledge; therefore, the utility of ritual actions (*karman*) as auxiliary factors in that regard is logically established. Furthermore, since this effect, namely destruction, is eternal, the fault of impermanence will not apply. With this intention, the opponent says: "The cause of bondage... [The author replies: But liberation is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), not the mere severance of the cause of bondage.

If it were to be accomplished by knowledge (*jñāna*), then knowledge would result in a fruit that is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) and would thus be unworthy of being pursued; and from what [other cause] would liberation (*mok�a*) then arise? For no other means for that [liberation] than knowledge is heard of in scripture. Anticipating this objection, he himself says: "Thus" (*iti*). The word "thus" indicates a reason (*hetu*); because the severance of the cause of bondage is the objective to be accomplished by knowledge, therefore, when that cause of bondage has been severed by knowledge, one is liberated due to the absence of that cause of bondage.

Furthermore, since knowledge has liberation as its fruit, it does not have a non-human goal as its fruit; nor is liberation impossible because there is no means [other than knowledge]. This is the intended meaning. To refute this, he asks: "What? The other replies: "Ignorance. He refutes that: "In that case, not... The point is that there is no cessation of ignorance distinct from and separate from knowledge that could be accomplished by knowledge, wherein action might serve as a cooperative cause. He explains why it does not exist: "Because..."

Non-apprehension (*avidyā*) is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of apprehension; its cessation is precisely the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), which consists in apprehension, because the arising of any positive entity (*bhāva*) necessarily involves the destruction of its own prior non-existence. Therefore, the cessation of ignorance is not something to be accomplished separately by knowledge, such that ritual actions (*karman*) could serve as its auxiliary cause. This is the sense. Here, an objection is raised: "It might be so. Granted that in the case of ignorance characterized as non-apprehension, the cessation of ignorance is simply the arising of knowledge and thus there is no separate effect to be accomplished; however, this is not so in the case of ignorance characterized as erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*). [p. 89]

The very arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cessation of error (*viparyaya*); therefore, the cessation of that [error] is not to be accomplished separately from knowledge. And thus, the idea is that there is an application of ritual actions (*karman*) as auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) in that regard. Anticipating the objection—"Why should the cessation of erroneous cognition not be the very arising of knowledge, just like the cessation of non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*)?"—he states the distinction: "Indeed, not... Non-apprehension is indeed antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); its cessation is logically possible only through the arising of a positive entity (*bhāva*). (P. 32-21)

But erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*) is a distinct entity from knowledge (*vidyā*); and knowledge is not a distinct entity that constitutes the cessation of erroneous cognition, which is itself a distinct entity. Why? He says: "For not... If entities were mutual absences, then one distinct entity would be the absence of another distinct entity; but this is not the case. Therefore, the absence of one distinct entity from another distinct entity is something to be established separately, and in that regard, the inclusion of ritual actions (*karman*) is possible; such is the sense.

He asks "Why? and says: "Because of being non-existence" (*abhāvatva*). For if things were by nature non-existent, they would lack the nature of existence and thus would be non-existent; consequently, everything would be void—this is the sense. The opponent himself raises the doubt: "If... It is certainly not the case that one who perceives reality possesses erroneous cognition; therefore, the non-apprehension of reality is the cause of erroneous cognition.

Therefore, when ignorance—which consists of the knowledge of reality—has ceased, false cognition will cease of its own accord simply through the cessation of its cause. Thus, even though it is a distinct entity, its cessation is not to be accomplished separately by knowledge such that there would be an occasion for the entry of ritual actions; this is the sense. Having raised this objection, he refutes it with the words "And that... It might be so if non-apprehension were the cause of something; but this is not the case, for non-apprehension is an absence (abhāva), and an absence is not the cause of anything.

Therefore, the meaning is that this is not the case for error either. Why? He says: "fainting and so forth. If non-apprehension were the cause of error, then since that [non-apprehension] exists during fainting and similar states, erroneous cognition would follow as a consequence; yet such is not the case. This is the meaning. If non-apprehension is not the cause of error, then what is its cause? He asks: "What then? He provides the answer: "beginningless... and so on.

It has been stated during the explanation of the phrase "the immortal, unborn" that beginningless, purposeless, and indefinable ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-avidyā*); this is the meaning. Nor should it be asked what the cause of that [ignorance] is, for he says "and there," meaning that because it is beginningless. Alternatively, the meaning is that when that beginningless ignorance exists, the objection as to what the cause of the error might be finds no ground.

If, however, you maintain that there is a cause for error other than beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), that too can be demonstrated; thus he says: "By error," etc. The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is the cause of the erroneous cognition that grasps the phenomenal world. What, then, is the cause of that?

It is said that even for that [error], the cause is precisely a contrary cognition (*viparyayajñāna*). Thus, since both are beginningless and established in a relationship of cause and effect—like a seed and a sprout—there is no fault such as being without a cause; this is the meaning. Therefore, in this way, the cessation of error does not occur through the mere removal of non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*), but rather it is brought about by knowledge (*vidyā*); consequently, there would be a requirement for an auxiliary factor for the correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) which is to be accomplished therein.

And since that [sublation] exists, he concludes that there is a connection between actions and their results. The proponent of non-connection (asaṃbandhavādī) refutes this with the words "And this... (P. 38-4); the meaning is that even this is without substance. He asks, "In what way is it without substance? and replies: "Not indeed... (na khalu). The word *svalpa* is used for the sake of indicating what is well-known (*prasiddhi*). This is well-known in the world: when correct knowledge arises regarding mother-of-pearl and the like following an erroneous cognition, people do not exert a separate effort for the cessation of the erroneous cognition, because the production of correct knowledge itself effects that cessation.

The meaning is that they do not depend upon any other auxiliary cause for right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) besides [the means of valid cognition], such that karma would enter into it as an auxiliary factor. Anticipating the objection—"Why do they not strive for the cessation of error by means of right knowledge, just as one strives with a sickle for the purpose of reaping? Or why do they not depend on an auxiliary [cause] in the same way?"—he says:

For if the cessation of erroneous knowledge were a separate effect from right knowledge—just as cutting is a separate effect from the sickle—then one would have to exert oneself separately for the cessation of error by means of right knowledge, just as one exerts oneself for cutting by means of a sickle; or else, one would require some other auxiliary cause. But this is not the case; for right knowledge is not produced first like a sickle and only later employed for the cessation of false knowledge. What then? The very production of that [right knowledge] is itself the cessation of false knowledge.

The meaning is this: since the very arising of another entity that is the opposite of ignorance constitutes the destruction of the preceding [ignorance], what need is there for a separate effort? By specifying "the opposite" (*virodhin*), it is indicated that if every other entity in general were the destruction of the preceding, then the existence of a jar would entail the destruction of the clay; thus, the inclusion of the term "opposite" is necessary. Furthermore, the previously mentioned fault—that everything would result in non-existence—does not apply here, because an entity is indeed the absence of others, whereas the absence of others is not itself an entity.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the destruction of the preceding thing is simply the arising of another contradictory entity, rather than a void? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is not a void. The meaning is that a void entity is nothing at all. Why so? He says: "Otherwise. If destruction were a void, then, like the horn of a hare, it would be non-productive; consequently, since there would be no causal operation upon it, it would be causeless. Yet, its being caused by a hammer or similar instruments is well-established—this is the sense.

One might object: "Let it be that the destruction of a preceding entity is simply the arising of another, contradictory entity; however, since *vidyā* (knowledge) belongs to the same genus as knowledge (*jñāna*), it cannot be the opposite of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And it is contradictory. The intention is as follows: being of a different genus (*vijātitva*) or the same genus (*sajātitva*) is not the basis for contradiction or non-contradiction. For there is no contradiction between two things of different genera, such as color and taste, when they exist in the same place; and conversely, there is contradiction even between things of the same genus, as when one poison neutralizes another poison, or milk [neutralizes] milk. [p. 91]

"It wears away" (*jarayati*); therefore, that which causes the cessation of something is its opposite. And since knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cause of the cessation of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), it is its opposite. He asks, "What follows from that? and says: "That" (*tat*). When the very arising of the opposite state is the destruction of the prior [state], and knowledge is the opposite, then the arising of knowledge itself is the destruction of false knowledge; thus, upon the arising of knowledge, false knowledge has indeed perished.

Therefore, just as one does not exert oneself separately for the purpose of reaping with a sickle once [the grain] is already cut, nor does one require auxiliary factors, the point is that there is no connection between knowledge and action for the sake of removing erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*). Now, it may be argued: this might be so if ignorance (*avidyā*) were the cause of bondage; however, actions are the causes of bondage, and knowledge is not their opposite, but rather the opposite of ignorance.

Therefore, since the destruction of karma is not identical to the arising of knowledge, it is not something to be accomplished separately by knowledge; thus, with the intention that there might be an entry of karma as a cooperative factor in that regard, he raises an objection: "Now, it might be said... He refutes this with: "And that... This is what is meant: actions are manifestations of ignorance, and upon the cessation of ignorance, they cease of their own accord through the removal of their cause; their cessation is not something to be accomplished separately, wherein actions would need to be required as cooperative factors.

Because ignorance is the root, as long as ignorance exists, there is merely the conventional distinction that "this is karma" and "this is its fruit. That [state] is described as such because in it all the various diversities of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) have been wiped away—that is, entirely eliminated. Therefore, the meaning is: when that pure consciousness arises, how could [such distinctions] possibly exist? The use of the word "merely" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of indicating their lack of ultimate reality. He confirms this point with scripture, saying "And thus... (*tathā ca*).

The meaning is that because action is mentioned alongside error and doubt—which do not depend on action for their cessation by right knowledge—as if they were equal in being removable by right knowledge, it is determined that [ignorance] too is removable by right knowledge independently of action. The "knot of the heart" is considered to be error (*viparyāsa*). Having raised the objection that there might be another way in which actions are connected with knowledge, he refutes it with the words "Now, however" (*atha*). For in the case of knowledge, only doubt and error are the impurities, and nothing else.

And since those [objections] have been refuted by the impossibility [of karma functioning] within knowledge produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the meaning is that even for the sake of its cessation, dependence upon karma is useless. Again, suspecting a connection between knowledge and karma through another method, he says: "Now, it might be thought... (*atha matam iti*).

That direct perception is realized in which even apart from the knowledge of Brahman produced by words, there is the dissolution of all distinctions—that is, the appearance of the manifold diversity of the phenomenal world—and therefore it transcends all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), being devoid of the conceptualization of the world beginning with space; that is the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattva*). And that very [perception] has Brahman as its object.

The meaning is: [the object] is not the subject matter for that [cognition] which has the habit of grasping the mutual association of distinct and manifold word-meanings produced by the words of the Vedānta. This is what is being said: non-dual Brahman can indeed be known only through perceptual knowledge in which all dualistic conceptual constructions have dissolved, but not through verbal knowledge; for the latter, having as its object the meaning of a sentence—which consists of the association of various word-meanings—is dualistic in nature, and therefore does not lead to the realization of non-dual Brahman. P.

33-17. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In its production" (*tadutpattau*). This is a locative of motive (*nimitta-saptamī*), as in the expression "one kills the leopard for its skin. It should be understood that, in the context of discussing the connection with action (*karman*), the connection with meditation (*upāsanā*) and so forth has been shown incidentally by the same logic. Meditation (*upāsana*) means constant reflection day after day. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and other such practices are included. Having raised this objection, he refutes it with the word "Who? (*kaḥ*).

What is the distinction between this perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) and verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*), by virtue of which one seeks that perceptual knowledge even when verbal knowledge has already arisen, and for the sake of which ritual actions are required? The sense is that there is no distinction whatsoever, because verbal knowledge such as "This Self is 'not this, not this'" (*sa eṣa neti netyātmā*) and "This alone is the one without a second" (*eka evāyamādvitīyaḥ*) is likewise non-dual in its object.
