The other [opponent] states the distinction of perception from verbal knowledge: "It is the quality of appearing clearly. He refutes that with "No."

Let it be granted that perception possesses clarity; nevertheless, it need not be sought for that purpose. The meaning is that clarity itself is useless. He states this lack of utility with the words "for knowledge... Knowledge is required for the attainment of the object of knowledge, and since that [attainment] does not fail to occur through verbal knowledge, what is the use of clarity? Therefore, the point is that perception need not be sought for that sake.

[Objection: "If that is so, then since every cognition produced by other means of knowledge culminates in perception (*pratyakṣa*), let perception itself be sought after; [the author] anticipates this objection with the words 'of cognition' (*pramiteḥ*). The analysis of the compound is: 'that for which perception is the supreme or primary' (*pratyakṣaṃ paraṃ pradhānaṃ yasyāḥ*); the meaning is 'because it culminates in perception. This connects with what will be said later, 'that is sought after' (*tadarthyate*). Why does cognition culminate in perception? To this he says: 'therein' (*tatra*)."

The meaning is that when that perception exists, there is a lack of curiosity on the part of the knower (*pramātṛ*). To illustrate: even though fire and so forth have been cognized at a distance by means of smoke and other signs, the knower desires to cognize them again through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "Not so. For not every act of cognition culminates in perception, since there is a deviation in the case of the Vedic cognition of *dharma* and the like; furthermore, even regarding fire and such, the knower requires proximity for practical activity (*vyavahāra*), but not necessarily the cognition of perception.

The sense is that, by chance, she may be present at that which is intended; however, when the sun’s motion and so forth are in proximity to Brahman, she is not there, and yet the knower remains free from longing. Therefore, valid cognition (*pramiti*) does not have direct perception as its ultimate goal, but rather has the mere apprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) as its goal. Once that object of knowledge has been apprehended, what else could be desired? The meaning is: nothing at all. Anticipating the objection that even when the object of knowledge has been apprehended, another means of knowledge might still be required, he refutes it with the words "another means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāntaram*).
For another means of knowledge... [p. 93]

The meaning is this: another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is required for the sake of establishing the object of cognition (*prameya*), not for its own sake; and since the object of cognition has already been established by the preceding means of knowledge, the requirement for another means of knowledge is indeed useless. If it is argued that it is not useless, because there will be a need for the re-establishment of an object of cognition even though it has already been established—this is not so. If there is a purpose in re-establishing what has already been established, then that will be accomplished by the very same preceding means of knowledge. Even so, the requirement for another means of knowledge remains entirely useless.

Anticipating this doubt, he says "again" (*punaḥ*). This has been stated while provisionally accepting the possibility of repeated establishment (*siddhi*); however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), since the knower (*pramātṛ*) achieves complete satisfaction through a single establishment alone, there is no reason for a desire for repeated establishment. Thus he says "of that which is already established" (*siddhasya*). [Objection: Even for an object of knowledge established through scripture (*āgama*), there exists perception (*pratyakṣa*) as another means distinct from scripture; therefore, a requirement for repeated establishment arises from that [perception].

And so, how can it be said that "there is no cause"? Having raised the objection that the existence of another means (*upāyāntara*) constitutes the cause, he refutes it with the words "another means. [The opponent suggests: "In that case, let another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) be required as something to be assisted. [The author replies: But regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*), there is indeed a lack of further expectancy on the part of the knower (*pramātṛ*) because it has already been established. Furthermore, once the object of knowledge is established, another means of knowledge cannot be required in itself; for the purpose of such requirement is precisely the establishment of the object of knowledge—this is the intended meaning.

Now, one might raise the objection: even for that which is already established as dear, there arises a special degree of affection upon its being established again; and the Self is indeed dear, according to the Vedic scripture, “This is dearer than a son. Therefore, since this special affection is the cause for requiring a further establishment [of the Self], the author refutes this by stating, “affection,” and so forth. The meaning is:

even if a special degree of affection arises from the repeated cognition of something already known and desired, nevertheless, that [affection] is established through repeated perception even from what was previously produced by a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa); thus, another means of valid knowledge need not be sought for the sake of establishing a special degree of affection.

Furthermore, if that which is already known through scripture were to be known again by means of perception for the sake of a particular pleasure, then even that which is seen through perception would be known by others through inference and so forth, because there would be no distinction [between them] since a particular pleasure could arise in those cases as well. Thus he says: "seen through perception. Nor can it be argued that it will not be known by those other means because they lack definitiveness; thus he says: "definitiveness."

In the reading "niścāyakatve," however, having stated the absence of distinction in the state of being determinative, the reason for that is given: "of the others. For that which is determinative is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and these [other means] are also means of valid cognition; therefore, the meaning is that they are determinative. "Because of the state of being a means of valid cognition" means "because of being a means of valid cognition. Now, it might be argued: perception has a proximate object, and what is proximate is fit for rejection or acquisition; whereas inference and the rest have remote objects, and by means of them one cannot engage in practical activity (*vyavahāra*).

[The opponent might argue: "Even that which has been cognized by other means will be sought to be cognized through perception, but not that which has already been cognized by perception will be sought to be cognized by others. Anticipating this, he says: *hānādi* (and so forth). That whose object is fit for rejection (*hāna*) and the like is described as such. That whose object is a proximate thing is [described as] "having a proximate object" (*saṃnikṛṣṭārtha*). "Because it has a proximate object" is the reason for its having an object fit for rejection and the like. He refutes that: if a proximate [object] were required... [p. 94]

In that case, it is the cause itself that brings the object of cognition (*prameya*) near to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), or else it is the movement of the cognizer toward the object that must be accepted as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); however, this is not the *pramāṇa*, for the *pramāṇa* is required for the sake of valid cognition (*pramiti*), and that [cognition] is already established by the preceding *pramāṇa*. This is the meaning. And in the present context, regarding the Self (*ātman*) as the object of cognition, there is no distinction characterized by being "near" or "not near," such that perception would need to be required for the sake of proximity; for the Self is eternally and most intimately proximate. With this intention, he says: "And in the present context... (P. 34-4).

Now, suppose it is thought: "Words and the like have universals as their objects, whereas perception has particulars as its object; therefore, even though something is known through a word in its universal aspect, perception is required to know it in its particular aspect. That is incorrect; for in that case, the particular form—which was not at all apprehended by the word as a means of knowledge—would become the object of perception. And thus our own position is established: there is no need for a further means of proof for what is already established. Anticipating all these objections, he says: "The universal... and so forth.

The other [opponent] now objects in the same manner: "Certainly! This is also our own view, namely, that perception has as its object that which is not already known through verbal testimony; therefore, for that purpose, there will be a requirement for ritual action, meditation, and so forth—this is the intention. He refers to what was stated: "And that [Brahman] is the domain of Brahman, not of verbal testimony. This is the meaning of what was stated there. He refutes this with the words "If... and so on.

If Brahman is not specifically understood through the means of verbal testimony (śabda), how then can meditation on that Brahman proceed in its specific form? The implication is that it is impossible to meditate upon what is unknown. Nor should it be argued that one will meditate upon the general form understood from words, while the specific form will become directly perceived (aparokṣa); for it is impossible to realize one thing when something else is being meditated upon. Thus he says: "Nor... (na ca).

Furthermore, the claim that words have only the universal (sāmānya) as their object is unproven, because from them there is also the cognition of specific qualities such as being free from evil (apahatapāpman) and bliss (ānanda). For if the nature of the human goal consisting of freedom from evil, bliss, and so forth were not understood from words, then for the sake of realizing what form would the injunction of sacrifices and other rites by the scripture stating "by sacrifice, by giving," etc., be intended? Indeed, it would not be intended at all. With this intention, he asks: "And of what [form]? (kasya ca).

He states both points—how the injunctions for sacrifices and the like are possible when the specific nature [of the Self] is known through scripture, and how they are not possible when it is unknown—with the words "Through scripture" (*śabda*). This is the meaning: if the Self, whose essential nature is Brahman consisting of bliss and so forth, were revealed by scripture, then, upon the need for means to attain human goals such as bliss, the injunction of sacrifices and the like would be logically established.

The sense is this: if, through verbal testimony (*śabda*), that which is of the nature of human ends—such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth—is not apprehended, while that which is its opposite, being of the nature of what is not a human end, is apprehended as the Self (*ātman*), then the injunctions for sacrifice and other rites would be "of non-existent purpose" (*asadartha*), meaning they would have no existing object and be rendered useless. Therefore, even the specific forms such as bliss are understood from verbal testimony; this is the intended meaning. The phrase "of that Brahman whose nature is indicated by verbal testimony as consisting of unsurpassed bliss, freedom from evil (*apahatapāpman*), and so forth" means the Self whose very essence is that [Brahman].
In that context, "unsurpassed bliss" refers to the human end consisting in the attainment of what is desired.

The distinction is that "one whose evil has been struck away" (apahatapāpman) means one whose undesirable states have ceased to exist. "Whose nature is the goal of man" (avidita-puruṣārtha-rūpa) refers to the self as the primary object denoted by the word. He concludes with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). When the Self, whose nature consists of qualities such as having evil struck away, becomes manifest through the authoritative verbal testimony (śabda) that is free from doubt and uncertainty, there remains no other means of perception (pratyakṣa) to be required; therefore, the intention is that verbal knowledge alone is the cause of liberation (apavarga).

Now, one might object: "If verbal knowledge alone is the cause of liberation, then once it has arisen, the attributes of transmigratory existence such as hunger and thirst ought to cease; yet these are seen even when the identity with Brahman—'I am indeed Brahman'—is understood from the word 'That thou art. Therefore, for the removal of those [attributes], some other direct realization (sākṣātkāra) must be required. Thus he raises the objection with the words "Now, [one might say]... (nanu).

Although the statement “That thou art” expresses the Self’s state of being Brahman, and not Brahman’s state of being the Self, nevertheless, by implication, that too is stated; thus it is called the identity of Brahman and the Self. He refutes this, saying: “No. The attributes of the body and senses—like the properties of lac applied to a gem—are superimposed upon the Self through false knowledge and do not exist in reality. Therefore, when that [superimposition] is destroyed by right vision, how could there be the possibility of those attributes, which are caused by it, in the Self? This is the meaning.

The analysis of the compound is: "one by whom the nature of Brahman has been realized. For this very reason, he is called "one who has known the reality of the Self," meaning one by whom the reality of the Self—that is, its form as the ultimate truth (paramārtha)—has been known. He states that there is not only logical reasoning (upapatti) for this point, but also scriptural authority (śruti), saying: "And it is heard [in scripture]. The sense is that if the attributes of transmigratory existence were to persist, the realization of the state of being Brahman for the knower of Brahman, as declared by scripture, would be impossible.

And he says "not" [in the verse] to show that these qualities do not belong to Brahman alone, such that even those who know Brahman would have to conform to them. The meaning is that, being caused by merit and demerit, they cannot exist in Brahman, who is "stripped of evil" (*apahatapāpmā*). By the term "evil" (*pāpma*), merit is also implied. On this very point, he cites another scriptural passage, saying "likewise."

If one should know the Self as supreme bliss, non-dual, then desiring what, or for the sake of what desire for sons and so forth, would he suffer—that is, burn with pain—the body, which is conditioned by the body? Thus [the text] states that the knower transcends the attributes of transmigratory existence. And another scriptural passage says the same: "Thus," where the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "indeed" (*eva*). Now, it might be argued that this scripture declares the absence of contact with the pleasant and unpleasant for one who is bodiless after the fall of the body, but not for one who is still living.

An objection is raised: "The involvement with the phenomena of saṃsāra was described as occurring even while the knower of the Self is alive, and that indeed occurs only while one possesses a body; how then can it be said, according to the scriptural texts concerning the bodiless state (*aśarīra*), that this does not exist? Anticipating this, he says: "It is false. For the connection of the Self with a body in saṃsāra is not caused by karma, because the Self is actionless (*niṣkriya*) according to the scripture, "Without parts, without activity" (*niṣkalaṃ niṣkriyam*).

For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence [of such a state] occurring even toward sons and others. Rather, it is caused by that false conceit of selfhood (*mithyātmakatvābhimāna*)—the notion "I" directed toward the non-self body—which is mistakenly regarded as real. When that connection with the body ceases due to the cessation of its cause through the vision of the true nature of the Self as distinct from the body, then, even while the mere residual impression persists and the appearance of the body continues, one is "bodiless even while living"; this is the meaning. (P. 34-22)

Having thus explained the state of being bodiless (*aśarīratva*), he applies the meaning of the scriptural passage to it with the word "therein" (*tatra*). "Therein," that is, in such a state of bodilessness, the non-contact with the pleasant (*priya*) and the unpleasant (*apriya*) is declared of the Self; the remainder of the sentence is "by this scriptural passage. He concludes with "therefore" (*tasmāt*). He states the distinction (*vyatireka*) with "but he who... (*yas tu*). "In that way" (*tathā*) means one who partakes in the attributes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). The particle "iti" marks the end of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It might be argued: “Since Brahman is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*), ritual action (*karman*) is of no use. Having begun with this and having refuted various types of connections between ritual action and knowledge, [the author] again raises the objection regarding a connection with ritual action, meditation (*upāsanā*), and so forth, for the sake of achieving direct experiential realization (*pratyakṣānubhava*). Then he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): “Liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) comes from verbal knowledge alone, not from direct experiential realization; therefore, even for that purpose, there is no need for ritual action or meditation. This is introduced with the words “It is considered” (*alocyata*). Here he provides an illustration with the words “Just as” (*yathā*).

The connection with the preceding [sentence] is as follows: for those persons who have ascertained the reality of the directions and the moon through the word of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*), errors such as the perception of two moons or the misapprehension of directions continue to occur. He applies this to the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "likewise" (*tathā*): for that person by whom the reality of the Self has been understood from the doubt-free sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), there persists the recurrence of false appearances due to the power of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). These impressions are produced by the repeated practice of beginningless false perception, are accompanied by it, and arise spontaneously.

Therefore, for its cessation, something other than verbal knowledge must be required. He states what that requirement is with the words "And that. The practice of the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), which sublates false perception, is established in the world itself through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as being the cause of strengthening mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Sacrifices and the like are also established by verbal authority (*śabda-pramāṇa*), as in the passage beginning, "Him [one reaches] by sacrifice" (*tam etaṃ yajñena*). Among these, he explains the utility of practice—which is synonymous with meditation (*upāsanā*)—with the words "For practice..."

The practice of the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) strengthens the latent impression (*saṃskāra*); once strengthened, that impression obstructs the latent impression born of prior false vision and continues and flows as its own effect, namely the vision of reality; from that, the manifestation of the true nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*) occurs—this is the sense. He states the utility of ritual actions (*karman*) as well: "and sacrifices, etc. Here he mentions another view: "the highest good" (*śreya*). The word "is utilized" (*upayujyate*) is to be supplied. He states the reason for this: "of the obligatory rites" (*nityānām*). [p. 97]

Thus, having shown that ritual action and meditation enter [the process] for the purpose of removing this false appearance, the opponent objects again regarding the view that verbal knowledge alone is sufficient—starting with the words "This might be so. Due to the conceit of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtvābhimāna*), there arises attachment to the instruments of enjoyment, such as one's own sandalwood paste and the like; from that follows activity (*pravṛtti*) characterized by auspicious acts such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and inauspicious acts such as the killing of a Brahmin.

Furthermore, the grasping of a body—namely, the conceit of being an agent of liberation and so forth—is accepted as a valid means of knowledge prior to [ultimate] awakening and serves as the cause for activity. Once that [conceit] is sublated by the verbal comprehension of the true nature of the Self as being a non-agent and so forth, it does not give rise to activity even while it continues to persist. For one who has understood the reality of the eastern direction through the rising of the sun does not, even if confused about directions, act toward the north; rather, he acts only in accordance with his certain conviction in the authoritative truth.

Therefore, for one who has realized the truth of the Self (*ātmatattva*), there is no engagement whatsoever in ritual action (*karman*), meditation (*upāsanā*), and so forth; thus, the sense is that ritual action, meditation, and the like are not required for the cessation of the persistence of false appearances. He refutes this with the words "It is said" (*ucyate*). Those whose objects are false are "false-objects" (*mithyārtha*); those which are like false objects are "as if false-objects" (*mithyārthā iva mithyārthāḥ*); however, they are not literally false objects, because it is impossible for those who have ascertained reality to possess false objects.

The meaning is that [erroneous cognitions] do not initiate an activity corresponding to themselves like a cognition of a false object; rather, even when sublated, erroneous cognition alone initiates an activity corresponding to itself. Here he provides an illustration with the word "just as" (*yathā*). Just as for one who is confused about directions and has not awakened to the true nature of the directions, even his determinations regarding them remain false because he has not reflected on the words of a trustworthy person—this connects with what precedes. He asks "Why? and answers with "as before" (*prāgiva*). He provides another illustration with the word "so" (*tathā*).

He concludes: "Therefore. What is intended is the cessation of the appearance of falsity—which possesses causes—by means of the suppression and destruction of its cause, namely *saṃskāra*. He confirms this point with scripture: "And thus. The meaning is that even for one who has attained the vision of reality through verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*) arising from the hearing of the Vedāntas—as indicated by the injunction "it is to be heard"—"it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*) prescribes further practice at a subsequent time. Likewise, he says "self-restraint" (*dama*) and so forth to show that self-restraint and other qualities are enjoined. He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "Otherwise."

The meaning is that if the cessation of worldly attributes occurred through verbal knowledge alone, then the instruction on meditation and so forth would be entirely useless. He again raises the opponent's view with the words "this might be so": the knowledge of reality arises from the sacred tradition (āmnāya) by means of the aids such as celibacy; therefore, the instruction on the means such as celibacy is solely for the sake of accomplishing verbal knowledge and is not useless. He refutes that with "that is incorrect": the production of verbal comprehension occurs from the word alone, independent of tranquility and the other [aids].

Therefore, there is no dependence on tranquility (*śama*) and the like for its production; nor can that which is not depended upon be an auxiliary means (*upakaraṇa*). This is the intended meaning. He establishes this very point through reasoning with the words "for not" (*na hi*). Prior to the specific means such as tranquility and the rest, the scripture is not non-expressive, because the relationship between word and meaning is innate (*autpattika*). Nor is it the case that the expressive word is dependent on tranquility and so forth, in the same way that the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning] is. [Page 98] 7.

It is appropriate [to consider] this; for the sense is that the comprehension of meaning from the word does not fail to arise merely because of the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning], even in the absence of tranquility (*śama*), the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and so forth. Nor should it be argued: "Even if the Veda was not non-expressive prior to the specific means [of knowledge], it would nonetheless be non-conclusive like the speech of an ordinary person; therefore, for the sake of certainty, it would require tranquility and the rest"; because there is no possibility of doubts regarding defects based on human agency in the impersonal Veda, he says: "Nor... (*nāpi*).

If, on the other hand, even the Vedic revelation (*āmnāya*), though not of human origin, were not determinative, then because there would be a lack of certainty even regarding the means such as tranquility (*śama*) taught in that revelation, engagement in them would be difficult to achieve; thus he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). Now, if the revelation is indeed determinative, then from it the certainty "I am Brahman" would also arise; and this being so, how could the persistence of the attributes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) continue? For once that certainty has arisen, the persistence of false attributes is not tenable.

As for the example cited regarding those who are disoriented about directions and the like, it is reasonable that their activity proceeds as before because they have forgotten the true nature of the situation; however, one might object that this is not the case here. Anticipating this doubt, he states another example with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). On the stage (*raṅge*), which is the theater, actors (*bharatāḥ*) enter having become Rāma and others, weeping out of grief due to separation from Sītā and so forth; even though the spectators know the truth—that "these are not Rāma and others, but rather actors"—they produce great sorrow [in them]. Likewise, having become tigresses, they produce fear, and in some cases, joy.

The meaning is that even when there is such certainty regarding the reality of the Self, the persistence of worldly characteristics still occurs. He provides another example with the words "and even when [it is] ascertained. He concludes with the words "therefore."

Since false appearances continue to follow along with the phenomena of saṃsāra—such as grief, fear, and so forth—even for those who know the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), it follows that for the cessation of those [appearances], even a person who has ascertained the nature of Brahman as the Self must still depend upon tranquility (*śama*) and other means for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that knowledge which removes the phenomena of saṃsāra like grief and the rest. The sense is that even for one who has known the true nature of the Self, engagement in action regarding unseen matters (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is established just as it is in seen matters (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

And it should not be argued that, this being the case, liberation would be an effect because it depends on causes such as sacrifice; thus he says, "Just as... Indeed, liberation is not produced directly by sacrifices and the like, but rather a particular state is manifested. Therefore, just as liberation is not an effect when the reality of the Self is manifested through the authority of scripture, so too it is not an effect in the manifestation of a particular state of bliss—which consists of direct realization—even when that occurs through means such as sacrifice.

Now, one might object: "If liberation does not arise from the mere knowledge of the word, but rather from that which depends upon sacrifice and other such acts, then how are those scriptural passages to be explained which teach liberation through knowledge, such as 'He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The scriptures... First, having understood the Self from the word...

The meaning is as follows: *tattva* is the contemplation of that [reality]; *abhyāsa* is the repeated practice of that; and when that practice reaches its perfection, there arises a state of knowledge that directly perceives all worldly phenomena such as sorrow and the like, having fallen away from them—that is the object [of the term]. This is what is being said: by the verb *vid* in the phrase “one knows Brahman,” it is not verbal (conceptual) knowledge that is denoted, but rather direct, intuitive knowledge (*sākṣātkāri-jñāna*) itself. Alternatively, he states this very point—that it is indeed verbal knowledge that is expressed by the verb *vid*—by saying “having sound as its means” (*śabdasādhana*). That which has sound as its instrument is so described.

The analysis of the compound is: "that which is both the means of verbal knowledge (*śabda-sādhana*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). The meaning is that the scriptural texts (*śrutayaḥ*) are "dependent on that" (*tad-apekṣāḥ*), because they require that knowledge as their object. An objection is raised: "It has been stated that liberation does not result from mere verbal knowledge, and it is the knowledge conducive to liberation that is denoted by the root *vid*; so how can it be called 'verbal knowledge'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because it is the cause of that" (*tad-dhetutvāt*). The meaning is that it is the cause of the subsequent direct realization (*sākṣātkāri-jñāna*) which arises from verbal knowledge.

The point is this: although verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*) is not the direct means to liberation, it is nevertheless designated as "knowledge" (*vidi*) because it is a cause of liberation through the intermediate step of being the cause for the direct realization (*sākṣātkārijñāna*) that constitutes liberation. Thus, having refuted the position that there is no connection between knowledge and action by demonstrating the relationship between them as that of means and end, he now restates the position regarding the discharge of debts (*ṛṇāpākaraṇa*) in order to refute it—beginning with the words "yadapi" ("as for what was said"). The phrase "ity uktam" ("thus it has been stated") is the ellipsis to be supplied. He refutes that [position] with the words "tadapi" ("that too").

As for what was stated—that one who has discharged his debts possesses the qualification for liberation—that too does not mean it is mandatory or obligatory. Why? He says: "Because of the [scriptural mention of] alternative stages of life" (*āśrama*). If the qualification for liberation belonged only to one who has discharged his debts, then, since the discharge of the three debts is impossible without the householder stage, the scripture would have taught only the householder stage; consequently, the scriptural hearing of the optionality of the stages of life (*āśrama-vikalpa*) would be purposeless. Therefore, this is not a rule: that only one who has discharged his debts has the qualification for liberation.

What, then, is this recollection of the classification of the stages of life (*āśrama*)? He says: "Of that" (*tasya*). It is not only *smṛti* [that teaches this], but he says "or if" (*yadi vā*) to show that even *śruti* declares that one situated in another stage of life is qualified for liberation. Likewise, he cites other *śruti* passages with the words "this" (*enat*): the debt to the gods is discharged by the obligatory rites such as the *agnihotra*, that to the ancestors by progeny, and that to the seers by the study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*).

The sense is this: if one who has not discharged the three debts were to possess the qualification for liberation, then the scriptural injunctions regarding the renunciation of the Agnihotra and other rites, of progeny, and of Vedic study by one desiring liberation would be inconsistent. Thus, the phrase "because the renunciation of karma is observed" is an illustration; the renunciation of progeny and Vedic study are likewise to be understood.

If one has the qualification for liberation even without having discharged the three debts, then what is the status of such Smṛti texts as, "Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation"? Anticipating this objection, he explains that text so as not to contradict the Śruti cited previously: *pratipanna*... [p. 100]. *Pratipanna* means attained or reached in the state of being a duty (*kāryatva*).

The genitive case in the phrase "of one who has not undertaken the householder's state" (*an-aṅgīkṛta-gārhasthyasya*) is used in connection with the idea that such a person, thinking "I shall accomplish my purpose by acquiring the knowledge of the Self alone," has no regard for the discharge of debts. This forthcoming Smṛti text demonstrates that [the householder's state] acts as an obstacle to the arising of the knowledge of the Self by virtue of its connection to that [discharge of debts].

In response to the question of "to what does this state of being an obstacle belong?", he says: The non-performance of that which is prescribed as a necessary duty—the repayment of debts—is the very cause of that evil (pāpman). Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) with respect to "of that evil," and in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) with respect to "of the arising of knowledge. Thus, the meaning of the Smṛti is this: being a householder, one should discharge the three debts and then fix the mind on liberation; however, one who desires liberation without having discharged his debts does not attain liberation because his knowledge is obstructed by the evil resulting from the non-performance of prescribed duties.

However, the meaning is that one goes downward because of that sin. Although there is no specific qualification such as "householder" in the Smṛti, it must nevertheless be inferred due to the contradiction with the previously cited Śruti; otherwise, the Smṛti would lack authority. As it has been said: "But in case of contradiction, [the Smṛti] should be disregarded. Having thus refuted the position regarding the discharge of debts, he accepts the position of the "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), which is consistent with the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) because it establishes that ritual actions are useful for direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). He states this with the words: "But this... (idaṃ tu).

The meaning is that it is logical that actions—though they have no further requirement for other effects such as heaven mentioned in their own scriptural statements—function as auxiliary members (*aṅga*) to knowledge (*vidyā*), because of the distinct connection with knowledge expressed in the passage: "Brāhmaṇas seek to know this very [Self] through the study of the Vedas. The word *tu* (but) indicates a distinction from the previously stated positions.

Having thus established the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*), and since this status as an auxiliary is observed to exist in both ways—with respect to origination and with respect to the result—just as in the case of substances and so forth, or the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, he qualifies it: "That too," namely the status of actions as auxiliaries to knowledge, "is for the sake of the origination of knowledge" in the manner already described; it is not, however, for the sake of a result in the same way that the *prayāja* offerings and so forth serve the purpose of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice and its results, such as heaven. Here, "origination" (*utpatti*) is intended to mean manifestation (*abhivyakti*).

Why, then, is it that the status of ritual actions as auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of knowledge does not occur solely through their utility toward a result? To this he says: "Of knowledge. For in the case of the *darśa* sacrifice and others, there is a result such as heaven; therefore, it is appropriate that acts like the *prayāja* offerings are auxiliaries by virtue of being useful for that [result]. But here, in the case of knowledge—which is characterized by direct realization—there is no other result. If it is argued that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the result, we say no; because that very [knowledge] is liberation, and if it were a result, it would be non-eternal. [Objection: But surely the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) will be the result. [Reply: Not so.

The cessation of that [ignorance] is indeed the very arising of knowledge, not something separate; as it has been said: “The destruction of the preceding state is simply the arising of a contrary state. Thus, having accepted the position of a separate conjunction as being consistent with one’s own doctrine and logical, one should now also accept this position—that there is an entitlement to knowledge for one who has been refined by ritual actions—as being consistent with one’s own doctrine.

Considering this to be indeed logical, he says: "Or the side of the *saṃskāra*s. The word "logical" (*yuktam*) is carried over [from the previous context] by changing its gender. But on what authority is this position established, such that it is called "logical"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "From *smṛti*. This means: from such *smṛti* passages as, "He for whom these forty *saṃskāra*s [exist]," and so forth. Now, if ritual acts are for the purpose of purifying the person (*puruṣa-saṃskāra*), then they do not serve the purpose of knowledge (*vidyā*); and that [point] was stated previously.

Anticipating the question "How so?", he says: "Of that which is conditioned" (*saṃskṛtasya*). For purification (*saṃskāra*) is not for the sake of the object to be purified. What then? It is for the sake of producing another effect in that which has been purified; and that [effect] is knowledge (*vidyā*), characterized by the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*). He confirms both positions with the words of the author of the Sūtras: "That has been said."

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: knowledge does not depend solely on [qualities] such as tranquility for its own sake; rather, it also depends upon the ritual actions connected with the four stages of life (āśramas)—such as kindling the fire, the Agnihotra sacrifice, austerity, recitation, and meditation—in their respective order, because these are prescribed by scripture. Regarding this, he raises an objection concerning both positions with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). That which has perceptible practice as its means is "one whose means are perceptible" (*dṛṣṭopāya*); this refers to the production of knowledge characterized by direct realization.

In this context, let it be understood that only those means of action (*itikartavyatā*) which are perceived and provide visible assistance—such as tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth—which destroy mental distraction, are required. For when a task has a perceptible means, only a perceptible procedure is observed; for example, in the case of cooking by fire, the kindling of the fire and so forth are of a perceptible nature. Sacrifices (*yajña*) and the like, however, have an imperceptible purpose; therefore, they are not required for the production of knowledge (*vidyā*). By describing them as "destroyers of mental distraction," [the author] states that tranquility and the rest provide visible assistance.

Now, one might object: "Even if tranquility (*śama*) and the rest constitute the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) that removes mental distraction, how can they provide a visible (*dṛṣṭa*) assistance in the production of knowledge? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of one who is concentrated" (*samāhitasya*). This is what is meant: because mental distraction is eliminated by means of tranquility and the rest, a person becomes one whose mind is concentrated; for one who practices with a concentrated mind, there arises clarity, serenity, and purity of knowledge—this is the meaning. Furthermore, anticipating the question, "Why then are sacrifices and the like not required? he says: "By those" (*taiḥ*).

The meaning is that the clarity of knowledge (*jñānaprasāda*) arises through practice alone, even without sacrifices and the like. He provides the answer by way of admission, saying "True. He confirms this very point, saying "And thus. The word "by them" means by sacrifices and the like. An objection might be raised: "Previously, it was stated that sacrifice and so forth are auxiliary parts of the injunction (*vidhi*); now, you admit that knowledge is independent of them. This involves a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Anticipating this, he says "But rather... (*kiṃtu*).

The sense is that because liberation is of a single nature, just like the creation and so forth, no distinction in its essential nature can arise from a distinction in the means; therefore, it is logical that any distinction here must be produced by time. He states that very distinction with the words "by the means" (*sādhanena*). Just as there is a distinction, that is, an excellence, in the cause, [p.

The meaning is this: in proportion as that absence—the absence of specific [auxiliaries] and the deficiency of means—occurs, so too is that knowledge manifested more slowly and even more slowly; whereas in proportion as those [auxiliaries] are present, it is manifested more quickly and even more quickly. This is what is being said: knowledge manifests itself slowly when based on mere practice alone; it manifests quickly when accompanied by each one [of the auxiliaries] such as sacrifice; and it manifests most quickly when accompanied by all of them. P.

36-23 He confirms this very point by means of the words of the author of the Sūtras: "That has been said. He states the meaning of the Sūtra: "This [is it]. The meaning is that even though knowledge can be attained through practice even without ritual acts, ritual acts are still required for knowledge, because of the scriptural statement, "by sacrifice" (yajñena). The example, "as without," is explained by its own wording. Here, he raises an objection: "But surely..."

According to the Vedic revelation, "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," Brahman has the nature of pure knowledge; and since knowledge, which is acquired through practice, also has the nature of pure knowledge, it is therefore Brahman itself and not something other than Brahman, for otherwise the consequence of duality would follow. Furthermore, Brahman is eternal; for that very reason, it is non-productive (not an effect). In that case, while Brahman exists—being eternal and non-productive by nature—how could anything depend upon sacrifices and the like? For it is a product that requires means and auxiliary factors to assist it, but not that which is non-productive; this is the sense. He provides the rebuttal: "It is said."

That which is placed near (*upa*) and held (*dhīyate*) is called an *upadhāna*, such as a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*). Just as a crystal gem, whose white form is obscured by such an adjunct, requires the removal or withdrawal of that adjunct—the hibiscus flower and so forth—even though it is not an effect [of that obscuration], for the manifestation of its white form; in the same way, Brahman, although not an effect, depends upon sacrifices and other rites for the manifestation of its own nature, which is obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*). This is the meaning.

Although the crystal gem is an effect, it is nevertheless similar [to the case of the mind] simply by virtue of the fact that it is not an effect produced by the operation of that [gem]. Now, one might object: all things are momentary; therefore, just as the wood [is transformed] upon the proximity of fire, the previous form of the crystal is destroyed and another arises due to the proximity of an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) such as a *japā* flower; and when the adventitious condition is removed, yet another white form arises.

Anticipating the objection that "therefore, only a produced white color requires the removal of an adjunct, whereas an unproduced one does not; thus, the example is dissimilar," he says: "For not... Why, then, is it not so? He says: "For not... The meaning is this: for a subsequent white moment—which is similar (sabhāga), that is, resembling, the preceding white moment that was separated by several dissimilar (visabhāga) and unlike moments of red crystal—it is impossible for that white moment to arise again "without cause" (akasmāt), that is, without a cause.

But surely the preceding moment alone is the cause of the succeeding one; so how can it be said that [the effect arises] "without a cause" (*akasmāt*)? It is replied: first of all, that immediately preceding red moment does not initiate a white moment, because they are dissimilar; for a preceding moment initiates only what is similar to itself. To illustrate: a moment of a jar initiates a jar, not a cloth. But surely it also initiates what is dissimilar, as in the case of wood—[page 103]...

The moment [of the black thread] is like the moment of charcoal. It is true that this occurs when a dissimilar cause falls upon it; for in that case, the cause is fire, which produces something dissimilar. But here it is not so, because dissimilar factors such as the *japā* flower have been removed. Now, one might argue that the preceding white moment could then be the cause of the final white moment. That too is impossible; being separated by many red moments, it cannot remain undestroyed and thus cannot serve as the cause for the subsequent one.

This has been stated: "separated by many dissimilar moments. Regarding that very point, he provides an illustration: "For not... Having thus established the example of the crystal, he applies it to the case at hand (the *dārṣṭāntika*): "Therefore... Now, one might object: the innate form of the crystal remains ever-present; a person does not exert effort to remove it for its sake, but rather for the sake of knowing it, and that [knowledge] is the effect.

Therefore, it is only knowledge that is an effect dependent upon something else in that regard, not the non-effect which is the nature of the crystal; thus he raises the objection again with the words, "It might be so. He refutes this by means of an alternative analysis, asking, "But what [is the purpose]? For a person engages in activity for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*), and that is for the sake of the object (*artha*), not for the sake of mere knowledge, because that would lead to the absurd consequence even in the case of false cognition. Therefore, knowledge is sought for the sake of the form of the object, and not for its own sake; consequently, the operation aimed at knowledge is for the sake of the object.

Therefore, although cognition is an effect, nevertheless the activity for the sake of cognition is required by the object itself, not by the cognition; the meaning is that [cognition] has the object as its primary focus. This is what is being said: this requirement regarding the object itself arises by way of cognition in the form, "Cognize it, and then act upon it. Thus, even that which is not an effect may have a dependence on something else, and the same will hold true for the Self as well. But if cognition is for the sake of the object, then it must surely produce some modification in the object.

For the status of being "for the sake of that" (tādarthya) is not conceivable for something that performs no action upon the object; moreover, modification is an effect. Therefore, suspecting that it is only the effect—and not the object—that is dependent [on another], he says: "And not... (na ca). The meaning is: this would indeed be so if a modification were produced in the object by knowledge, but such is not the case. Alternatively, if the object is manifested by knowledge, then there must certainly be some modification in the object resulting from the knowledge, because that which effects nothing cannot be a manifester.

Therefore, having raised the objection that if Brahman were manifested, it would likewise undergo modification and thus incur the defect of impermanence, [the author] says "And not," setting aside for a moment the case of Brahman, to show that even in the case of an object, no modification occurs through knowledge. Alternatively: Now, one might argue that knowledge manifests an object by modifying it; otherwise, since an object that has not changed in any way cannot be manifested as before, it would follow that dependence on something else is required for its manifestation. Furthermore, Brahman, being unmodifiable, could not be manifested. To this [he replies]: "And not. Or rather: [The author says] "And not" to show that even in the case of an object, no modification occurs through knowledge. Or again: Now, does knowledge manifest an object by modifying it, or otherwise? If it were otherwise, then since an object that has not changed at all would be impossible to manifest as it was before, it would be logical that there is a dependence on something else for its manifestation; however, Brahman, because it is unmodifiable, is impossible to manifest. To this [he replies]: "And not. Or yet again: Now, does knowledge manifest an object by modifying it, or otherwise? If it were otherwise, then since an object that has not changed in any respect would be impossible to manifest as it was previously, it would be reasonable that there is a requirement for something else in order to manifest it; but Brahman, due to its unchangeability, is incapable of being manifested. To this [he replies]: "And not. Or finally: Now, does knowledge manifest an object by modifying it, or otherwise? If it were otherwise, then since an object that has not become different in any way whatsoever would be impossible to manifest as it was before, it would be proper that there is a dependence on another factor for its manifestation; but Brahman, because it is not subject to modification, cannot be manifested. Therefore, having raised the objection that the analogy is dissimilar—asking how something else could be required for the manifestation of what is already meaningful—he says "And not... in order to demonstrate their similarity. Alternatively: [Objection] But surely the object, because it is insentient...

One might object: "If a thing's nature is unmanifest, then by that knowledge [of Brahman], its previously non-existent manifestation must arise; and for that manifestation, something else must be required. But how can Brahman—which is the light of the Self and whose nature is eternally manifest—be manifested, or require anything else for its manifestation? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says "And not... in order to show that in all cases manifestation is not real, but rather depends upon *māyā*.

If some modification, such as burning and so forth, were to occur in the object prior to its cognition, then its manifestation therein would be real (*tāttvikī*); but since this is not the case, that manifestation is everywhere dependent upon *māyā*. Why then should it not be so even in the case of Brahman? For the aforementioned defect of irrationality does not apply to *māyā*; the point is that *māyā* is defined precisely by its being irrational. He states the reason why there is no modification of the object from cognition with the words "of those two" (*tayoḥ*). For fire does not modify fuel that is unconnected to it.

Furthermore, internal cognition is not connected with an external object; therefore, the meaning is that it does not modify the object. If it is argued that even in the absence of other types of connection, there will be a connection between the object and the cognition characterized by the object's being in a suitable location, he says: "suitable location. Suitable location for the object consists in its being situated directly [in front]; and this is the same everywhere, including in the case of color, taste, and so forth, which reside in the same substratum. Therefore, the meaning is that the cognition of color would produce a modification in taste and so forth as well, just as it does in color—as explained previously.

Although the rebuttal here is that the capacity to transform is not observed in fire and other such things when they are not in contact, nevertheless, this other rebuttal has been stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]. Furthermore, if cognition were to produce the manifestation of an object prior [to its own arising], then once the manifestation had arisen through the cognition of one person, the object would become manifest to everyone—just as a jar that has become red through the baking of one person becomes red for everyone, and not only for that one person. Thus he says: "sarva... (everyone).

Furthermore, while it may be granted that an object existing in the present can be produced [as an effect] by cognition, such production is impossible in the case of past and future objects cognizable through inferential marks (*liṅga*) and the like, because the substratum (*dharmin*) itself does not exist. With this intention, he says: "destroyed" (*dhvasta*), etc. Having thus established the nature of the example, he concludes: "Therefore," etc. For the substance of crystal is not concealed by the *japā* flower as if wrapped in a red cloth, nor is it [concealed] by its radiance, since that radiance is not a substantial entity (*dravya*).

And yet it appears as if concealed, though in reality it is not concealed; for this very reason, because it is not concealed in reality, it is not manifested in its true nature, even so it requires an effort to remove the adjuncts (upadhāna) as if it were being manifested—this is the meaning. He applies the point established by the illustration to the subject of the illustration with the word "tathā" (so too): likewise, the reality of the Self is also concealed by beginningless ignorance, like a black blanket; nevertheless, because its own nature does not shine forth, it is as if concealed, such that [the removal of ignorance through] sacrifice and other means is required. [p. 105]

The meaning is that there is no fault because [the Self] is as if manifested through effort. This is what is being said: this triad—concealment, manifestation, and dependence upon effort—is not real for the Self; rather, it is merely an illusion of ignorance (*avidyā*). In reality, however, the Self is neither concealed, nor is it manifested because its nature is eternally manifest, nor does it depend upon effort.

Having thus stated the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman in the *Brahmasiddhi* with the words "famous from tradition" (*āmnāyataḥ prasiddhim*) and so forth, he now states the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman, which is the object of that cognition, beginning with the verse "In whom all distinctions have been withdrawn" (*saṃhṛta*). He explains the meaning of the verse: "From whom... (*yataḥ*). The phrase "by others, by Vyomaśiva and so forth" is used for the sake of honor; it is not intended to exclude his own view. "In whom all distinctions have been withdrawn" means that in whom all particular differences (*viśeṣa*) have been subsumed or dissolved. "The universal self" (*sāmānyātmā*) means whose very nature is the universal; that is the self described.

The meaning is as follows: just as, by the withdrawal of specific distinctions such as bracelets and the like, that which is indicated and defined as the commonality (*sāmānya*) of those various forms—bracelets and so forth—is [the gold itself]; "bracelet" (*kaṭaka*) is said to be a ring (*pārihārya*). He recites the passage from the *Brahmavidyā* treatise beginning with "This very great... That which is perceived through the abstraction of its specific qualities is possessed of those specific qualities; and that which is possessed of specific qualities is the commonality, just as the essence of gold is.

The reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is also apprehended through the removal of all particularities by means of the formula "not this, not this" (*neti neti*); therefore, the intended meaning is that it too is a universal (*sāmānya*) because it is apprehended through the removal of particularities. He explains the verse otherwise with the words "or those which": if it is being argued that what is devoid of particularity cannot be a universal, and thus the state of being a non-universal is established for that which is devoid of particularity, then this would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

For us as well, who maintain the doctrine of non-duality (*advaya*), since specific entities such as space (*viyat*) and the like do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*vastu-dṛṣṭyā*), the universal nature of the Self (*ātma-tattva-sāmānya*) is not accepted. How then is a "universal" spoken of by the proponents of Brahman (*brahma-vādibhiḥ*)? To this he says: "But the universal has been mentioned figuratively (*upacārataḥ*). Now, a figurative application arises from some common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*), just as the word 'fire' (*agni*) is applied to a young boy because of his intensity; so here, from what characteristic does the figurative application arise? To this he says: "Because of the specific... (*viśeṣa...*).

The meaning is that because the universal property, well-known in the case of gold and so forth, is defined by way of the exclusion of particularities (viśeṣapratyastamaya), there is a metaphorical application (upacāra) of it to the Self, which is common to all. In this interpretation, it should be understood that this verse is intended to demonstrate the similarity with the well-known universal essence of gold. Now, if one were to argue that the universal postulated by others—which is devoid of particulars—cannot exist, because it lacks particulars, like a hare's horn, and thus its non-existence alone is being proven;
then the reason would be inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to deviation (vyabhicāra) on account of the very particulars.

[Objection: But surely there are even further sub-distinctions (*viśeṣa*) among the distinctions; therefore, the reason "being devoid of distinctions" (*nirviśeṣatva*) does not exist at all in those [sub-distinctions]. Of what, then, would there be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? To this he says: "by those devoid of distinctions" (*nirviśeṣaiḥ*). Although they were previously called "distinctions," since even those are not ultimate constituents, the meaning is that there is a deviation by means of those which remain as "devoid of distinctions. And since this has already been stated in prose, one need not be overly concerned with the formal arrangement of the verse.
Thus ends the commentary on the Brahmakāṇḍa of the *Śrībrahmasiddhi*, composed by Śaṅkhapāṇi.
[Page 107] Yes.

The *Brahmasiddhi-vyākhyā* composed by Śaṅkhapāṇi: the section on Logic (*Tarkakāṇḍa*). In the section on Brahman (*Brahmakāṇḍa*), it was established that Brahman is the twofold sequence of the means of valid cognition consisting of scripture (*āmnāya*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*). Now, regarding that which was stated there as being non-authoritative because it contradicts perception and so forth—just like statements concerning "leaping over stones"—the scriptural tradition of non-duality (*advaya-āmnāya*) is likewise set aside by perception and other means of knowledge that apprehend the nature of differentiation (*vyāvṛtta-svabhāva*).

Therefore, having raised the objection that [the scripture] is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) on the grounds that it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, he first states the absence of contradiction with perception in order to declare the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of that reason, beginning with the words "They say" (*āhuḥ*). If perception were to determine that "a jar is not a cloth," then, because its object would be difference (*bheda*), it would contradict the scriptural teaching of non-duality (*advaya*); however, the wise do not say that perception determines such [a distinction]. Rather, they hold that it is the apprehender of the mere essential nature of the thing itself.

For that reason, the meaning is that this scriptural tradition (āmnāya), such as "this is indeed one, without a second," regarding the non-dual reality in its state of oneness, is not contradicted by perception. Now, even if there were a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, the authority of the scripture would not be undermined; for while a human statement—whose authority depends upon the validity of the speaker's cognition—would become invalid in the face of such contradiction, that which is not of human origin possesses independent authority.

Thus, even though there is a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, if that [scripture] were invalid, why could the opposite not be the case? For when perception and so forth and the sacred tradition (āmnāya) possess an equal independence, there is no specific reason to distinguish them such that the tradition would be invalid due to contradiction with perception and the rest, while perception and the rest would not be invalid due to contradiction with it. Therefore, the effort to establish non-contradiction with perception and so forth is entirely in vain; thus, he challenges the commencement of that inquiry with the words "Now, [is it not the case... (nanu).

"By whom the operation—the activity—of another means of knowledge, such as perception and so forth, is not required for its own validity, he is described as such. "In contradiction with that" means in contradiction with perception and so forth. Here, first, he states the resolution according to the opinion of some: "In that regard," etc. When there is contradiction with perception and so forth, the authority of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is weak; therefore, by virtue of that contradiction with perception and so forth, its lack of validity would follow.

The meaning is that it is not the case that perception and the other means of knowledge contradict that [scripture]; thus, for the sake of establishing the authority of the sacred tradition (āmnāya), the demonstration of its non-contradiction with perception and the rest is purposeful, and not in vain. He asks, "How is there weakness [in perception, etc.]? and answers, "Because of their dependence. He explains this dependence: "In that way... [p. 108]

The word "hi" (for) [indicates the following]: a certain portion of the Veda (*āmnāya*), established by its recitation, depends upon direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the Śrauta rites; likewise, in the case of Smārta practices, it depends upon inference (*anumāna*) because of the commonality of the performers; it depends upon presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) for that which is to be understood through the indicative power (*liṅga*) of mantras and so forth; and it depends upon analogy (*upamāna*) for the application of archetypal (*prakṛta*) injunctions to modified (*vikṛta*) rites. Thus, every portion of the Veda depends upon direct perception and the other means of knowledge; the meaning is that the establishment of its own nature (*svarūpa-siddhi*) is dependent upon them. He asks, "What follows from this? and says, "And thus" (*tathā ca*). The phrase "of those" (*teṣām*) refers to direct perception and the rest.

He asks "Why? and replies with the word "tat" (that). The meaning is that if the sublation (*bādhana*) of those [means of knowledge], such as perception and the rest, or of their validity, were admitted on the basis of the Veda (*āgama*), then the very establishment of the nature of the Veda itself would not even be possible, let alone that of the object, which is much further removed. Furthermore, it is not the case that the Veda depends upon perception and the others in the same way that they depend upon it, such that there might be an equality of strength. Therefore, he says "But it is not so," meaning that because the Veda is dependent upon perception and the others, it is weaker than them.

For this reason as well, he says it is weak: "because its deviation is observed. A sentence that accords with reality on one occasion in a certain manner may, at another time, disagree with reality in that very same manner; for even a corrupt speaker does not corrupt the word itself by means of a hoarse or nasal tone and the like. However, in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), that which is produced by a defective sense organ is deviant, while other [perceptions] are not; this is the distinction. The mention of "perception" is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); inference (*anumāna*) and the rest should also be understood to apply.

The sense is this: although no deviation [from truth] is observed in the Veda, nevertheless, because it shares the common nature of being "speech" (*śabdatva-sāmānya*), such a deviation is suspected there as well, since it is observed in the world. For this reason also, he states that the *Āgama* (scriptural testimony) is weaker: "Moreover" (*api ca*). He asks, "What follows from that? and replies: "They would be without scope" (*anavakāśāḥ*). First of all, the Self is not the scope for perception and the other means of knowledge, because it is not an object of the senses and so forth; if even the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) did not exist therein, then those [means of knowledge] would be without scope due to having no object. He says, however, that verbal testimony does have scope: "It has scope" (*sāvakāśa*).

He asks, "How so? and replies, "By way of being secondary" (*gauṇena*). He clarifies this very point with, "For instance" (*tathā hi*). The meaning is that although the world is diverse, because it is one in its essence as *sattā* (Being) and so forth, it is figuratively designated as "one alone, without a second. He states another way in which [the Upanishads] have scope: "of the intended meanings" (*vivakṣitārthānām*). He confirms this very point with, "the Upanishads" (*upaniṣadaḥ*); the meaning is that this statement of his own indicates the utility of the Vedāntas for the purpose of silent recitation (*japa*). Furthermore, he says, "Moreover" (*kiñca*), to show that the Āgama is weak; he states its confusion with, "ritual action" (*karma*).

For the domain of karma takes as its object the distinctions of means and ends, and so forth; whereas the Vedāntas take non-duality and identity as their object—this is the meaning. He asks, "What follows from this? and replies with the words "mutually," etc. Therefore, precisely because they are mutually contradictory, the Vedāntas are first of all difficult to establish as authoritative. On the other hand, those whose authority is established as being non-contradictory among themselves—either by way of establishing the nature of fire and other such things, or by way of establishing matters already accepted by all disputants—such as perception...

The meaning is that when there is a conflict with them [perception and so forth], the Vedāntas are all the more difficult to establish as authoritative. He concludes with "therefore" (tasmāt). The meaning is: because the consequence of the lack of authority of the Vedāntas arises when there is a conflict with perception and the other means of knowledge, therefore [it is so]. Regarding the fact that perception and the others are subversive of the Self when a conflict exists, he states another reason: "because they are primary" (mukhyatvāt). This means because perception and the others are prior. He explains this priority: "for they are primary" (mukhyā hi).

For a living being as soon as it is born, the primary means of knowledge are perception and the rest, which exist from the very beginning; whereas for someone who has mastered the meaning of words and is awakened, the Veda (Āmnāya) becomes a means of knowledge at a later time. The term "living being" (*jantu*) is used to highlight the superiority of perception and the rest over the Veda—which resides in only a few individuals—even though that Veda pertains to all living beings. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "That... (*sa iti*).

That [scriptural teaching] concerning Agni—whose subject matter is the nature of difference established by those means of knowledge such as perception, which are established because they are antecedent and thus free from contradiction—is "overcome," meaning its subject matter in the form of non-duality as it is heard is removed or set aside. For this very reason, it has a "meaning that must be inferred"; that is, because of the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, its meaning is something other than what is heard in the scripture, and thus it is sublated.

If [the scripture] is not to be favored, then, because it would contradict perception and other means of knowledge, there must be a relinquishing of the literal meaning, and no other meaning should be postulated; thus, this sublation is characterized by the removal of the subject matter (*viṣayāpahāra*). On the other hand, if it is to be favored, then, in accordance with perception and the rest, one must accept non-duality in the form of the universal (*jāti*) without abandoning the duality grasped by perception and so forth; such is the meaning of "it deserves to have its meaning postulated in this way. Alternatively, [the phrase *pratyakṣādi*] refers to an object established by perception and the rest.

The Vedic word (āgama), however, has its meaning to be determined in accordance with other means of knowledge; therefore, its meaning is not self-established. Consequently, because it is weaker, it is sublated [by perception], or rather, it ought to have its meaning determined in accordance with those [other means]. Having thus stated the primacy of perception and the others by way of their essential nature, he states their primacy also by way of their objective function, saying "by way of the object" (arthataḥ). He asks "How? and replies "By way of the word" (padataḥ).

When the distinction between words and their meanings is known, there occurs the determination of the nature of reality as being *sat* (truth) or *māyā* (illusion); and that distinction between words and their meanings depends upon perception and the other means of knowledge (*pratyakṣādyāyatta*). This is what is meant: the differentiation of words and their meanings is the domain of perception and the rest, and it exists prior [to the Veda], whereas non-duality is the domain of the scripture (*āgama*) and exists posteriorly; therefore, by virtue of its primacy regarding its object, perception and the rest also possess primacy. He concludes with the word "ataḥ" (therefore).

The meaning is that since there would be no authority for the Veda (*āgama*) in the event of a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge which are stronger by virtue of being primary, [this objection is raised]. He states another view: "Others" (*anye*). Due to the aforementioned reasoning, the superiority of the intellect (*buddhi*) does not exist; nevertheless, when there is a contradiction between perception and the Veda regarding duality and non-duality, there would be doubt and no definitive conclusion. Therefore, the absence of contradiction is established in order to reach a certain determination of that [truth].

One might object: "Surely there will be an option (vikalpa), as in the case of the taking up of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup and so forth, and not a doubt. Anticipating this, he says: "the thing" (*vastu*). The meaning is that while performance may be optional because it is yet to be accomplished, an already established thing (*siddha vastu*) cannot be optional.

P. 40-3. Having thus stated the purpose of resolving the contradiction between the two views, he states his own position with the words "anyād" (different). He sets forth the reasoning for the superior authority of the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*) with the words "paurva" (preceding). In the Soma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture that the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having joined hands with one another, exit the sacrificial hall in the following manner: "The *prastotṛ* should follow the departing *adhvaryu*; the *udgātṛ* should follow him; the *pratihartṛ* should follow the *udgātṛ*; the *brahman* priest should follow the *pratihartṛ*; and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) should follow the *brahman*."

And in that regard, an incidental rule is heard: “If the Prastotṛ should be cut off [from his share], he alone should be made to proceed after giving a boon to the Brahman; if the Udgātṛ should be cut off, the sacrifice should be concluded as one without a sacrificial fee (adakṣiṇa); if the Pratihartṛ should be cut off, all one's possessions (sarvavedasa) must be given. The word *apacchidyeta* means “should be severed.”

Then, when there is a double suspension (apaccheda) of the Udgātṛ and Pratihartṛ occurring in succession, since they are not of equal strength and because there is a conflict between the rules regarding the non-giving of fees and the giving of all one's possessions, and since neither option nor combination is possible, a doubt arises: which is stronger, the former or the latter? When it might be argued that the former is stronger due to its priority—just as in the case of direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and so on—the author replies: “In the case of succession, the former is weaker, as in the archetype.”

In the case of *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth, that which is obtained first—because it arises more rapidly—sublates the subsequent [indicator] even though it has not yet reached its object; therefore, in those cases, there is no sequence at all, since the subsequent [indicator] does not arise. But here, however, the subsequent [rule] is also obtained through direct *śruti*; thus, regarding the sequence of two contingent rules (*naimittika*), the former is weaker, because the latter does not arise without having set aside the former; therefore, that very [former] is sublated, as is the rule of the archetype (*prakṛti-vrata*).

The meaning is that just as ordinary *kuśa* grasses, which have been extended by analogy (*atideśa*) into a modified ritual (*vikṛti*), are set aside by the *śara* grasses explicitly heard in the direct scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), so it is here. He confirms this very point with the words of Bhaṭṭa: "without sublation of the prior. Now, one might object: let there be weakness of the prior when there is a sequence of priority and posteriority; but here that very sequence does not exist, because neither of the two directly revealed texts (*pratyakṣāmnāya*) has a claim to primacy. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For thus... (*tathā hi*).

The term "kila" (indeed) is used for the purpose of illuminating that the determination of a distinct and differentiated object—based on perception and other means of knowledge—is innate to every living being, established by the mere fact of birth, and thus the priority of the cognition of difference has been stated; however, this determination of the reality of differentiated objects is not [established] in ultimate truth (*tattvataḥ*), but is merely illusion (*māyāmātra*).

The realization of non-duality (*advaitāvagama*), however, depends upon the perceptual determination of distinct words, word-meanings, and objects; for this very reason, it is preceded by that [duality]; for this very reason, it is not innate (*anisargaja*)—that is, it is not established merely by birth; for this very reason, it is adventitious (*āgantuka*), occurring at a later time, and belongs only to certain individuals such as Janaka and others, and not to every person. Thus, the superiority of the realization of non-duality has been stated. Having thus explained the sequence between the knowledge of duality and non-duality, he states the sublation of the former: "That" (*sa*).

He states another reason for the strength of the *āmnāya* (scriptural tradition) with the words "for this reason also" (*itaśca*); the phrase "the *āmnāya* is strong" is understood to carry over. He asks "Why? and replies "Because they are possible" (*saṃbhavat*); those in which there exist various and manifold causes of error, such as the presence of defects and so forth, are described as such. [p. 111] These [causes] have dissolved—

"From which all suspicion of defect has departed"—thus he is so described; the meaning is that it is logical for the Veda, from which the suspicion of defect is impossible, to possess greater authority than perception and other means of knowledge, which are subject to the possibility of defects. The cause of error is not uniform everywhere, but rather diverse; therefore, the term "diverse" is used to indicate that even in the absence of defects in the sense organs and so forth, we may postulate some other defect in the cognition of the phenomenal world. Regarding this, he states the reason why the Veda is free from the suspicion of defect: "puruṣa... (due to the person).

It has been stated later that the attribution of defects to perception and the other means of knowledge follows solely from the force of the faultless tradition (*āmnāya*). However, the faultlessness of the tradition, though mentioned later, has already been established. For all defects in verbal testimony reside in the person [who utters it]; since such a person is absent in the case of the tradition, how could those defects possibly exist in it? Now, one might object: even in perception and the others, defects are not observed; those in which defects are observed are not true perceptions and so forth, but rather their fallacious counterparts (*tadābhāsa*).

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to assume something in one place based on what has been observed elsewhere without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, having raised the doubt—"What is the means of valid cognition for assuming defects that cause error when they are not perceived in those [perceptions]?"—the author states the means of valid cognition: "For it is possible... The meaning is this: from the very fact that the non-dual scripture (*advaitāmnāya*) possesses established validity due to its being free from defects, it is possible to both suspect and ascertain the presence of defects in perception and other means of knowledge which apprehend duality. Now, one might object: "Defects such as cataracts and the like are well-known in the world."

Anticipating the objection—"Since these [illusory objects] have been excluded by the non-perception of the capable in perception and other means of knowledge, how can they be postulated even from scripture?"—it is said: "beginningless" (*anādi*).
