This has already been stated: "For a defect does not necessarily take the same form everywhere"; the sense is that, even in the absence of cataracts and the like, we shall postulate another defect called the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Anticipating the objection that prior to the arising of the defect known as the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), perception and other means of knowledge, being free from defects, would possess equal authority with the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), the author qualifies [the defect] by stating "beginningless" (*anādi*). Alternatively, it is for the sake of indicating its firmness: because it is bound by this beginningless defect called the impressions of ignorance—consisting of the perception of duality, the impressions of ignorance, and then again the perception of duality—the perception and other means of knowledge are eternally weaker than the sacred tradition; such is the sense. Or, "impression" (*saṃskāra*) may simply mean ignorance itself.

The impression of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*) or the formation of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃskāra*) is so called because the self (*ātman*) is conditioned by it and thereby undergoes, as it were, a transformation. Here, certainty (*niścaya*) alone is intended; however, "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*) was mentioned as a bold assertion (*prauḍhavāda*), based on the mere possibility of defects, in order to show that perception and other means of knowledge are weaker than the Veda even when its defects are merely suspected—how much more so when its defects are certain! Furthermore, since that which is possible is what is to be established, certainty itself is stated here by way of the sequence of possibility.

As it has been said: "When a proposition is possible, the thesis shall be established by means of a reason. But what is well-known from the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) regarding the cause of error—the beginningless impression of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃskāra*) distinct from darkness (*timira*)—by virtue of which this [is established] here?

P. 40-10. Anticipating the objection that [the notion of self] is merely imagined (*kalpita*), he says: "In the body" (*dehe*). The cognition of the self as "I" within the body is the identification of the body with the self (*dehātmābhimāna*). The meaning is this: just as in each successive birth, the beginningless latent impression (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*)—arising from the Vedic revelation (*āmnāya*) which teaches a self distinct from the body—is the cause of the delusion regarding the body as the self, so it is here as well. Now, one might object: "The cause of the delusion in identifying the body with the self is the perception of distinction, namely 'my body,' and not the Vedic revelation. This is not so.

Because the cognition of distinction is observed even where there is no actual distinction—as in the case of the thought "my self"—this reason is not conclusive. Therefore, it is well said that the beginningless impression (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of delusion, is drawn forth from scripture alone as the cause for the conceit of the body being the self. This example merely illustrates the fact that the impression of ignorance is the cause of delusion. By this much, the objection—“How can the cognition of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) common to all people be a delusion?”—is also refuted; for even the cognition of the body as the self, though common to all, is seen to be a delusion.

But why, one might ask, is a defect (doṣa) that causes error postulated for perception and the other means of knowledge based on the Veda (āgnyāya), and not rather the Veda itself by the force of perception and the rest? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But it is not so. For sound is not defective by its very nature, but rather through the defect of the person [who utters it]; therefore, in the case of the Veda, even the suspicion of a defect—which lacks a substratum—is impossible, let alone its certain determination. He states the defect [that would arise] if such a suspicion were entertained: "If [it were] so," etc.

The meaning is that if there were a suspicion of defect, the Veda (Āgama) would not be a means of valid knowledge at all. Now, one might object: "In that case, how can perception and the other means of knowledge be valid, since they too are subject to defects? Moreover, the world recognizes them as 'means of valid knowledge'. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But as for perception and the others... The word "but" (tu) is intended to show a distinction. What is meant is this: validity is of two kinds—that which consists in the revelation of reality (tattvāvedana), and that which consists in non-contradiction in worldly practice (vyavahārāvisaṃvāda).

In that regard, since [the world] possesses defects, even for perception and the other means of knowledge, the validity characterized by the revelation of reality (*tattvāvedana*) does not truly exist; however, empirical validity (*vyāvahārika*) does exist. Therefore, there is no loss of established consensus. Now, one might object: "If it possesses defects, how can there be even empirical validity, as in the case of an illusion such as silver? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Through ignorance" (*avidyā*). For when defects are removed, there occurs correspondence with worldly practice (*vyavahāra-saṃvāda*). But this latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance and so forth, being beginningless, is stable and persists in worldly practice just as before.

The meaning is that because there is no contradiction with worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), the conventional validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*) of perception and the other means of knowledge is established. Now, one might object: "If conventional validity exists even when there is defect (*doṣa*), then where will invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) reside? For its existence is well-known in cases of delusions such as [mistaking] silver. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And where... The point is that although there is no difference between perception and the like and the delusion of silver in terms of having defects, the distinction between worldly valid and invalid means of knowledge is nonetheless possible.

Now, one might object: "If even perception and the other means of knowledge are authoritative despite possessing defects, then the same will apply to verbal testimony (*śabda*) as well when it possesses defects;

therefore, the statement that 'if [defects] exist, it would not be a means of valid cognition at all' is incorrect. Anticipating this doubt, he explains the point with the words: "But in the case of verbal testimony" (*śabde tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates the distinction from perception and the others. Even when a defect is merely possible in verbal testimony, neither of the two kinds of authority exists; how much less so when a defect is certain? Thus, the term "possible" (*saṃbhāvita*) is used for emphasis.

One might object: "Granted that the validity characterized by non-cognition of reality may not exist in a defective word, why should its conventional validity not exist, as it does in perception and the like? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because its object is unseen" (*adṛṣṭārthatvāt*). The analysis of the compound is: "that whose object (artha), i.e., its referent (viṣaya), is unseen. Since no subversion of worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) is observed in the case of perception and the like, conventional validity is appropriate for them; however, because the Veda (*āmnāya*) has an unseen object, there is no knowledge of the non-subversion of such practice [in its case].

Therefore, the meaning is that it possesses not even empirical validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*). For this reason as well, he states that a word possessing defects does not have validity characterized by non-contradiction in practical usage (*vyavahārāvisaṃvāda-lakṣaṇa*), saying: "From defects" (*doṣebhyaḥ*). Elsewhere, in cases such as the illusion of silver, a cognition that contradicts practical usage is seen to arise from defects in the causes of cognition.

Therefore, if there were defects even in the case of verbal testimony, those too would be inferred—by means of an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*)—to be causes of cognitions that contradict worldly practice, because they are defects, just like cataracts and the like; and consequently, from where could the validity characterized by non-contradiction with worldly practice arise? This is the meaning.

One might object: "If that is so, then even defects (*doṣa*) in perception and the other means of knowledge would have to be postulated as causes of cognitions that are non-concordant with worldly practice (*vyavahāra-visaṃvādin*), because they are defects, just like defects in the sense organs and so forth. Consequently, since perception and the others would themselves possess defects, their validity (*prāmāṇya*), characterized by non-discordance with worldly practice, would not exist due to contradiction. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But in the case of perception and the others... The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction from the [previous] argument regarding words; for in the case of perception and the others, concordance with worldly practice is observed.

Therefore, because there is no contradiction with perception, it is not possible to postulate, on the basis of this inference, that there exists a defect in those [cognitions] which causes a failure of correspondence in worldly practice (*vyavahāra*). For such a defect could only be postulated if there were a discrepancy in practical activity regarding them; however, it has already been stated that such a discrepancy does not exist. Thus, the sense is that even if a defect were present, the empirical validity (*vyāvahārikapramāṇya*) of perception and the other means of knowledge would not be contradicted.

If no defects that cause non-conformity with worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) are postulated for perception and the other means of knowledge, then what kind [of defect] is it, and from what source is such a thing postulated? In response to this inquiry, he states both the nature of that [defect] and the reason why it is postulated: "But of the vision of reality... and so forth.

Because the knowledge of the reality of non-duality (*advaitatattvajñāna*) arising from Vedāntic texts such as "one only, without a second" stands in opposition to the duality that is the object of perception and other means of knowledge, and because it sublates that [duality], one must postulate an beginningless connection with ignorance (*anādyavidyānubandha*) as the sole cause for the obstruction of that ultimate reality—the duality which is the object of perception and other means of knowledge. It is not [the case that this duality is real].

The meaning is that cataracts and the like are the causes of the obstruction of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*). This is what is being said: for in the case of perception and other means of knowledge, a defect is not something cognizable through another means of knowledge; rather, it must be postulated on the strength of scripture (*āmnāya*). Therefore, it deserves to be postulated only in accordance with that [scripture]. And since scripture reveals non-duality (*advaita*), it is opposed solely to the duality that constitutes the object of perception and the other means of knowledge; it does not subvert empirical usage.

Therefore, when a defect is postulated in accordance with that [observation], it is postulated as nothing other than the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is capable of producing the false cognition of duality; it is not postulated as something like cataracts (*timira*), which is capable of producing a cognition that contradicts worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Thus, he concludes: "Therefore," meaning that even though there is a defect in perception and the other means of knowledge, their validity—characterized by non-contradiction in worldly transaction—is not inconsistent, just as in the case of the conceit of the body being the self (*dehātmābhimāna*).

He concludes the point previously stated—that the authority of a faulty word would not exist—with the words "But the word... (*śabdastu*). In that very context, he also recalls the reasoning mentioned earlier with the words "For it is seen... (*dṛśyate hi*). And in the phrase "and of the obstruction" (*pratighātasya ca*), the word "because it was suspected" (*śaṅkitatvāt*) is to be supplied. Now, he concludes the superiority of verbal testimony over perception and other means of knowledge when there is a conflict, with the words "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).

For he who asserts that the Veda lacks authority when it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge necessarily accepts its authority as being free from defect when there is no such contradiction; this being the case, it is logical that the flawless Veda possesses greater force than perception and the rest, whose defects have been postulated by the aforementioned arguments. Now, he restates what was said—that the Veda is weaker than those [means] because it depends upon perception and so forth—with the words "As for that which... He states the refutation of that point with the word "Therein..."

It is true that verbal testimony (*śabda*) has a dependence upon perception and other means of knowledge regarding its object; however, this dependence does not pertain to its validity (*pramiti*)—that is, to the determination of its own meaning—but rather to the establishment of its own nature (*svarūpa-siddhi*). He confirms this very point with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). For if verbal testimony were dependent upon perception and the like for its validity, then, because validity is characterized by independence (*anapekṣā-lakṣaṇatvāt*), verbal testimony would not even be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Alternatively, the meaning is this: if the word does not depend upon perception and other means for the establishment of its own nature, then, failing to produce a cognition when it is not understood, it would not even be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). He asks, "If it is independent of that [perception] regarding the resulting cognition, then what? and answers with the words "And so" (*tathā ca*). Since the word is independent of perception and the rest with respect to its effect, which is characterized as the resulting cognition, the word is not inferior to perception and the rest, because there is no difference in their status as means of valid knowledge.

An objection is raised: "Surely, even though a word is independent regarding its effect, it depends upon perception and other means for the establishment of its own form (*svarūpa*), whereas perception and the rest do not depend on the word; why, then, should the word not be inferior to them? Anticipating this, he says: "Perception and the rest as well. Even in the case of perception and the rest, there is dependence for the establishment of their own forms due to their reliance on the sense organs and so forth; yet this does not bring about their lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). For dependence regarding the effect merely diminishes their capacity (*sāmarthya*) [p. 115].

It acts; moreover, that which has inferior capacity becomes non-authoritative when sublated by that which has superior capacity. Therefore, mere dependence is not the cause of non-authoritativeness, but rather dependence regarding the effect; and this [dependence] does not exist even for the word. Thus, the intention is that there is no non-authoritativeness of the word.

Now, since the establishment of the nature of the Veda depends upon perception and the other means of knowledge, their authority must necessarily be accepted for the sake of establishing that very nature of the Veda; therefore, it is appropriate that they possess greater force when there is a conflict with the Veda. He restates this objection with the words "But as for... Having thus restated it, he refutes it with the words "And who says...": "It is true that their authority must be accepted, but it is of the kind characterized by non-contradiction in practical usage (*vyavahārāvisaṃvāda*), not of the kind characterized by the revelation of ultimate reality (*tattvāvedana*). This is the meaning.

What, then, is the specific reason for which one accepts only conventional validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*) and not that characterized by the revelation of reality (*tattvāvedana*)? Anticipating this doubt, he states the specific reason: "from the Veda, which possesses conventional validity, as established through perception. The reason for its non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*) is that the non-contradiction of worldly practice is not in conflict with the establishment of the Veda; and the phrase "due to contradiction with that" refers to its sublation by the scriptural revelation of the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*).

By this, the following is stated: because these [means of knowledge] such as perception and the rest are sublated by the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), their validity characterized by the revelation of reality (*tattvāvedana*) is not accepted according to the standard of the Śruti; however, their empirical (*vyāvahārika*) validity is not sublated because it is consistent with its own sphere, and therefore it is accepted—this is the distinction. Now, one might object: this cognition of perception and the rest, which apprehends the Śruti, must itself depend on the cognition of reality produced by the Śruti, since it is the means thereto. It is logical that whatever is established by the force of something else should be considered weaker than that thing.

As it has been said: “If the establishment of X occurs by the very power of Y, how can Y be more powerful [than X]? Consequently, how can the realization of reality (*tattva*) produced by the Veda be more powerful than the cognitions derived from perception and other means? And how could it sublate them? For the relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists only when there is a contradiction; yet such a contradiction does not exist between the means (*upāya*) and the end (*upeya*), otherwise the very relationship of means and end would not be possible.

As it has been said: “And this [subsequent cognition], having been established, cannot sublate its own cause. This [author] refutes that by pointing out an instance of deviation, using the words “and it is observed. Here, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in *pūrvasyāḥ pratipatteḥ* (from the prior cognition), while the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in *parasyāḥ* (of the subsequent). He provides an example with the words “for instance. In the phrase *vanaspatipratipatteḥ*, the word *balavattvam* (the state of being stronger) is to be supplied as the predicate. Now, one might object: an example should be given where the subsequent cognition, which is required as the cause [of sublation], is stronger than the prior cognition.

Nor is there any proof that, in this case, the cognitions of elephants are required as the cause for the cognition of the forest tree; therefore, suspecting that the example is inconsistent with the subject at hand, he first asserts the similarity between the example and the subject by stating: "For they are required," etc. By saying "the cognitions of elephants," he shows that it is many such cognitions that serve as the cause, not just one. As [in the verse]: 8A [p. 116]

We shall explain this accordingly. Now, one might object: "Since it arises immediately after the contact of the sense organ [with the object], the cognition of the tree must be produced by that [contact] alone, and not produced by the cognition of the elephant; therefore, how can it be said to depend upon the latter? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not of that" (na tasyāḥ), meaning "not of the cognition of the tree. Why? He says: "Because of its sudden appearance" (āpāte). If the birth of the cognition of the tree were from mere contact with the sense organ, it would occur at the very first moment of approach; however, it does not so occur.

Therefore, its birth does not arise from mere sense-object contact; rather, the meaning is that even the cognition of an elephant must be required as a cause. Now, one might object: "Granted that its birth does not occur from sense-object contact alone, it will nonetheless arise from contact accompanied by a specific location; nevertheless, why must the cognition of an elephant be required as a cause? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not [from] the location," etc. The phrase "its birth" is understood to carry over. Why? He says: "Because of that location," etc.

This might be so in a case where a person standing at a distance first has a non-existent cognition of a tree, and later, as he approaches it, the cognition arises; but where [the cognition] arises for one who is already situated in that very place, its birth does not result from a particular location—this is the meaning. "One situated in that place" refers to the person; "that" refers to the place in which the cognition of the tree arose spontaneously.

Since the cognition of a tree does not arise from the mere contact of the sense organ with its specific location prior to the cognition of an elephant, but does arise immediately after the cognition of an elephant, it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that this [cognition] arises from the contact of the sense organ accompanied by the cognition of an elephant; thus he concludes that the cognitions of elephants serve as the means [to the cognition of the tree], stating "therefore."

The meaning is this: the "prior" refers to a preceding error or delusive cognition; the "mental continuum" (matisantati) is a series of cognitions that repeatedly apprehends that very [object] as an elephant; the "impression born thereof" (tajjaḥ saṃskāraḥ) is the latent trace produced by that; and the "conjunction of the sense organ" which has that impression as its "associate" (saciva)—that is, its auxiliary cause—is what produces the cognition of the tree. Thus, it is the cognition of the tree [that arises].

For when someone, having seen an elephant through delusion, applies his mind by means of its various parts, and as he perceives that very elephant again and again with its specific features, there arises—without being intentionally sought—the knowledge of the reality of the forest tree; in that case, the repeated perception of the elephant serves as the cause for the knowledge of the reality of the forest tree, which is termed a "stream of cognition."

For instance: having once perceived an illusory elephant and then disregarding it, for one who has moved on to another object, no true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) regarding that [elephant] arises. Now, one might argue that mental attention (*manaspraṇidhāna*) alone is the cause of such true knowledge here. If that were so, then it was not performed with the intention of attaining true knowledge of that [object], but rather to know the elephant again and again. But surely, even when the mind is directed toward one thing, it may cause the cognition of something else, just as the eye opened for a jar perceives a cloth.

In that case, the cognition of an elephant and the cognition of a tree cannot occur simultaneously in a single locus, as they are contradictory, unlike the cognitions of a jar and a cloth. Therefore, even while the mind is directed toward and producing the cognition of that [tree], it is preceded by a continuum of cognitions of the elephant.

It is established that [the cognition of the elephant] itself produces [the cognition of the true nature]; thus, even the stream of cognitions regarding the elephant possesses the status of being the cause for the cognition of its true nature. Now, one might object: "The cognition of the true nature arises from the cognition of properties distinct from the properties of the elephant; therefore, that [distinct cognition] alone is its cause. True; however, it is precisely that [cognition of the elephant] which arises for one who repeatedly observes the elephant more skillfully through various specific features, and not for one who, having known it once, becomes indifferent and moves on to another object—as has already been stated.

Therefore, the cognition of a property distinct [from the elephant] does not subvert the causality of the intermediate operation within the continuum of the cognition of the elephant, for that would entail the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that all causal factors (kāraka) are non-causes. As it has been said: "For in every single causal factor, there is indeed an intervention by its own operation. Therefore, everything is consistent. In this very context, he states another example: "In the same way" (evam); the analysis of the compound is: those for which the cognitions of numbers such as unity and so forth are the means (upāya). Viśvādi-... P.

41-10 Furthermore, the greater strength of cognitions [of number] should be understood as follows: the cognitions of numbers such as "oneness" and so forth override the delimiting nature [of other attributes] by acting as the delimiters of the substance itself, thereby initiating their own conventional usage. If this "delimiting nature" were the very essence (*svarūpa*) of number, then in the absence of that [higher number], the intermediate numbers within a large number would be utterly false due to the lack of their own essential nature; as it has been said: "Each preceding one is false."

This being the case, he now dispels another objection by way of a further consequence, beginning with the words "If this is so. The word "this" (evam) refers back to the logic of the elephant, the tree, and so forth, which was just mentioned. The connection is with what will be said next: "that which some describe is refuted. He states what they describe: "by itself alone. To the question "How so? he replies: "there is no non-difference. Why? He says: "because [non-difference] depends on difference"; for there is no apprehension of non-difference without the distinction of the knower and so forth. This is the meaning.

To the question, "What is the fault here?", he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). Non-duality (*advaita*) implies the duality of the knower and so forth for its own realization; yet duality and non-duality cannot coexist. Therefore, the meaning is that there is a mutual contradiction. To the question, "But how is this refuted?", he says: "Because" (*yataḥ*). He states the reason: "as false" (*mithyā*). And in this context, the examples are precisely the cognitions of elephants. If it is asked, "How can duality, which is absolutely non-existent, serve as a means? he says: "empirical" (*vyāvahārikam*).

Thus it is established that verbal testimony possesses greater force when there is a conflict with perception and other means of knowledge. The word *iti* marks the conclusion. As for the further argument stated—that verbal testimony is fallible because its deviation is observed—he demonstrates this by saying "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*). The sense is that even though the word itself is not inherently defective, its defect lies solely in being uttered by one who is more defective; for defects, which cause a reversal of the effect, possess a variety of forms. Now, if it is argued that perception produced by non-defective causes is non-deviant, he says "of the other two" (*itarayoḥ*), meaning that the same applies to verbal testimony as well.

He also refutes the argument stated [by the opponent] that the lack of scope (*anavakāśatva*) is the reason for the superiority of perception and other means of knowledge—[the text says] "In the same way" (*tathā*). The phrase "is equal to verbal testimony" (*śābdapratyakṣayoḥ samānam*) is understood to carry over. He states this equality: "If... (*yadi*). It must be said that the scope belongs to that meaning which is well-known as the subject matter of the Vedāntas, and not to any other, such as external violence—which, like the prohibition of violence, is sublated by the injunction regarding non-violence in sacrifice. And that [scope] must be either primary (*mukhya*) or secondary (*gauṇa*); it cannot be both, because that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

If, therefore, the primary meaning of the Vedānta were well-established, then figurative and unintended meanings would simply not exist; how then could there be any scope for them? Thus, the meaning is that the lack of scope applies equally even to the Āgama (scriptural tradition).

Now, if it is argued that—given the existence of duality—the meaning of the Vedāntas is either a figurative unity consisting of birth and so forth, or that their purpose is for recitation (japa) since their literal meaning is not intended; then, given the existence of duality, there is no contradiction at all between the Vedāntas—whether they express a figurative unity consisting of birth and so forth or are intended for recitation—and the means of knowledge such as perception which have duality as their object, because their objects are either different or [the Vedāntas] have no object [at all]. In that case, the consideration of relative strength (balābala) does not even arise; for such a consideration occurs only when there is a contradiction.

And while that [primary sense] exists, the other would be weak due to having no scope; he asks "whence is that? and answers with "Now" (*atha*). He states another objection against both positions with "How? (*katham*). The meaning [of the word] has its scope within the domain of the primary sense (*buddhakakṣya*). And it is not possible for the secondary sense to have the same scope as the primary, because that would contradict the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*); such is the intended meaning.

Likewise, the status of the word as a subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*)—its being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*)—in relation to the meaning to be expressed, by virtue of its being the signifier, is innate and natural. This is established by the principles: "For its purpose is seen to be the communication of ritual action" and "But the meaning of the sentence is uniform. How then could it be that the meaning is not intended? This is the sense. Now, it might be argued: where there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there the primary meaning cannot be set aside, nor can there be a figurative meaning or a lack of intentionality regarding the meaning.

But here, since there is a contradiction with other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) such as perception that apprehend difference, and because the primary meaning [of non-duality] is thus untenable, why should one of those two [perception and scripture] not be set aside? He raises this doubt with the words "by other means of valid cognition. He refutes it with the word "vārtam"; the meaning is that this is merely a rumor, or it is insubstantial. He states its insubstantiality with the word "no" (na). The sense is that the self-validity (svataḥ-prāmāṇya) [of perception] is established. It is the natural disposition [of perception] to have the primary meaning as its object.

He states the reason why that which possesses intrinsic validity (*svarasa-prāmāṇya*) does not abandon its own nature: "That" (*tat*). The meaning is: dependence on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntarāpekṣatva*) is the cause for the word functioning in accordance with that other means of knowledge; that is to say, "because. He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "Of that which is independent" (*nirapekṣasya*). But for a means of knowledge that is independent of other means of knowledge, what reason could there be for following another means of knowledge—whether by abandoning or adopting its own object—based on whether there is contradiction or non-contradiction? The meaning is: none at all. Now, one might object: in common worldly usage, as in "The boy is fire" (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*), the word functions in accordance with another means of knowledge... [p. 119]

The operation [of words] has been observed [in common usage]; therefore, one might suspect that it ought to be exactly the same here as well. Anticipating this, he states their difference with the words "But worldly... (laukikās tu). The meaning is: worldly words are employed for objects perceived through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, because they denote an object that depends upon another means of knowledge, it is logical that their function follows those other means of knowledge. He states the distinction by saying "But when it is equal... (tulye tu).

Since perception and scripture are equal in their independence from other means of knowledge, why does the reverse not occur? That is to say, why are perception and the other means of knowledge not themselves interpreted so as to conform to scripture? This is the meaning.

Why should there not be invalidity for both [the Veda and perception] as well, due to mutual contradiction, like the case of two contradictory non-erroneous reasons (*viruddhāvyabhicāri-hetu*)? The meaning is: why should there not be a sublation of the earlier—such as perception and so forth—by the Vedic revelation (*āmnāya*), just as the cognition of silver is sublated by the cognition of mother-of-pearl, according to the maxim that "in a sequence of prior and posterior, the former is weaker"? It is this very last position that is intended as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

It should be understood that the two preceding [verses] were stated as a bold assertion (prauḍhivāda) with the intent that, in every respect, the operation of the sacred tradition (āmnāya) would fail to accord with perception and other means of knowledge. He strengthens this very point with the example: "But certainly not" (na tv-alu). The word *alu* is used to indicate what is well-known (*prasiddhi*). It is well known in the case of the cognition of silver that, because of the contradiction with what preceded it, the subsequent [cognition] is not assumed to be without an object or to have a different object; rather, it is simply the sublation (*bādha*) of the former. The sense is that the same must hold true here as well.

The statement "beyond the scope" (*aviṣaya*) is made for the sake of establishing parity with the position that the meaning of the Veda (*āmnāya*) is not intended to be literal. Now, if a word does not abandon its primary meaning even when there is a contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then how is it that in passages such as "Water is indeed peaceful" (*āpo vai śāntāḥ*), there is a figurative eulogy (*guṇavāda*)? For in this case, there is no basis for a figurative eulogy other than contradiction with another means of valid cognition. Anticipating this objection, the author asks: "How? The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*), however, replies: "Where... (*yatra*).

In a sentence, to whatever extent its scope of authority extends, if the intended meaning as a whole—the subject matter of the sentence—is not established because the primary meanings expressed by the words heard therein do not cohere with one another, then, since in common worldly usage words are seen to function through a second mode of operation (lakṣaṇā), that secondary function is resorted to so that the word, as a means of valid knowledge, may obtain its object; for example, in the injunction, "He draws the fire with a branch of the *vetasa* tree and with *avakā* grass," the *vetasa* branch and the *avakā* grass are both enjoined.

Furthermore, water is praised in the passage, "Water is indeed peaceful. Since the injunction and the praise there have different objects and thus lack mutual connection, the meaning of the sentence remains unestablished; consequently, even though there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge, one must set aside the literal praise of water and instead adopt the view that the purpose is the praise of the *vetasa* branch and the *avakā* plant, on the grounds that by praising their origin, the noble-born [the plants] themselves are praised.

This is what is meant: in the Veda, contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not the cause for [a term] being secondary; rather, it is the impossibility [of the meaning] when the primary sense is established as the object of a means of valid cognition. Now, it may be argued that elsewhere it has been observed that injunction (*vidhi*) and praise (*stuti*) share a single subject matter; therefore, if they have different subject matters here as well, there is indeed a contradiction with that observation. [p. 120]

True; however, that [contradiction with other means of knowledge] is the cause for the non-establishment of the sentence-meaning, not for the abandonment of the fact that water is intended to be "tranquil" as heard in the text. And that abandonment occurs precisely because of the non-establishment of the sentence-meaning. Now, one might argue: in cases such as "The sacrificial post is the sun," figurative interpretation arises simply due to contradiction with another means of knowledge; for the identity of the sacrificial post with the sun is contradicted by another means of knowledge, namely non-perception. But even there, contradiction with another means of knowledge is not the cause of the figurative sense; rather, it is simply the non-establishment of the objective referent of the means of knowledge.

For that [figurative usage] has its power observed in things such as the *vetasa* branch and is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*). Since the identity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with the sun cannot be connected to the meaning of the sentence concerning the tethering of the animal, there is indeed a failure to accomplish the purpose of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, contradiction by another means of knowledge is deviant, because even in the absence of that [identity], one may resort to figurative usage in the case of the *vetasa* branch and so forth; and a non-deviant cause is what is appropriate. Therefore, it is established that even in the case of the sacrificial post and the like, the very failure to accomplish the purpose of the means of knowledge is the cause of figurative usage. This concludes the second application of the fivefold [reasoning].

However, since this is not the case in Vedānta, there is no figurative sense [intended]; with this intention, he states the distinction [from other systems] with the words "But where... They turn back; the meaning is that they return of their own accord. Here, he recalls the reasoning stated previously with the words "For not... He raises another view on this very point with the words "Now, if... The phrase "in this way" means that the scripture would have a figurative sense. He explains the reconciliation of both [views] with the words "For in this way..."

If the scripture (*āmnāya*) were secondary, then there would be no contradiction because their objects would be distinct—the non-difference of entities by way of genus and so forth, and their difference by way of their own nature—and thus both [scripture and perception] would be upheld; the meaning is that there is no absolute sublation of perception and the like by the scripture. He states the counter-argument with the words "otherwise": if, on the other hand, the scripture were primary in its literal sense, then since non-duality would be real, perception and the like, which have duality as their object, would be absolutely sublated, and there would be no upholding of both.

The sense is that when both [alternatives] are being favored, it is not logical for one to be absolutely sublated. He refutes this with the words "Not this. He asks "Why? and replies "On account of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*); the meaning is as follows: a certain conceptual construction regarding an object of knowledge (*prameya*) occurs in accordance with the capacity of the means of valid cognition. For example, there is a conceptual construction of an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the objects of knowledge such as rice and barley, in accordance with the capacity of the two injunctions that restrict them to rice or barley respectively; and likewise, there is a conceptual construction of a combination (*samuccaya*), in accordance with the capacity of the dual number in the phrase "by means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices."

And just as, in cases such as the *uditānuditahoma* (the oblation at sunrise or before sunrise), a systematic arrangement is devised according to different schools (*caraṇa*) by following the force of other scriptures; however, regarding the very nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no reason to abandon the primary meaning—which is established through its own natural essence and innate capacity—and to assume a figurative sense for the sake of reconciling both, as there is no basis for doing so. He concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The term "in the object of knowledge" (*prameye*) is understood to carry over. He refutes the reason stated by the opponent: [P. 42-5, p. 121]

"No," says the other—"those very ones. The meaning is that those two mutually contradictory means of knowledge (pramāṇas) known as perception and scripture are themselves the authority for reconciling both; one does not seek another means of knowledge for that purpose. He explains this very point with the words "If... and asks "Why? by saying "Because they are means of knowledge."

The meaning is as follows: the non-duality [established] by scripture and the like is established precisely because of their own inherent validity (*prāmāṇyatva*), and not by the force of another means of knowledge; for that reason, the object of perception and the like is duality, whereas the object of scripture is secondary non-duality. This is what is being said: if this were not so established, both perception and scripture would cease to be valid means of knowledge, since their objects would be contradictory; yet they are indeed valid means of knowledge. Therefore, the determination of the respective objects occurs solely through the power of their intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*).

Since both are to be accepted, those very two—perception and scripture—are the authorities (*pramāṇa*). Although one should have said "of those two" (*tayoḥ*) or "by those two" (*tābhyām*), the singular forms "of that" (*tasya*) and "by that" (*tena*) are used with a general intention in order to establish the underlying principle (*nyāya*) in a general sense. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), however, says: "Just as... If one establishes that [scripture] as an authority, then that [scripture] is an authority for an object exactly as it is understood from it; therefore, the object must be established as being exactly of that nature.

In this way, that [scriptural statement] is upheld; otherwise, if such a reality were abandoned, it would indeed be sublated due to a reversal of its meaning. Thus, when the non-dual tradition establishes a non-dual nature of reality, since duality—which is the domain of perception and other means of knowledge—is impossible, how could there be the possibility of upholding both? This is the intended sense. He states another defect in establishing [reality] otherwise than as it is perceived: "And [the scripture] would be without authority. To the question "Why?", he says: "Therefore..."

For an object that is not being perceived, when it is being established, it is not perceived from that word by its own inherent force (*svarasena*); nor is it perceived from anything else, because there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the meaning is that this establishment of the object is entirely without a basis in valid cognition. He states the fault in this very context with the words "mutually" (*itaretara*). He clarifies that very point with the words "from validity" (*prāmāṇyāt*). He then states that this fault does not apply if one relies on an object established by its own inherent force, with the words "by its own inherent force" (*svarasa*).

For when an object that is not being perceived is postulated, then its perception must be postulated on the strength of the validity [of the cognition]; and by virtue of that perception, the validity [of the cognition] would consist in its being the generator of that perception—thus there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). But when the primary object is grasped as established by its own nature, then validity arises from the perception established by its own nature, and the perception [arises] from validity; for that perception is established by its very own nature—this is the meaning. He concludes the subject at hand with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since it is not logical for both to be accommodated when there is a contradiction, therefore, the sublation of the prior means of knowledge, such as perception, by the scripture (*āmnāya*) alone is authoritative; this is because cognition occurs through the sublation of the prior, or because it is cognized in that manner in cases such as nacre-silver, and not because of the subsequent scripture.

The meaning is that the postulation of another object for the activity [of perception] conforms to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding this very point, he states an example: "Indeed, not... (*na khalu*). He further states that even what was said regarding the lack of scope (*anavakāśatva*) for perception and the other means of knowledge is unestablished: "And not... (*na ca*). To the question of how there is no lack of scope, he says: "That which indeed... (*yā khalu*). Lack of scope occurs when there is no other alternative (*ananyagati*); however, there exists an alternative for perception and the others, namely, their status as error (*bhrāntitva*), just like the delusion of silver and so forth. Therefore, there is no lack of scope; this is the meaning.

Although the objection regarding the lack of scope (*niravakāśatva*) was previously set aside by recalling the possibility of illusions such as that of silver, it is now refuted once more; thus there is no fault. He states that these [objects] are merely the objects of illusory cognitions of silver and the like with the words "If... (*yadi*). The phrase "of them" (*teṣām*) means "of the illusions of silver and the like. A young boy (*māṇavaka*), while existing in his own nature, becomes the object of the word "fire" through the mere application of a quality; whereas silver and the like are themselves [merely] figurative in their own nature. This was stated—"imagined" (*kalpita*)—in order to show this specific internal distinction.

"Imagined" (kalpita) means superimposed by the intellect; the ellipsis of the sentence is that even perception and the other means of knowledge have precisely such [imagined] objects. Now, if it is argued that because silver and the like are non-existent, errors regarding silver and so forth are without an object, and therefore perception and the others must likewise be without objects, he says: "Now" (atha). It has been stated that the status of the Veda as having a figurative meaning consists in its having a non-existent referent due to its not being intended [to be taken literally].

It should be understood that this was stated—in order to show that even perception and the other means of knowledge are of the nature of cognition—to indicate that perception and the rest have a figurative meaning (*upacaritārthatva*) and lack a real object (*avidyamānārthatva*), just like the error of silver and the like. He concludes the present topic with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The point is this: just as the Veda has scope because its meaning is figurative or not intended to be taken literally, so too do perception and the others; thus, there is no sublation of the Veda by them on the grounds that they would otherwise be left without scope. [The phrase] "of both" refers to...

The meaning is "of perception and scripture. This being the case, he states that other views are also refuted by saying, "And these. He sets forth another view with the words, "As they say. "Being such" (tathābhāvaḥ) means having a figurative sense or having a sense that is not intended to be primary. The opponent's intention is that a conceptualization following what is observed is logical. He explains how that is refuted with the words, "In perception and so forth. Just as there is scope for [interpretation], so too defectiveness is common to both perception and scripture without distinction.

Therefore, the point is that even on that basis, there is no [justification for claiming] that the Veda itself has a figurative or unintended meaning. If it is argued that such a perception occurs in the case of a pseudo-perception (pratyakṣābhāsa), we grant that; however, its status as a pseudo-perception is only postulated there because of contradiction with other means of knowledge, and not previously. Likewise, in the case of the Word (śabda) as well, whether it has a non-primary meaning or an unintended meaning, the situation is the same.

Now, he restates the alternative position mentioned previously in order to refute it: "Because [perception] is primary" (P. 48-5); that is to say, because it arises first and its objects are established without having encountered any contradiction, the Veda has its subject matter sublated by perception and the other means of knowledge; therefore, it is not a valid authority—this is the meaning. The analysis of the compound is: "those whose objects have become established," meaning those that have become fixed or immovable. He refutes that with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*): precisely because perception and the others occur first, for that very reason the Veda is their sublater—this is the meaning.

Regarding this, he states an illustration: "like the cognition of mother-of-pearl" (*śuktijñānavat*); the meaning is that just as the cognition of mother-of-pearl sublates a previously existing cognition of silver, so it is here. Now, one might object: since the Veda is primary, it must follow perception and other means of knowledge, and thus the Veda should not be interpreted in a way that contradicts them; anticipating this doubt, he says: "and not [so]," where again the illustration is "just like the cognition of mother-of-pearl. He states the reason: "because of its independence" (*anapekṣatvāt*). He explains this very independence: "not... [and so forth].

If the authority of the Veda were dependent upon perception and other means of knowledge, then it would depend upon perception and the rest for its own validity; however, this is not the case, because, being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), its validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Therefore, the meaning is that the Veda does not require the postulation of an object in accordance with those [other means]. Furthermore, if the Veda were to produce a single act of cognition in conjunction with perception and the other means, then it too would have dependence regarding that effect.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for two things with contradictory purposes to act together toward a single effect, the latter would have to be interpreted in accordance with the former; however, this is not the case, as he says: "not by them. Alternatively, if there were syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between these two, as there is between the words contained in sentences such as those regarding the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi* sacrifice, then it might be so; but even this is not the case, as he says: "not of the Veda" (*nāmnāyasya*). He provides the reason for both cases: "mutually" (*paraspara-*) and so forth. Or rather, "not of the Veda" is the reason for their not acting in concert; and syntactic unity consists in having a single intended meaning (*ekatātparyatva*).

When that [simultaneity] exists, there is the state of acting in combination (*saṃbhūyakāritva*). And this does not exist for the Veda and for perception and so forth, because in both cases cognitions arise independently of one another—thus the text should be construed. To the question, "What is logical in this case?", he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). In that case—when cognitions arise independently of one another—it is logical that the subsequent [cognition] possesses superior force (*parabalīyastva*), because it is observed to be so in instances such as the cognition of silver and mother-of-pearl; the meaning is that the object of the subsequent [cognition] is not to be postulated in accordance with the preceding one.

He confirms this with the words of an authoritative person (*abhiyukta*) by saying, "as it has been said. To the question, "In what case, then, does the primary sense prevail? he replies: "But where... The word *tu* (but) is used for the sake of distinction.

However, in a particular sentence where many word-meanings, through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), act together to produce the cognition of a single sentential meaning, there—because the preceding contradictory word has not yet been uttered—the primary first word remains established in its own natural function (*svarasavṛtti*) as the primary [sense] since no contradiction has yet arisen. Consequently, the subsequent words [cannot] provide the meanings required by the preceding word.

[Page 124] Since they are unable to achieve syntactic unity with the preceding word through the primary mode of signification (*mukhyā vṛtti*), they provide the meaning required by the preceding word through the secondary mode of signification (*gauṇī vṛtti*)—by virtue of, and through the power of, that syntactic unity; otherwise, there would be no syntactic unity at all for words whose meanings are mutually unconnected. For this reason, the primary preceding [word] possesses greater force. For example: "Prajāpati performed austerity. (*Prajāpatistapo'tapyata*).

Beginning with the passage, "From him, as he was performing austerity, the three Vedas were born," and ending with, "The Ṛk is recited aloud, the Sāman aloud, and the Yajus in a low voice," this is heard in the scripture. Regarding this, there is a doubt: do the words "Ṛk" and so forth denote the generic classes (jāti) of Ṛk verses and so on as they are defined, or do they denote the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas?

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was that the words *ṛk* and so forth denote the classes (*jāti*) of verses and the like because they are the primary meanings; however, since the word "Veda" is mentioned at the beginning of the section, and since that primary meaning remains established as it has not yet encountered any contradiction, the words *ṛk* and so forth—being unable to provide the required sense through their primary function (*mukhyā vṛttiḥ*)—are established by the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) as denoting the Vedas through their secondary function (*gauṇī vṛttiḥ*). As for what was said—that the injunctions of ritual action (*karmavidhi*) are intent upon the distinctions of the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), whereas the Vedāntas are intent upon non-duality (*abheda*)—[that too is addressed].

Therefore, the scripture (*āgama*), being itself mutually contradictory, is difficult to establish as authoritative; hence, it is indicated that its lack of authority is all the more evident when it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge. He restates this objection with the words "As for what was said... Having thus restated it, he refutes it with the words "In that case... [The principle is: "A word is a source of valid knowledge regarding that which it intends to convey"; and yet, the injunctions concerning ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) do not have the purpose of establishing the actual existence of difference (*bheda*).

However, by relying upon a distinction established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), [injunctions] have as their primary purport the meaning of an action beneficial to man, characterized by the three factors: "this is the goal," "by this means," and "in this manner one should accomplish it through this procedure. Therefore, they are not a means of valid knowledge regarding difference; thus, how could there be any conflict between them and the Vedāntas, which are means of valid knowledge for non-difference? This is the sense. Here, the opponent raises an objection: "It might be so... and so forth.

Even though the word does not primarily intend to express difference, but rather intends to enjoin an action (bhāvārtha-vidhi), nevertheless, it implies difference by necessity; for without difference, there can be no division into the three factors such as the goal to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth. And in the absence of that [division], an injunction of an action qualified by those [factors] is not possible—this is the meaning. He refutes this with the words "It is said": True, the instruction for one's welfare would imply the existence of difference if it were not possible without the three factors.

Just as in the case of injunctions such as the Śyena sacrifice, [an action] occurs even in the absence of the "object-to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) portion due to the prohibition "one must not injure," so too it will occur in all ritual injunctions even in the absence of the three constituent parts; thus, the sense is that they do not imply a difference [between the two types of injunctions]. Now, one might object: in the Śyena and similar sacrifices, injury is the object to be accomplished; yet it is not the case that it simply does not exist at all—like a sky-flower—since it exists once it has been performed.

Nor is it not pleasing, nor is it not desired; therefore, how can there be an absence of the *sādhya* (the goal to be accomplished) in those cases? Anticipating this objection, he says: "For thus... (*tathā hi*). For one who has not transcended the prohibitory scriptures, violence—which results in misfortune because it is given as a hidden treasure—is neither pleasing nor desired; nor is it a part of the *sādhya*. Therefore, the meaning is that for such a person, there is an absence of the *sādhya* element. It is called *anarthodayā* because misfortune (*anartha*) arises (*udīyate*) or emerges from it.

Now, for a certain person whose mind is overcome by intense anger, whose discriminative knowledge of what is beneficial and what is harmful is obscured by an agitated darkness, and who—consequently perceiving even harmful violence as beneficial—transgresses the prohibitive scriptures, for such a person, violence becomes something to be accomplished (*sādhya*); in this way, the possibility of an "objective factor" (*sādhyāṃśa*) is stated in the case of the Śyena sacrifice and others.

Likewise, even in the injunctions for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, all three parts imagined by ignorance are possible for those possessed of beginningless ignorance; thus, by relying on those very parts established through ignorance, the instruction of what is beneficial for the sake of those ignorant persons is justified. Therefore, that [instruction] does not imply the actual existence of the division into three parts. This is what he says with the words "Now" (atha). Having raised the doubt as to how injunctions for ritual action can exist for those possessed of knowledge given the non-existence of the three parts imagined by ignorance, he says: "But those who are awakened... (pratibuddhāstu).

Those who have directly realized the truth of the external self, considering the three factors [of action] to be non-existent or the self to be a non-agent, are not instructed by the injunctions for ritual action; therefore, the meaning is: what is the use of the reality of those three factors for them? Here he provides an illustration with the word "just as" (*yathā*). The phrase "are not instructed" (*nānuśiṣyante*) is understood to carry over from the previous context. "Krodhārāti" means one whose enemy is anger (*krodha*); those by whom that enemy has been conquered are so described. He concludes with "tadevam" (thus, in this way).

Therefore, although there is a cognition of the distinction between the three factors (the agent, the action, and the object) in those ritual injunctions whose basis is precisely that distinction established through conventional means—that is, through empirical instruments of knowledge such as perception and the like—nevertheless, because those ritual injunctions do not have the distinction itself as their primary purport, that distinction is not an authoritative means of proof (*pramāṇa*) regarding it. This is the meaning.

One might object: "If it is indeed perceived, why is there no validity (*prāmāṇya*) therein? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] provides an example to show that validity does not reside in mere perception, but rather in the intended meaning (*tātparya*), stating: "In the case of narratives" (*vṛttānteṣu*). The meaning is that just as there is no validity by mere perception in narratives such as the cutting of Prajāpati’s own fat—"Prajāpati cut out his own fat"—which are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), so too there is no validity in ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) apart from the distinction of the three factors (*trikāṇḍa*).

And since the Veda is not a means of valid cognition regarding difference, nor does it imply the existence of difference, there is no mutual contradiction within the Veda; thus, its weakness cannot be established on that account. With this intention, he says: "And so. Having thus resolved the mutual contradictions within the Veda, he now introduces them [in the world] in order to establish the weakness of perception and the other means of knowledge: "Moreover," etc. He asks "Why? and answers: "Because it is sublated," etc. He asks "Where? and answers: "In the case of silver," etc. [p. 126]

Here, the mutual contradiction has been stated with reference to the cognition of mere sensory objects, but the cognition of silver is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); rather, it is a semblance thereof (*tadābhāsa*). Now, regarding the proponent of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābhedavādin*), he provides another example of the mutual contradiction between the two intended meanings of direct perception: "Difference and non-difference," etc. In all cases, such as universals (*jāti*) and qualities (*guṇa*), both difference and non-difference are admitted by direct perception; yet these two are mutually contradictory.

Therefore, the sense is that because perception itself is sublated by having that [scriptural teaching] as its object, it is logical that it is weak. This should be inferred for inference and the other means of knowledge as well. Thus, since the authority of scripture is established as being more powerful, it follows that even when there is a conflict with perception and so forth, scripture alone is the valid means of knowledge; consequently, it would be redundant to undertake a section on "reconciliation" (parihāra) regarding such conflicts. Nevertheless, he states how it is nevertheless undertaken: "Thus, in this way... and so on.

The connection [of the following discussion] is with the statement: "The Vedas (*āmnāya*) have a figurative meaning when there is contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, because they are verbal in nature, like worldly speech"—this being said for the sake of instructing that dull-witted person who, deluded by such a fallacious inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumānābhāsa*), considers the Vedas to have a figurative meaning despite the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge; it is not, however, directed toward one who possesses discrimination (*vivekin*).

How, then, is there a fallacy of inference? It is said: worldly speech has its validity dependent upon perception and other means of knowledge; therefore, when there is a contradiction with those, it is logical that its meaning be figurative. But the Veda, possessing independent validity, why should it become figurative even when in contradiction with perception and the rest? Therefore, when there is dependence on perception and the rest, contradiction with perception and so forth is the cause for a word’s meaning being figurative, not contradiction alone; thus, [the opponent's argument] is a fallacy of inference. He states another method: "Or else... and so on.

Because it exists at all times for all those possessed of ignorance, it is "firmly established" (*rūḍha*) by way of being determined as such; it is "dense" (*nibiḍa*) by way of being firmly rooted, meaning it is extremely tight and, in other words, difficult to eradicate. Its state is its "nature" (*tattā*); thus, [the phrase means] "by way of that nature. However, in the reading *nirūḍhinibiḍatayā*, the compound is *nirūḍhyā nibiḍam*; and "establishment" (*nirūḍhi*) is simply the becoming rooted (*rūḍhi*) through determination. To the question "of what is there firm establishment and density?", he says: "of the darkness of the perception of difference."

The perception of difference is itself darkness, and that is due to its similarity with non-illumination. Since this [darkness] is firmly established and dense, and since the words of worldly people are seen to be sublated by perception and other means of knowledge, the meaning is that the contradiction with perception and so forth is being dispelled in order to awaken those who consider perception and the rest alone to be authoritative. Now, one might object: "There is no harm whatsoever to the Ātman even if it is defiled by the contradiction of perception and so forth by a wretched person of dull intellect and deluded mind."

Anticipating the objection, "What is the purpose of this effort to refute that? he says: "For indeed... Just as one who is bitten by a snake seen in a sluggish form by someone with impaired vision is treated with medical care even if he does not die, so too must the Self be treated medically even if it is defiled by contradictions such as those of perception for someone of dull intellect or one who is deluded; for him, too, the removal of the defect known as contradiction must be performed.

This is the meaning. Regarding the reading "mriyate" (dies), one might suspect that the fault stated by him [the opponent] is beyond doubt because it was spoken by one of dull intellect; however, the connection should be made as follows: just as one who is bitten by a mild poison and dies in a particular place is treated with medicine, so too the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*)—which, though corrupted by a person of dull intellect, is further defiled by many of dull intellect and thus meets the death of invalidity—must also be treated.

Having thus established the commencement of the definition of non-contradiction, he explains the verse beginning with "They say [it] is the creator" with the word "therein. He specifies those same three positions with the words "the entity," etc. [Direct perception... P.

44-10 Does the cognition "this is a jar" enjoin the mere nature of the object? Or does it exclude another object, such as "this is not a cloth"? Or does it both apprehend and exclude? Even when it performs both, does it perform the injunction and the exclusion simultaneously? Or does it exclude after having enjoined? Or does it enjoin after having excluded?

In that regard, among those positions, if it is admitted that the operation of perception consists either in the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*) or in both, then because difference (*bheda*) would be the object of perception, there would be a contradiction with the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). However, when the operation of perception consists merely in the affirmation of the nature of a thing (*vastusvarūpavidhi*), devoid of the exclusion of any other entity, difference is not the object of perception.

Anticipating the objection—"Why, then, when the operation of perception consists solely of affirmation (vidhi) devoid of exclusion (vyavaccheda), does difference (bheda) not become an object of perception?"—the author says: "For indeed" (na hi). For perception, while not excluding [other things], does not grasp the difference of a jar from that [other thing]; therefore, without exclusion, there is no establishment, no recognition, and no cognition of difference—this is the meaning. To the question, "Even if this is so, what follows from it?", he says: "Solely affirmation" (vidhimātra).

Perception grasps only the essential nature of an object and does not exclude anything else; therefore, since it lacks the quality of having difference as its object, there is no contradiction between it and the scriptural teaching of non-difference—this is the meaning. Here, the opponent asks: "How so? The meaning of the question is: how can perception be merely affirmative and not exclusionary? To this he gives the answer: "It is said. He states what was referred to by the words "that which is said": "Having obtained... He explains the verse: "Not indeed..."

The word "first" (*tāvat*) is used with reference to the position that negation is preceded by a positive injunction (*vidhi*), which is about to be refuted. First of all, the operation of perception is not merely exclusion (*vyavaccheda*); nor is it both exclusion and affirmation (*vidhi*) simultaneously; nor is it an affirmation preceded by exclusion. This is because, regarding an object already established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), only that which is already established therein is negated. He states the nature of this negation: [p. 128]

P. 44-20. “This is not here” and “this is not that. The presentation is made with a distinction: “This is not here” is the negation of relation (*saṃsarga*), while “this is not that” is the negation of identity (*tādātmya*). He provides an example for both cases with the word “established” (*siddha*). When a jar established by another means of knowledge is negated on a ground already established [by perception], this is an example of “this is not here. When a horse established [as present] in a cow is negated, this is an example of “this is not that.”

To the inquiry, "Why, moreover, is the well-known existence of the object of negation and the thing to be negated required for a negation? he says: "No. For a negation is not independent; rather, it must belong to something somewhere. Therefore, as long as the thing to be negated and the locus of the negation are not known, the negation itself is not possible; this is the meaning. Here, an objection is raised: "How then..."

The meaning is: if that which is established is negated regarding an object that is already established, how could there be a negation such as "primordial matter does not exist" or "a sky-flower does not exist"? Why, then, is negation not possible here? To this he says: "For not... For every negation is seen to occur when a specific place or a specific time is established; yet neither of these exists here. Therefore, the sense is that in this case, no established object exists as the locus of negation. Why is this so? He says: "Because of its absolute nature."

Wherever there is a negation of something that exists elsewhere, in that case the qualifiers of place and time apply; but this is an absolute negation, namely "it does not exist anywhere," and not "it does not exist here" in a particular place or at a particular time. Therefore, the meaning is that in this case those two qualifiers are not possible. Not only is there no object [of negation] here, but even the thing to be negated is not established; thus he says: "nor... (nāpi).

The meaning is that the primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth are not established anywhere by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like a jar or similar objects. He states the reason: "because of absolute non-existence. The absolute non-existence of a sky-flower is well-known to everyone. Primordial matter, however, exists for the Sāṃkhyas, though it is not something they themselves deny; rather, it is denied in other systems of debate, and its negation is unestablished [for them]. It is precisely because of this distinction that two examples were given. Regarding that, he states the rebuttal according to the opinion of one school: "In that case... He states what they say: "As for the sky..."

The word "first" (*tāvat*) is used with reference to the rebuttal concerning the negation of the *pradhāna*. The meaning is that regarding space (*khādi*) and other things established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), flowers and so forth—which are of the same nature as those—are here negated precisely because they are established by other means of valid cognition; thus, there is no lack of proof for the object of negation which is established by another means of valid cognition. Likewise, he says "the *pradhāna*" to show that even in the case of "the *pradhāna* does not exist," there is no lack of proof for either the subject or the object of negation: first of all, a cause is established for the world because its production is observed.

And the Pradhāna consists of the forms of sattva, rajas, and tamas; because of the non-difference between cause and effect, its effects are held by the Sāṃkhyas to consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

Furthermore, when it is stated that "the Pradhāna does not exist," once the cause of the world has been established, the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion—which is already established elsewhere—is precluded. Likewise, because there is absolute non-difference between cause and effect, the state of having an undifferentiated effect and the existence of the effect within the cause (satkāryatva)—which are established by such evidence as "this is clay, this is a jar" in the case of clay and a jar—are precluded by the negation of the Pradhāna. Thus, the point is that even here, there is no lack of establishment regarding either the subject or the object of negation.

Because that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*) is undivided and non-distinct, it is so described; the state of being that is *tattva*. Regarding this very point, he states another opinion: "But others [say]... The meaning is that others explain that the negation of external existence is made for those things such as sky-flowers—which have acquired form in the intellect due to some cause such as similarity, latent impressions, fallacious reasoning, or fallacious statements—and which, while existing as mental forms, appear externally.

To the objection that "if it is described in this way, then negation itself cannot be established," he replies with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). Otherwise—that is, if it were not described in this manner—since [non-existence] is in no way applicable to things like a sky-flower, which are excluded by their very nature, what negation could there be? The meaning is that there would be none; for that which is not applicable is not negated. Furthermore, if it were applicable, there could be no absolute negation. Thus, it is logically consistent that when an object is established, it is precisely that established thing which is negated.

He states another argument for the point that "the established is negated by the established" with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). If, in a negation, the object of negation and the thing being negated—such as a jar and a cloth—were not required, then the negation would occur without distinction, simply as "it does not exist"; it would not be "the cloth does not exist in the jar. Consequently, because everything would be negated everywhere without distinction, the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be universal emptiness, and not difference, since the two distinct things that constitute difference would be absent. This is the intended meaning.

That by which the object [of negation] and the thing to be negated are not required is described as such. In response to the inquiry, "What kind of negation is that which depends upon another? he says: "But that which... For a difference is apprehended in the form, "This is different from that"; and such a difference requires the establishment of both members of the pair through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). He then asks, "And what follows from that? and replies: "Not... and so forth.

The meaning is this: that establishment of two distinct [entities] through affirmation is not possible by means of apprehending the nature of a real thing (*vastu-svarūpa*) through its own valid cognition (*tat-pramāṇa*); therefore, affirmation must be accepted prior to exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). For this reason as well, he states that affirmation must be accepted prior [to exclusion]: "preceded by affirmation" (*vidhi-pūrvaka*); the meaning is that all disputants accept it in exactly that way. The particle *iti* indicates either a reason or the completion of the meaning of the verse.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: when a certain thing, such as a jar, which has already acquired its form through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and whose nature is thus established upon a locus such as the ground, is negated as being exactly that same thing established by a means of valid cognition; therefore, since negation is not possible without a prior affirmation, there must first be an affirmation. To the objection, "In that case, let there be exclusion preceded by affirmation," he says: "Nor... (nāpi). Why? He says: "Because... (yataḥ). This refers to the two operations of affirmation and exclusion, which constitute the functions of a single perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa-vijñāna*). [p. 130]

The sequence characterized by priority and posteriority does not cohere with reason; that is, it is not logical, because cognition is momentary—this is the sense. Furthermore, that perceptual cognition arises from what is proximate; it is produced regarding a proximate object. Therefore, it does not arise as "referring to another," meaning it does not arise as something whose nature is to refer (*parāmṛś*) to what is other than the proximate, i.e., what is not proximate. He explains the verse with the words "Indeed, not... (*na khalu*).

He asks "Why? and replies: "Because of momentariness"; the word "of cognition" (*jñānasya*) is to be supplied [as the subject]. But why is a sequence of two operations not possible for that which is momentary? To this he says: "Because they possess a sequence. The meaning is that, between two operations that possess a sequence, the operation which occurs later would not be an operation of that cognition. He asks "Why? and replies: "Because of the intervention."

The meaning is this: for that which is momentary, a subsequent operation cannot be separated by a preceding operation, because [the former] has already perished by that time. For this reason as well, exclusion is not preceded by a positive injunction; thus he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*). The very arising of cognition, which consists in the determination of an object, is its operation; unlike firewood and the like, there is no other operation distinct from its arising.
