As it has been said: "Therefore, the arising itself is held to be the operation of cognition with respect to its object."

Likewise, [it is said]: "For it does not remain even for a moment, nor is it born as having the nature of valid cognition. The qualification "in the form of the apprehension of an object" is intended to exclude the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). He asks, "What follows from that? and says: "If that... If that cognition arises in the form of the affirmation of an object, then the operation of this cognition is exclusively positive (*vidhi*), not negative (*vyavaccheda*); thus, how could there be the possibility of two operations, by which a sequence might occur? This is the sense. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose arising—that is, its birth—is in the form of the affirmation of an object."

The word *cet* (if) should be understood as in the phrase “if the Vedas are authoritative. Now, one might ask: why does that cognition arise in the form of a positive injunction (*vidhāna*) alone? Why could it not arise in the form of both an injunction and an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)? Anticipating this objection, he says: “simultaneously” (*yaugapadyena*). That cognition does not arise in the form of both, because simultaneity has just been refuted. Therefore, that cognition arises only in the form of a positive injunction; thus, there is no exclusion from it. Consequently, there is no sequence, for a sequence occurs only between two things—this is the intended meaning.

One might object: "In that case, there will be two successive births of cognition—one in the form of affirmation (*vidhāna*) and the other in the form of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*); thus, a succession is possible. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of [cognition] having arisen" (*utpannāyāḥ*). In this view as well, a sequence—that is, a priority and posteriority—between the two functions of affirmation and exclusion, whether they be understood as two births of a single cognition or as two operations of a single action, is not logically tenable, because a birth that has already occurred cannot occur again. This is how the meaning of the verse should be construed.
He explains the latter half of the verse with the words "Even if" (api ca). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And not...

The term "perception" (pratyakṣam) carries over [from the previous context]. To the question, "Why is perception unable to exclude that which is not manifest? he says: "For if it were not manifest," and so forth. In that case, if the object to be excluded—such as a jar—is not manifest within the perception, there would be a mere exclusion devoid of any specific thing to be excluded, such as "there is no jar on this ground"; however, there would be no exclusion of any specific object to be excluded, such as a jar, yet such an exclusion is indeed observed.

Now, if it is argued that the object of exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) must be postulated because its exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is otherwise untenable, then—inasmuch as no specific [object] is being apprehended—there would be a negation of everything on the ground; yet this is not the case. This is the meaning. He concludes with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says "And not" (*na ca*). Furthermore, this defect is common to all four positions previously mentioned. Why then was this defect stated here? It was stated for the sake of all [positions], as it applies to them all.

Here, he raises an objection again, asking: "How so? The meaning is that if a positive injunction is not preceded by a negation within a single cognition, or if there is no appearance of a non-present object to be negated in perception, then the subverting perception, "This is mother-of-pearl," would not be possible. He asks why this is so and says: "In that case. In that subverting perception, a positive injunction of the other thing, mother-of-pearl, is admitted within a single cognition, preceded by the negation of the previously perceived object, silver.

For the affirmation of mother-of-pearl as the locus of negation is not possible if there is no silver to be negated. Likewise, the manifestation of the absent silver—which is the object to be negated—must be admitted, because its negation would be untenable without its manifestation. Therefore, the negation is not prior, nor is there a temporal sequence within the operation of a single cognition, nor is there manifestation of what is absent in perception. Thus, this rule just mentioned does not hold, because it is subject to deviation; for in the case of a sublating perception, all three of these factors are present. This is the meaning.

The established doctrine (siddhānta) refutes this, saying: "This is not so. It states its lack of substance with the words: "Even there. Even in that case of subverting perception, where silver and so forth—as established by a prior cognition in the form "this is silver"—are the objects to be negated, the negation is necessarily preceded by an affirmation; for the negation is directed toward a general object present before one, which is not specified in its particularity by the very "this" portion of that [prior] cognition. This is the meaning.

This is what is meant: here too, the negation is preceded by a negation of the object and an affirmation [of its opposite]; thus, there is no deviation in the case of the statement, "The prior negation does not exist. Now, one might object: in the case of "This is not silver, this is mother-of-pearl," an affirmation is understood as being preceded by a negation; so how can it be said that "affirmation is not preceded by negation"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "mother-of-pearl" (śuktikā). The analysis of the compound is: that from which the negation of the contradictory silver (*rajata*) is prior.

And even if that were so, there would still be no destruction of the restriction we accept; thus he says: "vidhi... By the phrase "the prior negation is not," it is stated as a rule that a negation is preceded by a prescription of the object to be negated; nor is there an absence of such a preceding prescription for the negation.

It is set aside. Although the injunction regarding the mother-of-pearl is preceded by its negation, nevertheless, because the negation of silver is preceded by the general injunction of the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*) as being silver, there is no deviation; this is the sense. And this has been stated according to the view of another school. In our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, there is no sequence between the negation of silver and the injunction of the mother-of-pearl, since this was investigated under the statement, "The sequence is established through reasoning"; and he will say later: "And in that case, a single cognition does not have an operation characterized by sequence."

Having thus stated that there is no deviation in the principle that negation is preceded by a positive injunction, [the author] now addresses the deviation previously mentioned regarding the claim that "there is no sequence in the operation of a single cognition," by means of the subverting perception (*bādhakapratyakṣa*). He says, "And not... (*na ca*). Therein, he refers to the subverting cognition. To the question "Why?", he replies: "Because of both... (*ubhaya*). A subverting cognition arises as a manifold (*citram*) consisting precisely of the affirmation of the mother-of-pearl and the negation of the silver; and it has been stated that its very arising constitutes its operation.

Nor is it one, because that which has already arisen does not arise again; furthermore, succession occurs in multiple [cognitions], not in a single one. Therefore, it does not perform affirmation and negation simultaneously. Thus, the meaning is that there is no successive operation within a single cognition. Nor should it be argued that the production of both forms is impossible due to the absence of a previously established object to be negated, for those two were shown in the prior cognition in the form "this is silver. He says: "by the prior cognition," and how this is so has been explained.

Now, regarding the statement that in perception there is no appearance of what is not present (*asaṃnihitāvabhāsa*), he addresses the objection raised against that definition by means of a subverting perception (*bādhakapratyakṣa*). He says: "By the previous cognition," etc. The meaning is this: when the object to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*) is manifested by the cognition "this is silver," the questioner asks for the exclusion of silver; therefore, there is no undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the appearance of non-present silver in that perception.

If it is asked, "How can one thing negate what has been brought about by another? [The answer is: Just as that which was brought about by the injunction of the sixteen [purificatory rites] is negated by the injunction of its prohibition (*niṣedha-vidhi*). If this is so, then since perception excludes the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) brought about by memory, there is no fault even if perception manifests an object not present [at the time]. This is not so; for if that which is brought about by memory is non-different [from the perceived object], it cannot be the counter-correlate; if it is different, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). But surely this same fault applies even when the counter-correlate is brought about by perception? Let it be so.

What is our loss? Why, then, was this not stated? Because other refutations are available; furthermore, for one who believes that perception alone is both the means of apprehension and the means of exclusion, the fault of "not manifesting what is not present" has been stated. Now, raising the objection: since cognitions arise independently of one another, how can that which was manifested by a preceding cognition be excluded by a subsequent one? Anticipating this, he says: "of that which depends on the preceding."

This would indeed be the case if there were mutual independence between the preceding and succeeding cognitions; however, that very independence is unestablished. For a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) arises only in dependence upon the subverted (*bādhyam*); otherwise, its status as a subverter would be impossible—this is the sense. It depends on the preceding, thus it is "dependent on the preceding" (*pūrvāpekṣi*). For this very reason, it arises with two forms (*dvirūpa*); otherwise, like any other cognition, it would arise with only a single form. Thus he says: "the preceding," etc. [p. 133] It has two forms: affirmation (*vidhi*)...

It is of the nature of exclusion (*niṣedharūpa*). This means it is of a single form, namely, the form of a mere affirmation (*vidhimātrarūpa*). Furthermore, by that proponent who has rejected all exclusions (*sarvavyavaccheda*), even the exclusion of silver and so forth has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*); and it is not proper for there to be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the subject itself. Thus he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*).

Now, if it is argued that the exclusion of silver and so forth is established in the world and therefore there is a deviation [of the reason], then why is the mutual exclusion of villages and the like—which was made the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of being something not to be refuted—not likewise established in the world? Therefore, why is a deviation not asserted on its basis? If that [exclusion] does not hold up when examined, then the exclusion of silver and so forth is the same; thus, with the intention that worldly establishment is of no consequence, he says: "That is established. He states another opinion: "And that which..."

The very perception of the singular existence of one blue thing as "blue" is itself the exclusion of another [thing], such as yellow; however, there is no dual operation in perception by which there could be either succession or simultaneity. Therefore, even though these two [operations] are impossible, it is established that perception is a negator. How then can it be said that "it is not a negator"? And since it is established that perception has difference as its object by virtue of being a negator, its contradiction with the Veda follows—this is the sense. He explains this very point with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

For non-conceptual perception of blue arises with a fixed form of blue that is distinct from yellow and so forth; it does not, however, have a form of blue that is indistinct from yellow and so forth. Therefore, just as it establishes the blue object, so too, by being restricted exclusively to the form of blue, it excludes what is other than it. Thus, the point is that affirmation itself is the exclusion of the non-blue. Now, one might object: the cognition of blue, "This is blue," is one thing, whereas the well-known [cognition] "This is not non-blue" is another.

Therefore, having raised the doubt as to how the cognition of blue itself constitutes the exclusion of non-blue, he says: "That... This means that by the power (*sāmarthya*) of that indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-darśana*)—namely, its restriction to a single form—the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of "this" and "not this," which are manifested and produced through the force of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), set in motion the linguistic conventions of existence and non-existence. What is being said is this: it is true that there are these two cognitions; however, the latter is determinate (*savikalpaka*).

That which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and serves as the root of those [conceptual cognitions] is perception (*pratyakṣa*). And regarding that, we maintain that affirmation alone (*ekavidhi*) is the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*). Why, then, is it conceptualized in this way? To this he says: "For not... (*na hi*). That which has connection with another is "connected with another" (*anyasaṃsargi*); that which does not have connection with another is "not connected with another" (*ananyasaṃsargi*). This is an elaboration of the phrase "due to the restriction to a single form" (*ekākārapratiniyamāt*). And so he will say later: "For its restriction is the non-connection of that [object] with anything other than itself. [p. 134]

Having thus presented the Buddhist position, he refutes it by means of the fallacies of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and under-extension (*avyāpti*), saying: "To this it is replied. The very affirmation of one thing does not constitute the scope for the negation of another. Why? He says: "Lest there be no distinction. If the negation of something other than one [thing] were simply the affirmation of that one, then there would be a negation without distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible; the meaning is: "Lest that be so. The particle *smā* is for the purpose of completing the meter.

Having thus stated the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), he states the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) with the words "lest not" (*mā na*). The meaning is: lest there be no mutual exclusion (*anyonyavaccheda*) among blue, yellow, and so forth—which are mixed together in a painting and are objects of a single cognition—even though they are distinct, because for each one individually there is no single cognition [of them all]. He explains the meaning of the verse with the words "not one," etc. To the question "Why?", he says: "For its restriction," etc. This is the restriction of that [blue, etc. to the cognition of blue and so forth; therefore, there is no association (*asaṃsarga*) or non-entry (*ananupraveśa*) of another [color] such as yellow into that [cognition of blue].

If that were the case, and non-connection (*asaṃsarga*) with yellow and so forth were admitted as the means of exclusion, then because there would be no distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible, or between what is capable of being perceived and what is not, both of them would be excluded; yet such [an exclusion] does not exist—this is the sense. Now, one might think: "In this case, the exclusion of the perceptible and the imperceptible is indeed desired; therefore, this is not an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*), and an undesired consequence constitutes a fault. Anticipating this view, he raises the objection with the words "Now, if... (*atha*).

The phrase "the exclusion of both" continues [from the previous context]. He establishes this with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*). For instance, the perception of blue, by virtue of having the single form of blue, determines—"this is indeed of the nature of blue"—and thereby excludes, without distinction, all those entities that are not of the nature of this blue, whether they be visible or invisible; the meaning is that it excludes them. He confirms this very point with the words "and thus" (*tathā ca*).

All those things other than this blue—whether visible, such as yellow, or invisible, such as atoms and so forth—are non-self (anātman) of this blue, because it is contradictory for a single thing to have multiple natures. Therefore, the sense is that [the cognition] excludes the perception of all those things as being of that nature, due to the restriction that they do not possess its nature. In response to the question, "If other things were not the nature of another, what would they then be?", he says: "taddeśa... (having the same space and time as that); those whose space and time belong to that [blue] are so described.

The meaning is that others have different locations and times from one another, but they do not possess the same nature as it. Here he provides an illustration: "like color and so forth" (*rūpādivat*). The meaning is: just as taste and the other qualities share the same location and time as color, so it is here. He states the reason for this: "because there is no contradiction" (*avirodhāt*). For while it is contradictory for color to have the nature of taste, it is not contradictory for them to occupy the same location and time. If [the opponent] rejects perception without distinction between the visible and the invisible, for what purpose [is this stated]? [p. 135]

Anticipating the objection that "the specific characteristic called 'attainment of the conditions for perception' (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti) is relied upon with respect to the object to be excluded," he says: "In that case" (tatra). In that case—meaning when others possess the same place and time—the specific characteristic called "attainment of the conditions for perception" belongs only to that which has such attainment of the conditions for perception at that particular place and time; the exclusion applies only to that [object] at that place and time, and not to anything else. This is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and not for the purpose of restricting the exclusion to the self.

The meaning is that this [non-apprehension] occurs even in the case of something that has reached the conditions for apprehension (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). He states the reason for this here: "it is possible" (*saṃbhavati*). That entity which is non-apprehension—being of the nature of a non-self (*anātman*) and lacking a specific form (*arūpa*)—is indeed possible even when another thing is being apprehended; therefore, there is no exclusion of it, but rather [the exclusion applies] only to that which is capable of being apprehended. Thus, it is logical that in that context, the condition for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) is adopted as a qualification (*viśeṣa*). Regarding this, he provides an example: "form," etc. (*rūpa*).

The meaning is as follows: just as there is the non-apprehension of taste despite the apprehension of color—because taste, which consists of that same place, time, and substrate as the color, is possible even while not being apprehended during the apprehension of color—and thus the exclusion of taste [from the color] does not follow from the restriction to the color; likewise [in the case of the self]. However, that which is of the same nature as it (the color) possesses the capacity for simultaneous apprehension with it, and therefore it is impossible for it not to be apprehended when that [color] is apprehended.

Therefore, with the intention that even though [an object] has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), it may still be excluded [from the negation], one need not rely on "perceptibility" as a qualification for that purpose; thus he says: "not equal. The phrase "is possible while not being perceived" is to be supplied. One whose "perceptibility" (*upalambhayogyatā*) is equal is described as such. Why is it not possible? To this he says: "necessarily."

If there is a fitness for simultaneous apprehension, then that which possesses such fitness with another is necessarily apprehended when that other is apprehended, just like the object currently being apprehended; otherwise, it would not have that very fitness for simultaneous apprehension. If it is not apprehended, then it simply does not exist—this is the point. Thus, in the exclusion of its location and time, visibility (*dṛśyatva*) is the defining characteristic.

When the Buddhist establishes his own position—that perception excludes the object's very nature (*ātman*) without distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible—the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) says: "True. It is true that when there is an exclusion of place and time, the perceptible is excluded, but not the imperceptible; likewise, for the sake of determining the exclusion of that place and time, "perceptibility" (*dṛśyatva*) is the distinguishing characteristic (*viśeṣa*), and not the exclusion of its own nature—this distinction indeed exists.

The meaning is that the restriction of perception to a single form does not, at this point, possess the capacity to exclude other things. Now, one might object: "But isn't it the case that the restriction to the ground has the capacity to exclude visible objects such as jars? Therefore, why is it said that the restriction of perception lacks capacity? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). Just as the perception of color—that is, regarding the object which is color—is exhausted merely by the affirmation of color and terminates precisely there, in whatever location [p.

The meaning is this: just as color at that time does not exclude taste, so too the restriction to the perception of a portion of the earth would not exclude other visible objects. If the restriction of perception possesses the capacity to exclude others, then the same should apply to the perception of color. Alternatively, if in that case there is no capacity extending to the exclusion of others because the operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) terminates in the mere affirmation of color, then the same would hold for the ground as well.

The sense is that there is no difference whatsoever between the specific restriction of perception here and there. Now, if it is claimed that even when the operation of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) results solely in a positive affirmation (vidhi), the exclusion of others occurs by its own inherent power, then it would follow that everything—both the perceptible and the imperceptible—is excluded; thus he says: "exclusion" (vyavaccheda). He concludes with: "therefore" (tasmāt).

Having established the incapacity of the restriction of perception (*darśanapratiniyama*), he says "And so" (*tathā ca*) while applying it even to the exclusion of that nature in cases such as "A pot is not a cloth. The sense is this: if another reason (*hetvantara*) must be relied upon there, then here too the exclusion will be established from that very [reason], and not from the restriction of perception. The word "from that" (*tataḥ*) means "from the restriction of perception."

If, however, a single affirmation were to exclude another, then—since it would consist in the exclusion of the non-existence of its own object of affirmation—it would exclude the non-existence of its own object of affirmation; but it would not exclude the existence of yellow, which is a different nature from blue, as in the case of "blue is not yellow. Thus he says: "Kāmam" (Granted). "Affirmation" refers to the perception of blue and so forth; the "object of affirmation" refers to the domain of blue and so forth.

Although affirmation (vidhi) manifests the existence of the thing to be affirmed (vidheya), it does not [directly] exclude the non-existence of that which is to be affirmed; nevertheless, since the thing to be affirmed cannot be conceived as existing without its own exclusion [of non-existence], it is said to have the nature of excluding the non-existence of the thing to be affirmed due to their necessary connection (nāntarīyakatva). Alternatively, it should be understood that this was stated by one who considers that, because a positive entity (bhāva) is of the nature of the negation of its own non-existence, the thing to be affirmed itself is the exclusion of the non-existence of the thing to be affirmed, and that there is no separate affirmation of the form of the thing to be affirmed.

Regarding this, he states an illustration: "In that place," etc. The meaning is: just as the perception of blue does not exclude the existence of an unperceived blue atom (paramāṇu) in its location or at its time, so it is here. [Objection: If perception excludes the non-existence of the perceptible, then the existence of the perceptible world follows as a consequence. Therefore, even if perception does not grasp difference, mere difference would not exist.

But as for the visible world, since it is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), by whom can it be denied? Therefore, non-duality (*advaita*) is not established. It is replied: If there were an absence of difference, the world would be a single reality (*tattva*); yet even that [single reality] is not visible, because, being insentient (*jaḍa*), its distinctness from itself is not established due to the absence of difference within it. Therefore, the Self (*ātman*) is self-established, and thus it is established that the Self alone is the one reality; this is the non-duality of the Self, or at least it is merely a statement of provisional acceptance (*abhyupagamavāda*).

For an injunction does not exclude the non-existence of that which is to be enjoined, since we observe injunctions even when the object to be enjoined is non-existent, as in the case of "the snake in the arm" (*svaksa-rpa*) and so forth. If it is argued that this is an error, then what indeed is this [error]?

How this [cognition] is erroneous has already been explained in the section demonstrating the authority of the sacred tradition (āgama), so we shall desist here. Now, it might be argued: "It is not possible for one thing to have many natures; therefore, the perception that is restricted to a single form excludes multiple natures. To this, he says: "Not of one" (*naikasya*). Here, he states the reply: "From another" (*anyataḥ*). Your position is that the very affirmation of one thing constitutes the exclusion of others.

The sense is that, because there is contradiction, [the distinction] would not be established for you once exclusion has occurred. Now, one might object: "Our purpose is served by the exclusion of the non-self; if that [exclusion] occurs through contradiction with a constituent part, let it be so. By that much, difference is indeed established. What is the use of our grasping at the exclusion of the restriction of perception? Anticipating this, he says "asati" (when it is non-existent) to show that even due to contradiction there is no exclusion—for multiplicity belongs only to things that are mutually excluded.

Furthermore, exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)—which must reside within the locus of a dispute—is not yet established. Therefore, in the absence of exclusion, how can there be plurality? Even if plurality exists, if there is no exclusion of plurality and unity, how can there be contradiction, given the absence of a second contradictory factor? If it is argued that contradiction arises from exclusion and exclusion arises from contradiction, then there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Thus, the point is that even through contradiction, exclusion does not exist.

Alternatively, one should apply the reasoning: "If there is no exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), how can there be multiplicity? And in the absence of that [multiplicity], how can there be contradiction? In this case, the word *vā* (or) has the sense of *ca* (and). He concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Now he explains the quarter-verse "May it not be so": "Furthermore" (*api ca*). "Of those possessing a single perception" means "of those being grasped by a single variegated cognition" (*citrajñāna*). He asks "Why? and answers: "Because of oneness" (*eketi*).

The meaning is this: because blue and other colors are related to a single variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) by way of being objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*), there is no restriction of the variegated cognition to one specific color, such as blue or yellow; therefore, difference is not established by the capacity of a cognition that possesses a restricted form. The intention is that if there were some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for difference in that case, that same would apply everywhere, and thus the restriction observed in perception would be without cause. Thus, having refuted the view that the exclusion of another is simply the affirmation of one thing, the proponent of a difference that is non-distinct from the entity itself (*bhāvāvyatiriktabhedavādī*) raises an objection with "But surely... (*nanu*).

"By its very nature" (prakṛtyaiva) means by its own essence (svabhāvena). "Of that kind" (tadvidhān) means having distinct natures (bhinnasvabhāvān). Now, one might object: "Exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is different from that which possesses exclusion (vyāvṛttimat); therefore, even when that which possesses exclusion is apprehended, [the exclusion] is not apprehended. Anticipating this, he says: "For not... If there were a difference between the exclusion and that which possesses it, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā); therefore, the point is that an entity has exclusion as its very nature (vyāvṛttisvabhāva). To the question, "What follows from this being so?", he says: "In that case... He asks, "Why? and says: "Because..."

He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*); the meaning is that if something whose nature is X is not perceived as that very nature, then, due to the non-perception of its own nature, it would not be perceived at all. Having thus established the general principle (*nyāya*), he applies it to the present case with the words "excluded" (*vyāvṛtta*). The phrase "according to their respective [natures]" (*yathāyatham*) means that they appear in cognitions in their own unmixed forms. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), however, extends the previously mentioned fault to this case as well, saying: "here too... (*atrāpi*).

Since blue appears as unmixed with yellow and so forth, if it is admitted that blue exists as something unmixed with yellow and the rest, then just as the ground appears unmixed with jars and other objects that are perceptible, so too would it appear unmixed with atoms and other things that are imperceptible; therefore, there would be a distinction (vyavaccheda) between those two as well—this is the meaning. Regarding this very point, he states another objection: "Moreover" (*api ca*). Difference (*bheda*) is not a form (*rūpa*) or essential nature (*svarūpa*) of an entity that is non-different from the entity itself.

Why? Because it would entail the consequence that there is no difference between entities. If, on the other hand, [the exclusion] were distinct [from the entity], then the entity’s being different from its own nature by way of that non-nature (i.e., the exclusion) would not be possible; this is the meaning. He explains the verse: "Exclusion is not... Why? He says: "That... The meaning is that this exclusion is asserted to have multiple substrata, like duality and so forth. Not only is it merely asserted, but it is also perceived in exactly that way; thus he says: "...and it is perceived."

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And thus... To the question "Why?", he says: "Not from one... The meaning is this: whatever is non-different in nature from one thing is not different from it, just as that very same single thing [is not different from itself]; and the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the two distinct counter-correlates is one and the same; therefore, due to their non-difference, there would be no difference between those two either. Now, if—out of fear of the fault of contradicting one's own statement—one maintains that exclusion is distinct from the entities, then, because exclusion would lack the nature of a real entity (*avastu*), there could be no difference among entities by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*).

And for this reason, with the intention that "it must therefore be one alone," he says, "Now" (*atha*). He states another interpretation of the first half [of the verse] as "Another" (*apara*). Because blue and yellow are not identical to each other, their difference consists in the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svarūpa*). If that [difference] were the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity, then, since entities would be asserted to have the nature of non-existence, and since difference would be asserted to have the nature of non-existence, it follows that there would be no existence of entities; such is the meaning. In this interpretation, in the phrase "its non-existence" (*tad-abhāva*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the entity (*vastu*).

He states another explanation of that very point: "The other [says]... He describes that manner: "And division... Why? He says: "Because of difference. For division consists in being split into two; the meaning is that if a thing has that as its nature, the unity of the object cannot exist. Now, one might object: there exists no single entity that is either distinct from or non-distinct from atoms; therefore, the object is merely the atoms themselves joined together in a superior-inferior arrangement, and since those atoms possess a manifold nature, the object is rightly held to be manifold.

Therefore, since a thing has the nature of difference, the consequence that a single entity would be non-existent does not apply to us, as it would result in an undesirable conclusion for the Buddhist position.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "The atom (*paramāṇu*). The meaning is that even an atom, because it is divisible, would not be a single entity if it were divided into two parts by means of its inherent differentiation. He asks, "What follows from that? and replies: "And so" (*tathā ca*). Since the one does not exist, the many—which consists of a collection of those ones—cannot be conceived as the nature of this object; the meaning is that there is neither the one nor anything at all. Thus, an object as either one or many is not tenable, and there is no third possibility.

Therefore, with the intention that the non-existence of the entity follows from its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). An alternative explanation of the meaning of the verse is begun with the words "by means of formlessness" (*arūpeṇa*). He states this [alternative] as "another" (*anyā*). He explains that [alternative] as "as something distinct" (*vyatirekitā*). The meaning is: some people object to this aforementioned alternative regarding the entity—namely, the dilemma of whether the difference is distinct or non-distinct. He states the objection as "the entity" (*vastu*).

A cognition devoid of a real object (*vastu*) is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); he whose body is fashioned by that [construction] is so described. He elaborates on this very point with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the real object (*vastu*); its state is "the nature of being that object" (*vastutvarūpatvam*). That which cannot be determined as either different from or non-different from the object is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) in terms of difference or non-difference. Now, one might object: if difference is neither distinct from nor non-distinct from the object, then it does not exist at all, like the horn of a hare.

To explain how conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) proceeds, he says: "beginningless" (*anādi*). That is to say, that differentiation (*bheda*) whose body is constructed by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which has as its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) the latent impression (*vāsanā*) born from that beginningless conceptual differentiation of difference—that is what is meant. This is what is intended: a rabbit’s horn does not appear; however, although difference is non-existent in reality, it appears through the power of latent impressions and thus becomes the cause of conventional discourse.

The meaning is that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no such thing as "difference" (*bheda*) as a real entity (*vastu*) for which identity or otherness could be investigated. To this, he gives the answer: "In that case" (*tatra*). The meaning is that difference does not exist in the ultimate sense; it is not possible, just as in the case of a double moon. He explains this very point with the words "If... (*yadi*). The gloss of "formless" (*arūpa*) is "devoid of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*).

If difference does not exist as a real entity but is merely of a conceptual nature, then, because difference is absent in the ultimate sense, an entity could not possess difference ultimately. For it is not logical that a thing should possess an ultimate state of being "possessed of two" by virtue of a conceptual, false nature—such as the duality [of the moon]—but rather, you yourself have accepted that such a state would be merely conceptual. Why, then, do you not agree with this which we are stating?

We too say this very thing: that so-called difference does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*); rather, the meaning is that this state of being distinct is a mere play of ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding the word *bhāvataḥ*: it means "by way of having the nature of existence" (*sadrūpatayā*), which is to say, "from the perspective of ultimate reality"; or else, in the sense of being "other than entities," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in connection with the meaning of "other. This entire meaning of the verse is intended by the author as a double entendre (*tantra*), so there should be no confusion regarding alternative interpretations of the commentary. [p. 140]

P. 48-16. Having restated what was previously said, he raises a certain objection regarding it with the words "yad uktam" (as for what was said). The meaning is that the opponent says this concerning the statement: "If a thing has the nature of difference—that is, if its very essence is difference—then because unity is contradictory to difference, there would be an absence of any single entity; and due to that absence, since there is also an absence of any other entity consisting of a collection of many parts, and because neither unity nor plurality is possible and there is no third alternative, there follows the non-existence of all things. This is what the opponent asserts.

Regarding what they have said, he says: "dependent on another" (*parāpekṣam*). An object such as a jar is distinct from another object such as a cloth due to something external, but not by itself; for it is inherently one. Therefore, since there is no contradiction between difference and the unity of the object, there is no fault of the non-existence of a single entity—this is the meaning. To this, he gives the reply: "In that case" (*tatra*). "Pauruṣeyī" means belonging to a person; since an object does not conform to that dependence—that is, the object is not in accordance with the dependence—[it cannot be established].

Therefore, the fault of the nature of difference in an entity remains exactly as previously stated by the aforementioned reasoning; this is the meaning. If dependence were a property of the entity, then the entity could be established as different by virtue of that property; however, this is not the case, as he says: "not dependence. Why? He says: "but not thus. The word *svataḥ* is for the purpose of indicating what is well-known: an entity arises with whatever nature it possesses from its own causes alone; otherwise, it would not even be that entity.

Therefore, it is established that it is not logical for it to depend on another entity for the sake of establishing its own intrinsic nature; this is the meaning. Those things whose arising or birth is brought about by their own causes are described as such. In that context, the cognition of a person—which is the subject here—is what possesses this property called "dependence"; for a person, when cognizing a distinct object, cognizes it by depending upon its counter-correlate (pratiyogin). He says "therein" to indicate this. To the question "What follows from that?", he says "And not... To the question "Why?", he says "From their own causes..."; [the rest of the sentence continues the argument].

The meaning is that the determination of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing depends upon its own causes. If things were to conform to the cognitions of persons, then things would take on whatever form a person perceives them to have; consequently, even mother-of-pearl perceived by a person as silver would itself become silver. Thus, the true nature of a thing would not be established. But this is not the case. Therefore, he says "hence" (*ataḥ*), meaning that the determination of the nature of a thing does not occur in accordance with the cognition of a person.

However, it is appropriate that the determination of a person’s cognition conforms precisely to the nature of the object, because that cognition is preceded by the object; thus he says: “established. In this way, if a jar has a distinct nature produced by its own causes as that very nature, it does not depend on a human [convention] regarding a counter-correlate; this is to be applied to the present context. Furthermore, if the difference of the jar were dependent on the cloth, then the difference of the cloth would also be dependent on the jar, resulting in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*); thus he says: “mutually. He explains the meaning of this verse again in another way: [p. 141]

Alternatively: if the difference between two things that stand in a relation of mutual exclusion were one and the same, and if that [single] difference were not distinct from them, then—because of its non-distinctness from that single difference, and because those two possessors of difference would also be one—the consequence would follow that there is no difference at all. Thus, regarding the statement, "Difference is not the nature of an entity," the opponents reply: this would indeed be so if a single difference had multiple substrates; however, it is not one, because of a contradiction in its nature. For difference, by bringing about the distinctness of each individual thing, is properly understood as having a distinct nature for each respective thing.

Whence does its unity come? If it were one, then, due to the connection with a single property, the unity of things would be caused by that [property], and there would be no diversity. Alternatively, if difference and unity were identical, then because they are not distinct from that [unity], the unity of things would be nothing other than that very difference. Therefore, difference varies with each object; the meaning is that there is a mutual difference between a jar and a cloth, and between a cloth and a jar. Here, the proponent of the established doctrine asks: "How so?"

The meaning is: if difference resides in each individual locus separately, how then will the well-established fact that difference has multiple loci be maintained? To this, the opponents reply: "Because of dependence. Even though it exists in one [locus], it depends upon a second; thus, difference has multiple loci, not because it actually exists in more than one. Anticipating the objection—"If difference exists in only one, how can it depend on another? For the whiteness of a jar does not depend on a cloth"—he says: "For instance... (tathā hi).

For difference arises for something from something else. Consequently, its own nature is established in relation to that which it arises from—that is, in dependence upon its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Thus, the meaning is that even for that which resides in a single locus, dependence on another is logical. He asks, "What follows from this? and says: "And so it is. This being the case, all things are distinct through their respective individual differences—which are distinct in each entity, dependent upon their counter-correlates, constitutive of the entity's own nature, and non-different from the entity itself.

The intended meaning is this: because each manifestation is distinct due to its difference [from others], it cannot be a single unity, since that would entail the absence of distinction among the distinct things themselves—a fault resulting from the non-existence of difference. To this, the refutation is stated: "That which is produced by a person" (*pauruṣeyīm*). He explains this as follows: "For a person," etc. For a person, having taken a single lump of clay, requires other factors such as a wheel; for the production of an effect such as a jar is accomplished by that much alone.

If entities were to acquire their own nature while being deficient in some form [of distinction] due to their own causes, then they would require something else for the sake of acquiring that form; however, since they have already acquired their complete forms from their own causes, what need would they have for anything else? This is the meaning. Others say: "But surely... This is the very nature of distinction, that even though residing in one thing, it requires a second counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); the question is: "Doing what? Anticipating the objection that "this nature is not observed in the case of whiteness and so forth," he says: "Not manifold... and so on. And that...

The meaning is "its own nature" (*svarūpa*). Since difference, which is included within the category of the probandum (*sādhya*), is established for all people as requiring a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), he cites that very example with the words "for instance" (*yathā*). Here, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntavādin*) says: "In that case, then not... If difference were a positive entity (*bhāva*)... [p. 142]

If an intrinsic nature depends on something else, then things must be admitted to have arisen from their own causes with an incomplete intrinsic nature; for otherwise, dependence on another would be impossible. And this is not desired [by you]. Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of an entity arises from the very causes of that entity at the same time as the entity itself, just as heat arises from fire.

However, difference (*bheda*), which arises subsequently once the entity has come into being from its own causes through another cause—the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—could not have the nature of an entity (*bhāvasvabhāva*); therefore, this thesis of yours that "difference is of the nature of the entity" would be abandoned. Thus he says: "from another cause. Here, however, he objects again: "It might be so. This objection of yours might hold if an entity devoid of the form of difference were produced from its own causes.

That [entity], however, is born from its own causes as entirely complete and undivided in all its forms, including difference (*bheda*) and so forth. This, then, is the distinction: that while other forms have a nature independent of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the form called "difference" is dependent upon a counter-correlate; for it is never observed to exist independently of a counter-correlate. This is the meaning of the reason. He asks, "Why? and says: "Of that... (*tasya*).

The meaning is that because this form called "difference" (*bheda*) is of such a nature—that is, its very essence is dependent upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Therefore, an entity (*bhāva*) arises together with that difference, which is of precisely that same nature; for this reason, there is no manifestation or birth of an entity devoid of difference, by which the fault you have mentioned would occur. Here he states the refutation: "In this regard... Let it be granted that an entity manifests only as being of such a kind, namely, accompanied by difference.

However, the meaning or purpose of the requirement for a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) must be stated; and your position is that such a purpose does not exist—this is the sense. Why? He says: "For that of which... For when something exists dependent upon another, it requires that other; anything else is independent of it. This is the established distinction between the dependent and the independent, and nothing else—this is the meaning. He asks what follows from this and says: "In that case. First of all, the arising of difference is not dependent upon the counter-correlate, such that difference would require the counter-correlate for the sake of its own arising—this is the meaning.

He asks, "Why? and replies: "From its own [causes] (*sva*). The meaning is that even prior to its production, an entity that is already complete and accompanied by difference arises solely from its own causes. Now, if it is argued that the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) of a jar and the like for fetching water and so forth depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—that is, its difference—[the author] says "no" to that as well. He asks, "Why? and replies: "Because of that (*tat*). Even when a counter-correlate such as a cloth is not present, the causal efficiency of the jar is observed. The point is that if that efficiency were dependent upon a counter-correlate, it would not occur in the absence of such a correlate.

He raises the objection that the cognition of difference is dependent upon a counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*) with the words "the cognition" (*pratīti*). He confirms this very point with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). Since a difference is not cognized without depending on its counter-correlative—that from which the difference of a given thing is perceived—therefore, the cognition of that [difference] [is dependent].

The meaning is that [the cognition] is dependent upon the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Having raised this objection, he refutes it with "No. If this were so, then the nature of the entity called "difference" would not depend on the counter-correlate; rather, it would follow that once that difference has first become established, the subsequent cognition of the entity called "difference"—which is its own existence—would be dependent on the counter-correlate. Therefore, the intended thesis that "difference itself is dependent on the counter-correlate" is abandoned; such is the sense.

And lest one should think that because the cognition is dependent, the object of that cognition must also be dependent, he provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as). The analysis of the compound is: "those which are established by their own causes have acquired their own nature, and for that very reason possess a non-dependent nature. Alternatively, it may mean "those whose nature is non-dependent in their state of establishment. Anticipating the objection—"Let it be that the cognition of difference itself is dependent; for that purpose alone, difference, though independent in itself, will depend upon a counter-correlate"—he says "itaretara... (mutually...).

The meaning is this: since difference must be cognized from that which is already cognized as different, and that [cognition] likewise depends on the former, there is a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). Therefore, even the cognition of difference—which would be mutually dependent and reliant upon one another—is not possible. Now, one might object: "Difference will be cognized from the mere thing itself when its difference has not yet been grasped; therefore, there is no circularity. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not... He states the reason: "In a single [thing]... If this were the case, then a thing would be cognized as different from itself by its own nature.

And such is not the case; this is the sense. He concludes the topic under discussion with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). There is another explanation of this very point; he states it with the word "No" (*na*). He provides the reason with the word "Relative" (*apekṣika*); the meaning is that since that difference is perceived in dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). He asks, "What follows from that? and answers with "And that" (*sa ca*). For "dependence" (*apekṣā*) is a particular cognition of a person; and it does not conform to reality (*vastu*), nor is the determination of a thing dependent upon the cognition of a person. He provides the reason for this with the word "Established" (*vyavasthita*).

For it is logical that the cognition of a person corresponds to the actual object; otherwise, it would be without a basis—this is the intended meaning. The word *iti* marks the completion of the sense of the verse. Now, if the nature of an object is not relative (*apekṣika*), then how can fatherhood and so forth be the nature of an object? For they too are indeed relative; they do not exist without depending on a son and so forth. With the intention that just as these are the nature of an object despite being relative, so too is difference (*bheda*), he asks: "How? (katham).

Nor are they non-existent like a sky-flower, nor are they unreal like a city of the Gandharvas; thus he says, "nor... Let it be that there is no conventional usage [at all]; however, that which is unreal is deceptive. But fatherhood and so forth are established in the world as the causes of conventional usage, and that [usage] is non-deceptive; therefore, the meaning is that they are neither non-existent nor unreal. To this, he provides the answer: "It is said... [p. 144]

If even fatherhood and the like are relative, then let them not be the nature of a distinct entity either; let them simply be unreal—what loss is that to us? Nor can it be argued that they differ from difference (bheda) because they are established as the cause of non-contradictory worldly transaction; for why is difference itself not established in the world in the same way—as the cause of non-contradictory worldly transaction, just like fatherhood and the like, or like the entity itself? Indeed, it is certainly so established. Therefore, the meaning is that this too is not a point of distinction.

Having thus stated the lack of distinction between differences such as fatherhood and so forth, he now states the distinction with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). In the case of objects such as a father, there is a dependence on a son and so forth based on acts such as procreation. Even in the case of the short and the long, there is mutual dependence, which arises from a specific difference in degree regarding the action of occupying space by one or the other. The point is that in the case of [absolute] difference, no such cause for dependence exists. He explains this with the words "when established" (*vyavasthite*).

When the innate [relationship] is established—that is, when it exists through mutual independence, rather than being produced by a dependence on another subsequent to the existence of the entities themselves—the powers of being father and son, which constitute the designations "father" and "son," belong to the father and son respectively. (The correspondence of the terms here is not intended. And this has been stated with the view that "the power is the causal factor" (*kāraka*). Even under the position that "the possessor of the power is the causal factor," everything should be inferred accordingly. Anticipating the objection, "How then can there be mutual dependence between the two? he says: "But those... (*te tu*).

When the causal powers (*śakti*) of the produced and the producer—the factors of agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*)—are co-present, the operation called "producing" (*janana*), existing with respect to that [object], causes those two terms "father" and "son" to apply to it; that is, they take it as their referent. Alternatively, the meaning is that those two powers, acting as the agents, cause those two words to apply to themselves as their objects, taking them as their own designators. This is what is meant: when in a single act of producing one person is the agent and another is the object, then those two become denotable by the words "father" and "son."

"Not otherwise. Why? Because of the difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāvabheda*). The meaning is that such is the specific nature of these two words that they function only with respect to such an object and not with respect to another. He asks, "What follows from this? and says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). For equality belongs to an action between two things; therefore, that whose action is equal to another's has a requirement for it—that is the meaning. He clarifies the stated point for its application to the present context: "This... (*etad*).

The meaning of the words "father" and "son" is dependent upon the father and so forth in that context; it is not, however, a real entity known as the power of producer and produced, for it has already been stated that such a thing is established from the very beginning. This is what is meant: when the producer performs the same act of producing as the produced, then he becomes the referent of the word "father," and not otherwise. Therefore, since the producer becomes the referent of the word "father" only in dependence upon that produced person with whom the act is common, the meaning of the word is said to be dependent. Thus, it is merely a matter of words [p. 145].

In this case, however, it is not the entity itself that is dependent. The reason for this dependence exists in the common generative action (*janakakriyā*) found in the father and so forth; although the two entities known as the "capacity to be produced" and the "capacity to produce" are established as mutually independent, the sense is that there can be no commonality without a second [factor]. Regarding the difference, he states the disparity with the words "in the case of existence" (*bhāve*). "Residing in the reality of the entity" means it does not reside in the word; therefore, the sense is that in this case, it is the entity itself that is dependent.

Even in the case of [measurements] such as the *hasta* and so forth, whatever object has a certain dimension is produced from its own causes with that very dimension, independently of anything else. However, the mere application of a word is dependent [on something else]; and the cause for this dependence is the state of deficiency or excess in the action of spatial pervasion belonging to things of the same class. That whose action of spatial pervasion is greater in comparison to another is called "long" (*dīrgha*) in relation to it; that which is less than another is called "short" (*hrasva*). Whatever extent of space one thing pervades, another does not pervade to that same extent, nor is it less than that extent.

"The other is greater" constitutes the distinction between the deficient and the excessive; by this, there is no fault of mutual dependence between the deficient and the excessive. The opponent objects—"If," he says—"dependence on the father and so forth is desired because of the specific nature of the act of procreation, then let the difference in the entity itself also be accepted as arising from the difference in the effect. Furthermore, even if it were the case that perception, whose operation consists solely in the affirmation of an object, does not exclude [other possibilities] and thus is not a means of knowledge regarding its difference, nevertheless, we shall infer it from the difference in the effect.

Therefore, he states "moreover" (*kiñca*) to show that difference is not even unauthoritative. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose function consists of mere affirmation (*vidhi-mātra*), devoid of the exclusion of others (*anya-vyavaccheda-rahitam*). He states the exclusion from the contrary (*vipakṣa*) because a reason that does not exclude the contrary is non-probative; thus he says "not in unity" (*naikatve*). There is no fault in not stating the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), for it is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the Advaitin and is not accepted by the Buddhists. Here he states the reason: "because of the cause," etc. He explains that: "that," etc. But the proponent [of the Siddhānta] holds that even the difference in effects is unestablished for us.

Therefore, there can be no inference of a difference in nature [of the cause] on that basis. A single thing cannot possess multiple natures, because if it did, it would follow that the thing itself is divided; thus, he says "this very [point]" to show that establishing a difference [in the effect] from a [supposed] difference [in the cause] is untenable. As for what was also said—that if the cause is one, a difference in the effect is not possible—that too has been addressed; he says "moreover" to show that even when [the cause] is one, such [difference] is observed. The meaning is that due to the difference in effects such as burning and so forth, there is merely a difference in designations such as "burner" or "cooker," but not a difference in the actual entity. The rest is easy to understand.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "when a difference based on causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is accepted. Now, one might object: even here, fire is merely a collection of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; a single composite whole (*avayavin*) that is either different or non-different [from its parts] is not possible. Therefore, the difference in effects arises solely from the difference in qualities such as color-form and so on. Anticipating this objection, the author says: "Now" (*atha*). The proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*), however, says: "Let it be so; nevertheless—" [p. 146]

Since there is indeed a difference in the effects of burning and cooking due to the contact with hot touch, the reason’s failure to exclude the counter-example remains exactly as it was; thus he says, "Granted" (*kāmam*). Nor should it be argued that the difference between cooking and burning is unestablished; thus he says, "And those two. Although cooking is also a transformation resulting from contact with fire, and thus the general property of being a transformation exists in both cases alike, nevertheless, their internal distinction cannot be denied because it is well-known in the world. This is the meaning.

The difference in effects due to a single cause is not only established by common worldly experience, but is also accepted by all disputants; thus he says: "Action. For Kaṇāda, the action of the motion of a released arrow—the disjunction from and conjunction with preceding and succeeding locations—is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the impression (*saṃskāra*) called velocity (*vega*); and the self (*ātman*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of desire, pleasure, and so forth. This is what is accepted by the follower of Kaṇāda.

In the same way, it should be understood that *sattva* and the other qualities (*rajas* and *tamas*), being individually non-different—that is, lacking any distinct parts—are the causes of lightness, activity, and illumination, respectively. In some versions, the reading is "due to non-difference" (*abhedāt*); in that case, the meaning is as follows: it cannot be said that they are different. Why? Because *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are non-different within each [quality]. Thus, the sense is that even from a single [cause], there is a diversity of effects. In this regard, it is the doctrine of Kapila that *sattva* is the cause of lightness and so forth, while *rajas* is the cause of activity and suffering.

Likewise, according to the Buddhist doctrine, form and the other [objects] are each causes for the cognitions that have them as their respective domains, serving as objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*); specifically, form is the material cause (*upādāna-pratyaya*) for moments of form, and taste is the material cause for moments of taste. Now, the opponent raises an objection: "We do not assert a difference in entities merely on the basis of a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); rather, when there is a difference in something from another, there is a causal efficiency that is impossible because it has never been observed in that case. Thus he says: "But surely... (*nanu*). He provides an example for this very point: "Just as... (*yathā*).

The meaning is as follows: just as in the case of a deaf person, even though the eye exists, the cognition of sound is impossible because it is not perceived; therefore, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is postulated as distinct from the eye. Anticipating the objection, "In this way, how is difference established elsewhere?", he says: "Generally" (*prāyeṇa*). Those things whose effects are mutually impossible are so described; generally, in all cases, the effect of one thing is not seen elsewhere. Therefore, difference is established.

The term "mostly" (*prāya*) is used for the purpose of excluding the case where an arrow and a horn have the single effect of disintegration. Raising the objection, "How then is there a distinction between those two?", [the author replies that] even though they share the single effect of disintegration, other effects—which generally do not occur together—are also present in them; thus, the word "mostly" is to be applied once again. The proponent, however, says "Now" (*atha*); the meaning is: how is the impossibility of one effect occurring in another to be understood? The opponent says "But surely" (*nanu*). He refutes this with "No" (*na*).

For Advaitins, every effect is observed in one and the same place; therefore, there is no case of an effect belonging to one thing not being seen elsewhere. In that regard, if difference were real, one would have to say that the effect of one thing is not seen elsewhere. Thus, there would be a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*): difference existing because the effect is not seen, and the non-perception of the effect existing because of difference. Therefore, the meaning is that the difference between entities cannot be inferred from a difference in their effects. Now, even though the cloth exists, the effect of the pot is not seen therein, and subsequently, by its cause— [p. 147]

"The difference of the jar is inferred; for if there were no difference between the two, then like the effect of a cloth, the effect of the jar would also have been seen previously"—thus he anticipates the opponent's view with the words "Now" (*atha*). He refutes that with the word "That" (*tat*): the meaning is that even for a single person performing successive purposeful actions such as eating, an action not previously seen is seen later, yet there is no difference in that person.

Now, if there were absolute non-difference [between the self and its states], then because that person is capable of all purposeful action (*sarvārthakriyā*), and because it is impossible for what is capable to be delayed, all effects would be seen simultaneously; consequently, the non-perception of a certain effect previously and its perception later would not occur, since there would be no distinction from the prior state. Therefore, there must be some distinction from the previous state by whose arrival the effect, previously unseen, is seen later. Thus, he raises the objection that there is neither absolute difference nor absolute non-difference, by saying: "It might be... (*syāt*).

To this, he states the following reply: "In that case, not so" (*na tarhi*). If a difference in effects is possible even when there is only a difference in specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), then a difference in effects does not sublate the non-difference of the entity; rather, on the basis of the difference in effects, one should infer only a difference in specific qualities without rejecting the non-difference of the entity, since the difference in effects is accounted for by that much alone even in the case of a non-different entity. Therefore, the intention is that the claim that "there is a difference of entities because of a difference in effects" is refuted under these circumstances.

Now, raising the objection that non-duality is not established even if there is a difference consisting merely of a particularity (*viśeṣa*), he says: "And that" (*tacceti*). It is true that we accept a mere particularity as being different; however, it is not real, but rather conceptual (*kālpānika*); and since that is a non-entity (*avastu*), it does not bring about duality—this is the sense. Raising the further objection, "Why should that not be real?", he says: "In reality" (*vastviti*). The meaning is that, from the standpoint of the actual nature of things (*vastuvṛttyā*), such a mere particularity is impossible because it is untenable. He states the reason for this: "And that" (*tacceti*).

The state of being that (*tadbhāva*) is identity (*tattvam*), meaning non-difference; the sense is that, in reality, it is impossible for particulars to be both different and non-different. If they are not different from the entity, then the entity alone is supreme, and they do not exist separately. If, on the other hand, they are different, then they cannot belong to the entity, because there would be no connection. For there is no identity between two distinct things, such as a tumor and gold. Nor can there be inherence (*samavāya*); for that too must be either different or non-different from the two things that inhere in it. If it were non-different, it would not exist separately.

If it were distinct, there would be no relation between the two, because they would lack a connection; and if one were to postulate yet another inherence (*samavāya*) for that [inherence] to connect with those two, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued that inherence, though distinct, is connected to those two by its very nature, then let those two themselves be so [connected]—what is the use of that [inherence]? For it is that which lacks a connection which requires a connection, not that which is already a connection, just as one lamp does not require another lamp. If this is said, we reply: no, for this inherence is a connection between the two inherent things (*samavāyin*), not with itself.

Therefore, it is logical that for the self to be related to its two inherent causes (samavāyin), there must be dependence on another inherence; thus, an infinite regress is unavoidable. As for the lamp, since the eye perceives it just as it perceives other things, it is logical that no further lamp is required there. Furthermore, if a relation does not require another relation, [then the same applies to the relation between the self and its inherent causes].

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) also would not require inherence (*samavāya*); yet such an asymmetry does not exist. Furthermore, inherence must be connected by another inherence with its two related relata, because it is a relation, like conjunction. Thus, that [second inherence] would likewise require this [third], leading to an infinite regress. Moreover, inherence is the cause of the cognition "here" (*ihapratyaya*); however, no such "here"-cognition occurs in respect to universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*). For there is no cognition for anyone of the form "the cow is here in the cow," but rather everyone has the cognition "this is a cow."

Therefore, since inherence (*samavāya*) does not exist, it too cannot be the relation between two particular entities. Nor is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*). For that [conjunction] also exists as non-different from the conjoined things; if it were different, how could it be related to them? If you say "by means of inherence," that has already been refuted. Furthermore, it cannot exist independently. Therefore, that [conjunction] also does not exist. Consequently, conjunction either cannot be the relation between two particular entities, or—since it does not exist—it follows that a particular (*viśeṣa*) which is distinct from the entity itself is not possible. Thus, it is well said.

Having thus established the distinction between effects—even when the underlying entity is one—based solely on the difference of conceptual qualifications for the sake of those who maintain the doctrine of permanence (sthiravādin), he states it specifically with regard to the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādin): "But as for him... The word "but" (tu) is used for the purpose of distinction.

But as for the proponent of momentariness who does not accept even that identity—that non-difference of the particular from the nature of existence and so forth—who maintains that particulars alone are utterly distinct and momentary entities, and that there exists nothing stable such as a single genus (*jāti*) and so on—for him, since the nature of the effect follows the nature of the cause, how could an effect called a rice-sprout of a uniform nature arise from those rice-moments if there were no difference [between them] in terms of that common form?

Now, if it is argued that even though those [effects] are absolutely distinct, they possess an equality of effect due to their non-difference from the imagined form of the universal (*jāti*), then, in that case, since the distinction between effects is established even when the cause is one—due solely to an imagined distinction—the postulation of a distinction in the cause for the sake of establishing a distinction in the effect is seen to be unnecessarily cumbersome; this is the meaning. The analysis of the compound is: "those whose destruction is without persistence" (*niranvaya-vināśa*). For the proponents of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), when a jar is destroyed, there is no persistence (*anvaya*) of "jar-ness" in another jar, nor of "clay-ness" in its own shards and so forth; thus it is called "without persistence."

Now, if it is argued that even from distinct causes—namely, the visual object (*cakṣurviṣaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)—a single cognition arises, and therefore a difference in the cause is not required for a non-difference in the effect; and that for this reason an effect of identical form is produced even from entirely distinct moments (*kṣaṇa*), then [we reply]: since there is thus a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the principle that the nature of the effect follows the nature of the cause, just as a single-form effect can arise from what is distinct, so too can a diversity of effects arise from a single cause. Consequently, a difference in the cause is not established for the sake of proving a difference in the effect.

It must be postulated; this is what he says with the words "Now" (*atha*). Furthermore, as for the example of the eye and so forth cited to show that distinct things can have a single effect, even that is unproven for him. For instance, he who asserts that the operation consists in the restriction of the eye to the apprehension of form, the nature of the immediately preceding cognition being that of consciousness, and the object having the form of that [cognition].

The distinctness of the objects of the operations of the causes, such as the eye and so forth, has already been stated by him [the author]; therefore, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*) to show that even in that case there is no difference in the effect. He states another fault regarding the fact that the sameness of the effect does not depend on the non-difference of the cause: "If, moreover" (*yadi ca*). The meaning is that, in that case, there would be no inference of a rice-sprout covered by earth from a rice-sprout. Why? He says: "Because of the difference" (*bhinna*); the meaning is because the production of a rice-sprout is possible even from a moment of barley. He establishes this very point with the words "Because of the cause" (*hetu*).

If [you argue that] the identity of the cause is not required because the effect is identical, then just as a rice-sprout arises from one rice-moment which is absolutely distinct from another rice-moment, it would likewise arise from a barley-moment; for, apart from the conceptualization of non-difference, there is no distinction between those two. This is the sense. In this regard, you too must necessarily accept the conceptualization of the identity of the cause in order to account for the identity of the effect; thus, our positions are equal. He establishes this with the word "tatra. Here, the opponent raises an objection with the word "syāt."

That which performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is real; anything else, such as a rabbit’s horn, is not. If difference (*bheda*) is also the cause of purposeful action, then it is not imagined (*kalpita*), but rather it is indeed real—this is the meaning. The established doctrine (*siddhānta*) replies: "It is equal. The meaning is that for you, non-difference (*abheda*) too would not be imagined, since it is the cause of the equality of effects. Now, if it is thought: "We do not assert a difference in reality merely from a difference in purposeful action, but rather from a difference in contradictory purposeful actions; for such contradiction cannot occur in a single thing," to this he says: "Even that which... (yo 'pi).

He elaborates on this very point with the words "Thus, indeed" (*tathā hi*). He states the reply to that with the words "Of that too" (*tasyāpi*). Objection: It was stated that the difference between entities arises from the difference in their contradictory causal activities (*arthakriyā*); yet burning and cooking are not contradictory. With the intention of asking how this can be a reply, he asks: "How? The proponent establishes its status as a reply with the words "This... (*idam*). If, first of all, the meaning of the word "contradiction" is the impossibility of birth, death, and so forth in a single locus, then that is unproven for us Advaitins.

For us, indeed, everything that is contradictory is unified within a single self. Now, if it is argued that contradiction consists in mutual exclusion (*mitho vyavacchinnatā*), and that birth, death, and so forth are likewise [contradictory], then the difference between entities is established by means other than [mere conceptual exclusion]. This is because even in the case of a single fire, one observes burning and cooking, which are mutually exclusive. Nor is their mutual exclusivity unestablished, since it is proven by their distinctness (*nānātva*).
