Therefore, if there were a distinction between entities based on such states, then even earth and other elements—which possess multiple properties such as color and taste—would not be unitary; this is the meaning. Now, suppose it is argued that joy consists in the absence of sorrow, and sorrow consists in the absence of joy, such that this constitutes their opposition: if these two were to exist simultaneously in one place, then there would be the existence of sorrow and the non-existence of joy (since joy consists in the absence of sorrow); likewise, there would be the existence of joy and the non-existence of sorrow (since sorrow consists in the absence of joy).
Yet, existence and non-existence of the same thing in the same place at the same time are not possible. [p. 150]

If it is argued that, because of such a contradiction between those two, a difference in the nature of their substrates is thereby determined—and likewise from birth and so forth—that is incorrect. For in this way, since they would consist of mutual non-existence, the properties themselves would not exist as positive entities; how then could a cognition of a difference in the nature of the substrate arise from the contradiction between them? Furthermore, in the case of a broken pot and similar objects, there would be the undesirable consequence of joy and sorrow being of the nature of mutual non-existence due to their absence [in the object]. He states all of this with the words "Now" (atha).

Now, if it is argued that the relationship between the slayer and the slain constitutes their opposition, that too is not correct; for since the slayer, having been born, kills the one to be slain, and since they do not exist in different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*), the slayer must first come into being in the same substratum as the victim and then kill the victim. Consequently, because the relationship of slayer and slain exists only when they share a single substratum, no understanding of a difference in substrata can be derived from it.

It might further be argued: "Even so, because we observe that [existence and non-existence] reside in a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatva*), the inference of a difference in substrata is not non-erroneous (*avyabhicāra*); for we see even two things that kill and are killed residing in a single substratum. To this he says: "Now" (*atha*). The analysis of the compound is: "that of which there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) exists. If it is then said: "The properties consisting of existence and non-existence are contradictory; just as, for example, permanence and impermanence, or corporeality and incorporeality. Since it is impossible for these two to belong to a single property-bearer (*dharma*), a difference in the property-bearers (*dharmī*) is determined"—even that is not so.

For a property that exists in a certain locus does not necessarily pervade it; indeed, chariots or the conjunctions of chariots do not pervade the sky or the earth and so forth, because chariots are limited and their conjunctions are likewise limited by virtue of being dependent on limited substrates. Just as chariots and their conjunctions are thus, so too are other things that are limited. Furthermore, properties such as eternality and non-eternality are not unlimited.

For this very reason, even though they rely upon an object called the infinite self, they do not pervade it. Consequently, for them, the existence and non-existence of that which consists of eternity are not contradictory. Therefore, it is not the case that a distinction between the substratum is understood from the contradiction between existence and non-existence. He states all of this with the words "Now" (atha). [Objection: Granted that existence and non-existence are logical in the case of conjunction and so forth because of their non-pervasiveness; however, the eternity of the self is pervasive.

Consequently, since it is impossible for that non-existence (the impermanence) to have that [Self] as its sole locus, the locus of earth and so forth is indeed perceived as distinct from the Self. To this we reply: This would be so if there were such a thing as a real entity called "impermanence"; however, that is merely an illusion (*māyā*) imagined within the Self in the form of earth and so forth. Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the case of an illusion; for the idea is that the duality of a single moon is not contradictory. He raises the objection of another view with the words: "But he who... (*yastu*).

He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "in the case of oneness. He states the lack of fixed order (*avyavasthā*) with the words "and likewise. "Otherwise" means: if oil were produced from sesame alone and not curd, and if upon the destruction of one, the other were to be destroyed—that being the sense. Here he cites the opponent's statement: "that," etc. "Everything would be useful everywhere" means that everything, such as milk, sesame, and so forth, would be applicable in every instance. [p. 151]

The meaning is that [the sesame seeds] are employed as the cause for oil, curd, and so forth. Having raised this objection, he refutes it with the words "of that too" (tasyāpi). The syntactical connection is as follows: if the diversity of effects constitutes the established rule (*vyavasthā*), and by means of that one asserts the distinction between sesame seeds and milk, then this very [point] is the answer. [Objection: But surely it was stated that the production of curd occurs from milk and not from anything else; this is what was called the "established rule," not merely the diversity of effects. Therefore, why this unprovoked reproach? [Reply: It is true that you have stated this.

However, this distinction [of function] exists only if there is a difference between sesame and milk; and since their difference is established by that very distinction, they are caught in a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*) and thus the position is untenable. Therefore, intending to show that one who asserts such a distinction must actually be asserting a plurality of effects, he said this [in the verse], and thus there is no fault. Now, he states the aforementioned distinction itself, to which it is replied: "Now" (*atha*). For a distinction is the means of proving the difference between entities; and a means of proof must be already established, not unestablished.

The point is this: if the definition of the restriction were that "the production of curd occurs from milk and not from anything else," then that otherness (*anyatva*) which is unestablished as the probandum would have to enter into the definition of the restriction that serves as the probans. But that is not tenable; for if the unestablished otherness were to enter into it, it would follow that the restriction itself remains unestablished. Consequently, there would be a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*). Therefore, the restriction consists in the capacity to produce curd and the absence thereof.

Consequently, a distinction between sesame and milk is reckoned; for it is not logical that a single substance, such as milk, should possess both power and lack of power with respect to one and the same object. Therefore, it must be stated that the distinction between the two is established by the fact that milk possesses power while sesame lacks it. To this he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*); the meaning is that since the aforementioned arrangement is difficult to maintain, this [distinction] must be asserted. The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), however, says: "And that" (*sa ca*).

Furthermore, this reason was refuted by us immediately following [the previous argument] in the passage: "Therefore, there is no contradiction between the existence and non-existence of a single thing. Thus, the sense is that even this is not a definition of systematic order (*vyavasthā*). He confirms the previously stated lack of contradiction between existence and non-existence in a single locus by means of an illustration, beginning with "just as" (*yathā*).

Just as Devadatta and others, who exist for a long duration, when connected with limited periods such as childhood or youth, possess those attributes at that time and later become devoid of them without falling into contradiction; likewise, the earth and other vast objects, like the chariot and its conjunctions which occupy limited space, and even infinite entities such as the Self, do not become subjects of contradiction when connected with [attributes] such as impermanence. This is the meaning. Here, he raises an objection: "How so?"

The sense is that, because the property (*dharma*) is not distinct from the substratum (*dharmī*), it is also appropriate for that [substratum] to be infinite. For this very reason, he provides the following answer by not accepting the position of non-distinction: "In the case of distinction" (*vyatireke*). If the property were non-distinct from the infinite, it too would be infinite just like it. But in the case of distinction, however, whether that [property] is false or not, there is no possibility of an infinite [substratum] possessing a finite property; such is the meaning. He states that even in the case of non-distinction, that [possibility] does not exist: [p. 152]

"Even in the case of non-distinction" (P. 53-16): properties that are not distinct from long duration are themselves long-durationed like it, and do not instead become limited in time; therefore, the meaning is that in the same way, even for the infinite, there may exist a property that has an end.

However, regarding the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādī*) who does not admit that an object persists over a long duration, [the author], fearing that for such a person the coexistence of existence and non-existence in a single locus cannot be established because the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is unproven, restates the meaning of the previously mentioned verse in order to demonstrate to him the coexistence of existence and non-existence in one place—beginning with "He who... He explains that [verse] as follows: "One... A single moment of fire burns and cooks only certain things, such as grass or rice, but not water and the like.

And likewise, [fire] is a burner and a cooker with respect to grass and such, but not so with respect to water and the like, yet it does not thereby become divided. Therefore, the meaning is that since one observes the properties of existence and non-existence—characterized by capacity and incapacity—even in a single entity, there is no understanding of a difference in the entity itself from that [observation]. On this view, the distinction must be explained as follows: in some cases there is the presence of burning and cooking, while in others there is their absence. Now, one might object: "In this case, non-contradiction is appropriate because of the difference in objects."

Anticipating the objection that "capacity and incapacity regarding a single object are contradictory for one [agent]," he restates the meaning of the verse in another way with the word *tathā* (so). Even a single moment of fire performs a certain burning and cooking upon a single combustible object; therefore, it is both a burner (*dāhaka*) and a cooker (*pācaka*). Since it does not perform anything other than that, it is also a non-burner (*adāhaka*) and a non-cooker (*apācaka*), and the phrase "it is not divided" (*na ca bhidyate*) continues to apply. This very distinction between burning and cooking is to be understood here.

Thus, in order to demonstrate the convergence of these two positions upon a single point while raising a doubt against the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇavādin*) alone, he states another example, beginning with "In the same way" (*tathā*). The Buddhists maintain: if a seed were incapable, it would not produce a sprout even when in contact with earth and other factors, just like sand; if it were capable, it would not depend on earth and the rest. If it is argued that it produces the sprout by means of a specific quality imparted by earth and the rest, then it is not inherently capable; and what is incapable does not produce [the effect] even when a specific quality is imparted, just like a defective seed.

Moreover, that [specific condition] would be the cause because the effect exists when it is present and does not exist even when the seed is present; it is not the seed itself. Furthermore, such a specific condition cannot be established as being either different, non-different, or both different and non-different [from the seed]. Therefore, the moments of soil, seed, and so forth—attaining a succession of similar moments—are each individually capable, yet they produce only a single sprout, not multiple ones for each individual factor. [Objection: But since there is no production of what has already been produced, what has been produced by one should not be produced by another. [Reply: This would indeed be the case if there were a temporal sequence.

But when an action is performed simultaneously, there is no such thing as "having been done. Even for one for whom the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer, that complex produces only a single sprout, not other sprouts. And this being the case, even a single entity possesses both the state of being a producer and the state of not being a producer.

The phrase “and yet it does not differ” (*na ca bhidyate*) also carries over here. The word *iti* marks the end of the example. Regarding the terms “causality” (*janakatva*) and “non-causality” (*ajanakatva*): the meaning is the presence and absence of the power to produce. Now, it was stated that the contradiction between the power and the lack of power in a single thing regarding a single object implies a difference between sesame seeds and milk; in that case, an exception (*vyabhicāra*) must be pointed out. But such is not the case here. To explain: seeds possess the power to produce a sprout in one and the same instance; yet there is no lack of power in that regard, but rather [a lack of power] with respect to something else.

Anticipating the objection that "therefore, due to this disparity, there is no deviation [of the cause] from the seed and so forth," the opponent says, "Now (atha). The sense is that incapacity in other cases is not contradictory precisely because the objects are different. However, the proponent of the established view (siddhāntin) states the parity through a quibble regarding words: "another. Let it be that the capacity exists in one [case] alone; nevertheless, there is also the past and the future. Therefore, since capacity resides in one [time] and incapacity resides in another, the objects of capacity and incapacity are identical; thus, the parity remains exactly the same.

Now, one might raise this objection again: "Since power (*śakti*) is known through its effect, the power of those [seeds] resides only in the sprout that has just arisen; it does not reside in the past or the future. Nor is there a lack of power in that very [sprout]. In the case of sesame seeds and milk, the power for curd and the lack of power reside in the same distinct entity. Therefore, because of this disparity, there is no deviation [from the rule] regarding seeds and so forth. This is what is meant by "Now" (*atha*). To this, he gives the reply: "Even though there is non-difference" (*abhede 'pi*). What is meant is this: whatever has arisen from milk as curd, because of its non-difference [from the milk], has necessarily already arisen from the sesame seeds as well.

Therefore, just as in the case of milk, there is only potency (*śakti*) therein and not non-potency (*aśakti*), so that there is no contradiction between potency and non-potency; so it is also with sesame seeds. Consequently, their difference cannot be understood from that. Now, if curd were the potency of sesame seeds, it would produce another curd; but it does not do so. Therefore, since non-potency also exists, it is said that there is a contradiction between potency and non-potency. To this we reply: for curd is produced only from milk, and the potency of sesame seeds lies in [producing] oil, not in another curd—just as, for example, the potency of seeds and the like relates to the past and the future.

Therefore, where there is capacity, there is simply no incapacity; how could there be a contradiction? As for that incapacity which exists elsewhere, it is not contradictory because its objects are distinct; thus, there is no contradiction between capacity and incapacity. If it is argued that if there is capacity in one case, there must be capacity in other cases of the same kind—and therefore even sesame seeds should produce curds—the author says "no" to this: "For it is not so. He raises another view with "Now," and states the difference in application with "For curds... He refutes that as well with "That too..."

He states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) with the words “even in the case of oneness. He elaborates upon that very point with the words “that same [thing]. Even a single entity is employed for an effect only when accompanied by auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), not in its isolation; therefore, because both employment and non-employment exist even in a single thing, there is inconclusiveness, and thus it cannot be the cause for the cognition of a difference between entities. Anticipating the objection that “the entity is indeed different from its isolated state due to the difference in the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) consisting in the proximity of auxiliary causes, so there is no inconclusiveness,” the proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*) says: “Now [if you say]... [p. 154]

He says: "It is adventitious" (*aupādhika*). If the difference [in the cause] arises from the distinction of adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) consisting in the proximity of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), then it is indeed adventitious. And that which is adventitious is perceived only as a secondary appearance; it does not touch the reality of the thing itself, just like a reflection in relation to its original object (*bimba*). Therefore, it is not ultimately real (*aparamārtha*). Furthermore, we accept that the difference between entities is ultimately unreal. Thus, the sense is that you have merely resorted to our own position.

However, for the proponents of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), the milk-moment accompanied by auxiliary causes is absolutely distinct from the milk-moment alone; likewise, sand is also [distinct]. Consequently, that [sand] too would be employed in the production of curd. If it is argued that sand is not employed in the production of curd because its capacity is unobserved, then the new milk-moment as well would not be employed, since it was non-existent previously and its capacity has not been observed. Nor can it be said that its capacity is observed by way of a single genus (*jāti*), for the point is that they do not admit the existence of a genus.

Now, if it is argued that the application [of water] is established because the capacity is observed in a moment of water due to its non-difference from a previous moment whose capacity was observed—this being mediated by a single birth (jāti) constructed through beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā)—and not so in the case of sand, which consists of heterogeneous moments; then, for the opponent who maintains non-difference (*abheda-vādin*), the application and non-application of water and sand will likewise be established based on the difference constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, the intention is that the postulation of a difference between entities (*bhāva-bheda*) for the sake of distinguishing between application and non-application is entirely useless.

Thus, he says "even that which" in response to the proponent of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda-vādin*). The meaning is that just as the contradictory properties of difference and non-difference coexist in one place, so too do [the properties of] being a producer and so forth; therefore, the distinction between sesame and milk is not established by that. The mention of "by way of being a producer and not being a producer" is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*); all other factors such as capacity and incapacity are also to be understood. Now, drawing upon all the previously stated points, he concludes his own position with "therefore" (*tat*); the meaning is "for that reason. *Sahaḥ*; [this refers to the capacity].

The meaning is "it is possible. He explains the meaning of the verse [beginning with] "In one case" (*ekatra*). Everything that was stated starting from "in the difference produced by causal efficiency" (*arthakriyākṛte bhede*) up to that point is here relied upon by the word "thus" (*evam*). That very same [argument] is recited for easy recollection by the passage beginning with "in one case" (*ekatra*) and ending with "because of the possibility" (*saṃbhavāt*). In the phrase "and because of the established order" (*vyavasthāyāśca*), the words "because of being inconclusive" (*anaikāntikatvāt*) or "because of being unestablished" (*asiddhatvāt*) are to be supplied. He confirms this very position of his own through scripture, saying: "This, therefore... (*tadetad iti*).

He explains the scriptural passage (*śruti*) with the words "This... (*etad iti*). In the phrase "that which has become" (*yadbhūtam*), the word "even though he is one" (*yadeko'pi*) is understood to carry over. To provide the answer to the doubt raised by the phrase "greater than this" (*ato jyāyān*), he first states the doubt itself with the words "The former... (*pūrva iti*). The meaning is: how can he, being a single entity, be the substratum for the attributes, actions, and worldly dealings that were described in the two preceding verses as being mutually contradictory? Among those, his having a thousand heads is contradictory because it is not observed [in reality];
however, for one who pervades all the worlds, it is improper that he should be only ten fingers in height. [p. 155]

To this, he states the answer: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). By this word "therefore," that which is proximate is denoted; and that [proximity] occurs either through perception (*pratyakṣa*) or through verbal testimony (*śabda*). In that regard, relying on perception, it is said: "from this which is regarded as perceived" (*ataḥ pratyakṣābhimatāt*); and relying on verbal testimony, it is said: "from that indicated by all the words [of the verse], namely 'This is indeed the Person' (*puruṣa evedam...*)", or "from that indicated by the phrase 'or rather, of immortality' (*utāmṛtatvasya...*)"—thus it should be distinguished.

How is the manifold world of gods and so forth indicated by this? It is said: by the phrase "the lord of immortality for the mortal [consisting of] the gods and so forth," there is an indication of the manifold world of gods and so forth. Or, this is an indication by means of a representative sign (*pratīka*): by the phrase "that which here rises up as food," there is an indication of the manifold world of gods and so forth; for whatever is to be eaten by someone is that person's food, and for the gods, food consists of nectar and the like. Consequently, "that which here rises up and manifests" and "the lord of that"—this is the indication of the manifold world of gods and so forth.

“*Medeneti*”; the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe*), meaning "by way of being characterized as such. And all of this is an adjective qualifying the word *prapañcāt*. "*Dṛḍhataraḥ*" means "surpassing [all] in every respect" or "infinite" (*ananta*). By this, he shows that the substitution of *jyā* for *pra* occurs according to the rule "*dṛḍhasya ca*" (Pāṇini 6.1.85). Thus, even though this one infinite Person (*puruṣa*) is single, the coexistence (*samāveśa*) of limited and even contradictory attributes—such as eternity and non-eternity—is not untenable.

Therefore, with the intention that the comprehension of the distinctions between entities arises from this infinity, he says: "By that. He states that the Śruti demonstrates this very infinity by way of another method: "That indeed... He explains that [verse]: "Even the whole... The word *viśvāḥ* [is used] because the elision of the case-ending *śi* occurs frequently in the Vedic language (*śerundasi bahulam*). A "quarter" (*pādaḥ*) means a fourth part; "smaller" (*kanīyān*) means formless (*arūpa*). The phrase "as if a portion" (*bhāga iva*)...

The word "as it were" (*iva*) is used to show that, since there is in reality no division for that which is partless, this [division] is merely imagined through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the delimited phenomenal world (*prapañca*). In response to the inquiry, "How is it that the portion delimited by the phenomenal world is small, while the Person (*puruṣa*) is greater? he joins the next quarter-verse of the Ṛgveda with the words "For thus" (*tathā hi*). "Feet" (*pāda*) means parts; the analysis of the compound is "that which has three feet"; the word "form" (*rūpa*) is the external referent of the compound. By specifying the feet as being three, the intention is to convey that, in terms of magnitude, they are infinite compared to a single foot.

Alternatively, "immortality" (*amṛtatva*) means non-perishability; and this is intended to indicate attributes such as being unborn (*ajatva*). For that [immortality] belongs only to the unborn, not to that which possesses birth. This is the meaning: it is immeasurable, and for that very reason infinite; it is empty of that phenomenal world (*prapañca*) whose properties are death and so forth. The form of this Puruṣa exists in the sky—in the state of radiant light, the state of pure consciousness, the state of joy, or the state of eternal, unsurpassed bliss—or in the solar orb, or in the heavenly realm.

"It exists," it is said. This is what is meant: because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is limited, the form of Brahman with the phenomenal world is "with form" (*sārūpa*), whereas the one without the phenomenal world is "immeasurable"; therefore, this is the effect of its contradictory and non-contradictory attributes.

"It is appropriate that [the sun] is the locus of worldly transaction (vyavahāra). Now, one might object: "Since the Infinite (ananta) exists everywhere, why is it said to be 'in the solar orb' or 'in the celestial station'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For there... He explains that: "For that... Here, "perception" (upalabdhi) is intended to mean the knowledge of meditation (upāsanā-jñāna). He provides an alternative explanation for the verse beginning with "of the one alone": "The other... In this context, "kalpa" means "meaning" (artha).

Even if you postulate a difference between the two causes, sesame and milk, based on the distinction between their respective effects as previously stated or by some other arrangement, we ask you: why does curd, which is a different effect from the oil produced by sesame, arise from milk? Why do the two not together produce only a single effect? Or, even if sesame and milk each produce a separate effect, why do they not produce one of the same kind? In that case, the term "different effect" should be understood as referring to something of a different genus.

And why is it that both [oil and curd] are not produced from both [sesame and milk]? This would be a confusion (*saṃkara*). Or why should there not be a reversed arrangement, such that oil comes from milk and curd from sesame? Furthermore, even though there is no difference in the distinction between milk on one hand and sesame or sand on the other, why is it that oil comes from sesame and not from sand? Moreover, it is logical that distinct things should have either a single effect or effects of the same kind, simply because this is what is observed.

For it is observed that the eyes and other sense organs have a single common function, and that arrows, horns, and the like produce effects belonging to the same class. Furthermore, even though sesame seeds and milk are distinct, why is it that oil comes from sesame and curd from milk, and not the reverse? This is merely an explanation of a contrary arrangement. Now, if it is thought that the difference in effects and the fixed order of effects arise from the inconceivable potencies of things (*bhāvasāmarthya*), and that because such an order exists, no reversal will occur; [we reply:]...

Therefore, it is better that this excellence of capacity belong to a single [cause] alone, such that from even one [cause], multiple effects arise in their established and non-erroneous forms; for since the distinction between effects and so forth is established by a single cause alone, or merely by the excellence of capacity of one [cause], the assumption of a manifoldness of entities is baseless and cumbersome—this is the meaning. The explanation of the term “from the inconceivable” is: “they are inconceivable.”

It is impossible to conceive of them in terms of their origin by asking "from what do they arise" or "how do they arise"; rather, the arrangement of their potencies is determined through the observation of their effects. For the effect is seen to be distinct from both sesame and milk, established, and unerring; therefore, the sense is that those [potencies] are established in exactly that way. And this has been stated with reference to a potency whose nature is ignorance (*avidyā*); for in reality, there is no potency that is either different, non-different, or both different and non-different [from the substrate].

It is observed that even from a single cause, multiple effects arise; as it has been stated, for example, burning and cooking result from fire. To this, an objection is raised: "It might be so. He refutes that with the words: "In that case," etc. Even though there is a difference in the capacities (*śakti*), [on page 157...]

The sense is that [the difference in effects] arises from the oneness of the fire. Now, one might object: even from a single fire, the difference in effects is based on a difference in powers (*śakti*); yet for those who maintain non-duality, there can be no difference in powers. To this we reply: not so; for even for us, a difference in powers consisting of *māyā* is accepted, so there is no fault. Alternatively, one might suspect: since the effect is not observed when the power is impaired by mantras and the like even while the fire exists, it is intended that powers alone are the causal agents; and these powers are distinct. Therefore, the difference in effects there arises precisely from the difference in causes. Thus he raises the objection with the words "atha" (now).

To this it is replied: "As follows" (yathā). Regarding the word "form" (rūpa), the term "undivided" (abhinna) is understood to carry over from the previous context. He explains the meaning of the verse with the words "of one" (ekasya): the meaning is that because it is contradictory for a single fire to be related to multiple effects such as burning and so forth, a diversity of powers (śakti-bheda) must be postulated. The remainder is easy to understand. Furthermore, if the multiple powers were non-different from the single fire, then the fire would have to be both one and many.

In this regard, if the unity of fire is not contradicted by its own multiplicity, it is even less so by the multiplicity residing in its effects. Therefore, since multiple effects can arise even from a single cause, the distinction of causes cannot be established by the multiplicity of effects; with this intention, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*) in a mocking tone. Furthermore, if the potencies are distinct from the single fire, it must be explained how that fire can be their substratum.

If it is argued that their conjunction with it consists in their being supported by it, is that characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or by contiguity (*nairantarya*)? It cannot be characterized by identity, because identity is impossible for distinct things. For if there were identity, there would be only oneness between the two, not difference. And if conjunction and support consist in contiguity, then even a piece of wood in close proximity to fire possessing the power to burn would have that contiguity, leading to the absurd consequence that it too must be its support.

For that which is in contact with one substance is not thereby out of contact with its power; indeed, that which is in contact with the substance of the eye is not out of contact with its color-form (rūpa), otherwise the perception of color-form would simply not occur. And thus, since all-pervading entities are in contact with all things possessing powers, it would follow that they possess all powers. Therefore, it must be stated that fire, by performing some service for its powers, is the substratum of multiple powers.

And that [capacity] is distinct for each capacity due to the difference between capacities. Thus, just as from a single [cause] there is the accomplishment of multiple auxiliary effects, so too would there be the accomplishment of multiple primary effects; therefore, the distinction of causes is not established by the distinction of effects. He states all of this with the words "Now" (*atha*). Having now summarized and stated the meaning of the section, he introduces another view in order to refute it with the words "In this way" (*evam*).

That very inference which was stated by the Buddhists by way of the exclusion of counter-examples (vipakṣa) such as the difference in effects, is what others consider to be *arthāpatti* (presumption), because it cannot otherwise be accounted for; thus it was said: "or by presumption. For difference is indeed mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and that is not within the range of the senses, since the sense organs are capable of grasping only positive entities (*bhāva*). Nor is it cognizable through a logical mark (*liṅga*), because there is no relation with respect to a non-existent correlate, which is not an object of any other means of knowledge.

Because no connection has been observed between that [subject] and any mark (liṅga) possessing it; nor is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) a means of knowledge for difference in the form of mutual exclusion (anyonyābhāva), since it is afflicted by the fault of circularity (itaretarāśrayatva)—that is, when it is based on the premise that the production of curd from milk does not occur from anything else.

Therefore, for those who maintain that there must be another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—characterized by the non-arising of other means of valid cognition—from the causes for the apprehension of existence such as the eye and so forth; or that there must be another means of valid cognition in the form of the cognition "it does not exist" as a negator from the affirmative cognition of an entity, which serves as the basis for mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), since the non-confusion of entities with one another depends upon that [negation]—to them it is replied: "Mutual... and "another means of valid cognition. The word *pramā* is derived either as an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*) or as the state of the result (*bhāvasādhana*).

And this has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "because of the causes for the perception of existence" (*sadupalambhahetubhyaḥ*). The meaning is that, because there is a distinction between the locus (*viṣaya*) and the object negated (*pratiṣedhya*), the two kinds of negative cognition—"this jar etc. is not on this ground" and "this is not a jar, it is a cloth"—do not occur without such a distinction. Now, the opponent has stated that difference (*bheda*) is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*); and that is an absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*), not an absence of the relation between locus and located (*ādhārādheyābhāva*). In that case, one should say only "this is not that," and not "this is not on that. True; yet it is not redundant.

That is indeed for the sake of an illustration! He explains the verse with the word "not" (*na*). The particle *khalu* is used to indicate what is well-known. Why? He says: "not without dependence. For a negation such as "this is not here" or "this is not that" does not occur without depending on that which is being negated; or, if it did occur, it would be merely the word "not. Consequently, because no specific distinction would be apprehended, it would result in universal nihilism.

It has been stated in the passage, "Moreover, when the exclusion of an object to be negated is not required, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the objective referent of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," that the distinction between two specific entities does not consist in their mutual non-existence. Furthermore, this point is demonstrated by the words beginning with "having grasped," as it is also accepted by our opponents.

Thus, when there is a cognition of both the object and the thing to be negated, if that [cognition] were to establish the objects as mere entities whose mutual difference is not apprehended, then—due to the absence of any distinction such as "this is the thing to be negated" and "this is the object"—negation itself would be impossible. For if mere entities whose difference is unapprehended constitute the object, they could not be the thing to be negated; and if they are the thing to be negated, they could not be the object.

Furthermore, if there were no object [to serve as the locus], the absolute negation "the jar does not exist" would pertain to the jar itself, rather than to a specific location where it is established elsewhere; for the absolute negation of something established nowhere is not tenable, nor is that of something absolutely unestablished, because it has never been presented [as a possibility]. This has been stated in the passage beginning: "Otherwise, what negation could there be of that which is prohibited by fate and whose form has not been attained? The term *viṣaya* (object/locus) is intended here as that in which exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is delimited—that is, the locus within which the negation occurs.

Now, if it is said that it is not the mere entity as such that is to be negated as the object, but rather any two specific entities whatsoever, then there would be a negation of everything everywhere, because there is no distinction—[p.

Because of the ninefold apprehension (*navadhāraṇāt*). Therefore, having first cognized the object and the negandum as qualified by distinct intrinsic natures (*bhinnasvabhāva*), the negation must be understood through that [prior cognition]; for only in this way would it be possible. Otherwise, if the distinction between the object and the negandum were not cognized, it would not be possible. Furthermore, when those two are cognized as qualified, there would be the rule that negation occurs only in a specific place; otherwise, as has been stated, everything would be negated everywhere. Moreover, the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the negandum.

Nor is it the case that he has not apprehended the difference; otherwise, it would be as if one were [the negation] of oneself by oneself. Or rather, a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is one that is apprehended merely as a universal while its difference [from the subject] is not apprehended. Consequently, when a post is perceived without distinction, a person too—being perceived through the commonality of verticality (*ūrdhvatā-sāmānya*)—would become the counter-correlative; thus, there would be a cognition of its non-existence. But this is not so. Therefore, it is established that the absence must be understood by first taking two distinct objects of negation into the intellect.

And so, even in the world, that cognition is observed in each individual case to be exactly thus. This being the case, the meaning is as follows: if there is a cognition of the difference between the object and the thing to be negated, then there is the cognition of non-existence; and if that [cognition of non-existence] exists, then there is the cognition of the difference consisting of mutual non-existence between those two—thus there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Now he states the [fault of] mutual dependence in a summary manner with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*): the cognition of the non-existence of a thing does not arise from mere non-apprehension alone, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of such cognition occurring even during deep sleep.

However, non-apprehension [serves as a means of knowledge] only when the totality of the conditions for apprehension is present. For in deep sleep, there is no such thing as a "residual nature" characterized by non-apprehension, whose superior capacity—like that of the eye and other senses—could make known the absence of form and so forth. Rather, in that state, non-apprehension occurs due to the deficiency of the causal complex of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-sāmagrī*). But when there is no such deficiency, since non-apprehension is impossible without the absence of the object of cognition, it necessarily leads to the understanding of the non-existence of the thing.

And thus, like smoke and other such signs, that [non-perception] becomes a means of cognition (*gamika*). That [non-perception] is held to be of two kinds: either the non-modification (*apariṇāma*) of the self in the form of the perception of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), or the cognition of an object other than that [counter-correlate]. As it has been said: "It is either the non-modification of the self, or the cognition of another thing. In this regard, if non-perception were the cognition of another object, then it could not be established unless the difference between the things is already established. Therefore, for the sake of cognizing that [non-perception], the difference between the things must be known.

Nor should it be said: "Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is a cognition other than the cognition of the object to be negated; therefore, in this case, a difference in cognition is understood, not a difference in the real entity (*vastu*); so how can it be stated that 'the difference in the real entity is not established'? For since that cognition is to be inferred from the object of cognition (*jñeya*), its difference is also to be inferred from the difference in the object of cognition; thus, the difference in the real entity as the object of cognition is what must be understood.

Furthermore, since difference cannot be established otherwise than through distinction, the cognition of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) would occur only when difference is known; and when that [non-apprehension] is known, there would be the cognition of difference consisting of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). Thus, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Alternatively, if non-apprehension is defined as the non-modification (*apariṇāma*) of the self (*ātman*), that too does not belong to the self.

The state of stupor (*stimitāvasthā*) consists in the emptiness of all cognition, because when there is no apprehension of anything at all, there is an absence of any specific object such as a cloth. Therefore, it must be said that the transformation of cognition regarding a cloth—which is distinct from a jar and so forth—is the cause for the cognition of the non-existence of that [jar] which is distinct from it; yet this distinction from non-apprehension is not established prior to the cognition of the difference between the jar and the cloth. Consequently, as before, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). [Objection: But surely the difference is grasped by perception itself.

For instance—the author of the *Vārttika*, while refuting the view that non-conceptual perception has only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, stated: "That is incorrect," and so forth. Now, one might object: "But he also stated that 'the establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends upon its validity'"; certainly, that statement was intended to refer to the non-confusion consisting of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*). As for those who say this, they have already been refuted previously under the section beginning with: "They say that perception is a producer [of knowledge]."

As for the followers of Kaṇāda who previously asserted: "That which arises from the sense-organ—assisted by the procedure consisting of the perception of the locus (such as the ground) and the recollection of the counter-positive, and produced through the contact of the qualifier with the conjoined [object]—is a distinct type of perception that apprehends absence. Nor should it be argued: 'If that were born of the senses, it would have to occur first, like the cognition of the object itself, and not later; and how can that which is produced when the operation of the sense-organ has been interrupted by the recollection of the counter-positive be considered sense-born?'"

Just as determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) occurs after indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) because it depends on the recollection of words, and yet is not "non-sensory" (*anakṣaja*) because it arises from the sense organ aided by that [recollection] even when there is an intervention by the recollection of words; likewise, the cognition "it does not exist" also occurs later because it depends on the recollection of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and is sensory because it arises from the sense organ aided by that [recollection] even when there is an intervention by the memory of the counter-correlate. To those who argue thus, this alone must be said: "Because of mutual dependence" (*anyonyasaṃśrayāt*).

"Another means of valid cognition" (pramāṇāntaram) means another form of perception (pratyakṣāntaram). Even by means of perception, one must first apprehend the object and the negatum as distinct, and then apprehend their mutual non-existence; therefore, the same circularity (itaretarāśrayatvam) that applies when non-existence is understood through [another] means of valid cognition applies equally when non-existence is understood through perception. For this reason as well, he states that the knowledge of the non-existence of one thing in another is impossible, beginning with "Furthermore" (kiñca). The analysis of the compound is: "those things (bhāvānām) for whom the single, being-measured entity is the nature of pure existence (sanmātra). He explains that further with "Moreover" (api ca).

For the determination of the object of knowledge (prameya) follows the nature of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa). And that [means of knowledge] cognizes both the jar and the cloth as having the nature of pure Being (sanmātra), not as having a specific form; therefore, those two have the nature of pure Being alone and do not have distinct natures. Consequently, there is no mutual dependence between them; thus, in the jar, which is intended as "the other," there is no [dependence on] the cloth, which is the "other."

The non-arising of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) constitutes non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because both [the object and its absence] possess the same single nature of pure existence (*sanmātraikarūpatva*); for when one is apprehended, the other is also apprehended by that very same form. Therefore, the meaning is that the cognition of the absence of one thing in another is not possible. Here, the proponent of the denial of existence (*sattāpahnavavādin*) objects: "But surely... Because of the recognition of a single form, "cowness" (*gotva*) is admitted in individual cows. Yet, just as it exists in one cow for someone who has seen it, it does not exist in the same way in Mount Meru for someone who has seen a mustard seed.

Therefore, there is no such thing as the universal "existence" (*sattāsāmānya*). How then, in the absence of a single objective basis, can the word and the cognition "existent, existent" occur with respect to infinite things that are absolutely distinct? [The answer is: It will occur through connection with an adjunct (*upādhi*), as in the case of "cook" and so forth. But what is this adjunct? It is the state of being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇaviṣayatā*). For whatever is an object of valid cognition, people call that "existent," whereas they do not apply it to things like a sky-flower which are not such objects; this is the meaning. He refutes this: "Not so."

Indeed, for two things, there can be no cognition of difference without their mutual negation; nor is a cognitive operation termed "negation" possible as something isolated, occurring either simultaneously with an affirmation or subsequent to it. Furthermore, it has been explained in passages such as "in some case where a form has been apprehended" that the affirmation of a real entity itself is the negation of another. Therefore, difference is not the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, if even a non-different form were not grasped, the means of valid cognition would be entirely without an object.

Therefore, a single, undivided form that pervades all states of being must be accepted. And that is our *sattā* (Being). That alone is the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not the particular differences (*bheda*). Consequently, the claim that "only the differences, by virtue of being objects of valid cognition, are the denotable meanings of words" is also refuted. As for the argument that there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the word "existent" (*sat*) with respect to both Mount Meru and a mustard seed, that is unproven; for indeed, there is very well a recognition there too, by way of their common nature as Being (*sadrūpatā*).

Now, if it is argued that [the cognition does not arise] because of dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*), even though there is a persistence of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa-anugama*), then for one who has seen a single cow, the cognition would likewise not occur with respect to another cow—because the individual manifestations (*vyakti*) differ. If it is replied that in that case, despite the difference in individuals, there is a synthesis of the prior and subsequent [cognitions] in the form "this is that very same [cow]," whereas such a synthesis does not exist between one existent mustard seed and another existent Mount Meru; [we respond: no. For even in the case of the mustard seed and Mount Meru, there is indeed a synthesis of the prior and subsequent in the form "this is existent, that is existent," provided there is a recollection of the previous experience. Therefore, since the synthesis of the prior and subsequent exists in both cases, the cognition must arise in both as well. Thus, the distinction between the two cases is not established. Furthermore, if the synthesis of the prior and subsequent were the cause of the cognition, then the cognition would arise even when one sees a series of different cows, such as a black cow followed by a white one, because the synthesis of the prior and subsequent is present there too. And if it is argued that the cognition arises only when the synthesis of the prior and subsequent occurs with respect to the same object, then the cognition would not arise with respect to a second cow, because the synthesis of the prior and subsequent occurs with respect to the first cow, not with respect to the second. Consequently, the cognition of "existence" would never occur with respect to a second cow, nor would it ever occur with respect to a second individual of any kind. Thus, the claim that the cognition of "existence" arises from the synthesis of the prior and subsequent is untenable. Therefore, the cognition of "existence" must be admitted to arise from the persistence of the nature of existence itself. This concludes the section on the proof of the universal "Existence. Now begins the section on the refutation of the universal "Being-ness" (*sattā*). Some maintain that there is a universal called "Being-ness" which inheres in all three categories (*padārtha*). Others hold that this is merely the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) and that there is no separate universal. To refute them, he says: "The universal Being-ness is not distinct from existence. Why? Because it is not perceived separately from existence. Just as the nature of a cow is not perceived apart from the cow, so too the nature of being is not perceived apart from the existent. Nor is it perceived through inference, because there is no probans (*liṅga*) for it. If it were perceived through inference, it would have to be inferred either from its own nature or from its effects. It cannot be inferred from its own nature, because that would lead to an infinite regress. Nor can it be inferred from its effects, because there is no effect of Being-ness other than existence itself. If existence were the effect of Being-ness, then existence would be something distinct from the existent, which is contradictory. Furthermore, if Being-ness were distinct from existence, then the cognition "this is existent" would not arise with respect to an existent thing, just as the cognition "this is a cow" does not arise with respect to a horse.
