For those who maintain the doctrine of existence (*sattāvādinaḥ*), oneness arises from the synthesis of the prior and the subsequent in the form "this is that," and not from the cognition of an identical form. Therefore, they argue that although there is a continuous cognition of an identical form between Mount Meru and a mustard seed, they do not constitute a single entity because there is no synthesis of the form "this is that. This is incorrect; for even without synthesis, the certainty of oneness occurs at the very first sight of a single individual object simply through the cognition of an identical form. Indeed, synthesis occurs only upon a subsequent perception when there is a difference in space and time.

And that [distinction] does not exist at the time of the first perception. Therefore, it is established that the determination of multiplicity and unity arises solely from the cognition of an undifferentiated form; likewise, from the very first non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-pratyaya*) of the form "cow," which is undifferentiated despite being uttered within a herd of buffaloes, the individual cows within the cow-herd are [cognized] even when they occupy different locations.

P.59-14. This is because the ascertainment of a single genus (*gotva*) is indeed desired; as it has been said: “Non-conceptual [perception]... and so forth. For even here there is no synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*); for that [synthesis] occurs when what was previously seen is seen again at a different time. And in a herd of cows, although the individuals differ in location, there is no difference in time. Therefore, in this case too, the determination of non-difference arises solely from the cognition of an identical form.

Furthermore, if oneness were due to mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*), then just as there is a synthesis upon seeing one water-jar (*maṇika*) when seeing another water-jar, it would not occur in the same way upon seeing a bowl (*śarāva*); in that case, even the universal of "clay" (*mṛjjāti*) would not exist. Now, if it is argued that just as with a water-jar, there is indeed a synthesis upon seeing a bowl when seeing another water-jar, yet this is the distinction: that in the case of two water-jars it is intense because of the greater number of common parts of the jars, whereas in the case of a water-jar and a bowl it is not intense because only the universal of "clay" persists; therefore, the universal of "clay" does exist.

In that case, just as there is a non-intense synthesis (anusaṃdhāna) between a water-jar and a shallow bowl, and from that the genus "clay-ness" (mṛjjāti) is established, so too, having observed this among mustard seeds, even on Mount Meru, although there is no intense synthesis in the form of "mustard-seed-ness," there exists a non-intense synthesis in the form of "existence" (sat-rūpa); therefore, the genus "existence" (sajāti) is also established. Thus it is well said: "among those things whose single form is being measured. Having raised an objection against this very point according to the view of another, he resolves it with the words "bheda" etc. That which is differentiated is "bheda"—that is, a particular form (viśeṣa-rūpa) that is excluded (vyāvṛtta).

Non-difference is the inclusive nature of the universal, which is the opposite of that [particularity]; there exist two cognitions, "existent" and "jar," which manifest both of these. The cognition "existent" is inclusive across all things, while the cognition "jar" is excluded from cloth and so forth. The same should be understood for such cases as "the cow is brindled. If, however, these two cognitions were not admitted, then the twofold empirical usage would not occur; yet this [usage] does indeed exist.

For instance: a calf, seeking its mother, runs toward a herd of cows with a cognition of generality (*sāmānyabuddhi*), and toward its own mother with a cognition of particularity (*viśeṣabuddhi*). Therefore, there are two cognitions from that [act], having the forms of the inclusive (*anuvṛtta*) and the exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*). And the determination of objects depends upon cognition; otherwise, even non-difference would not exist for you, since even that is accepted by you solely through the power of cognition. If it is argued that, therefore, the world is indeed of two forms and not of one form, we say: no.

For the determination of the reality of an object does not arise from mere cognition alone, as this is absent in cases such as the cognition of a fire-brand circle (*alātacakra*). Therefore, even if a cognition has arisen, it must be examined by reasoning whether it is contradicted or not; for this very reason, one should investigate whether it is produced by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not, rather than simply accepting it as "cognition. Alternatively, the investigation concerns contradiction or non-contradiction with reasoning—whether it is contradicted by reasoning or not. Furthermore, the distinction is that "produced by a valid means of knowledge" refers to an investigation into the capacity or incapacity of that means of knowledge.

But how can perception be sublated by reasoning? True; it would not be sublated if it were genuine perception; however, that is merely a semblance of perception, as they say: "Perception is that which establishes [an object].

This has already been explained in such passages as those cited above. Therefore, just as the cognition of a fire-brand wheel (alātacakra) and the like seen in a dream—or even when awake—is not the cause for following after that [object] despite its apparent existence, so too is the cognition of difference (bhedajñāna). Now, it may be argued that according to the principle stated—namely, "Difference is not [known] by itself, nor accompanied by an injunction, nor subsequent to an injunction; the operation of a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) does not occur"—the cognition of difference cannot arise from anything other than a means of valid knowledge.

Who else would say otherwise? We too, while denying difference, simply state that there is no arising of the cognition of difference; for in ultimate reality, there is no comprehension of difference. If such [comprehension] were to exist, then since a cognition without an object is impossible, how could we deny difference? And if it is denied, how can there be a comprehension of difference by the reasons previously stated? For a comprehension cannot occur without something to be comprehended, because comprehension is necessarily transitive (sakarmaka).

Now, if neither difference nor the cognition thereof exists, then what is this world that appears as distinct from Brahman? It is called *avidyā* (ignorance). He clarifies that very term through a synonym: "delusion" (*vibhrama*). The meaning is that ignorance is *avidyā*, or rather, delusion has that [ignorance] as its material cause (*upādāna*). And that [delusion] is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*); for instance, if the object of knowledge existed in the manner it appears, it would not be a delusion, but rather right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). On the other hand, if it were non-existent, like a flower in the sky, its cognition would be impossible.

Therefore, in the world, an error (*vibhrama*) is not spoken of as being determined as either existent or non-existent. Consequently, it is indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), because such a state alone is established in all philosophical systems. This was stated in the passage: "And this would be accepted by all proponents in this manner. Although it has already been stated, it is repeated here due to the context of the indeterminability [of the object]. Alternatively, the distinction is that in that [previous] case the indeterminability of the error of the object (*arthavibhrama*) was stated, whereas here it is the indeterminability of the error of cognition (*jñānavibhrama*).

And at that time, since there is no cognition without an object of cognition (*jñeya*), one must pose the question: "How is it that this cognition of all things as distinct appears? Furthermore, the phrase "when the object of knowledge exists" is an indication where the object is not intended to be emphasized; rather, it means "when the manifestation exists," which is to say, "when cognition exists. Thus, even though these two types of cognition exist, it must be examined whether they are contradicted by reasoning or not.

Furthermore, we have already explained that in those cases, the cognition of difference does not arise from the power of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, it contradicts the reasoning presented in the passages "the proponents [say]" and "the sequence is consistent. Therefore, the sense is that difference is not ultimately real (*paramārthataḥ*). However, for this reason as well, those two cognitions must be examined; hence he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*), and states that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) [arises] "from the difference of cognitions" (*jñānabhedāt*).

Because of the distinction between inclusive and exclusive cognitions, and because the determination of things conforms to their cognition, the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) assert that there are two types of entities, distinguished as the universal (*sāmānya*) and the individual (*vyakti*), who maintain that the relation between the universal and the individual—which are absolutely distinct—is inherence (*samavāya*). Alternatively, because the two cognitions "it exists" and "it is a jar" are established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and because such coreferentiality would be impossible if there were absolute difference, [they posit the universal].

A single entity consists of particularity (*viśeṣātmaka*); as the proponents of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*) say, those who maintain that there is neither absolute difference nor absolute identity between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*). Alternatively, the individuals themselves are the entities, and the universal is not a separate entity. There is non-difference in the form of the universal. And because a universal that is both different and non-different is impossible, and because all persons possess an innate [disposition], they lack the capacity to ascertain the absolute difference residing in the individuals due to the force of beginningless mental impressions (*vāsanā*); thus, the object of conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), which takes individuals as its material cause and has individuals as its domain, is [perceived] in this way.

Nor is this unseen; for the Buddhists observe that the conceptualization of non-difference as "a forest" occurs with respect to distinct trees. Reality is one and non-dual. Because that [Reality], which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth—and for that very reason infinite—cannot be determined in its true form due to ignorance (*avidyā*), and because ignorance is beginningless, there arise conceptualizations of difference that have that [Reality] as their object. These conceptualizations of difference are beginningless, do not depend on adventitious causes such as defects of the senses, and take non-difference as their material cause (*upādāna*), since they originate from that [ignorance] and arise within that very [Reality]. This is not unseen.

For it is observed that there is a conceptualization of difference in the moon, which is in fact non-different, due to the distinction between its waves; such is our own view. Thus, because there is doubt arising from conflicting opinions (*vipratipatti*), one cannot reach a certainty regarding that [object] without investigation. Therefore, the meaning is that even when there are two types of cognition—one characterized by favorability and one by exclusion—an investigation must be performed. Regarding this, when the occasion for investigation has arisen, he says: "Not, first of all... (*na tāvat*).

First of all, there are not two entities called the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) that are absolutely distinct, because the cognition "the pot exists" would be untenable if the universal and the individual were non-different by way of identity (*aikātmya*). For co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is never observed between two things that are absolutely distinct, such as a pot and a lotus. If it is argued that this cognition of identity is produced by the relation called inherence (*samavāya*), that is not so; for even in that case, since their difference in form remains unaltered and undiminished, the same problem persists: a cognition of identity between two things of distinct forms is logically impossible. This is the meaning.

He explains this with the word "no. It should be understood that it is not the case that the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are two entirely distinct entities, like blue and yellow, because they differ in their manifestation as being either inclusive or exclusive. He states the reason for this: "because of the non-appearance of a relation" (*saṃbandhasyāpratibhāsanāt*). Where there is a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between two distinct things, there the relation—which is the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matup*)—appears, as in the case of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*). However, here in the expression "the jar possesses existence" (*sattāvān ghaṭaḥ*), there is no such appearance of that relation.

However, the meaning is that there is identity [expressed] in "the pot exists" (*san ghaṭaḥ*). Even if these two appear as co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*), he asks "even so, why? and replies with "And not... (*na ca*).

If the universal and the particular were two distinct entities, then even though they might be related, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) such as "the pot exists" (san ghaṭaḥ). This is because, through that relation, the pair of universal and particular would be grasped either by two distinct cognitions apprehending the qualifier and the qualified respectively, or by a single cognition apprehending the qualified as characterized by the qualifier—just as in the case of "the man with a staff" (daṇḍī puruṣaḥ)—and not as a single identity. And here, "existent" [p.

The cognition of "the jar" as a single identity is experienced by all people. Furthermore, if there were a disagreement [regarding their nature], the universal (sāmānya) and the particular (viśeṣa) would have to be cognized as distinct; since they are established by cognition as being distinct, the Sāṃkhyas would not disagree regarding that distinction. Yet they do disagree. Therefore, for this reason also, they are cognized as a single identity. Moreover, if they were cognized as distinct, then upon the perception of the universal, there could be no conceit of perceiving the particular.

Furthermore, as in the case of seeing smoke, there might arise the conceit of [perceiving] something imperceptible due to its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with fire; but this is not the case here. For this reason also, the cognition of those two occurs through their identity (*aikātmya*). Moreover, even if a relation exists between them, that [identity-cognition] would not occur; rather, it was stated that it occurs through the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), like a staff [and its bearer]. Here, an objection is raised: "It might be so. If we were to say that the cognition of identity arises from conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then it would indeed be like the case of a staff; however, our position is that it arises from inherence (*samavāya*). This is the meaning.

Regarding the question, "What is its specific distinction?", he says: "For that [proximity]," and so on. The meaning is that because it consists of the state of immediate contiguity even between two distinct things, it conceals their difference and makes known their non-difference. He refutes this with: "Not so. He states the reason: "Even in the case of inherence," and so on. Even in the case of inherence, because it is a relation, it exists between two distinct things, not within a single one. If, however, the difference between those two were not manifest, then, due to having distinct substrata, the relation itself would not be manifest either.

Therefore, even in the case of inherence (*samavāya*) as a relation, there must be a distinction between those two [the universal and the particular], because the difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the two inherent entities remains unaltered by them. And thus, a cognition of identity is not logical. Yet such a cognition does exist. Consequently, the non-difference of appearance (*prakhyābheda*)—which is contradictory to that [identity]—is incapable of establishing the difference between the entities of the universal and the particular; this is the meaning. Thus, having relied upon the difference between the cognition of non-difference of appearance and the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it has been stated that the former is contradicted by the latter.

But when a single cognition itself makes known two objects as being in a relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he says: "itself" (*svayam*). Or rather, because it is self-contradictory, the difference in cognition does not serve to establish a difference in the objects. He states the reason for its being self-contradictory: "single" (*eka*). The meaning is that the difference in cognition arises through coreferentiality in a general sense.

This is what is meant: if the appearance of the inclusive and the exclusive were to occur in the pot with a lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), just as the appearance of a cloth [is distinct from it], then there would be no self-contradiction; but when [the cognition] does not show the universal and the particular as distinct, then, because it displays both contradictory difference and non-difference, it is self-contradictory. Here, an objection is raised with the words "But surely" (*nanu*); to this, the author provides the reply with the words "Difference... (*bheda*).

The meaning of this is as follows: Now, if it is admitted that even though there is absolute difference between the universal and the particular, inherence possesses the power to conceal their difference, then why is such a power not admitted for the single Self itself? For it is by virtue of a specific power that it appears in manifold forms. The function (*vṛtti*) has been explained by the words themselves.

P. 61-16. It was stated that there is no distinction [between the two cases]; to this, the opponent objects with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). In the case of fire, iron, balls, and so forth, it is observed that the conjunction of distinct entities—such as fire and an iron ball—has the power to conceal their difference. For instance, people perceive the iron ball as "this is fire. Since this is observed, it is accepted in that case; however, a single entity does not have the power to appear as manifold, because such a thing is never observed. Anticipating this objection regarding the alleged distinction, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) again asserts the lack of distinction, saying: "It is observed."

If it should be argued that there is a distinction because it is observed that conjunction possesses the property called the "capacity to conceal the difference" between two distinct things, to that it is replied: this is not a distinction; for even a single variegated color and a single cognition appear as manifold—this is the meaning. He explains this with the word "observed."

Nor should it be argued that there is no such thing as a distinct color called "variegated" (*citra*) belonging to the cloth, but rather that the colors of the threads themselves—such as blue, yellow, and so forth—when combined and joined together, are called "variegated"; for since the colors such as blue and the rest are inherent (*samaveta*) in the threads, the cloth would then be devoid of color. And if it were devoid of color, it would be invisible to the eye, like the wind, due to the absence of that specific excellence of objective refinement which constitutes the definition of color.

If it is argued that even though the cloth itself is formless (*arūpa*), it might still be visible because it inheres (*samavāya*) in the threads which possess form (*rūpin*), just as number such as unity and actions such as motion [are perceived] in relation to their substrates; that is not so. For it has been stated in the Vaiśeṣika system: “The visual perception of an object that is a large substance, such as a triad (*tryaṇuka*) and the like, arises from its inherence in multiple substances and from its color. In this context, the phrase “from its inherence in multiple substances” is stated in order to exclude the visual perception of an atom (*paramāṇu*), even though it possesses color.

In this context, "manifoldness" (*anekatva*) is intended to mean plurality (*bahutva*); by this, it is stated that even a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is not visible. Furthermore, the phrase "from color" (*rūpāt*) is mentioned to exclude the visibility of air (*vāyu*), even though it is inherent in multiple substances. Alternatively, "inherence in multiple substances" (*anekadravyasamavāya*) serves as an indicator for "largeness" (*mahattva*); thus, the meaning is "from largeness. In that regard, largeness excludes atoms (*paramāṇu*) and dyads, while the phrase "from color" excludes air and the like.

This is what is meant: even though qualities, actions, and so forth are formless (*nīrūpa*), they possess visual perceptibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) due to their inherence (*samavāya*) in a substance, but not the substance itself; rather, the substance's visual perceptibility arises from its own color/form (*rūpa*). Therefore, if one does not admit a variegated color for a cloth, it would follow that the cloth is imperceptible to the eye. Furthermore, if something were visually perceptible despite being itself formless, then even a jar or similar object would be formless, since its visual perceptibility is admitted to arise through inherence in parts that possess color.

Now, if it is not accepted that a substance devoid of color (*arūpa*) is visible, then it would follow that jars and the like are themselves colorless; consequently, this would also apply to a multicolored cloth, which would likewise not have color. Therefore, there exists a variegated color (*citram rūpam*). And although that [color] is one, it appears through the distinctions of blue and so forth; thus, there is a manifold appearance of the one. Likewise, even though there is no difference between the cognition of a city and the cognition of the three worlds, and although they are inherently one, they appear as manifold through the distinctions of houses, palaces, and so on.

The state of being an appearance has been observed. To show that this is established even in the case of the dependent nature (*paratantra*), it was stated: "the form of the object," and so forth. Nor should it be said that it is the forms of cognition that appear as manifold, and not the cognition itself; therefore, it is not the case that a single [entity] appears as manifold. Because they do not differ from the single reality of cognition (*buddhitattva*), there is in truth no mutual difference between them either, but rather it is an illusion. How much less so in relation to cognition itself? Therefore, it is cognition alone that appears as manifold.

Furthermore, for our opponents, the non-difference [of qualities] from the cognition is established in their own system. Now, it might be thought: "In those very things where qualities such as blue and yellow are inherent (*samaveta*), there is the composite whole (*avayavin*) called 'cloth. In that case, the inherence (*samavāya*) which belongs to the variegated quality (*citraguṇa*) is itself the relation characterized by 'inherence in that which is inherent in a single object' (*ekārthasamavetasamavāya*) with respect to the blue and other colors. It is precisely because of this that the multiplicity residing in the blue and other colors appears in the variegated [whole]. Therefore, this too is the power of the relation."

If it is argued that, therefore, it is precisely the greatness of that [universal] which causes both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), though distinct, to appear as non-distinct, he says in response: "And not... (P. 62-7). A relation preceded by a connection—that is, a conjunction (*saṃsarga*)—does not occur; why? Because of an intervention (*vyavadhāna*); this is the meaning. But surely a conjunction can occur even when there is an intervention, as in the case of the eye conjoined with a substance [perceiving] color; to this he says: "For conjunction is indeed... Conjunction is indeed a contact (*saṃśleṣa*).

And from that [contact], there occurs the appearance of another object, such as a glowing iron ball, in its own form before [the observer]; this does not happen through just any kind of connection. Furthermore, that intimate contact (*saṃśleṣa*) is possible only when there is no separation whatsoever, not even when there is a single layer of separation. The meaning is that an intimate contact is certainly not possible between the blue color residing in the threads and the variegated color residing in the cloth, because of the separation by both the threads and the cloth. He says "moreover" (*kiṃca*) to show that this postulation of an absolute difference between the universal and the particular is futile.

The meaning is as follows: when every cognition that serves as a factor in linguistic usage regarding a substrate consisting of a genus (*jāti*) and a quality (*guṇa*), such as "Bring the cow with a horn," is in accordance with reality, then the conceptualization of a difference between the two entities—the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*)—is useless. He explains this [with the words] beginning "of which" (*yasya*).

For one who maintains the absolute difference between the universal (sāmānya) and the particular (viśeṣa), cognitions such as "the white cow"—which serve as the basis for linguistic usage—arise with respect to substances through the imposition of qualities and universals, by being colored by them, by being excluded from what they are not, and by appearing non-different from them. For such a person, those cognitions do not correspond to reality; the meaning is that they are cognitions of things otherwise than they actually are. Why? Because the substance is a different entity from the universal and the quality, due to their distinction; the object is distinct, yet the cognitions present it as non-distinct.

Therefore, the meaning is that these [notions] do not correspond to the actual state of things (*yathāvastu*). The mention of "qualities" (*guṇa*) is either because they follow the same logical principle (*nyāya*), or for the purpose of demonstrating the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛttabuddhi*). He asks, "What follows from that? and says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*); the meaning is that, such being the case, linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) based on distinct entities would not exist. He asks, "Why? and says: [p. 168]

"By means of cognition" (*buddhyā*) means that only what is known serves as a factor for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), not what is unknown. And a distinct object is unknown; therefore, it does not serve as a factor for linguistic usage—this is the meaning. "Because of being such" means "because of being a factor for linguistic usage. To the question "Even so, what [follows]? he says: "And thus. Even though there is a distinction between substances (*dravya*) on account of genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*), linguistic usage is observed to be inclusive, such as "cow," and exclusive, such as "white," by means of an object that is non-different from the genus and quality as they are apprehended solely by cognition.

Therefore, the meaning is that since the distinction between entities is useless for conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), whereas non-distinction alone is useful for it, the postulation of a distinction between entities is futile. Furthermore, it is futile for this reason: a distinction between entities is postulated so that conventional cognitions may correspond to reality (*yathārthatva*); yet, even when such a distinction is postulated, because conventional cognitions such as "white" arise through the non-difference of the universal (*jāti*), the quality (*guṇa*), and the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), their lack of correspondence with reality is not avoided. Thus, the postulation of a distinction between entities is useless.

The opponent, however, states that the conceptualization of a difference between things has a purpose: "It might be so," he says. It is observed that the cognition of a person in a post, or the cognition of silver in a white object, is caused by a commonality of form such as height. Therefore, even though the non-differentiating cognition "This is a cow" or "This is white" may not correspond to reality, it must have a cause. And if there were two distinct entities, they would appear [to us] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

If there were no difference between entities, there could not be a conventional, non-corresponding cognition that grasps both inclusive and exclusive forms, because of the absence of a cause; therefore, although the conceptualization of a difference between entities is not itself a constituent of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), it is not useless, as it serves as the seed for the cognition of real co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) which is a constituent of linguistic usage. He refutes this, saying: "It is replied. If [the cognition] is not an error without a seed, then it must have ignorance (*avidyā*) as its seed; thus, enough with the conceptualization of a difference between entities. This is the meaning.

Having thus refuted the view of those who advocate conjunction (*saṃsarga*), he introduces the view of the proponents of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*) in order to refute it, saying: "Let it be so. The meaning is: let there be a single reality consisting of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). He states the distinction of this view from the previous position of absolute difference by noting the absence of the faults inherent therein, saying: "In this way. It was previously stated that if there were absolute difference between the universal and the particular, the manifestation of their identity—as in "this is a cow" or "this is white"—would not be possible.

To begin with, that [distinction] does not exist here, because the cognition of non-difference is established through the fact that a real entity consists of both the universal and the particular. Furthermore, as for the imagined capacity of the entity known as "inherence" (*samavāya*)—which is of the nature of a relation—to cause the disappearance of difference, that is contrary to reality; for since a related entity has difference as its object, it cannot be the cause of the opposite, namely non-distinction between two things that are actually distinct. Moreover, that [capacity] does not even exist, because a single entity, by virtue of its internal nature, is itself non-different. Thus, when an entity possesses a dual nature... [p. 169]

The conventional usage such as “the cow is white” is based on a real entity; therefore, the claim that empirical cognitions are non-correspondent (ayathārtha) because they involve external adjuncts (*paropādhi*) in worldly practice is also not tenable. Consequently, let this position alone stand as correct. He raises an objection regarding contradiction with the words “it might be,” and states the contradiction with the words “one. The meaning is: one is that [entity], while the opposite of that is many.

He states that it is difficult to comprehend the oneness of two things due to contradiction in another way—with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). He refutes that with "No" (*na*). That which is perceived by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory, such as color in that which possesses taste; that which is other than this is contradictory, such as coldness in what is hot. Therefore, in whatever manner a thing is cognized by a means of valid cognition, it is logical only in that very manner. If contradiction were asserted while disregarding the means of valid cognition in that regard, then the distinction between contradiction and non-contradiction would be entirely without basis.

Therefore, that which is cognized by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory; and yet, a single [entity] is cognized as having a triple nature. For its triple nature follows from the difference in cognition due to its forms of persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), while its oneness follows from its being apprehended through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); such is the meaning. Having thus introduced the view of the proponent of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*), he refutes it with the words "This very... He states the reason with the word "Because": the cognition of an entity as having a triple nature is invalid, because its object is contradictory, like the cognition of doubt; such is the meaning.

In this context, "contradiction" (vipratiṣedha) refers to a reversal of essential nature (svarūpaviparyaya), not to non-coexistence (sahānavasthāna); and since that [reversal] exists between unity and multiplicity, one should not suspect the reason (hetu) to be unestablished (asiddhi). However, if the cognition of a single thing as having a dual nature were to be a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) despite its object being contradictory, then by parity of reasoning, even doubtful cognition would be a valid means of knowledge; and consequently, even an object under doubt would possess a dual nature. Since this is not accepted, he says "otherwise" (anyathā). He provides the reason for this with the words "having a dual nature" (dvyātmā).

Just as the cognition "this is a cow" has a form consisting of both the inclusive and the exclusive, so too the cognition of doubt has a form consisting of the two aspects of a post and a person; and just as there is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the universal and the particular in that case, so too in doubt there is [co-referentiality] between those two forms, the post and the person. Therefore, the meaning is that because it is similar to an object consisting of two natures, the object of doubt must also consist of two natures. Here, he raises an objection regarding this lack of similarity with the words "Now, however" (*atha*).

The meaning is that just as there is a cognition of a conjunction (samuccaya) regarding an object possessing both general and particular properties—as in "this is a cow" and "this is a Śābaleya"—such is not the case with doubt. To this, he states the reply: "Let it not be so. The opponent says: "Even that [is not so]. For it is not tenable that one and the same thing is a post in one alternative and a person in another; because it arises from its own causes with a fixed, single form. As it has been said: "A real entity is not subject to conceptual oscillation. However, the proponent [of the Siddhānta] argues: if the conceptual oscillation of a real entity is not admitted because it is untenable, then even for a single thing, there would be a dual nature. [p. 170]

The meaning is that because of contradiction, that [cognition] would also not be possible. Here too, contradiction consists in the subversion of the essential nature (*svarūpa-viparyaya*), and not in non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), since the latter is what is yet to be proven (*sādhya*). This being the case, regarding that which possesses the sacrifice, he says: "therein" (*tatra*). Immediately after the phrase "due to having a common substratum" (*aikādhikaraṇyāt*), the word "invalid" (*apramāṇam*) is to be supplied. Now, one might object: doubt-cognition is not invalid due to contradiction, but rather because it is sublated (*bādhana*) by a determinate cognition (*nirṇaya-jñāna*) of either the post or the person.

And that [cognition] does not exist because there is a cognition of both the general and the particular. Therefore, even though there is a contradiction, since there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). With the intention of showing that the statement—"the cognition of the general and the particular is not a valid means of knowledge because of conflict, like doubt"—is improper, he raises an objection with the words "it might be" (*syāt*). The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), however, says "where... (*yatra*).

If it is argued that doubt lacks validity because it is sublated by a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*), then in a case where there is a doubt such as "is this the middle or not the middle" based on the pointing out of a pillar used as a marker for the earth buried according to the *Pāśupata* rite, there would have to be a dual nature for one and the same thing being conceptualized; and this is not desired. Therefore, its invalidity arises precisely from contradiction. If this is so, then even in the absence of sublation, the cognition of both the general and the particular is invalid due to contradiction, just like doubt; thus the statement is well-said—this is the meaning.

Thus, it has been stated that because the cognition of a universal and a particular possesses contradictory natures, it lacks validity, just like doubt. Now, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*) to show that when two cognitions of unity and multiplicity—which have contradictory objects—are negated by one another, there is no dual nature; however, when they negate each other, they are equivalent to doubt.

Just as the invalidity of the cognition of silver arises from its sublation—that is, its rejection by the stronger cognition of mother-of-pearl—so too, despite the contradiction between the cognitions of unity and multiplicity, there is invalidity for one or both of those cognitions. Why? Because when two contradictory forms, namely unity and multiplicity, are apprehended, the cognitions grasping these contradictory forms mutually reject one another.

In that case, if one [of the two cognitions] is stronger, then, as in the case of the cognition of silver and so forth, there is a determination from the other [cognition] upon the negation of the first, just as from the cognition of mother-of-pearl. In that situation, the object would be either a single entity or dual-natured; it cannot be both single and dual-natured simultaneously. However, when two equally strong reasons—like two non-deviating contradictory reasons (*viruddhāvyabhicāri-hetu*)—mutually negate each other, there is no determination of either unity or dual-naturedness due to the sublation involved; consequently, the apprehension of the general and the particular results in a state equivalent to doubt.

Therefore, this is merely a description of one's own position, asserting that "neither is the object exclusively one, nor is it many; rather, it is both one and dual-natured," and that the cognition grasping this is well-ascertained; the meaning is that it is not actually so. For this reason as well, he says "moreover" (*api ca*) that it is neither one nor dual-natured. He explains the verse with the words "necessarily" (*avaśyam*), etc. One must necessarily establish the distinction between difference and non-difference regarding categories such as genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*). [p. 171]

While doing so, he must necessarily state the definitions of difference and non-difference for both the universal and the particulars individually. Furthermore, for each of these two, the definitions of difference and non-difference consist respectively in the contradiction and non-contradiction of their natures, which take the form of mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*) and its opposite; for it is from the contradiction of nature—consisting in mutual exclusion—that the mutual difference among particulars arises, and from the opposite of that, the universal remains non-different within those particulars that are themselves different.

In this regard, if such a contradiction between the universal and the particular—characterized by difference and non-difference—were of the nature of mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*), then there would be no mutual unity between them, just as there is none among distinct particulars. Alternatively, if the cognitions of the universal and the particular arise in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), then they do not possess the state of being contradictory; thus, their unity is asserted through the absence of contradiction.

Therefore, because there is an absence of contradiction between their forms—which is the defining characteristic of difference—and because difference is absent, there is an absence of duality as the substratum of that difference. Just as the universal aspect and the particular aspect are not divided, being each devoid of internal subdivisions and thus not possessing two forms, so too, since there is no contradiction between the forms of the universal and the particular, and since difference is absent, there is an absence of duality as the substratum of that difference; therefore, a single entity cannot be dual in nature. The phrase "because of the cognition of co-referentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇyabuddheḥ) is the reason for the absence of contradiction between their forms. (P. 64-15)

The meaning of this very point has been clarified in brief by the passage beginning with "yadi" (if). Now, [the opponent] might think: if plurality were due to a contradiction in nature characterized by mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*), and unity were its opposite, then because there is no contradiction in nature between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), duality would not exist for them—as it does not for either of their constituent parts; yet such is not the case. Rather, wherever there is a cognition of two forms, there is plurality, and wherever there is a cognition of a single form, there is unity.

And therefore, because the universal and the particular are perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the cognition "this is a cow," they possess oneness despite the absence of contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*); thus, because a real entity is cognized by a cognition of two forms, it has a dual nature. To this, it is replied: "oneness and otherness" (*aikānya*). A cognition of oneness and otherness (*aikānyabuddhi*) is a cognition of a single form.

If there were oneness between the universal aspect and the particular aspect, then this cognition of a single form would not exist regarding an object that possesses two forms; if it does not exist, how can there be oneness? Or, if it does exist, then because it is cognized by a cognition of a single form, it would have oneness like a single part; the meaning is: "How can there be a dual nature? The term *vṛtti* means manifestation. Now, if it is thought: "Both the difference in the form of the cognition and the mutual non-identity [of the aspects] constitute the definition of difference."

In that case, since both [existence and non-existence] exist in cows, horses, and so forth, there is indeed a difference [between them]. However, as for the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), even though there is a difference in the form of their cognitions, because they are perceived as having a mutual identity through the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), they lack mutual non-identity; thus, there is no difference [between them], and consequently, there is no destruction of unity. To this we reply: that too is not correct. For if, due to the perception of the universal and the particular as having a mutual identity, there is no mutual non-identity, even so— [p.

It has been stated in the passage "How could there be a dual nature? that a dual nature would not exist because of the absence of the combined characteristics of difference, as if one were pointing out a location. Now, suppose the following view is held: the non-difference of form within cognition and the mutual apprehension of each other's essence are two separate characteristics of non-difference; and the combination of the absence of both of these constitutes the characteristic of difference. Consequently, because of the characteristic of non-difference—the non-difference of form within cognition—there would be unity for each part, namely the universal aspect and the particular aspect.

However, because the universal and the particular are understood to have each other as their own nature, they possess oneness through the characteristic of non-difference. On the other hand, particulars possess only difference because they lack both characteristics of non-difference. Consequently, although the universal and the particular are dual in terms of their essential form (*svarūpa*), they also possess oneness due to the aforementioned characteristic of non-difference; thus, it is established that a single entity possesses a dual nature. This is incorrect; [The argument continues: ...because the two characteristics of non-difference do not exist for particulars, there is only difference. Therefore, even though the universal and the particular are dual by virtue of their own nature, oneness also exists due to the previously mentioned characteristic of non-difference; thus, it is established that a single entity possesses a dual nature. Because even if there were thus a mutual identity characterized by non-difference, and for that very reason the characteristic of difference—which consists in the absence of both—were non-existent, the dual nature of the universal and the particular would not be possible. Furthermore, it is not logical for a single non-difference to have two characteristics designated as "the cognition of non-difference" and "the mutual identity of forms. Why? Because the non-difference of characteristics establishes non-difference in all the objects characterized.

For example, the non-difference of the definition of inference establishes the non-difference of all inferences insofar as they share the nature of being inference; whereas the difference in definitions establishes their distinction, as in the case of inference and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). In that regard, it is logical that there should be a plurality of the defined objects due to the difference in their definitions. If, however, the reality of the defined object remains non-distinct despite such differences, then since the difference or non-difference of the definitions would be irrelevant, there would be plurality even in the absence of difference [in the definitions]; consequently, the definition itself would be rendered useless.

The word *iti* marks the conclusion. Furthermore, he states that the identity of the universal and the particular is untenable with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). If there were non-difference between the two, then since one would be grasped by the very same cognition as the other, it would follow that when either one is grasped, a second cognition apprehending the other—which would have a distinct object—would be rendered useless; just as, for example, when the aspect of the universal or the aspect of the particular has been grasped by its own respective cognition, no further cognition is required to describe it.

Now, if it is argued that because they are both different and non-different, there is also multiplicity between them, and thus the apprehension of one does not entail the apprehension of the other—thereby establishing the meaningfulness of distinct cognitions—then the meaning is: why would their unity not also be rendered purposeless? The term "in differences" means "in particulars. The phrase "as in the case of the parts consisting of the universal and the particular" [is used].

Just as when either the universal aspect or the particular aspect is apprehended by its own cognition, another distinct cognition is not sought to refute it, so too, when the universal is apprehended, another cognition is not sought for the apprehension of the particular, because the two are non-different. Likewise, when the particular is apprehended, the same applies to the universal; this is the meaning. Now, due to their non-difference, it is logical that both are apprehended by a single cognition, and not that they are unapprehended due to their multiplicity.

He says: "The general rule" (*autsargika*). In the absence of a seed, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the sprout is established as a cause that is independent [of other factors] because it is beginningless. The presence of the seed is an exception (*apavāda*) to that prior non-existence of the sprout; for by that [presence], [the non-existence] is set aside—this is the meaning. Having stated this in general terms, he applies it to the subject at hand with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

In that case, since the cause for the apprehension of both the universal and the particular is present when they are non-different, it is logical that there occurs through a single cognition the result of their apprehension, which is the negation [of non-apprehension]; it is not logical that there be an absence of the result called the apprehension of both, which follows as a general rule. For if the two are one, whatever cause there is for the apprehension of one is the very same as that for the other; thus, when they are one, it cannot be said that the cause for the apprehension of either one is absent.

Therefore, the meaning is that having set aside the general absence of the realization of both, there must exist the realization of both as an exception. Now, if one argues that since there is also a distinction, the absence of oneness means there is no cause for the fruit of realizing either one; and thus, due to the absence of that cause, the general absence of the fruit of realizing both is asserted—even so, there still exists a cause for the realization of both, because of their oneness, since even one of them is present. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In that case."

The meaning is that when there is oneness due to the cause for the realization of both, there is the existence of the fruit which is the realization of both. Why? He says: "of that" (*tasya*); the meaning is "because of the causal nature of that," i.e., because of its being the cause. An objection is raised: "But since those two are distinct, there is also the absence of the cause for the realization of either one; therefore, why should the aforementioned fruit not exist? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But not... (*na tu*). It is not the case that the absence of the cause is the cause for the prior non-existence of the fruit, because a causal relationship between two absences is never observed. This is the sense.

To the question, "How then could this be so?", he says: "By its own nature" (*svabhāva*). For the prior non-existence of the effect is established by its very nature as the general rule; the meaning is that it does not depend upon a cause. He states the exception to that: "Of that" (*tasya*). To the question, "What follows from that?", he says: "And that" (*sa ca*). And because the universal and the particular are one, that [prior non-existence] serves as the cause for the apprehension of both. Therefore, since the other is also cognized by a single cognition, it is established that there is no need for another cognition due to their non-difference—the meaning is that [the distinction between them is untenable].

Although there is no reason for their difference, nevertheless, there is [a reason] for their non-difference; this is the meaning of the word "tāvat" (for now). Now, one might object: "But difference does not exist at all; therefore, due to the absence of a cause, why would there not be an absence of the effect? To this he says: "asattvam" (non-existence). The meaning is that non-existence cannot be a cause. The word "iti" marks the end [of the section]. He states another objection against the position that a single entity consists of three aspects: "api ca" (furthermore). It is not merely the universal (*sāmānya*) that is the essence—that is, the true nature—of a thing that possesses two aspects.

It is not merely a particularity, for that would entail the consequence of two distinct entities; rather, the word is manifold, consisting of both the universal and the particular. That is the nature (*ātman*) or essential form (*svarūpa*) of the object. Since such a thing does not persist (*anvaya*) or follow through (*anugama*) into another such entity, the meaning is that by asserting "one entity is dual-natured," one has actually resorted to a doctrine of absolute difference under a different terminology. This is explained by taking the ablative *śabdāntarāt* as expressing either the agent of the suffix *-lyap* or the causal sense (*hetau*) expressed by the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Now, one might object: "Since the universal aspect persists across other instances, there is no consequence of falling into a doctrine of absolute difference. Anticipating this, he says: "of the persisting entity" (*anugantuḥ*).

In the view that a single entity possesses a dual nature, a mere universal that persists through individuals cannot be the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the real thing. Consequently, since this [universal] is a non-entity (*avastu*) consisting of a conceptualized form, the persistence of the real thing does not follow from the persistence of that [universal]; thus, the consequence of absolute difference (*bheda*) follows. To this, the opponent objects: "It might be so" (*syāt*). The sense of the objection is: even if it is not a real entity, we do not deny that the universal is a constituent part (*aṃśa*) of the real thing; otherwise, the very dual nature of the entity would not exist. Therefore, it is not an object of conceptual construction, and thus there is no consequence of falling into the doctrine of difference.

"But if that is not accepted, then even the conception of the seedless would not be possible," he says—"otherwise. The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), however, asks—"What [is it]? [The opponent replies: "The consequence of duality. This means that there would be two entities: the universal and the particular. Nor is a part (*aṃśa*) itself an entity distinct from the entity, as he says—"nor is it... Now, if it is said that the part is neither the entity itself nor something other than the entity, but is itself an entity, then by process of elimination, it must be merely an object of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

The meaning is that since it is neither different nor non-different from the entity, it is therefore inexpressible (anirvācya). Here, the opponent raises an objection with the word "nanu": the part is neither absolutely different from the whole, nor is it non-different. He states the reason for this with the phrase "ubhayathā" (in both ways): even if there were difference, it would not be a part, just as a cloth is not a part of a jar; nor [would it be a part] if there were non-difference, just as a jar is not a part of a jar. Therefore, the meaning is that the part is neither different from the whole, nor is it non-different.

One might object: "Since it cannot be defined as either real or unreal (*tattvātattvābhyām anirvācyatvāt*), it must then be a non-entity (*avastu*. Anticipating this, he says: "Nor [is it a non-entity]. "Precisely for that reason" means: precisely because it is a part (*aṃśatvāt*). For a non-entity is never observed to have parts; indeed, a non-entity such as a sky-flower does not become a part of anything—this is the meaning. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In that case. "Because it is non-different from that" intends to express non-distinction (*abheda*). He refutes this, saying: "This is not so."

The meaning is this: if it is argued that the persistence of a thing is due to the persistence of its generic aspect (*sāmānyāṃśa*) in other particulars (*viśeṣa*), then why would there not also be non-persistence due to the non-persistence of its particular aspects? One might object: "But since there is indeed persistence of the thing through its generic aspect, the consequence of an absolute doctrine of difference does not follow. Anticipating this, he states the non-persistence of the thing with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). Since a thing consists of both a generic and a particular aspect, if one particular aspect is absent in other locations, the thing itself is absent in them; therefore, even if the generic aspect persists, [the thing does not]. (p. 175)

The meaning is "the following of the object. He establishes this very point with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*). "Aggregation" (*samāhāra*) means a collection (*samuccaya*). The rest is easy to understand. Having thus led to the consequence of a doctrine of difference (*bheda-vāda*) due to the following of the specific aspects (*viśeṣāṃśa*), he now leads to the consequence of a doctrine of non-duality (*advaita-vāda*) by accepting the following of the general aspect (*sāmānyāṃśa*): "Or if... (*yadi vā*). Since that [general aspect] is not distinct from the object, when the following of the object is accepted through the following of the general aspect, the consequence of non-dualism would follow.

For instance: a cow is first of all a cow by itself; yet, because it conforms to the common factors of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth shared with a horse, it would also conform to the entity that is a horse, and thus the cow would also be a horse. Consequently, the cow would be both a cow and a horse; likewise, the horse would also be both a horse and a cow. Thus, the cow would possess both cowness (*gotva*) and horseness (*aśvatva*), and the horse would also possess both horseness and cowness. This state of being one thing is the state of being another; through these two, there is no difference between the cow and the horse. The same applies to other entities as well. Therefore, the meaning is that non-duality (*advaita*) has been stated by means of a different mode of expression.

The phrase "by means of its existence and the existence of something other than it" (*tadbhāvānyabhāvābhyām*) is an explanation of the term "by way of its being that or not being that" (*tadatattvataḥ*). To this extent, the word "that" (*tat*) is connected individually with each of the two terms; thus it is said that the suffix *tasi* follows a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyantāt*). Its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is as follows: "that" (*tat*) and "not-that" (*atat*) together form "that-and-not-that" (*tadatadī*); the state of being that and not-that is "the state of being that or not-that" (*tadatattvam*); [the suffix indicates] "from that" (*tataḥ*). Now, it is true that non-duality (*advaita*) exists; however, you yourself have stated that there is non-difference by means of the existence of that and the existence of something other than it. Consequently, if the cow is the absence of the horse, then duality (*dvaita*) also exists.

With the intention that "therefore everything consists of both duality and non-duality, and that is precisely what we accept," [the opponent] objects with the word "True. The proponent, however, says: "This is not so. We have stated that there is no otherness for the sake of instructing others, having in mind an otherness established by worldly convention. But in reality, if there were no difference between a cow and a horse, how could there be otherness? For if that were so, even duality would not exist; this is the meaning. [The opponent objects: "But if there were no difference between a cow and a horse, their designation as distinct—as 'cow and horse'—would not occur."

Anticipating the objection that "therefore, difference also exists," he says: "And the cow... The distinction in designations is merely stated for the sake of communicating with others, as it is already established in common worldly usage; however, the meaning is that there is no underlying cause for such [designation] based on the cow and horse being individually defined as "cow-ness" or "horse-ness. One might object: "Even if there is non-difference due to the persistence of the generic aspect, nevertheless, because the specific aspect is excluded, difference also exists; therefore, the world would consist of both duality and non-duality, and that is precisely what we desire. To this, he raises the challenge: "But surely... (nanv iti).

The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*), however, analyzes this in order to refute it, beginning with "Now" (*atha*). An object possesses both forms; therefore, because it is excluded from that which is distinct from it, there is no persistence (*anugama*) in another particular. He illustrates this: "The entity 'horse' is not the entity 'cow'. Now, if there were persistence of an object in another object, he illustrates that: "The horse also becomes a cow. Regarding the first case [on p. 176]:

P. 67-19. He states the fault in that position: "In that regard" (*tatra*). Among those two positions, first, regarding the position that an entity does not follow through into another entity: because an entity does not follow through into another entity, the universal aspect—which would have to follow through—is itself a non-entity; for, according to the logic previously stated, it falls within the domain of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Thus, it results in the consequence of the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*), as was stated in the passage "because of its non-inherence" (*tasyānanvayataḥ*).

Now, even though there is exclusion based on specific differences (*viśeṣavyāvṛtti*), that entity is nevertheless inherent (*anugata*) in other entities; he illustrates this with the words "it exists" (*bhavati*). The meaning is: in that case, there would be no difference at all between a cow and a horse; how then could their distinctness be established? If it is thought: "The horse is the entity 'cow' by way of its nature as a divine being (*divyatva*) and so forth, yet it is not inherent [as a cow] by way of its specific form; therefore, there is no consequence of either absolute difference or non-difference"; [we reply: by saying "the horse becomes a cow," one who asserts that the horse possesses the nature of a cow has already stated its inherence [in universals] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*).

By the statement “a cow is indeed a cow,” it is stated that a cow does not follow after (is not present in) a horse by way of its own form as a cow. But how is it that a cow is excluded from horses and the like by way of its own form as a cow? To this he says: “It indeed exists. If, in the case of a horse being a cow, the cow’s own specific nature—the cow-form—did not exist [in the horse], then it would not be excluded from the horse; but since it indeed exists [in the cow], and since that thing which is the cow-nature lacks its own essential form (*svarūpa*) in that [horse], then, because it is excluded by its own essential form, its distinctness (*anyatva*) is established.

Having raised the opponent’s view with the words “If it is thought,” etc., he refutes it by means of an alternative analysis, beginning with “Now” (*atha*). Here, “now” (*atha*) is used in the sense of an objection; or rather, the opponent must state in what manner that entity—which is by its own nature excluded from horses and so forth—is constituted. Does the cow exist only as the form of a cow, or does it not also exist [as another]? This is what is being asked: Is the cow only the unique form of a cow, or is it also the form of a horse? If the cow is only the form of a cow, then the horse too is only the form of a horse; thus, there is the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*).

Now, even though the cow has the form of the horse, and likewise the cow has the form of both the cow and the horse, and even the horse has the form of both the cow and the horse—this is the doctrine of non-difference (*abheda-vāda*). Anticipating the objection that "even if such non-difference exists, we shall establish the reality of the cow as distinct from the horse by means of some other specific property; therefore, difference (*bheda*) also exists," he briefly explains the present context of the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda-vāda*) with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*).

Having thus refuted the view that a single entity consists of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), he extends that same refutation to the view that a single entity consists of substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*) by means of the word "substance" (*dravya*). He explains the verse with the words "those who also" (*ye 'pi*): jars and the like are the particulars of clay, while necklaces and the like are the particulars of gold. Those which arise successively are called "modes" (*paryāya*). By the term "perishing" (*apāyin*), he indicates their difference from the persisting substance such as clay. By the term "non-distinct" (*avyatireka*), he indicates non-difference; those things for which there is no distinction (*vyatireka*) are so described.
It is said that they are both different and non-different. He establishes this very point with the words "And not... If the necklaces and so forth [p.

[If they were identical,] they would be nothing but the substance gold; consequently, upon their destruction, the gold itself would perish. Therefore, when the *rucaka* (necklace) is destroyed, the *vardhamāna* (bracelet) would not persist; yet this is not the case, for there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) even in that instance. Nor are they distinct from the substance, because no difference is perceived, as it is the very substance that is perceived in the form of the *rucaka* and so forth. Thus, since the substance and its modes (*paryāya*) are neither different nor non-different, a single entity consists of both; it is neither substance alone nor mode alone.

For if the object were merely substance (*dravyamātra*), since there would be no [existence] of the necklace (*rucaka*) and so forth, joy and grief would not occur for one desiring it upon its production or destruction. And if the object were merely a mode (*paryāyamātra*), then because gold itself would undergo production and destruction, neutrality (*madhyasthatā*) would not exist. However, when the object consists of both [substance and modes], joy and the rest are indeed possible.

Therefore, for those who maintain that a single entity consists of two natures—namely, those for whom the object (*artha*) or entity (*vastu*) is composed of substance and mode (*dravyaparyāya*), i.e., those for whom the object is of the nature of substance and mode—their doctrine is also refuted by this very same method of rejecting the consequence of an absolute doctrine of difference and non-difference. He elaborates on this very point: "For instance" (*tathāhi*). For that which is stable is called "substance" (*dravya*); if, because of the non-difference of the golden parts within the two objects—the necklace (*rucaka*) and the *vardhamānaka* vessel—non-difference is asserted, then there would be only one single entity.

And since that [entity] is impermanent and non-abiding, the doctrine would be that the world is merely a substance (*dravyamātra*). Now, if it is argued that because an object possesses both forms—as in the case of gold and a golden ornament—the object itself is excluded when the ornament is excluded from the *vardhamānaka* (a specific type of golden vessel), yet the mere portion that is gold persists even in the *vardhamānaka*, and therefore the object does not persist through that persistence because that [gold-portion] alone is not a real entity (*avastu*) according to you; [This argument is addressed as follows:]

Consequently, the doctrine that the world is merely a succession of modes (*paryāya*) would follow; for it is said that mutually exclusive modes are [transient], whereas substance (*dravya*) is said to be persisting. And there is no persisting entity whatsoever in mere modes, because they are subject to arising and destruction. As for the conceptualization that the mere gold-element persists even when the *rucaka* (necklace) is destroyed and becomes a *vardhamānaka* (a type of vessel), that is merely a conceptual construction; for the real entity is manifold, consisting of both substance and mode.

The meaning is that even a mere portion of gold does not possess such a nature. On this very point, he states another objection: "Moreover" (*api ca*). If there were a difference between the substance (*dravya*) and its modes (*paryāya*), then because the substance would remain constant while the two modes undergo destruction and origination, the established distinction between neutrality, sorrow, and joy for those seeking them would be possible. However, if there were no difference, then that very same thing would persist, that very same thing would be born, and that very same thing would perish; thus, persistence, birth, and destruction would all coexist in one and the same locus.

Furthermore, for one who seeks the substance (*dravya*), there would be neutrality because the substance remains constant; yet this would not be the case, because since the destruction and arising of the *rucaka* (necklace) and *vardhamānaka* (earring) are non-different from it, the substance itself would undergo destruction upon their destruction, and there would be no persisting substance during their arising. For this very reason, joy and sorrow would also occur simultaneously. However, if the substance were to remain steadfast, then neutrality alone would prevail.

It might be so; however, when [an object] arises and perishes due to non-difference [from the substance], then it follows that the triad of sorrow and the rest would also occur, which is an untenable consequence. Likewise, even upon the destruction of a *vardhamānaka* (a type of golden vessel), the triad of sorrow and the rest would occur for one who desires it; and likewise, even upon the production of a *rucaka* (a necklace), the triad would occur for one who desires it. Now, if it is argued that there is both difference between the substance and its modes (*paryāya*) and mutual difference among the modes themselves, and therefore the aforementioned faults such as doubt and infinite regress do not apply—

In that case, why should the previously mentioned defect not apply to those who maintain both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), since for them non-difference also exists? Now, suppose it is true that non-difference exists, but it is not absolute; therefore, the defect of the confusion of grief and so forth, which depends upon that [non-difference], does not occur. [The opponent objects: "In that case, since difference also is not absolute, the distinction (*vyavasthā*) regarding grief and so forth, which depends upon that [difference], would not exist. To this he says: "Now" (*atha*). Furthermore, that which is called a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) is that which does not exist elsewhere.

And for one who maintains the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda), if there were anything absolute anywhere, then "absoluteness" could be predicated as a qualification regarding non-difference; however, for one who desires non-absolutism in all cases, nothing whatsoever is absolute. Therefore, since nothing at all is absolute, that which is stated as a qualification regarding non-difference—namely, the non-confusion of grief and so forth—is not established. Thus he says: "But not... [na ca...]. Now, one might object: even if the doctrine of non-absolutism applies everywhere, the fault of confusion does not arise here either. Anticipating this, he refutes the doctrine of non-absolutism itself by saying: "If that were so... [tathā ca...].

The phrase "and likewise" (*tathā ca*) introduces the presentation of a refutation. He states that if all things were non-unique (*anekānta*) in every respect, then the world would be devoid of both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*). The word *hi* signifies "alas" (*kaṣṭa*). The expression "this is not so" (*asāvatathaiva*) means that there is no proof for what is intended. He explains the verse differently: "Now" (*atha*)—for me, who maintains the doctrine of non-uniqueness in all cases, even joy and the like both exist and do not exist.

Therefore, as for the difficulty previously mentioned—that pleasure, indifference, and sorrow might either exist or not exist—it is precisely what we desire; thus, the suspicion that "this is not difficult for me" is addressed by the words "not absolute. The rest is easy to understand. Having thus refuted the two positions—that the universal and the particular are two distinct entities, or that a single entity is of a dual nature—the two remaining positions are that "the particulars are real and the conceptualization of non-difference arising from them is an error," or [the reverse]. To determine between these, he says: "In that case... [tatreti].

The meaning is: "of those two alternatives. The meaning of the verse is stated as follows: Difference indeed depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); therefore, difference cannot be grasped by having the apprehension of difference as its prerequisite, because that would involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). Nor can that which is not itself apprehended serve as the material cause for the conceptualization of non-difference; for two cows, such as a *śābaleya* and a *bāhuleya*, do not give rise to the conceptualization of their non-difference as "this is a cow, this is a cow" unless their difference has been apprehended. Therefore, an unapprehended difference cannot be the cause for the conceptualization of non-difference. However, the cognition of non-difference does not depend upon non-difference, nor does it depend upon difference, for that would entail the loss of its own nature (*svarūpahāna*).

Because it follows from this context: therefore, since it is capable of being known, that which is known in its mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) ought to be the material cause for the conceptualization of difference. And it is observed that a single entity serves as the material cause for the conceptualization of difference; thus he says, "Just as... (P. 70-16). The meaning is: just as a single composite whole (*avayavin*) is the cause for the conceptualization of its parts. Now, one might object: since a composite whole distinct from its parts is impossible, the conceptualization of the whole must have the parts as its material cause, and not the conceptualization of the parts having the whole as their material cause.

Anticipating the objection that "here too, the conceptualization of non-difference is based upon difference," he says: "Not there. Here, the word "difference" (*bheda*) refers to the distinct parts (*avayava*), while the word "non-difference" (*abheda*) refers to the undivided whole (*avayavin*). He states the reason: "For difference... Just as the whole (*avayavin*) such as a jar is conceptual and unreal, so too the [features] such as the conch-shaped neck would be unreal because they are wholes relative to their own parts. Therefore, difference resides only in partless atoms (*paramāṇu*).

The meaning is: for this very reason, they would be distinct from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Nor can those [atoms] themselves be the basis for the conceptual construction (*kalpanopādāna*), because since they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it is impossible for them to serve as the basis for a conceptual construction. It has already been stated that a single cognition does not depend upon difference for its arising; regarding that, he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). "Synthesis" (*anusaṃdhāna*) refers to the act of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

And that [cognition] consists of the synthesis of the prior and the subsequent in the form "this is that," occurring only when there is a difference of place and time, and not otherwise; for in the absence of a difference of place and time, since the relation of prior and subsequent would not exist, what could be synthesized as non-different with what prior? Therefore, even the cognition of non-difference is dependent on a difference of place and time, and thus it suffers from the same defect as the cognition of difference—this is the meaning. To this, he states the reply: "It has been refuted"; the meaning is that this has already been refuted in the argument that an object cannot be a single entity if its place and time are not non-different.

He recalls what was already stated with the word "not. He says "it would be useless" because, in the absence of a single object, the act of synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) would be purposeless. For synthesis would be meaningful only if it were to establish the non-difference of a single object whose difference might be suspected due to differences in place and so forth; but in the absence of a single [object], that [synthesis] would indeed be meaningless—this is the meaning. Furthermore, since it is established for all people, it is logical that difference is subsumed under non-difference, and not the reverse; thus he says "moreover."

The meaning is as follows: through the first-occurring non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) arising from conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), the mere object (*vastumātra*) is perceived as undivided and unitary, grasped while devoid of all conceptual constructions such as difference; subsequently, conceptual distinctions such as "this is a cow" or "this is white" arise—a fact established for all people. Therefore, it is logical that the conceptualization of difference has non-difference as its substrate. He explains the second half of the verse as a response to an objection, beginning with the word "syāt": "grasping a qualified form" means grasping a differentiated form.

The phrase "just as in the case of conceptual cognition" (*vikalpabuddhau*) is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the passage beginning with "But he who... (*yas tu...*), its meaning is as follows: we do not say that "difference appears in perception and yet is not perceived," which would constitute a contradiction. Rather, perception clearly manifests the jar as excluded from all other things, such as cloth, which are different from the jar's own nature. Therefore, for one who says there is no contradiction, the answer has already been stated by the verse beginning with "They say it is an affirmer" (*āhur vidhātṛ*). This is the sense.
