Furthermore, if it has been stated that the universal and the particular cannot exist as two distinct entities, and that one thing cannot possess a dual nature, then since one of the two must be considered false, it is more appropriate to regard the cognition of difference (*bhedajñāna*) itself as false, rather than the cognition of non-difference (*abhedajñāna*). Thus he says: "Furthermore" (*kiṃca*). In illusions such as "this is silver," the cognition that apprehends only the undifferentiated object in its general aspect—as "this"—is well-established and non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*).

Therefore, subsequently, even at the time of sublation, because the "this" aspect (the *idamaṃśa*) appears in the cognition "this is a piece of mother-of-pearl," whereas in the case of the differences—the specific particulars such as silver—it is observed that the cognition lacks stability and is erroneous. And the postulation of error applies only to that which is observed to be erroneous, because its capacity for error has been established; in the other case, regarding the aspect of the mere object (*vastumātra*), that [postulation] would be more cumbersome as it would have to be inferred. Thus, the sense is that here too, it is only the cognition of difference that is false, not the cognition of non-difference.

It was stated [above] that "this applies even to sensory cognitions"; in order to state the counter-argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) from which that statement is to be distinguished, he begins with the words "it might be" (*syāt*). The word "also" (*api*) should be understood as meaning "also because of conformity" (*anuvidhāyitvāt*). Here, the example of two moons and so forth is given. Furthermore, by one who asserts that "all entities are excluded," it must be stated whether those entities are of the nature of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) or have mutual non-existence as their qualifier, since mutual non-existence is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "excluded. He says "mutual... (*anyonya...*) because neither of those two possibilities is tenable.

In that case, when this limiting adjunct (upādhi) of mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) is accepted as a qualifier, the meaning is that while entities may be perceived in the form of difference, they would not be different by their own nature (svarūpataḥ). Having stated "mutual," etc., one might suspect that [difference] is produced by that [adjunct]; therefore he says, "in one," etc. If one positive entity were independent of another, then another positive entity could be established; but when everything is of the nature of non-existence, then in the absence of one, the other—which is of the nature of its non-existence—could not exist.

The meaning is that if that [otherness] were absent, this [the object] would not exist; thus, there would be a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). To illustrate the cognition of something that does not possess that nature, one should cite the example of a gem placed nearby. Here, the opponent objects with "But surely" (*nanu*). By "establishment of the object," he means that the very nature of the thing itself is its mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and there is no other such thing. The proponent, however, replies: "No. [p. 181]

Furthermore, other faces arise in proximity to a face, and not otherwise; therefore, the face itself is a cause. And it is fitting that the effect conforms to its cause. In that case, it would be logical for those [reflected faces] to possess exactly the same dimensions as the original; yet this is not so, because they are perceived to be smaller in a sword and similar objects. However, if they are distinct from ignorance (*avidyā*), then the impossibility of their being small is not a fault. This is merely an illustration; the other faults have already been stated previously.

The formal argument for that purpose is as follows: "This manifold diversity has non-difference as its material cause" is the property to be proven (the *sādhya*), because it possesses the nature of difference (*bhedatva*), just like the diversity of faces in jewels, swords, and so forth. Now, the opponent also counters by means of inference alone: "It might be so. This is his inference: "Non-difference is the subject (*dharmin*); 'it has difference as its material cause' is the property to be proven, because it possesses the nature of difference, just as the non-difference denoted by the word 'forest' has the diversity of trees as its material cause. He refutes this, saying: "No."

If every distinction whatsoever were false because it has distinction as its material cause (*upādāna*), then even a single atom would not exist; its non-distinction (*abheda*) too would have distinction as its material cause, and likewise for each part and sub-part of that, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, nothing at all would be a unity. Therefore, there is no such thing as non-distinction consisting of a collection of individual atoms.

How could there be the conceptualization of non-difference (*abheda-kalpanā*) regarding [the question] "from where does the forest come"? Now, if one were to go even further and maintain that some single reality exists which is devoid of being the material cause of non-difference, then for that very reason the logical mark (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of that" (*tadabhāvataḥ*): the meaning is due to the absence of difference (*bheda*) in the form of gross objects such as trees, which consist of a collection of individual atoms. He states another inference (*anumāna*) to prove that difference is false (*mithyātva*), beginning with "furthermore" (*api ca*).

The subject (*dharmī*) is "difference" (*bheda*), and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is "being false" (*mṛṣā*). This is because [each instance of difference] is followed by a non-differentiation (*abheda*) through such terms as "this," "that," "object" (*artha*), "entity" (*vastu*), and "existent" (*sat*) respectively; the meaning is that whatever is a particular difference is false, just as the various differences in the moon's reflections on waves are each false because they are permeated by the non-difference expressed as "the moon. However, the difference between trees—though permeated by the non-difference expressed as "a forest"—is not false; therefore, the word "respectively" (*pratyekam*) is used so that there may be no fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to that case.

Furthermore, even on the grounds of parsimony of conceptualization (*kalpanālāghava*), it is appropriate to postulate a distinction based on the assumption of non-difference, rather than the reverse; thus he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*). The word "of distinct things" (*bhinnānām*) is not [the subject]; rather, the word "magnificence" (*mahimā*) must be supplied and "to be postulated" (*kalpya*) is to be understood as the predicate. Now, one might object: "You must postulate the capacity for a single entity to appear as manifold, whereas I do not; therefore, the parsimony belongs to me alone. Anticipating this, he replies: "The postulation of capacity is equal for both of us. Nevertheless, you must postulate many capacities for many entities, whereas I postulate only a pre-eminent capacity for a single entity. (p. 182)

P. 72-25. He begins to demonstrate the parsimony of conceptualization (*kalpanālāghava*) regarding the similar class (*sapakṣa*) with the words "This... [referring to *idam*]. For the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), how can there be the appearance of non-difference (*abhedāvabhāsa*) as "cow, cow" among individuals that are absolutely distinct? Indeed, no cognition occurs without a cause. Nor is difference itself the cause of the cognition of non-difference by its very nature; for when it is said, "Bring the cow," one brings whichever individual [cow] [is intended], and when it is said again, one brings that very universal (*sāmānya*), and not just any individual such as a horse.

Thus, if there is absolute difference [between individuals], how can there be a recurring appearance and linguistic usage? If it is argued that the recurring appearance and usage arise from the similarity (*sādṛśya*) among individual cows, that is incorrect; for similarity occurs through the persistence of common parts (*avayava-sāmānya*), and such [common parts] do not exist for one who maintains the doctrine of absolute difference. Furthermore, if it is claimed that the mutual exclusion (*anyonya-vyāvṛtti*) among individual cows is not perceived, yet their distinction from individuals such as horses is perceived;

Therefore, although individual cows are distinct, there occurs the manifestation and linguistic usage of a recurring [universal]; yet, even though that [recurring nature] is no different [in other cases], such [usage] is not possible regarding individual horses and the like. Furthermore, it is said that although individual cows do indeed possess differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*), its non-apprehension occurs due to subtlety, like the color of coral hidden by molasses; but that is incorrect, because for you, what is called "differentiation" is simply the very nature (*svabhāva*) of entities and not distinct from them. In that case, if that [differentiation] were not apprehended, their own natures would likewise not be apprehended.

The point is that otherwise, it would not possess that very nature. Now, suppose it is argued that perception is non-determinative by virtue of being indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*), whereas determinate (*savikalpaka*) cognition is determinative; and since the latter is not perception, there is a difference in the essential nature between determinate cognition and perception. Therefore, although the mutual exclusion (*anyonya-vyāvṛtti*) inherent in the nature of individual cows is indeed perceived when those individuals are perceived, nevertheless, because there is no determination of it, the appearance and linguistic usage of "continuity" (*anuvṛtti*) occur. This is incorrect.

If there were no certainty regarding exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) would be based solely on the universal "cow" (*gosāmānya*), and not on the exclusion from other particulars; yet such [convention] is observed. For instance, when it is said, "Bring the black-eyed cow," one brings precisely that cow which is excluded from other cows; and this would not be possible if there were no certainty regarding that exclusion. Therefore, this position as well is not tenable. Now, suppose one individual cow performs a certain purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by milking and so forth, and another [individual] performs that very same [action].

If it is argued that—just as one [cow] is excluded from horses and other things that do not perform that function, so too is another—and thus, because the exclusion from non-performers of that function is identical, there occurs a linguistic usage characterized by the appearance of a single form even among cow-individuals that are absolutely distinct; that too is not tenable. For the purposeful action (arthakriyā) performed by one cow-individual is not the same as that performed by another, nor is it of the same kind, since they do not admit a universal (jāti). Therefore, cow-individuals do not possess the property of performing a single purposeful action.

And therefore, just as there is the exclusion of one individual cow—which does not perform the causal function of that [other object]—from that other object, so too is there exclusion from another individual cow; since that [other cow] is also [excluded] from it, how is the exclusion of what does not perform that function the same? Furthermore, if exclusion is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity, [p.

If there is a difference between entities, how can that [cognition] be identical? If, on the other hand, it lacks an intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), then, due to the absence of any relation such as identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth, how could it belong to those entities? Consequently, from that perspective as well, there would be only one single reality, not difference. Now, if it is argued that the appearance of a single form among distinct individuals is based on beginningless latent impressions (*anādivāsanā*), and that the corresponding linguistic usage arises from this, without any need to depend upon any particularity residing in the individuals themselves—that too is incorrect.

For if one did not rely upon individual particulars (*vyaktiviśeṣa*), there would be no such restriction that the uniform appearance of "cow" occurs only with respect to cow-individuals and not with respect to horse-individuals; yet such a restriction does exist. Therefore, this appearance of non-difference is not based solely on mental impressions (*vāsanā*). Nor can it be argued that, due to the diversity of impressions, only certain impressions produce the appearance of non-difference in certain individuals and not all [impressions do so].

For that [cognition], being of the nature of being permeated by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) born from previous experiences, would produce the appearance of non-difference only among individuals previously experienced, not among those that are different. If it is argued that it produces this appearance even there [among different things] due to similarity; no, for that [notion of similarity] has already been refuted. Therefore, certain individuals must be postulated as possessing a superior capacity (*sāmarthyātiśaya*), such that they are by their very nature capable of producing the appearance of non-difference for someone, while all [individuals] are not so for everyone.

It is logical that specific capacities (sāmarthyātiśaya) serve as the causes for the manifestation of difference among distinct individuals; however, these [other capacities] are said to be contrary to their own nature, as they are the causes for the manifestation of non-difference. In that case, one would have to postulate infinite entities and infinite specific capacities for them, which results in a heavy conceptual burden (kalpanā-gaurava). For me, however, only a single reality needs to be postulated, which results in a lightness of conceptualization (kalpanā-lāghava). Therefore, let there be the majesty of the One alone, such that it appears as many.

But they are not distinct; the meaning is that they appear as non-distinct. It is logical for worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) to accord with reality; if it is asked how there can be a practice of distinction such as "pot" and "cloth" regarding that non-different reality, he says: "Distinction... For practice follows appearance, not the actual state of things, as is seen in the case of fleeing from the appearance of a snake in a rope. And distinction does indeed appear. Therefore, practices of distinction will be established in accordance with that appearance.

For example, among those who maintain the theory of difference (*bhedavādin*), there is the non-different usage of the term "cow" with respect to individual cows that are distinct. This is not only the case for them; it is also so for those who maintain the existence of a relation called *samavāya* (inherence) between the universal (*jāti*) and the individuals, which they hold to be absolutely distinct. Since, according to the followers of Kaṇāda (*Kaṇabhujas*), the universal is an entity separate from the individuals, there is no usage based on the manifestation of difference as it actually exists—such as "Bring the individual possessing cowness"—but rather, the usage of the general term with respect to particulars occurs only through the manifestation of non-difference, as in "Bring the cow."

Likewise, even for those Bhāṭṭas who assert that the universal is not a distinct entity from the individuals, the object is still dual-natured. And there is no persistence of such a word in another object; rather, that which does persist is merely the generic aspect, and that is a single non-entity. Consequently, [p.

This common usage in the form of a recurring cognition, such as “this is a cow, that is a cow,” is exactly as it appears and not according to the actual state of things; this has been demonstrated in the passage beginning with “because of its lack of continuity” (*tasyānanvayataḥ*). The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the logical exposition belonging to the Section on Reasoning (*tarkakāṇḍa*). He summarizes the point just mentioned in a verse, beginning with *yathā*. “The outsiders” (*bāhyāḥ*) refers to those who maintain the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavādinaḥ*), namely, those proponents who stand outside the discernment of Vedānta. The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the text of the Section on Reasoning. Thus ends the commentary on the Section on Reasoning in the *Brahmasiddhi*, composed by Śaṅkhapāṇi.

**The Section on Injunction (Niyogakāṇḍa)** Now he begins another section with the word "evam" (thus). The mention of what has been discussed and what is about to be discussed is for the purpose of demonstrating the connection between the two sections. Once it is established—by refuting the view that they have a figurative meaning—that the Upaniṣads possess a primary meaning, the following inquiry arises: what is that primary meaning? Is it the nature of the Self (*svarūpa*) or an action to be performed (*kārya*)? It does not arise otherwise. For the authority of the Veda lies only in an action to be performed; this is established by way of a general principle. (P. 74.8)

The intention is that even the Upaniṣads, which are included within the Vedas, possess authority regarding their purpose as something to be accomplished (*kārya*). He establishes the proposed point by means of its being accepted by the sages, saying "thus" (*evam*). He explains that [point] with the words "injunction" (*codanā*). Since the mantras, arthavādas, and Upaniṣads form a single syntactical unit with the injunctions and do not constitute a separate Veda, the entire Veda consists solely of injunctions. Therefore, the meaning of that [Veda] alone is the meaning of the Veda; there is no other whatsoever. Now, it might be objected: by this, it has only been stated that the meaning of the Veda is such that it is based on the authority of injunctions.

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And [it is] *codanā*. For *codanā* is an impelling statement; yet it does not impel like the wind. Rather, by making known the object (*artha*) which serves as the cause for activity, it prompts action. The cause of activity is its own effect (the task to be accomplished). To illustrate: no one engages in action without first apprehending that even a desired means is "this is my task to be accomplished" (*mamedaṃ kāryam*). Therefore, the meaning is that the Veda is the authoritative source (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object as a task to be accomplished (*kārya*). But surely this may be so in other cases; [however, it is not so in the case of eternal things].

Anticipating the objection—"But what injunction of action (*kāryavidhi*) is there in the Vedāntas, wherein their authority [might reside]?"—he says: "Of the Vedāntas... The authority [of the Vedāntas] consists in the necessity of realization (*pratipatti-kartavyatā*), expressed as "The Self is to be realized. For those who follow them, their function is to bring about an understanding by way of the necessity of realizing that established nature of the Self (*siddharūpātmatattva*) which is connected with and inherent in that necessity of realization; they do not [function] independently. Therefore, the meaning is that even these [Vedāntas] are indeed grounded in the accomplishment of an action (*kāryaniṣṭhā*).

This is what is meant: the authority of the Vedāntas consists in their providing the nature of the Self that is to be realized, as required by the injunction regarding the duty of self-realization. He confirms this very point with the words of the Commentary: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). Raising the objection—"If the Veda is authoritative only with respect to what is to be done (*kārya*), how then do the meanings of the Mantras, along with the Upaniṣads, declare established facts (*siddha-artha*)?"—he states: "For the injunction... (*codanā hi*), and so forth. The meaning is this: since the Mantras and others form a single syntactical unit with the injunction, there is only one such injunction; and that [injunction] pertains to what is to be done (*kārya*).

Because it leads [the mind] toward that goal through total devotion, it expresses the meaning of the elements and so forth only partially, and not as something established in its own right. Therefore, for those who maintain that even the Upaniṣads are solely concerned with the duty of realization (*pratipatti-kartavyatā*) and not concerned with an already established fact (*siddhārtha*), it is replied: "The three... The knowledge of the Self that arises from the word known as the Vedānta is not enjoined by an injunction such as "the Self is to be realized."

The sense is this: since for one who has studied the Veda, the knowledge of that [Brahman] arises from the very power of the words themselves, just like the understanding of ritual action (*karman*), what need is there for an injunction (*vidhi*) in that regard? Now, one might object: "Why is it said here that verbal knowledge alone—not knowledge born of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is not to be enjoined? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For Brahman... The rest is easy to understand. He provides the analogy "just like the understanding of ritual action" and states the lack of dependence on an injunction therein with the words "in the case of heaven... (*svarga-*) and so forth.

"In the verbal comprehension of the sentence-meaning of 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice,' no other injunction is required, because if that injunction's own sentence-meaning were to require yet another injunction, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor is it the case that this very injunction 'one should sacrifice' is what is required, for that injunction is fixed upon the ritual act (*karman*); the meaning is that by it the act is enjoined, but not the cognition of it. Here, he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*).

Just as the injunction "One's own Veda should be studied" (svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ) is required for the study of sentences such as those concerning the desire for heaven, yet no further injunction is required for the study of that very injunction regarding Vedic study, and thus there is no infinite regress; so too, let there be a requirement for an injunction even for the comprehension of their meaning. However, for the comprehension of the meaning of that injunction, no further injunction is required; therefore, there is no infinite regress—this is the sense. Nor is it the case that there is no injunction for engaging in the knowledge of the Veda's meaning; he says: "And it exists."

He refutes that [position] with the words "It is unequal. He states the inequality: "Even if it has not been set in motion," etc. If the injunction to study, having itself been studied, causes other sentences to be studied, then the study of that [injunction] would likewise depend on another injunction to study, resulting in an infinite regress.

The meaning is that, although a person does not initiate the study of the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) on their own, they proceed to study that injunction and other sentences because it has been studied by another person; therefore, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in that case. Now, one might ask: how can a person be prompted to act by an injunction to study that has been studied by another? For it is a studied sentence that prompts action, not an unstudied one, since that which is not grasped cannot function as a prompter. To this, he says: "By the branch" (*śākhā*).

The meaning is that formal study (*adhyayana*) is not the sole determinant for the performance of a rite, but rather its comprehension (*grahaṇa*); and that comprehension indeed occurs even from mere hearing. For example, even though one has not personally studied a subsidiary statement (*aṅgavākya*) mentioned in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), when it is heard from those who have studied that branch, the integration of that subsidiary element is performed during the ritual applications.

Now, one might object: "How is it that even other persons study the injunction regarding the study of the Veda? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as... (yathā). Thus, it has been stated that there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding the study of sentences such as those concerning the "desirer of heaven" (*svargakāma*). However, regarding the comprehension of their meaning, there can be a dependence on another injunction, namely: "The entire Veda is to be mastered. For that [injunction] too, if its meaning is not understood, it is not capable of impelling one toward the knowledge of the meaning of sentences such as those concerning the "desirer of heaven"; therefore, its meaning also depends upon an injunction.

Nor does that very [injunction] itself impel one toward the understanding of its own meaning, because it is impossible for something whose meaning is not yet understood to be an impeller; for there would be a circularity: activity arises from the understanding of its meaning, and the understanding of its meaning occurs for one who has already engaged in activity. Consequently, regarding the injunction "the entire Veda is to be mastered," another injunction would be required for the understanding of its meaning, and since the same would apply there as well, there would be an infinite regress. Thus, [the opponent] remains silent, saying: "This is an unequal comparison. Furthermore, what was said—that "there is an injunction"—is also incorrect.

Since an injunction (*vidhi*) is that which brings about a previously unknown matter, this [injunction regarding study], however, being for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), is merely a restatement of what is already established by logic; thus he says: "And not... Having provisionally accepted its status as an injunction, he states that there is no need for a separate injunction for the comprehension of the Veda's meaning, such as "The Self is to be realized," by saying: "Now..."

Objection: If the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda is already implied by the injunction for the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*), as expressed by the statement "the entire Veda is to be mastered," then this [injunction regarding the knowledge of meaning] would merely be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already obtained through the injunction for study; how, then, can it be accepted as an injunction (*vidhi*)? Reply: It is said: even that which is implied by an injunction may itself be enjoined, just as the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth are enjoined though implied by the injunction for sacrifice (*yāga-vidhi*). For the implication of a meaning is a delayed process, whereas the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) occurs immediately; thus, prior to the operation of implication, the scripture enjoins that which was not yet established.

But the result is the cessation of the other; for if there were an implication by the sense (*arthākṣepa*), then something else might also be implied, and thus there would be no fault. This has been stated as being "like the injunctions regarding ritual action" (*karmavidhivākya*); explaining that, he applies the verse again with the words "just as" (*yathā*).

If, even when an injunction exists, another injunction is required, then that too would require another, leading to an infinite regress. Therefore, just as in the case of sentences such as "one who desires heaven [should perform sacrifice]," activity toward the comprehension of meaning is established by the general injunction "the entire Veda is to be studied," and thus no other injunction is required for that purpose—neither one contained within the sentence concerning the desire for heaven, because that pertains to ritual action (karma)—so too in the Vedānta texts, since the comprehension of their meaning arises from the power of the sentences themselves, there is the [general injunction]: "The Self is to be realized."

The meaning is that no further injunction need be expected. Now, one might object: "Just as in the case of ritual injunctions (*karma-vidhi*), here too it should simply be stated that [the knowledge of Brahman] is established by a general injunction (*sāmānya-vidhi*); so why was it said, 'by the power of the sentence' (*vākya-sāmarthyāt*)? It is replied: In the Vedāntas, there is one who maintains a specific injunction (*viśeṣa-vidhi*) stating, "The Self is to be realized. This proponent considers that the scope of the general injunction must therefore be something other than that [Self]. It is with this intention that it was stated, "by the power of the sentence," because [for him] the matter is not established by a general injunction.

Furthermore, even if the Upaniṣads were general rules or subordinate details, they would not have established things as their meaning; thus, there is no fault in this statement made by one who does not even desire them to be subordinate to something else. [p. 188] P. 76-3.

For the following reason as well, he says "for this reason" (*itaśca*) that the knowledge of the Self arising from the word is not something enjoined: the fruit of an injunction is the activity that occurs subsequent to the comprehension of what is to be enjoined, and not the understanding of the thing to be enjoined which arises directly from the word itself. Why? Because of mutual dependence (*anyonyasaṃśrayāt*): activity would occur once the meaning of the word is understood, and the understanding of the word's meaning would occur for one who has engaged in activity; thus, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatā*).

However, that realization of reality which arises from the Vedānta texts through the excellence of that comprehension is not something subsequent to the understanding of the word’s meaning; rather, it is that very Self itself. Therefore, the meaning is that the result of the injunction "the Self is to be realized" is not something external. For this reason as well, he states that the knowledge arising from words is not something subject to an injunction—beginning with the words "Moreover" (api ca). Furthermore, once the comprehension of the object has arisen from the word, a person cannot be impelled by the injunction "the Self is to be realized. For one is impelled toward that which is yet to be accomplished (sādhya), not toward that which is already established (siddha).

Now, if the word is indeed non-informative regarding its object, then one should not be prompted toward the knowledge of that [object], because the comprehension of the word’s meaning is impossible even there; for no one is prompted toward an unconnected subject. If it is argued that, once the knowledge of the object has arisen from the word, one is prompted toward the ascertainment (*niścaya*) of it, to this he says: "By the word" (*śabdena*). One is not to be prompted even toward ascertainment; for that too must be either produced by the word or produced by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

First, there can be no application of an injunction toward that certainty regarding an object which arises from a word and its comprehension; for that [certainty] has already been produced by the word itself at the very outset—what, then, would be the use of an injunction there? Alternatively, if it is argued that one is to be impelled by an injunction toward the certainty that arises from another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) regarding what has been understood from the word, then there would be a requirement to seek another means of knowledge. Consequently, the word would not be the cause of certainty in that regard, and this is not an accepted position. This is the meaning.

Now he introduces another alternative view with the word "atha" (now/if). "Upaṣṭhavaḥ" means comprehension. The pointlessness of the literal meaning is the reason for the lack of purport (*atātparya*); and since a lack of purport is also observed [in some cases], there is doubt. He refutes that with the words "tadvārtam" (that is mere talk); that is without substance. Why? Because in both worldly and Vedic usage, the dependence of words upon their meanings is the general rule (*autsargika*), according to the maxim "But the meaning of a sentence is not distinct [from its parts]. However, the primacy of the verbal form itself occurs due to other causes.

For this very reason, the state of having an unintended meaning (*avivakṣitārthatva*) is its exception; as in the case of "He said 'gavi'," where the meaning is determined by the word *iti*, or as in the case of mantras for silent recitation (*japa*), where the purpose of the recitation—which consists of utterance—is restricted to the mere form of the sound being uttered. The point is that no such other cause exists in the Vedāntas.

For this reason as well—that the Vedāntas have a meaningful intended sense—one need not require an injunction such as "the Self is to be realized. To this he says: "dṛṣṭa" (seen). In the study of the injunctive passages concerning ritual action (*karma*), there is a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) enjoined by the rule of Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*); that same [purpose] is not different here in the study of the Vedāntas—it is not distinguished from it, meaning it is identical. Therefore, precisely because they possess a seen purpose through the injunction of Vedic study, just like the ritual passages, the lack of an intended sense in the Vedāntas is already set aside.

The sense is: "What is the use of an injunction for practice, since that [understanding] is its purpose? Otherwise, if the study of the Vedānta did not have a visible purpose, then—by establishing an injunctive meaning through the phrase "the Self is to be realized"—the meaning of the Vedānta would become unintended as an object of instruction. Regarding the "postulation of another fruit": another fruit has been stated either by way of the Viśvajit rule (which implies heaven as the default result), or by way of the Rātrisatra rule, or as the streams of curd and honey and so forth.

Likewise, the construction of a different fruit [for the Vedāntas] based on their study, despite their having no intended meaning, follows from the fact that even there, the realization of the Self is seen to be like the realization of ritual action (*karma*); this is the logical connection (*anvaya*). Now, it might be argued: "It is appropriate to say that ritual injunctions have an intended meaning because they possess purpose through their utility for engaging in or desisting from activity; however, this is not the case for the cognition of an established entity (*siddhārtha*) arising from the Vedāntas, since it would be useless due to its lack of utility for engagement or desistance."

Anticipating the objection that, for this reason, the status of the *svādhyāya* injunction as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) would be distinct [from other injunctions], he says: "And not... Furthermore, the futility (*vaiyarthyam*) is exactly the same even in the case of an injunction for comprehension (*pratipatti-vidhi*). He says: "In the case of comprehension... and so on, stating that this will be explained in the passage beginning with "That is equal in the injunction for comprehension. He explains the half-verse beginning with "It would be... as follows: "It must necessarily be understood thus: that by virtue of the *svādhyāya* injunction having a visible purpose, the Vedāntas also have an intended meaning (*vivakṣitārthatā*)."

Otherwise, the entire Vedānta would lack intended meaning along with the injunctive [passage] stating "the Self is to be realized. Why? Because the intended meaning of these other Vedānta passages is contingent upon the words that enjoin realization; however, for the injunctive [passage] itself, there is no basis or reason for its having an intended meaning.

Therefore, since the injunctive [portion] does not have its literal meaning intended (*avivakṣitārthatva*), the other Vedānta texts cannot have their literal meanings intended by virtue of that [injunctive portion]. Thus, together with the injunctive portion, all Vedāntas would be of unintended meaning. Now, if it is argued that the injunctive word has its meaning intended because words by nature tend toward their own meanings and because [the injunction] has a perceptible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), then the other Vedāntas as well will likewise have their meanings intended; what then is the use of the injunctive [portion]? This is the sense.

Now, since an injunction is not capable of impelling one toward that which does not accomplish a human goal (puruṣārtha), the status of being a human goal is dependent upon an injunction; therefore, for the sake of establishing that the knowledge of the Self arising from the word possesses the status of a human goal, an injunction such as "the Self is to be realized" is desired. To this he says "of knowledge," meaning: even that is not so.

He states its lack of excellence with the words "jñeya" (the object of knowledge). The attainment of the object of knowledge is the visible fruit of knowledge. There is no injunction regarding a visible fruit, because since it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it does not depend upon an injunction. If it is argued that liberation is the invisible fruit of knowledge and that there will therefore be an injunction for its sake; that is not so. For it is not something to be produced (*sādhya*). Why? Because of the loss of its nature as liberation (*mokṣatva-hāni*). For liberation is defined as the absolute cessation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

If that [liberation] were an effect, it would perish like a jar or similar objects, and consequently, there would be a recurrence of saṃsāra. Therefore, liberation’s very nature as liberation—characterized by the absolute cessation of saṃsāra—would be lost. Now, one might argue that even if liberation is an effect, it will not perish like a jar; this is not so, because every positive entity that is an effect is necessarily concomitant with destruction. Furthermore, liberation is a positive entity, since it is characterized by unsurpassed bliss and sovereignty.

[Objection: But has it not been stated that liberation (mokṣa) is defined as the absolute cessation of transmigratory existence? Having said this, how can you say that liberation is of the nature of a positive entity (bhāvarūpa)? [Reply: It is said in response: there is no contradiction, because it is figuratively stated that "that [cessation] exists in liberation," and thus that very cessation is called liberation; or rather, the meaning is that that [cessation] is described in liberation by means of scripture and other authorities. [Objection: But liberation is the absence of future conjunction with body, senses, and intellect; and since it is an absence, even if it were produced, it would perish like the absence of a jar. [Reply: Not so; for that is an antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva).

Nor is this [liberation] something to be produced, because it is beginningless, like the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a jar or similar objects. [Objection: But surely liberation is the destruction of the cause of bondage; and that, like the destruction of a jar, though produced, is not impermanent. [Reply: True; however, this [destruction] is not distinct from knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, it is not its effect. Since bondage arises from ignorance (*avidyā*), and knowledge alone—which is its opposite—is the absence of that [bondage], it is not distinct [from knowledge]; and only that which is distinct becomes an effect. Alternatively, this is another explanation of the sūtra-portion "and on account of the departure therefrom" (*tadvyuccheḥ*).

Liberation, characterized as the abiding in one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), is declared by the Śruti; if it were something produced (*kārya*), it would fall away from being liberation characterized in such a manner. The point is that what is produced cannot be the eternal nature of the Self. If liberation were a product, its impermanence would entail a return [to worldly existence]. Since this would contradict the scriptural teaching of non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*), the inference that "whatever is produced is impermanent" is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) in this context.

He restates the objection—that even if liberation (*mokṣa*) were an effect, because it is eternal, the claim that "if it were an effect, it would perish and there would be a return to transmigratory existence" is incorrect—with the words beginning *yac ca*. He refutes that with the word *dṛṣṭā*: all observed effects are perishable due to their impermanence; yet, even if liberation were an effect, one might resort to its eternality on the strength of the scriptural teaching of non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*), provided there were no other way to understand the scripture. However, there is indeed such another way. He states that alternative way with the words *yadā tu*: [the phrase] *anavayavena* means...

"Without remainder" means as much as possible. Ignorance (*avidyā*), moreover, is the cause of rebirth; when that has been completely eliminated by knowledge (*vidyā*), [rebirth ceases] precisely due to the absence of its cause.

The meaning is that there is also an absence of returning. This present-tense scriptural statement, "And he does not return again," restates that fact as an *arthavāda* (a commendatory or explanatory passage). Therefore, the meaning is that the attainment of liberation as an infinite fruit cannot be established on the basis of the authority of that [statement]. He confirms that this scripture is indeed an *arthavāda* with the words "For it is so. The point is that a description in the present tense refers to something already begun but not yet completed, and not to a future goal to be accomplished.

Furthermore, if there were a connection with a desire (kāmopabandha), as in the case of "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) and so forth, then even from that, it would follow that what is desired is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and not something eternal; thus, non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*) would be understood as something to be accomplished. But such a connection does not exist here. Therefore, the meaning is that the scriptural mention of non-return is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). [Objection: But is it not observed that even from an explanatory passage a fruit is postulated? For example, in the *Rātrisatra* and other rites, [the fruit] such as "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is so postulated. To this he replies: "From an explanatory passage... True; that [postulation of a fruit] occurs in cases where the supreme end (*pārārthya*) is not otherwise known.

However, regarding those things whose purpose is already known, the following principle is recited: "In the case of substances, preparatory rites, and actions, the mention of a fruit is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), because they exist for the sake of another. And since knowledge has its purpose already established by the visible result—the manifestation of the object of knowledge and its true nature—it is free from further expectancy. Therefore, the [mention of a fruit] is not appropriate here; this is the meaning. [Objection: But surely, even the manifestation of the true nature of the Self, which is the object of knowledge, is itself not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); therefore, there certainly remains an expectancy for a human goal.

To the question, "In what way, then, is there freedom from expectancy? he says: "Because it has the human goal as its purpose. He raises another view: "Others [say]... Without an injunction (*vidhi*), a statement whose content is a mere fact (*bhūtārtha*) and devoid of a task to be accomplished would be a restatement (*anuvādaka*), since that factual matter is already within the scope of other means of knowledge; and a restatement occurs regarding an object already within the scope of another means of knowledge. Therefore, such a restating statement, being dependent on other means of knowledge, would transcend the status of authority characterized by independence and would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

However, when a statement is established—that is, culminates—in an action that is its meaning (a *kārya*) which is not the object of any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), it attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) by being independent of other means of knowledge; such is the case, for example, with sentences concerning rituals like the *agnihotra*. Therefore, although there is no fruit of an injunction here subsequent to the realization of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), nevertheless, for the sake of establishing the authority of the Vedāntas, an injunction must be resorted to. The rest is clear. To this, it is said: "The means of knowledge... and so forth.

That speech whose object (*artha*) has been reached—that is, attained—by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is so described; its state is "being such" (*tattā*). That speech whose object is established as being thus is "having an established object" (*bhūtārtha*); its state is "being such" (*tattā*). Is this "having an object attained by another means of valid cognition"—that is, being made known by way of being already known through another means of valid cognition—the same as being a restatement (*anuvāda*), or is it merely the state of having an established object? In that regard, if "having an object obtained by another means of valid cognition" is intended to mean being a restatement, then that which is non-human (authorless) Vedic discourse (*vedāntavacaḥ*) does not, as something already known by another means of valid cognition, bring about understanding [of its object].

It is not a restatement; therefore, it is not dependent; therefore, it is not invalid. The point is that what is of human origin (pauruṣeya) has its object already obtained through another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Now, if being a restatement consists merely in having an existent object (bhūtārthatā), he says [in response]: "Because of dependence. This means: because in the case of memory (smṛti), we observe that contact with another means of valid cognition is the cause for its dependence on another means of valid cognition. He states this very point: "For that... (sā hi).

For that memory, by delineating the very jar previously apprehended through the pronoun "that" in the form "That jar," arises for the purpose of contacting another apprehension; thus, the meaning is that it requires another apprehension as its cause. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose object (viṣaya) is a thing (artha) mixed with—that is, contacted by—another apprehension. It has been stated that even in the case of an authorless (apauruṣeya) statement whose meaning is an established fact (siddhārtha), there is no ground for dependence; regarding this, the opponent says: "It might be... [syād iti].

Other means of valid cognition, such as perception and the like, have established objects as their domain. Therefore, since another means of valid cognition can also apply to the object of a Vedic statement whose content is an established fact, it is logical that such a statement requires that other means; this is the meaning. To the question, "Even if another means of valid cognition is possible regarding an established fact, why does [the Veda] depend upon it? he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). The implication is that if there were a requirement for corroboration by another means of valid cognition, the authority of the Vedāntas—characterized by independence (*nairapekṣya*)—would not exist.

But when the Vedāntas culminate in the meaning of an injunction for realization (*pratipatti-vidhi*) whose nature is an effect (*kārya-rūpa*) that lies beyond the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), then, since no other means of knowledge is possible there, there can be no suspicion of contradiction from any other means of knowledge; thus, another means of knowledge need not be required for corroboration. Consequently, validity characterized by independence (*nairapekṣya*) is established. The point is this: corroboration and contradiction may occur regarding the object of another means of knowledge, but not elsewhere. To this, it is replied: "Not so."

It is not appropriate to claim that verbal testimony (*śabda*) depends on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) merely because of the possibility of such a means existing regarding its object. Why? Because in that case, there would be no distinction between those two—namely, the other means of knowledge and the word—such that it is the word alone that is dependent and not the other means of knowledge; this is the meaning. [Objection: There is indeed a distinction, for in common worldly experience, it is observed that the word is dependent upon another means of knowledge, whereas the other means of knowledge is not.

If it were argued that "therefore, dependence belongs to the word alone and not to another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because such is not observed," then, since the authority of a word is not observed in the world even with respect to an effect that is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge, its authority would be all the more non-existent there, just as in the case of the words of the Buddha. He states all of this with the words "if" (*yadi*). He uses the expression "not at all" (*natarām*) to indicate an intensification of the point, saying "by another means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāntara*);

for even in the case of an object within the scope of another means of knowledge, the authority of a word is possible only because of its correspondence with that [other means], just like the speech of a trustworthy person (*āpta*).

It might be argued: "Since no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is possible regarding an action (*kārya*) that is beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition, its validity—as in the case of the words of the Buddha—is difficult to establish. Now, the fact that worldly speech has as its object what is already apprehended by another means of valid cognition is caused by its human origin, not by the inherent power of the word itself; whereas the word possesses an inherent power to denote an object even when it is beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition. Therefore, its validity regarding an action beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition is not difficult to establish. This is not so.

If a word possesses a capacity that is independent of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, because their capacities are equal, it would not be the case that the word alone is dependent on another means of valid cognition when another such means is possible regarding that same object; rather, the other means of valid cognition would also be dependent on the word regarding that object. What follows from this? If this were so, then the following would result: since the other means of valid cognition would be dependent on the word, it would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*); and since its authority is lacking, corroboration or contradiction by it is useless, and thus the dependence of the word upon it is not tenable.

If it is argued: "That which depends on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot itself be a means of valid cognition. But verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a means of valid cognition. Therefore, another means of valid cognition is not invalid by depending upon it; rather, it is indeed a means of valid cognition because it is independent. To this, it is replied: "In that case, the invalidity of verbal testimony itself has been established. The opponent says: "Because it depends on other means of valid cognition. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), however, says: "The validity of the other means of valid cognition also [remains] because it does not depend on verbal testimony; and that independence [of the other means] exists because verbal testimony is invalid."

Therefore, if verbal testimony were not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇya*), then other means of knowledge would possess validity because they do not depend upon it; but if those [other means] were valid, then verbal testimony would lack validity because it depends upon them. Thus, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). [The author] establishes that other means of knowledge are independent precisely because verbal testimony is not a means of valid knowledge—with the words "For if [verbal testimony] were a means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇe hi*). If verbal testimony were a means of valid knowledge, then, since the possibility of verbal testimony exists within the domain of other means of knowledge, those other means of knowledge would also depend upon verbal testimony, just as verbal testimony depends upon their possibility.

Therefore, because verbal testimony lacks intrinsic validity, it is logical that it depends on another means of knowledge; thus, there is a mutual dependence. The meaning is that there is no distinction such that verbal testimony is dependent when another means of knowledge is possible, but not so when verbal testimony itself is possible.

Furthermore, if a word that has already established its object were to depend on other means of knowledge merely because such other means are possible, then it would follow—without distinction—that even perception and inference would be mutually dependent, just like the word. This is because, in the case of wind, both touch and trembling (as their respective inferential marks) operate upon the same single object; consequently, those two [perception and inference] would also lack validity. Likewise, if a sense organ were to operate upon the object of another sense organ, that too would be dependent.

As it has been stated: "Of perception and inference," and so forth. Regarding "existence" (*sattā*): the five qualities, such as color and the rest, are graspable by the five sense organs because they possess existence and the quality-nature; however, substances such as a jar are graspable by the skin and the eye—this is the distinction. Now, if it is argued that only verbal testimony (*śabda*) is dependent upon other means of knowledge when another means of knowledge is possible, whereas this is not the case for perception and inference, then [the response follows on page 194].

A specific reason must be stated; yet no such reason exists. If it is argued that in common worldly experience, a word is seen to have as its object something already apprehended by another means of knowledge, and therefore, on account of this distinction, only verbal testimony is dependent when other means of knowledge are possible, whereas perception and inference are not—then the answer to this has already been stated at P. 81-11: "In that case, it would be even more so regarding what is not the object of any other means of knowledge. He elaborates upon the point already stated with the words "If... (yadi).

If this quality called "the state of having an object already apprehended by another means of knowledge" were a property belonging solely to words—whether human or non-human—then, precisely because of the possibility of such other means of knowledge, the word would lack authority, just like the statements of the Buddha and others; conversely, it would possess authority, just like the statements of a reliable person (*āpta*), precisely because of the possibility of other means of knowledge. Therefore, the argument that the Vedāntas lack authority when their meaning is an established fact (*siddha*) due to the possibility of other means of knowledge, but possess authority when their meaning is a task to be accomplished (*kārya*) due to the impossibility of other means of knowledge, is incorrect. This is the intended sense.

Now, if the nature of a word were to depend upon its being produced by a person (*pauruṣeya*), then, since the Vedic text—which is not produced by a person—does not have its object already apprehended by another means of knowledge, it would not be dependent even when its subject matter is one that could potentially be accessed by other means of knowledge, because it establishes what was previously unknown (*siddhārthatva*). Therefore, there is no lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). The compound *saṃbhavatpramāṇāntaraviṣaya* is analyzed as follows: that in which another means of knowledge is possible is *saṃbhavatpramāṇāntara*; that whose object is such [a thing] is *saṃbhavatpramāṇāntaraviṣaya*. For dependence is caused solely by the fact of being produced by a person.

The meaning is that even though a word is of non-human origin, it ceases [to function] when its cause ceases, provided it is within the scope of other means of valid cognition; however, it does not follow [as a consequence] merely by virtue of the universal property of being a word (*śabdatva*).

Furthermore, if that which is observed in one place were to exist in another place by virtue of some commonality, then the inference of a son from his voice—which is specifically observed to have its object already apprehended through perception—would, by virtue of the commonality of being an inference, imply that the inference of the sun’s motion based on its reaching another location (the *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* type) must also have its object already apprehended through perception. Moreover, since perception regarding the discrimination of notes such as *ṣaḍja* is observed to be preceded by the science of music (*gāna-śāstra*), it would follow that the perception of jars and other objects must likewise be so preceded; yet this is not the case.

Therefore, just as something seen in one place does not exist elsewhere, so too dependence, though observed in the case of human [utterances], cannot belong to that which is non-human, even if it possesses a real object (*bhūtārtha*). If what is observed in the human were also present in the non-human, then—since a human utterance is seen to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when its object is apprehended through other means of knowledge—the non-human would lack validity because other means of knowledge are impossible in its case; this is the meaning of the phrase "all the more so" (*natarām*).

It has been stated: "But when [the Veda] is established in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*), which is not the object of another means of knowledge, it attains the status of a valid authority by virtue of its independence. To this, he states the refutation: "Not so" (*anicet*). If it is argued that the word's validity arises from its independence due to the impossibility of other means of knowledge regarding the focus on the *niyoga* (injunction), then, because other means of knowledge are equally impossible in the case of the injunctions to drink poison or eat sand, those two sentences would also possess validity by virtue of such independence.

And this is not accepted; the meaning is that in one case it would be a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*), while in the other it would lack authority due to being devoid of a basis (*nirbhūlatva*). Here, regarding the worldly and Vedic injunctive sentences (*niyoga-vākya*) intended by the opponent on page 195:

He raises a specific objection with the word "nanu" (but). This is addressed by the passage beginning with "atha" (now). The phrase "the relation of the end and the means" (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is an explanation of *viniyoga* (application); and this [relation] is to be seen between the destruction of fever and the drinking of medicine, as well as between heaven and the eating of sand. The phrase "or rather" (*yo vā*) provides another interpretation of *viniyoga*. In that case, the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is one who desires freedom from fever; the object (*viṣaya*) is the drinking; and the injunction (*niyoga*), however, is expressed by the optative suffix in the word "pibet" (one should drink).

This is what is meant: even if this statement were independent with respect to *niyoga* (the injunction), it would nonetheless be non-authoritative with respect to *viniyoga* (the application) because of its dependence [on other means of knowledge]. However, in the Veda, there is no dependence even regarding *viniyoga*; thus, because of its independence, it possesses authority. When the opponent has thus stated the distinction between the sentences of worldly *niyoga* and those of the Veda, the proponent replies: "By human intellect," etc. The word "hanta" (well then) indicates assent.

As you have stated, it is precisely in this way that the dependence of speech upon other means of knowledge (pramāṇāntara) is based on its being preceded by human intellect; for in the world, when such [human intellect] exists, there is dependence, whereas in the Veda, when it does not exist, there is independence. It is not the possibility of other means of knowledge regarding that subject which is the cause [of dependence], because even in the absence of other means of knowledge, dependence is observed in worldly injunctive sentences (niyoga-vākya); this is the meaning. Furthermore, he raises another distinction in this very context with the word "atha" (now/if).

Therefore, one should apply this: in the Veda there is no dependence on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas in common worldly usage there is such dependence. The sense is that a statement is appropriately either dependent or independent based on whether its subject matter falls within the scope of other means of knowledge or not; this does not apply elsewhere. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), however, says "No. The phrase "as for example" provides a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). It has been stated that this distinction is not caused by the mere nature of the word; regarding that, he raises an objection with "Now [if you say]... (*atha*).

Having understood the meaning from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a person employs speech regarding that [meaning]. Therefore, that human speech is "established in application" (*viniyoga-niṣṭha*), meaning it is established in the application which is the domain of another means of valid cognition. But the other [type of speech], the non-human (*apauruṣeya*), stands otherwise as being established in the mandate (*niyoga*) itself; this is the meaning. What is intended is this: by the inherent power of words, establishment in the mandate is the general rule (*utsarga*). However, in the case of human speech, establishment in application is an exception (*apavāda*); yet this distinction is not produced by the inherent power of words alone.

"But the Vedic," he says; the meaning is that the Vedic [text], by the power of its words, has *niyoga* (the injunction) as its primary focus, because the *niyoga* is what is to be accomplished (*kārya*). It is explained: "by another means of knowledge" (*mānāntara*). That which has another possible means of knowledge is "one for which another means of knowledge is possible" (*saṃbhavyanyapramāṇaka*). This is the sense: well then, since this human speech depends on another means of knowledge, its subject matter—the application (*viniyoga*)—is one for which another means of knowledge is possible; it is not, however, [the case] for us, for whom another means of knowledge is possible. [Page 196] 18A.

P. 83-10. "Because this human speech depends upon another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). Regarding the phrase "of that kind": it means [the speech] of one for whom there exists another possible means of knowledge regarding the application (*viniyoga*). He concludes the stated point with supporting reasoning: "Therefore," etc. Having understood the matter through another means of knowledge—that is, having known it—a person employs speech for the sake of communicating the meaning to another, the listener.

Therefore, since that [scriptural] statement of a person (*puruṣavacas*) is possible through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), there is no dependence upon another means of knowledge for the statement of a person because of the possibility of another means of knowledge. Thus, the meaning is that the statement of a person does not depend on another means of knowledge due to the possibility of another means of knowledge. By virtue of its dependence on another means of knowledge, the application (*viniyoga*) of the statement of a person has become an object (*viṣaya*) for which another means of knowledge is possible; it is not, however, the case that this [statement] depends on another means of knowledge simply because it has as its object something for which another means of knowledge is possible. Regarding the word "there" (*tatra*):

The meaning is: "in the case of human speech. He states the result of this consideration in the words "where... The intended distinction (*vivakṣā*) is as follows: for the phrase "it is possible for this [to exist]," the negative instance (*vyatireka*) is the statement of a Buddha or others regarding an unperceivable object, which lacks the possibility of perception; and for the phrase "nor is it unperceivable," the negative instance is the statement of an unreliable person regarding a perceptible object, even though the sequence of its perception is possible. He strengthens his own stated point with the agreement of the venerable master (*ācārya*), using the words "non-human" (*apauruṣeya*).

The meaning is: "by that very reason" refers to the fact that dependence and independence are based respectively on being of human origin and not being of human origin. The compound *anapekṣavyapekṣatvayornimitte* is a genitive tatpuruṣa (possessive) compound, meaning "the grounds for independence and dependence. Since dependence is based on being of human origin, therefore, a Vedāntic statement produced by human intellect, even though it concerns an existing reality (*bhūtārtha*), is not dependent; consequently, it is not invalid (*apramāṇa*).

Therefore, the sense is that the assumption that [the Veda] has action as its purport is useless for the sake of establishing its authority through independence. To the question, "How is independence established by way of being innate (autpattika)? he says: "For in the case of what is innate... (autpattike hi). The meaning is that when the relationship between word and meaning is eternal, there is independence from other means of knowledge because it is not of human origin (apauruṣeya). Now, it might be argued that the impossibility of other means of knowledge was also stated by the Sūtra on "contact with the existent" (satsaṃprayoga).

Then, with the intention that "non-occurrence" is the reason for independence, and that if [the Vedāntas] were for the sake of establishing an already existing fact (*siddha-arthatva*), their non-authoritativeness would follow from dependence due to the possibility of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara-sambhava*), one objects with the words "But surely... (nanu), thinking that the fact that the Vedāntas have an effect as their purpose (*kāryārthatva*) must necessarily be accepted in order to preclude that [possibility of other means]. The proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*), however, says: "It is true that the non-occurrence of other means of knowledge has been stated; however, if other means of knowledge existed, there could be no such restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) as 'only the Vedic injunction' (*codanā eva*); therefore, it was stated for that purpose."

But he says "True" to show that it is not for the sake of establishing the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) through independence; for if the authority of the injunction were established even when other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are possible, what would be the point of refuting them? Therefore, the refutation of other means of knowledge was made so that the authority of the injunction might not be undermined by such dependence. Consequently, it is logical that the Upanishadic texts (*vedānta*), which have as their purpose the establishment of [the Self], can indeed exist.

The opponent asks with the intention that, because [the Veda] would be dependent on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of having another purpose, it would lack authority; therefore, one must resort to the view that it has "action" (*kārya*) as its primary purport in order to preclude the possibility of other means of knowledge. He asks: "Now then" (*atha*). The proponent, however, says "Dharma... with the following intention: since other means of knowledge are indeed possible, let there be no dependence; thus, the purpose of this [Vedic inquiry] is not the refutation of those [other means], but rather the knowledge of the true nature of Dharma. Furthermore, because the Veda is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), any charge of dependence is dismissed far in advance. Thus he speaks.

To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of [the existence of] other means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). For if other means of valid cognition were possible, then even the worship of the Buddha and so forth, as perceived by the Buddha and others, would constitute *dharma*; in that case, it would not be determined that the *agnihotra* and similar rites alone are the true essence of *dharma*. If it is asked, "What is the use of that being determined?", he says: "That" (*tat*). This refers to "this effort"; the meaning is that this is the effort to exclude other means of valid cognition. Now, one might ask, "Why could that effort not be for the sake of establishing the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) itself? To this, he says: "The Vedic injunction" (*codanā*).

The authority of *codanā* (Vedic injunction) is also investigated solely for the purpose of determining the true nature of *dharma*. Therefore, that [the nature of *dharma*] alone is primary, not the authority of *codanā*. The sense is that when it is possible for something to serve the purpose of the primary, it is not appropriate for it to serve the purpose of the non-primary. Alternatively, if other means of knowledge were possible, [the Veda] might sometimes have even contradictory meanings; for example, the perception of the Buddha regarding the non-dharma-nature of the killing of animals in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, and the dharma-nature of entering a monastery (*vihāra*), and so forth.

In that case, if the injunction were weak, it would be sublated by that [other means of knowledge]; and if they were of equal strength, doubt would arise. Therefore, in order to eliminate the invalidity arising from such sublation or doubt, the impossibility of another means of knowledge is established by the *satsaṃprayoga* sūtra; it is not for the sake of eliminating invalidity based on dependence when another means of knowledge is possible—as he says with the words "or rather" (*athavā*). But surely, if another contradictory means of knowledge were possible, verbal testimony would not be a valid authority?

"In that case, for the sake of its validity, the absence of any other contradictory means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must be required; and therefore, the state of being dependent (*sāpekṣatva*) remains as it was. Furthermore, regarding those Vedānta passages whose subject matter is already established (*bhūtārtha*), since other means of knowledge are possible there, their absence [of such contradiction] would not exist, and thus their validity would not obtain. With this intention, he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). The proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*), however, replies: "Granted, let the absence of a contradictory other means of knowledge be required; even so, the word itself does not become dependent on it."

For dependence consists in the requirement of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and the mere absence of another means of valid cognition is not itself another means of valid cognition, because it does not produce knowledge. Thus he says: "Granted" (*kāmam*). Furthermore, if invalidity were to result from the mere possibility of another contradictory means of valid cognition regarding matters of fact (*bhūtārtha*), then that would apply to perception and other means as well when they concern matters of fact. Thus he says: "Contradictory" (*virodhī*). Moreover, invalidity resulting from the possibility of another contradictory means of valid cognition cannot be avoided even if the Vedāntas are held to have a purport directed toward action (*kāryaniṣṭhatva*). Thus he says: "Furthermore" (*api ca*).

He asks "Why? and replies: "Because it is something to be done (*kartavya*). Even though the Vedāntas have as their ultimate goal an effect (*kārya*), they nonetheless culminate in the comprehension of the true nature of the Self, which is the object to be comprehended and required for the performance of that comprehension; and in that regard, there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is that there is a possibility [of its existence]. Thus, for now, the objection raised by the opponent—that "its absence need not be taken into account"—has been refuted. Now, having restated the opponent’s intention and reiterated the previously mentioned fault therein, he applies the meaning of the verse—which is intended as a conclusion with the words "even though it be a real thing" (bhūtārtham api)—while relying upon that very fault: "Of the real thing" (bhūtārthasya). "By him" (tena) means by the opponent. The word *kila* is used to indicate a lack of conviction [in the opponent's position].

However, when [the word] is restricted to its function (*kārya-niṣṭhatva*), the phrase “it conveys a meaning” (*arthaṃ pratipādayati*) is to be supplied after the word “independently” (*svatantraṇa*). In this context, the section ending with “because it is within the range” (*gocaratvāt*) restates the opponent’s position; the section beginning with “by what has been said” (*uktena*) and ending with “and mere possibility does not constitute dependence” (*na ca sambhava-mātraṃ sāpekṣatvam*) reiterates the faults already mentioned; and the section beginning with “even though it refers to an existing fact” (*bhūtārtham api*) constitutes the conclusion—such is the analysis (*nirveka*).

Now, anticipating the objection raised by others—that if the Vedāntas are not subordinate to injunctions (*vidhi*), then in the absence of action, there could be no connection between word-meanings at all—the author says: "Now" (*atha*). The sense is: without action, word-meanings do not enter into relation; therefore, for you, there would be no connection between the word-meanings of such passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite. He refutes this with: "What [of it]? (*kim iti*). If there is no connection without action, then let there be action.

What has come about from the Creator (vidhi), such that the Vedāntas are said to enter into it? This is the meaning. [Objection: But even that [action] is difficult to find in the Vedāntas since it is not heard there. To this he says: "That too. That action, consisting of forms such as "is" (asti) and so forth—where is it not easily available? On the contrary, it is easily available everywhere; for where no other verbal root is heard, the action of "being" (asti) is certainly available by the maxim: "The verb 'to be' (asti), accompanied by the present tense suffix (bhavantī), should be employed. By the word "asti," he indicates its meaning through the verbal root.

“As in the case of [the injunction] ‘one who has performed the sacrifice [should give] substance, deity, and action. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), other actions are included as far as possible; for example, in the phrase “door, door,” [the implied actions are] “let it be covered” and “let it be closed. In the Vedāntas, however, only the action of existence (*astikriyā*) is intended. He explains this with the words beginning “If... The meaning of a verb is action; without it, there can be no syntactic connection between the meanings of nominal stems.

For this reason, the action has been made the cause of the mutual connection between the meanings of the verbal roots and the nominal stems, according to the principle of the *aruṇaikahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow). This is because the action is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) in the absence of mutual connection among the meanings of the nominal stems; for the action is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), whereas the meaning of the nominal stem is already established (*siddha*). That which is to be accomplished requires what is established, and that [accomplished thing] becomes qualified by its connection with another distinct entity, as in the case of the *ekahāyanī* and the *vāruṇī*. Therefore, the action does not require connection with other things for the sake of anything else.

The connection of word-meanings is caused by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Therefore, action is the cause of their connection. Thus, the meaning is that without such [action], the establishment of a connection between real entities does not occur. To the question "What is the fault in this?", he says: "Therefore" [p. 199].

Thus: "not within the range of words" means not being an object of words (*padārtha*). Since Brahman, as the denoted object, has no known relation [to words], the apprehension of it through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the cause [for its being understood]. To this, the proponent says: "In this way. "The establishment of the word-meaning" refers to the intended meaning of the word *brahman*. The word "meaning" (*artha*) here signifies "purpose" (*prayojana*). And that [purpose] is the connection with the action of "being" (*asti*) and so forth. He states the reason for this with the words "the verb 'to be' (*asti*)."

The maxim has been shown that "where another verb is not perceived [the verb 'is' is understood]. The particle *iti* here denotes a reason; the meaning is "for this reason. *Bhavantī* refers to a verbal suffix (*vibhakti*) expressing the present tense. Thus, since the action of "being" (*asti-kriyā*) is obtained, there is no fault regarding the connection of word-meanings in the Vedāntas based upon that [action]; so he says: "Therein" (*tatra*), which means "when the action of being is obtained."

Now, if a sentence is indeed grounded in the sense of existence (*asti-artha*), how can it have as its primary aim the comprehension of the essential nature [of Brahman]? For it is not logical for a single sentence to aim at two things simultaneously, as that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, one might suspect that if the Vedāntas are grounded in the sense of existence, the specific reality of Brahman—characterized by truth, infinity, and so forth—cannot be established from them.
