Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of existence" (*sattāyāḥ*). In the sentence "Devadatta cooks," the agent is subordinate to the action; the action itself, however, is primary because it is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

The meaning of "is" (asti) in the statement "Brahman exists as having the nature of truth, knowledge, and infinity" has Brahman as its primary referent; it is not perceived as being primarily the action [of existence], as in the case of cooking. Now, one might object: "But there is no accusative case here; how can it be said that the primary referent is the grammatical factor (kāraka)? To this he says: "By its very nature. This is the inherent nature of existence (sattā): that it has existence as its primary referent. Furthermore, in the cognition "Brahman exists," Brahman is perceived as qualified by existence; therefore, because it is the substantive (viśeṣya), it is primary by its own nature. This is the meaning.

Here, those who deny the existence of the universal "Being" (sattāsāmānya) say: "Existence is nothing other than being cognizable by a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). He states this with the words "here. He provides the reason for that with the words "for thus. "The opposite" means that which is not cognizable by a means of valid knowledge. Now, one might ask: why should this [cognizability] not be the cause for the distinction between the existent and the non-existent? To this he says: "Certainly not. But why is another cause not perceived? For surely the presence or absence of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) will serve as the causes.

To explain: having raised the objection that "that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*) is real, while other things, such as a human horn, are called unreal," he refutes this with the word "no" (*na*). The presence or absence of causal efficacy is itself determined by the presence or absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends that causal efficacy, and not by anything else. If this is so, then let the reality or unreality of an object also be established by those very two [the presence or absence of the valid cognition]; what is the use of the presence or absence of causal efficacy? This is the intended meaning.

One might object: "Surely the presence and absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) will themselves depend upon the presence and absence of causal efficiency, and not upon the presence and absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For it is thus" (*tathā hi*). "From its opposite" (*tadviparyayāt*) means "from the absence of a means of valid cognition. Having thus established that existence consists in being the object of a means of valid cognition, he applies this to the subject at hand: "And so" (*tathā ca*). And so, if the Vedāntas were concerned with an existent entity (*astyarthaniṣṭhatva*), they would be dependent on other means of valid cognition... [p. 200]

The sense is that, because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of [their] being authoritative, their being directed toward an effect must be accepted for the sake of their authority. He refutes this with the words "In this case" (atra). The word "iti" indicates both the cognition and the word; therefore, the meaning is as follows: it is not held that the cognition "it exists" and the word [expressing it] have an object that is apprehended by a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa); the point is that existence is not the state of being apprehended by a means of valid knowledge. The expression "it exists" is a reference to time without intending to specify it; for this very reason, there arises the cognition: "it was," "it exists," or "it will exist."

For when a means of knowledge (*māna*) has arisen, there is the state of being an object of that means of knowledge, but not prior to it; therefore, the state of being an object of a means of knowledge is not the object of the cognition "it exists. Consequently, once a means of knowledge regarding fire and so forth has arisen from smoke and so forth, the cognition "it exists" would subsequently occur. However, that [cognition] arises as "it exists" precisely as a self-evident means of knowledge (*svayam-māna*). Thus, the point is that existence (*sattā*), which is the very nature of the thing, exists as something other than the state of being an object of a means of knowledge.

Since the refutation is applicable only against the notion that "it exists," the introduction of the notions of past and future objects is for the purpose of stating the refutation that is about to be explained. Now, if it is argued that the notion "it exists" arises only after the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has occurred, he says in response: "It would differ. If the notion "it exists" occurs at a time subsequent to the means of valid cognition, it would not differ in its mode according to whether its object is past, future, or present; rather, it would have only the present as its object.

Although an object exists in the three periods of time, nevertheless, the connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs only when it is present; this is the meaning. The word "or" (*vā*) is used for the purpose of indicating an alternative position. Regarding the phrase "of the cognition that [it] does not exist": it should be construed as follows—that which is cognized by a means of valid cognition through the cognition that "[it] exists" is not the object [of the cognition that it does not exist]. Regarding the phrase "due to a specific filling": the mention of "specific" is intended to refer to the particularity residing in the filling caused by a dam. And regarding the phrase "due to a specific arising of clouds": this is for the purpose of excluding clouds that are joined with opposing winds. Regarding the phrase "due to a difference in explanation":...

The meaning is that [this objection arises] out of audacity. Now, if it is argued that the very objectivity belonging to the Self is what is grasped by the means of knowledge produced from the three marks such as smoke, and therefore the cognition of "existence" (asti), though it has the means of knowledge as its object, does not occur at a later time, nor can it be said that it would apply to what has already been measured (*mita*); even so, since objects in the three times exist as being cognizable by those means of knowledge, the cognition of "existence" would not be divided into three kinds.

Furthermore, this being the case, since the meaning of "is" (asti) would be apprehended by the means of knowledge precisely as its own object, there would be no dependence on another means of knowledge even regarding a statement whose content is the meaning of "is. Therefore, what was said—that a sentence whose content is the meaning of "is" depends on another means of knowledge—is incorrect. He states all of this [in the words] beginning with "atha": "Now, if the state of being its own object is not apprehended by the inferential means of knowledge, but rather the state of being the object of another means of knowledge..."

If it is asked, "What is that other means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara)? we reply: it is indeed perception (pratyakṣa). And that pertains to all three times; for instance, the past is perceived by some as past, the future as future, and the present as present. Therefore, since perception extends across the three times, its objects likewise extend across the three times, and thus the threefold distinction—"it was," "it is," and "it will be"—is logically established. If it is argued that, because they depend on another means of valid cognition and because the Upanishads (Vedāntas) would otherwise result in being non-authoritative if they were restricted solely to the sense of "existence" (astyartha), they must instead be accepted as being restricted to "what is to be done" (kāryaniṣṭhatva); we reply: that argument is without substance.

For this being the case, since atoms—which are always to be inferred—are not objects of perception, they would not be inferred by one who perceives only gross objects, as they would lack the status of being objects of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Likewise, the *śruti* that enjoins [a ritual act], which is itself to be inferred from the indicative power (*liṅga*) of a mantra, should be cited here as an example. Furthermore, if this were so, it would not only be the case that the Vedāntas lack authority due to their dependence on other means, but even the indicative power of smoke and the like would be subject to it; consequently, inference itself would not be a valid means of knowledge. He states this with the words "anyā" (another). Here he raises an objection: P. 86-18.

Regarding the phrase "tatsiddhāṃśena": the meaning is that if there is independence (*nairapekṣya*) of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) from another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), because that [object] is established—meaning proven, well-known, or known—from that very mark such as smoke. For they declare independence to be the lack of dependence on another corroborating means of knowledge. But here, another means of knowledge is not required for corroboration; rather, it is itself being cognized. And in the cognition of that [object], the mark is indeed independent. Through that [cognition], the object is established, just as in the case of the words of a trustworthy person (*āptavākya*).

Therefore, the intention is that the inferential mark (*liṅga*) possesses validity. The word *vā* is for the purpose of completing the meter. Alternatively, if it were the case that its establishment [of the object] occurs from that very [mark], then there would be no independence; thus one should connect the phrase "if it were so. To this, he gives the reply: "No. Such independence as has been described cannot be prevented—even by royal punishments or by clubs—in the case of the Veda, which is established in the sense of existing reality. This is the same even regarding the Vedāntas.

For even in their case, since another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) is established through them, and the establishment of the object occurs by way of that cognition, their status as a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is unimpeded—this is the meaning. Regarding this, the opponent states the disparity between the Vedāntic [texts] and inferential marks (*liṅga*) with the words "the possibility of that" (*tatsaṃbhava*). In the case of an inferential matter, such as the swelling of a river or smoke, there is the "possibility of that"—the possibility of another means of knowledge—with respect to the perceived object. Therefore, in those cases, it is appropriate that they possess validity, because the establishment of the object occurs by way of that cognition.

However, the claim that "in this case, Brahman is known solely through the Vedānta" is inconsistent. Why? Because even regarding Brahman, since direct realization is admitted, there exists a knowledge that is directly realized (*sākṣātkāri-jñāna*). Therefore, the sense is that the authority of the Vedāntas is unimpeded, as the object is established by means of that valid cognition. The phrase "in this way" (*evam*) means: because the object is established either through the establishment of its cognition by another means of knowledge, or through the establishment of that [other] cognition, or through the object itself. The phrase "of that in the object" (*tasyārthe*)...

The meaning is that the object of that indicative mark (*liṅga*) is possible through another means of valid cognition, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*). The phrase “of the statements of Buddha and others which teach supersensible objects” connects with the distant [term]. By virtue of being human speech, it is inferred that “this person knows thus,” which is what is appropriate; however, there is no basis for knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*) in the words of Buddha, because knowledge regarding a supersensible object is impossible. Therefore, [the two phrases] “of those who have a basis in knowledge” and “because of the impossibility of knowledge” [refer to this]. [p. 202]

There is a contradiction. Now, one might object: "If Brahman shines forth directly, then why is it said in the passage, 'Its establishment is from scripture and tradition' (p. 87-12), that it has scripture as its sole means of valid knowledge? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of those possessed of ignorance" (*avidyāvatām*). Although even for those possessed of ignorance the Self shines forth directly, nevertheless it does not do so in its form as Brahman; rather, it shines in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), accompanied by the experience of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). However, for those possessed of knowledge, it shines forth directly as one whose knots of the ego-sense and other such bonds have been severed; this is the distinction.

[Objection: Is it not the case that existence (*sattā*) is the state of being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that the manifestation of the eternal self-luminous [Brahman] is the means of valid cognition? For that [manifestation] is not perception, because it is not produced by the sense organs; as for inference and the other means of knowledge, their scope is far removed [from Brahman]. Nor can Brahman be the object of that [means of knowledge], for the relationship of object and subject occurs only between two distinct things; and there is no difference between Brahman and its manifestation, since that would entail the consequence of duality (*dvaita*). [Reply: It is said: Even by one who maintains that existence is the state of being an object of a means of valid cognition, experience (*anubhava*) is declared to be the fruit of that means of valid cognition.

It is not an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) is admitted. Consequently, it would lack existence; yet this is not desired. Therefore, the opponent maintains that being an object of a means of valid cognition consists merely in appearing (*pratibhāsamānatāmātra*), and not in the relation of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*). And the proponent considers that such [appearance] exists even in the case of Brahman. As for the argument that "this is not perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is not produced by the sense organs" and so forth, we reply: the definition of perception is not "that which is produced by the sense organs."

Moreover, it is direct perception (*sākṣātpratīti*); otherwise, experience would not be perceptual. And since that [direct perception] exists even with respect to Brahman, there is no fault. That which was stated by the author of the Sūtras as being born of the senses is direct perception regarding its own specific object; it is not born of the senses in the case of [objects like] dharma. Therefore, for the Buddha and others, cognition arising from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding dharma and so forth is not tenable. Thus, all is consistent in order to demonstrate that with respect to dharma, the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

As for what was stated—that because the connection with other means of knowledge occurs across the three times, there is a threefold division [of existence] as "it was," "it is," and "it will be"—that too is incorrect; thus he says, "Moreover" (*apica*). If being-measured (*mīyamānatā*) is existence (*sattā*), then even another means of knowledge is indeed existent because it is being-measured; and what is existent is present. Therefore, the threefold temporal division is unestablished in that very case; this is the collective meaning. Now, wishing to state another refutation, he offers an alternative analysis, beginning with "Moreover."

The phrase "connection with a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasaṃbandha*) is an explanation of the term "yoga" found in the verse. "Its opposite is non-existence" (*tadviparyayo'sattā*); this means that non-existence is the lack of connection with a presently operating means of valid cognition. Regarding the expression "not depending on a specific time," the phrase "existence is connection with a means of valid cognition; its opposite is non-existence" should be supplied as a continuation. In that case, the "opposite" intended is simply the absence of connection with any means of valid cognition whatsoever. Regarding the first of these two positions, he states the fault: "In that case" (*tatra*). The word "in the view" (*mate*) refers to the desire to express both existence and non-existence together. For what was previously cognized is remembered; therefore, for this [memory], there is no present... [p. 203] means of valid cognition.

The point is that the relation itself is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Here, an objection is raised with the words "Now [one might ask]... (nanu). The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) replies: "True. The intention is that [the object] would be non-existent because, in the case of memory, there is an absence of connection with a presently existing means of valid cognition. Regarding the second alternative, he states the fault: "By a means of valid cognition... (*pramāṇa*). If existence were merely the connection with a means of valid cognition without depending on a specific time, then even a jar that was pure through a past connection with a means of valid cognition would have to exist now.

Furthermore, even if it has perished, [an entity] would perform functions such as holding honey as if it had not perished; yet this is not the case. Therefore, existence is not merely the connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that there is a distinction between those two states due to being "perished" or "not perished," and thus there is no contingency of something seen as "not perished" performing a function, we say: no.

If you assert a distinction based on being destroyed or not destroyed, setting aside the application or non-application of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then let that very distinction characterized by being destroyed or not destroyed be the cause for the linguistic usage of "existent" and "non-existent"—namely, "that which is not destroyed is existent, and that which is destroyed is non-existent. This is just as, in the determination of an effect, one says "the effect [arises] from that which is not destroyed, not from that which is destroyed," and not because of the application of a valid means of knowledge; such is the meaning. He confirms this very point through common worldly experience with the word "tat" (that).

At that time, one reflects upon the distinction known as "perished" and "unperished," and upon the established rule for the linguistic usage of "existent" and "non-existent. The word *upacarati* means either "teaches" or "knows," because the root *car-* has the sense of "going" (movement) and thus implies "knowing. Furthermore, if existence were merely the connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then even what was previously cognized would be existent at present; consequently, there would be no further desire to investigate its existence or non-existence now, yet such a desire does exist. Therefore, the meaning is that existence is not merely the connection with a means of valid cognition.

Now, having raised another alternative position, he refutes it with the words "atha" (now/if). If it is argued that "existence" (*sattā*) is the property of an object consisting in its fitness for being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇayogyatva*), and that this [fitness] has departed from a destroyed object—in other words, it is lost when the substratum (*dharmin*) is destroyed—then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a destroyed thing possesses existence, because it still possesses fitness for valid cognition. If it is then said that this is not so, because in some cases where an object is being remembered, [this fitness] has merely shifted due to the destruction of the substratum and is not lost everywhere, and thus there is no undesirable consequence of existence for everything; even that is not satisfactory. This is the meaning.

In this regard, by the statement "and [the cognition] fallen from that which has perished," the consequence that a perished object must exist, as well as the impossibility of inquiry regarding what has already been cognized, are both refuted. Furthermore, by the phrase "regarding that which is being remembered," the position that existence consists in connection with a presently functioning means of valid cognition is refuted by the consequence that everything being remembered would have to exist; this is how one should distinguish [the arguments]. He states its lack of elegance with the words "accepted" (*abhyupagata*). He states the abandonment of what was accepted with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*).

The opponent’s position is that the linguistic usage of "existent" and "non-existent" is conditioned by the presence or absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not that there exists an objective reality consisting of existence as an intrinsic property of things; this position has been abandoned by one who maintains that existence as an objective reality consists in the suitability of an object for a means of valid cognition. "The nature of the object" (*arthasvabhāva*) means that which consists of the object itself, and not [the aforementioned].

It consists in the fitness for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yoga*); the meaning is that it is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the object. Furthermore, since this is so, he begins to state that even the fault of the Vedāntas being dependent on something else that has an existent entity as its referent does not apply: "fitness for a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa-yogya*). This is a designation where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is primary, meaning "fitness" (*yogyatā*). This was stated with the intention of expressing the non-difference between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). Alternatively, the meaning is that the nature of the object, which consists in fitness for a means of valid cognition, is itself "fit for a means of valid cognition" because it is an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*).

One might object: "Is it not the case that existence is defined as the fitness for being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yogyatā*)? Therefore, even if the Vedāntas have that [existence] as their object, their dependence on other means of knowledge remains exactly as before due to contact with those other means. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But of that... The meaning is as follows: the very means of expressing the nature of that object is what is called its "connection with a means of valid cognition"; however, fitness is essentially the nature of the object itself, existing entirely outside of the means of cognition, and does not consist in a connection with the means of cognition. Consequently, there is no contact with the means of cognition in that [fitness].

The following is what is meant: when it is said that "fitness" (yogyatā) means "an existent object," one might understand fitness to be anything whatsoever; therefore, in order to convey its specific nature, it is designated as "fitness for a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇayogyatā). However, the means of valid cognition is not included within the very constitution of fitness, such that the means of valid cognition would be a limiting adjunct (upādhi) to the existence of the object within fitness. Regarding the principle that whatever is mentioned for the sake of conveying a specific quality becomes a limiting adjunct for that term's application, he provides an illustration with the words "just as" (yathā).

The analysis of the compound is: "that which has the cognition of blue as its limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*). He now states the absence of the defect mentioned by the opponent: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). The word "it" (*sa*) refers to the nature of the object. Here, the opponent objects: "It might be so" (*syāt*). But the proponent replies: "Let it not be so" (*mā bhūt*). The meaning is: let there not be a single existence (*sattā*); this—that there is a single existence—is not what we seek to prove. To the question, "What then is to be proved?", he says: "In every way" (*sarvathā*). Let existence be one, or let it be many.

In every respect, the word "is" (asti) denotes an existence whose essence is the object itself; it is not the case that "being" (sat) has its cause in connection with a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—this is what is not to be proven, as this connects with the preceding [text]. Why, then, is only the absence of having connection with a means of valid cognition as its cause being proven, and not the oneness of existence? To this he says: "pramāṇa... If the word "is" had connection with a means of valid cognition as its cause, then in the Vedānta passages which are centered on the meaning of "is," the object would have to be something touched by a means of valid cognition.

If that were the case, they would be dependent [upon something else], and thus the claim that the word "existent" (*san*) arises based on its connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yoga*) would not be established. However, since the multiplicity of existence (*sattā*) does not entail any fault, its unity is not what must be proven; this is stated as a criticism of their own accepted position. But in ultimate reality, if a single existence is not admitted, then because it would be impossible to grasp the relationship with infinite paths and because it would lead to the absurdity of postulating infinite powers, the single word "existent" could not apply to them.

The meaning is that, for this reason, one single reality must be admitted. Now, it may be objected that the application of a non-different term is indeed observed even with respect to things that are different; for example— [p.

Having raised the objection that the word "cow" applies to individual cows, the word "staff-bearer" to those with staffs, and the word "die" to vibhītaka fruits and the like, [the author] replies: "True, it is seen; however, it occurs in three ways. Keeping in mind that here, apart from the single universal *sattā* (Being), not even one of those three ways exists, he first sets forth those three ways, beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*). The analysis of the compound is: that whose cause for application is a triad of distinct universals, such as the nature of being a vibhītaka fruit and so on. (P. 89.6)

In this context, that by which something is qualified through one’s own cognition is indeed a *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier); whereas an *upalakṣaṇa* (indirect indicator) is merely a mark, and it may even be something past. To show that none of these modes exists for the application of the word "exists" (*asti*) regarding things that are fit to be objects of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he first sets aside the term "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) with the words "not, first of all" (*na tāvat*). The analysis of the compound is: "those [things] which are infinite and are the intrinsic natures of objects. He states the reason with the words "because of the relation" (*saṃbandha*). For a relation is to be grasped only after the relata have been grasped.

Furthermore, it is not possible to grasp all the infinite related [individuals]. Therefore, the meaning is that those [words] lack the capacity to grasp the relationship with that [referent]. However, in the case of words such as *akṣa*, it is appropriate for them to be common [to multiple referents]; thus he says: "limited," etc. The words *akṣa* and so forth have as their objects universals (*jāti*) such as the *vibhītaka* tree and others, which are indicated by those [universals]. Consequently, the sense is that in those cases, it is possible to grasp the relationship with even infinite individuals through those three limited universals, or rather, through the medium of them.

One might object: "Surely the word 'sat' (existent) will serve as a common term even for my infinite objects, which are characterized by the three universals such as *dravyatva* (substantiality) and so on; what is the use of a separate *sattā* (existence)? Thus he raises the objection with the words "It might be. This was stated from the perspective of one who holds that *sattā* is common to the three categories (*padārtha*). He refutes that with "That is not so. To the question "How so?", he replies: "Indeed, it is not..."

The meaning is this: the argument used for the denial of existence (*sattā*)—namely, that one who has seen a mustard seed does not have the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "this is that very same thing" when looking at Mount Meru—is equally applicable to the denial of substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the other categories. Furthermore, the word "existent" (*sat*) is applied even to universals (*jāti*) and so forth; if [existence] were caused by substance-ness and the like, that word would not apply to them. Thus he says: "Moreover" (*apica*). [An objection: "But the word 'existent' is used for those things only figuratively. To this he replies: "Not in those cases," providing the reason: "because of the cognition" (*pratyaya*).

For where there is a difference in the cognition (*pratyaya*), the word for one thing is applied metaphorically to another, as the word "fire" is used for a young boy. However, in the case of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, there is no difference in the cognition "existent" (*sat*); therefore, there is no metaphorical usage. As it has been said: "Even in the case of universals and so forth, because the cognition of 'being' exists, existence (*sattā*) resides in those universals. Furthermore, metaphorical usage is observed for words such as "heroic" based on common properties like bravery; however, there is no single common property shared by the triad of substance and so forth with the triad of universals and so forth.

Therefore, he says "and not" to show that this is not a mere figurative usage. Then, he says "if it exists" to show that if there were a single universal (*sāmānya*), our desired point would be established. "Because of equality" means because the cognition "existent" (*sat*) is indistinguishable with respect to substances (*dravya*) and so forth.

206] He raises the suspicion that the word "existent" might be a common name for other reasons, saying "now": in the doctrines and scriptures of the teachers such as Kaṇāda and Sugata, all categories (*padārtha*) are subsumed under certain limited properties—either six or five—through divisions such as the "six" or "five."

Consequently, the common term "existent" (*sat*) will apply to infinite objects, even though they are characterized by a limited number of properties such as six or five; the meaning is that this is just as the word "akṣa" applies to infinite individual instances characterized by three universal classes, such as *vibhītaka*-ness and so forth.

In that regard, the six categories beginning with substance (*dravya*) are subsumed under the doctrines of Kaṇāda by means of these properties: possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*), being the substratum of qualities (*dravyāśrayatva*), being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), being the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction (*saṃyoga-vibhāga-anapekṣa-kāraṇatva*), being the cause of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛtta-buddhi-hetutva*), being the cause of exclusive cognition (*atyanta-vyāvṛtta-buddhi-hetutva*), and being the cause of the notion of "here" (*ihapratyaya-hetutva*). The same should be stated for other systems as well. He refutes that [position] with the words "tadā" (then). He states its impropriety with the word "saṃgraha" (subsumption).

For indeed, without a single "cowness" (*gotva*), six individual cows cannot be subsumed by the expression "six cows. In that case, if one were to accept "existence" (*sattā*) and effect a subsumption under the term "existent"—that is, if it were maintained that the meaning of the word "existent" consists of six varieties—then it would follow that the meaning of the word "existent" is the number six, rather than being a distinct category of reality (*padārthāntara*). Consequently, the entire universe would not be subsumed [under that term].

Just as when it is said, "The referent of the word 'cow' is ninefold," the ninefold nature of the referent of the word 'cow' is stated, but it is not meant that there are no other referents besides the referent of the word 'cow'; so too, the meaning is that if it were understood from mere verbal reports that "there are only this many varieties of objects in the world and no others," one would not attain the true nature of reality (*arthatattva*). Therefore, since such verbal reports are undertaken for the sake of encompassing the entire world, they would be rendered useless in their absence. The opponent says: "But surely... [nanv iti].

The point to be proven for you is that the word *sat* lacks commonality [with other things], not that the various doctrines (*pravāda*) are meaningful. Therefore, even if those [doctrines] do indeed have meanings, nevertheless, because the commonality of the word *sat* is established by the limited properties (*dharma*) indicated by them, your intended probandum is not proven; this is the sense. Furthermore, this constitutes the "point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "refuting another's tenet" (*siddhāntāntaradūṣaṇa*). The proponent of the established tenet (*siddhāntin*), however, says: "No. He states the probandum with the words "Moreover" (*kiñcit*). The "proponents of doctrines" (*pravādinaḥ*) are the speakers, such as Kaṇāda and others.

He states the reason, beginning with "since": Just as in the case of "six cows," the application of the number six is not possible without a single unifying factor such as "cowness" (gotva), so too, in the collection of categories such as five or six, the application of numbers like five or six is not possible without a single universal (sāmānya). Therefore, they refute [the existence of] some single universal for those who maintain such a doctrine; and that [universal] is "Being" (sattā)—this is the meaning. For the Buddhist Vijñānavādins, there are five categories known as form (rūpa), consciousness (vijñāna), sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and mental formations (saṃskāra).

The six categories, beginning with substance (*dravya*), are the "parts" (*kaṇasuja*); by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the twenty-five principles and so forth as taught in Sāṃkhya and other systems are to be understood. Now, one might object: "If a number cannot be applied without a single unifying factor, then let there be a unification within the single capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) and the fitness for being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇayogyatā*); what is the use of 'Being' (*sattā*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Now" (*atha*). [p. 207]

Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "by those two" (tābhyām). If it is intended that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) or the fitness for a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operating upon the world is the inclusive definition, then it would be better to characterize the meaning of the word "existent" (*sat*) by those two alone; that is to say, let it be that "that which is fit for a means of valid cognition or capable of causal efficiency is the meaning of the word 'existent'," and that these two alone are the grounds for the application of the word "existent. Consequently, the presentation of limited attributes (*parimitadharma*) is redundant.

And thus, he says "therein" (*tatra*), [showing] that even the commonality (*sādhāraṇatā*) of the word *sat* would not exist. A single word applied to different objects based on different causes is "common," such as the word *akṣa* and so forth. However, if the two causes—the capacity for valid cognition (*pramāṇayogyatva*) and the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*)—which reside in the world, were indeed one and the same, then the word *sat* would be merely a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*), and not a common one. If, on the other hand, those two were distinct for each object, then they would not be inclusive; the sense is that there is no single inclusive factor.

He states another defect regarding the word *sat* being a common term (sādhāraṇaśabda) with the words "bhinna" and so on. Just as when it is said, "Bring the *akṣa*," a doubt arises as to which specific object among the various classes (such as the *vibhītaka*) that serves as the basis for the application [of the word] has been brought, so too would there be such a doubt in the case of "the pot exists" (*san ghaṭaḥ*). Consequently, there would be no cognition of a specific property called "existence" (*sattā*); yet such a doubt does not arise, because, as in the case of "the white cloth," the cognition of "the existing pot" is complete in itself and requires no further expectation. This is the meaning.

One might object: "But even regarding existence (*sattā*), there is doubt as to whether it is a substance, a quality, or an action; likewise, regarding form (*rūpa*), there is doubt as to whether it is an object or consciousness. Thus, there is indeed a similarity to the case of the sense organs and so forth. Anticipating this, he says: "But he who... The meaning is: while it is true that such a doubt exists, it pertains to disputants (*vādins*) and not to common people (*laukikas*); therefore, we understand that common people perceive the ground for the application of the word "existent" (*sat-śabda*) as being indeed non-different.

Furthermore, from a common term (*sādhāraṇa-śabda*), there arises a doubt originating from the word itself, such as "What is its meaning?", as in the case of the word *akṣa* and others. Having perceived the meaning of a genus-term (*jāti-śabda*) without doubt, there arises a doubt regarding its specific nature originating from the object itself, such as "What is the nature of this?", for example, among disputants who, having perceived "cowness" (*gotva*) from the word "cow," wonder whether it is different or non-different from the individual (*vyakti*). However, in the case of the word "Being" (*sat*), there is no doubt as to "What is its meaning?"

However, having first perceived the object known as "existence" (sattā), one subsequently [perceives] its internal distinctions, such as "it is a substance," "it is a quality," or "it is an action. Therefore, this is a common term (sādhāraṇa-śabda). He states this: "But here... There is no doubt here arising from the word itself; rather, it arises from the meaning. He asks for the reason: "Why? He provides the answer: "Because of the distinction..."

The meaning is that there is no doubt arising from the word here, because even without the cognition of those specific features regarding existence (*sattā*)—such as "Is it a substance, a quality, or an action? which are subjects of disagreement among disputants—one attains a state of cognitive completion through the mere cognition of the existence of the jar, namely, "The jar exists. Now, one might object: "Even when a doubt arises from the object itself, there is still a desire for its specific features; how then can there be a state of cognitive completion? To this, he says: [p. 208]

Regarding the phrase "wherein" (yatra): [it means] "otherwise. That is to say, if there were still an expectation for a specific means (*sādhana*) even in that case, then from that expectation for a specific means, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. Therefore, having gone as far as possible, one must reach a state of non-expectation by taking up some [means] whatsoever; the point is that it is better to assume that this [non-expectation] exists right at the beginning. To the question "Where, then, does the state of having an expectation occur?", he says: "wherein" (*yatra*).

However, where there arises a doubt as to "what is the meaning of this" regarding the word *akṣa*—which has multiple meanings—upon hearing the command "bring the akṣa," there is a lack of engagement due to the non-determination of the object itself; thus, there is an expectancy for a specific meaning. But from the word *sat*, there is no such expectancy as "what is its meaning? rather, the distinction is that there is the expectancy, "what is the nature of its meaning? This is the intended sense. He concludes with "na hi"; the meaning is "therefore. With the word "evam," he points to the method of reasoning just mentioned.

The word "real" (*sat*) is to be supplied [to the beginning of the sentence]. Now he refutes the view that [valid cognition] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), stating: "the qualifier. But surely, valid cognition is a property of the knower (*pramātṛ*); how then can it be a qualifier of the object? This is not a fault, as this is stated as a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*). He states another refutation with the words: "Moreover" (*api ca*). Since the result of valid cognition is experience (*anubhava*), it is only the past activity of the knower that is inferred; in that case, from where could there be the qualification of the object by valid cognition? Such is the meaning. He states the reason for this with the word: "no" (*na*).

That whose qualifier, called "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), is not present because it has passed away is described as such. The meaning is that at the time of the experience "the jar exists," since the means of valid cognition has already passed away, the jar would not appear as qualified by it, i.e., as "the jar exists. He states another objection with the words "and not" (*na ca*). The term *ciranikhātānidhayaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those [places] in which there are treasures buried long ago. And this is the reason for the certainty regarding the absence of a means of valid cognition. Alternatively, the two locative endings may be in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇe*).

In the phrase "santi," one should connect it by making "nidhayaḥ" (treasures) the nominative case. He concludes with "tasmāt" (therefore). Regarding "sadarthaḥ": the meaning is "the referent of the word 'sat'. Now he states that even an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*): "nāpnoti" (does not obtain). He provides the reason: "pramita... (because of what is cognized). The meaning is that since the word "sat" is not used in common parlance for something that has perished after being cognized, and because there is doubt regarding whether [something] exists or does not exist when it is merely being remembered.

[The opponent objects: "Surely, because the connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has already passed away, the non-application of the word 'existent' and the doubt regarding what has perished after being cognized will be justified. To this he replies: "Because it has occurred" (*vṛtta*). Even though it has passed away, it serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the application of the word; it has not perished [as an indicator]. Therefore, since even that which is past serves as an indicator of its having been a means of valid cognition, it must indeed be existent, not non-existent. And in the case of something being remembered, there would be certainty of existence alone, not doubt—this is the meaning. The term *vṛttapramāṇasaṃbandha* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that of which the connection with a means of valid cognition has occurred."

Now, let it be granted that there is neither a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*); nevertheless, it is precisely the fitness for being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇayogyatva*) that differentiates those two. Even so, existence (*sattā*) does not [belong to them].

It is established. And how is it said that even a single qualifier (*viśe�ṣaṇa*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? For that [qualifier] is said to be distinct for each object of cognition (*prameya*); there is no such thing as "fitness for being a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇayogyatva*). Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), one considers that the means of valid cognition itself must be understood here as either the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or the secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). If it is asked, "How can an object be an object of cognition (*prameya*) without fitness for being a means of valid cognition?", we say: no, for its status is established precisely through the capacity of the means of valid cognition, just as in the case of the past and the future.

For that which is non-existent, such as the past and the future, there is no fitness for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yogyatva*), because a property cannot subsist in the absence of a substratum (*dharmin*). Therefore, it has been said that fitness for a means of valid cognition alone should be the qualifier; what is the use of "existence" (*sattā*)? Furthermore, according to their logic of denying existence, they do not even accept a single [universal] fitness for a means of valid cognition, because since these [individual instances] are infinite, they cannot serve as the basis for the application of a single word.

As for the claim that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is distinct for each object of cognition (*prameya*) and not one and the same, that too has been shown to be untenable because it can be explained in the manner of [the term] "cook" (*pācaka*) and so forth. Now, he refutes the view that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) functions as either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) in the application of the word "existent" (*sat*): "Even that which... and so on. That which possesses causal efficiency is existent. In that case, prior to the production of the sprout, the seed would not be called "existent."

Now, if it is argued that in the case of the direct perception of a seed, the seed itself is also a producer [of that cognition], otherwise—since there would be no distinction in the capacity of the sense organ—the cognition would not be restricted to that specific object; therefore, even for this reason, the performance of a causal function (*arthakriyā*) consists solely in the production of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its own object, and consequently, the seed is designated as "existent" (*sat*); [we reply: that is not so. For if the cognition "it exists" were to arise only after one has first recognized the causal function called the production of a valid cognition, then it would not arise from the valid cognition itself. But such is not the case; the meaning is that the seed is known to "exist" at the very moment it is being cognized.

Now, non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, the cognition that "it exists" (*asti-buddhi*) is conceptual (*savikalpika*) because it is permeated by words. And conceptual cognition is preceded by non-conceptual cognition. Therefore, it is said that the cognition "it exists" occurs only after the [initial] means of valid cognition, and not from the means of valid cognition itself; the meaning is that, if this were so, the cognition "it exists" would not arise regarding fire and the like from a mark such as smoke. For inference is held to be exclusively conceptual.

The meaning is that there is no subsequent non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) therein, by the arising of which a subsequent conceptual cognition (*savikalpikā buddhiḥ*) of the form "it exists" might occur through purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Now, it might be argued: even if a non-conceptual cognition is not admitted in inference, and its existence is not grasped by a cognition of "it exists," nevertheless, the cause is to be inferred from the effect. Therefore, fire and so forth are subsequently cognized by means of the mark (*liṅga*) such as smoke, which has its relationship with the effect—such as smoke and the like—already ascertained in the form "this is the effect of that."

It has been stated that existence (*sattā*), which is characterized by the possession of effects such as smoke, is itself understood through the possession of effects such as smoke; to this he replies with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). Existence is the possession of effects. If that [possession of effects] is already known from fire and so forth, what further thing is being inferred? Furthermore, the idea that the possession of effects is understood through the possession of effects is unsound, because it is contradictory for one and the same thing to be both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). By this, the view that the possession of effects, while itself unknown, will be inferred through the possession of effects, is also refuted. [p. 210]

For that which is known is the means of proof (*sādhana*), while that which is unknown is the object to be proven (*sādhya*). And it is not possible for one and the same thing to be both known and unknown. [Objection: But even for you, there is certainly this same fault, since it is precisely the mark (*liṅga*) whose relationship has been known—as in "this is pervaded by that"—that brings about the cognition; [Reply: It is said: for me, the relationship exists between two universals (*sāmānya*), whereas the valid cognition (*pramā*) occurs in terms of particulars (*viśeṣa*); thus, this is not a fault. However, for the Buddhists, there is no universal, and this is the distinction. Furthermore, in the inference of "tree-ness" from "śiṃśapā-ness," the fact that the relationship with the effect is already known should also be understood to apply.

Furthermore, for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda), at the time of the effect-moment, the cause-moment is non-existent; therefore, this [cause] does not possess the qualification of being an effect. Consequently, with the intention that the existence of the cause would thus be impossible, he says: "The effect... (kārya...). Now, if it is argued that "possessing an effect" is merely an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) for the application of the word "existent" (sat), that too is not so, because of the previously mentioned fault; thus he says: "Now... (atha). He concludes: "Therefore... (tasmāt).

Just as the referent of words such as "blue" is not something characterized by its effect or its means of cognition—such that one might say, "the referent of the word 'blue' is that which has this as its effect or that which has this as its means of cognition"—because there would be an infinite regress: the effect and the means of cognition themselves would have to be characterized by another effect and another means of cognition, and those two by yet others, and so on.

Moreover, the meaning is this: just as [entities] established by their own nature are determined according to the means of knowledge—insofar as a means of knowledge is merely that which makes something known—so too is the word "existent" (sat). Expounding upon what was stated regarding the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), he confirms that its own referent is not characterized by being an object of a causal means of knowledge (*kāryapramāṇa*), using the words beginning with "kārya. The phrase "of that" (*tasya*) means "of the distinction in linguistic usage" (*vyavahāravibhāga*).

Having thus fortified his own position, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). When the position that the meaning of the word "existent" is "fitness for being a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇayogyatā*) has been refuted under the view that existence is not a single entity, he turns back and anticipates a counter-argument regarding the position that existence is indeed fitness for being a means of valid cognition, saying: "Now" (*atha*).

If existence (*sattā*) were the very nature of an object consisting in its fitness for being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yogyatvam*), then even in the case of the Vedāntas—which are established in the sense of "it exists"—the opponent’s position that "that which is established in the sense of 'exists' is dependent [on other means of knowledge]" would be abandoned, because they do not depend on other means of valid cognition. However, if that fitness consists in the possibility of the causes of a means of valid cognition, then when the cause exists, a means of valid cognition must necessarily follow. Therefore, since there is dependence [only in this sense], there is no abandonment of the subject under discussion. Nor does it follow from this that things such as a human horn would possess existence; to this he says: "And not... (*na ca*).

And by this much, it has been stated that practical activity (*vyavahāra*) arises from the existence of the cause that is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Although there is a refutation here—namely, that if the cause known as the "river-flood" exists, then even a past rain would have to exist—nevertheless, because this has already been mentioned previously and because there is room for a further response, he states another refutation with the word "that" (*tat*). By saying "on the ground, in a windless place," he indicates the absence of the cause of perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is sensory contact, due to the fact that the ground portion is concealed; by "without a mark" (*nirliṅga*), he indicates the absence of the mark (*liṅga*) which is the cause of inference (*anumāna*);
and by "unperceived and unestablished" (*avedya-anupapanna*), [he indicates the absence of the cause of verbal testimony].

The reason for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is that which cannot be otherwise accounted for (*anyathānupapanna*). The analysis of the compound is: "that in which [the fact] being known is not otherwise accounted for. Likewise, regarding the reason consisting of tradition (*āgama*), it is said to be "one whose observer has perished. And as for analogy (*upamāna*), because its object is similarity, it is utterly remote from being a cause for the cognition of the actual nature of a hidden treasure. Thus, the substance of a hidden treasure transcends the applicability of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); yet it is not non-existent, but rather doubtful. The meaning is that according to your position, it would be non-existent, and not merely doubtful.

Now, [the opponent argues that] existence is not the presence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or its cause; rather, existence is said to be a certain specific excellence residing in the object itself, which is fit for a means of valid cognition. To this we reply: that too is not correct, as it involves the fallacy of abandoning the subject under discussion (*prakṛtahāna*) and other faults. He explains the verse differently: "Alternatively" (*athavā*). It is said that "existent" (*sat*) is that which is qualified by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaviśiṣṭa*). Therefore, when there is doubt regarding the presence or absence of a means of valid cognition, a doubt such as "Is it existent or non-existent?"—informed by the word "existent" which denotes being qualified by a means of valid cognition—is appropriate.

Regarding the treasure (nidhi), however, because there is a certainty that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are absent, there would be a certainty of its non-existence, not a doubt; this is the meaning. Furthermore, existence is not fitness for being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇayogyatā*), because that [fitness] exists even for a non-existent absence (*abhāva*); therefore, with the intention that [existence] would thus also not exist, he says "Moreover" (*apica*). Some are in disagreement regarding the fact that absence is an object of valid cognition; for that purpose, he establishes that it is indeed an object of cognition, saying "For instance" (*tathāhi*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the refutations, or it has the sense of "even"—not only the existent, but even the supreme non-existent.

In whatever manner—whether as being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or as being devoid of all causal capacity—the opponent establishes non-existence, in that very form it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*). Why? Because if it is measured (known) in that way, in that form, why is it thus of that nature, and not otherwise, i.e., of another nature? He explains this very point with the words "And not... (*na ca*). "Attachment to one side" (*ekapakṣānurāga*) means that between the two states of being thus and not being thus, attachment to one side without a means of valid cognition is not tenable.

He states another reason for the fact that non-existence (*abhāva*) is an object of cognition (*prameya*), beginning with "furthermore" (*api ca*). Non-existence is indeed an object of cognition; otherwise, how could one place a foot upon the ground or similar surfaces after having cognized—that is, determined—the absence of a thorn? If it is argued that the placing of the foot does not result from the determination of the absence of a thorn, but rather from the determination of something else, such as the ground which is other than the thorn, he says in response: "not of another" (*nānya*).

The placement of the foot does not result from the cognition of something else, such as the ground; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of placing the foot even when grasping something else like the ground while a thorn is present. Furthermore, since it is possible to grasp some other thing even before grasping the ground, there would be the consequence of placing the foot right there [on that other thing]. Now, if it is argued that it is not due to the grasping of another, but rather that the placement of the foot depends on the absence of the cognition of the thorn; then, because a subtle thorn or the like might pass by unnoticed, the placing of the foot would occur, yet there would be no inquiry into it.
Therefore, even due to the absence of the cognition of the thorns and so forth, there is no placing of the foot; thus, it is solely from the determination of non-existence that this occurs.

This is the meaning. "From effort" means from an effort directed toward ascertainment. The purport of the passage beginning with "preceded by a desire to know" and ending with "is appropriate" is as follows: according to the view that there is no delimitation (*apariccheda*), the subtle desire to know is fruitless; however, if there is a delimitation (*pariccheda*) of what is to be delimited, then it is fruitful. Furthermore, it is not the mere non-delimitation of the throat that is the object of the desire to know, because prior to its delimitation, it is already established by itself, and thus the desire to know would be deficient. Moreover, that which is to be known (*prameya*) is the object of the desire to know.

And "non-discrimination" (*apariccheda*) is the absence of discrimination; moreover, an absence is not an object of knowledge (*prameya*). Therefore, the meaning is that it is not something to be investigated. Now, if it is thought: "The act of stepping forward does not occur merely due to the non-discrimination of thorns and the like, but rather because, while the eyes and other organs—which are the causes for perceiving thorns and so forth—are present, there is a non-discrimination of that subtle thing which exists and is capable of becoming an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," to that he says: "That is incorrect. That is incorrect.

The sense is that since no utility for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is observed here in this non-delimitation, it would therefore have only an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). To the question "Where, indeed, is this useful?", he says: "asat" (non-existent). The word "hi" has the sense of "tu" (but); however, in the case of the cognition of absence (*abhāvabodha*), the status of being an object of a means of valid cognition is useful. How so? By virtue of having no other cause. From the non-delimitation of thorns and the like, there arises the cognition of their absence.

Non-apprehension (*apariccheda*) is of two kinds: that caused by the deficiency of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or that caused by the absence of the object itself, such as a thorn. Among these, non-apprehension caused by the deficiency of the means of valid cognition is not a cause for determining the absence of existence, because it can occur even when the object exists. However, non-apprehension occurring when the means of valid cognition are complete is a cause for determining the absence of the object. Thus, the meaning is that when the conditions for apprehension are present, the fact of being an object of a means of valid cognition is what serves to produce the cognition of absence.

If it is argued that the placement of the foot occurs because of the apprehension of something else, and that even when thorns and the like exist, [the placement] would occur if there were an apprehension of the ground alone—as has been stated—the author anticipates the opponent's view with the word "atha" (now). "Now, where the activity of placing the foot occurs on a portion of the ground or the like, there it occurs through the cognition of the ground alone. Therefore, it is said that in the presence of thorns and the like, it does not occur because of the absence of such exclusivity. To this, he replies with the words "jijñāsetā" (by the desire to know).

In this regard, the following must be examined: Is this isolation (*kaivalya*) characterized by the cognition of the ground appearing as the ground alone? Or does it belong to the ground, which is the object of the cognition? Even if it belongs to the object, is its isolation [due to] its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), or due to the absence of qualifying attributes (*viśeṣaṇa*)? If the first alternative is held, then in a case such as a thorn where the ground appears [only] because of its subtlety, there would be a placement of the foot due to the isolation of consciousness (*saṃvitti*).

Or rather, it is for that purpose that the person acts. Nor is the mere nature of the object, such as the bare ground, desired in its absolute isolation; for even when the ground is mixed with thorns and the like, its essential nature remains unaltered, which would entail the consequence of one stepping upon it. If, on the other hand, it is desired through its connection with a qualification, then [it is the ground] as qualified by its isolation—[p.

The meaning is that since there is no other [object] such as a thorn, it cannot be a qualifier of another; thus, it follows that the placement of the foot occurs precisely through the determination of the absence of the thorn, which establishes the status of absence (*abhāva*) as an object of cognition (*prameya*). "Restriction to a single object" (P. 98.9) is an explanation of the isolation of this cognition. "Non-connection with other objects" is an explanation of that restriction; the meaning is that its object is exclusively the ground. He says "moreover" (*api ca*) to show that for this reason as well, absence is an object of cognition. "What is being trampled? means:

The meaning is: "What is the offense? In the verse, the mention of *dhī* (cognition) is illustrative; *śabda* (word) should also be understood. Since the scope of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is precisely the scope of cognition and word, it is not mentioned separately in the commentary, as it is already established by the definition of those two. Alternatively, *vyavahāra* is a word (*śabda*), in the sense that "by this [word] one communicates. He explains the verse with the words "Moreover" (*apica*). For one for whom non-existence is not an object of knowledge (*prameya*), he must state the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the cognition and the word "it does not exist"—namely, what is the support for these two?

In this regard, first of all, the entity of the ground itself is not the object of these two [cognition and word], because it would follow that the cognition and the word "it does not exist" would apply even to a ground mixed with thorns and the like. Nor is the entity of the bare ground their object; for in that case, they would have the absence of thorns and so forth as their object, since no qualifier called "bareness" other than the absence [of those things] is possible—as it has been said: "There is no qualifier other than the absence of another. The opponent says: It is a contradiction to say that what is non-existent and indefinable is precisely what is apprehended.

Therefore, it is not that non-existence (*abhāva*) is cognized by the word "it does not exist," but rather that the meaning of this [word] is "it is not cognized as existing. To this, it is replied: in that case, the absence of cognition would be the object of both the cognition and the word "it does not exist. And if that were so, what fault would there be in [accepting] the absence of the object of knowledge (*prameyābhāva*), such that you bypass it and claim that the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) is the object of these two? This is the sense. He raises the opponent's view with the words "Now, if... (*atha*).

The meaning is that when there is no apprehension—that is, no cognition—of the thorn and so forth, there arises the delusion of apprehending a non-existent thing, which is a delusion of perceiving an absence; likewise, when there is an absence of the linguistic usage regarding the thorn, there occurs the error of the linguistic usage of an absence. However, it does not mean that the apprehension of an absence or the linguistic usage of an absence actually exist. He states that the non-perception of what was previously seen is a delusion of perception: "in the case of non-seeing" (adṛṣṭau); the meaning is that just as when light is not seen, there is the delusion of seeing darkness, such as thinking "I see darkness."

When the opponent has stated that there can be neither the cognition nor the linguistic usage "it does not exist," and the proponent has questioned how this is so, the opponent replies again with the words "it is said. One should construe the text as follows: [The opponent objects: "But surely the object darkness itself is visible, and it is not merely the absence of light; thus, the illustrative example is unestablished. Anticipating this objection, he says: "For indeed... If darkness were a visible object, then, because it possesses color, it would be perceptible by the eye; consequently, it would not be seen by a blind person. Yet even such a person perceives it.
Therefore, the intention is that it is merely an illusion. He refutes this: "Not so... [p. 214]

He asks "Why? and replies with the word "Thus" (*ittham*). According to what you have stated—that the perception of non-existence occurs upon the non-perception of existence—there would arise the delusion of perceiving the absence of the three worlds during the states of deep sleep, intoxication, and fainting, because there is no perception of them then; yet this is not the case. [Objection: But how can there be delusion for one who is in deep sleep, whose collection of sense organs has ceased to function? [Reply: True, but erroneous cognition (*anyathākhyāti*) is produced by the sense organs, whereas non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) is not. This was said with the intention that you yourself are an adherent of the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyātivādin*).

But surely, non-apprehension of discrimination (*vivekākhyāti*) also occurs between that which is being remembered and that which is being perceived; yet these two do not exist for one who is in deep sleep. Therefore, how can this delusion consist of non-apprehension? It is said in reply: we shall explain immediately after this that those two do not exist in the delusion consisting of the perception of existence and non-existence.

Thus, if there were an error here even without the perception of non-existence, then one might think that even for a person in deep sleep, there would be the error of perceiving the non-existence of the three worlds due to not seeing them; thinking this, the author has raised an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by stating, "In this way, it would occur in deep sleep and so forth. Therefore, there is no fault. Furthermore, for anyone who does not discern anything at all, an error would not be possible.

For instance—one who does not know the mother-of-pearl, which is the locus of superimposition (*āropaviṣaya*), nor the silver, which is the object superimposed (*āropya*), does not experience the delusion of silver. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Not by non-existence" (*nābhāvena*). "Conduct" (*vyavahāra*) means that which is conducted; for she (the delusion) is conducted as qualified by non-existence; thus the meaning is "conduct regarding non-existence. And the absence of that [delusion] does not fall within the domain of cognition, i.e., is not an object of the intellect. This is what is meant: you maintain that when there is an absence of conduct regarding existence, there occurs the delusion of conduct regarding non-existence.

In that case, the absence of the conventional usage of existence has as its object of superimposition the mother-of-pearl (as the locus), while the conventional usage of non-existence is that which is superimposed as silver. Furthermore, for one who maintains that non-existence is an object of valid cognition (*prameya*), those two [the locus and the superimposed] cannot be known [simultaneously]. Therefore, error would be impossible. The phrase "conventional usage is not distinct from non-existence" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be stated that the cognition of non-existence, mentioned in the preceding verse, is likewise intended. For this very reason, he says: "And there is no absence of cognition. [He adds: "Otherwise..."

The meaning is as follows: regarding the ignorance of both the locus of superimposition (*āropa-viṣaya*) and the object superimposed (*āropya*): if there is ignorance of both, then there is non-apprehension; if there is ignorance of the locus of superimposition alone, then there is the recollection of silver; if there is ignorance of the object superimposed alone, then there is the perception of the general property (*sāmānya*) of the substance present before one, whose specific features are not determined. Here, the intention is that from the ignorance of both, there would indeed be non-apprehension; however, the mention of recollection and the apprehension of the general property is stated incidentally. Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "nor the absence of cognition," the ignorance of the locus of superimposition has been explained.

The distinction is that, by the words "not the cognition of absence" and so forth, it is shown that ignorance is what is superimposed. In the case of "cognition of absence" and "usage of absence," absence (*abhāva*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); however, in the case of "absence of cognition" and "absence of usage," it is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, the phrase "of the qualifier" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), and it should be understood to apply to the qualificand as well. Furthermore, he states that the example "darkness is seen when there is no seeing" is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*)—namely, "darkness. In that context, the statement "that which is shadow" was made by relying on the Puranic view; for it is said in the Purāṇa [p. 215]: [The text continues with the Puranic citation.]

Regarding the phrase “because of the hearing of qualities belonging to real entities,” here the state of being a quality of a real entity (*bhūtaguṇatva*) is stated merely as dependence upon a substance (*bhū*), but shadow is not a quality; for it is perceived separately from a substance, and is rather another substance. It possesses qualities, and that which possesses qualities is a substance. Its quality is dimension (*parimāṇa*), known as large or small. And it is mobile. Therefore, because it possesses action, it is also a substance; as it has been said: “large, small, moving, and unmoving.”

That [shadow] is produced by means of subtle visible parts, having taken some substance as its substrate, just as a flame is produced by means of fiery parts depending upon wood. For this very reason, the flame follows after the substance; and that [shadow] is also a substance, because it possesses the nature of a real entity (*bhāva*). Furthermore, the existence of the subtle is established by the gross itself as its mark, as in the case of earth and other elements. Or, just as air is formless yet possesses touch, so too shadow possesses both form and touch, due to the manifoldness of the nature of entities (*bhāva*). Therefore, it has the essential nature of a real entity (*bhāva*). And for this very reason, it is perceptible to the eye (*cākṣuṣa*).

However, as for the view of one who holds that shadow is simply the absence of light—since it exists when there is an absence of light and does not exist when light is present—why resort to the burden of conceptualizing [it as a substance]? For when light is removed from a large area by a large tree, the shadow is large, and when removed by a small [tree], it is small. Furthermore, it is mobile with respect to substance; wherever the light is removed, there the shadow appears to move. But since it is neither large nor small nor mobile [in itself], no substance is established thereby; thus, according to that view, it is said that [shadow] is indeed the absence of light.

[Objection: But in that case, how can a blind person—who does not see either a shadow or the absence of light—have the perception of darkness? [Reply: It is said: Just as for one who has never seen silver, an error consisting in the mere appearance of a similar object arises even though the mother-of-pearl has not been seen and the light is not perceived; this is possible. As for the statement that "one who does not know both the locus of superimposition and the object superimposed cannot have the delusion of silver," that refers to a delusion regarding a specific object such as silver, and thus there is no contradiction.

Now, having accepted existence as fitness for being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yogyatā*), he says "Let it be" (*astu*) to show that even if the Vedāntas are established in the sense of "existence," they do not suffer from the defect of dependence on other means of knowledge. Let existence indeed be fitness for being an object of valid cognition; let that very [fitness], which is the referent of the word "exists," be the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for the Vedāntas. Thus, when that fitness for being an object of valid cognition has been cognized, the existence of the entity Brahman—which is fit for that [cognition]—becomes the meaning of the Vedāntas.

What has been stated is that the establishment of the authority of the Vedāntas regarding the nature of Brahman, as well as the establishment of the nature of Brahman itself, occurs by way of the valid cognition of its fitness (*yogyatā*). Nor is there the defect of dependence on other means of knowledge; why? Because there is no intermingling with other means of knowledge. For where the establishment of an object depends upon another means of knowledge through contact with that other means, there dependence is a cause of defect.

In this case, however, only this much is understood: "this is fit for a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇayogya*); there is no commingling or contact with another means of valid cognition; that is to say, the establishment of the object does not depend on another means of valid cognition. Therefore, there is no dependence (*sāpekṣatā*). For instance—even those who assert that existence (*sattā*) is nothing other than being graspable by a means of valid cognition or having a connection with a means of valid cognition—they too [must admit] an intermediate state of the object's distinctness from other means of valid cognition.
[Page 216]

They do not desire a confusion [of categories], as it has been said: "Because the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is included within the range of the objects of valid cognition (prameya), they do not [desire it]. By them also, another means of valid cognition should not be sought through contact with another means of valid cognition; how much less so by those who assert that existence (sattā) is the fitness residing in the object, which constitutes the very nature of the object. "That is the object of valid cognition" (tat-prameyam) means that the object of valid cognition exists through an inseparable connection (avinābhāva) with that existence. Here, the opponent raises an objection: "How?"

When the Vedāntic statement, which culminates in the sense of "existence," has its operation exhausted merely in [establishing] the fitness [of the object], and does not thereby convey the existence of the qualified Brahman—that is, of the fit [Brahman] characterized by the fitness of having the nature of bliss and so forth—then, for the sake of establishing the existence of that qualified object, why should one not depend upon whatever means of knowledge that object is fit for? On the contrary, it must indeed be depended upon; this is the meaning. The proponent, however, asks: "For what purpose? The opponent replies: "For the sake of the qualified [object]," and so on.

The meaning is that a statement whose terminus is the sense of "existence" (asti) ceases its operation once it has conveyed mere fitness; it does not bring about the cognition of the actual existence of a qualified object. Therefore, another means of knowledge must be sought for that purpose. Again, the proponent asks: "What?"—that is to say, what is this actual existence of the qualified object, for the cognition of which, having not been conveyed by the statement whose terminus is the sense of "existence," another means of knowledge must be sought? The opponent replies: "By a means of knowledge. The proponent says: "It is already cognized."

If the fitness for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇayogyatva*) constitutes the existence of a qualified object, then, in that case, that [existence] is already understood because speech is directed toward the meaning of "is" (*astyartha*); for the meaning is that the very fitness for a means of valid cognition is the meaning of "is. Although there is an answer to the effect that no other means of valid cognition need be required for that purpose—since it has been stated that what is fit is established through its invariable concomitance with fitness—nevertheless, another answer has been stated because the former answer was not fully developed.
