It has been stated that because there is no commingling with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no fault of invalidity in the Vedānta texts which have as their object an existent reality; now, however, he says—"pramāṇāntara..."—that even if one admits a commingling with other means of valid cognition, there is still no fault. The word "no" has a prohibitive sense. Even that speech whose object is distinct from—that is, conjoined with—another means of valid cognition is not non-authoritative, but is indeed authoritative, just like the statement of a trustworthy person (*āpta*). [Objection: But if its object is distinct from another means of valid cognition, then it would be dependent (*sāpekṣa*).

Anticipating the objection as to how that which is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could be independent, he says: "independent" (*nirapekṣam*). The meaning is this: regarding the word "that" (*yat*), which refers back to what was intended by the pronoun [in the previous verse], namely, "this object has been cognized by me"—here, in this sense consisting of the speaker's intention, when it is not cognized through another means of valid cognition by the listener, but is understood from the word alone without depending on anything else, then that speech is "independent. For instance, from a human utterance, the cognition is "this person knows it thus," but not "the object is thus."

By the statement of the speaker, "It has been cognized by me," the manifestation of his own means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is expressed; however, the listener understands it as, "It has been cognized by him. To the question, "In what respect, then, is that [the listener's understanding] dependent upon it? he says:

Regarding the word "artha" (object): that statement is dependent upon something else with respect to the mere object. He states the reason for this: "anyāpekṣaḥ" (P. 95-18). The meaning is that it makes the object known by means of the speaker’s own authority, and not independently of it. It is "dependent on another" (*anyāpekṣa*) because it requires another—the speaker’s authority—for its own establishment; that [authority] and the object itself constitute the "object dependent on another" (*anyāpekṣārtha*). Therefore, "from the making known of the object dependent on another" means from the cognition of that object.

Thus, since that speech makes its meaning known independently of any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for apprehending the speaker’s form, it attains validity due to that independence; and it is established that the object [of knowledge] is reached through that [speech]. Now, it was argued that the object depends upon that [speaker]; therefore, how can validity be asserted in that regard? There is no fault, because it is said that the object is validated by that [speech] with the intention of referring merely to its non-contradiction regarding the object, since the object is uncontradicted.

Now, one might object: "If even a statement that is dependent [on other means of knowledge] is considered a valid authority (*pramāṇa*) provided its meaning is not sublated, then why is the human speech regarding the worship of *caityas* and so forth declared to be invalid due to the defect of dependence, even though its meaning is not sublated? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is un-sublated. Although there is no sublation of the object in that case, nevertheless, the foundational authority of the speaker is itself sublated; for instance, that speech does not have perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the like as its basis, because *dharma* is not within their scope.

Furthermore, the Buddha does not possess a connection with the Veda as Manu and others do. Thus, in respect to the factor of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he is sublated by that [Veda]; and due to the absence of that [connection], he is also sublated in respect to the object (*artha*). As it has been said: "In that case, the possibility of its being subject to exception arises from human incapacity. This means that because a person lacks the capacity to perceive *dharma*, there is the possibility of an exception—namely, a lack of validity—in such cases as the words of the Buddha. Therefore, neither in respect to the speaker’s authority nor in respect to the object does that [Buddhist teaching] attain the status of a valid means of knowledge.

In this manner, the same should be applied as far as possible even to the speech of an unreliable person (*anāpta*). Regarding the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*), however, he states its authority (*prāmāṇya*) by way of contrast to that: "The reliable person," etc. By the phrase "the portion that is a means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇāṃśa*), it is implied that the object (*artha*), on the other hand, is dependent [on other means]. Having thus established the authority of the speech of reliable persons even when there is contact with other means of valid knowledge, he states that the Vedāntas likewise possess authority even when there is contact with other means of valid knowledge: "By me," etc.

Since this is so regarding the words of a trustworthy person (āptavākya), for that very reason, the Vedāntas likewise should make known—by means of another means of knowledge called self-luminosity—that which is devoid of the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge, being free from the division such as "this is knowledge" and "this is the object of knowledge"; and precisely because of this, they are non-worldly (alaukika), meaning other than worldly perception and the like which are possessed of the distinction between knowledge and its object. And by way of establishing that [self-luminous reality], there is the establishment of the object—the reality of Brahman—just as in the case of the words of a trustworthy person.

The intention is this: even when there is a convergence with other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the authority of the Vedāntas is not undermined, just as in the case of the words of a reliable person (*āpta*). Is it then the case that there is no distinction at all between the Veda and human speech? No; for in the case of human speech, the listener understands the means of knowledge as being communicated through the speaker’s use of the statement, “This has been known by me. In the Veda, however, because of the absence of a speaker, one understands merely another means of knowledge, devoid of any contact with the word “by me.
This is what was stated: “devoid of the convergence [expressed by] ‘by me’” (p. 218).

Having thus concluded the argument based on concession (*abhyupagamavāda*), he summarizes the subject at hand with the word "thus" (*evam*). The term "knowability" (*meyatā*) is illustrative; "fitness for being a means of knowledge" (*mānayogyatā*) and so forth should also be understood. Here, the opponent objects: "But surely" (*nanu*). "Other" (*anyā*); that is to say, having the nature of a universal (*sāmānyarūpā*). He states the reason for this: "For not" (*na hi*). "Prior recognition" (*pūrvāvamarśaḥ*) refers to the subsequent reflective awareness of what was previously perceived in one individual within another individual.

The meaning is that for one by whom a mustard seed and the like are seen as "existent" (sat), it is not so with respect to Mount Meru within that same [category of] existence. Nor should a single universal (*jāti*) be postulated on the grounds that the application of the single word "existent" would otherwise be inexplicable; for, as in the case of "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth, it is explicable otherwise. Thus he says: "A single... etc. Although the similarity to "staff-bearers" and the like was already refuted previously, it is raised again here by relying on the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a "Being-ness" (*sattā*). The intention is: this is better than postulating a "Being-ness" that is not actually perceived. To this, he states the reply: "In this regard... etc.

The word *nu* is used for emphasis. As for this "prior reflection" (*pūrvāvamarśa*) mentioned by you as the cause for the conceptualization of a universal (*sāmānyakalpanāhetu*), what is it? The opponent replies: "Prior... [and so on]. The form or aspect of cognition regarding one individual (*vyakti*) previously perceived—that which follows, accompanies, or recurs in another individual (just as the form of "cowness" recurs in every instance in the cognition "this is a cow, that is a cow")—is called "prior reflection. To point out the flaw in that, he says: "In the case of another existent... (*sadantareti*).

For a person who has seen [something], that [object] indeed exists within the existent, even though many forms do not persist [in it], by some degree—that is, in the form of a mere portion; otherwise, just as the non-existent appears as utterly devoid of description and absolutely distinct [from the existent], so too would existents appear to be mutually absolutely distinct; but this is not the case. The word "khalu" (indeed) is used to indicate what is well-known. Now, if it is argued that there is no persistence of the previous form of the cognition in that [subsequent state] in its entirety, he says in response: "sarva... (all...).

However, the persistence of the prior form in its entirety does not exist even among individuals such as the broken-horned and hornless [cows]; the point is that, in that case, even the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth would not exist. If, on the other hand, there were a persistence of form in its entirety in those [individuals], then they would necessarily be one and the same. Consequently, it would follow that universals such as cowness do not exist; for a universal is not admitted to reside in a single individual—like space (*ākāśa*)—since it must have multiple individuals as its locus.

The mention of "the broken and the hornless" is an introduction of a distinction between individuals for the purpose of showing the absence of the persistence of form in its entirety. If it is argued that the kind of manifest persistence of form found in the broken and the hornless does not exist between "being" (*sat*) and another instance of "being," we reply: it is not then proper to deny the persistence of the cognizable form between "being" and another instance of "being" merely on account of internal differences.

Otherwise, since the recurrence of the form of cognition upon seeing Devadatta again is not the same as that which occurs in the case of individuals such as Khaṇḍa and others, even "cowness" (*gotva*) would have to be denied. The inclusion of the term "perceived" (*vedya*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the contradiction with consciousness (*saṃvit*) that would result from such a denial. Furthermore, it is not only in a single individual that the recurrence of the form of cognition is of such a nature; rather, it is the same in the case of individuals such as Khaṇḍa and others—namely, the recurrence of the form of cognition as the generality of clay (*mṛtsāmānya*).

Even the object of perception (*gocara*)—such as a water-jar (*maṇi*) or a begging bowl (*mallaka*)—is everywhere uniform in its conformity with the form of cognition (*buddhirūpānvaya*). To explain: the kind of conformity of form that arises among water-jars themselves is not the same as that which is seen in a water-jar compared to a begging bowl. And it does not follow from such internal difference alone that the water-jar and the like lack the universal of "clay" (*mṛjjāti*), because they appear as somewhat identical insofar as they consist of the nature of the universal of "clay. Now, regarding the synthesis of the prior and the subsequent expressed as "this is that," which constitutes the prior reflective awareness (*pūrvāvamarśa*), it is said here: "the prior... [and so on].

The phrase "like a broken jar" (*svaṇḍamuṇḍavat*) is an example of a dissimilarity (*vaiṣamyadṛṣṭānta*). Now, even if for one who has seen a jar there is no subsequent synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) such as "this is that very same [jar]" when looking at a small bowl (*mallaka*), nevertheless, for one who reflects, the thought "this belongs to the same class as that" arises later; therefore, the genus "clay" (*mṛjjāti*) is accepted in that case. Consequently, since this is observed in one existent thing, it is the same in another existent thing as well; so why not accept "Being" (*sattā*) too? He says this with the words: "for one who reflects."

Now, if—as in the case of water-jars (maṇika)—the universal "jar-ness" (maṇikatva) exists in both the jar and the small bowl (mallaka), then, since the possession of a commonality is equal for both, what is the reason that the recognition "this is that very same thing" occurs immediately in the case of the jars but not in the case of the jar and the bowl? To this question, the answer is given: "The commonality... and so on. "That indeed" means that non-difference shines forth as "this is that. In the case of the jars, there is a mutual clay-ness, jar-ness, and many recurring commonalities of parts.

The meaning is that because there is only the cognition of "jar-ness" (mṛttva) in the small jar (mallaka), the prior mental grasp (pūrvāvamarśa) occurs quickly with respect to the water-jars (maṇika), but not with respect to both the water-jar and the small jar. It was stated that "the application of a single word [to multiple objects] is possible, as in the case of 'staff-bearer' (daṇḍin) and so forth"; he refutes that by saying "pramāṇam" (the means of knowledge). The cognition "it exists" (asti-dhī) arises first, even before being conjoined with the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) which is to be inferred from the effect, namely, the valid cognition (pramiti); therefore, it is not caused by the conjunction with the means of knowledge. For if it were caused by that, then the cognition would arise only after the means of knowledge has arisen and been conjoined with it, and not beforehand.

For indeed, one does not become "possessing a staff" (*daṇḍin*) prior to the conjunction with the staff; therefore, the meaning is that there is no similarity to the case of [the cognition of] a staff-bearer and so forth. Nor is the cognition of existence itself the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is contradictory for a single cognition of existence to be both the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*); furthermore, since its own relation cannot be known by itself, all the aforementioned defects would follow as a consequence. This is the intended sense. Here, the opponent asks, with a view toward what has been observed: "If... (*yadi*).

If the object does not possess a connection with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could the object itself possess the three times—namely, "it was," "it is," or "it will be"—given that the connection with the means of valid cognition occurs across the three times? Therefore, the intention of that [opponent] is that the very connection with the means of valid cognition constitutes the meaning of "existence" (*asti*). To this, he states the reply: "That" (*tat*). The meaning of "existence" appears and is designated as possessing the three times through a distinction imagined by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of time. Thus, it is said that the meaning of "existence" is that which has its distinction imagined by the limiting adjunct of the time of the means of valid cognition.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Devadatta," etc. Just as the existence of Devadatta is conceptually constructed by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of a particular location...

The distinction [of existence] resides only there and not elsewhere; thus it is established by way of spatial distinction (*deśabheda*). Likewise, the meaning is that the distinction imagined through the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of temporal difference is established by way of temporal difference. This is what is meant: existence (*sattā*) is indeed the universal (*jāti*); and a universal is perceived through its individual instances (*vyakti*). Therefore, in whatever place or at whatever time an instance is perceived by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there [existence] shines forth and is designated; thus, its occurrence in all three times (*traikālyopapatti*) is established. Thus far, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been presented, having accepted for the sake of argument that there can be no connection between categories of meaning (*padārtha*) without action (*kriyā*).

11-10. [The opponent’s position was] refuted; now, however, he states that even that is unestablished—“saṃbandha... and so on. The connection between the king and his servant, as well as between two fruits, is understood merely as a relation; therefore, the syntactical connection is that they utter words which are "akriya," meaning devoid of such actions as "to be" (asti) and the like. The remainder is easy to understand.

Now, even if it were the case that there is no sentence devoid of a verb, and if, in the case of the verb "to be" (*asti*), the Upanishads were subject to the defect of dependence on other means of knowledge because the existence [denoted by] *as* is caused by its connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yoga*), nevertheless, we shall postulate the action of being born (*jani*). And birth is not caused by a connection with a means of valid cognition; therefore, there is no defect of dependence, and the nature of Brahman will be established. Thus he says: "birth."

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: from such a cause, which is conscious and of the nature of a divine form and so forth, this world arises; thus, even from a sentence that culminates in the act of originating or results in the state of having originated, a specific cause characterized by consciousness and other attributes can be understood. He states that this meaning is also supported by scripture with the words "And likewise": "From space alone" means "from Brahman. "They issue forth" means "they emerge"; "they merge" means "they dissolve."

Unable to tolerate the statement, "What has now come of [the authority of] injunction? the opponent objects, asserting that in the Vedāntas, an injunction must be resorted to for the purpose of connecting word-meanings, beginning with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). Those whose connection of meanings is dependent on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are so described. The analysis of the compound is: those whose mutual conjunction (*ātmasaṃśleṣa*) is dependent on an injunction. He demonstrates how, in the case of statements made by persons, the connection of word-meanings is dependent on another means of valid cognition, with the words "of the words" (*padānām*).

The syntactical arrangement (*samabhivyāhāra*)—the simultaneous utterance of words such as "fetch water from the well with a jar" which are mutually connected—fulfills the speaker’s intention regarding a specific meaning; that is, it conveys that meaning in its complete form. For that complete cognition is not derived from the single word "fetch" alone. Since the speaker's intention is established in respect to an object accessible through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), the connection between word-meanings (*padārthasaṃsarga*) in that case is dependent solely upon those other means of knowledge.

For instance: where there is contradiction by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is a lack of syntactic connection (*asaṃsarga*), as in the case of the sentence "jaradbhava" (O you who have become old) and so forth. In the Veda, however, because there is an absence of other means of valid cognition, it is for the sake of establishing that object which is the injunction (*niyoga*) in the form of a mandate; for an injunction has as its object a meaning qualified by the syntactic connection of word-meanings (*padārtha*). And [without such connection,] there is no syntactic connection of word-meanings... [p. 221]

Without [an injunction], there can be no establishment of a qualified object. Therefore, since the connection between word-meanings depends solely upon Vedic injunction (*vidhi*), an injunction must be resorted to. Now, one might object: "In the case of [the text] *satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma* (Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite), there is an understanding of a qualified object even without an injunction. To this he replies: *tadabhāve tu* ("But in its absence"). The meaning is that in the absence of an injunction—which is the cause for the connection [of words]—there is no connection of word-meanings in passages such as *satyaṃ jñānam*; therefore, whatever understanding of a qualified object occurs there is of a nature similar to error.

Regarding the phrase "for the accomplishment of the intended object": the meaning is, "How indeed might that entire collection of specific causal factors—the intended object such as the fetching of water—be brought to completion? [The opponent claims] "it cannot be accomplished by a single word"; that is, the complete object cannot be conveyed by a single word, nor can it be established by a single word. However, the proponent (siddhāntin), having raised various alternatives, refutes this with the words "In this case... (atra).

If it is argued that because the connection [of the word] with its object is apprehended by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), that connection is said to be dependent on another means of knowledge; that is incorrect, because that very connection is perceived by the sense of hearing even when it is *apūrva* (unprecedented) and not previously apprehended by another means of knowledge. The word "also" (*api*) is used in consideration of cases such as "fire is hot," where the connection is understood even though it has already been apprehended [by other means]. The phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: if the capacity to signify were restricted solely to that which has been apprehended by another means of knowledge.

By the words "not previously apprehended" (*anadhigata*) and so forth, [the author] further confirms that the hearer’s comprehension of an object not yet understood is precisely what is intended. Now, one might object: "Since it was already specifically stated earlier that 'the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) is established regarding an object accessible through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),' what is this criticism of something that was not mentioned? It is replied: This criticism is leveled here first because, once this point is refuted, the other will not follow; thus, by refuting this first, the other is also refuted, and there is no fault. Furthermore, it may be argued: if the relation were established as known through another means of knowledge, then the verbal statement would be redundant.

But this is not so; rather, by means of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), only the fitness for relation (*saṃsargayogyatā*) is cognized between the action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), and those [factors] are thus fit to be related with it. Therefore, in common worldly usage, the relation is dependent upon other means of knowledge. This is incorrect; for even in the Veda, the fitness for relation is indeed dependent upon other means of knowledge. To illustrate: in the injunction "He buys Soma with a one-year-old reddish-brown cow" (*aruṇayā ekahāyanyā somam krīṇāti*), the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) possesses the fitness for relation with the action because it functions as an instrumental factor (*karaṇakāraka*). Likewise, the mandate (*niyoga*) has as its object that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

The meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*); therefore, by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatva*), it alone is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), whereas substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) are not, because they are already established (*siddha*) and thus unfit. Thus, by the very power of fitness as understood through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [the relationship] is determined; consequently, even in the Veda, the connection (*saṃsarga*) would depend solely on the means of knowledge and not on the injunction. This is the sense. Having thus refuted this position, he now restates the position put forward by the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to refute it—starting with "Now" (*atha*). He refutes that with "In this way" (*evam*).

The intention to convey a specific meaning, such as "fetch water from the well with a jar," is not understood from the single word "fetch" alone; for from that word, only the act of fetching is perceived, and it remains undetermined as to what is fetched, by what means, or from where.

Because it is not useful for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), knowledge [of isolated word-meanings] is purposeless. Therefore, the cognition of the intention to speak a specific meaning does not occur with respect to word-meanings that are not mutually related. If it is argued that this [cognition] is brought about by the relation of the word-meanings themselves, it is replied: In that case, since it is prompted by the intention to speak, the relation of the word-meanings is based solely upon that [intention], and not based on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For no other means of valid cognition is either the cognizer or the motivator of that [relation].

As for the claim that, regarding what is established by other means of knowledge, the relation [of words] in common usage depends upon another means of knowledge according to the speaker's intention; to that it is replied: let there be an intention toward what is established by other means of knowledge, but there is no utility for another means of knowledge with respect to the relation itself, because the cognition of the relation between word-meanings occurs even without another means of knowledge, as in the case of the speech of an unreliable person.

As for the reason stated regarding the claim that "the relation [of words] is dependent on other means of valid cognition"—namely, that in cases such as the sentence "The old cow... there is no relation when there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition—it is replied: Granted, let there be no relation due to that contradiction; nevertheless, the relation does not arise from that [contradiction], because even in the case of the speech of a deceiver, that [relation] is indeed perceived. Furthermore, if something does not occur when another thing is contradicted, it cannot be dependent upon that [contradicted thing]; for it is not the case that "shade" is dependent on "heat" simply because shade does not exist when heat is contradicted.

Furthermore, the claim that there is no connection [of meaning] when there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is also unproven; for in the case of the speech of an unreliable person (*anāpta*), when there is such a contradiction, it is not the case that there is no connection, but rather a connection is indeed perceived. This, however, is the distinction of the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*): namely, that although a connection is perceived here, it is sublated by another means of valid cognition, whereas in the other case, no connection is perceived at all. If, in the case of the speech of an unreliable person, the perception of a connection had not even arisen to be sublated, then there would be no such thing as "false" speech distinct from the "meaningless."

Consequently, the threefold classification of speech established in common worldly usage—namely, "false," "meaningless," and "true"—would be contradicted. Now, if it is argued that a person, desiring to communicate an object already apprehended by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), conveys it to another through a sentence, then the object of the statement of a distinguished authoritative person (āpta) is simply that apprehension by another means of valid cognition; and it is "distinguished" by virtue of having a distinguished object as its content, not intrinsically, because [the cognition] is devoid of form (nirākāra). Furthermore, the distinguished object is that which is accomplished through the relation of word-meanings (padārtha-saṃsarga).

[The relation] is to be established by a single word, because that [word] has only the general property (*sāmānyamātra*) as its object. Therefore, since that specific [relation] is not understood from the sentence regarding word-meanings that are unconnected, it implies their connection. However, in the case of the Veda, since there is an absence of any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) that could serve to prompt the connection between word-meanings, the connection is not established; thus it is said that an injunction (*vidhi*) must be resorted to for its establishment. To this we reply: even if there is no apprehension through another means of knowledge in the Veda, nevertheless, an injunction need not be resorted to therein.

What, then, is it that brings about the connection between word-meanings (*padārtha*) in that case? It is the qualified object itself, whose nature is Brahman—truth, knowledge, and infinite. If, in the case of human speech, the object is something apprehended through other means of knowledge, and therefore that [human statement] brings about the connection of word-meanings for its own comprehension, then since the object of the Vedāntas is the qualified Brahman consisting of bliss and so forth, that very [Brahman] will bring about the connection of word-meanings within the Vedāntas for its own comprehension; what need is there for an injunction? Thus it is said. Now, [page 223]...

The capacity of words is to be understood through worldly usage; and in the world, it is observed that the apprehension of a means of knowledge other than verbal testimony (pramāṇāntara) is the motivator for the connection of word-meanings. Therefore, since such [external] means are absent in the Vedāntas, a qualified meaning cannot be the motivator for the connection of word-meanings; thus it is said that an injunction (vidhi) must be resorted to. Consequently, even if there were an injunction in the Vedāntas, because the external means of knowledge that serves as the motivator is absent, and because an injunction itself is non-worldly (alaukika), no connection of meanings would be possible.

Therefore, the intention is that there is the affliction of imagining the presence of injunctions (*vidhi*) with respect to them from the perspective of [ordinary] perception. Now, if words were intended solely for the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*), the cognition of a qualified object would be untenable; furthermore, since there is no practical activity (*vyavahāra*) based on mere word-meanings, and because the employment of words for those meanings would thus be unjustified, there arises an *arthāpatti* (presumption). By means of this *arthāpatti*, it is understood that the employment of words has as its purport the relation (*saṃsarga*) itself.

However, it is not the case that [the sentence] has as its purport a specific relation necessitated by the apprehension of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), because both usage and comprehension are possible even without such a relation, through the mere purport of a relation. Therefore, it might be argued that even in the absence of apprehension by other means of knowledge, a relation would indeed exist if there were an injunction; but that is not so, because in common worldly experience the apprehension of other means of knowledge is not a necessary factor. For even without it, the understanding of a qualified meaning in the Vedāntas is established solely through the capacity of words to have as their purport a mere relation.

Therefore, what is the use of a formal injunction? Now, if it is argued that in the world, the connection [of meanings] is not necessitated by the apprehension of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather is produced solely by the words' own orientation toward connection; and that the truth of the connection depends upon other means of valid cognition—for instance, even in cases where the listener has no means of valid cognition, there too, because the words of the Buddha and others would be untrue without the speaker's means of valid cognition, the connection acquires truth only through another means of valid cognition arising in the speaker; [we reply:]...

If it is argued that, even though not produced by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its truth is dependent on another means of knowledge, and thus in common worldly usage a connection (*saṃsarga*) is said to be dependent on another means of knowledge; let it be so in the world. However, in the case of the Veda, because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), there is an absence of contact with the authority of a speaker; since the determination of its meaning occurs independently, there is no need for another means of knowledge even for the sake of its truth. For the truth of the connection is understood from the word itself; therefore, it is based solely upon the word.

This being the case, the intended meaning is that in the Vedāntas, an injunction is not enjoined for the sake of the knowledge of a relation, nor for the sake of its truth. Now, let it be as it may in the world; however, an objection is raised regarding the Veda: "How is it so?"—that is, how can it be said that in the Veda the relation between word-meanings is dependent upon an injunction? For an injunction does not denote either relation in general or a specific relation.

Now, if it is argued that an injunction has a qualified object and does not have a single word-meaning as its object, and that the establishment of a qualified object is not possible without a relation (*saṃsarga*), and therefore an injunction would be purposeless if it lacked a relation and thus had no object—therefore, it must imply a relation—this is not so. For this same principle applies equally even when the matter is stated by a word other than the injunctive word; since another word-meaning also leads to the comprehension of a qualified meaning.

It is employed for its own establishment. Here it is objected: "How indeed can there be a specific comprehension of its own meaning? It is for this purpose that the relation between word-meanings is conveyed by the word; that is to say, without the relation of word-meanings, there is no establishment of the qualified meaning, and without that, there is no cognition of a new (transcendental) meaning.

Since every individual object (*padārtha*) has already been cognized previously at the time of knowing the relation [between words and their meanings], the words are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the relation by way of denoting objects associated with that relation. Words do not cause their own meanings to be understood as being restricted solely to themselves; rather, they are for the sake of the comprehension of a qualified meaning, because only in this way is practical activity (*vyavahāra*) possible. And this being so, there is an expectancy for a relation for each individual object.

Therefore, since any other word-meaning (*padārtha*) is also devoid of purpose without a relation (*saṃsarga*), it is capable of implying that very relation; what, then, is the speciality of an injunction (*vidhi*)? And thus, even without an injunction, in the Vedāntas, the word-meanings such as "Being" (*satya*) and "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) will be employed for the sake of their mutual relation; what is the use of an injunction? This is the sense. In common worldly usage, it is improper for words intentionally employed by an intelligent agent to be purposeless; therefore, their status as having a relational meaning is appropriate there. However, in the case of the Veda, since there is no evidence for the meaningfulness of word-meanings being produced unintentionally, it is not so.

If it is argued that even if a word-meaning is devoid of purpose when it does not imply a relation, let it be so; yet it is not capable of implying a relation. Therefore, a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) is resorted to there for the sake of establishing that relation—if this is said, it is not so; for even in the Veda, the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) is the authority for its meaningfulness. As for what was said—that because words used with conscious intent in common worldly usage must not be meaningless, they must convey a relation—that is without substance.

Since you do not assert that these [injunctions] possess the status of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for what reason would a positive injunction (*vidhi*) not be useless? For it too, being Vedic, possesses meaning like any other word-meaning, as there is no difference in the absence of a valid means of knowledge [to establish its purpose]. Therefore, the intention is that it too would not bring about a connection [with a result]. And if there were futility for those employed intentionally without a connection [to a result], let it be so.

Nevertheless, without the capacity of word-meanings to denote their own referents as prompted by a mutual relation (*saṃsarga*), that relation cannot be apprehended, as it would lack any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For if it were apprehended through a non-valid means of knowledge, then because there is no distinction in being non-valid, the apprehension of any random relation whatsoever would follow, rather than a specific one. Therefore, this must necessarily be accepted: that the capacity of word-meanings to convey their own referents as prompted by a mutual relation is understood from linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

If this is so, then even in the Vedānta, the exclusion of the connection between the referents of such terms as "Being," "Infinite," and "Knowledge" is equally present; therefore, what is the need for an injunction (*vidhi*) for that purpose? Alternatively, it might be argued that while other words besides those expressing an injunction may be employed to denote a matter already established by another means of knowledge, an injunctive word itself is not used in that way, because an injunction is not within the scope of any other means of knowledge.

Therefore, "injunction" (vidhi) is the meaning of that which enjoins; since it is measured from an injunctive word as something not otherwise obtainable—that is, not within the scope of other means of knowledge—it is therefore an object that is both "unprecedented" (apūrva), even while being dependent on other means of knowledge, and yet possesses a composite form.

One might argue that [the injunction] would project the connection preceded by the association [of word-meanings]; however, the other [element], namely the word-meaning established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), being merely restated exactly as it is established by that other means of knowledge, is brought under the control of the "restraint" (*aṅkuśa*) of that other means of knowledge and would not project a previously unknown object. Therefore, even if an injunction is not explicitly heard in the Vedāntas, one must still assume an injunction for the sake of the connection between word-meanings. If this is argued, it is incorrect; for in this way, the cognition of the relationship of that word with its meaning would be denied by an injunction that does not fall within the scope of any other means of knowledge.

Furthermore, even for one who has not mastered the language and does not know the relationship [between word and meaning], there would be activity prompted by a word that is injunctive; yet this is not the case. Moreover, if this were so, the word would overstep its own nature—which consists in its dependence on the knowledge of the relationship—and would instead adopt the nature of the sentence, which is characterized by independence from such knowledge.

Otherwise, if the cognition of the relationship were denied, then since the word for that [related] object would lack the capacity to produce a cognition of the relationship when the injunction is unknown, the injunction would result in being "established by another," meaning established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And that being the case, there would be no distinction between the injunction and other objects of words, as both would be equally mere restatements (*anuvāda*). Therefore, the meaning is that just as another object of a word—being a restatement—is unable to imply a novel connection (*apūrva-saṃsarga*), so too is the injunction.

It has been stated that the knowledge of a relationship is impossible in the case of an injunction (*niyoga*) which is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To this, he raises the view of another school—the view of the opponent—with the words "from the word" (*śabdāt*). [The opponent holds: "The knowledge of the relationship does not occur when the meaning of the injunction is ascertained by another means of valid cognition; rather, it occurs when it is ascertified by the injunctive word itself. Even for one who maintains that the grasp of the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācaka-sambandha*) takes place with that very word, the same [objection] applies"—this is to be connected with what follows later. [Objection: But in that case, the knowledge of the relationship would occur once the meaning of the injunction is known from the word.

Fearing that if there were knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning], there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*) insofar as knowledge arises from the word, he says: "not a circular dependency. Nor is there the fault of the defect known as circular dependency. Why? Because a child does not grasp the convention (*saṃgati*) regarding the meaning of an injunction through his own direct perception. How so? He explains: "by another."

When the meaning of an injunction has been understood from a word by another—an elder who is the instigator—and when the child observes the activity of that instigator upon being told "Bring the cow," and [thus] it is indicated that "surely this person has understood from this [word] the object which serves as the cause for his activity," then the grasping of the connection—the knowledge of the relationship—is easy with respect to that meaning of the injunction; this is the meaning. He states the refutation of that [position] with the words "of that" (tasya).

For one who thinks thus: "When the activity of the person to be prompted (*prayojya*) leads to the inference of a specific cognition belonging to him, and since the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) is an object of that [cognition]—either as its qualifier or as a distinct category like other word-meanings (*padārtha*)—how can that meaning of the injunction be said to have the word alone as its domain (*śabdaikagocara*)? If it is argued that because that inference is preceded by the word, the meaning of the injunction is said to have the word alone as its domain, then why does it not also have inference alone as its domain? For even the understanding of the meaning of the injunction arising from a word is preceded by inference. To explain:

Even the person being prompted (the *prayojya*) understands at the time of grasping the relationship that the meaning of the injunction is precisely what was inferred from the activity of another prompted person; he now awakens to it from the word. That other prompted person likewise [understood it] from yet another prompted elder. Thus, like the sequence of seed and sprout, between the word and inference, there is no "firstness" for either one that can be established as primary. Therefore, one should not say that [inference] is "exclusively within the domain of the word" because it is preceded by the word at the outset.

However, for every cognizer who is to be prompted to action, inference stands prior to and precedes the verbal cognition; for even he, at the time of knowing the relationship [between word and meaning], understands the meaning of the injunction as already established through the word. Just like any other word-meaning, that word which enjoins the heard meaning of the injunction is merely reiterative (anuvādaka). Therefore, like any other word-meaning, it is not capable of implying a novel connection (*apūrva-saṃsarga*), nor is it the exclusive domain of the word alone—this is the intended sense.

An objection is raised: "A child who understands through inference does not understand the meaning of an injunction from the word alone; therefore, it must be inferred. Now, one might argue that the child indeed infers what was already understood from the word. True; however, this is inferred by means of the person being prompted (the *prayojya*). Furthermore, the verbal cognition occurring in one person being prompted does not serve as a restatement (*anuvāda*) for another child's inferential knowledge. Therefore, it is logical that the meaning of an injunction is solely inferable, and not something whose sole domain is the word—this is the doubt [raised].

Furthermore, through the activity of the person being prompted (*prayojya*), the linguistic understanding (*vyutpatti*) has occurred only with respect to the general cause of activity; therefore, that alone would be the meaning of the word. Now, if it is argued that because there is no worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding that generality, a specific [non-worldly] entity is postulated for it—even so, since the status of being a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatva*) is established through worldly [experience] alone, a non-worldly *niyoga* cannot be postulated. The point is this: in the case of Vedic activities, since a worldly cause of activity within the scope of other means of knowledge is impossible, a non-worldly cause of activity [must be assumed].

If it is argued that [the cause of activity] is postulated [as something supernatural], this is not so; because, according to the maxim "those very [words] which are worldly," a word whose capacity is understood in common worldly usage is what conveys meaning in the Veda. In that regard, since worldly activities are preceded by a known connection with a worldly cause of activity, that very same [worldly cause] must be understood in the Veda, as it is not supernatural. Or, if such a thing were impossible, it would be more logical to conclude that the knowledge of the cause of activity in the Veda is simply false, rather than postulating something supernatural for its sake. For the relationship between a word and its meaning is non-deviating.

Furthermore, because specific causes of activity (*pravṛttihetu*) vary in many ways and thus involve logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*), they cannot be the meaning of a word. Therefore, it is the universal (*sāmānya*) alone that is the cause of activity and constitutes the meaning of a word in both common usage and the Veda. As for the fact that another extraordinary particular (*viśeṣāntara*) is perceived in the Veda, this is because such particulars—being objects of other means of knowledge for worldly people—are impossible within the Veda, which is preceded by [the cognition of] non-authoritative [particulars]; it does not, however, arise from the word itself. Thus, if it is argued that there is no fault of abandoning the worldly meaning of a word in the Veda, even so, the universal of "word-ness" (*śabdatvasāmānya*) would be the meaning of the word in the Veda.

At the time of cognizing the relationship in that world, it has already been known; thus, like any other category of object (*padārtha*), its status as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) does not cease. Now, if it is argued that it falls within the scope of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with reference to a non-worldly (*alaukika*) distinction, that too is not the case; for even that is established by inference through elimination (*pāriśeṣya-anumāna*) due to the impossibility of it being anything else. This has been stated while granting the opponent's position for the sake of argument. But in reality, [p. 227]...

Inference by elimination (*pariśeṣa-anumāna*) is also not possible regarding a non-worldly particular (*alaukika-viśeṣa*); for that [inference] occurs only when other [possibilities] are impossible, and here there is no impossibility of another particular, since a worldly particular—namely, being a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatva*)—is possible. Now, if it is argued that the two usages of the world and the Veda are beginningless and follow separate paths;

In that regard, since a worldly motive for activity is impossible in the case of Vedic activities, the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning] regarding the non-worldly motive for activity arises solely from Vedic usage. Therefore, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth in the Veda is not something to be understood through worldly means; rather, it is established in an entirely different way. The objection that this contradicts the principle "it is like the worldly" (as stated in *Nyāya-sūtra* 2.1.56) should be refuted by noting that it is similar to words such as *śrāddhavanīya*. Consequently, there is no falsity [of the Veda] simply because [its meaning] cannot be established through worldly means.

Nor should it be argued that even in Vedic activities, the cause of activity is not exempt from being inferred from the activity itself—thus remaining a mere restatement (anuvāda)—because in those cases, the cause of activity is not inferred from the activity; rather, the cognition of the elder who is prompted (prayojyavṛddha) arises, and the establishment of the cause of activity occurs through the force of that cognition. And since that cognition of the cause of activity in the person prompted originates from the word, the mandate (niyoga), which is the cause of activity, is cognizable solely through the word.

As for what was said—that because worldly means of attaining the highest good (*śreyaḥsādhana*) are possible, the Vedic injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) does not denote a non-worldly (transcendental) meaning—that is incorrect; for worldly efficacy as a means to the highest good is cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since we observe the use of the optative suffix and so forth in reference to what is cognizable by other means of knowledge. Furthermore, the meaning of words in the Veda must be followed in accordance with their usage in the world.

In this regard, if the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the Veda were merely the state of being a means to the good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatā*), then another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) would also have to be the word-meaning, because linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) occurs in that very way; yet it is not so, because the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) and thus lacks any other means of knowledge [to confirm its content]. Therefore, the meaning of the optative suffix in the Veda is indeed *alaukika* (transcendental), falling within the domain of a means of knowledge other than [empirical] ones, and is not subject to mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

If it is thought that, for this reason, [the Veda] is capable of implying a previously unknown connection, to that we reply: let it be granted that, based on Vedic usage, there is in the Veda a correspondence between word and meaning—that is to say, a relation or knowledge of the connection; nevertheless, the fact that the meaning of an injunction is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not thereby excluded.

To explain: when the expressive capacity of a word such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is understood with respect to an extraordinary injunction (*vidhyartha*), is that injunction then already cognized, or is it not cognized? If it is cognized, then it cannot be known from that very word—the optative suffix and so on—at that very moment; for a word does not cause the cognition of something whose relationship [to the word] was previously unknown, since its relationship is being known at that time. Therefore, one must necessarily admit that the cognition arises through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). Consequently, it follows that [the injunction] falls within the domain of another means of knowledge.

Now, if it is not established [by perception], then even when the word is established, its injunctive meaning (*vidhyartha*) is not established; and consequently, because both related members are unknown, the relation based upon them cannot be known. This has been stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]. In reality, however, the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. are not exclusively Vedic; therefore, it is logical that their derivation of meaning occurs from ordinary worldly usage, just as in the case of words such as "cow" (*paśu*).

There is also one who thinks: "The relation of a word is its *śakti* (potency). And that [potency] does not reside in the object, which is the cause of activity, because that [object] is mediated by being cognized through the cognition of that [potency]. Rather, it resides in the cognition of that [object]; for that [cognition] is the direct effect of the word. And that very [cognition], inferred from the activity of the elder who is prompted, is not itself the cause of activity. It is precisely through that [cognition] as a logical mark (*liṅga*) that the knowledge of the word's relation [to its meaning] occurs. Therefore, the cause of activity is not within the scope of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

Nor is there an impossibility of knowing the relationship [between word and meaning], because even when the cause of activity is not directly perceived, that [relationship] is established by means of the perception of that [cause] as it is perceived through the cognition [of the word]. He should be asked this: is the capacity of the word grasped in the mere cognition, or in the cognition of the cause of activity that is non-worldly (alaukika)? If the first alternative is held, then from that cognition of the one being prompted, which is inferred from his activity, the child might perceive something or other, but not the non-worldly cause of activity.

Now, the child understands the word’s capacity for that [object] by means of inference regarding the cause of the listener’s activity—which, because such activity is impossible in the worldly realm, must by process of elimination (pāriśeṣyāt) have an extraordinary object as its domain. Consequently, when there is an inference of the specific cognition in the listener, the cause of the activity—which serves as a qualifier of that [cognition]—is also inferred through the aforementioned process of elimination regarding the activity; thus, it follows that this [cause] falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For instance: either a qualifier remembered is a factor in the cognition of the qualified, as for example, when at the time of knowing the relation [in the inference] "there is fire because there is smoke," the fire being remembered is a factor in the cognition of the mountain qualified by that [fire]; or [the qualifier] is already cognized, as for example, whiteness in the cognition of a cow qualified by that [whiteness], as in "the cow is white."

Therefore, in this case, whether the qualifier of the cognition of that [object] which is the cause of activity pertains to memory or to valid cognition (*pramiti*), in either instance it is the object of another means of knowledge and is not accessible through verbal testimony alone, because at that time the relationship [of the word] has not been grasped. In that regard, if the qualifier of the cognition of that [object], drawn forth by memory, is the cause of activity, then—since memory is produced by a valid cognition—one must necessarily seek another means of knowledge for the establishment of that memory. Consequently, because it is already known through valid cognition, it is not accessible through verbal testimony alone.

Now, if [the object] is a qualifier in the valid cognition [itself], then even so, since the qualifier is also inferred in the qualified inference, the cause of activity would fall within the scope of another means of knowledge. Alternatively, it may be thought: "True, by the activity of the person being prompted, it is inferred through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that the cognizer's cognition is indeed qualified by a worldly cause of activity already perceived; nevertheless, the validity of the inference pertains only to the cognizer's cognition itself, and not to its qualifier—the cause of activity."

In that case, however, there is for him mere cognition (*pratīti*), but not valid knowledge (*pramiti*); his valid knowledge, rather, arises only from the cognition of the person being prompted, which is itself inferred from his activity. And since that [cognition] is verbal in nature, it is not something to be inferred. Now, this status of being a qualifier for what has not yet been validly known—is this seen anywhere else? We say it is seen: for example, the word of a reliable person (*āptavacana*) is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding a specific cognition of a charioteer, but not regarding cognition in general; and the specificity of that cognition is due to its connection with the object, not inherent in itself. And that object is [as follows]: [p. 229]

It is precisely that which is already known (*pratīta*) that qualifies the cognition (*pratyaya*). Nor is it established by the authority of a trustworthy person’s word (*āptavacana*), because such a word has its validity only with respect to the speaker’s cognition; and because the object is only subsequently established through that very cognition of the speaker, while the qualified cognition is already apprehended prior to that. Therefore, that which is merely known is the cause for activity and serves as the qualifier when inferring that cognition; it is not something remembered, nor is it something [newly] established by valid means of knowledge (*pramita*). This is incorrect; P. [continues].

For cognition is fivefold, consisting of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), error (*viparyaya*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and memory (*smṛti*). Among these, that cognition by which an object is said to be merely cognized as the cause for activity must necessarily be one of the aforementioned types. It cannot be memory, because [the object] was not previously apprehended; for what has been apprehended is remembered. It cannot be doubt, because it lacks contact with two alternative possibilities (*koṭi*). Nor can it be conceptual construction, for that is devoid of a real entity (*vastu*).

As it has been said: "Conceptual construction (vikalpa) is that which follows upon the cognition of a word and is devoid of a real object. In this context, if the cognition that serves as the cause for activity were devoid of a real object as its referent, then—since the cause of activity would be absent—the cognition of the elder who is prompted, which is inferred by the child, would also result in being a conceptual construction due to its lack of a real object. And in that case, the real object that is the cause of activity would simply not exist; what, then, would be the meaning of the injunction? Nor can it be a case of error (viparyaya).

Since, in that case, when the cognition of the person being prompted is accepted as having a real object—that is, as being true with respect to the cause of activity—how could the cognizer’s own cognition, which is the cause of his activity and which grasps a real object, be devoid of an object? Furthermore, its status as memory has been refuted. By process of elimination, it follows that the cause of activity falls within the scope of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And since the cognizer’s cognition of the cause of activity arises from the cognition of the person being prompted, and that cognition in turn originates from words, it is stated that [the Veda] has no other means of valid cognition as its source.

That too is incorrect; for the cognition arising from the word belongs to the elder who was prompted, not to the child. Moreover, one person cannot be made to understand by means of another's cognition. Therefore, since the child understands through a different kind of cognition, the meaning of the injunction is not cognizable by the word alone. Now, if it is argued: "The child does not understand by means of the elder's cognition, but rather by his own cognition; however, this [cognition] arises from the capacity of the elder's cognition—which is inferred from his activity—produced by the word; thus, for him, the meaning is cognizable by the word alone. [Response: [This is not so.]... [The argument continues with the refutation of the opponent's position.]

In this regard, we ask: is that knowledge which belongs to the child considered a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)? It cannot be verbal (*śābda*); for verbal knowledge is that knowledge of an object which arises from the knowledge of a word. Now, in the case of the child who has not yet been trained in language, there is no knowledge of the object from the knowledge of the word, but rather [such knowledge belongs] to the person being prompted. Since the child’s knowledge of the object—which serves as the cause for activity—is inferred by the child from his own activity, that knowledge of the child is not verbal. Consequently, it follows that the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), which is to be understood from that [knowledge], falls within the scope of another means of cognition. Now, if it is argued: "We do not say that the child's own knowledge is verbal..."

However, when the cognition of the person being prompted—which has as its object the cause of activity—is inferred by the child through that activity, and when the child understands the cause of activity by means of that [cognition], then, provided that cognition is valid, it confirms for the child the cause of activity regarding its object; not otherwise.

And its validity arises from a faultless word (*śabda*). Therefore, in that case, the certainty regarding the cause of activity in the child's cognition is dependent upon the word. Even though the child perceives the cause of activity through his own cognition as a qualifier of the person to be prompted (*prayojya*), nevertheless, because the certainty therein arises by the power of the faultless word, it is said that the word possesses validity regarding that cause of activity; it is not the child's cognition that possesses it, because that [cognition] lacks the capacity for certainty. This too is without substance.

For verbal cognition (*śābda*) is that knowledge of an object which arises from a word; it is not, however, that wherein a certain determination is dependent on a word even through a mediated succession. As it has been said: "When the speaker's knowledge is apprehended from the words of a reliable person (*āpta*), the object is established from that [knowledge] alone; for by the mere apprehension of the speaker's knowledge, the object serves as its qualifier"—this too is incorrect. Because even the speech of a person is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the object itself; for it is impossible to apprehend a specific cognition without first apprehending the object.

Therefore, the object must be understood as a qualifier of the speaker’s cognition. And a qualifier is either remembered or cognized. In that regard, since it is impossible to remember an object previously unexperienced, the object being cognized is itself the qualifier of the speaker’s cognition. Nor is that cognition [of the object] by means other than the word, because such [a means] is not perceived. Therefore, the apprehension there is based solely on the word as the means of valid cognition; thus, the object is not a qualifier merely by virtue of being apprehended.

Nor can it be by the speaker’s own verbal cognition, because one person cannot perceive the cognition of another. Therefore, the human statement (*puruṣavacana*) is not a valid example. [Objection: If the listener understands the object through their own verbal cognition and not through the speaker’s cognition, then why is it said—in the passage beginning with "Furthermore, from a human statement"—that the establishment of the object depends upon the speaker’s cognition? [Response: That is because when the speaker’s cognition is false or impossible, as in the case of sentences such as "one should worship the *caitya*," the cognition of the speaker’s cognition that arises from the human statement...

It is sublated [only] when there is no sublation of the cognition of the speaker; it is not, however, the case that the meaning of human speech lacks an object. Rather, the intention is that the hearer’s cognition of the meaning arises through the speaker’s cognition. For if the meaning of human speech were not its object, then the dependence of human speech regarding its meaning—which was stated in the passage "and there is dependence regarding the mere object"—would be untenable. Dependence and independence apply to an object (*viṣaya*), not to what is not an object.

And so it has been said by the author of the *Vārttika*: “The establishment of validity, however, occurs because of the possibility of a cause for the speaker’s cognition. This is what is meant: the validity of the meaning of human speech is intrinsic (*svataḥ*); yet, it is established through the possibility of a cause for the speaker’s cognition. If, however, a cause for the speaker’s cognition were not possible—as in the case of the worship of a *caitya*, where there is no cognition of a Buddha—then it would be sublated. Therefore, what is intended here by “establishment” is non-sublation, and not validity itself.

Thus, it has been stated that there is the "establishment of validity" (*prāmāṇyasthāpana*), but not "validity" (*prāmāṇya*) itself. And this establishment of validity belongs to the sentence, not to the speaker’s cognition alone. Therefore, validity does not belong to the object of the speaker’s cognition, but rather to the sentence. Furthermore: "The relation of a word with its meaning is innate" (*autpattikastu śabdasyārthena saṃbandhaḥ*). [p. 231]

The relationship of a word, characterized by the fitness between the signifier and the signified, is grasped with respect to an infinite [number of instances], and not through cognition [of a specific instance]. Furthermore, since that relationship cannot be known if the related object (*saṃbandhin*) has not been cognized, it follows that the meaning of an injunction (*vidhyartha*) must fall within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Nor should it be argued: "This would indeed be so if the relationship of cognition and so forth were grasped when the meaning of the injunction is already cognized; however, it is merely a matter of apprehension (*pratīti*). For that apprehension is not a doubt, as it lacks contact with both extremes (*koṭi*).

In that case, if it were to possess an object, then memory would either be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or [itself] a recollection. And regarding that [memory], it has been stated that the meaning of an injunction falls within the scope of another means of knowledge. Alternatively, if it consists of the nature of a misconception or a conceptual construction and thus lacks an object, then the meaning of the injunction does not exist at all.

With what [other means] would there be a connection for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth? Furthermore, if the meaning of an injunction were understood through some other, non-authoritative cognition distinct from the cognition arising from the word itself, then, by overstepping the principle that it is cognizable solely through verbal testimony, one would have to suspect that it is also cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As for what was also said—that the status of being a means to worldly welfare (*śreyaḥsādhanatā*) falls within the scope of other means of knowledge, and therefore, if that were the meaning of the optative suffix, then the state of being accessible through other means of knowledge would also enter into the verbal meaning—that too is incorrect.

For a word does not have something as its meaning merely because it is employed when that thing exists, or because it is not employed when that thing is absent; otherwise, since the word "śiṃśapā" (a type of tree) is employed when "treeness" exists and is not employed in the case of jars and the like when it is absent, "treeness" would also have to be the meaning of that word. What indeed could be considered a second meaning of a word? Similarly, since a sprout does not arise even when earth, wind, and so forth are present if the seed is absent, the seed is understood to be the cause.

Thus, where there is one efficient cause (*prayojaka*) for the employment of a word, yet the word is not employed due to the absence of a second [cause], even that [first cause] is understood to be the efficient cause for its employment, as in the case of the word *goṇa* (red). For in that case, although redness (*aruṇatva*) is present, because the word is not employed for cows and the like, horsehood (*aśvatva*) is also an efficient cause; such is the established position elsewhere. And here, in the case of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, since these are observed when there is a cause of welfare (*śreyas-hetu*), and they are not observed when there is no cause of welfare—even though that [latter] may be within the scope of other means of knowledge—therefore, being a cause of welfare is first of all the meaning of the word.

Although the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are observed in the case of the cause of the good (*śreyas-hetu*) which is cognizable through other means of knowledge, and they are not observed in the case of things like a human horn—which are cognizable through other means of knowledge precisely because of the absence of such cognizability—nevertheless, if non-observation were due to the absence of cognizability by other means while being the cause of the good, then, by the logic of the "red cow" (*śoṇa*), cognizability by other means would also be the meaning of the word; but this is not the case.

However, where—as in the case of a human horn and the like—there is no cognizability by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), there is likewise no status as a cause of the highest good (*śreyas*). Therefore, since the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are not employed when both [properties] are absent, it is doubtful whether their non-employment is due to the absence of being a cause of the highest good, or rather due to the absence of cognizability by other means of knowledge; thus, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is uncertain. In this regard, since it has been previously determined that being a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥsādhanatā*) is the motivator (*prayojaka*), the non-employment [of the suffix] is based solely on the absence of that [status], and not on the absence of cognizability by other means of knowledge.

Thus it is determined. Consequently, since there is the application [of a word] when there is the quality of being a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatva*), and its non-application when that is absent, the logical consistency of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is established; therefore, there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that being cognizable by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara-gamyatva*) constitutes the meaning of a word. Hence, the argument that if the quality of being a means to the highest good were the meaning of a word, then being cognizable by other means of knowledge would also have to be the meaning of the word, is refuted.

If, however, the denotation of a word were to consist merely in positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) without the aforementioned manner [of essential identity], then existence (sattā), treeness (vṛkṣatva), and so forth would also be the denotations of the word "śiṃśapā"; for these are present when the word is applied to a *śiṃśapā*, and they are absent when it is not applied, as in the case of a "man's horn" and the like.

Now, if it is argued that because the object denoted by "śiṃśapā" (the tree *śiṃśapā*) is absent in things such as a human horn, its non-employment is logically accounted for, and thus the absence of existence (*sattā*) is not the cause of its non-employment—therefore, existence and the like are not the meaning of the word "śiṃśapā"—then that same [argument] applies equally to the case of the human horn and so forth. How this is so has already been stated. Furthermore, if the means of achieving the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatā*), which is cognizable through other means of knowledge, were the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi*), then the Veda would lack authority, since other means of knowledge do not apply to the Veda.

Therefore, it is said that the meaning of an injunction (*vidhyartha*) in the Veda is indeed not cognizable by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*); however, that is incorrect. For it is not the case that whatever is the object of a particular means of knowledge in one instance must be the object of that same means in another instance, nor does something become false merely because it is perceived in the absence of that specific means of knowledge. Since fire is an object of the sense organ when nearby, but an object of inference and so forth when at a distance, it is not the case that it is always the object of only one sense organ; nor is it false simply because it is being perceived.

Therefore, even if in the world the status of food and such things as means to a superior end (*śreyas*) is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding other results, nevertheless, in the case of sacrifices and the like which have remote results, because positive and negative concomitance are absent, this status will be cognizable solely through verbal testimony (*śabda*) in the Veda. What is the fault in this? If it is argued that the fault is that the Vedic status as a means to a superior end is sublated by the non-perception of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just as the existence of a hare’s horn is sublated by its non-perception through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); [we reply: no.

This is not a fault, because other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have as their object that which has been perceived, whereas verbal testimony (*śabda*) has as its object that which has not been perceived. Therefore, what is unperceived does not fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition at all. Furthermore, that which is not an object for a particular means of cognition is not sublated by the non-perception of it through that means—just as taste is not sublated by the non-perception of it through the eye. Moreover, a rabbit's horn is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition whatsoever; however, the fact of being a means for attaining the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatā*) is understood through verbal testimony. And that which is apprehended by one means of cognition is not sublated by the absence of knowledge of it through another, just like taste.

Now, if the status of being a means (*sādhanatā*) expressed by the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) in the Veda were to have as its object another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), then, because there would be a contradiction with that other means of valid cognition regarding its own object, the Veda would lack authority. Furthermore, since no immediate fruit is perceived in the case of sacrifices and the like, such a contradiction indeed exists. However, if it is argued that this fault does not apply when the object of the injunctive suffix is not the object of another means of valid cognition, and therefore one must accept that the meaning of the injunction in the Veda has as its object only that which is not the object of another means of valid cognition, and not the other [kind], that is incorrect.

For if the immediacy of the result were enjoined in the Veda, then there would be a contradiction due to the non-perception of an immediate result; but this is not the case. As it has been said: "Indeed, immediacy is not enjoined.

Now, even if immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not enjoined, and being cognizable by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not the meaning of the word, nevertheless, if the status of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatā*) is established by another means of knowledge, then that which is expressed by the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) in the Veda must be of the same kind as it is established in the world. And that [status] established by another means of knowledge is the state of being a means to a good that occurs immediately [after the action]. Therefore, in the Veda, only such a [status] should be accepted; otherwise, it would not be verbal in nature.

If it is argued that because the means to the highest good (*śreyas*) does not occur immediately after [the performance of] sacrifices and the like, that [immediacy] is not the meaning of the word in the Veda, we reply to this: as for what was stated—that the status of being a means to an immediate fruit is established in common worldly usage—that is not so, because there is deviation in the case of agriculture and similar activities whose fruits are delayed. Now, if it is argued that even in those cases, although the attainment of pleasure and so forth is delayed, nevertheless intermediate effects such as the production of impressions (*saṃskāra*), sprouts, and birth occur immediately, then that same [logic] applies to sacrifices and the like as well.

For even among those [actions], it is established by logical necessity (*arthāpatti*) that something unprecedented (*apūrva*) arises immediately thereafter. As it has been said: "An action enjoined for the sake of a fruit, being momentary, cannot otherwise bring about that fruit which occurs after a long time; therefore, the *apūrva* is postulated. Furthermore, where a specific capacity to be a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatā*) is established as immediate, there its qualification—the mere capacity to be a means to the highest good—is also established.

Therefore, just as when the word "cow" is applied to an individual qualified by cowness (*gotva*), it is cowness alone—the qualifier—that is its meaning, and not the particularity of that individual; so too here, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes merely the state of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatā-mātra*), and not immediate succession as a particularity. Consequently, even if no immediate fruit is observed in the case of sacrifices and the like, there is no discrepancy whatsoever. Thus, since the optative suffix functions without defect even in the worldly sense of being a means to the highest good—which is the cause of engagement—the postulation of a non-worldly (transcendental) meaning for the injunctive suffix is entirely redundant.
