Furthermore, just as when someone’s experience of pleasure is perceived through the serenity of their face and so forth, that pleasure itself becomes an object of inference and no separate means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is required for it; likewise, when the cause of an action is perceived through the activity of an elder who is being prompted, that cause of action is also inferable. Therefore, it is not the case that this [cause] is cognizable by verbal testimony alone. Even according to this view—that the meaning of a person's speech is simply the speaker’s cognition;

And that cognition of the speaker cannot exist without an object, which is established through *anupapatti* (logical inconsistency); or else, the object is established by inference: "The cognition of a reliable person (*āpta*) is accompanied by an object, because it is the cognition of a reliable person, like previously observed cognitions of reliable persons. Yet even this [inference] is based on the activity of the person being prompted, for the cognition that is the cause of activity cannot exist without an object that causes such activity—just as the meaning of a reliable person's word is itself inferred as the cause of activity. Therefore, the status of being cognizable by verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not established.

In the commentary on the phrase "in being inferable," one should also understand that it is cognizable through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), due to its similarity to inference. Now, from whatever causal cognition there is activity...

It is argued that the cause of activity (*pravṛttihetu*) is perceived (*anubhūyate*), and because it is understood through words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), it is said that the cause of activity is cognizable solely through verbal testimony (*śabda*). This is incorrect; for although the cognition of the cause of activity is brought about by the word, the cause of activity itself remains something to be perceived, and the word does not become that [cause] itself. Otherwise, when the knowledge of a reliable person (*āpta*) contained in their statement is produced by the senses, then the object perceived by that [knowledge] would have to be a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇaka*) for the listener. But this is not the case.

Therefore, [the injunction] is not cognizable by verbal testimony alone on the grounds of being a cause for activity. Consequently, the statement beginning with "If that [injunction] is thus to be inferred" is well-said. Now, if that meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) is manifested by its own word—the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth—in the form of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, because a means of valid cognition is impossible without an object of cognition (*prameya*), it is said to imply a novel relation between words (*apūrva-padārtha-saṃsarga*) and to be independent of other means of valid cognition, owing to its independence from the knowledge of [previously established] relations.

For if this [word] were dependent upon the knowledge of a relation, like the word "cow," then, since the knowledge of a relation is based upon the knowledge of the related terms, it would require another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of knowing those related terms; and in that case, being restated as something already established, it would not imply a previously unknown connection. But this is not so; rather, it is said to be independent with respect to other means of valid cognition. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Now" (*atha*). He refutes that with: "Even so" (*tathāpi*).

Even though the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) consists in being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, if that [meaning] is not established by another means of valid cognition, there would arise two defects in the statement of something unprecedented (*apūrva*): namely, the failure of the word to incite activity in one who is untrained, and the transgression of its own nature as a linguistic item. On the other hand, if it is established by another means of valid cognition, it becomes a restatement (*anuvāda*), that is, something already known. And when it is restated exactly as it was previously understood, it cannot imply a new relation (*saṃsarga*). Furthermore, where the validity of the object of knowledge—the meaning of the injunction—resides, it resides in the scripture itself, that is, in the very word being heard.

Consequently, the meaning is that this [injunction] would be rendered useless. Now, one might object: if the word is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then because it would be merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*), there could be no comprehension of a previously unknown object (*apūrva-artha*); therefore, the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) denoted by that word must itself be accepted as the means of valid cognition. This is not so; for if the word were reiterative, then even the means of valid cognition called the "meaning of the injunction" denoted by it—being reiterated exactly as it was already understood—how could it bring about the cognition of a new object known as a "syntactic relation"? Nor is it the case that the means of valid cognition is reiterated, while its object of cognition (*prameya*) is not.

It must be said that it will cause one to understand that previously unknown object; for if a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is restated, its object of cognition (*prameya*) must necessarily also be restated. There is no apprehension of a qualified means of valid cognition brought about by contact with an object of cognition that has not already been perceived. Therefore, when a means of valid cognition is being restated, it is understood precisely as it was previously known in respect to its object; thus, the implication of a previously unknown object of cognition is not established—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, is this meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the action? It cannot be so in the case of a sacrifice and the like, because it would not be "expressed by its own word" (*svaśabdaka*). That which has its own word—namely, the word *yajati* and so forth—is "expressed by its own word. What is meant is this: the sacrifice and such are already expressed by the word *yajati* itself; what, then, is the use of the meaning of the injunction to you? Nor can it be the meaning of the word (*padārtha*)... [p. 235]

The novel relation (*saṃsarga*) is its object of cognition (*prameya*); for in ordinary speech, such as "O Brāhmaṇa, a son has been born to you," even though there is no injunction—that is, even in the absence of an injunction—a novel relation between word-meanings is perceived by the listener. Therefore, the sense is that this [relation] is not based on the authority of an injunction. Now, if it is argued that the mandate (*niyoga*) applies to one who desires creation and so forth, [we reply: it is not possible for a mandate to apply to a sacrifice or similar act which is not a means toward that desire; for a mandate applies to a person desiring something only when the object is something that ought to be done.

And the means for desire must be employed, and no other. In that regard, since a non-desirous means such as sacrifice would not be performed by one who possesses desire, it is a "means for desire. If it is argued that this means for desire does not belong to one who is incapable, and thus the injunction (*niyoga*) is the authority regarding the capacity of sacrifice and the like to produce a result, he says in response: "The word is not defective regarding that capacity to produce a result. Even in the verbal expression "one should accomplish heaven by means of sacrifice," the word is sufficient to make known the sacrifice’s capacity to produce the result.

Therefore, what fault is there in that [the Veda], by virtue of which one would bypass it and resort to another means of knowledge (*vidhi*)? Nor should it be said that "verbal testimony (*śabda*) depends on other means of knowledge, and therefore it is not capable of making known the power to accomplish a result not previously known," because the dependence of Vedic verbal testimony upon other means of knowledge has already been refuted in the passage: "Since it is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), [Vedic testimony] is independent; and thus authorship itself [is denied]."

Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) because the result is not seen immediately after the means to the result is understood through verbal testimony; for this same contradiction applies equally even when [the means] is understood through an injunction (*niyoga*). If it is argued that there is no contradiction in that case because immediate succession is not enjoined, then that [absence of contradiction] is equally true in the case of verbal testimony as a source of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, there is no fault. Alternatively, another point: the word is not defective regarding its capacity to be the means to the result therein. However, the understanding of being the means to the result cannot arise from the injunction alone.

This point is to be understood from the *Vidhiviveka* and the *Bhāvanāviveka*. For therein it is stated: "An injunction (*niyoga*) depends only upon the object and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), not upon its being a means to a fruit. And the person to be enjoined is the qualified agent (*adhikārī*). Since there can be no qualified agent who is unspecified, the phrase 'desiring offspring' (*sargakāma*) serves as a qualification of the qualified agent in that context."

Furthermore, since the desire for creation can function as a qualification of the eligible person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa) by way of being a causal condition (*nimitta*), just like the distinction between various types of living beings, it cannot be understood—on the basis of an injunction—that creation is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and that sacrifice is the means to achieve it; this has already been stated. Moreover, if the capacity of an injunction to bring about a result were its object of knowledge (*prameya*), then because such capacity is absent in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*), the object of knowledge would be untenable.

Thus, since there is no distinction in the case of the *niyoga* (the mandate) as a means of valid cognition, it is equal to other word-meanings which—being cognized through a dependence on the knowledge of their relations—are incapable of implying a novel synthesis (*apūrva-saṃsarga*). Therefore, the synthesis of word-meanings is not based on that expectancy for a relation which exists solely for the sake of establishing the object of the *niyoga*; rather, all word-meanings themselves, by their own words, possess a mutual connection in the form of action, factors of action (*kāraka*), and so forth, according to what is appropriate.

Being manifested by that [cognition], they become participants in a relation (*saṃsarga*). For how else could a qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*) be understood? Therefore, the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhṛti*) or employment of words in that context is appropriate; it is not prompted merely by the presentation of isolated word-meanings (*padārthamātra*), because such mere meanings are not constituent parts of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). A word-meaning cannot possess qualification without a relation. Consequently, even in this way, all word-meanings indeed imply a relation, and not the injunction (*niyoga*) alone. Thus, even in the absence of an injunction, the relation among word-meanings is established.

The meaning is that, in the Vedāntas, the entry of an injunction (*niyoga*) for the sake of ritual association is not to be postulated. (P. 112-6) There, another objects: "How so? The meaning is that since words in common usage are understood through their orientation toward injunction, an injunction must necessarily be accepted in the Vedāntas. He refutes this deviation: "This is not so. The meaning is that because there is also an understanding [of words] directed toward the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of things], this is not an absolute rule. Nor should an injunction such as "bring this" be postulated even here.

Since the engagement of one who desires that object is established by the mere cognition of the thing itself, it is not possible to assume that the sentence possesses the capacity to enjoin. Furthermore, the connection with an injunction must be postulated because the use of words for the mere meaning of individual terms and the resulting cognition of a qualified meaning would otherwise be inexplicable; yet, since those two [the word-use and the cognition] are equally explicable through connection with any other word-meaning whatsoever, there is no evidence for their connection specifically with an injunction.

Furthermore, if it is argued that because an association with an injunction (*niyoga*) is observed in common worldly usage, the same must be accepted in the Veda as well, then—since in the world such an association is observed to be the object of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—it would likewise have to be so in the Veda. Yet, no other means of valid cognition exists there [regarding the Vedic injunction]. Therefore, it has been stated that the meaning of the Veda would not have the word itself as its sole means of valid cognition. Moreover, if activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*) are the only purposes of a sentence and nothing else, and these two depend upon the knowledge of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*), then without that knowledge of what is to be done, the sentence would be purposeless.

Therefore, it is said that in the Vedāntas, an injunction (*vidhi*) is being enjoined. To this, it is replied: even though there exists an injunction for realization in the form “the Self is to be realized,” the futility of the statement is equal [to other injunctions], because after the realization of the Self, there is an absence of both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*). If it is argued that even in the absence of those two, the purpose of the injunction is simply the realization of the nature of the Self, then this is the same in the case of a statement whose goal is the nature of reality itself. Now, it may be objected that the futility is not equal in the case of an injunction for realization.

To the extent that the injunctions regarding qualification for wisdom, ritual action, and meditation are untenable without an understanding of the essential nature of the Self—which is the object of meditation—the injunction of realization (pratipatti-vidhi) supplies the required meaning, namely, the essential nature of the Self as the object of meditation; therefore, it is not purposeless. To this, the reply is: "The same applies here," which should be understood as following [from the previous argument]. It is the same in that even those Vedānta texts whose primary focus is the essential nature [of the Self] serve to supply the essential nature of the Self as the object of meditation and so forth.

Therefore, even in this way, the meaning is that it is solely for the purpose of an injunction for practice; for the statement, "Having understood, one should exercise discernment," refers to the act of discernment (*prajñākriyā*), which is meditation (*upāsana*).

Action (*kriyā*) is being discussed: "He should perform a sacrifice" (*kratuṃ kurvīta*); here, *kratu* is a mental operation, and that too is indeed meditation (*upāsanā*). And "one should meditate upon the Self alone" (*ātmetyevopāsīta*)—this is simply meditation. Thus, although there is no difference in meaning, they are presented separately because of the difference in injunctions (*vidhi*). However, in the verse, since the term "intellectual action" (*prajñākriyā*) is intended as an illustration, "sacrificial action" (*kratukriyā*) should also be understood [as included]. Alternatively, "action" (*kriyā*) may be mentioned separately from "sacrificial action" (*kratukriyā*) itself. In the aphorism (*sūtra*), the word "qualification" (*adhikāra*) is connected individually with each of the terms beginning with "intellect" (*prajñā*).

The syntactical connection is as follows: those injunctions for which one seeking liberation is qualified are "authoritative" (*adhikāra*); their accomplishment is what is required. With the intention that the Vedāntas present the nature of the Self just as they do when they are focused on the Self—rather than being subordinate to something else even while being centered on injunctions—the commentary uses the term "all the more" (*sutaram*).

Now, one might object: "If the words of the Vedānta are each connected with wisdom (*prajñā*) and the rest, thereby presenting them as their respective objects, then its status as being established in its own nature (*svarūpaniṣṭhatā*)—which belongs to that [Vedānta] when it enters into the injunctions regarding wisdom and so forth—is lost. To this he replies with the word "hanta" (alas). The answer here is: "It is the same."

The meaning is as follows: if, according to my position, the state of being restricted to its own form (*svarūpaniṣṭhatā*) is lost because of the entry into the injunction regarding discernment (*prajñā*) and so forth, then for you as well, that injunction of performance (*pravṛttividhi*) would not be restricted to the injunction of comprehension (*pratipattiniyoga*) contained within its own sentence, due to the entry into the injunction regarding discernment and so forth. In the passage "And a sentence completed [only] through connection with another sentence," both the words "if" (*cet*) and "this is equal" (*tulyam etat*) are to be understood as carrying over (*anuvartate*).

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: if it is argued that the sentence enjoining the act of meditation (pratipatti-vidhi-vākya), having concluded its own inherent injunction and being thus finalized, is connected with each of the qualities such as wisdom (prajñā) and so forth—that is, it is construed with the sentences concerning wisdom and the rest—and that consequently the sentence enjoining the act of meditation does not lose its status as being grounded in its own inherent injunction, we reply: this which you have stated applies equally to the Vedānta sentences even if they were grounded in their own essential nature (svarūpa).

The meaning is that even for this [injunction], just like an injunction regarding performance (*pratipatti-vidhi*), its status as resting upon its own essential nature (*svarūpa-niṣṭhatā*) will not be lost, even though it enters into the application (*niyoga*) of wisdom and so forth. By the passage beginning with “This very [injunction] belonging to the context,” the *Vṛtti* has strengthened the point that this connection with another sentence occurs only for that which terminates in its own application, not for that which does not terminate in it; for instance, the connection of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings with the sentences concerning the *darśa* sacrifice.

However, regarding the definition of a sentence as something that must reach its completion [in meaning], this is like the case of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) which are connected with injunctions (*vidhi*). Furthermore, this connection of the Upanishads is with an injunction for realization (*pratipatti-vidhi*) that pertains to the context. Therefore, the sense is that [the Upanishads] do not terminate in their own literal meaning. Now, if this were so, since it would follow that they are purposeless without entering into a mandate (*niyoga*), even those Vedānta texts that are established in the nature of reality must enter into a mandate, just like the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings.

Therefore, with the intention that their validity as you desire cannot be established for those [means of knowledge] independent of an injunction (*niyoga*), he raises the objection: "By means of an injunction" (*niyogena*). To this, he provides the answer: "And not... (*na ca*). If the injunction regarding the realization of the reality of the Self is for the purpose of presenting its object, then the Vedāntas themselves present it.
[Page 238]

They will [understand]. What is the use of that method of comprehension? Thus, the claim that the Vedāntas possess a portion consisting of a method for the comprehension of reality has been extracted and refuted. However, the idea is not that, in the ultimate sense, the Vedāntas enter into the sphere of injunction (*niyoga*), because it has already been stated that their function consists solely in the production of linguistic proficiency and the realization of the nature of things. At this point, an objection is raised: "But surely... (P.113-20).

Just as the originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi), such as "There is an eight-potherd offering to Agni," is established for the purpose of making known the nature of the ritual action—namely, the Agni-offering and so forth—and is intended for the knowledge of the ritual's nature rather than for inciting activity, so too the injunction for the realization of the reality of the Self is established for the realization of that reality; let it be intended solely for the knowledge of that reality and not for inciting activity. As for activity, however, it follows from the injunctive qualification (adhikāra-vidhi) contained in the passage, "One should cultivate wisdom."

Just as in the case of the Agneya and other rites, there is the injunction regarding the qualification for the ritual, namely, "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Since the two purposes of an injunction consist precisely in engagement and withdrawal, the wise declare that injunction is of two kinds; this is the meaning. What is intended is this: just as an originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi) is not purposeless because it makes known the essential nature of the ritual act, so too the injunction for the realization of the reality of the Self is not purposeless because it makes known the essential nature of the Self. Therefore, it need not be discarded.

The distinction is that an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) makes known what was previously unknown, whereas an injunctive rule concerning qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) impels one to act who has not yet acted. The word "atha" (now) is intended to indicate that the injunctive rule concerning qualification is preceded by the originative injunction. He refutes this with the words "this [is]... ("etad"). The phrase "of such a kind" (*tādṛśam*) means "insubstantial. He states its insubstantiality with the words "action... (*karma*).

In that regard, the meaning is as follows: in an originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), the result of the injunctive word—which is so called because "by it something is enjoined"—is not merely the comprehension of the essential nature of the ritual action such as the *Āgneya* sacrifice; rather, since an injunction is untenable without a result, the result of the originative injunction, which requires a purpose, is its connection with a fruit-bearing sentence concerning the result, namely the sentence regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

And here, because of the connection with the statement regarding the fruit, the fruit such as heaven and so forth—which belongs to that [injunction] itself—is figuratively stated to be the "fruit" in the context of the connection. Nor is it the case that the same fruit belongs to the injunction for comprehension (*pratipatti-vidhi*) as well; thus he says: "In this [world]. In this injunction regarding the realization of the reality of the Self (*ātma-tattva*), whatever reality of the Self is connected to the qualification—as being that which is to be known and that which is to be meditated upon, as in the texts "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kuryāt*) and "one should meditate [on him] as the Self alone" (*ātmety evopāsīta*)—that is what is enjoined there. For it is an action (*bhāva-artha*) that is enjoined.

Nor is there an injunction regarding curd and the like, because they function as *kārakas* (factors of action). That which is enjoined is the comprehension [of the object]; the meaning is that this comprehension does not enter into the scope of an injunction such as "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*). Now, one might raise the objection: since it is impossible to meditate upon what has not been comprehended, the comprehension of that [object] must also enter into the scope of the injunction. Anticipating this, he says: "For not... For it is not the case that rice and so forth, being imperceptible, are not auxiliary factors; rather, their perception enters into the scope of the injunction—it becomes a constituent part of the performance (*prayoga*), to put it another way. This is because, for those things which have been cognized, there is the scope [for action].

There is a connection; therefore, the valid cognition (*pramiti*) regarding those previously established [entities] is implied by their eligibility (*adhikāra*), just as in the case of "he gives a cart" or "he gives a garment," where because carts, garments, and so forth are already accomplished, they are connected to eligibility, whereas the acts of carpentry or weaving do not enter into that eligibility—it has this meaning. Thus, it has been stated that verbal comprehension is within the scope of injunction. Now, there is a third form of comprehension which consists of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) in which all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have been uprooted.

115-1 That is stated as the injunction for practice (*pratipatti-vidhi*). He says this with the words "Now" (*idānīm*). An objection might be raised: "Is it not improper to bypass the injunction regarding the second form of practice known as meditation (*upāsanā*) and instead refute the injunction regarding the third form of practice? Anticipating this, he says: "And that [injunction] concerns the realization of reality" (*taccāvabodha*). By the connection that the injunction concerning the third form of practice has as its object the realization of reality—which consists of valid means of knowledge—that very [realization] becomes present in the intellect immediately thereafter, and not the object of the second form of practice.

The meaning is that it is not an object for the realization of reality through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather an object for the repeated practice of reality in the form of recollection (*smṛti*). In this regard, he presents the position of the injunction for the third type of realization: "together with the means" (*sopāyam*). If verbal knowledge is not enjoined by the injunction for realization, then this knowledge—which is different from verbal knowledge and whose nature will be described immediately hereafter—is enjoined together with its means, namely, tranquility (*śama*) and the other [disciplines].

In response to the inquiry as to what that knowledge is like, he says: "in which the manifestation of the distinction between the grasping [subject] and the grasped [object] has dissolved. The analysis of the compound is: that in which the manifestation of difference—the appearance of distinction such that "this is the grasping" and "this is the grasped"—has dissolved, i.e., has set. The meaning is that it is non-dual knowledge (*advaya-jñāna*), because there is an absence of a second such knowledge, or because of the lack of duality such as the knower and the object of knowledge. It was stated that this is other than verbal knowledge; he states the reason for this with the words "for not... (*na hi*).

The meaning of a sentence consists of the connection between distinct entities, or has that as its nature; the cognition thereof has the word-meaning as its object, not the non-dual reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), because [the latter] is devoid of manifoldness (*niṣprapañca*). Therefore, the meaning is that this knowledge is different from verbal knowledge. The meaning of a sentence consists of the connection of various objects, whereas the reality of the Self is non-dual and of a nature contrary to that; thus, it is stated that it is not the object of such a cognition.

One might object: "Granted that the reality of the self may not be established by the means of knowledge that is the sentence (*vākya*), why could it not be established by the means of knowledge that is the word (*pada*)? Anticipating this doubt, the commentary states, "For [the word] has the nature of a sentence," and so forth. The intended meaning is that [the word] is a means of knowledge consisting of the word alone. As it has been said: "The word is not distinguished from that which merely causes recollection, because there is no additional [cognitive content]. The phrase "by following that" provides the reason why the relation (*saṃsarga*) has the sentence as its domain: the meaning is that since the relation is perceived only when the sentence exists, it therefore has the sentence as its domain.

Alternatively, the meaning is that the object of a sentence consists of the cognition resulting from the following of various word-meanings, or rather, the relation between those various word-meanings. Regarding the phrase "of the manifold," etc.: "saṃbheda" means the conjunction or relation of various "arthamātrās," which are word-meanings; the meaning is "of that cognition which illuminates such a [relation]. [p. 240] Unexamined...

P. 116-7. *Viti* means "untouched. He refutes that [position] with the word *enaṭ*. *Pelava* means unskillful, not firm, or insubstantial; that is to say, it is flimsy. He states its flimsiness with the words *advaya-*. *Advayātmaprakāśaḥ* is the manifestation of the non-dual Self. *Anavacchedavibhramaḥ*: limitation (*avaccheda*) is the finitude of the infinite [Self] through the body, senses, and objects; the delusion (*vibhrama*) having that as its object is the "delusion of limitation" (*avacchedavibhrama*). That in which such a delusion does not exist is *anavacchedavibhramaḥ*.

"Abiding in its own self" (*svātmaniṣṭhiti*) means abiding by itself, in its own nature. "Perfectly tranquil" (*supraśāntā*) means exceedingly peaceful; the meaning is that it consists of unsurpassed bliss, manifesting as all auspicious qualities such as the complete cessation of sorrow and the like. By this, it is established that the non-dual Self-knowledge possesses fruitfulness, since the cessation of suffering and the attainment of bliss constitute the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*).

Thus, this is the meaning of the sentence: the fruit is that abiding in one’s own self, which is the manifestation of the non-dual nature, free from the delusion of limitation and perfectly tranquil; it is not an object of injunction, nor is it something to be enjoined—this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "due to the turbidity caused by limitation": limitation (*avaccheda*) is that by which one is limited, namely the body, senses, and so forth; due to the turbidity caused by that, [the Self] appears as if it were of the nature of the non-Self.

There is no cognizer other than that non-dual nature of the Self; rather, it is of the very nature of the manifestation of the non-dual Self. The meaning is that it consists of reality (*satya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and bliss (*ānanda*). Nor can it be argued: "One does not engage even in a fruit [the goal] if the means are unknown; therefore, how can there be spontaneous engagement in that [Self]? Rather, it must be said that engagement occurs only through an injunction by way of making the means known"; for desire is the precursor to engagement. Indeed, one engages by means of desire, and that desire exists even with respect to the fruit. Nor does it occur through an injunction.

Therefore, the meaning is that since activity toward that [result] is already established by that very [means], there is no requirement for an injunction (*vidhi*) in that regard. Furthermore, if one does not engage with a result when the means to it is unknown, then one must necessarily be directed toward the means with the result as the aim, by making known that means; but one is not directed toward the result itself, because that would entail the fault of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). And since the means has thereby become known, activity toward the result is established from that alone; thus, one need not resort to the operation of an injunction for the sake of engaging with the result.

As it has been said: “The desire for that [result] is characterized by the object. This means that the desire to obtain that result is characterized by the object—that is, characterized by the purpose—not characterized by an injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, the result is not enjoined; rather, it is its means that is enjoined. As it has been said: “its means. Now, one who desires a result certainly desires its means as well, since a result cannot be accomplished without a means. Consequently, just as with the result, activity toward the means is also characterized by the object—that is, motivated by the purpose—and not characterized by an injunction.

Therefore, when the opponent objects that the operation of the injunction does not extend even to the means (*sādhana*), the proponent asks: "What then? The opponent replies: "The 'being-measured' (*itthamāna*)," meaning the aspect of being something to be performed (*kartavyatva*). He refutes this: "It would not exist," for the specific means is not known prior to the injunction; thus, there can be no indication by implication (*arthalakṣaṇā*).

[The activity of] engagement (*pravṛtti*) is as follows: Now, if [the injunction] pertains to the general means (*sādhanasāmānya*), it is equally applicable to the general mode of being (*itthaṃbhāvasāmānya*); for just as one who desires a result seeks the general means thereto, so too does he seek that which generally assists it, since a means devoid of assistance is incapable [of producing the result]. If, however, a specific mode of being (*itthaṃbhāvaviśeṣa*) is enjoined, then a specific means (*sādhanaviśeṣa*) will likewise be enjoined; thus, in that case as well, there is no activity characterized by [the pursuit of] a further purpose. This is the meaning.

And he says that the operation of the prescriptive injunction (*vidhi*) lies in the accomplishment of the fruit [of action], beginning with the words "apekṣita" (required). An injunction is of the nature of impelling one who has not yet acted. And the property (*dharma*) that is the cause of such activity is "impulsion" (*pravartanā*). That [impulsion] is of two kinds: being desired (*iṣṭatā*), and being a means to that which is desired (*tatsādhanatā*). For a person acts toward what is desired, or toward a means to that which is desired, and nowhere else. In that regard, when there is the state of being desired—which consists in the property of a desired fruit—the person certainly knows: "This must be done by me."

When an action is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a person’s engagement in it occurs spontaneously; it is not a case of being impelled to act where there was no prior inclination. Therefore, that [action] is not an injunction (*vidhi*). However, the fact that sacrifice and the like are means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) cannot be determined by any other means of valid cognition; rather, it is accessible through verbal testimony alone. Consequently, engagement with that which is a means to the desired end arises from the word itself and not from anything else; thus, that [status of being a means to the desired end] alone is the cause of engagement. Therefore, it is precisely this status of being a means to the desired end, when established by the authority of the word, that is celebrated as the "injunction" (*vidhi*).

Granted that the means of achieving a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*) is the cause of activity, and that this is the injunction (*vidhi*); but how is it understood that the performance of action has that [means] as its object? Or rather, why should it not have something else as its object? To this he says: "for one who performs. It is not the case that the means of achieving a desired end is the cause of activity for just anyone, like the wind; rather, it is for one who performs [the action]. And for one who performs, the means of achieving a desired end becomes the cause of activity only when it is something to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*); it is not self-evident by itself, like the wind.

Therefore, for one who performs [an action], the injunction (*vidhi*) consists in the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*). And since the injunction pertains to one who performs [it], it follows that this very performance—being dependent upon what is to be performed—is understood from the injunctive word, such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), as having precisely as its object a means to a desired end that constitutes the thing to be performed; it does not have anything else as its object. This is the meaning. It was stated that "the means is the cause of engagement" because of the non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to things like the *godohana* vessel, which are not themselves to be performed; for that [vessel] is not a means to the desired end by its own nature.

Moreover, it is the act of carrying [the fire] (*praṇayana*) that is to be accomplished by that [injunction]; for this very reason, it depends upon that which is contextual (*prākaraṇika*). And since that [act] must necessarily be performed, there is no deviation [from the injunction]. Now, those who know the injunction (*vidhi*) describe the injunction as having the characteristic of determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth; how then can the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) be the injunction? Anticipating this objection, he says: "From that" (*tataḥ*).

The determination that "this is my task" is the resolve (*niścaya*); from that arises *ākūta*, which is a specific form of volition (*saṃkalpa*); from that follows the initial activity. Likewise, the mere activity not delimited by the three times, such as "one should cook," and the relationship between the action—such as sacrifice—and its agent, which is unknown through other means of knowledge, is understood from the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) alone; thus, this resolve and so forth arise precisely because [the action] is a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), and not spontaneously without a cause—this is the meaning.

This is what is meant: the determination and so forth occur only with respect to that which is to be understood as the means to the desired end; it is not otherwise. Therefore, that alone [is the object]. 16 [p. 242]

Since that which is the root cause of activity is the injunction (*vidhi*), it is that alone which is the injunction, and not determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth. If it is argued: "Determination and the rest will arise simply from the denotation (*abhidhāna*) by means of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so on; what is the use of a separate injunction?", he says in response: "Not from denotation" (*nābhidhānataḥ*). The production of these [mental states] does not come from denotation, but rather there is merely their cognition (*pratīti*). And they do not possess the status of being causes for activity through mere cognition alone. For it has been stated in the *Vidhiviveka* that jars and other such things are not causes for activity through mere cognition.

But their origin [is] from the fact that [the action] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*); therefore, the meaning is that the injunction (*vidhi*) consists precisely in that. Another interpretation: "denotation" (*abhidhāna*) is that by which something is denoted, namely the word in the optative mood (*liṅ*) and so forth; one might then object, "Since the determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth will arise from that very [word], what is the use of 'being a means to a desired end'? Anticipating this, he says: "Not from denotation. There is no production of determination and so forth from the word in the optative mood and so forth; for that [word] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of determination and so forth, not a producer (*kāraka*). If it were a producer, it would impel even one who lacks understanding, just like the wind.

And for this reason, there would be no need for the cognition of a relationship in the case of a word; yet this is not so, as has been stated in the *Vidhiviveka* itself. For from that [injunction] arises determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth. As for the other view—the view held by one who thinks that the injunction (*vidhi*) is a non-worldly command (*alaukiko niyoga*), which is the meaning [of the Veda], namely, that from which the determination “this is my duty” and the cognition “I am commanded” arise—it is in response to him that it is said: from that very [injunction] arises the determination that it is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), and so forth.

Therefore, even though the cause of determination (*adhyavasāya*) is the injunction (*vidhi*), the injunction is simply the state of being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatā*); the meaning is that it is not some other worldly thing. For instance, regarding agriculture and the like as a means to what is desired, the notion arises in the world among agents: "This must be done by me. In the absence of a means to what is desired, there arises the notion that it is "not to be done. Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), those two notions are understood to have as their objects whether something is a means to what is desired or not a means to it. For instance, the cognition "I am engaged in action" occurs as a perception of the cause of engagement.

Furthermore, it is also your own view that one does not consider oneself to be set in motion by the wind itself. Nor is there any other non-worldly (*alaukika*) factor possible besides the fact of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), since that alone is observed in the world to be the cause of engagement in activities such as agriculture. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to say, without any reason, that in the world the capacity of a person (*nṛsāmarthya*) is not the cause of engagement, but rather that some other non-worldly factor is; for there is no evidence for postulating a non-worldly factor while abandoning the worldly one.

For this reason as well, the postulation of something non-worldly (alaukika) is not appropriate, because its denotation is held to be by means of a word. And the denotation of something non-worldly is not possible, because the relationship [between the word and its object] cannot be grasped; this was stated in the passage, "The word would overstep its own function. Therefore, determination, the undertaking, the intention, the performance, and the completion of what has been performed—all of these occur solely because [an action] is a means to a desired end, and not from anything else.

For one who has been enjoined acts only because of the very cognition that [the action] is a means to what is desired; for men do not act upon the injunction of an untrustworthy person who, without knowing that something is a means to what is desired, issues an injunction. Therefore, being a means to what is desired is itself the injunction (*vidhi*).

Objection: One engages in action because of the cognition, "This must be done by me. Otherwise, if one did not engage in action due to the understanding that something "must be done," then whatever was understood as a duty from the Veda—which is an authoritative means of knowledge—would remain unperformed. Yet, that is not the case. Furthermore, even regarding a means to a desired end, no one engages in it until they perceive, "This must be done by me. Therefore, engagement proceeds solely from the understanding of a duty (*kartavyatā*), and not from being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

It is said: Certainly, activity arises from the cognition that something ought to be done (*kartavyatā*); however, its production does not occur "accidentally" (without cause). For that [cognition] arises with respect to a means of attaining a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*) by means of this motive: "From this, the desired object is obtained. Objection: We do not say that it arises accidentally; rather, we say that the cognition that something ought to be done arises from the word itself. To this, it is replied: "Not from denotation" (*nābhidhānataḥ*). For the cognition that something ought to be done does not arise from words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*); because you maintain that the meaning of the word is the mandate (*niyoga*).

And that [impulse], consisting of the form of instigation and so forth, would either be a property of the instigator, or it would not be a property of the instigator but rather independent, because the fruit is accomplished [by it]; therefore, it is perishable. The state of being "to-be-done" (kartavyatā) is a property of the object—namely, the action (bhāvārtha) currently being performed—and is neither a property of the instigator nor independent. Therefore, it cannot be denoted by that [word] and the like.

Now, if it is argued that *niyoga* (the mandate) is the property of the object (*viṣaya-dharma*), then—since there is no other property for the object than its being a means to a desired end—it follows that *niyoga* is simply the state of being a means to a desired end. Alternatively, if it is argued that the cognition of "what ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*) does not arise from the word itself, but rather from the *niyoga*; even so, the word is not the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for that cognition, because the word merely expresses the *niyoga*. Nor can the cognition of "what ought to be done" arise through implication (*arthāt*) based on the impossibility of the *niyoga*, for we observe mandates (*niyoga*) directed toward things that are not to be done.

Now, it might be thought: "That [injunction] is said to be the *dharma* pertaining to liberation, which is the object of what is to be done; therefore, because it is a means to liberation as its object, it follows that it is an injunction. Thinking that liberation is something distinct [from knowledge], the opponent objects: "It might be so," and so forth. He establishes through scriptural citations that the knowledge of the non-dual Self is the means to liberation: "It is heard," etc. Regarding the phrase "having known, he understands": the meaning is that having first known [the Self] from the sacred word (*śabda*), he subsequently knows it specifically through direct perception (*aparokṣatayā*).

One might object: "If liberation were something to be accomplished by means of a causal instrument (*sādhana*), it would be non-eternal like a jar; and consequently, the liberated one would undergo a return [to transmigratory existence]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not... He states the reason: "By the word... He provides the scriptural statement: "And not... Now, one might further object: "Since liberation is something to be accomplished, reasoning (*tarka*) establishes that it must have an end, just like a jar; therefore, how can there be no return? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For indeed... Indeed, the injury involved in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and similar rites is not a duty (*dharma*) as understood from scripture, unlike external injury.

The sense is that it is unrighteous because it is violence; thus, by means of reasoning, it becomes unrighteous. With reference to knowledge (*vidyā*) as being the eternal nature of the self, he states another refutation: "infinite," etc. [This refers to the proponent of momentary cognition (kṣaṇikajñānavādin) on p. 244, 16A].

On page 119, he states that even for one who has died, knowledge is infinite—saying "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*). Here he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with "but not" (*na ca*). In order to explain the meaning of the verse and to define the nature of liberation (*mokṣa*), he asks: "But what [is it]? In that regard, liberation is certainly not the non-arising of future bodies and so forth, because that, being a state of living, is not something to be accomplished; thus he says: "If... In the passage "Indeed, the bodiless one," the particle *vāva* is used for the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇārtha*).

Thus, having refuted this position because it is untenable, [the author] sets forth several alternative views on liberation (*mokṣapakṣa*) in order to distinguish between what is essential and what is not, beginning with the word "Now" (*atha*). "As in the case of Caitra and the village": this refers to the attainment of Brahman characterized by conjunction preceded by motion. "Going" (*āyan*): the meaning is "moving. "As far as" (*sa yāvat*): this expresses the swiftness of the yogin who goes to the world of the sun for the sake of attaining Brahman, even though the mind itself is swift. "This indeed is the path" (*etadvai kham*): this is a praise of the path. "The flame" (*arcis*): this is the description of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*).

"Madhukṛtaḥ" means honey-bees. "Vidhūya" means having removed or cast off. "Nirañjanaḥ" means devoid of the distinguishing marks (añjana) such as the body and so forth. "Yogavyāpravad" means just as those who have attained the eightfold supernatural powers (aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya) through the power of yoga transform themselves into the form of a tiger, so too [is the case here]. In the phrase "brahma saṃpadyate," the word "darśanāt" (because of seeing) is understood to carry over from the previous context. "Rāgādyapakarṣaṇe" refers to the removal of the intense passion caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the rosary used for recitation (japa).

*Rāga* (attachment) is that by which one is colored, namely *japā* (the hibiscus flower) and so forth; the meaning is "in the removal of that. Therein, he first refutes the position that there is the attainment of Brahman preceded by movement for one whose nature is distinct [from Brahman], starting with the word "therein" (*tatra*). He states the reason with the word "all" (*sarva*): the attainment of Caitra and the village is logical, but not that of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, because Brahman is omnipresent (*sarvagata*); and the sense is that what is omnipresent is eternally attained. He establishes this omnipresence through two scriptural citations, starting with "that" (*tat*).

The meaning is that the Śruti passage, “It is within all this, and it is outside of all this,” as well as the Śruti passage, “eternal and omnipresent,” declare the all-pervasiveness of Brahman. The term “omnipresent” (vibhu) is explained by the word “all-pervading” (sarvagata). Alternatively, there is no tautology, for “vibhu” may also mean “because of its manifold existence. Furthermore, it is logical that Caitra, who is separated from a village, must first undergo the act of going in order to reach that village; however, the individual soul (jīva) is not other than Brahman, being Brahman itself.

Therefore, he says that the attainment of Brahman is not caused by the movement of the one who has superimposed [the world upon It], stating: "And because of non-difference" (*ananyatvācca*). He states the reason for this non-difference: "That" (*tad*). The scriptural statement, "When the Self is known, all this becomes known," is consistent with the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, but not with their difference; for when one thing is known, another thing does not thereby become known. Hence, there is non-difference. Likewise, in the passage "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), by addressing the individual soul with the word "thou" (*tvam*), its non-difference from Brahman—the referent of "that" (*tat*)—is declared.
Similarly, [in the passage] "By this living self" (*anena jīvenātmanā*).

Thus, by the word *ātman*, which refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and denotes one’s own self, the individual soul (*jīva*) is indicated; and nothing other than this constitutes one’s own self. Likewise, the perception of difference between the individual soul and the Supreme is prohibited through the censure: "He who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know. Therefore, the meaning is that there is non-difference (*ananyatva*) between these two. Precisely because there is non-difference between the individual soul and Brahman, liberation is not the attainment of non-distinction (*avibhāga*) between them—unlike the various flavors in honey or like the rivers and the ocean.

For that [non-distinction] occurs in the case of division, not in the case of non-difference; with this intention, he says "therefore. Furthermore, non-distinction among things possessing parts is characterized by the mutual intermingling of their parts. And the Self, according to the scriptural text "partless" (*niṣkala*), is without parts. Therefore, non-distinction is not possible for It; thus he says "without parts" (*niravayava*). By the term "partless," the partlessness of the Self is stated through Its being devoid of the sixteen constituents (*kalā*), namely the eleven organs and the five great elements.

Likewise, based on such scriptural passages as, “Just as pure sparks fly forth from a blazing fire, even so [sparks] from this Self,” the view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is an effect of Brahman—and that liberation (*brahmaprāpti*) is the attainment by the effect of the state of its cause—is also not tenable; thus he says, “Nor...”. For an effect is at all times of the nature of its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). Therefore, its attainment of that state would be eternally established and not something to be accomplished through knowledge (*vidyā*); yet liberation is heard in scripture to be accomplished through knowledge. This is the sense.

Now, even if the effect is eternally of the nature of its cause, if the destruction of the individual soul—which is of the form of an effect—were its dissolution into the causal Brahman, then liberation would be the mere annihilation of the soul. In that case, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural text: "By knowledge, one attains immortality. For then it would follow that annihilation results from knowledge, rather than immortality. Furthermore, no one desires the annihilation of their own self, nor can a result be established without valid means of knowledge; thus, in that view, knowledge itself would be fruitless.

Furthermore, since the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), like that between space and the space within a jar, there is no relationship of cause and effect at all. Even where such a relationship is well-known, it has been stated that it does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*). Is this so independently? No; for the scripture stating "an origin from speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) establishes the unreality of modifications (*vikāra*). To explain: a modification such as a jar, and its name "jar," are merely originated by speech (*vācā kevalam ārabhyate*), but they do not exist in reality.

But only the cause is real, as in the statement, "The clay alone is real. By the word "speech" (vāk), conventional usage is indicated; thus, the meaning is that this jar and so forth are merely the means for conventional usage and do not exist in reality.

Furthermore, liberation is not the transformation of the individual soul (*jīva*) into the form of Brahman in the same way that a yogi transforms into the form of a tiger; for it would imply that one thing becomes another through transformation, as in the case of the yogi becoming a tiger. Moreover, it has already been stated that there is no difference between the individual soul and Brahman. Furthermore, in the case of transformation, there must be the acquisition of new qualities distinct from the previous state; however, such a distinction does not exist here, because there is no difference among individual souls insofar as they possess the nature of consciousness and Brahman.

If it is argued that there is a distinction because previously there was consciousness characterized by sorrow, delusion, and so forth, whereas upon the transformation of Brahman—which has pure consciousness as its sole nature—the absence of sorrow and other such states has come to be for the individual souls (*jīvas*), we say no; for even under this view, if sorrow and the rest were inherent to the nature of the *jīvas*, then because the *jīvas* are eternal, those [afflictions] too would be indestructible, just like the *jīvas* themselves.

Now, if the qualities (*guṇas*) are distinct from the living beings (*jīvas*) and are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), then, precisely because they are momentary, they perish by themselves; thus, no means known as "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is required for that purpose, and knowledge would be rendered futile. Nor can it be argued that a means is required to prevent the future arising of grief and so forth; for that [prevention] is simply their prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), and it has already been stated that such non-existence cannot be produced by a means. Therefore, there is no need for a means even for that purpose. Now, if it is claimed that there is a particular excellence of sovereignty (*aiśvaryaviśeṣa*) belonging to Brahman;

The attainment of that [Brahman] itself, which is the transformation into the nature of Brahman, is called liberation (*mokṣa*). For instance, the scripture states, "He becomes self-radiant," which declares the self-luminosity of the liberated one. That is incorrect, because it is logically untenable for there to be multiple lords (*īśvara*). To explain: the sovereignty of the liberated ones would have to be either inferior to or equal to that of Brahman. In that case, if it were inferior, there would be no attainment of the nature of Brahman, nor would there be self-luminosity; for we observe that the liberated lords remain subordinate to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

If that were the case, liberated souls would come under the sovereignty of another king. Regarding subjection to another king, the scripture states: "Now, those who know otherwise than this, they have other kings and their worlds are perishable. Consequently, the sovereignty of the liberated would be finite, and like those in heaven, there would be a return to rebirth. Therefore, the grammatical connection is: "those who know otherwise than the state of being the Self that is Brahman. Those for whom there is another king are described as such.

Nor is it untenable that [liberated souls] possess a limited sovereignty, for in the world we observe that even lesser lords may have their sovereignty fall away by the will of the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, it is simply impossible for liberated souls to simultaneously possess a sovereignty equal to that of Brahman; for if there were but one Lord who were the sovereign ruler and governor of the entire universe, then there would be nothing left for another to do. What could he possibly be doing to be considered a Lord? Moreover, due to contradiction, an equality of sovereignty cannot coexist at the same time.

Indeed, there is no reason for a rule that whatever is intended by one Lord must also be intended by another. In that case, between two Lords who hold contradictory intentions regarding a single object, if that object were to conform to the intention of only one, then it would not conform to the intention of whichever Lord it does not follow; thus, that Lord would not be a Lord, as his intention would not be realized in that object. Furthermore, if an object were to conform to the intentions of both Lords— [p.

This is indeed possible, because of the contradiction [between their wills]. Furthermore, if he does not conform to the intention of both, then the object would be something entirely different from what the intentions of both were; thus, both would likewise lack sovereignty (*anīśvaratva*). Now, it might be argued: this would indeed be so if there were no cause for unanimity (*aikamátya*); but that is not the case. For if there were discord among the Lords (*īśvara*), the effect would not be accomplished due to their mutual opposition. Therefore, the very accomplishment of the effect is the cause of their unanimity.

If it is argued that there is a consensus among many for the sake of accomplishing a task—just as in legal proceedings and the like, where there is a formal assembly (*pariṣad*)—that is not so; for in this way, each individual would lack sovereignty. And this [lack of sovereignty] is the same even in the case of a consensus based on karma. Now, if it is said that their sovereignty exists in turn (alternately) in order to avoid the contradiction mentioned above, then for one whose sovereignty has ceased, the liberation characterized by that sovereignty would be finite. This is because, upon attaining the infinite, there is the scriptural teaching of non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*).

For this reason as well, the sovereignty of the liberated is not equal to that of Brahman: because Brahman creates the world, whereas the liberated do not. They, however, attain [liberation] by worshipping the Lord after the time of creation has passed. Therefore, they do not exist at the time of creation; how then could they possess the status of creator? Thus, due to their lack of creative agency, their sovereignty is not equal to that of Brahman.

Therefore, just as in the case of a crystal whose nature is purity, when its redness—falsely attributed through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of a hibiscus flower—is removed, its pre-existing pure nature simply becomes manifest and no new quality is produced; likewise, for the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is Brahman as established by such scriptural texts as "That thou art" and "By this living self," and whose true nature is concealed by ignorance (*avidyā*), the attainment of Brahman is merely the manifestation of its own innate Brahman-nature upon the removal of ignorance through knowledge (*vidyā*), and not the acquisition of a different form.

And thus, the word *sva* (own) in the scriptural passage "in its own form" (*svena rūpeṇa*) is appropriate [only] when there is no production of another form. This word *sva* denotes both the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). If another form were produced that is non-different [from the original], then [the original] would be "that" (*tat*); if it were different, then it would be "belonging to that" (*tadīya*). Therefore, one might argue that even in the production of another form, the word *sva* is appropriate due to either non-difference or a relationship [of belonging]. This is not so, because it would follow that the qualification "by itself" (*svena*) is redundant. A qualification is meaningful only when [the qualified term] is possible and yet subject to deviation [from the intended meaning].

Ownership or one's own possession is indeed possible for that which is being produced in another form; it does not deviate from this. Therefore, the qualification "by oneself" (*svena*) is redundant. [The opponent objects: "Because of ownership"; the word *sva* denotes both the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). If liberation is merely the manifestation of one's own nature as Brahman, how then can it be said to be "produced"? For production is birth, and that is the appearance of something previously non-existent, not merely the manifestation of an already existing form. [The author replies: No.

For even in the case of manifestation, we observe the use of such specific verbal expressions; for example, when whiteness is manifested by the removal of impurities, one says, "the jar has become white," "it is produced," or "it has come into being. Therefore, this too is not a fault. Likewise, this scriptural passage as well—"Being Brahman, he attains Brahman"—[p.

He states that liberation is nothing other than the manifestation of the soul’s existing nature as Brahman; otherwise, the scriptural statement "being indeed Brahman" would not be possible. Having thus defined the nature of liberation, he explains the meaning of the verse—"liberation is not something to be accomplished, nor is it anything else"—while justifying it, saying: "Thus, therefore. The negative particle *na* functions like the "crow's eye" (shifting between both), connecting with both "not to be accomplished" (*na sādhyaḥ*) and "nor anything else" (*na cāparaḥ*). Alternatively, in the phrase "not to be accomplished," the particle may be understood as carrying over from the preceding [verse].

Alternatively, the word “na ca” (and not) is connected with the word “sādhya” (the goal to be accomplished). The phrase “aparaḥ” (another) means that it is not something else. In some places, however, the reading is “na nāparaḥ”; in that case, the meaning is that it is neither the goal to be accomplished nor another. The phrase “na cānyatvam” (nor is there any otherness) means that there is no otherness between liberation and knowledge. This is an explanation of the term “nāparaḥ. He states the reason for this non-difference with the word “yat” (because).

Since liberation is precisely the manifestation of the eternal knowledge that constitutes the very nature of Brahman, therefore there is nothing other than knowledge [that brings about liberation]. Furthermore, [liberation] is not something to be accomplished (*sādhya*); thus, it is not to be accomplished by knowledge—this is the application to the subject at hand. Although it was stated in the verse that "liberation is the cessation of ignorance" (*avidyāstamaya*), nevertheless, because it will be stated later that knowledge itself is the cessation of ignorance, there is no fault in the commentary stating that the attainment of knowledge is liberation. In the reading "the disappearance of ignorance" (*avidyāvigama*), however, there is indeed no contradiction. Regarding the phrase "as has been stated":

The meaning is that this has been stated by him [the author] according to the analogy of the crystal, namely: "This is the manifestation of the non-dual Self. He establishes that liberation (*mokṣa*) consists in knowledge (*vidyā*), which is of the nature of the manifestation of the non-dual Self, by means of the verse beginning with "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). Even though liberation is the cessation of ignorance, there is no fault, because it is well-known that "liberation is the cessation of saṃsāra. Now, one might object: even so, liberation is the cessation of ignorance, not knowledge itself. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Knowledge alone. Whether ignorance is of the nature of non-apprehension (*agraha*) or of the nature of erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*); [in either case, its cessation is brought about by knowledge].

In this regard, if non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*) is indeed ignorance (*avidyā*), then knowledge (*vidyā*) alone is its cessation, because apprehension is the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of non-apprehension; its cessation is simply the presence of apprehension and nothing else, just as the presence of a jar is the cessation of the prior absence of the jar. Alternatively, if erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*) is ignorance, even so, its cessation occurs only through the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) which is opposed to it. He establishes this by means of an illustration with the words "for not... (*na hi*). Therein, he states the reason why [ignorance] is not to be remedied by the knowledge of mother-of-pearl with the words "of those two" (*tayoḥ*).

If the cessation of the cognition of silver were to be accomplished by the cognition of mother-of-pearl, then there would be a temporal sequence between the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the cessation of the cognition of silver; yet such a thing does not exist—this is the meaning. He states the reason for its not being achievable through a further effort: "by a further effort" (*prayatnāntara*). For one does not exert a separate effort for the cessation of the cognition of silver once the cognition of mother-of-pearl has arisen—this is the meaning. [p. 249] He confirms this point with scripture—that the attainment of Brahman is indeed knowledge itself manifested, and is not something to be accomplished by it: "And so," (P. 122-3). For that which exists prior is the cause.

In that case, if the attainment of Brahman were something to be accomplished by knowledge (*vidyā*), then there would be a temporal sequence between knowledge and becoming Brahman, as expressed in "having known [it], one becomes Brahman"; likewise, there would be a sequence between knowledge and the cessation of fear, as in "having known [it], he does not fear"; and similarly, there would be a sequence between the vision of unity and the absence of delusion. However, they are not simultaneous. In this context, however, simultaneity is heard in the statements: "he knows and becomes," "the knower does not fear," and "what delusion can there be for one who perceives thus?"

For instance: the form ‘veda’ is a usage derived from the root *vid* with the suffix *liṅ*, where by the rule “*vido laṭo vā*” (Pāṇini 3.4.83), the suffix *tiP* is replaced by *ṇal*; and in ‘vidvān’, by the rule “*videḥ śaturvasuḥ*” (Pāṇini 7.1.36), the suffix *śatṛ* is replaced by *vasu*. In ‘anupaśyataḥ’, the present tense is clearly expressed. Thus, because they share the same single time—the present—there is no relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between the attainment of knowledge and [the state of being a knower]. However, in the passage “He knew that Self... became fearless,” since the forms ‘aveda’ and ‘abhayat’ have the sense of the past, a multiplicity of times is to be understood.

For instance: in the word ‘avet’, from the root *vid* in its *leṅ* (optative) form, the suffix *tip* is elided by the rule “*hallaṅghābbhyaḥ*,” resulting in a usage denoting the past tense (*bhūtārtha*). Anticipating the objection that the sequence [of knowledge and liberation] is heard in the scripture, “Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death,” he says: “As for that which... (*yattu*). He raises an objection: “But surely, if knowledge and the attainment of Brahman are identical, even simultaneity is not tenable; for simultaneity occurs only between two distinct things. He provides the answer: “No. Just as the very arising of the potsherd is the destruction of the jar, yet they are designated as distinct; so too is the case here.

Likewise here as well, the meaning is that although there is a difference in the nature of the boon (*vara*), there is only a difference in designation (*vyapadeśa*). Alternatively, even here, the difference in designation occurs precisely by way of existence and non-existence; for this is indeed manifest from such [scriptural passages] as "the knower does not fear" and "what delusion can there be for one who perceives oneness? However, in the case of "he becomes Brahman itself," the absence of non-Brahman-hood is intended by the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*); thus, there is a similarity between the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*).

Now, if liberation is indeed the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*)—which consists in the manifestation of one's own true nature as the non-dual Brahman whose essence is consciousness—then one would be liberated only at that very place where such knowledge arises.

Then, since there would be no movement [of the soul], how are scriptural passages concerning the path such as, "They quickly attain the rays, from the rays to the day," and so forth? And how are those scriptural passages that teach the dissolution of even the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—such as, "Just as the bees in the world," and "As rivers, my dear, flow into the ocean," and so forth—possible if there is no distinction [between them]? Furthermore, how are scriptural passages such as, "He becomes singlefold, he becomes twofold," possible regarding the manifestation of the nature of the non-dual Self? Thus he asks: "How? (katham).

To this, he states the following reply: "In that regard" (*tatra*). The word "the teachers" (*ācāryāḥ*) must be supplied as an ellipsis. And that [mention of the teachers] is stated for the sake of honor, not for the purpose of excluding their own view. Knowledge is both with attributes (*saguṇā*) and without attributes (*nirguṇā*). Among these, the scriptural passages concerning the path and so forth do not have knowledge without attributes as their object; for in that case, there is indeed a negation of movement, as it is heard in the scripture: "Being Brahman itself... This scripture, declaring the state of being Brahman for one whose very nature is Brahman, negates movement elsewhere because that [Brahman-]nature is easily accessible right there in that very place.

Likewise, the scriptural text beginning with "Nor do the vital breaths (prāṇas) depart from him" states that the vital breaths of the knower do not depart from the body, but rather are absorbed and dissolved right here; thus, it negates the departure of the knowing self (vijñānātman). And the instruction regarding the path has the sense of movement; the intention is that such an instruction would be purposeless in the case of the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā), since there is no movement. Now, one might object: "This negation of movement applies to the vital breaths, not to the knowing self. Anticipating this, he says: "The vital breaths... [and so on].

He states the reason for this with the words "for not" (*na hi*). Just as the state of being a reflection belongs to the original object itself through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) such as a mirror, yet appears as distinct from the original object, so too the state of being a cognitional self (*vijñānātmatva*) belongs to Brahman itself through the limiting adjunct of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), yet appears as distinct from Brahman. In that case, when the vital breaths depart, because the limiting adjunct is absent, the state of being a cognitional self no longer exists; therefore, the question "whose departure could there be? implies that it is the departure of the cognitional self itself that has been stated. This is the meaning.

To this, he says: By the statement, “The vital breaths do not depart from him,” the departure of the vital breaths having the living soul (*jīva*) as their point of departure is prohibited, not their departure having the body as their point of departure. Therefore, this is its meaning: the vital breaths do not depart leaving the living soul behind, but rather they depart from the body together with the living soul. And thus, regarding the scriptural passage from another recension, “His vital breaths do not depart,” when the question arises, “From what do his vital breaths not depart? From the body, or from the embodied one (*dehin*)?”—it is established that they do not depart from the embodied one, based on the authority of the scriptural statement, “Not from him.”

Furthermore, since a prohibition presupposes a prior attainment, the departure of the ignorant person for the purpose of taking up another body—which is heard in the text, "As he departs, the vital breaths (prāṇas) depart after him"—is what is prohibited in the case of the knower by the statement, "The prāṇas do not depart from him. It does not refer to the departure intended for the attainment of the Supreme Brahman. As it has been said: "That departure which is for the sake of another body is what is prohibited there. Therefore, even for the knower there is departure; thus, the scriptural texts concerning the path pertain to the higher knowledge as well.

And likewise, they are recited even in that specific context. This [objection] is incoherent; for instance: if the departure belonging to the ignorant is what is being denied for the knower, then how can that departure—which is heard in scripture as being from the body—be denied as being from the individual soul (*jīva*)? Or, if it is said that the denial of departure is indeed from the body, but that it is for the sake of another body and not for the sake of attaining Brahman; then by this, the departure for the sake of another body is denied for the knower.

But by whom was this [prohibition] enjoined for the purpose of attaining Brahman? Not by this very text itself, because that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Nor is it established by implication (*arthākṣepa*), since the prohibition of departing from the body is logically consistent even without it, and the attainment of Brahman is likewise possible. For instance: that which is other than oneself and situated at a distance is attained by going there; but Brahman is the soul’s own essential nature and is omnipresent; therefore, it is not something other [than the self]. [p. 251]

Nor is it situated at a distance; therefore, what would be the use of going there, such that one would be drawn away from the caravan? Furthermore, the Śruti, by stating "right here they are completely dissolved," declares the dissolution of the vital breaths in that very place, indicating the non-departure of the knower. If you argue that "here" refers to Brahman and not to a specific location, then you are a great connoisseur of the function of words!

For when it is said, "The king has not gone; he remains right here," the word "here" does not refer to a place other than that from which he did not go. Therefore, for the knower, there is no departure for the purpose of attaining Brahman; thus, the scriptural texts concerning the path—even those recited within the context of the Supreme (Brahman)—are rendered purposeless. Where they do have a purpose, they are like the mantra for the consecration of Pūṣan; let there be no further elaboration on this point. To the inquiry, "Of what subject matter, then, are those scriptural texts concerning the path? he says: "But where... and so forth.

The meaning is that those [passages] concern knowledge with attributes (*saguṇavidyā*). Nor is it the case that they are useless there as well, according to the same logic applied to the knowledge without attributes (*nirguṇavidyā*); with this intention he says, "And in that case... For the Supreme Brahman is the innate nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), and although it is eternally attained, it is—as if it were a coin in one's hand—as though unattained due to ignorance (*avidyā*). Upon the cessation of ignorance through knowledge (*vidyā*), it is easily obtained right there; thus, it does not require a journey. Therefore, the lack of utility for the scriptural texts concerning the path in that context is appropriate.

Furthermore, the effected world of Brahman (kāryabrahmaloka) resides in the third heaven from here; therefore, it is situated at a distance. Since its attainment requires a movement like that of a bird, the scriptural texts concerning the path are applicable there.
