He demonstrates the existence of the effected world of Brahman through its presence in scripture with the words "where," etc.; even those who do not know the supreme Brahman go to that effected world of Brahman.

In this regard, the scripture confirms that those who worship faith, truth, and austerity attain the effected world of Brahman (*kārya-brahmaloka*), stating: "And so it is. Now, one might object: why should those who worship the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa*) not also attain Brahman itself? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The higher," etc. He provides the reason for this: "By means of knowledge. The syntactical connection is: "He transcends death. But if those who worship the qualified Brahman attain the effected world of Brahman, then since that world perishes at the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), they must necessarily undergo rebirth.

Now, one asks how the scriptural statement regarding non-return—"they do not return to this whirlpool of human birth"—is to be understood; thus he says, "non-return. Here, he provides the answer according to different viewpoints, saying "herein. He elaborates on that with the words "that," pointing to the location of the effected world of Brahman (*kāryabrahmaloka*).

Having attained that station in the world of the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahmaloka*), those who have there acquired the realization of the reality of Brahman as liberated from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) reach the supreme state gradually when the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) occurs; thus, because there is no return for them even then, the scriptural statement regarding "non-return" (*apunarāvṛtti*) is justified. On this point, he cites the text: "Just as... Those for whom the object is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta are so described; that is, they are those who have produced the mere knowledge of the meaning of the [great] sentence. [p. 252]

This means they have not yet attained the direct realization of the unborn, non-dual Self. For this very reason, they are not liberated immediately; rather, having gone to the *kārya-brahmaloka* (the effected world of Brahmā), they are liberated thereafter. Anticipating the objection that the phrase "in the worlds of Brahmā" (*te brahmalokeṣu*) refers to the Supreme Brahman itself—and thus it would mean the attainment of that [Supreme Brahman] rather than the attainment of the *kārya-brahmaloka*—he says: "Brahman. The Supreme Brahman is one and partless. Therefore, multiplicity cannot be attributed to it either inherently or by way of its parts.

Although the effected world of Brahman (*kārya-brahmaloka*) is indeed one, nevertheless, the use of the plural number there is justified by its many constituent parts; thus, it is that very [effected world] which is meant, and not the supreme [Brahman]. On this point, some say that the plurality is not intended to be enjoined—just as in the case of the "oneness of the cup" (*graha-ekatva*)—and therefore, they claim that here the "world of Brahman" refers only to the supreme Brahman. That is incorrect, because of the mention of waiting for the time of the final end (*parāntakāla*).

For it is the consensus even of those [who hold this view] that the attainment of the Supreme Brahman by the wise does not occur at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), but rather after the fall of the body. And thus says the Sūtra: "But upon the falling away" (*pāte tu*). Furthermore, the word *loka* is primarily used for the realm of experience (*bhogabhūmi*) and not for the Supreme Brahman. Moreover, the status of being a substratum (*ādhāratva*) is appropriate only for that effected world of Brahmā (*kāryabrahmaloka*), as it is the place of residence. Therefore, this is indeed a reference to the effected world of Brahmā.

This being the case, even the plural number can somehow be justified; thus, it has been stated that this [plural number] also functions as an indicative mark (liṅga), and so there is no fault. All this—beginning with the agent—is due to the meditation (upāsanā) on Brahman. By the word "yoga," mere meditation is meant, and not the knowledge (jñāna) of That; this is what is being said. For this very reason, the fruit is the attainment of the world of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahmaloka). Regarding this very point, he cites a Smṛti passage, beginning with "tathā ca."

The meaning is that all those who have perfected themselves and possess refined intellects go to the world of Brahman; at the end of the Supreme Pradhāna—that is, upon the completion of their office—when the re-absorption, the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), occurs, they enter the supreme state together with Brahman.

Others, however, understand the meaning of the scriptural statement regarding non-return (*anāvṛtti*) as follows: Just as those performers of ritual actions who have gone to the world of the moon by the path of smoke and so forth remain there until the time of their descent, having enjoyed pleasures while staying there, they return even while that [world] still exists; it is not the case that for those who have gone to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), there is no return from it while it persists. Rather, they remain right there until the dissolution of the world of Brahman. Nor should it be argued: "Even so, since they return at its dissolution, how can there be a scriptural statement of non-return?"

Because when that [state] exists, there is no return from it; but at its dissolution, that very state does not exist—how, then, could there be a return from it? And for this reason, non-return is heard in scripture. However, where the reading is "for at its dissolution there is a return from it," the meaning there is that before that dissolution there is no return, and consequently, non-return is heard in scripture.

And thus, the specific qualifications "this human," "here they do not return," and "this here" refer to non-returning within this present creation that is currently present. If there were non-returning in every respect [absolutely], these [qualifications] would be difficult to justify. Furthermore, the phrase "by means of non-returning" refers to those living beings who attain non-returning even before the end of the dissolution (pralaya).

Even for those who die at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), immortality is established just as it is for the gods. Thus, the Smṛti states: "The state lasts until the destruction of the elements" (*ābhūtasaṃplavaṃ sthānam*); that is, they possess the nature of beings (*bhūtatva*) for as long as the aggregate of beings persists, and they die only at the dissolution. As for the view that this transformation of the elements and their derivatives belongs only to a limited portion of Brahman and is not universal—therefore, there exists an untransformed portion of Him—[that is refuted].

And thus, the Śruti passage beginning with "That which is beyond this" shows the self-luminosity shining beyond the sky, unassailed by the modifications of the world; and liberation occurs therein. Therefore, since there is utility for the scriptural texts concerning the path in attaining the Supreme Brahman, they do not have the effected (kārya) Brahman as their object. This must be examined: first of all, this instruction regarding the path is not for one who has not yet produced non-dual knowledge, because [the scripture] speaks of the knower of Brahman.

Even for one who has realized the non-dual Self, since all ignorance is completely removed by that realization, the manifold world of duality born of that ignorance dissolves everywhere; thus, Brahman remains unmodified and easily accessible even here, and so no journey elsewhere is necessary for its attainment. Therefore, the instruction regarding a path is not for the sake of reaching That, but is properly intended only for the world of the effected Brahman (kārya-brahmaloka).

As for the scriptural teaching of the non-distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman by means of the illustration of the honey-stream (*madhu-nadī*), that too does not intend to mean that there is a mutual non-distinction between the *jīva* and Brahman as substances upon their union—just as there is a non-distinction of the floral juices in honey or of rivers in the ocean—because those two are substances that do not undergo such union. Rather, it intends to show that just as there is an absence of knowledge through discrimination in those cases, so too it is with the *jīva* and Brahman; for an illustration is employed even on the basis of some degree of similarity.

Likewise, although the scriptures concerning creation appear to have creation as their primary purport, he explains them incidentally as well—in the words "In creation," etc.—in order to remove the suspicion that the non-duality [of Brahman] might be destroyed because the world being created would be real. Those [scriptures] also do not have creation as their primary purport; rather, they are intended to establish that the Self alone is the reality of the world, and that there exists no second thing other than it. Therefore, their purpose must be determined as the support of the oneness of the Self, and not otherwise; for [otherwise], the oneness of the Self, which constitutes the meaning of the sentence, would be contradicted.

How is it said that these [scriptural passages] have as their purport the oneness of the Self? The opening statement is: "Venerable sir, when what is known, does all this become known? For if the Self is one and the reality of all things, and there is no other reality apart from it, then when the Self is known, all this becomes known; it cannot be otherwise. Thus, it is understood that the opening is made with reference to the oneness of the Self. Likewise, in the passage beginning "Being alone, my dear," the opening is made with reference to oneness by stating "one only, without a second."

Likewise, there is a conclusion in terms of oneness with the words, "All this has that as its self. Therefore, this statement is intended to establish the oneness of the Self. In that context, if it were taught as a reality by being devoted to the creation of the elements, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Thus, just as in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja* sentence: "A flaw is indeed created in the sacrifice... [p. 254]

Since the opening statement, "The two cakes [are] after the two horses," and the concluding statement, "He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between for the sake of non-redundancy (*ajāmitva*)," establish that these form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), the intervening injunctions such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to silently" do not attain independent status due to the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*). Consequently, because they are supplementary to the *upāṃśuyāja*, they must be interpreted in accordance with it as follows: "So great is this *upāṃśuyāja*, so highly esteemed, that when it is performed, Viṣṇu and the others also become objects of sacrifice."

Thus, these [passages] are established as being for the purpose of praising the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice; likewise, the *sṛṣṭi* (emanation) scriptural passages are intent upon conveying the diversity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) that is being emanated, which constitutes the meaning of the sentence. This is because in all cases, both the opening and the conclusion are heard as being in unity, and that which is heard through those two is the meaning of the sentence; and that which is the meaning of the sentence is the primary matter, and whatever is the primary matter, everything else is connected for its sake. Furthermore, the knowledge of difference is fruitless.

The knowledge of the oneness of the Self, however, is fruitful by virtue of its visible result, namely the cessation of grief and the like. Therefore, according to the maxim that "that which is fruitless stands as a subordinate part when in proximity to that which is fruitful," the scriptures concerning creation are likewise intended to establish the identity of the Self. In this context, the fact that the result is visible is stated by the words beginning with "therein, being purified" (*viśuddha*), while the fact that it is heard [from scripture] is indicated by the words beginning with "what delusion is there? (*tatra ko mohaḥ*). It has been stated that the scriptures concerning creation are established as a means to that unity; he now demonstrates that status as a means: "And [their] status as a means... (*upāyatvaṃ ca*) and so forth.

The meaning of the Śruti passage, “How could the existent be born from the non-existent? is stated as: “This [world] does not have the non-existent as its root. However, the meaning of the Śruti passage, “In the beginning, this was Being alone, one only, without a second,” is that it has the non-dual, single Being as its root. Now, one might object: if there is thus a difference between cause and effect, how can there be the oneness of the Self? Anticipating this doubt, he says: “The cause...”. This would indeed be so if there were a distinction (vyatireka) between the two; but that very distinction does not exist, because of the perception of non-difference in such expressions as “this clay is the pot. The word “this” (idam) means the world (jagat).

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Like a pot, etc. The meaning is that just as there is oneness of pots and so forth in the form of clay, so too is there oneness of the world in the form of Being (*sat*). Now, one might object with the intention: "If the world has Being as its root, then a primary relation of cause and effect would have been asserted; and consequently, the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would follow, which would entail the loss of non-duality (*advaita*). With this in mind, he raises the objection: "Now [if]... He refutes it: "No. He elaborates upon this: "Not [as] their own [nature]," thereby explaining that [the distinction between cause and effect] is merely a means for entering into the realization of oneness.

As it has been said: “The creation taught in the Śruti by means of clay, sparks, and so forth, is a pedagogical device for the sake of introduction; there is no difference whatsoever. This means that because of an excessive attachment to duality, one who is unable to comprehend non-duality all at once is instructed that the world—which is non-different from Being (sat) in its form as Being due to having Being as its material cause—is non-different in its form as clay, just like a jar and other objects made of clay. But [one might object]: [p. 255]

One might object that even if the causal relation is primary, there will still be a means for establishing unity; even so, the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would not be contradicted. Anticipating this, he says: "And that... That [primary causal relation] is opposed to unity; therefore, the meaning is that the non-primary [relation] is what is grasped. Now, one might further object that even if the causal relation is primary, there is multiplicity in the form of the effect and unity in the form of the cause, so there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding unity. Anticipating this, he negates it by saying: "one."

Furthermore, if there were multiplicity in the form of the effect, then because the effect would also be real, the Śruti would not have determined the unique reality of the cause—denoted by the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "That is real" (*tatsatyam*)—to the exclusion of others; yet it does so determine it. Therefore, he says "That is real" to show that there is no multiplicity in the form of the effect. But surely, there is also the term "real" applied to the effect, as in "Clay alone is real" and "The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed real."

It is said in reply: Just as when the innermost, primary Self is intended to be expressed, the word "Self" (ātman) is applied to the "sheaths" such as the one consisting of breath (prāṇamaya) in order to indicate that which is declared by the term "Self" in the passage, "There is another inner Self consisting of breath"; yet this does not imply that those sheaths possess the status of the primary Self. Similarly, with the intention of expressing the primary reality of the root cause, the word "Real" (satya) is employed in reference to clay—which possesses a reality established for the ignorant—and to the vital breaths (prāṇas), whose reality is not so established, in the phrase "Of these, this is the Real. Thus, there is no fault.

Regarding the absence of multiplicity in its nature as an effect, he cites another two scriptural passages with the words "elsewhere. Here he states another reason with the words "difference," etc.; what was explained under the phrase "unity without contradiction" should be remembered here. Therefore, in accordance with all these scriptural texts, just as reflections are variations of the original image and words are variations of phonemes, so too the world-variation has the Self as its material cause. He says "this" to show how the scripture on creation is thus described.

He explains the two examples with the words "Just as" (*yathā hi*). Just as it is said that reflections arise from an original object (*bimba*), yet they do not exist in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), so too it is said: "From the Self, space was produced; from space, air. Furthermore, there is scriptural mention of creation even in a dream; however, the chariots and other things therein do not possess reality merely on that account. He says "Moreover" (*api ca*) to show that this creation of the elements will be similar, since its purpose is the realization of the unity of the Self.

Furthermore, if the creation of beings from the chariot were ultimately real (*pāramārthikī*), then it would have been stated as such by the scriptural passage on "the origin of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa-śruti*) itself, which determines that only the cause is real by stating, "clay alone is real. But this is not the case, as he says: "by itself" (*svayam*). Having thus explained the purport of the scriptures concerning creation, he speaks of the scriptures concerning lordly power (*aiśvarya*): "lordly power," etc. In the knowledge of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-vidyā*), various states such as being manyfold and so forth—which correspond to results like heaven—are heard of here as the fruit; but liberation (*mokṣa*) is not. That [liberation]... [p. 256]

The meaning is that [the non-return] is caused by knowledge devoid of qualities (*nirguṇavidyā*). But how is it that even there, in some places, there is a scriptural statement regarding non-return? Anticipating this objection, he says: "As for that which... The phrase "there are two paths" means that the scriptural hearing of non-return has been explained as intending either gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) or the non-return of the current creation (*vartamānasargānāvṛtti*). Regarding the scriptural texts on lordly power (*aiśvarya*), he states another opinion: "Others..."

Since Brahman is the self of all, the Lord of all, the enjoyer of all enjoyments, and omniscient; and since the bliss of the gods and others are but minute portions (*mātrā*) of the bliss of Brahman—therefore, whatever lordship and so forth exists among beings from Brahmā down to the immovable, all that is in Brahman. And whatever is in Brahman, all that the knower—who has manifested the true nature of Brahman—attains, because Brahman is the self of all. Thus, for him, it is said: "He attains all desires," and so forth.

The meaning is that this is stated for the purpose of praising liberation, which is characterized by the manifestation of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). Now, an objection is raised with the words "But surely" (*nanu*): if the knower, having manifested the nature of Brahman, attains all desires because he is the Self of all, then, precisely because he is the Self of all, he would also incur the sorrow and other afflictions residing in all beings; consequently, there would be suffering even in liberation. With this intention, the opponent objects. The author refutes this with "No" (*na*). The meaning is: the knower attains the form of Brahman, but sorrow and the like are not the form of Brahman.

He states the reason for this: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*). Since knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth are the very nature of Brahman, he says "knowledge" (*jñāna*) to show that it is logical that these are attained upon the attainment of Brahman. But how is it understood that knowledge and the rest are the nature of Brahman? He replies: "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*). The distinction is as follows: the scripture "There is no other seer than He" establishes their nature as knowledge; "Of this" establishes their nature as bliss; and "The Lord of all" establishes their nature as sovereignty.

Thus, since grief and the like are superimposed upon [the Self] by ignorance (avidyā), while knowledge and the like are the very nature of Brahman, it is logical that the knower, having manifested his true nature as Brahman, experiences knowledge and the like, but not grief and the like; so he says: "And thus... Here, an objection is raised: "But surely... He refutes this: "This is not so... He illustrates this with two examples: "By the established... Now, an objection is raised: even if Brahman is of the nature of light and independent of objects to be illumined, since Brahman is non-dual, how can there be omniscience when nothing else exists? Anticipating this, he says: "And thus..."

This being the case—that is, when Brahman is of the nature of light independent of anything to be illumined—the meaning is that even though everything is absent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), during the state of ignorance (*avidyāvasthā*), the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is encompassed by the self-consciousness of the Self, as established by such scriptural texts as "By its light" (*tasya bhāsā*). Thus, the Self possesses omniscience. Having raised the objection that if there is an absence of everything in non-dual Brahman, its status as the Lord of all (*sarveśvaratva*) would be untenable, he establishes that very point with the word "all" (*sarva*).

Here too, even in the state of ignorance (*avidyāvasthā*), whatever sovereignty belongs to the lords such as Brahmā, Indra, and others, each over their respective objects of rule, all that belongs to Brahman alone because He is the Self of all; thus, the meaning is that His is the status of being the Lord of All (*sarveśvaratva*) by virtue of that very sovereignty. He states that the same interpretation applies to passages such as "He is the lord of beings" (*eṣa bhūtānām adhipatiḥ*).

Thus it is said. Even in that case, during the state of ignorance (*avidyā*), the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of Brahmā, Indra, and others over the elements and the worlds is actually the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord Himself, manifested in them as something delimited through specific ritual actions and meditations (*upāsanā*). Therefore, the meaning is that the sovereignty belonging to Indra and the others is what has been described as belonging to the Supreme Lord in such passages as, "He is the lord of beings" (*eṣa bhūtādhipatiḥ*).

Having raised the objection that the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of all desires (*sarvakāmāvāpti*) is untenable because there is an absence of any desire for heaven or the like with respect to one whose nature is the manifested non-dual Brahman, he establishes its validity as well by saying "all" (*sarva*). Here too, within the sphere of ignorance (*avidyābhūmi*), whatever various desires are attained through action, the blisses associated with each of those are, according to the scripture—"Of this very bliss, other beings live on a mere fraction"—nothing but the bliss of Brahman itself.

And for this reason, it is said that "he attains all desires" because the wise man who has reached Brahman attains all those joys; the meaning is not that he attains all desires in their own literal form. He extends this very interpretation to another scriptural passage with the word "thus. Here he provides an illustration with the word "just as. Anticipating the objection that the illustration is unestablished, he proves its validity with the words "for not. For play and sexual union occur only by means of a second [entity]; and for one who has attained non-dual Brahman, there is no second.

Therefore, just as he is called "one whose self is his companion" (*ātmamithuna*) here because of attaining the bliss of union, so too expressions such as "rejoicing with women" are stated according to the aforementioned principle by virtue of attaining that same bliss; this is the meaning. He confirms with the *Gītā* the point that those very qualities of Brahman, such as knowledge and the rest, which are unlimited, appear as if limited through superimposition within the elements, and there are no others: "And because... (*yataśca*).

Precisely because those very qualities—knowledge, bliss, and so forth—which are unlimited in Brahman alone, exist in all beings in a limited form, therefore, wherever among beings there is no absolute limitation or diminution of knowledge and the rest, those beings such as Vyāsa and others are proximate to the Blessed One due to the excellence of their knowledge and other attributes. Having declared Himself to be "Vyāsa among the sages" by way of identity, that which was said regarding "the sages" and so forth refers to the principle: "Whatever being is possessed of glory... (BhG 10.41).

The meaning is that they thus concluded. It is understood that the knowledge of the Supreme Self alone, being unlimited, is the cause of such worldly activities as seeing and so forth; therefore, he speaks specifically regarding this knowledge with the word "tathā" (thus). The meaning is that the fact that the seeing, hearing, and other functions of all beings are based upon the knowledge of the Supreme Self is heard in such scriptural passages as, "the unseen Seer," and so on. Having thus established omniscience and other attributes, he states another view regarding that matter with the word "anye" (others).

That for which name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are the basis of word and meaning is described as such. Meditation itself is *adhyāna*. He states an illustration regarding that: "just as" (*yathā*). He establishes this with: "for not" (*na hi*). Regarding the phrase "of one established in his own majesty": [this refers to] the support. [Page 258, line 17]

He states its independence [from external causes]. The specific location is the solar orb; the form consists of the golden [egg] and so forth. Now, one might ask: "How is it known that this specific location and form belong to the Supreme Brahman alone? To this he says: "The Supreme. He cites the scripture: "Risen" (*udita*). By the word "evil" (*pāpman*), merit is also implied; thus, it means risen above or gone upward from all merits and evils—that is to say, untouched by them.

Furthermore, it has been heard from another [scriptural source] that there is no contact with merit or demerit "except for the Dharma. Therefore, this specific location and form were heard of as belonging to the Supreme Being alone; yet these two are not possible for Him who is all-pervading and formless. Consequently, meditation is enjoined upon Him by means of that form. In the same way, omniscience and other such qualities are also to be understood.

Thus, having resolved the scriptural passages concerning the path to liberation and so forth—which have that manifestation of one's true nature as their defining characteristic—as well as other passages occurring by way of context, he establishes that very liberation [with the words] "Thus, in this manner. Regarding the phrase "of the Brahman-Self": he is called such because for the knower, Brahman itself is the Self; the meaning is the manifestation of that form. And since that attainment belongs to the Self, and because the Self is of the nature of knowledge, it is indeed knowledge itself; thus he says, "And that..."

This being the case, he concludes what was stated—that "liberation is not something to be accomplished, nor is it other than knowledge"—with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He raises an alternative view with "Now" (*atha*). To provide authority for the stated point, he says "It is heard" (*śrūyate*). An objection is raised: "Indeed, it is heard that only evil (*pāpman*) is burnt away by knowledge, not merit (*puṇya*); yet even that [merit] is a cause of bondage. Therefore, knowledge is not the cause for the destruction of all causes of bondage. Anticipating this, he says "Evil" (*pāpma*). He states the reason for this with "That which is accompanied by fault" (*sāvadya*).

The analysis of the compound is: "that whose fruit is blameworthy (sāvadya) and possessed of defect (sadoṣa). Defect (doṣa) consists in being bound to saṃsāra and being subject to falling [from one's state] and other such things to be avoided. Regarding the point that by the word *pāpman* merit (*puṇya*) is also expressed, he states another reason for this: "elsewhere. The meaning is that since the word *pāpman*, which begins with "good and evil deeds" (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*), occurs there in reference to both of them. Furthermore, if liberation were possible without the exhaustion of karma, then it would not be something to be accomplished; but that is not the case, as he says: "nor is it... (*na ca*).

Since an action is destroyed only by its fruit, there is no cessation of an action that has not yet yielded its fruit; therefore, raising the doubt as to how such [karma] could be exhausted by knowledge, he says: "Of expiations. Expiations are prescribed in connection with faults such as the killing of a cow, and it has been stated that they are not merely for the sake of the occasion [of the fault]. Therefore, it is understood that these are causes for the destruction of the fault. By means of that expiation, the sinful karma whose fruit has not yet been given is exhausted. Likewise, by means of knowledge, there is the exhaustion of the karma that is the cause of bondage; this is the meaning.

One might object: "If the destruction of the karma that causes bondage is accomplished by knowledge (*vidyā*), then liberation does not result from knowledge. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That very [knowledge]" (*saiva*). Thus, the claim that liberation is the manifestation of one's true nature (*svarūpāvirbhāva*) is also refuted.

Now, one might object: if the destruction of karma were an effect of knowledge, then because it is an effect, it would be finite—just like a jar; and consequently, due to the reappearance of karma, there would be rebondage for the liberated person. Anticipating this, he says: "In this way" (*evam*). The point is that the destruction of a jar is not perishable, since we do not observe the re-appearance of the jar. Having thus set forth the opponent's view, he refutes it with the word "therein" (*tatra*). By that same logic which applies to expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), [the destruction of karma is not perishable].

The destruction or exhaustion of the karma that is the cause of bondage does not occur [independently]; for when all ignorance (*avidyā*) has dissolved, no karma remains to be severed. He states the reason for this with the word "bandha" (bondage). Karma is the cause of bondage because it has ignorance as its material cause (*upādāna*); therefore, it possesses the very nature of ignorance. In that context, when knowledge (*vidyā*) exists, ignorance is utterly destroyed. Consequently, by the very cessation of ignorance, that which is the cause of bondage consisting of it also ceases; thus, the meaning is that nothing remains separately to be severed.

The very arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is itself the cessation of the cause of bondage consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, the sense is that [bondage] is not something to be accomplished by that [knowledge]. The commentary (*vṛtti*) has a clear meaning. He shows the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the destruction of karma through the destruction of ignorance with the words "And because" (*yataśca*). The meaning is that the mention of karma together with doubt and error—which are being destroyed by the destruction of ignorance—in the passage "the knot of the heart is severed," indicates their destruction through the destruction of ignorance. By "knot of the heart," error (*viparyaya*) is intended.

Here he raises an objection: "Now then" (*nanu*). To this, he states the fault: "Of that" (*tasya*). For one who has attained knowledge, the delay lasts only as long as it takes to be liberated from the body; there is a Vedic elision of the letter *t*. The meaning is that immediately after liberation from the body, one shall attain Brahman. To the question, "Whose [scriptural statement] would not be contradicted by this? he replies: "Of whom" (*yasya*).

The meaning is that for one who understands from the scripture that knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cause of the destruction of karma, a systematic arrangement becomes possible according to the scripture: that for some karmas there is destruction by knowledge, while for others there is destruction through experience. He states this in accordance with the scripture: "In that case" (*tatra*), meaning in that view; "thence" (*tataḥ*), meaning from knowledge. He provides the reason for the following point: when, as a general rule (*utsarga*), the destruction of all karma by knowledge would result without distinction, that [rule] is set aside by the scriptural statement that liberation depends upon the falling away of the body; he says "for not... (*na hi*) to provide the reason for this.

If all karmas were destroyed by knowledge (*vidyā*), liberation would occur immediately upon the arising of that knowledge; consequently, the waiting for the fall of the body would be untenable, yet such waiting is indeed heard of in scripture. Therefore, the meaning is that it is understood that some karmas are exhausted through experience (*bhoga*). He states that this path is favored by the Teacher: "That has been said. Having caused the destruction of those merits and demerits whose effects have not yet begun—that is, those which have not yet yielded their fruit and do not initiate the present body—by means of knowledge acquired previously...

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: as for others, however, whose work has already begun, they reach Brahman after exhausting those works by means of their momentum, since scripture declares that liberation occurs at the limit of that [work], namely at the fall of the body. But in the case of one whose engagement with the fruits of karma is cut off by knowledge through its very perception, there would be liberation immediately thereafter due to the destruction of all karma without distinction upon the destruction of all ignorance by knowledge; consequently, the scriptural statement regarding the limit of liberation being the fall of the body would be contradicted. To this he says: "By knowledge... He refutes that objection: "This is not so."

The meaning is that there is no defect of contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding the limit of the body's fall. He states the reason for this: "For not... (na hi). The sense is that if this scripture were to declare that liberation is characterized by a long duration ending at the fall of the body, then this defect would arise; however, such is not the case. In response to the expectation of what it actually says, he says: "But rather... (kiṃ tu). Here he provides an illustration: "Just as... (yathā).

Just as someone who is commanded, "Go more quickly," and wishing to demonstrate that greater speed, says, "That [time] which it takes me to bathe, eat, put on my sandals, or mount a horse is indeed long for me"—the meaning is that it is exactly so in this case as well. For if mere duration were intended in the Śruti, then it would simply say "long" (cira); it would not specify a particular limit by saying "only that much" (tāvadeva).

The intention of the Śruti, which indicates that the limit [of liberation] is the fall of the body, is this: since the body, which is born of ignorance, must fall immediately upon the cessation of ignorance through knowledge, liberation occurs very quickly. Thus he says "otherwise" to show that the Śruti is observed to have ceased its task. He concludes with "therefore": "it need not be awaited"; the meaning is that one need not wait for the exhaustion of commenced karma (*ārabdhakarman*) by means of experience (*bhoga*).

And since liberation occurs immediately thereafter, because that [liberation] is impossible without the falling away of the body, the falling away of the body also necessarily occurs immediately; thus he says: "the body" (*deha*). He states another meaning for this scripture: "or else" (*athavā*). He points out the fault in both interpretations: "otherwise" (*anyathā*). This being the case, he states the meaning which results from the scripture: "therein" (*tatra*). The meaning is that, having restated the fact that for some the duration of liberation is long as established by other sources, the release from the body is prescribed as the limit.

In that regard, he raises an objection concerning the meaning of the first scriptural passage with the words "Now, [is it not the case]? (nanu). The meaning is: since the wise one (*prājña*) who abides in liberation immediately after the dawning of knowledge has no body at all because his body has fallen away, for whom is this characteristic being stated? He also raises an objection concerning the meaning of the second scriptural passage with the words "In the second [case] as well" (dvitīye 'pi). The meaning is: if all karma is destroyed by knowledge, then the body born of karma falls immediately thereafter; thus, for anyone in liberation, there can be no state of duration (*ciratva*). Consequently, it is not tenable to enjoin a specific limit by way of restating that [state].
In this regard, he first addresses the following objection: "It is said. When all ignorance has dissolved, [the Self] is established; when it has dissolved...

One who has attained perfection (*siddha*) through that knowledge in which all ignorance has been dissolved is one for whom all ignorance has vanished. He who, through the ripening of the practice of yoga, attains the light of the direct realization of the non-dual Self and is liberated immediately thereafter, is not the "one of steady wisdom" (*sthitaprajña*). Rather, it is one who is still a practitioner (*sādhaka*) regarding the mode of the direct realization of the non-dual Self, who has reached a particular stage but remains in a state slightly prior to perfection—this one who is considered "perfected" (*siddha-bhrānta*) but is not yet truly perfected, is the one of steady wisdom.

The meaning is that it is appropriate to state the characteristics of that [self] which has not yet attained a body. He refutes the second objection with the words "And not... (*na ca*). Regarding the point that [liberation] would follow if there were no dependence on karma whose effects have already begun, he says "In that case" (*tatra*). The sense is this: if one expects the exhaustion of karma through experience, then everyone would attain liberation only after a long time. However, if there is no such expectation, then for some it might be at that very moment, while for others it would be after a long time. For one who attains it after a long time, it is logical to first state that duration and then prescribe a specific limit (*avadhi*); this is the intended meaning.

Now, one might object: even when one does not wait for the exhaustion of karma that has already begun to bear fruit through experience, nevertheless, once ignorance is removed by knowledge and all karma produced by it ceases, there must be an immediate separation from the body born of that [ignorance]; therefore, how can liberation (apavarga) last for a long time for anyone? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as... [and] "from its residual impression" (tatsaṃskārāt). By the word "that" (tat), fear, trembling, and so forth are meant.

The meaning is that it is based on that latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which arises when the fruit of the karma whose effects have begun is being experienced and ripened—an impression consisting of the notions "I am the embodied experiencer" and "this is the object of experience"—and its continued persistence. He provides an illustration for the persistence of an effect due to a latent impression with the words "as in the case of a lineage" (*kulaletivat*). Here, he raises an objection with "But surely... (*nanu...*) and states the fault in that position with "And thus... (*tathāca...*).

Now, if it is argued that, out of fear of this defect, the perception of the distinction between the enjoyer and so forth—which is caused by ignorance (*avidyā*)—does not continue because ignorance is severed by knowledge (*vidyā*), then there would be no perception of the distinction between the enjoyer and so forth even for a moment; thus, that same contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding the limit of the body's fall remains. He says "Now" (*atha*) to state that this is like a rope with a noose at both ends, due to the defect on both sides. Therein, without even accepting the position of non-continuation, he refutes the defect stated against the position of continuation, saying: "It is said" (*ucyate*).

"And not from the root cause": the meaning is that just as trembling and so forth are more intense when accompanied by *abhiniveśa* (clinging) due to fear—the root cause—so too [is it] due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that [fear]. And this has been stated for the purpose of the distinction to be explained later: namely, that the fruit of the root cause, which is karma, is accompanied by *abhiniveśa*, whereas the fruit of its latent impression is not. "From that alone" means: from the very perception of the rope-ness [of the object].

But is it not the case that [the realization of truth] is momentary; therefore, how can there be a gradual cessation [of fear]? It is said: just as the accomplishment of a fruit from a momentary act such as a sacrifice occurs by means of the production of *apūrva* (unseen merit), so too, from the vision of reality, the cessation of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of fear occurs by means of the production of a [new] impression; thus there is no fault. [p. 262] It [ceases] of its own accord.

In the phrase "or [it ceases] by itself," the example is the momentum (*saṃskāra*) of a spinning wheel. And all of this has been stated for the purpose of supporting the point that "the persistence [of the impression] does not continue merely because fear has ceased, nor does it last for a long time. In the phrase "or by itself," the word "gradually" (*krameṇa*) is understood to carry over. Now, one might object: the destruction of a momentary thing is seen to have a cause; so how can it be said to be "by itself"? Even the momentum of the wheel is destroyed only by its fruit.

If it is argued that [the karma] perishes through contact with a substance such as a portion of the earth, then the example is unestablished. It is replied: who says that it does not have a cause? Time itself will be the cause; for this very reason, it was stated "gradually. Furthermore, it is observed that time also possesses the power to destroy things such as the impurity (*sūtaka*) resulting from birth or death. The same will be the case here as well. How then is it said to be "by itself"? There is no fault, for it was stated with the intention of expressing merely the non-dependence on any other effort.

Having thus established the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he applies it to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "so" (*tathā*). Regarding the phrase "in actions whose effects have begun and those whose effects have not yet begun," the term "ceased" (*nivṛttāyām*) from the feminine singular must be applied as "ceased" (*nivṛtteṣu*) by changing the gender and number. The compound *rūḍhābhiniveśa* is analyzed as follows: one for whom there is an "established" (*rūḍhaḥ*, i.e., manifested) "adherence" (*abhiniveśaḥ*), meaning an intense attachment.

Therefore, this is the meaning: through knowledge, when ignorance and the karmas—both those whose effects have already begun (*ārabdha*) and those not yet begun (*anārabdha*)—have ceased, the fruition that has already begun (*ārabdha-vipāka*), which is being experienced as the fruit of karma whose effect was initiated, leads the knower to perceive himself as a mere reflection, a physical enjoyer devoid of any sense of identification due to the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that commenced effect. He does not, however, perceive himself as possessed of the intense sense of "I-ness" as the ignorant man does.

This is what is meant: even when that karma whose fruit has already begun has ceased, as long as its fruit is being experienced, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of embodiedness and so forth that has arisen causes one to continue to regard oneself as an embodied enjoyer for a subsequent period of time. In this context, before completing the intended point, [the author] first describes the nature of the man of steady wisdom (*sthitaprajña*) in order to justify the statement regarding his characteristics, saying: "And he, this... etc.

Previously, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) was described as one whose wisdom is established (*sthitaprajña*); now, however, he is described as one who has attained perfection (*siddha*). This is the distinction. To bring about his characteristics—such as "when he casts off desires," "satisfied in the self by the self alone," and "with a mind undisturbed in sorrows"—the Lord says: "one whose [fears] have departed," and so on. Here He provides an illustration with the word "just as. He applies the stated meaning to the subject of the illustration with the word "so. The analysis of the compound is: "one from whom ignorance born of action has departed" (*vigata-kṣaṇa*), or "one for whom actions and ignorance have departed" (*vigata-kṣaṇi*).

Regarding the phrase "due to the impression of that" (*tatsaṃskārāt*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to action (*karman*); even in the second analysis of the compound, it refers to action and ignorance (*avidyā*). In that case, it should be understood that the impression of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃskāra*) is also indicated. By the expression "merely as a shadow" (*chāyāmātreṇa*), he shows the absence of attachment (*abhiniveśa*). He confirms the absence of attachment to the body and so forth in the case of the knower through scripture with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). Just as the slough of a snake (*ahinirvayanī*)—the skin of a snake—is cast off [p. 263].

Having been rejected and abandoned due to the emptiness of the notion of "I," that [body] lies as if deficient; the meaning is that for the wise man, the body merely follows along with residual impressions (*saṃskāra*). Anticipating the objection—"Why, then, should there not be attachment even to the body, which persists through residual impressions, just as there is to karma?"—he says: "Because... (P. 132-3). Furthermore, the incomparability [of the body] is illustrated by the residual impression of fear.

Now, regarding the statement that if the perception of distinctions such as the enjoyer and so forth persists due to residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), it must persist even after the fall of the body—that is now refuted with the words "trembling, etc. Here he states the reason: "insignificant, etc. An objection is raised: "If residual impressions persist, another means must be practiced for their cessation; yet the knower possesses no such means. Anticipating this, he says: "in the very same way. The suffix *vati* is applied here according to the rule *tatra tasyeva*, following a word in the seventh case.

The meaning is that, just as in that case [of the spinning top], no other cause is required for the cessation of the momentum (*saṃskāra*) such as its trembling, so it is here as well. Now, by this very context, he shows liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) as well—starting with "And that" (*sā ca*). If it is asked how the destruction of the momentum is known, he says in response: "The prārabdha... [etc.]. But surely, in some places it is called the momentum of the ripening being experienced (*bhujyamāna-vipāka-saṃskāra*), while in others it is called the momentum of karma (*karma-saṃskāra*).

What is this confused statement? It is not confused, because both alternatives are intended as options (*vikalpa*); and so he will say later: "Either from the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of a cause whose function has been realized, or from the residual impression of the effect itself. Alternatively, even there, by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound—such as "one whose fruition (*vipāka*) is being experienced" or "one whose fruition has begun"—it is karma that has commenced its effect (*prārabdhakārya*) which is expressed; thus there is no contradiction. He asks "How? and replies with the word "that" (*tat*).

At that very moment, upon the fall of the body, because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the karma whose effects have begun (*prārabdha-kārya-karma*) have been exhausted, it is impossible for the fruit of that karma—which is caused by those impressions—to be perceived even as a mere appearance of fruition after the body has fallen. Thus he says: "iti" (thus). The word "iti" signifies a reason and is connected to both [parts of the sentence] like the eye of a crow. The sign (*liṅga*) for the exhaustion of the latent impressions of the karma whose effects have begun has been stated; now the logical justification (*upapatti*) is being stated: "yena hi" (for by which...).

The meaning is this: by whatever action a particular body has been initiated, that action yields its fruit in that very body and not elsewhere; and wherever that fruit is yielded, it is logical that even from the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) there arises the appearance of the remainder of that fruit. Now, one might ask: just as the impression of an action whose fruit has already begun persists even after the action itself has ceased, why does the impression of actions whose fruits have not yet begun not likewise persist? And if such persistence were to occur, the impression would become long-lasting.

Therefore, suspecting that this very point contradicts the scriptural statement regarding the limit being until the fall of the body, he says: "anārabdha" (unbegun). He states the reason for this here: "labdha" (obtained); that by which the activity or operation has been obtained for its effect is so described. He establishes this by means of an illustration: "na svalv" (not indeed). Because its activity has not been obtained, for that very reason there is no arising of trembling and so forth; this is the relationship between cause and effect. That by which the activity has not been obtained... [p. 264]

The analysis of the compound is: "that by which trembling and so forth have not been produced"; the word *bhaya* (fear) is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). He concludes the present topic with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). By this, the objection raised in the passage beginning with "Now, even for one who knows Brahman... and ending with "...liberation would not be inevitable," has been refuted. Now, since the desired goal is established in every respect, he shows disregard for the determination of specific residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) with the words "And here... (*atra ca*). The cause is action (*karman*), and the effect is its fruit.

The meaning is that, due to the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of the action whose momentum has been acquired and whose effects have already begun, or from the impression of its effects, a remainder of the work continues even for the wise one. He shows that this same direction applies to the illustrative example as well with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). In response to the expectation—"Therefore, why is a specific residual impression not taken into account?"—he says "in every way" (*sarvathā*). The reason here is fear; the "remainder of the work" consists of trembling and so forth produced by residual impressions. He concludes the subject at hand with the word "hence" (*ataḥ*).

The sense is that, therefore, there is no contradiction with the scriptural statement that liberation lasts until the fall of the body. By this, the objection raised—that [liberation] could not exist even for a moment—is also refuted. He strengthens his own position by showing it is established in the *Kāpila-tantra*, stating: "As it has been said. For it is impossible for knowledge to obstruct those karmas whose fruits have already begun to manifest, just as it is impossible to stop an arrow already in flight or a potter's wheel already set spinning.

Therefore, it is well said that "their destruction is expected through experience," as he presents the view of the venerable Bhagavatpāda: "But having exhausted the others through experience. He refutes that [view] with the words "That... Even an arrow whose momentum has already been set in motion can be obstructed by those such as a hunchback; therefore, the illustrative example itself is unestablished.

The point is this: just as in that case [of the arrow] there is an obstruction of the arrow—even though its momentum has already begun—by means of a hunchbacked woman or others, so too is there an obstruction of karmas by means of knowledge (*vidyā*); therefore, it is not logical to wait for their destruction through experience. Let the matter of obstruction stand for a moment; however, since even destruction is possible, the word "to destroy" (*nāśayitum*) is used to demonstrate, by way of the maxim of the "stick and the *apūpa*" (the stick being found where the cake was), that obstruction is established as a matter of course. If it is argued that while the obstruction of an arrow with a visible purpose is possible, it is not so for karma which has an unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*), he says: "its own nature" (*svamā*).

That karma whose ripening—the fruit—is indicated by such signs as the dream of ascending a tree and manifested by such events as the swoop of a vulture, and which is to be experienced in the present body—that karma is thus concluded. He concludes his own position with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). By the phrase "from residual impressions alone" (*saṃskārādeva*), he refutes the expectation that the exhaustion of karma must await the completion of its commenced effects. [Objection: But if this is so, then the statement previously made—that "when all ignorance has been dissolved, nothing remains to be cut away"—is contradicted.

That is not so; for, since the residual appearances of the effects of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) dissolve by themselves, they are not things to be dissolved. With this intention, it was stated: "nothing remains to be cut.

Since even those two, ignorance and the self, are incapable of producing any effect, their non-existence is superimposed according to the analogy of "having no son"; thus, with the intention of referring to what is to be cut away, it is said, "in the dissolution of all ignorance"—this is the intended sense of the resolution in both cases. He states the reason for showing their equivalence to being dissolved: "akiñcit" (incapable of anything). If something is dissolved, it is incapable of any effect, it is no longer bound, and it does not require any other cause for its own cessation. The same applies to the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the remainder of their effects; therefore, the meaning is that these two also are as good as dissolved.

In that regard, the fact that [the world] ceases by itself, without dependence on any other cause, has already been stated in the passage beginning with "from that very [knowledge], it ceases gradually," or "it ceases by itself"; thus, setting that aside, he describes how the semblance of the remainder of effects is almost entirely dissolved, preceded by the demonstration of the logical impossibility of its being either productive or binding—starting with the word "pure" (*viśuddham*). The semblance of the remainder of effects belonging to the karma whose results have begun to manifest (*prārabdha-karma*) is the semblance of its maturation (*vipāka-ābhāsa*); that does not touch the one who perceives the Self as pure, untouched by the impurity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

And that which does not touch darkness does nothing to it, yet it binds it. Therefore, the meaning is that he is as if already dissolved, like a cloud with a hole. Although it was previously asserted that even residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) are incapable of acting [upon him], nevertheless, his incapacity was stated by way of the appearance of a remainder of effects; thus, since that [residual impression] is incapable of acting upon him, its own incapacity is also implicitly stated, and so it is mentioned here separately. He provides an illustration for this: "Just as... and so forth.

In the phrase "the appearance of the source and so forth," the word "dissolved" (*pravilīna*) is understood to carry over; the meaning is "as if dissolved. By the words "of passion and so forth," their inefficacy is stated. He provides another illustration with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). Regarding the word "self" (*ātmānam*): by the term *ātman*, the worldly self consisting of the body is meant. "Pure" (*avadātam*) means fair-complexioned. "The opposite" (*viparītam*) means not pure (*anavadātam*).

In this context, the meaning is as follows: although a dark appearance arises in a bright face when reflected in a sword or the like, and a bright appearance arises in a dark face when reflected in a mirror or the like, because one knows the true nature of the face, that appearance finds no room for contact with the self and is thus almost entirely dissolved. He confirms this state of being "almost dissolved" with the words, "And so it is. By this, a great distinction is established between the two types of bodily persistence—one caused by the latent impressions of karma (*karma-saṃskāra*) and the other [caused by ignorance]; for in the case of the knower, the exhaustion of karma is understood through the cessation of the fruits of karma as previously described.

And thus, because karma is exhausted, it is said that there is no waiting for its destruction through experience. He confirms with the *Gītā* that for the knower, the appearance of fruition is neither welcomed nor desired—“so too” (*tathā ca*). He also confirms with the *Gītā* what was stated—that the knower does not consider the appearance to touch the Self—“so too” (*tathā ca*). Here, one who thinks that liberation comes from the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence alone raises an objection: “But surely” (*nanu*). “Of that” (*tasya*); the meaning is, of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

He refutes this, saying: "It is said... For that which is of the same class (*samānajātīya*) is contradictory, not that which is of a different class (*vijātīya*). And the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which is indirect (*parokṣa*), is of a different class from the direct appearance of the phenomenal world (*prapañcābhāsa*) which is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, because there is no contradiction between the two, it is impossible for that indirect knowledge of reality to bring about the non-contact, the inefficacy, or the lack of connection of the direct appearance of the phenomenal world. This is the meaning. Here he provides an illustration, saying: "And that which..."

Just as, through inference—such as "this sugar-candy is sweet because it is sugar-candy, like a sugar-candy previously experienced"—or from the authoritative word of another, one has already cognized the sweetness in a substance that is sugar-candy, there nevertheless arises a sensory appearance of bitterness that is perceptually similar [to the actual taste]. This appearance does not touch the substance of the sugar-candy; rather, being neither welcomed nor disliked merely as an appearance, it persists by not touching the self, but instead it is actually disliked. He confirms this very point with the words: "And so it is."

The statement "it leads to suffering" expresses the state of being hated [by the wise]. Likewise, it has been stated that this occurs "due to the abandonment of the burden. However, when meditation (*upāsanā*) is present, for the knower who has directly realized the reality of the Self through that meditation, there is a contradiction between the immediate knowledge of the reality of the Self and the immediate appearance of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because they belong to the same class [of immediate experience]. Consequently, even though the appearance of the phenomenal world exists, it is rendered equivalent to non-existence by that [knowledge]; it no longer touches the Self nor does it lead to happiness. Thus, the point is that meditation is indeed useful.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Devadatta," etc. Furthermore, he states that meditation must be resorted to for the direct realization (*aparokṣa*) of the reality of the Self: "And eternal," etc. The manifestation of the reality of the Self—the manifestation of the Self which consists of knowledge, as stated in "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite"—is eternal, according to "Indeed, this Self is indestructible. Therefore, when that [manifestation] has become manifest, the appearance of the delusion of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca-bhrānti*) does not occur again. By means of that, the absolute cessation of saṃsāra is logically established. Verbal knowledge, however, is momentary.

Therefore, when that non-attention to the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has perished, the delusion of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca-bhrānti*) once again finds an opportunity; its recurrence would follow. Consequently, the meaning is that meditation (*upāsanā*) is appropriate for the manifestation of the eternal self-luminous Self. And this is observed: when there is non-attention to the means of valid knowledge, delusion arises, and that is a cause of suffering; thus he says, "It is observed. Now, if delusion occurs again when there is non-attention to the means of valid knowledge, then in this case as well, the verbal knowledge of the Self alone should be continuously attended to.

One might suspect that for this very reason, error will not arise again; what then is the use of *upāsanā* (meditative worship)? To this he raises an objection with the word “But” (*nanu*). He refutes that with the word “What? (*kim*). Continuous contemplation (*saṃtatānusaṃdhāna*) itself is *upāsanā*, and nothing else. Therefore, if that is accepted, how could *upāsanā* not be desired? This is the meaning. Having thus resolved the contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding the limit of the body’s fall, and having stated that there is no means other than the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, he concludes with the words “therefore,” summarizing what was said: “nothing remains to be cut away. [p. 267]

Having thus established, by means of the visible [result] through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), that knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cause for the destruction of both previously commenced and uncommenced karmas, [the author] now seeks to refute those who believe that knowledge—by means of its unseen power (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*)—renders one untainted by the sin arising from negligence (*pramāda*) occurring at a later time after the realization of the true nature of the Self (*ātma-tattva-bodha*) has arisen. To that end, he extends the same principle—that knowledge is the cause by means of the visible alone—to this case as well, stating "In the same way" (*evam*). Therein, he first cites the scriptural text regarding the non-clinging of future evil: "Just as... (*yathā*).

And just as in that case knowledge is the cause by means of what is directly perceived, so he demonstrates it with the words "by the agent" (*kartṛ*). For there is a connection between an agent and the action to be performed; therefore, as long as one perceives oneself as an agent through ignorance and conceives of sinful action as something to be performed, for that long it remains connected to that [action]. But when knowledge has arisen, because ignorance has dissolved, the very distinction between agent and action to be performed no longer exists; whose connection could there be with what? Thus, the meaning is that even regarding the non-clinging of future evil, knowledge is the cause precisely by means of what is directly perceived.

Now, demonstrating the validity of his own position—that knowledge itself, as something directly perceived, is the cause for the destruction and non-clinging of prior and subsequent karma—and indicating the untenability of the position that knowledge is the cause of those two through the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), he says: "In this way. For those who maintain the doctrine of the unseen power, an unseen power must first be postulated; moreover, since that power would be manifold due to the distinction between the destruction and non-clinging of prior and subsequent karma, there is the fault of conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava).

Furthermore, there is the defect that one must assume that statements such as "and yet he does not return" (na ca punarāvartate), which are presented in the present tense, are injunctions for a fruit by means of a transformation [of their meaning]; however, this is not the case for us—this is the sense. Now, since it is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), like other forms of ignorance, it ought to be removed along with the remainder of the effects of impressions (*saṃskāra*) by means of residual ignorance; therefore, how can it be said that those two persist even when they are almost entirely dissolved? This is an inference, and it is invalid because it contradicts the fallacious inference (*abhāsānumāna*), the presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and the scriptural statement regarding the limit of the body's fall (*dehapātāvadhi-śruti*).

Furthermore, a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) persists even after its own cause has ceased, like the impressions of fear and so forth. Now, having set forth the argument of the proponent of the injunction for the third mode of apprehension—who claims that Brahman, being non-differentiated (*aprapañca*), cannot be the object of verbal cognition consisting of the connection of various word-meanings—he refutes it with the words "That which... (*yaditi*). If Brahman were not accessible to the cognition produced by the words of the Vedānta, then the injunction of the cognition of Brahman in the form "The Self is to be known" would be impossible.

For an injunction cannot exist if its locus is not defined and its object is not understood; moreover, the object of an injunction is not merely the undifferentiated reality (tattva) itself, but rather a particular state of cognition. And this particularity, for a cognition that is inherently formless, is dependent upon an object. Furthermore, an object that is unestablished and unknown is incapable of defining or specifying a particular state of cognition. Therefore, it is only when the object—Brahman—is already known that one can enjoin the knowledge of Brahman. Nor is there any means other than the Word (śabda) by which that [Brahman] can be known.

Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman must be accepted as accessible through verbal testimony (*śabda*). Furthermore, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*) to show that for one who holds that the Vedāntas are solely intent upon injunctions regarding specific modes of realization, the reality of the Self would be without any means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇaka*). An injunction (*vidhi*), that is, a mandate (*niyoga*), culminates in its own accomplishment, which is its own effect.
[Page 268]

It culminates in that [realization]; or rather, it is intent upon the accomplishment of the action, for from that, the status of the object—which is the essence of the action—as a task (*kāryatā*) is understood. In the first case, the injunction (*vidhi*) culminates in itself; the word, too, as the mandate (*niyoga*) whose object is the realization of the non-dual self, culminates precisely in this being the task. In the second case, the injunction culminates in the accomplishment of the object, and the word does likewise; consequently, the realization of the non-dual self would be without cause and lack any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*).

Now, if it is argued that the nature of the Self will be understood either through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words such as "free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow" in certain instances, or otherwise through their connection in a non-coreferential relationship (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) elsewhere, the author says: "Because of the application" (*viniyogāt*). That which is the understanding of the nature of the Self resulting from its application has for its purpose—that is, is subordinate to—the injunction of the act of knowing expressed as "the Self is to be known"; it does not have the nature of the Self itself as its primary purpose.

It has been stated that [the scripture] is intended to convey that "the Self must be known as having the nature of Viraja and so forth," but not that "the Self is of the form of Viraja and so forth. Therefore, the realization of the Self—which culminates in knowledge and action—is not intent upon the essential nature of the Self; being thus not focused on the Self's own nature, it does not constitute a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the Self's nature. This is just as the cognition arising from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), which is intent upon injunctions and praise, culminates only in the thought "worship is to be performed," and not in the essential nature of the Self as "the non-dual Self."

In that case, there is an absence of being intent upon the nature of non-duality in either way. For in common worldly usage, that which a word is intent upon is its meaning. Therefore, the realization of a non-dual self lacks a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇikā*), just as in narrative accounts such as "Prajāpati cut out his own omentum. The phrase "in the narrative or otherwise" means "by way of a different grammatical coreference" (*vaiyadhikaraṇyena*). Furthermore, in that context, the injunction of examples such as "from which indeed these beings are born" is neither established in itself nor established in the accomplishment of an action.

But if it is argued that the very nature of the Self is what is enjoined, and therefore, because the word is intent upon that [nature], the Self alone is the means of valid knowledge there, and thus the realization of the non-dual Self is not without authority—then he says: "An injunction" (*vidhi*). For an injunction impels persons toward an object that is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*); and action is what is to be performed. Therefore, since it has as its domain action, an injunction is not capable of prompting activity with respect to the substance of the Self—which is established by its own word and is not something to be performed. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the suffix *-vat* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) in the expression *siddhavat*.

The meaning is that just as other established things such as a jar are referred to by their own names, so too is the self. Now, if a substance is not being enjoined, how then can there be an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhi) in cases such as "one offers with curds" (*dadhnā juhoti*)? It is said: even there, it is the action itself that is enjoined. But surely that [action] is already obtained from the statement "one performs the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*)? True; however, it is not obtained as qualified by the specific accessory. How then is it called an injunction of an accessory? Because of the principle of what is already obtained versus what is not yet obtained (*prāptāprāpta*). [p. 269]

There is no fault [in our position], because through differentiation (*viveka*), it results merely in a quality (*guṇa*) within the context of an injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, since the cognition of a substance endowed with existence (*sattva*) is associated with one of the three times—past, present, or future, as in "such a thing was," "is," or "will be"—an injunction alone is not capable of enjoining a substance; on the contrary, it becomes defective, because it would result in the loss of its own nature. For that [injunction] does not have as its object a verbal meaning (*bhāvārtha*) that is unconditioned by time or agent.

For in such cases as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), existence qualified by any one of the three times is not perceived. [Objection: But that which is enjoined will be performed, and what is to be performed will exist; therefore, its existence is perceived as belonging to the future time. [Reply: This is not so. That which is enjoined is not necessarily performed; for otherwise, there would be no non-performance of it, and consequently, the scriptural declaration of fault—"By failing to perform the enjoined action"—would be purposeless.

Therefore, it is silent—meaning that it becomes faulty when it comes into contact with any one of the three times (past, present, or future). Now, an objection is raised: just as the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" is itself the authority for the Soma that qualifies the act of homa, and not a separate authority, so too the very authority for the necessity of realization—that "the Self is to be realized as being thus"—is itself the authority for the nature of the Self; therefore, how can there be a cognition of the reality of the Self that lacks an authoritative basis? Anticipating this, it is said: "qualified," etc.

In any other sacrificial act qualified by Soma, the injunction itself serves as the authority for the qualifier, Soma. However, the act of realization enjoined in the statement "The Self should be realized as being thus" is an act of realization qualified by the nature of the Self; it does not, however, necessarily or invariably establish the existence of the Self—the object of that realization—as possessing such qualities as freedom from old age and so forth.

Why? The meaning is that [superimposition] is possible even by superimposing a form onto that which does not possess that form through metaphorical attribution (*samāropa*), as in the case of "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire. In the Śruti, the word "world" (*loka*) refers to the celestial realm (*svarga-loka*) and so forth. Two examples are given in the commentary based on the distinction between Vedic and worldly [usage], or the distinction between injunctive and descriptive statements, or the distinction between singular and plural qualifiers. Not tolerating the statement that "it is possible for the intellect through metaphorical attribution," the opponent objects with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*). The particle *no* has the sense of negation.

That cognition whose object is a contrary thing is one that apprehends one thing as otherwise; it is of such a nature. Why? Because whatever object appears in a particular consciousness, that alone is its object and nothing else. In this case, it is contradicted by experience to say that silver appears while the object is actually mother-of-pearl. Furthermore, if cognition were to apprehend one thing as another, then due to the suspicion of error, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases, and the certainty that "it is exactly so" would not arise.

If the mother-of-pearl does not appear as silver, then what indeed is this cognition of silver with respect to the mother-of-pearl? In response to this inquiry, he says: "Silver... This cognition of silver is certainly not produced by contact with the sense organs, because there is no contact between the sense organs and the silver, which is not present.

Nor is it produced from a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, because such a mark does not exist. However, there exists a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born of prior experience which is the cause of recollection. Therefore, since this [cognition] has recollection as its cause, the meaning is that this cognition of silver is indeed a recollection. Furthermore, if the cognition does not conform to the form of its object—the mother-of-pearl—meaning it does not take the form of the mother-of-pearl but rather takes the form of silver, then that cognition would be without a basis (*nirālambana*). And this is not tenable.

The analysis of the compound is: "that which has no object (*ālambana*) or domain (*viṣaya*). It is said to be "without an object" because it does not conform to the object known as mother-of-pearl. Furthermore, the term "without an object" was stated so that, by providing an illustrative example, there might be room for the Buddhists' inference regarding the lack of an external object (*nirālambana-anumāna*). And the term "ungraspable" (*agrāhya*) was stated to indicate the impossibility of the action of cognition (*vijñāna-kriyā*) with respect to an object (*karman*). This is the distinction. Now, one might object: even if mother-of-pearl is not the object insofar as it is what is cognized (*vedyatayā*), it will nonetheless be so insofar as it is the cause (*hetutayā*).

Anticipating the objection that the error must have a cause because an error without a substratum is impossible, he says: "The cause... (hetu). If the mere cause were the objective support (*ālambana*), then the eyes and other sense organs would also be the objective supports of cognition; however, this is not observed. Therefore, only the two [the shell and the silver] are the objective support, and since the mother-of-pearl is not so, it is not the objective support—this is the meaning.

And if the object were the objective support (ālambana) merely by virtue of being a cause, and not by virtue of being cognized, then, since cognition would lack the capacity to apprehend [the object], the establishment of the object from that cognition would not occur even through dependence on another means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), much less without such dependence. Therefore, with the intention that the validity of cognition would thus not be independent, he says: "And so" (*tathā ca*). The proponent asks—"How?"—meaning: if this cognition of silver is not one whose object is contrary [to reality], then what is this cognition of silver? The other replies: "The mother-of-pearl... (*śukti*).

He states the cause for the arising of memory with the words "sāmānya" (commonality) and so forth. The meaning is that because one perceives a commonality—such as the form of whiteness and so on—between the mother-of-pearl and silver, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is awakened in one who has seen the similar mother-of-pearl, and thus memory of silver is produced. As it has been said: "The awakening of the seed of memory occurs through similarity, perception, and reflection."
