The proponent asks again: "If there is the apprehension of the nacre as 'this' and the recollection of silver, then since both are [individually] true to their objects, how can they constitute an error? The opponent replies: "Regarding perception. The specific features of the perceptible fragment of nacre—which serve as the causes for distinguishing it from silver and so forth—are not known because they are overwhelmed; only the general property of the nacre, such as its whiteness, is known.

Even by means of memory, due to a defect of the mind, the silver—being apprehended without the mental imprint of "that" (*tad*)—is not distinguished from the piece of mother-of-pearl as belonging to its former place and time. Thus, because there is no discrimination between the perceived and the remembered, for one who proceeds toward the mother-of-pearl with the cognition of silver, there is a failure in practical activity (*vyavahāra*); therefore, the meaning is that even though both the memory and the perception are of real objects, they constitute an error. Now, [an objection]: since there is a cognition through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form "this is silver," there must be an apprehension of identity.
[Page 271]

To the question, "How is this stated? and anticipating the objection that it is due to the non-apprehension of distinction (*vivekāgrahaṇāt*), he says: "This is that" (*so'yam iti*). Here he provides an example: "Just as" (*yathā*). Similarly, when light is not apprehended, the conceit of knowing a form consisting of black darkness should be cited as an example for the blind. He concludes his own position with: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) refutes this with: "In this regard" (*atra*). As for what was said—that there is no appearance of one thing as another;

If the piece of mother-of-pearl in contact with the eye were not perceived as "silver," or if silver located in another place were not perceived as being present right here before one, then a person seeking silver, desiring to take up silver, would not act toward the piece of mother-of-pearl; for the piece of mother-of-pearl would not be cognized as having the nature of silver. Indeed, a person seeking silver does not act toward that which is not cognized as silver, just as one does not act toward clods of earth and the like.

If it is argued that the activity occurs toward silver itself when it is being remembered, that is not so; because the remembered object lacks presence in the location before one's eyes, there would be no activity directed toward that present location, but rather one would act toward the very silver seen previously. If it is further argued that by a memory devoid of the notion of "that" (the past), only the silver is presented and not its connection with the previous location—and thus, since only the silver is perceived while its non-presence is not perceived, activity toward the mother-of-pearl is explained—this too is not so.

For in this way, since all this is no different elsewhere, [the cognition] would apply there as well, and not only to the mother-of-pearl. But that which necessarily applies to the mother-of-pearl is caused by the proximity of silver; and that proximity occurs only if the mother-of-pearl is apprehended as being silver, and not otherwise. For there is no actual proximity of that object [silver]. Therefore, the point is that the mother-of-pearl is apprehended as being silver.

Now, it is said that when objects in other places possessing specific qualities are apprehended through perception, there is no [erroneous] activity because the distinction—the differentiation from silver—is grasped; whereas in the case of mother-of-pearl, activity occurs because the differentiation is not grasped. And this non-apprehension of the differentiation is due to the similarity based on the common feature of the bright appearance of the mother-of-pearl, as well as because the specific qualities of the mother-of-pearl are not perceived by those who fail to differentiate.

Even so, in the case of lumps of earth and the like which have not been seen, because they were never seen and thus forgotten, one would fail to grasp their distinction from silver due to a lack of discrimination, and consequently, one might still act toward them. If it is argued that one does not act toward them because the cognition of "silver" does not exist in them, then the same would apply to the mother-of-pearl: since the cognition of "silver" does not exist there either, one should not act toward it. If, on the other hand, it is claimed that the cognition of "silver" does exist in the mother-of-pearl, then you have arrived at the theory of the misapprehension of an object contrary to reality (*viparītārthākhyāti*).

How could it be refuted? The analysis of the compound is: "that whose object is contrary. Now, if it is argued that there is no engagement because [the object] has not been seen in clods of earth and the like, then silver would likewise not have been seen as such in mother-of-pearl; thus, one seeking silver would not engage with it either. If it is argued that mother-of-pearl was seen in its general form, such as being white, lustrous, and so forth, that is not so; for the cause of engagement for one seeking silver is not the perception of it in its general form. [p. 272]

Rather, it is in the form of silver. Therefore, because the piece of mother-of-pearl is not seen in that form [of silver], just like a clod of earth and so forth, there would be no inclination toward it either—this is the point. If it is argued that action occurs due to the non-discrimination between the perceived and the remembered mother-of-pearl and silver, then how could such a contingency apply to unseen objects like clods of earth?

In this regard, the following must be considered: Is it because of the absence of the apprehension of the distinction—which would effect such a distinction—that there arises a cognition of the identity (*tattva*) between the mother-of-pearl and the silver, due to the perception of the silver as being present in front when it is actually near by; and that, consequently, activity toward the mother-of-pearl occurs because of the cognition of silver in the mother-of-pearl? Or is it because of the non-cognition of their difference (*atattva*)? If the position is taken that activity proceeds from the cognition of identity (*tattva*), then in that case one would be grasping the piece of mother-of-pearl as being silver. Therefore, the cognition of silver would have a contrary object (*viparītārthatā*).

But in the other view, just as the distinction from silver is not grasped from the perceived fragment of mother-of-pearl, so too it is not grasped from the unperceived clod of earth and the like. Therefore, there would be no difference between the perceived and the unperceived; the meaning is that activity would occur toward the unperceived just as it does toward the perceived. [Objection: But activity occurs only toward an object (*viṣaya*), not toward what is not an object. And an unperceived clod of earth and the like is not an object. Therefore, how can there be activity toward it? [Reply: Quite true; even silver [in the case of error] is not seen as being present before one. Thus, for you, there would be no activity even toward that [silver].

The mother-of-pearl that is actually seen is not the object of activity for the purpose of silver; thus, according to the opponent as well, the activity has no object at all. The point is: if this is so, why should it not also occur in the case of what is unseen? Now, one might object: "Error is the non-discrimination of what is being perceived; how then can there be such a contingency regarding things that are unseen? This would indeed be the case if there were a difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) between the non-apprehension of discrimination in the seen and the unseen; however, [the opponent] maintains that such a difference does not exist because that [non-apprehension] is a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

As for the claim that there exists a common form consisting in the non-apprehension of the distinction between erroneous and correct knowledge of silver, and that because of this similarity in form, practical activity occurs even in an error that is similar to correct knowledge of silver—that too is incorrect; for practical activity does not follow from some degree of similarity, since that would entail the consequence that even cognitions which are causes of pleasure and pain would be identical on the basis of their commonality as "cognitions."

Therefore, it is logical that when there is an equal basis for activity (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) in the case of a correct cognition of silver, there is an activity similar to that [of the erroneous cognition]. In a correct cognition of silver, the non-apprehension of the distinction (*vivekāgraha*) is not the cause of activity, but rather the apprehension of the distinction (*vivekagraha*); and since that [apprehension] does not exist for you in the case of an error, how can the activity be similar? [Objection: But surely there is a difference between those two cases, because in the case of what is seen there is contact with the sense organ (*indriya-yoga*), whereas in the case of what is unseen there is not; so how can there be non-difference? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "No."

For instance, since the non-apprehension of the distinction between the seen and the unseen is equal [in both cases], the perception of the contact with the sense-faculty is not useful. The point is that there is no utility for those two in the case of non-apprehension, because that [non-apprehension] consists in the nature of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). In response to the expectation as to where indeed they are useful, he states their utility in his own position: "Those two," etc. This means they are useful in the superimposition (*samāropa*) of silver upon mother-of-pearl.
On this point [p. 273]:

He states the reason: "No. This illusion of silver is visual; and that [illusion] is possible only with respect to an object perceived as "this" through its general features when it is in contact with the eye, and not otherwise. Therefore, the meaning is that [the two means of knowledge] are useful for the perception of their respective connections therein. He states another refutation: "Recalled. Recalled silver appears as distinct—that is, clearly differentiated—from the piece of mother-of-pearl and so forth by the very power of the capacity for discrimination arising from the cognition produced by direct perception, which takes the form of the recollection of silver.

In that case, how could there be a non-discrimination between memory and perception? On the contrary, there is indeed discrimination. Under those circumstances, how could one who seeks silver act toward mother-of-pearl due to a lack of discrimination? The argument beginning with "of the knowledge of memory" is merely an elaboration of the previously mentioned alternatives. Furthermore, if memory, by its own power, does not discriminate its own object [from others], then whenever one perceives a common feature such as height and remembers something else—such as a post or a person—there would always be an error.

And this is not so, because doubt—such as "Is it a post or a person?"—is also observed. In that case, the term "error" (*viparyaya*) refers by metaphorical extension to the delusion characterized by the non-apprehension of distinction, due to its similarity to the non-apprehension of distinction; however, the opponent's intended "error" is not meant here, which would entail the aforementioned consequence. If you think that in the case of a single recollection, there is error due to the non-distinction between the object present before one and that [recalled] object, whereas in the case of multiple recollections, there is doubt due to the non-distinction between the two remembered objects—that is not correct.

For even in the case of a post and a person, an error regarding one or the other is sometimes observed in memory; however, such an error would not occur according to your position. Now, if it is argued that what is remembered is not distinguished from cognition, but rather that when a thing such as mother-of-pearl (*śukti*)—which is present before one, undetermined in its specific qualities, and perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in its general form—is seen, then the specific cognition that brings about the distinction from silver and so forth is what is meant by "from that," we say: no.

For even then, if this specific cognition occurring through perception were absent, there would always be doubt when both [objects] are remembered; how then could there be a misconception of a single form? Yet such a misconception does indeed sometimes occur. Therefore, this position also is not superior. However, when memory—by its very nature of discerning its own object—distinguishes the remembered from the perceived, and a misconception distinct from memory is admitted, then even when both are remembered, a misconception in the form of non-discrimination is logical due to a particular defect of the sense organs and so forth.

Therefore, memory is by its very nature the discernment of its own object, and error is indeed distinct from that; this alone is the superior position. Furthermore, even that which has been remembered is discerned through the very cognition characterized as memory, and not through the specific cognition of what is currently being perceived; for this has been shown in the *Vibhramaviveka*: "Even when there is the perception of a common feature such as height, if one remembers only one alternative—either a post or a person—there is no doubt because of the absence of remembrance of both alternatives.

"And because the defects [of memory] are not perceived, there is no error. In this regard, if memory itself did not distinguish its own object, then for one who remembers a single alternative (koṭi), there would be an error regarding it; but such is not the case. Therefore, what is remembered is distinguished by the very cognition of itself, and not from the thorough knowledge of the specific features of the object being perceived, because at the time of perceiving the mere universal (sāmānyamātra), that [knowledge of the particular] is absent.

Furthermore, since memory is by its very nature distinct from what has been remembered, how could there be a lack of distinction between the remembered and the being-perceived, such that the error called "non-apprehension of distinction" (vivekākhyāti) could be asserted? Moreover, if the non-distinction between the remembered and the being-perceived were the error, then the well-known error of duality seen in the moon—due to defects such as ophthalmia—in a person who remembers the established oneness of the moon but does not remember its duality, would not occur; for it is impossible for there to be a non-apprehension of distinction regarding that which is being remembered.

If it is argued that the functioning of the sense organ, due to defects such as *timira* (ophthalmia), produces two cognitions—one of a distinct object and one of a non-distinct object—and that consequently, due to the failure to discriminate between these two cognitions or the failure to discriminate between these two functions of the sense organ, there arises the illusion of duality regarding the moon, that is not so; for in that case, since both the cognition and the function of the sense organ are inferable, they are not objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor can it arise from what is being remembered, because those two are not remembered. [Objection: But surely, through inference, there will be a failure to grasp the distinction between the cognition and the function of the sense organ. [Reply: It is not so.

Once the experience of two moons has arisen, there is subsequently an inference. Therefore, the delusion of two moons does not occur because of a failure to distinguish between the two functions of sensory cognition as they are being apprehended by that [inference]. And this was stated with reference to inferential cognition. Even though the experience is perceptual, nevertheless, since it is itself formless and its difference is not cognized intrinsically, the cognition of its difference arises only from the difference in objects; thus, there is no delusion regarding a difference in objects for you. Hence it is well said: "How then could there be a delusion of two moons?"

Furthermore, if someone desiring to drink water were to have their attention fixed upon a mother-of-pearl shell [mistaken for silver], then, because of the non-recollection of silver, the error of silver would not occur; yet that error does sometimes occur. Or, if such an error were to occur, it would be of the water itself—due to the recollection of water and because that recollection does not distinguish its own object—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, if it is maintained that the memory of silver arises from the perception of similarity to mother-of-pearl, and that this memory constitutes an error due to the non-apprehension of the distinction [between the remembered and the perceived], such that error is thus held to be based on similarity, then—since there is no similarity between white and yellow, or between bitter and sweet—there would be no erroneous cognition of white as yellow; yet such an error does exist. Therefore, error is not in every case invariably and necessarily based on similarity.

Now it is said: It is not our intention that error occurs everywhere solely through the authority of memory, such that it would always be based on similarity; rather, it also occurs in some cases due to the non-apprehension of a distinction between what is being perceived and something else. Therefore, the bile located in the eye is experienced as yellow, and the bile located in the tongue as bitter, but these are not remembered; and from the non-distinction of those two, error arises. For instance—even though yellowness is devoid of substance—it is its own pervasiveness [that causes this]. Likewise with bitterness. [p. 275]

And [the substance] is perceived, yet due to a defect in the sense organ, the substance appears devoid of its own quality, like a crystal gem colored by a *japa* flower. Thus, this error arises from the failure to understand the lack of connection between the substance and the quality, which are mutually dependent. The sense organ must be directed toward external objects. How so? It is said: because it does not function externally, that which has entered the eye is not seen by the eye, just as collyrium (*añjana*) is not seen. Now, collyrium merely obstructs the functioning of the ocular light; however, by bile (*pitta*), the functioning of the light is obstructed, as if by glass (*kāca*).

Furthermore, the visual light (*nāyanatejas*) that causes the perception of yellow must be radiating outward, not remaining within its own substrate. That is incorrect; for if the sense organ perceives the quality of yellowness residing in itself, then it would perceive it even when not directed toward external objects. Consequently, a person would experience sensations such as yellowness even when the external sense organ is not functioning. But this is not the case. Why then is the yellowness of the bile in the eye not perceived when the eye is inactive and obstructed by collyrium? It is certainly not so.

For in that case, one would likewise perceive the blackness inherent in one's own eyes and the water present within them, since even those two do not obstruct the function of light. Therefore, although the ocular light spreads outward, it perceives only what is external, not what resides within the eye. If it is argued that there is some degree of similarity between the yellow color of turmeric and the conch-shell, or between the bitter taste of neem and sugar-candy, such that upon perceiving the conch-shell and sugar-candy, the recollection of yellow and bitter is an error—this is not so.

For if that were so, where indeed would there be no such similarity? There would be no error at all regarding a conch-shell or a piece of gold; rather, every kind of error would occur in every case. Thus, having pointed out the defect in the opponent's position, he states the validity of his own position by saying "Therefore": since a certain sensory defect has the capacity to produce a specific error, and because the defects of the sense organs—such as the eyes and so forth—are distinguished according to their objects, there arises a restriction among errors such that a particular error occurs in a particular case.

If there were merely a non-apprehension due to a defect and not an error (*viparyaya*), then, because of the various defects such as jaundice (*kāmalā*) and so forth, there would be no fixed rule regarding errors. For that fixed rule of error is not caused by similarity, since an error is observed even in the case of a yellow conch-shell and the like, which are not similar [to what is being perceived]. This is the sense. When the proponent (*siddhāntin*) states, "The remembered is distinguished from the cognition itself; therefore, how can there be a non-discrimination between the remembered and the perceived?", [the opponent replies: "It is true that the remembered is distinguished from the cognition itself."

However, this is the distinction: just as even in perception that grasps particulars, there may sometimes be a non-apprehension of the particular due to defects such as distance when one perceives only height and so forth, so too in memory, there may sometimes be a non-apprehension due to a defect of the mind. In that case, there is an absence of discrimination and it constitutes error. But when, due to the absence of a mental defect, there is apprehension of the particular—even when there is the perception of the common feature of height in both a post and a person standing before one who is in contact with the senses—the absence of non-discrimination occurs because they have been distinguished by the knowledge of their specific features.

Consequently, doubt arises when there is recollection of both alternatives; however, when there is recollection of only one, there is neither doubt nor error. Therefore, having raised the objection from the perspective of another school—that "otherwise, whenever a universal is perceived, error would always occur for one who remembers something else," and so forth—it is stated that even in this case, of the two...

If there were recollection of two distinct things, there would be no error; yet such [recollection] does sometimes occur. Although this fault exists, he states another refutation, beginning with "viśeṣa" (the particular). Furthermore, even the non-apprehension of a particular never occurs in recollection; for it is not the mere object whose particularity has been determined that is remembered, but rather the specific object itself, such as silver and so forth. Now, it might be argued: "We do not say that the specific object is not remembered."

However, when that [object] being remembered is remembered as being associated with a specific place and time previously apprehended, it is then distinguished from the object currently being perceived by its own cognition. But where there is no apprehension of a specific place and time, there it is not distinguished. Therefore, what is remembered is distinguished by virtue of a specific place and time; in their absence, however, due to non-discrimination, there is error. To this, he says: "place," etc. Here he states the reason: "by many," etc. The non-apprehension of place is illustrative; [it refers to] that which has been apprehended in infinite places and times.

Therefore, due to the distinction of place and time, that which is being remembered or perceived is not understood as being separate [from the object]; rather, memory itself distinguishes it. For otherwise, although there may be a recollection of the place and time of silver and the like known at a specific location and moment, it would still be impossible to remember the infinite places and times of the infinite instances of silver and the like. Consequently, it is precisely from that [remembered] specific place and time of the silver and so forth whose memory occurs that the visible object is distinguished.

Nor [could it arise] from another [cause], because no specific place or time is being remembered. Therefore, for one who has apprehended silver and so forth as existing in infinite places and times, since it is impossible to remember all those specific places and times, and since memory would thus always be indistinct, the result would be error; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, if there were a distinction between the two combined factors of place and time, then even if there is a difference in time when an object perceived in a certain place is remembered in that very same place, there would nonetheless be a constant non-distinction due to the absence of any difference in place; consequently, this would lead to the undesirable consequence that [all cognition] would always be erroneous, which is not the case. Therefore, the specificities of place and time are not the cause of distinction. Thus, it is also not tenable to claim that error arises from the non-apprehension of their distinction.

Now, it is said that the distinction of what is remembered arises from the cognition of its being remembered through the mental impression "I remember," while in its absence there is no such distinction; therefore, cognitions of silver and the like that lack the cognition "I remember" are the causes of error. To this, he replies: "Memory. A cognition of the form "I remember," which grasps the memory-status of "this is a memory of silver," is cited as something entirely distinct from the memory of silver itself. Therefore, even in the absence of that [cognition], the memory of silver remains complete.

Nothing of its own object is left ungrasped by it such that there could be a loss (*pramoṣa*) of that [grasping]. And thus, it itself distinguishes its own object from what is being grasped. Why would there be a non-distinction between the remembered and the being-grasped, such that an error (*bhrānti*) might occur? This is the meaning. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the two words "error" (*viparyaya*) refer solely to delusion (*bhrānti*). [p. 277]

Now, if it is argued that memory does not have the nature of discriminating its own object in order to avoid the aforementioned fault, then, since other things such as a post or a person would also lack discrimination between memory and perception when there is a sight of their common features, confusion would always prevail. But this is not the case, for doubt is also observed. And this has been stated in the passage beginning with "otherwise, however... (anyathā tu).

Furthermore, if the cognition of memory, namely "I remember," were distinct and separate from the experience which is the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then [the distinction] would be established; but it is not so without that [experience]. Therefore, since memory makes manifest only that which was previously remembered as distinct, how could there be a non-distinction from what is being perceived such that an error might arise? This is the intended meaning. In the *Vṛtti*, the text is divided as follows: "The objection is 'I do not remember'; [the reply is] 'this is not a fault, because of the distinction in the thought "I remember"' (P.141.21). As for the phrase "that very same": [The text continues: "That very same [object] appears as if it were present, due to the similarity between the form of the object and the form of the cognition; however, it is not actually present, because it is not perceived by the sense organs. Therefore, this is an error consisting in the superimposition of the form of one thing upon another. This is the meaning. For the superimposition of the form of one thing upon another occurs only when there is a similarity between the two forms. And here, the similarity between the form of the object and the form of the cognition is indeed evident. Furthermore, the superimposition of the form of one thing upon another is seen only when both are perceived, as in the case of a mother-of-pearl shell and silver. Hence, the conclusion is that the superimposition of the form of one thing upon another is possible only when there is a similarity between the two forms

The meaning is that this very discrimination (*viveka*) expressed as "I remember" would not exist if memory were incapable of discriminating its own object. Furthermore, if the discrimination [of the object] were due to the cognition "I remember," and if there were an error in memory due to the absence of such discrimination, then when one of these two—the discrimination of memory—is being proclaimed as "I remember," the other, which is observed as the error of recognition (*pratyabhijñā-bhrama*) in the form "this is that very same person," would not occur. Nor, in this case either, is the remembered object discriminated by the cognition "I remember."

However, because there is no discernment (*viveka*) between the object currently present before one’s eyes—which is grasped by direct perception—and that which is remembered, it is an error (*bhrama*). For if there were discernment of the remembered from the perceived, then the discernment of the perceived from the remembered would also be established; indeed, the cognition of discernment cannot arise from what is undiscerned. Furthermore, if this were the case, then due to the lack of discernment from the remembered, this would be an error of memory (*smṛti-bhrama*); yet this is well known to be an error of perception (*pratyakṣa-bhrama*). Therefore, the lack of discernment does not arise from the "forgetting" (*ucchitti-pramoṣa*) of the thought "I remember."

If it is argued that an object such as silver, though not present, is said to be "undiscriminated" (avivikta) because it is known as being present and situated in front, then the memory—which presents [the object] as non-present—would have a contrary meaning (viparītārthatā). Consequently, there would be *viparītārthakhyāti* (the appearance of a contrary object), not *akhyāti* (non-apprehension). The analysis of the compound is: "that whose object (viṣaya) is a contrary thing. Alternatively, if it is argued that "non-discrimination" does not mean the cognition of a non-present thing as being present, but rather the failure to grasp its absence—that is not so.

If that object were not present, why would its non-presence not be known? If you say it is due to a defect of the mind (*manas*), then this would indeed be the case where there is impairment of the mind by defects in dreams and the like. However, in the case of an error in external sensory cognition occurring even when the mind is healthy, due to the impairment of the eye by defects such as cataracts (*timira*), there is no lack of awareness of the non-presence [of the object], because the mind is not impaired by defects.

Since the cause of error is the absence of apprehension, and that [absence] does not exist in the case of the mind with respect to that [object], there could be no error because the non-perception of its non-proximity would be impossible; yet such error does exist. Furthermore, on this view, activity would occur toward the mother-of-pearl alone and not elsewhere; [this is the consequence].

It has been stated [by the opponent] that "there would be no restriction [of activity]," and [the reply was] "if [you argue] that there is no restriction of activity because of the non-perception of non-proximity, from where [does that follow]? Furthermore, if something were not remembered in its entirety simply because it was not remembered in its entirety, then even mother-of-pearl (śukti) would be false merely on the grounds that it was not apprehended in its entirety; consequently, all cognitions whatsoever would be false. For indeed, no object is ever apprehended in its entirety by any cognition.

Furthermore, if error were merely the non-apprehension of distinction (*vivekāgrahaṇamātra*), then what healthy-minded person—possessing a sound self and a sound internal organ—who observes the persistence of errors such as the cognition of two moons in someone who has already ascertained the distinction through other means of knowledge, such as authoritative testimony, inference, and so forth, thinking "the moon is one, not many; this direction is east, not north"—would deny it? For even when distinction exists, the error of two moons and the like persists.

Therefore, it is stated that the non-apprehension of the distinction [between the two] is not the error. For this reason as well, he says "prasakta... [and so on], explaining that the position of Akhyāti (non-apprehension) is untenable: "If there were a cognition of 'silver' with respect to mother-of-pearl, then, since silver would have been reached by that [cognition], the cognition of 'this is not silver'—which consists in the negation of what was reached and takes the form of the negation of what was reached—would be possible and consistent. Error does not consist merely in the non-apprehension of the distinction between the remembered and the perceived; for it is that which has been reached which is negated."

Furthermore, the non-apprehension of distinction (*avivekāgraha*) cannot be the cause of attainment (*prāpaka*). For that [non-apprehension] is simply the absence of the apprehension of distinction, and an absence cannot be a cause of attainment precisely because it is an absence. In response to the question, "What, then, is the cause of attainment?", he says: "The cause of attainment" (*prāpikā*). That cognition which presents mother-of-pearl as silver, or silver as being present before one, is a cognition of a contrary object (*viparītārthā dhīḥ*) that is the cause of attainment. Now, even on the view that there is no apprehension of distinction, the memory of silver and the cognition "this" regarding the object conjoined with the eyes—that is, the cognition of the thing present before one—is indeed the cause of the attainment of the silver.

Anticipating the objection that this negation—"this is not silver"—must therefore apply to the "silver" and the "this-aspect" as they have been presented by those two [cognitions], he says: "And those which... When there are two modes of manifestation (*khyāti*) consisting of memory and direct perception regarding the silver and the object before the eyes, this negation "this is not silver" is not understood as applying to the object brought forward by those two; rather, it is a negation of the "silver-ness" in the mother-of-pearl, or of the "presence-in-front" of the silver. And such a negation is not possible for something that has not been previously presented.

Furthermore, non-apprehension cannot be the cause of attainment because it is a mere absence. Therefore, one must accept that erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*) is what brings about the attainment of silverness in a mother-of-pearl shell, or of the shell's presence-in-front as silver. Nor does the non-apprehension of the distinction between the remembered and the perceived sublate this very cognition "this is not silver"; for if all cognitions of jars and the like were produced through the sublation of non-apprehension, then every cognition of a jar and so forth would necessarily take the form of a negation of what was previously assumed (i.e., "this is not a jar"), which is not the case.

Furthermore, in the cognition "this is not silver," it is the silver that appears as the object of negation here, not the non-apprehension [of the difference]. Therefore, this position contradicts direct experience (*pratīti*). Nor should it be argued that there is no consequence of the previously mentioned defect because the cognition "this is silver" consists of memory and perception, while the cognition "this is not silver" is a knowledge of discrimination (*viveka-jñāna*), and not a cognition consisting of the negation of what was previously presented (*prasakta-pratiṣedha-dhī*); for in doing so, one who has understood the subject (*dharmin*) denies his own cognition.

The point is this: for one who is not fatigued, when there is a sequence between nacre and silver—such as perceiving the silver first and subsequently seeing the distinctness of the nacre—or when there is simultaneity, such as seeing the distinct nacre and silver at once, the cognition of distinction that arises is not of the form "this is not that. Rather, [the opponent] maintains that these two are distinct in such a way that this [subsequent cognition] would arise in the form "this is not that"; yet even so, he denies it. And this is not consistent with those who follow actual experience. This is the sense.

If it is argued that such a [subsequent cognition] would occur upon the perception of nacre and silver as non-distinguished, [the author] says, "Because of attainment" (*prāpteḥ*), meaning: when there is a contrary cognition, "This is silver," which brings about the attainment of the identity between nacre and silver, then there occurs the realization "This is not [silver]," which consists in the negation of what was previously attained; for this would not occur if there were merely a non-apprehension of their difference, since that [non-apprehension], being of the nature of an absence, does not bring about attainment, and thus there is no attainment [to be negated].

For this reason as well, he states that the cognition of discrimination (*vivekabuddhi*) is not of a negative nature: "of silver" (*rajatasya*), where the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Recalling the silver and seeing the common features such as brightness in the object of mother-of-pearl (*śuktivastu*) which is in contact with the eye, one does not initially perceive the distinctness of the mother-of-pearl from the remembered silver due to the lack of clarity in the eye, even though no error has arisen. Subsequently, when the specific features are known through the clarity of the eye, one discriminates the mother-of-pearl from the silver, thinking, "This is mother-of-pearl," and [realizes] "This is not [silver]."

One does not cognize [silver] by means of the negation of another, such as "this is silver," because there is no non-discriminative grasping (*avivekagrahaṇa*) of the shell and the silver, and because the negation of what has not been presented is untenable. Therefore, just as in that case the discriminative cognition is not of the nature of a negation, so too would it be in the present case; yet it is not so. Now, one might object: even where there is no error upon seeing a common feature, doubt (*saṃśaya*) may still arise; and the determinative cognition (*nirṇayajñāna*) that removes it must indeed consist in the negation of one alternative.

Therefore, one might ask: "How can it be said that 'one perceives it here as manifold'? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The universal," and so on. This would indeed be the case if doubt necessarily arose from the perception of a universal. However, that [doubt] arises from the recollection of two alternatives; in the absence of that, it does not occur at all. It was with this intention that we stated: "'One perceives it here as manifold'. But surely, if there is no doubt upon the perception of a universal, then there must be error?

And the cognition that sublates that [erroneous perception] is indeed of a negative nature. Therefore, having raised the objection—"In that case, how can it be said that 'he cognizes thus'?"—it was stated in the commentary: "Nor...

Regarding the term "contradiction" (*viparyaya*): by the passage beginning with “it exists” (*bhavati*) and ending with “nor is there oneness” (*na caikatvam*), the very absence of contradiction is demonstrated. As for what was stated, “nor otherness” (*nānyatvam*), it should be understood that this was mentioned incidentally for the purpose of showing the object of that which is not perceived as distinct. Therefore, wherever doubt and contradiction do not exist upon the perception of a generality (*sāmānya*), there is merely the knowledge of distinction (*vivekajñāna*).

Nor is it of the nature of a negation of what has been apprehended (*prasaktapratiṣedha*), because oneness is not perceived between the mother-of-pearl and the silver, since there is no prior apprehension (*prasakti*) of silver in the mother-of-pearl. [This is] because of the absence of the grasping of their distinction (*viveka*). Furthermore, regarding the silver that is remembered, its "presentness" refers to its being present in time; the mention of time is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for space as well.

If it is accepted that for the sake of accounting for the negation of silver—which is assumed to be obtained because of its proximity due to cognition, or because it appears as if present before one like silver—there must be an admission of the perception of proximity for what is not proximate, then "misapprehension" (anyathāgraha), which is "contrary manifestation" (viparītakhyāti), would be the intended position.

If the non-apprehension of either extreme proximity or the nature of being mother-of-pearl were the cause of the erroneous apprehension (*anyathāgraha*), then it would be so because [the error] exists when that [non-apprehension] exists and does not exist when it is absent; however, the sense is that this is precisely what is not intended. Alternatively, the non-apprehension of proximity is not the cause, because a non-entity (*abhāva*) cannot be a cause; rather, the apprehension of proximity itself is the cause, as it is a positive entity (*bhāva*). In response to the question of what kind of such [apprehension] serves as the cause, he says: "of difference" (*bhedeti*).

For the apprehension of the distinction—that "it is not silver that is present here, but rather mother-of-pearl"—is the sublation (*apavāda*) of the apprehension of proximity; as long as that [sublation] persists, the apprehension of proximity, being devoid of it, serves as the cause for the erroneous cognition (*anyathāgraha*), provided it has not been sublated by the sublation. Furthermore, if one does not accept the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), then error is simply the non-apprehension of the distinction; thus, by asserting that such [error] is based on non-apprehension, one would be saying that non-apprehension itself is based on non-apprehension.

And this is merely a verbal construction; the point is that there is no distinction between cause (*nimitta*) and effect (*naimittika*) for a single entity in reality. The statement in the *Vṛtti* that "this is well-refuted" is a word of censure. Furthermore, if the non-apprehension of the distinction between what is being remembered and what is being perceived were error, then in a dream—since there is no second thing being perceived—the non-apprehension of the distinction, or the failure to distinguish the remembered object from nothing else, could not constitute error.

Now, even though there is an absence of an object currently being perceived (*gṛhyamāṇa*), that which is remembered appears in a dream as if it were being perceived because it is not distinguished from its state of being remembered due to a defect of the mind. Nor does this lead to the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because memory is simply a specific kind of perception—namely, the perception of what has already been perceived—and nothing else. Therefore, when the aspect of "having been perceived" (*gṛhītāṃśa*) is lost, only the act of perceiving (*gṛhīti*) remains. Consequently, in a dream, the appearance of its object as something being perceived is false. As it has been said: "For memory is a specific kind of perception, namely the perception of what has been perceived. That [perception], through the loss of the aspect of 'having been perceived,' remains as the mere act of perceiving. [p. 281]

And if it is argued that in that case, discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) is sublated by its being a memory, he says: "By being a memory" (P. 144-5). If non-discrimination is admitted on the grounds of its being a memory, then just as in the case of a memory there is a sublation of the cognition of the property of "being remembered"—whether it be the cognition of the property of being unknown or the cognition of the property of reality—or just as in that case the memory is an error when it grasps merely that property devoid of the quality of "being remembered," so too, when a substratum such as Devadatta is known from a distance with its specific form undetermined, and one subsequently perceives him nearby as "this man is fair-skinned," [that cognition is sublated].

Thus, the cognition of a subsequent property would sublate the preceding one, and the cognition of the mere substratum (dharmin) alone would be erroneous. Furthermore, memory grasps an object that is not present to the senses; even when it loses its hold on the previously apprehended portion, it persists in the form of a grasp of an object not present to the senses. For you, however, there would be no manifestation of the object as if it were directly perceived (aparokṣa). Nor is it the case that every non-grasping is a direct perception of an object not present to the senses, because this is contradicted in the case of inference and so forth. Therefore, this [position] is untenable. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the meaning of the verse.

As for the claim that it contradicts experience to say that silver is perceived while the mother-of-pearl is the object, that objection is merely a false attribution; for, because there is a cognition through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form "This white substance standing before me is silver," there is a perception of non-difference between these two. He states [the following] to show that this contradicts the proponent of the theory of non-apprehension of distinction (*vivekāgraha*): "He who... Because the nature of being mother-of-pearl was unknown at first, and only the "this" aspect—the mere whiteness—was known, it was said to be "white."

In this regard, although this single cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) appears as grasping non-difference, nevertheless, since the existence of one thing in another is untenable, we shall treat these two cognitions—as consisting of recollection and perception—as distinct. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Cognition... [and so forth]. If it is established by the experience of coreferentiality, what contradiction is there in one thing being otherwise than itself? For there is no contradiction in what is established by experience; the point is that contradiction is based on a lack of such experience.

[Objection: But surely this cognition of silver is not produced by the sense organs, because there is no sensory contact with that which is not present; nor is it produced from a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, because such a mark is absent. However, there exists a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born of a previous experience, which serves as the cause of the cognition. Therefore, since the cause of memory is present, we conclude that the cognition of silver is indeed memory itself. [Reply: Do not speak thus. This cognition of silver is produced by the sense organs alone. [Objection: But there is no sensory contact with the silver, because it is not present. [Reply: Quite true.

How, then, is it that knowledge is not born of the senses? It arises from the contact of the sense-organ with the mother-of-pearl. However, this is the distinction: when the sense-organ is unimpaired, it manifests the object as it is; but when it is impaired, it causes it to appear otherwise due to the power of the defect. Thus, there is no fault. Now, he addresses what was said regarding "lack of confidence" (*anāśvāsa*): "Lack of confidence. That lack of confidence—which consists in doubting the reality of an object whenever it is known because one has observed its falsity in one instance—is sublated by that very cognition which determines its reality.

It is thus stated that knowledge which determines suchness does not require further arising, as it is free from the suspicion of any other state. For instance, even for the sake of removing lack of confidence:

That which this [cognition] depends upon for its status as supreme knowledge is likewise devoid of certainty and merely determines the state of things as they are. And such a cognition does exist. Therefore, what fault is there in it that another [cognition] must be sought? [Objection: But surely for one who does not accept the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) regarding another [object], there is no lack of certainty at all; so how can this be said in reference to him? [Response: The point is that for him too, because of the non-apprehension of distinction in one instance, there arises a doubt regarding the non-apprehension of distinction everywhere, and thus his lack of certainty is equal [to ours].

Now, it might be argued that because of the occurrence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in some cases, knowledge that is incapable of determining an object in all instances would be invalid (*apramāṇa*); and if that were so, even lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) could not be eliminated. To this, he says: "Because of deviation. Deviation does not imply an incapacity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the determination of an object, because the determination of the object—which is its effect—is obtained; for it is precisely from this that the validity of the cognition is established, as its fruit is the very determination of the object.

And therefore, if there is ascertainment (*pariccheda*), then validity (*prāmāṇya*) is established even when there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*); because validity and invalidity depend respectively upon ascertainment and non-ascertainment, and not upon deviation and non-deviation, since those two are irrelevant to validity and invalidity. For instance, even though smoke and the like do not deviate [from fire], they are not valid when they fail to produce ascertainment at some time due to a deficiency in the recollection of the relationship and so forth, provided that no ascertainment occurs.

Furthermore, even though the visual faculty (*cakṣus*) may deviate with respect to objects such as black and so forth, its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is observed when there is correct discernment. Moreover, it is seen that in all cases it is only subverting factors (*bādhaka*) and defects in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*) that destroy validity, not deviation (*vyabhicāra*); for the visual faculty remains a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even when deviation exists. And it has been said: "And where a [defective] instrument is perceived," and so forth. But surely, invalidity is also seen to result from deviation?

For example, in the case of sound, when its permanence or impermanence is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), [the reason] "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) that is common to both sides. This is not so; it is not that there is invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case, but rather that the very effect called "ascertainment" (*pariccheda*) is not obtained there because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*). For a logical mark must be non-deviant; and "knowability" and the like are not such.

However, in cases such as the eye and other [senses], non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) is not the cause of determination (*pariccheda*). In that regard, it is undisputed that validity (*prāmāṇya*) exists when there is determination, even if there is deviation. Knowledge—even if deviating like the eye and so forth—is the instrumental cause for determination, but it is not non-deviating like a logical mark (*liṅga*). Now, it might be argued: "Deviation undermines validity by producing doubt as to whether 'the object is thus, or otherwise'."

Just as the twofold nature of verticality—by virtue of its presence in both a post and a person—is a cause of doubt, so too might the twofold nature of cognition—by virtue of its contact with both alternatives of "being thus" and "being otherwise"—be a cause of doubt. That is not so; for since cognition, upon arising, determines the object as "exactly thus," how could that non-existent twofold nature be a cause of doubt? For when the post has been determined [p. 283], [doubt does not arise].

Because there are two types [of cognition], people have doubts regarding that which is subsequent. Now, if the term "in that very way" (*tathaiva*) functions as a restrictive particle, let there be no doubt; however, it might arise when it is not a restrictive particle—this is what is being addressed. That is incorrect; because that [subsequent cognition] is simply not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Furthermore, in this context, it is precisely a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is under consideration while being examined as to whether it is "a means of valid knowledge due to non-deviation" or "not a means of valid knowledge. In that case, how could there be the possibility of it being a non-means of valid knowledge? And from a means of valid knowledge comes the restriction: "in that very way."

Nor is it logical for there to be an uncertainty expressed as "or otherwise" (*anyathā vā*) because of contradiction. Thus, for us, there is no lack of confidence; on the contrary, it is precisely that person who seeks confidence through the non-erroneousness of all cognitions who lacks confidence. [Objection: But surely the cognition of a cognition’s non-erroneousness is itself true; therefore, how can there be a lack of confidence for another? [Reply: Not so, because even the cognition that grasps the non-erroneousness of all cognitions does not provide confidence.

Now, does the cognition that grasps non-erroneousness grasp the non-erroneousness of all cognitions in a general sense? And if so, being itself non-erroneous, it grasps the non-erroneousness of all [others]; and if, in doing so, its own non-erroneousness were established by itself, then it would grasp the non-erroneousness of itself and of other cognitions; and thus, when its own non-erroneousness is self-established, there would be the determination of the non-erroneousness of others.

And if that [non-deviation] were established upon the determination of the object, then there would be a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*). If, on the other hand, the establishment of its non-deviation were through another cognition, then the same would apply to that as well, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, if there is no confidence in the cognition’s own nature—characterized by its capacity to determine the object—then, because the object itself remains unestablished, the non-deviation of the cognition with respect to that object cannot be grasped. Therefore, it must be admitted that confidence in the object arises precisely from the nature of the cognition itself.

If this is so, then the same will apply to us as well. Furthermore, the very nature of knowledge—which consists in its capacity to determine an object as it truly is—is incompatible with the capacity to determine an object erroneously, which is its opposite form; thus, the non-erroneousness of knowledge is said to arise from the very nature of knowledge itself. Consequently, if the nature of knowledge must be relied upon even for the sake of non-erroneousness, then the establishment of the object will follow from that very nature.

Therefore, why is there no confidence? For it is because of that [lack of confidence] that one seeks a determination of the matter, and from that, one desires the non-deviation (avyabhicāra) to be established by itself. Nor should it be said that "if deviation exists, validity itself would not exist," because it has already been stated that deviation does not destroy validity; this is the meaning. Furthermore, defects of the cause, such as cataracts and the like, are not the causes of *udvega*—that is, the excess of the effect. What then? They are the destroyers of the causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) that a cause possesses toward its effect.

Therefore, because those [defects] exist, there is non-apprehension due to the obstruction of the capacity of the cause for its effect, which is called apprehension; and because they do not exist, there is apprehension due to the lack of obstruction of the capacity for the effect. Thus, the existence and non-existence of defects [is the cause] for the failure to distinguish between the remembered object and the object in the heart, which constitutes error in this case.

Regarding "the non-apprehension of discrimination" (*vivekāgraha*): even when one perceives the opposite of that which is accepted by the opponent as the cause for determining discrimination—that is, the certainty that "it is not here"—one does not subsequently ward it off with sticks. Therefore, with the intention that there is no lack of confidence in a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) due to the deviation of its semblance (*ābhāsa*), because one discriminates between the means of knowledge and its semblance upon perceiving the contrary, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*). He states the reason for this: "In the case of the contrary" (*viparyaye*).

Since it has been stated that "defects are those which obstruct the capacity for the effect [of knowledge]," this is all the more applicable and logical in the case of their opposite. To the question "How so? he says: "In the case of the perceived," etc. In the case of non-apprehension, there is merely the obstruction of the desired effect called apprehension by the defects. But in the case of that characterized by error (viparyaya), there is not only the obstruction of the apprehension of reality by the defects; rather, there is also the arising of a contrary cognition which is the opposite of that [reality].

Therefore, the intended meaning is that the apprehension of reality (*tattvagrahaṇa*), by its very nature as an effect, is utterly obstructed by defects through the arousal of opposing factors; this is the sense of "excess" (*atiśaya*). Consequently, regarding non-apprehension (*agraha*): since defects exist prior [to the cognition], there is non-apprehension; and since defects are absent, there is apprehension. Thus, he states "therefore" (*tasmāt*) to show that the distinction between apprehension and non-apprehension also applies to the definition of error (*viparyaya*). It has been stated that where a defect is absent, there is apprehension of reality from a defect-free sense organ, which serves to dispel doubt.

He refutes that [position] with the words "the defect" (*doṣa*). He states the reason for this with "for not" (*na hi*). If the existence of the effect were necessarily (*niyogataḥ*) present whenever the cause exists, then, given the presence of a faultless sense organ, the suspicion of non-apprehension would be removed because the effect called "apprehension of reality" would exist; however, this is not the case. For instance, even when the eye is faultless and wide open, the non-arising of cognition is observed. Nor can it be argued that the eye alone is the causal factor, but rather the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) as well; and since that complex is absent there, the effect does not arise. This is what must be said.

For the causal power resides in each individual factor, not in their collective aggregate. Indeed, the combination of causal factors serves for the accomplishment of the effect; it is not that the combined factors possess the status of being the instrument (*karaṇa*) as a whole. Therefore, the eye is also a cause. And since the effect is not accomplished even when that [eye] is not defective, it is well said: “For when the cause exists... Thus, the meaning is that the opponent’s distinction between perception and non-perception is not established. Furthermore, he states that if this were the case, the opposite would follow: “perception,” etc.

It is logical that the cause is inferred through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as consciousness; however, for the opponent, it is the reverse: the effect, characterized by consciousness, is inferred through an unimpaired instrument (*karaṇa*). But in the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), since there is an absence of the defect which is the cause, the absence of the effect is appropriate. Therefore, he says "misapprehension" (*viparyaya*), meaning that in that case, because of the absence of the defect, it is logical to infer the absence of the result called the perception of error.

Likewise, it should also be understood that it is logical to infer the occurrence of defects in its cause from the effect, which is characterized by error, and from the sign (liṅga) that is the cause; therefore, the distinction between valid cognition and its semblance is established for us through the presence or absence of defects, but not for the opponent—this is the intended meaning.

He states that the fault alleged by the opponent—that in the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) there would be no objective support (*anālambana*)—applies to the opponent himself as well: "Anālambaneti. Just as in the theory of misapprehension, because the form of silver (*rajata*) is presented as distinct from the form of the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*), it follows that the cognition lacks an objective support; so too, for you who maintain the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), even in the case of non-grasping, since the specific nature of the mother-of-pearl standing before one is not presented in the cognition "this is [it]," it would follow that the cognition lacks an objective support. This is the meaning.

Now, even if no specific feature is presented therein, there is indeed the presentation of some common aspect, such as the luster of mother-of-pearl, by the cognition "this"; and since that [aspect] is the own-form (*svākāra*) of the mother-of-pearl, when it is apprehended, the mother-of-pearl itself becomes the objective support (*ālambana*). Thus, it is argued that even if the specific feature is not grasped, there is no consequence of being without an objective support (*nirālambanatā*). This is equally true for the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), because even in that case, there is certainly the manifestation of the "this" aspect; thus he says: "of something."

Another explanation: [The opponent] might object that since there is indeed the apprehension of some other object, such as a jar, in its own form, even if the object *śukti* (mother-of-pearl) is not presented in the form of *śukti*, it is not the case that [the cognition] is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*). Anticipating this, he says: "of something" (*kasyacit*). This is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*). The phrase "because it has its own form" (*svākāratvāt*) should be construed immediately after [the statement] "there is no lack of an objective basis. In the first explanation, the reason for the similarity is given as "of certain of its own forms," namely, the brightness and so forth of the mother-of-pearl.

In the second explanation—that [the cognition arises] because certain objects such as jars appear—the reason based on "similarity" (*tulyatva*) is to be inferred from the phrase "of certain [objects]. Alternatively, in the two-fold explanation—"of certain [objects]" refers to objects such as jars and their own forms, and "because of the appearance of [things like] mother-of-pearl and luster"—two reasons have been stated.

Now, regarding that non-apprehension of distinction (*vivekāgrahaṇa*), if it is argued that the object conjoined with the eye is not accepted as the objective support (*ālambana*) in that manner, then for the opponent who maintains the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), the conjoined object is likewise not accepted as the objective support in that case of misapprehension.

Now, it might be suspected that since [the theory of] misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) is established there in that manner, and because it remains without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), this same state of being without an objective basis would apply to all correct cognitions (*samyagjñāna*) as well; to this it is said: "If, even in that case, the absence of an objective basis were observed when the distinct power is not apprehended, then this would be suspected everywhere"—this has been explained by the passage beginning with "just as" (*yathā*).

In that regard, just as in the case of erroneous perception (*viparyayadarśana*), because it is without a cause (*animitta*) and without an objective support (*nirālambanatva*), its lack of cause and lack of objective support are suspected—just as they are suspected in the case of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)—so too, when that lack of objective support is established in the non-apprehension of a capacity (*śakti*), it is suspected even in the apprehension of everything such as jars and the like; therefore, the sense is that the lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) is equal everywhere in those cases as well.

Now, in the cognition of a jar and so forth, since the object is established through the very cognition that determines the object, the object’s status as a cause (*nimittatva*) and its status as an objective support (*ālambanatva*) do not differ from those of other proponents of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension). Furthermore, even the cognition of silver has the mother-of-pearl itself as its objective support, for it is that very thing which is grasped under the form of silver; otherwise, the cognition would not have that object as its support.

It becomes objectless (*nirālambanatva*). This being the case, that which was stated—that because the cause alone is objectless, it is like the eye and so forth—is also refuted. We do not say that the cause alone is the object; rather, that which is apprehended either as such or otherwise is the object. Since the eye is not apprehended even in another way, it is not the object of error.

For this reason as well, the mother-of-pearl is apprehended otherwise: because that which has a certain form is not the objective support (*ālambana*) of a cognition, since cognition is devoid of form (*nirākāra*). Rather, when a cognition exists, that object which becomes fit for a particular type of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is its objective support. And in the case of the cognition of silver, the mother-of-pearl becomes fit for transaction as silver, not as mother-of-pearl; thus, one who is deluded acts in that way through the very cognition of silver, and not through a cognition of mother-of-pearl.

Therefore, it is established that the mother-of-pearl is not the objective support (*ālambana*) of the cognition of silver by way of its own true nature, but rather as silver. In the *Vṛtti*, the word “supported” (*ālambitā*) is understood to follow after the phrase “in the form of silver. Regarding the injunction “The Self is to be known,” since it is centered on the act of knowing, there is no focus on the true nature of the Self; thus, fearing the failure to establish the true nature of the Self—consisting of freedom from evil, bliss, and so forth—someone says “by threshing,” etc., in order to establish that [nature].

Just as in such injunctions as "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) and "one sprinkles the rice" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), the visible and invisible purifications (*saṃskāra*) are established as being for the sake of the rice—since the accusative case in "the rice" (*vrīhīn*) indicates its primacy as that which is most desired to be reached (*īpsitatama*)—so too, knowledge by its very nature exists for the sake of the substance of the Self, which is the object of knowledge, because of the instruction that the Self is the object of the action in the passage, "The Self, verily, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ*). Therefore, even though the injunction to know the Self has the Self as its objective domain, it touches upon the essential nature of the Self, such as bliss and so forth; it does not terminate in mere knowledge alone.

Since the necessity of performing knowledge (*jñāna*) is understood from the injunction (*niyoga*) precisely through the capacity of the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*), the implication is that the nature of the Self—characterized by bliss and so forth—is also established by that injunction; thus, its realization occurs. Here, the opponent raises an objection: "Let it be so. Granted that knowledge has its purpose, nevertheless, from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the establishment of the intended [Self] as qualified by freedom from evil, bliss, and so forth derived? The word "the Self is to be known" (*ātmā jñātavyaḥ*) is certainly not the authority in this regard.

For that [injunction], namely “the Self whose nature is free from evil and so forth must be known,” culminates in making knowledge the task to be performed for the sake of the Self; at that time, one is enjoined with “the Self of such a form must be known,” and not with a statement resting on the essential nature of the Self as “the Self is of such a form. And whatever a word aims at, that is its meaning. Therefore, verbal testimony is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the essential nature of the Self as being free from evil and so forth. Nor does any other means of valid cognition apply there. Thus, even in this way, there is no establishment of the essential nature of the Self—this is the intended objection. Having raised this doubt, he says: “knowledge... [p. 287].

Knowledge is enjoined as something to be performed by virtue of its being for the sake of the object of knowledge; and it is not logical that something which accomplishes nothing regarding that object should be established as having such a duty to perform. Therefore, some purpose must be accomplished by knowledge with respect to the object of knowledge. And what else could that be than the manifestation of the nature of the Self, which is the object of knowledge? Indeed, it is that very thing. For when the visible [result] is possible, the postulation of an invisible one is not appropriate.

Therefore, just as from the injunction regarding sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth—wherein the sprinkling, though performing no visible function upon the rice grains (*vrīhi*), which are its object—is understood to produce an unseen refinement (*saṃskṛti*) in those grains due to the impossibility [of its effect otherwise]—so too, from the injunction regarding knowledge, even though the knowledge has the Self as its object, the nature of the Self as "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*) and so forth is understood. This is the meaning. It is just as in the case of [the injunction]: "one who desires heaven... (*svargakāma*).

The meaning of this section of the *Chatti* [commentary] beginning with these words is as follows: It is established by experience that whoever desires a particular end understands that the means to it must be performed and proceeds to perform it; one does not perform what is not a means. For indeed, that which is not a means would not be performed by one who desires that end, since we never observe someone desiring one thing performing another. Consequently, for one who desires heaven, neither the mandate (*niyoga*) nor the performance can apply to a sacrifice that is not a means to heaven.

Therefore, just as the relationship of means and end between heaven and sacrifice is understood from the injunction whose object is the sacrifice, so too the injunction regarding knowledge directed toward the Self characterized by being free from sin and so forth would not be intelligible if such a Self were not cognized through that knowledge; thus, the nature of the Self is made known even from the injunction whose object is knowledge. The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) refutes this with the words "It has been said" (uktā). It is true that in this way it is established that the Self is cognized through knowledge, but not [cognized] in its own essential nature (svarūpeṇa).

For it has just been demonstrated by establishing the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) that cognition illuminates an object even through its own form as if it were another. In this regard, there would be no certainty from words alone as to whether the self is perceived by cognition in its own form or in the form of another. Nor is there any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here by which such certainty might arise. Furthermore, one must necessarily accept that there is a perception of the self in a manner other than [its true nature]; otherwise, the prescription of the practice of knowledge would be entirely fruitless.

For although that Self is devoid of phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), it manifests in the form of the phenomenal world consisting of words; thus, the purpose [of the scriptures] is the realization of that [Self] through the comprehension of that [phenomenal manifestation]. This is seen, for example, in the cognition of the nature of mother-of-pearl through the comprehension of the silver that constitutes its appearance. Consequently, since there is a perception of the non-proliferated Self as having the nature of the phenomenal world, the establishment of the Self's nature—such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpman*)—does not necessarily depend on its being known in that very form.

It is thus stated that even through superimposition (*adhyāropa*), that [attainment of the goal] is possible, as in the case of the injunction: "One should meditate upon speech as a cow. Now, the following view may be held: this ignorance (*avidyā*) is twofold; one consists in the non-cognition of the reality (*tattva*), which, being the seed and veiling the reality, is called "obscuring" (*ācchādikā*); for example, the non-cognition of the reality of a rope, which fails to manifest the reality of the rope. The other, however, is its effect, which [superimposes] the very rope in the form of a snake, a staff, and so forth. [Page 288] 20A.

That which expands the non-proliferated name (*nāmaprapañca*) into the form of proliferation is called "distraction" (*vikṣepikā*). Among these, the first remains in deep sleep (*suṣupti*) in the form of a mere seed; the second exists in the states of dreaming and waking as the self of proliferation (*prapañcātman*). Now, although the cessation of distraction is not the fruit of the injunction for the knowledge of the Self, one might suspect that the cessation of the concealing [ignorance] will be the fruit, and thus the injunction for knowledge would not be fruitless; anticipating this, he says: "dissolution" (*laya*).

The activity of a discerning person is for the sake of attaining knowledge in order to bring about the cessation of the various worldly sufferings of saṃsāra. Furthermore, distraction (*vikṣepa*), which consists of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), is the cause of sufferings such as grief in both the dreaming and waking states; it is not dissolution (*laya*), nor is it the concealing ignorance (*avidyā*). For that [ignorance] residing in deep sleep is not a cause of suffering, and it is the cause of suffering that must be removed. Therefore, dissolution is not to be removed in the same way as distraction. Indeed, it is distraction—and not dissolution—that is the cause of suffering even while being itself devoid of pain.

However, because it consists of suffering, that [state] is not only not to be removed, but on the contrary, it is to be sought after. Thus, in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the cessation of manifold sufferings results in a dissolution (*laya*) produced by the latent impression of bliss (*ānanda-vāsanā*), as heard in the Śruti. Furthermore, there is another refutation: for you, who maintain that error is merely the non-apprehension of difference (*akhyāti-mātra-bhrama-vādin*), the well-known twofold nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) would not be possible. He states this with the words "laya" and so forth: dissolution is the non-apprehension of reality, while distraction (*vikṣepa*) is the perception of error; if error consisted of mere non-apprehension, there would be no distinction between these two.

Therefore, two types of ignorance (*avidyā*) must be accepted, characterized respectively by non-apprehension and erroneous apprehension. These are established such that the former is the cause and the latter is the effect. Thus, for example, due to the non-apprehension of the true nature of a rope, an error such as [perceiving] a snake is observed. This being the case, the former [non-apprehension] exists in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), while the latter [erroneous apprehension] exists in dreaming and waking; in this way, the division of ignorance is logically established. And so it has been shown by Gauḍapāda: "Bound by cause and effect... (GK 1.13).

The effect is the ignorance of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca-avidyā*), which consists of projection; the cause is the ignorance of non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa-avidyā*). Bound by these two, both the Selfs designated by the terms Viśva and Taijasa—the one abiding in the waking state and the other in the dreaming state—are manifested. However, the Prājña, the Self abiding in deep sleep, is bound by that cause, which is the ignorance consisting of non-apprehension.

But both of those types of ignorance do not exist in the fourth state (*turya*). The meaning is that, in relation to the three previously mentioned states, they do not prevail in the fourth—the state of liberation—according to the grammatical rule: "For the word *catur*, [the suffix] *cha* is substituted and the first syllable is elided. Now, one might object: "Why this inversion? Let there be a different classification of ignorance based on the distinction between non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*) and incorrect apprehension (*asamyag-grahaṇa*). In that case, the systematic arrangement would be established such that non-apprehension occurs in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), while incorrect apprehension occurs in the waking and dreaming states."

Now, one might ask: "Is there any difference between incorrect apprehension (*asamyag-grahaṇa*) and non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*)? Certainly there is; for instance: the incorrect apprehension of the reality of the Self—which is non-dual, unitary, devoid of the distinctions of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and partless—is its apprehension as something divisible; whereas the non-apprehension of that same non-dual, unitary, or partless reality is simply not apprehending it at all. Thus, because they consist respectively of apprehension and non-apprehension, they are perceived as distinct; therefore, there is a difference between these two. This, however, is not sound; for: [p. 289]
