If, first of all, "incorrect apprehension" is intended to mean merely an apprehension that lacks the aspect of error and is distinct from erroneous cognition, then what is this "indistinct appearance"? Or is it the apprehension of an object in some form, but not in its entirety? In that regard, if the first position is held, then an indistinctly appearing cognition occurs with respect to an object that is distant or subtle; yet, that is not ignorance (*avidyā*).

Likewise, in the second alternative, ignorance would consist in the fact that regarding a distant post, only the general property of "uprightness" is known, while it is not known in its entirety due to the lack of knowledge of its specific particulars; yet this is not the case. Furthermore, if this were so, every cognition would fail to grasp its object in its entirety, and since all cognitions would thus be non-correct, they would necessarily result in being false. Therefore, the statement that "ignorance is the apprehension of something as non-correct" is first of all untenable.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that the non-apprehension of the non-difference of the partless, undivided Self is the second type of ignorance (*avidyā*): even in that case, if ignorance were merely the non-apprehension of non-difference devoid of the apprehension of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), then there would be nothing for that ignorance to remove. For the non-apprehension of non-difference is not what is to be removed; rather, that which offends the person by being the cause of the threefold suffering is what must be removed by him. And non-apprehension is not such [a cause]. Rather, it is the differentiation of the phenomenal world; for that indeed is the locus of the two kinds of suffering.

In that case, you would have to accept the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*). Now, if you say that we do not claim that what is different appears as different—which would indeed entail misapprehension—but rather that the non-dual reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), though undivided, appears as if divided by the distinctions of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), then it is replied: what similarity is there here between the different and the non-different, such that it could be the meaning of the word "as if" (*iva*)?

If the meaning of the comparison is that just as a distinct [object] appears while its unity remains unmanifest, so too the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) appears while its unity remains unmanifest despite being non-distinct, then—since the reality of the Self is apprehended as devoid of unity—it would be an apprehension by some part rather than in its entirety. Thus, it would be stated that "apprehension characterized by oneness" is an incorrect apprehension. And in that case, since no cognition whatsoever would grasp an object in its entirety, it has been said that this leads to the undesirable consequence of all cognition being false.

If it is argued that the non-different reality of the Self appears as if different, though it does not actually appear so—and thus there is no consequence of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension)—even then, what similarity can be stated between the appearance of difference and the appearance of non-difference? If it is claimed that this is the similarity: just as the engagement in the conventional usage of difference proceeds from the appearance of difference, so too does the conventional usage of difference proceed from the non-different reality of the Self; then [the response follows].

No; for if the conventional usage of difference occurs even when the self is non-different, then there must be an appearance of difference in that very self, since the manifestation of difference is the cause of the conventional usage of difference, and an effect cannot exist in the absence of its cause. Consequently, because the cognition of difference arises even though the self is non-different, the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) results. Now, if it is argued that this is merely a conceit based on the non-apprehension of the non-difference of the non-different reality of the self, and not actually an apprehension of difference—and that this alone is the cause of the conventional usage—[we reply:]...

If it is argued that, for this reason, there is no consequence of the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), we reply: that is incorrect; for the non-apprehension of non-difference is indeed an absence of apprehension. And this [absence], for those who do not admit that an absence is an object of cognition, cannot be grasped either in its own form or in the form of another. Furthermore, as long as that [absence] is not grasped, the conceit of apprehending difference is not possible.

In a mother-of-pearl shell, there arises the conceit (*abhimāna*) of perceiving silver. Furthermore, since the non-dual Self appears as the manifold world (*prapañca*), from where could there be a perception of difference? But was it not said that there is no perception of difference, but rather a conceit thereof? True, it was so said; however, no such thing as "conceit" can be defined apart from the perception of difference. Therefore, this is simply the perception of difference. And since that [perception] is not tenable if difference does not manifest, what has been stated is well-said.

Furthermore, by abandoning our own position—that ignorance (*avidyā*) is a false cognition (*viparīta-jñāna*) consisting in the conceit of difference within the non-different reality of the Self (*ātma-tattva*), manifested as the nature of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*)—and instead accepting the conceit of grasping at difference when there is a failure to grasp the non-difference of the non-different reality of the Self, you have merely accepted the theory of erroneous cognition (*viparīta-khyāti*). Therefore, what has been resolved by that? Consequently, it is well said: "In the case of mere non-apprehension (*agraha-mātra*), there would be no distinction between dissolution (*laya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*). Moreover, if the Vedāntas were intent upon injunctions for knowledge (*jñāna-vidhi*), the nature of the Self as free from evil (*apahata-pāpmā*) and so forth would not be established.

P.151-1. Since it has been stated that cognition does not manifest by way of its own nature [as the Self], an objection is raised there with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). If the manifestation of the Self were seen through a form that is not its own—that is, through attributes such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth—then, because there would be no visible purpose, one would have to postulate an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*). However, when there is the manifestation of the Self’s own nature, such as freedom from sin, the very establishment of that nature is the visible fruit. This is because, even elsewhere, the fruit of knowledge is simply the establishment of the true nature of the object to be known. And when a visible fruit is possible, it is not appropriate to postulate an invisible one.

Therefore, the meaning is that even though the Vedāntas are intent upon an injunction regarding knowledge (*jñānavidhi*), the Self is established as having the nature of being free from evil (*apahatapāpman*) and so forth. To this, he provides the answer: "Not from mere perception" (*na dṛṣṭamātrāt*). Knowledge does not have a perceived result merely because some perceived thing—even one that is not a human goal—is seen; rather, since an injunction cannot be satisfied without a human goal, the perceived result follows the human goal by virtue of its contact with the human goal.

Furthermore, whether the manifestation is of the nature of the Self—characterized by freedom from evil and so forth—or of the nature of the non-Self, there is no difference or distinction in the existence of the human goal (puruṣārtha); the meaning is that in both cases, the state of having the human goal as its fruit is indistinguishable. He elaborates upon this lack of distinction with the words "Just as... (yathā).

The meaning is this: just as in the view that [the self] is empty of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there is the abandonment—that is, the relinquishing—of suffering such as grief, of karma, and of afflictions such as passion, once the reality of the self, which is pure and free from evil, has been revealed by knowledge; likewise, even if that which is free from evil and so forth were not the true reality, their abandonment would occur once it is revealed by knowledge. As it has been said: "Therefore, whether it be real or unreal, whatever is intensely meditated upon, when the fruit of that meditation is accomplished, the cognition becomes clear and is the result."

And he who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) in his conduct is also approved by Manu; for thus he said: "An alms-bowl, the roots of trees, solitude, lack of assistance, and equanimity toward all beings—this is the characteristic of the liberated one.

Furthermore, one who is merely freed from passion and the like is not intended here as "liberated," because no such specific qualification is mentioned. Therefore, since no specific distinction is perceived, it is understood that the one described here as "liberated" is liberated from all bonds. For ignorance is the root cause of bondage; and when that [ignorance] has been destroyed without leaving a trace, bondage ceases precisely through the cessation of its cause. Thus, liberation for the knower is established even while he is still living.

As for the persistence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as a mere appearance even though it has been sublated, its justification has already been stated previously and thus is not repeated here. In this context, what is intended by "one liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*) is one in whom the light of the non-dual Self has manifested, not merely one who knows the meaning of the great sayings (*vākya*). Thus, the reality of the Self—pure, non-dual, and so forth—is manifested through the knowledge of the Self; this alone is appropriate here. For in this way, there is no contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge that apprehend duality.

Furthermore, the injunction regarding ritual action (*karmavidhāna*), which concerns the distinctions between the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), possesses a real object. For if the ultimate reality were the voidness of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca-śūnyatva*), then the means of valid cognition such as perception, which apprehend phenomenal proliferation, would be sublated. Moreover, rituals would then have non-existent objects. Therefore, it is logical that this is an injunction for knowledge concerning the unreal non-duality of the Self (*abhūtātma-advaita-viṣaya-jñāna-vidhi*), similar to [the statement] "One should meditate on speech as a cow. Regarding the phrase "having non-figurative objects" (*anaupacārikārthā*): the analysis of the compound is "those whose objects are non-figurative, i.e., imagined meanings" (*anaupacārika-kalpita-artha-viṣayāḥ*).

The analysis of the compound in the commentary (*vṛtti*) is as follows: "the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of that which is non-existent (*abhūtasya*); that very [conceptualization] is the appropriation (*upādāna*) for that which is both established by conventional usage (*vyavahāra-siddha*) and an object (*artha*); those whose range is that [object]. Now, one might raise the objection: "The verb 'to know' (*jānāti*) has that [non-dual reality] as its object of cognition; therefore, it is true that the non-dual form of the Self is indeed the object of knowledge. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The verb 'to know'... To that, he gives the reply: "No. The verb 'to know' does not apply to the cognition of that [reality].

Why? Because knowledge is qualified by terms such as "false" (*mithyā*), "correct" (*samyak*), and "doubtful" (*saṃśaya*)—as in "false knowledge," "correct knowledge," and "doubtful knowledge. Otherwise, in the term "correct knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*), there would be a redundancy between the substantive and its qualifier; furthermore, in the cases of "false knowledge" and "doubtful knowledge," there would be a contradiction. [Objection: But in the injunction "the Self is to be known," knowledge of the Self is prescribed. In that context, if the knowledge of the pure, non-dual, and so forth were to occur through a superimposed form of the Self, then the Self would not truly be known.

For the self becomes known only when it is perceived in its own form, and not otherwise. Therefore, one might raise the objection that since there is an injunction to know the self in the form of non-duality and so forth, the self must be established as having that very form—this is expressed by the words “not the self. To this, he gives the reply: “not in that form. If this sentence were merely “the self is to be known,” and thereby the knowledge of the self’s own nature were being enjoined, then it would indeed be so; but this is not the case.

If the self were established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then [the scriptural statement] would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already known; furthermore, it would be impossible to know that whose essential nature has not yet been ascertained. Therefore, whether the self is established by another means of knowledge or otherwise, there is certainly no injunction regarding the essential nature of the self. If, however, the knowledge of that self is enjoined in the form conveyed by words such as "free from evil, free from old age, free from death," then by that [means], [the self is known as] free from evil...

Even though [the Self] is superimposed in the form of sin and so forth—as in the case of the injunction, "One should meditate on speech as a cow"—knowledge of the Self is still possible. The point is that through this injunction for knowledge, the reality of the Self's essential nature, which is free from sin and the like, is established. Furthermore, the knowledge characterized by the manifestation of the non-dual Self is not for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), for no unseen effect is produced by it. If it is argued that it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), it is said in response: "Knowledge" (*jñāna*). P.152-7.

The means for that [attainment] is not known; therefore, because of this ignorance of the means, a person does not engage even in knowledge that has a visible result without an injunction. Anticipating this objection—that "knowledge is enjoined"—he says: "That" (tad). To this he gives the reply: "Of that" (tasya). Now, anticipating the objection that even knowledge with a visible purpose will be enjoined like threshing (*avadhāta*) and so forth, he says: "Like threshing" (*avadhāta*). In that case as well, there exists an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) consisting of a restriction pertaining to the rice grains.

The meaning is this: the removal of the husk is distinct from threshing; the rice-grains are distinct from that; the flour is distinct from that; and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is distinct from that. Thus, since the primary *apūrva* (transcendental result) is accomplished through such a sequence, there is an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) therein. Now, if it is argued that the knowledge of the non-dual Self is unprecedented and extraordinary, and therefore it is enjoined even for the sake of an unseen result, to that he replies: "extraordinary. For what purpose is it enjoined? Certainly not for the sake of establishing or realizing the essential nature of the Self.

Since an injunction does not have mere practice as its sole fruit, but rather the performance of what is to be done arises from the injunction; and that performance is established through the very visible fruit found in knowledge, just as in the case of eating and so forth.

What is the use of an injunction? Therefore, when the reality of the Self—which is non-worldly and characterized by being "free from evil" (apahatapāpman) and so forth—is first presented by means of words as something indirect, a person spontaneously turns toward it in order to make that [Self] immediate, because that immediate knowledge has the Self, which is the object of knowledge, as its means. For instance, having heard from someone's statement about a Gandharva city or the like, a person spontaneously turns toward making that immediate upon hearing it. Thus, the sense is: what is the use of an injunction?

He asks, "Where indeed is injunction (vidhi) applicable? and answers: "That" (tad). He concludes: "By injunction" (niyoga). Therefore, the entry of injunctions regarding knowledge into words such as "free from evil" (apahatapāpman) destroys their authority with respect to an existing, established object, because they do not have that as their primary purport. Thus it is said: "In this invocation. The meaning is that one who seeks to understand the nature of an existing, established object—such as being free from evil—should not resort to or entertain in the mind an entry into injunctions.

Thus, among the three modes of apprehension previously mentioned, it was stated that the first—the verbal apprehension—and the third—which consists of the manifestation of the non-dual Self—are not enjoined. Now, regarding the second mode of apprehension, known as meditation (*upāsanā*), its injunction is refuted by the words "therefore, prior...

The meaning is that [if it were otherwise], there would be the consequence of a lack of means of valid cognition regarding an existing reality (*bhūtārtha*). After the word “*niṣṭhatā*” (the state of being grounded), the phrase “of the established Vedāntas” is to be supplied. By the words “for this very reason,” he shows the point upon which [the previous argument] depends: “even there. “As before”; the meaning is: just as, if it were intent on a third kind of injunction (*vidhi*), the sentence would not achieve the realization of the nature of the Self because it would not have that as its purport, so it is here. However, if the passage beginning with “free from evil” (*apahatapāpmā*) is indeed grounded in the nature [of the Self] itself and not grounded in an injunction (*niyoga*);

Therefore, since the true nature of the Self has already been ascertained from that [scriptural passage], the injunction for meditation (*upāsana*)—as seen in such statements as "it should be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*)—is accepted; this would indeed be so, and there is no fault whatsoever. Thus, regarding the statement "having known, one should exercise wisdom" (*vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta*), he says "of its own nature" (*svarūpa-*) to show that by the use of the gerund suffix (*ktvā*) in "having known," the knowledge of the reality of the Self arising from the Vedānta is shown to be already established prior to the exercise of wisdom. Furthermore, that injunction for meditation is valid because an injunction must have a subject matter not already established by other means.

And because this [meditation] is attained precisely through its having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*), like eating and so forth, he says: "because it is attained" (*prāpteḥ*). He states its having a visible purpose: "by means of practice" (*abhyāsena*). This is what is meant: if liberation were an unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*) like heaven and so forth, then the contemplation of that fruit—which would not otherwise be attained due to its being an unseen purpose—would have to be enjoined. However, it has been described that liberation is merely the manifestation of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). And the manifestation of one's own true nature is the direct realization of the Self, which is known from scripture only in an indirect manner.

And this reflection has a visible fruit, like the satiety resulting from eating food, because one observes an intensification of cognition through the practice of knowledge. For it has been said that even that which is unreal, when it is experienced, attains the status of a direct experience; how much more so, then, that which is real? Thus, reflection has a visible object. And that which has a visible object does not require an invisible fruit, because its requirement is satisfied by what is visible.

Therefore, he concludes that reflection upon an already attained object is not something to be enjoined because its purpose is already perceived—this is expressed by the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is introduced with the words "even though" (*yadapi*) and so forth. When the Teacher says, "One should maintain the non-difference between Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*), which are the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam* in the phrase 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*)," the use of the first-person pronoun "I am Being" (*sadasmi*) is intended from the perspective of the disciple. The term "should maintain" (*dhārayet*) refers to maintenance (*dhāraṇa*), which is here synonymous with reflection (*anucintana*).

The opponent maintains that even though an injunction (*vidhi*) is not explicitly heard in the phrase “That thou art,” it is to be inferred there, just as it is in the case of “Pūṣan has the ground meal as his portion. By the word “from hearing” (*śravaṇāt*), the meaning is: something other than the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedāntic statements, which is characterized by the hearing of the Vedāntas. In scriptural passages such as “He should perform the sacrifice” (*sa kratuṃ kuryāt*), reflection (*anucintana*) is expressed by the two words *kratu* and *prajñā*.

The synonymic definition "meditation (dhyāna) is the continuous reflection for the purpose of seeing non-difference" is given so that, if there were a difference between those two [samādhi and meditation], the description of them as being equal would be untenable. Furthermore, "a flow of cognitions" is the explanation of meditation. "Like ritual action" means: just as ritual actions such as the Agnihotra have heaven and so forth as their fruit, so too [is this].

P. 154-8. The scriptural passages concerning the meditation on *bāṣkala* have been stated; among them, the passage "He should perform the sacrifice" (*sa kratuṃ kurvīta*) does not enjoin a meditation on the reality of the Self—which is free from all distinctions and devoid of limiting adjuncts—as having the fruit of becoming the non-distinct Brahman. Rather, because of the continuity [of the context] with the description "consisting of mind, having breath as its body, and having light as its form," it is the contemplation of the Self as possessing limiting adjuncts—characterized by attributes such as being "consisting of mind"—that has sovereignty as its fruit.

Having experienced sovereignty, it subsequently bestows the fruit of liberation characterized by the manifestation of one's true nature (*svarūpa*) through a gradual process, but it does not directly grant the fruit of liberation. Therefore, the application of such scriptural passages as "free from evil, ageless, deathless" or "neither gross nor subtle" to that [state] is not tenable for those who maintain the doctrine of a non-differentiated Self (*nirviśeṣātman*). The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is the meditation upon that Self consisting of mind (*manomaya*), etc., for which name and form—meaning word and object—are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Likewise, in the passage, "Having known that very [Self], the wise man should practice wisdom," the injunctive sense is transferred to the subordinate term (*upapada*), just as in the expression, "The cloth becomes red. Therefore, this does not have its purport in an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*); rather, its purport lies in the exclusion of other [objects] by the phrase "that very [Self]. For instance, having established the distinction between the principles (*tattva*) such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, the non-difference of the Self is subsequently established. Thus, in the preceding portion, "He is stainless and beyond space," His transcendence of space has been stated.

In that context, the purpose of the restrictive particle (*eva*) in the phrase "in that very [Self]" (*tam eva*) is as follows: the instruction for forming the cognition is not that one should form a cognition of the Self as being something distinct from space; rather, the intent of the particle *eva* is that one should do so by including space within itself, [so that] the Self alone [remains]. If, however, it were not explained in this way, the particle *eva* would be redundant. Furthermore, there is no other thing for it to exclude. Thus, the Self alone is the object of meditation, and not space or anything else.

This very point is elaborated by the statement, "One should not meditate upon the Veda, for that is merely weariness of speech," which functions as a sentence establishing the means of wisdom (*prajñākaraṇavākya*). Nor should it be said that this is a prohibition against meditating on the word and not its meaning; for since meditation on the mere word is not even possible, it cannot be the object of prohibition. Therefore, because the word is the precursor [to the meaning], this is indeed a prohibition against meditating on both the word and its meaning.

Likewise, in the passage "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self' (ātmeti)," this injunction—due to the hearing of the particle *eva* ("only")—is intended for the exclusion of other [notions], not for meditation (*upāsanā*). Similarly, the injunction "It should be deeply contemplated" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*) is also not an injunction for meditation; because, starting from the opening "But for the sake of the desires of the Self" and ending with the conclusion "All this is what this Self is," this entire statement has the nature of the Self's true essence as its sole purport.

Therefore, just as—starting from the opening statement, "Indeed, this would result in repetition (*jāmi*)," and concluding with the closing statement, "One performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between for the sake of non-repetition"—once the status of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) is established, the constituent parts such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to silently" (*upāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ*) do not possess independent injunctive force (*vidhitva*); likewise, not only are the constituent parts such as "He is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*) not separate injunctions, but rather, because the Self has such a nature, it is fit for seeing and so forth—thus, the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya*) is used in the sense of fitness (*arha*).

Because they are recited [in proximity], they are intended for praise (*stuti*). However, if they were intended as separate injunctions (*vidhi*), the unity of the passage—understood from the continuity of a single meaning between its opening and conclusion—would be lost. As for the injunctional force (*vidhikaraṇā*) in the statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), which lacks an explicit injunction and is established as a statement of essential nature (*svarūpaniṣṭha*), that too is to be disregarded as a mere fabrication of one's own imagination, since there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as textual ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) to support it. In the case of "Pūṣan has the ground-meal as his portion" (*pūṣā prapiṣṭabhāgaḥ*), however, the necessity of performing the grinding is understood from the sense of the sentence itself: that Pūṣan becomes one whose portion is ground only if the grinding is performed.

Therefore, since injunction is impossible even for the various types of knowledge mentioned in the statement "there are indeed three ways of approaching Brahman," and since the comprehension of the meaning arises from the Vedānta texts even without an injunction—because they are independent due to their non-human (apauruṣeya) origin—the establishment of the authority of the Vedāntas regarding an already existing reality is thus a summary of the entire subject matter taught in the subsequent section (kāṇḍa). This, moreover, is also the consensus of the author of the Sūtras.

“But that [Brahman], because of the harmony [of the texts]”—by the word "but" (tu), Brahman is distinguished from Dharma, which is characterized by injunction (codanā). That [Brahman] is the object; "harmony" (samanvaya) refers to the mutual connection of words, which is expressed as their syntactical application (viniyoga); it has been stated that the text concerning that [Brahman] is not accessible through injunction. Now, one might object: since immediately after the study of the Veda, the Sūtra states, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma," and since Dharma serves as the indicator, the entire meaning of the Veda is proposed as the object of inquiry.

By this, in the *codanālakṣaṇa* sūtra, the entire meaning of the Veda is stated to have *codanā* (injunction) as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And thus, *codanā* becomes the means of valid cognition for the entire meaning of the Veda only if the mantras, arthavādas, and Upaniṣads do not constitute a separate Veda [from the injunctions], but rather form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the injunctions; otherwise, this would not be the case. Consequently, the entire Veda is indeed *codanā*. Furthermore, since that *codanā* has only "what is to be done" (*kārya*) as its object, the author of the Sūtras has stated without distinction that the entire Veda is a means of valid cognition only with respect to an object that is something to be accomplished.

Therefore, the authority of the Upaniṣads regarding an already existing entity (bhūta-artha) is contrary to the Sūtra. This is not sound. For if the nature of the Vedic meaning as something to be accomplished (kārya-ātmatā) were dependent upon the authority of the injunctions (codanā), then, since the Vedic meaning in its form as an action would be unestablished prior to the authority of the injunction, it would be impossible for it to be a restatement (anuvāda). Consequently, the Vedic meaning could not be proposed as the subject of inquiry merely by way of restating the authority of the injunction. Furthermore, it is an established fact that only what is already established is restated.

In that case, the demonstration of the authority of *codanā* (Vedic injunction) immediately following [the first sūtra] via the *Autpattika-sūtra* would be inappropriate. Furthermore, if this were so, it would constitute a definition of the object of knowledge (*prameya-lakṣaṇa*), not a definition of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Consequently, what was stated at the beginning of the second chapter—that "in the first chapter, the definition of the means of knowledge has been established"—would also be inappropriate. Moreover, if the fact that the entire Veda has action (*kārya*) as its purport were determined right here, then there would be no room for the subsequent disagreement regarding whether mantras and arthavādas have action as their purport.

And that [objection] will be refuted later in the section concerning the *arthavāda* passages of the Veda and so forth. Therefore, because this position is vitiated by such defects as these, it was only the inquiry into the nature of Dharma (*dharmamātra*) that was proposed there; and it was only in that regard that *codanā* (Vedic injunction) was stated to be the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), not with respect to the entire meaning of the Veda. Enough of this digression. Furthermore, the three causes of validity regarding an action (*kārya*)—namely, being non-repetitive (*ananuvādatva*), being produced from a flawless cause due to its origin in an authorless scripture (*apauruṣeyāgamaja*), and being independent (*nirapekṣatva*)—are equally applicable even when the object is an already established fact (*siddha*). Therefore, he says "just as" (*yathā*) to show that validity is likewise appropriate in that case as well.

The "intermingling" (*vyatibheda*) of other means of knowledge, such as perception and so forth, refers to their contact [with the object]. Liberated from that, the cognition—born from the non-human (authorless) scripture—attains validity regarding this effect (*kārya*) because of its independence; the meaning is that it attains validity regarding an established (*siddha*) object as well. Here, by the phrase "other means of knowledge," the absence of being a mere restatement (*ananuvādatva*) is expressed; by "non-human," the absence of defects in the cause is expressed; and by "due to the state of independence," the lack of dependence on corroborating means of knowledge is expressed—this is the distinction. Thus ends the commentary on the *Niyogakāṇḍa* in the *Brahmasiddhi-vyākhyāna* composed by Śaṅkhapāṇi.

*Brahmasiddhivyākhyā* by Śaṅkhapāṇi. The Fourth (*Siddhi*) Chapter. Now, the proponent of non-authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇyavādī*) raises an objection, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*). First of all, words such as "Brahman" and so forth are not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman, because they depend upon the knowledge of their [conventional] relations; and since Brahman is not established by any other means of valid cognition prior [to the word], the words lack the capacity to serve as a cause for its cognition. Nor is it a sentence (*vākya*); [for a sentence depends on its constituent words].

For that [word] is not a direct denoter; rather, it causes the cognition of a qualified meaning by means of two word-meanings mutually related through a primary and secondary relationship. Otherwise, even one who does not know the word-meanings would understand the sentence-meaning. But this is not the case. Therefore, since it is established that the sentence-meaning consists of the word-meanings themselves in mutual contact, Brahman—being a non-word-meaning—cannot be cognized through a sentence.

If, however, words were to have [only] word-meanings as their objects, then since their objects would already be known, the referent of the word *brahman* would be something else entirely, falling within the scope of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, the thesis that [Brahman] is knowable solely through the Veda (*āmnāya*) would be abandoned—this is the intended meaning. "They would not be conjoined" is stated according to the view that the sentence-meaning is a conjunction (*saṃsarga*); and that is the mutual relation of the word-meanings. "They would not be excluded" is stated according to the view that the sentence-meaning is exclusion (*bheda*); and that is the differentiation from what they are not, as in the case of "a blue lotus," where there is the exclusion of the non-blue and the non-lotus.

The term *codanā* refers to the intention of non-human (authorless) speech. For it is not the case that *codanā* is introduced here as the subject of inquiry; rather, this is stated with the intention that, according to the reasoning previously set forth, the entire Veda is of the nature of *codanā*. The phrase "the comprehension of the category of the unprecedented (*apūrva*)" means the comprehension of the category of Brahman, which is unprecedented by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By the words beginning with "sā hi" (for that), it is stated that it is established that only in the case of a task to be accomplished (*kārya*) is non-human speech a valid means of knowledge.

Now, having raised the objection—"But if [the Vedāntas] lack authority, since they would be fruitless, how can there be acceptance of them by those learned in the three Vedas?"—the purpose is stated with the words beginning "those learned in the three Vedas" (*traividyā*). Thus, when it is urged that Brahman cannot be the meaning of a sentence because it is not the meaning of a word, the following is refuted: "By means of the universal" (*sāmānyena*).

Just as in the world, when a bird is established as a category of object through the possibility of knowing its relationship once it has been apprehended by other means of knowledge, there occurs the communication of a previously unknown specific type of bird—unshared with other birds—by means of a sentence through qualities such as having feet like emeralds; so too, when the mere cause or the mere "Being" (sanmātra) is established in the world as the referent of the word "cause" or the referent of the word "Being," there occurs the communication of this specific cause of the world—which is devoid of all particularities such as grossness—by means of the [Vedic] passage beginning with "from which...

The meaning is that [the nature of Brahman] cannot be established by means of the two sentences, "From which indeed these beings [are born]" and "Not gross," because their word-meanings are already established in common worldly usage. This is what is intended: just as a specific, unprecedented bird is understood through the association of the general, worldly object "bird" with other words such as "emerald" whose meanings are likewise established in common usage, so too is the general cause established in common usage [understood] through the association with words whose meanings are established in common usage, such as "From which indeed these beings [are born]" and "Not gross."

Through association, the unprecedented cause of the world is perceived as devoid of all particularity; therefore, the Vedāntas are neither non-informative nor merely repetitive. He states another resolution: "All... etc. The Supreme alone is the single Light, which is cognized—that is, it shines—in all cognitions in various forms such as blue, etc., which are imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*); the term "cognized" (*vedya*) is used here without intending the sense of an object of action (*karma*).

For instance—in every particular such as blue and so forth, a single, pervasive, common light (prakāśa-sāmānya) appears. When the light of Brahman shines, nothing else shines. Thus, by the negation of all differences in the passage, "This Self is 'not this, not this'," Brahman, which is the remaining universal form, is shown to be the Truth.

Now, by means of the illustration, “The modification is a verbal handle, a mere name; only ‘clay’ is real,” it is shown that the causal state alone—which permeates all differences—is real, just like the clay. Therefore, as clay is extremely well-known in relation to jars and other objects, so too is Brahman. Thus, the sense is that because it is the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), it is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). Anticipating the objection, “If Brahman is established through all cognition, what then is being propounded by words? he says: “Of the phenomenal world (*prapañcasya*)... [and so forth].

That [Brahman] is established as being with conceptual proliferation (*saprapañca*); however, it is taught as being without conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*) by means of words such as "not gross" (*asthūla*). The point is that there is no failure to perceive the connection [of meanings] here due to the meanings of the words being unknown, nor because the referents of the words, such as "gross," are not well-known. Now, one might object: "In this way, Brahman would fall within the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, how can it be asserted that it is the exclusive scope of scripture (*āgama*) alone? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "in which [all] has dissolved," and so forth.

The meaning is that [the object] is said to be within the scope of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is established by another means of knowledge in its phenomenal form (*prapañca-rūpa*), whereas it is not established in its non-phenomenal form (*aprapañca-rūpa*). However, the opponent objects in another way, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*). To this it is replied: "Of the means of knowledge" (*pramāṇasya*). Even indifference (*upekṣā*) is accepted as a fruit of a means of knowledge. Furthermore, being possessed of human purpose (*puruṣārthavattā*) is not the definition of a means of knowledge, but rather the quality of being determinative (*paricchedakatva*); and the sense is that this [determinative quality] exists here as well. And this [objection] is merely a challenge from the opponent.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate that the subject matter of the injunction for study—which belongs to an identical tradition—should have negligence as its result. Since the injunction for study does not have recitation (*japa*) as its purpose, but rather the purpose of understanding the meaning, he states another solution out of dissatisfaction [with the previous one], beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*). Now, is there not seen a fruit consisting of a human goal other than knowledge, wherein knowledge itself—[p.

This is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). However, this knowledge of the reality of the Self, which is by nature free from defects, is itself considered a human goal because it removes undesirable states such as sorrow arising from ignorance and because it brings about the manifestation of the desired bliss. Therefore, it is not a non-human goal, nor does it depend on any other human goal; this is the intended meaning. The very arising of a contradictory state is the cessation of the previous one. Thus, since knowledge itself is the cessation of sorrow and so forth arising from ignorance, and nothing else, there is a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "knowledge is that cessation."

Nor should it be argued: "Even though the false cognition of being a mourner and so forth has been sublated, it persists due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance; therefore, its cessation does not even exist. How then can that [cessation] be the fruit of the knowledge of the reality of the Self?"

For although that [delusion] persists, it nevertheless causes a person possessed of ignorance—who regards it as true—to become attached and thus suffers distress; however, this is not the case for one whose knowledge has been strengthened by the realization that sorrow and so forth are false, who perceives his own deceitfulness in maintaining the notion of being "free from sorrow" and the like. For such a person is not subject to the influence of illusion in the same way that a person is influenced by it when there is a dependence on another object, since that [illusion] has been sublated.

Furthermore, false cognition such as sorrow and the like, even while persisting from past impressions (*saṃskāra*), does not simply fail to cease; rather, it ceases gradually. Moreover, a result may indeed be mediated by an interval, as in the case of heaven and so forth. And it is observed that the attainment of knowledge constitutes a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); thus he asks: "In what [does it consist]? (P. 158.8).

The meaning is as follows: just as for someone who is curious and intensely desires to see a particular wonder, being agitated by that desire and suffering, the very sight of it is the human goal (puruṣārtha) that dispels that suffering; so it is here. Furthermore, if there were a rule that only that which is the object of engagement (pravṛtti) or withdrawal (nivṛtti) constitutes a human goal, then the Vedāntas, which are established upon already-existent reality (bhūtārtha), would lack human purpose; yet this is not the case, because perception and other means of knowledge provide counter-examples (vyabhicāra). Thus he says: "In perception and so forth."

The mention of "engagement" (pravṛtti) should be understood as implying "disengagement" (nivṛtti) as well. Now, objects such as water are known through perception and other means; therein lies the human purpose (puruṣārtha), for by means of that water, services such as bathing and drinking are rendered to the person.

Therefore, it is said that even perception and the other means of knowledge, though they culminate in established objects, serve the human purpose by way of their respective objects of cognition. In this regard too, Brahman—the object of knowledge produced by the knowledge of reality arising from the Vedāntas—is itself the supreme human purpose, because it is perfectly serene and consists of the cessation of the suffering of birth, old age, and so forth, as well as bliss.

The word "itself" (*svayam*) is used in order to demonstrate the distinction of Brahman as the cause of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), which is distinct from water and other such things; for it is that very Brahman which, being itself the human goal attained, is taught as the non-different Brahman to the disciple who is to be instructed through the mouth of Śvetaketu with the words "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). Thus it has been said: "There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self."

The meaning of the passage beginning with "for it is non-different" (*abhinnaṃ hi*) is as follows: that [Brahman] is indeed distinct from the disciple; yet, even though it is non-different, it is perceived as different due to ignorance (*avidyā*). In either case, there is no fulfillment of the human goal (*puruṣārthatva*). However, in the case of non-difference, when the disciple possesses the knowledge of identity—that "I am that very Brahman" as described—and because the disciple thus comes to possess that state, he attains the state of the aforementioned Brahman for all [beings].

Because there is the cessation of that which is inauspicious and unwholesome—consisting of sufferings such as those beginning with birth—and because there is the manifestation of the supreme bliss known as *śiva*, this becomes the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). While elsewhere the cessation of suffering and happiness are each incomplete goals for man, here both are present; therefore, it is said to be "complete."

If it is argued that the validity of perception and other means of knowledge [is established] because they serve as auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) for another person’s subsequent activity of rejection or acquisition, then—by the same logic—it must be accepted that the knowledge arising from the Vedāntas has validity as an auxiliary factor for the activity of meditation (*upāsana*) and so forth directed toward the realization of Brahman once it has been known through verbal testimony (*śabda*). Thus, the sense is that the Vedāntas, though not themselves [directly] human goals (*puruṣārtha*), possess validity. The word "iti" marks the completion of the composition of the treatise.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourth (Siddhi-) section in the *Śrībrahmasiddhivyākhyāna* composed by Śaṅkhapāṇi. The *Brahmasiddhivyākhyāna* is completed.
